About this text

Toh 5 in the Kangyur is the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya Vibhaṅga, known in Tibetan as the Dge slong ma'i 'dul ba rnam par 'byed pa, which may be rendered in English as The Analysis of the Discipline of Nuns. It is a Vinaya text — one of the foundational categories of Buddhist canonical literature concerned with monastic discipline and the rules governing the conduct of ordained practitioners — and this particular work focuses specifically on the code of individual liberation for fully ordained nuns, the bhikṣuṇīs, providing a detailed analysis of each rule along with its origins, scope, and application. As such, it is the counterpart to the monks' Vinaya Vibhaṅga and forms an essential part of the Vinaya division of the Kangyur, the collection of texts attributed to the Buddha himself. The text opens with verses of homage celebrating the Buddha as the lord of discipline and extolling the rarity and blessedness of encountering and practising the Vinaya, setting a devotional and exhortatory tone before proceeding to its systematic exposition.

Translation

In the language of India: Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya Vibhaṅga. In the language of Tibet: The Analysis of the Discipline of Nuns. The first section.

Homage to the Omniscient One.

Born into the lineage of the king of discipline,
He who trained disciples and subdued the wayward,
The Buddha, lord of discipline, and the attachment-free Dharma,
And the assembly free of dust — to these I pay homage.

The individual liberation of nuns,
The analysis thereof — neither too condensed
Nor too elaborate — shall now be set forth.
Hear this discipline from me.

Even across ten million aeons,
It is rare to hear the Vinaya,
And rare to find one who can receive and retain it.
To practise it is rarer still.

Blissful is the arising of buddhas.
Blissful too is the teaching of Dharma.
Blissful is the harmony of the Saṅgha,
And blissful is the austerity of those in harmony.
Blissful is the delight in solitude
Of one who has heard and seen the Dharma.
Blissful is the perfect vow of non-harm
Toward the living beings of the world.
Blissful is the freedom from attachment in the world,
And blissful is the victory over desires.
Whatever tames pride and arrogance —
That is the supreme bliss.
Blissful is the sight of one who holds moral discipline.
Blissful is the sight of one of great learning.
Blissful is the sight of arhats (foe-destroyers)
Who are freed from renewed existence.
Blissful is the sight of noble ones.
Blissful is the company of the holy.
Should one never encounter the childish,
One would dwell in constant bliss.
Blissful is a river with pleasant banks and gentle waters.
Blissful is the person well practised in Dharma.
Blissful is one who has attained wisdom.
Blissful is the exhaustion of pride.
Blissful is the world's esteem for ascetics.
Likewise blissful is its esteem for brahmins.
Blissful in the world is the one who leans to the far shore,
And likewise blissful is the one who leans to the near shore.
Blissful are those who are resolute and have subdued their senses,
Those who have grown old in peaceful hermitages.
Blissful is the dwelling of the greatly learned
Within the forests, past the flush of youth.

While the bodhisattva was residing in the Tuṣita heaven, there lived in the city of Nyagrodhāvatī a brahmin great as a Śāla tree, named Nyagrodha — wealthy, of great riches, of vast resources, holding much under his sway, wide and expansive in his affairs, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivalling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He had sixteen servant villages, thirty villages on the borders of his estates, sixty villages that brought produce, nine hundred and ninety-nine serfs, sixty cartloads of golden barley, and enough gold barley — refined according to the royal standard of the mighty king Padma — to make eighty measures. He took a wife from a family of equal rank, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and took his pleasure.

Since they had no son and no daughter, he made petition for a child to many hundreds and thousands of gods — namely: Brahmā, Śakra (Indra), Upendra, Yama, the Sun, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Skanda, Karmāntaka, Rohiṇī, the gods of the earth, nāgas, water gods, fire gods, wind gods, Dhṛtarāṣṭra (guardian of the realm), the noble-born, Durgā, Vaiśravaṇa, Maṇibhadra, Pūrṇa, Maṇibhadra the Auspicious, Pañcārṣika, Pañcaika, and the other twenty-eight commanders of the yakṣa armies; to Hārītī with her retinue of five hundred sons; to the gods of pleasure groves, the gods of forests, the gods of crossroads, the gods of triple junctions, the gods who receive torma offerings, the gods of the body, the co-born deities, the congruent deities, the ever-following gods — to all of these, and yet further to many hundreds and thousands of gods, he made petition.

Now there is indeed a worldly saying that sons and daughters are born as a result of making petition to gods — but in truth it is not so. For if it were truly thus, then —

Just as with a wheel-turning king, every single one of his attendants would have a thousand sons. Yet in truth, sons and daughters are born when six conditions come together and are present. What are those six? First, the father and mother must have accumulated and gathered the karma by which they will obtain a child. Second, the child too must have accumulated and gathered the karma by which it will obtain a father and mother. Third, the mother must be sound and in her proper season. Fourth, the father and mother must be united in desire and come together. Fifth, a gandharva (a being in the intermediate state) must be nearby. Sixth, the gandharva must have obtained a mind in either of two states: a mind that is attached to and desirous of the two, or a mind that is wrathful toward them. It is when these six conditions come together and are present that sons and daughters are born.

And yet, despite all this, Nyagrodhā sat there diligently petitioning hundreds and thousands of gods — and still there was no son, no daughter. Then he went up to the upper terrace of his fine house and, leaning his arms upon the railing, he stood there with the thought penetrating his heart: "All this great wealth and prosperity of my household — because there is no son, it will be taken away by others."

Then his relatives came before him and spoke these words: "Nyagrodhā, why do you sit in such discomfort?" He then told his relatives at length, and they said to him: "Resort to the gods and to sacred trees." He replied: "There is not a single god or sacred tree I have not already resorted to — and yet I have neither son nor daughter."

Then the mother of Nyagrodhā, who was like a great śāla tree, came and spoke thus: "Son Nyagrodhā, why are you so discomforted?" He replied: "Mother, is my discomfort a small thing? All this great wealth and property of our household — because there is no son, it will be taken away by others." His mother said: "My son, in your father's grove there is a great nyagrodha tree, full and complete with branches, crown, twigs, and foliage, its leaves wide and its boughs swaying — and the city is known by the very name Nyagrodhavān, 'the city of the nyagrodha tree.' Your father too, when he had no son, made petition for a child to many hundreds and thousands of gods — and still he had neither son nor daughter. Then your father went before the nyagrodha tree and made petition to it, and it was from there that you came forth. For that reason you were named Nyagrodhā. Since you too have no son, do likewise."

Then Nyagrodhā, like his father who was as a great śāla tree, went to where the nyagrodha tree stood. Arriving there, he had the area around the nyagrodha tree swept and cleaned, had it filled with incense, flowers, and perfumed smoke, and had victory banners and pennants raised. He then fed eight hundred brahmins, had them clothed in fine lengths of cloth, and afterward made petition to the deity dwelling in the tree: "Grant me, I beseech you, the joy of obtaining a son. If I am given a son, I shall offer you unmeasurable worship such as this every single year. But if not, I shall have this tree felled to the very base of a ficus shoot, split into pieces and pieces, dried out in the wind and the sun, and then burned in fire. Once burned, the ashes shall be scattered to the great wind or cast into the swift current of a great river."

Now the deity of that tree was of limited power, and so when petition was made to it, it was gladdened, delighted, deeply joyful, and felt strong — but when threatened, it became afraid, thinking: "Surely I will be driven from my dwelling place."

That deity, being hemmed in on all sides by the four great kings, went to the great king Virūḍhaka and, having arrived, spoke to him: "I am about to be driven from my dwelling place. Please inspire the wish that, in the city of the banyan tree, the brahmin shall find a son through the nyagrodha tree, as with the great sāla tree."

Virūḍhaka thought: "By the force of the cause of past karma, sons and daughters come into being. Over this matter I have no power." And so he said to the deity: "I am not able to give a son or daughter. But come — let us go together to the great noble king Vaiśravaṇa."

The two of them went to Vaiśravaṇa and, having arrived, told him the very same matter. Likewise, the great king Virūḍhaka went to Virūpākṣa and to Vaiśravaṇa in turn, and having arrived and spoken, those two also said: "Sons and daughters arise through one's own karma. Over this we have no power."

Then those four great kings went to Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, and spoke: "Kauśika, one of those in our retinue is about to be driven from his dwelling place. In that city of the banyan tree, please inspire the wish that the brahmin shall find a son through the nyagrodha tree, as with the great sāla tree."

Śakra replied: "Sirs, sons and daughters arise through one's own karma. I am not able to give a son or daughter to anyone."

Then a great radiance appeared in that divine assembly. Seeing it, Śakra, lord of the gods, instructed the four great kings: "Sirs, do not depart from this place. Just as this great radiance has appeared without interruption, so the Great Brahma (Brahmā) shall appear in this assembly." And they remained.

Into that assembly Brahmā indeed came down — young, youthful, a youth with five crests — and he sat upon the lap of Śakra, lord of the gods. And the purpose for which he had been summoned was fulfilled.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, pressed his palms together and made this supplication to the Great Brahmā: "Great Brahmā, you who are Brahmā, Great Brahmā, the Sovereign, the Creator, the Projector, the Emanator, the Supreme, the Supremely Exalted — you who have become the far shore of the world — have you not drawn beings forth? Now there is one belonging to our retinue, a wanderer upon the earth, who is about to be driven from his dwelling in the tree. In that city of the banyan tree, please inspire the wish that the brahmin shall find a son through the nyagrodha tree, as with the great sāla tree."

The Great Brahmā thought: "If I say I am unable to give a son or daughter to anyone, and if I then say 'I am unable to give a son or daughter,' then the names by which I am called — Brahmā, Great Brahmā, Sovereign, Creator, Projector, Emanator — those names shall no longer fit me. But if I say 'I shall give a son or daughter,' then when I have no power over the matter, how shall I give?" Thinking thus, he spoke in secret to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, I have not drawn the world forth, nor has the world drawn me forth."

Śakra replied: "Great Brahmā, if that is indeed so, nonetheless look within your own domain. If there is anyone whose nature is to die, please cause that one to be reborn in the household of the brahmin with the great sāla tree."

Brahmā said: "Kauśika, why do you not look within your own domain yourself?"

Śakra replied: "In this domain the gods are known to be of limited power.

That brahmin is known to be of great power, and so one of lesser known power cannot bear to take rebirth in his household. Then, when Brahmā gave his consent and searched within his own domain, he saw there a certain Brahmā-being whose life was exhausted and whose signs of death had appeared. He spoke to him: "Friend, if you are to pass away from this pleasant realm, it would be fitting to take a good rebirth. Therefore, take conception in the household of the brahmin of the great sāla tree in the city of Nyagrodha, and you will not be troubled by want of provisions."

That one, displeased, replied: "Great Brahmā, let it go, let it go. What use is such effort? That brahmin holds wrong views, and to take rebirth in a brahmin's household is like a person who, out of attachment to a golden fetter, places his own foot in that fetter. Now the bodhisattva, having thoroughly perfected himself among the six classes of gods of the desire realm up to three times over, has passed away from the Tuṣita heaven, and at midnight, resembling the son of the earth-guardian, has become a white elephant calf, snow-white in color, with six tusks and seven well-formed limbs. Not far from the slopes of the Himālayas, on the bank of the river Gaṅgā, not very far from the hermitage of the yellow-robed sages, in the place where the Śākyas dwell, there reigns a king called Śuddhodana. The bodhisattva has taken conception in the womb of that king's queen, called Mahāmāyā, and after ten full months will be born, and from birth will fully and perfectly awaken to the highest, complete, and perfect awakening. He will raise the Dharma stūpa, beat the drum of the Dharma, and bestow the offering of the Dharma. As for me, when I pass from this realm and take rebirth in the household of one known to be of lesser power, I must without doubt go forth from that household and into the teaching, and comprehend the nectar of the deathless. But as for being born in the household of a wealthy brahmin — because I would be their only child, no one would allow me to go forth. Therefore there is no need for me to take birth in a brahmin's household."

Great Brahmā then said: "Even if that is so, nonetheless please take conception there as I have requested, and at that time I will periodically urge your parents on your behalf." Then that one also gave his consent.

And so that divine being, through the ripening of his merit known to be of great power, who had planted roots of virtue in the presence of former buddhas, who was in his final existence, who sought to live the conduct, who had worn down his fetters, who had taken hold of the provisions for liberation, who was turned toward nirvāṇa, who had turned away from saṃsāra, who neither sought death and rebirth in all the destinies of existence nor clung to a final body — he passed away from the divine world and took conception in that queen's womb.

Now, certain women who are wise by nature know five matters that are to be understood: they know whether a man is attached and whether a man is free from attachment; they know the right time and the right lunar sign; they know that conception has occurred and from whom the conception has come; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, the child rests leaning to the right flank, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning to the left flank.

That woman, perceiving that her right side felt uncomfortable and thinking, "My child has been obtained without interruption," was filled with joy and delight and great gladness of mind, and spoke to her husband: "Noble lord, I have a pleasant word to tell you."

He spoke these words: "Good woman, may you hear a pleasant word — a word pleasing to gods and humans alike. What is this pleasant word? It is this: just as my right side felt uncomfortable, without any injury to myself, I have obtained a son."

Then the brahmin Nyagrodha, great as a towering śāla tree, overjoyed and delighted and in the fullness of gladness, his face like a blossoming lotus, spoke these joyful words: "Good woman, may your son be born in ease. May I see the face of a beloved son. May the son I have long desired and inwardly cherished come to fulfillment. May he be born in harmony with me and not be born at odds with me. May he perform my works. May he repay my nurturing with nurturing in return. May he make use of my wealth and possessions. May our family lineage long endure. May my prosperity not diminish. And when we have died and our time has come, may he make offerings on our behalf — whether modest or great — perform acts of merit, and, wherever we two have been reborn, may he go there and follow after us, dedicating the merit toward that end."

Knowing then that a sentient being had entered the womb, he had her settled comfortably in an upper chamber on a good foundation, free from harm. In cold weather he provided her with the things suited to cold, and in warm weather with things suited to warmth. He attended to her with particular foods and drinks prescribed by the physician — neither too cool, nor too warm, nor too sharp, nor too hot, nor too salty, nor too sour, nor too sweet, nor too astringent, nor too oily, nor too rough — indeed, foods and drinks from which sharpness, heat, saltiness, sourness, sweetness, astringency, oiliness, and roughness had all been removed.

And to preserve and nurture the one dwelling in the womb, he had her adorned in this manner: she was dressed in garments of many colors; her hands were decked with gold bracelets, jewels, and pearls; she wore necklaces, pendants hanging down, armlets, shoulder ornaments, and earrings and ear-rings; her eyes were drawn with eye-medicine; her face was beautified with dots of red lac; and her teeth were as free from stain as the kumuda flower, silver, snow, a pearl necklace, the kunda blossom, the moon, a swan, a mare's milk, a conch, or the root of a lotus. Her waist was girdled with a golden sash, and her feet were made beautiful with ankle ornaments — so that, like a golden pillar of offering wreathed in flowers, she moved as a divine daughter moving through a pleasure grove, with musicians making the sounds of song and melody. He placed her on the upper floor of the fine chamber and had a great and well-appointed throne set there, and she passed from throne to throne and from seat to seat, never descending to the ground below; and no one was permitted to utter any sound that was unpleasant to the ear.

Before long, that household grew and flourished abundantly in livestock, grain, gold, silver, storerooms, granaries, servants male and female, workers, those who lived on wages, bipeds, quadrupeds, and all the rest — just as the great ocean is daily filled by five hundred rivers, so too that household grew and flourished.

Then the brahmin Nyagrodha, great as a towering śāla tree, thought to himself: "If I were to have a son, how should I proceed — should I go about it in the ordinary way, as common brahmins do, extending the lineage of kings by playing games with the great king Padma?"

He thought to himself, "For that purpose I will have golden barleycorns planted." And so before long he had golden barleycorns sown. Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth there came a boy — handsome of form, pleasing to behold, beautiful, fair as the color of the root of a lotus, possessed of a head like a parasol, with long arms, a broad brow, fine eyebrows, a face like a lion's, an upper body like a lion's, and long shoulders.

When the birth celebration was to be held, the great Nyagrodha tree was cleared throughout of all stones, gravel, and weeds, sprinkled with sandal water, bedecked with many different flowers, and censed with various perfumes from golden censers. Victory banners and pennants were raised, and silk streamers and tinkling ornaments were hung. Scales and weights for honest measure were set in order. Then at the four gateways and at the center of the four crossroads, gifts were given and merit was made: food was given to those who desired food, drink to those who desired drink, garments to those who desired garments, garlands, perfumes, and ointments to those who desired garlands, perfumes, and ointments. In this way, for twenty-one days — three weeks of seven days each — gifts of many kinds were given and merit was made.

Then the relatives gathered and assembled together, and it was declared: "Since this boy was obtained by prayer to the Nyagrodha tree, let the boy's name therefore be Nyagrodha-born." And so the name was given. The brahmins then said: "Since his father too is of the Kāśyapa clan, let the boy's name be given as Kāśyapa." And so some knew him by the name Kāśyapa, and some knew him by the name Nyagrodha-born.

Now eight wet-nurses were assigned to care for him: two to carry him in their laps and keep him alive, two to suckle him at the breast, two to cleanse his impurities, and two to play with him and keep him company. They held iron arrows and carried protective coverings and many peacock-feather fans, and they nourished and raised him with milk, curds, fresh butter, clarified butter, butter oil, and all the other finest provisions and necessities. And so he grew and flourished like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

When he had grown to maturity, he was set to the study of letters, and in just a few days he mastered the alphabet entirely. At that time he became skilled in the brahminic way of conduct, behavior, ritual purity, conduct in all its forms, taking up ashes, taking up a water-pot and clay, the offering of praise, the scattering of libations, the recitation of mantras, perfect restraint, what must be determined, what is to be practiced at the proper time and season, the Veda of precise recitation, the Veda of sacrifice, the Veda of poetry, and the Veda of the protection of worldly existence. He became proficient in the six brahminic occupations: performing sacrifice, causing others to perform sacrifice, reading aloud, causing others to read aloud, and skill in giving and receiving.

He became learned in all eighteen branches of knowledge, namely: secret mantras, tantric texts, subtle ritual procedures, the science of logic, the Veda, grammar, the definitive arrangement of phonetics, clear understanding, precise terminology, compendium of prosody, the science of astronomy, the science of interpretation, the science of falling into water, the science of great conduct, the science of casting far into the world, the particular sciences, the sixty-section Tantra, the science of swallowing, and the science of posture and dwelling — in all these eighteen branches of knowledge his intellect became exceedingly sharp.

Before long his father entrusted him to five hundred brahmin boys of pure brahminic conduct, to lead them in reciting whatever they had heard.

He did as his father said, and it was done accordingly.

Then the brahmin Nyagrodha, great as a śāla tree, thought to himself: my lineage is of high standing, and I am endowed with great wealth. In a household such as this, one does not take a wife of inferior birth for one's sons without good reason. The custom among brahmins is to observe pure conduct for forty-eight years in full, and then in old age to sport with one's wife, to delight in her, and to enjoy her company. I therefore ought to obtain a bride for my son from the very beginning.

With this thought he spoke to the boy Nyagrodha and said: "Son, such is the way of nature in the world — for the sake of one's lineage, you should take a wife." The boy replied: "Father, with all due respect I request your leave — I will dwell in the forest of austerities." His father pressed him again and again, urging him to establish his lineage. And then the boy thought to himself: is there any means by which I might neither disobey my parents' wishes nor become entangled with a woman? Having reflected in this way, he said to his father: "Father, I would ask of you some gold from the Jambū River." The father summoned his treasurer and spoke these words: "Give this boy Nyagrodha as much gold from the Jambū River as he needs." The treasurer replied: "It shall be done."

Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha secretly summoned a skilled smith he had learned of from his father, and had him fashion the likeness of a woman in gold from the Jambū River. He presented it to his father and said: "Father, if a girl is found who resembles this form, she will be my bride — other than one such as this, I have no need of a bride."

His father looked at it and thought: on reflection, it seems this son of mine has given no thought to us at all. Even a girl of ordinary golden complexion is hard to find — what need is there to speak of one like this figure made of Jambū River gold? He held this thought inwardly, brooding over it. The brahmin boys who were with him noticed this and came to him and asked: "Master, why do you sit brooding?" He then explained to them at length the whole matter of obtaining a bride for the boy, and said: "On reflection, it seems as if my son has given no thought to me at all. Even a girl of merely golden complexion is difficult to find — how much more so one like this supreme figure made of Jambū River gold? Where would such a one come from?"

They said to him: "Master, do not be displeased. For whatever kind of man appears in the world, a correspondingly perfect array of companions and circumstances appears for him. Let us do this then: have three more figures made just like this one, and we will search in all four directions until we are certain to find a girl." He listened to his students' words and had three more figures made. The brahmin boys took the four figures and, fully equipped with musical instruments and finery, set out to travel through villages, hamlets, cities, and districts, setting off in groups of one hundred in every direction. And Nyagrodha, great as a śāla tree, charged them: "You must find — in a family of no low rank or lineage — only a girl whose appearance matches this figure."

Those brahmin boys thought to themselves: "How could we possibly go from house to house? We must devise a stratagem." And so they devised one. In every village, town, hamlet, and district they visited, they would enter and set the figure in the middle of the place, and offer it worship with incense, flowers, fragrant substances, and the sound of music, while proclaiming aloud: "If young women pay homage to this goddess who has gone ahead in the form of a girl, then the five excellent blessings will be granted to them — birth into a high lineage, marriage as a bride into a high lineage, dwelling in a supremely well-appointed home, a husband who will come under their sway, and the gift of sons." When these words were heard, the assembled womenfolk — young and old alike — would make offerings, pay homage, and offer prayers. After a time, however, those who had gone to the east, the south, and the north returned without having accomplished their aim. When Nyagrodha, great as a śāla tree, saw them, he fell into deep reflection. The brahmin youth Nyagrodha was delighted, joyful, and utterly glad, and he said these words: "It is well if she has not been found."

As for the brahmin boys who had taken the figure of the goddess and gone westward, they traveled through village after village, hamlet after hamlet, country after country, and palace after palace, until at last they came to the region of Kapila, to the city known as Kapila. There lived a brahmin named Śerśkya, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, with vast and extensive estates, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa himself in fortune. He had taken a wife from an equal lineage, and with her he lived in sport, in joy, and in delight. In the fullness of time, a being entered into his wife's womb. After eight or nine months had passed and she gave birth, a girl was born — beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and fair. Her kinsmen gathered and assembled, and over the course of three times seven, twenty-one days, they made gifts, performed meritorious deeds, and gave her a name. Now in the central lands, it was customary to call one who was beautiful of form "Bhadra," the Lovely. So they named her thus: "This girl is beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and fair, and her father is named Śerśkya, so let this girl be named Śerśkya's daughter Bhadra." And so she was named.

Then Śerśkya's daughter Bhadra was entrusted to eight nurses — who were these eight? Two nurses to hold and nurture her in their laps, two to suckle her at the breast, two to cleanse her of impurity, and two to play with her as companions. They bore iron arrows and carried quivers of many peacock feathers as a guard, and they nourished and raised her on milk, curds, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other finest provisions of various kinds. She grew vigorously, like a lotus dwelling in a pond, until at last she was fully grown.

The brahmin boys then went to the center of the marketplace, set up the figure, and made offerings to it with incense, flowers, fragrant substances, and the sound of music, proclaiming: "If young women pay homage to this goddess who has gone ahead in the form of a girl, then the five excellent blessings will be granted to them — birth into a high lineage, marriage as a bride into a high lineage, dwelling in a supremely well-appointed home, a husband who will come under their sway,

and will be blessed with sons." With these words they continued their proclamation.

Then the young women who lived in the city of Kapila went to the presence of the girl-goddess, made offerings, and presented their supplications.

Now the wife of the brahmin Śerśkya heard it said that such a girl-goddess had arrived and was granting the five excellent blessings. When she heard this, she said to her daughter, the fair one Bzangmo: "Go, daughter — you too should make offerings to the girl-goddess." The daughter replied: "What benefit would come from worshipping the girl-goddess?" The mother said: "If you present your supplications, she grants the five excellent blessings. And what are those five? Birth into a high lineage; being taken as a bride into a high lineage; dwelling in a supremely well-appointed home; a husband who will come under one's sway; and being blessed with sons."

Then the brahmin's fair daughter Bzangmo said to her mother: "Mother, I was born into a high lineage, I am fair of form and pleasing to behold — yet if one's wishes are not sought on my behalf, what excellent blessing is there left for me to request?" But her mother urged her again and again, and so, in order to protect her mother's feelings, the brahmin's fair daughter Bzangmo took flowers, incense, powder, cloth, and the like, and went to where the girl-goddess was.

The closer she came to the figure, the more deeply blue the figure became. When she drew near, the girl-goddess appeared to her as though made of iron. The brahmin boys thought: "What marvel has appeared? Whose power is this?" And as they reflected, they suspected that this apparition was the doing of this very girl, and they questioned her: "Whose daughter are you?" She answered: "I am Bzangmo, daughter of the brahmin Śerśkya."

The brahmin boys then heard this from the girl and went to where the brahmin Śerśkya's home was. They arrived and stood at the doorway of the house, calling out: "Wise one, please give us alms." When the brahmin Śerśkya heard the word "alms," he thought the brahmin boys had come seeking alms, and he gave instructions to the household that the brahmin boys should be given flour the colour of the blossoms of the mālūta tree, along with butter, molasses, grapes, round cakes, and tamarind. For in that land it was the custom that girls gave alms from their father's house — because alms given from the father's house were considered the gift of the essence.

Then the fair daughter Bzangmo took the alms and went to where the brahmin boys who were begging stood, and she presented the alms to them. But those brahmin boys did not accept them. Word of this reached the brahmin Śerśkya. The brahmin Śerśkya then said to the brahmin boys: "What do you wish?" They replied: "It is alms in the form of the girl that we want — not alms in the form of flour." The brahmin Śerśkya became angry and said to them: "I will not give you my daughter as alms." They replied: "We do not seek the girl as alms for our own sake." Then the brahmin Śerśkya said to the brahmin boys: "This matter, I did not understand the meaning you intended."

Then those brahmin boys spoke to the brahmin Śerśkya in these words: "O wise one, have you not heard that in the land of Magadha, in the city called Nyagrodhavana, there lives a brahmin named Nyagrodha — great as a great śāla tree — who is wealthy, possessed of great riches, of vast property, well established, broad and eminent, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa (the god of riches), a rival to the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, and who possesses sixteen villages of serfs, thirty villages of those who work the borders, sixty villages of those who tend the gardens, nine hundred and ninety-nine bondsmen, sixty loads of gold, and those by whose means King Padmachenpo's eighty bushels of refined gold grain are held — and that to him a son has been born called Nyagrodha, who is handsome, pleasant to behold, and beautiful, skilled in the six brahminical duties, who has gone to the far shore of the Vedas and their branches, and is extremely keen-minded in all eighteen fields of learning? It is for his sake that we have been begging for the girl as alms."

Then the brahmin Śerśkya said to those brahmin boys: "I have indeed heard at length of the qualities of that great brahmin who is like a great śāla tree — of his lineage, his moral discipline, his purity, and the nature of his conduct. However, since he lives far away, how should a marriage be arranged with him?" They replied: "O wise one, have you not heard what was said before:

Whatever fire there may be, whatever wind,
poison that is mingled with blood,
a brahmin who has been duly prepared,
and whatever horse — none of these are hindered.

That brahmin, moreover, is of very great wealth, and you too are likewise wealthy and rich. He has both mounts and people who can travel back and forth between them. Furthermore, to forge a friendship with one who lives far away is indeed something stable." When those brahmin boys had made the brahmin Śerśkya understand with these words urging him on, he then gave them bathing requisites — namely a bathing cloth, a tooth-cleaner, powder, grain oil, tooth-powder, and the like. The brahmin boys took those bathing requisites and went outside the city of Kapila to the ponds, in order to bathe. Then the brahmin Śerśkya thought to himself: "While the brahmin boys are away at the pond to bathe, I should deliberate with my friends, my relatives, and my kinsmen." Thinking thus, the brahmin Śerśkya remained inside the house and sat together with his wife and the assembly of relatives, and he told them the matter. They said: "Since that brahmin is like a great śāla tree, even if he were unwilling, we would strive earnestly to give him the girl. Since he himself desires this — what need is there even to say so? She should be given without any hesitation. To form a marriage alliance with him is entirely fitting and appropriate, and the girl too will be happy." Thereafter the two parents bathed the girl, dressed her in white clothes, performed the auspicious rites and the benedictions, had the brahmin boys recite the purificatory texts, and gave her to the brahmin boy Nyagrodha as his wife. After this, those brahmin boys reckoned the month, the day, the constellation, and the moment, and said to the girl's parents: "On such and such a great month, with the day, constellation, and

moment, the boy will come to live with you very soon." Then, their mission fully accomplished, those brahmin boys set out joyfully and gladly, their hearts overjoyed, heading toward the city of Nyagrodha, and in due course arrived at the city of Nyagrodha. The brahmin boy Nyagrodha saw them coming from a distance. Upon seeing them, he thought to himself: "How is it that those brahmin boys look so joyful and glad and overjoyed as they come along? It seems they have found just what I hoped for, without anything going wrong." Then those brahmin boys went straight toward the brahmin Nyagrodha, who was like a great sāla tree, and having arrived, they bowed to the brahmin Nyagrodha and took their seats. He in turn greeted each of those brahmin boys warmly and individually. Having greeted them all warmly, he spoke to those brahmin boys as follows: "Come now, brahmin boys — has everything been completed just as we imagined and hoped?" Full of joy and delight and great gladness, they spoke to their teacher: "Venerable teacher, please be pleased. We have found something even more excellent than what the venerable teacher had in mind." He replied: "How so?" And they said: "Did the venerable teacher not instruct us that in examining a girl, one should not scrutinize lineage, clan, and family line, but should examine only the beauty of her form? We have found one who is beautiful in form, and who also possesses lineage, clan, family line, and wealth." Those brahmin boys then related in full detail everything they had been asked about, speaking of the month, the day, the constellation, and the precise moment as well, and said: "Venerable teacher, we have settled all of this with certainty and have come; venerable teacher, please now know that the appointed time has arrived." Then the brahmin Nyagrodha, who was like a great sāla tree, upon hearing this account became joyful and glad and overjoyed, and honored those brahmin boys with various fine foods, drink, refreshments, garments, robes, and ornaments. Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha, hearing that the girl was so beautiful and radiant in form, became distressed, and thought: "Having heard that she is so beautiful, and lest something go wrong, I am greatly drawn to her by desire — I should go to my mother and examine her more closely beforehand." And so the brahmin boy Nyagrodha said to his parents: "Mother and Father, I will go and draw close to her personally beforehand, and only afterward take her as my bride." They both gave their consent to this. Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha set out from the city of Nyagrodha together with one brahmin boy, and heading toward the city of Kapila, traveled in due course through villages, hamlets, districts, and royal estates, and arrived at the city of Kapila. Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha, weary from the road and resting from his fatigue, took up a leaf-bundle and entered the city of Kapila to beg for alms. He went from house to house begging, and came to the door of the vaiśya household, which was like a great sāla tree. At that moment the good vaiśya girl came out carrying an alms-vessel, and the brahmin boy Nyagrodha saw her. Upon seeing her he thought to himself: "That girl — she is the one." Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha spoke to the girl as follows: "Whose daughter are you?" She replied: "I am a vaiśya's daughter." "Have you been given to another?"

"I have heard that in the city of the Nyagrodha tree, that very brahmin Nyagrodha — great as a sāla tree — has a son called Nyagrodha-born, and that your parents have given you to him." Then he said to her: "Good woman, what use do you have for such a husband? Know that one who becomes such a husband is as good as having no husband at all. How so?" She replied: "If he has no interest in the things of desire, what use is such a husband?" Then she thought: "Excellent! Excellent, son of a noble one! You have drawn out my every breath. You alone have anointed me with nectar." She then said: "Why is it, brahmin boy, that I too have no interest in the things of desire?" And she also spoke these words in verse:

That ease with which I look on rich and poor alike —
that salve which accords with the heart —
it is not sandalwood or camphor and such things.
Yet I have no power over myself: if my parents give me in marriage, what is to be done?

Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born said to the good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā: "Good woman, be steadfast and have patience. I myself am the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born." Then, upon hearing those words from the brahmin boy, the good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā breathed out at great length in deep relief, and said to Nyagrodha-born: "Brahmin boy, go now, and hold firm to your pledge. Those of noble character keep their pledges firm." Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born, having consulted together with the good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā, returned once more to the city of the Nyagrodha tree.

There the brahmin Nyagrodha — great as a sāla tree — performed all the customary rites of a householder, and the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born took Bhaṅgamā as his wife. When Bhaṅgamā was brought to the city of the Nyagrodha tree, the two parents of the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born placed the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born and the good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā in one dwelling, and made two beds for the two of them. Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born said to the good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā: "Good woman, remember the pledge we made before." The good vaiśya girl Bhaṅgamā likewise said to the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born: "Son of a noble one, bear it in mind yourself as well." And so the two of them reminded one another, and they lay as a mother and son lie together.

Then the brahmin Nyagrodha — great as a sāla tree — together with his wife asked the maidservants who attended the two of them: "How do the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born and his wife dwell together?" They replied: "Like a mother and son, or like a son and mother." Hearing this, the brahmin Nyagrodha — great as a sāla tree — spoke to his wife together with him, saying: "The fault is entirely ours, not theirs, for we made two beds for the two of them," and thinking this, he put one bed and one chair in place.

Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born thought to himself: "Alas, our parents have undertaken this great endeavor on our behalf — the affair of a teaching that is not wholesome."

The brahmin girl Bhadrā, having understood the intention of the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born's parents, spoke to the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born, saying: "Son of a lord, this arrangement has been made for your sake and mine. Yet please bear in mind the vow we made before." He replied: "Be at ease, dear one, and remember your vow as well."

So it was that in the first watch of the night, the brahmin girl Bhadrā lay down on the bed, while Nyagrodha-born remained sitting on the chair. In the middle watch of the night, Nyagrodha-born lay down, and Bhadrā sat up. Again in the last watch of the night, Bhadrā lay down, and Nyagrodha-born sat up without sleeping. And so the chair was removed as well. Again the brahmin girl Bhadrā spoke to Nyagrodha-born, saying: "Son of a lord, this arrangement has been taken up for the sake of warming ourselves — yet please bear in mind the vow we made before." He replied: "Be without doubt or suspicion, and do you too remember the former vow." And so Bhadrā lay down in the first watch of the night, while Nyagrodha-born walked about. In the middle watch, Nyagrodha-born lay down and the brahmin girl Bhadrā walked about. Again in the last watch Bhadrā lay down, and Nyagrodha-born walked about. In this manner, dwelling together in one place on one bed for twelve full years, not even once did the two of them give rise to a mind of attachment toward each other.

The Differentiation of the Nuns' Vinaya, the Second Fascicle.

Then Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, thought to himself: "How remarkable — while not yet free of attachment, these two conduct themselves as though free of attachment. I must put these two to the test." Thinking this, he manifested himself in the form of a serpent, went to where the two of them were sleeping, coiled himself up as a great serpent, and lay beneath their bed. The brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born saw a great black serpent, fierce and venomous with poisonous fangs, lying beneath the bed. Seeing it, he thought: "Alas, one with a form such as this will bring ruin." The arm of the one who was sleeping dangled out over the side. Then the brahmin boy Nyagrodha-born thought: "What am I to do now?" He took a fan with a jeweled handle and gently lifted and repositioned the arm. Then the brahmin girl Bhadrā was awakened by the touch of the jeweled handle of the fan, and being startled and displeased, she spoke to Nyagrodha-born, saying: "Son of a lord, what is this touching? Have you touched me with a mind of attachment?" He replied: "Bhadrā, it is not so. But thinking it would be wrong if that venomous serpent were to seize her, I lifted and repositioned the dangling arm." "With what?" she asked. He said: "With the jeweled handle of the fan." She then spoke these words: "Son of a lord, it would be better for me to be seized by that venomous serpent than for you to touch me with the jeweled handle of the fan. Why? Because:

A fine tree is ruined when the vine of the mālatī twines about it.
By the occasion of touching women, the world is brought to ruin.
Therefore it is not fitting that a man's hand should touch
an excellent woman — better he be seized by a swift and deadly serpent.

Moreover, through a man of power touching the body of a young woman,
the great austerities of one possessed of the horn-mark are undermined.
By the path of wind a man of power's exceptional conduct —

he came home, and then departed into the forest on foot. After that, while the two of them lived together in that manner, at another time the father and mother both died. Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born thought to himself: when our father and mother were alive, the two of us lived together with very little concern for the household; now our father and mother have died, and so we must see to the livelihood and provisions of our own home. Thinking thus, he spoke to the lovely daughter of the merchant, Bzang-mo, saying: "Bzang-mo, when our father and mother were alive, we lived together with very little concern for the household. Now we must attend to our household's livelihood and provisions, so Bzang-mo, for the time being you are to look after the affairs and tasks of the home, while I shall go out to the village fields." Having said this, the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born went off to tend the fields. When the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born surveyed his father's fields, he found nine hundred ninety-nine plowshares abandoned there, and besides, countless tiny living creatures being harmed and afflicted in wrongful ways. He saw the oxen with their nostrils pierced through, their flanks worn thin, their haunches split open by blows of the whip; and the workers there with their hair and beards grown long, their hands and feet cracked and yellow, wearing ragged garments, their bodies smeared with the dust of the earth, looking like charred stumps, like ghosts — quarreling with one another over the harrows, iron goads, plowshares, and ox-whips, falling to blows and working in that way. Having seen all this, he went among them and spoke these words: "Good people, who are you?" They replied: "We are workers employed by the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born." He then asked: "By whom were you appointed?" They said: "We were not formally appointed by him — rather, his father set us to doing the livelihood work of this household." Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born spoke to those farm laborers: "Good people, if the father of the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born set you to carrying out this household's livelihood work, then good people, why do you quarrel, why do you fall to blows and labor in such a way? Good people, why do you engage in such conduct of body and speech? Will not the karmic maturation of this bring you to experience suffering for a very long time in cyclic existence?" Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born thought to himself: though I am not engaging in the slightest wrongdoing through body, nor through speech, nor through mind, still from this situation a source of demerit has arisen close to me. Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born returned to his own home and said to the lovely daughter of the merchant, Bzang-mo: "Bzang-mo, keep the household with care and diligence." The lovely daughter of the merchant, Bzang-mo, said: "O son of a lord, where are you going?" He replied: "I am going to the forest of austerities." And he recited this verse:

A small monkey, whatever fruit it finds,
produces happiness on a single bed.
One must hold a mended piece of cloth.
The remainder — delusion seizes it all.

For a time after that, Bzang-mo also began to look after the household. And she saw that the maidservants had their hands and feet cracked and yellow, wore ragged garments, their heads disheveled, and were stabbing one another with verbal spears over the mortar, the pestle, the great elephant, the throne, and such things, and she went among them and spoke these words: "Good women, to whom do you belong?" They replied: "We belong to the lovely daughter of the merchant, Bzang-mo."

She then spoke these words: "Were you then appointed by Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant?" They replied: "We were not, in fact, appointed by Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant. Rather, it was Sgyug-mo who appointed us to manage that household."

For a time, she too grew disenchanted, and spoke this verse:

Whatever little rice is fit to eat,
one single bed produces happiness.
One must hold a mended piece of cloth.
The remainder — delusion seizes it all.

Now at that time buddhas had not yet appeared in the world. She thereupon gave generously to others: to tīrthikas who were wanderers, to those who roamed about, to the naked ascetics, to those who subsisted on whatever came their way, to the ash-smeared and their like; and to the poor, the destitute, and the beggars. She made the impoverished no longer poor. She released her slaves, hired servants, and bonded workers from their service. She divided all her wealth among friends, ministers, relatives, and the allied families of her kin, and then entered the house. Thinking to take whatever worn garments there might be, she looked into the treasury of cloth goods, and found there a great bolt of uncut outer cloth, some hundred thousand lengths in extent. She thought: "I shall take one such bolt, and give one like it to Bzang-mo. The house I shall entrust to the relatives." Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born said to Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant: "Bzang-mo, where do you wish to go?" She replied: "I wish to go with you alone into the ascetic forest." He said: "It is not fitting for a woman to dwell together with a man in the ascetic forest." Bzang-mo replied: "If that is the case, then release me from the household first." "Why?" She then spoke these words: "The reason is this: if you depart before me, a woman who has ripened and colored like cooked rice will be sought after by many people. If you leave and some among them should come to court me, there is the possibility that what is unsuitable may come to pass." Then the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born thought: "This girl is learned and exceedingly settled in her mind." And he said to Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant: "Bzang-mo, come. Let us leave the household together, the two of us alone." And the two of them departed from the household together, alone.

Then, having gone together with the brahmin youth Nyagrodha-born as far as the city's outskirts, he said to Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant: "Bzang-mo, go now and remain in whatever manner of practice you desire."

Now at that time in Rājagṛha there lived a naked ascetic called "Perfector of Nakedness," who, though not omniscient, claimed to be omniscient. He was surrounded by many naked ascetics and their disciples. Then Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant, went to the place where the naked ascetic called Perfector of Nakedness resided, and when she arrived she said to him: "Venerable one, I wish to go forth under you." He gave her the going forth and placed her among the community of naked female ascetics.

Then those naked ascetics, seeing that Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant, was beautiful in form, lovely to behold, radiant, of glowing complexion, and endowed with the highest qualities, said to one another: "Whatever going forth we have undertaken is entirely for the sake of the five desirable qualities of the gods. And this Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant, resembles a woman of the gods. So for now, whether or not she obtains the desirable qualities of the gods is beside the point — let us enjoy ourselves with this Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant." Having said this, some five hundred naked ascetics made their way toward the place where the naked ascetic Perfector of Nakedness was staying. And when, after a time, the occasion had been fully related, they then roused Bzang-mo, the lovely daughter of the merchant.

He permitted it out of affection for his disciples. Then, day after day, through the condition of karmic maturation, the five hundred naked ascetics would take their pleasure with her. After some time had passed, she became disgusted and appealed to the Perfector of Nakedness, and he said, "Go to whomever falls to you by lot."

At that same time, the Blessed One, while still a bodhisattva, was twenty-nine years of age. Having taken his pleasure among the desirable things of the senses, and having seen an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, his mind turned away from the world. At the stroke of midnight he mounted his noble steed Kanthaka the Praised One and rode into the forest. For six years he practiced austerities of every kind that proved to be of no benefit whatsoever, then bathed in the river Nairañjanā. From Gayā and Gayābala, the two women, he accepted a porridge of milk that had been reduced sixteen times by boiling. The nāga king Kāla praised him with verses, and from the grass-seller Svastika he accepted grass. He entered beneath the tree of awakening and spread his seat, undisturbed and unentangled by anyone. Sitting cross-legged as a nāga king coils in sleep, he formed the firm resolve and spoke it aloud as well: "Until I have attained the exhaustion of all defilements, I shall not break this cross-legged posture." After a time, having subdued Māra together with his hosts of thirty-six billion classes of demonic beings, he fully and completely awakened to unsurpassable and perfect awakening.

Urged by Brahmā, he went to the region of Vārāṇasī and turned the wheel of Dharma endowed with the Dharma, setting forth the truths to Kauṇḍinya, who came to know all, and to eighty thousand gods. He also tamed the group of five, and the assembly of the nearby five, and fifty principal sons of the town. He went into the forest of Śalmali trees and tamed the assembly of sixty belonging to the group of Yaśas. He went to the town of Senānī and set forth the truths to Gayā and Gayābala, the two daughters of that town. He went to the region of Uruvilva and tamed the five hundred, headed by Uruvilva Kāśyapa with his eighteen miraculous displays. He went to the region of Gayā and, by means of the three miracles, gave teachings to the river Kāśyapa and to those thousands of matted-hair ascetics. He went to the region of Rājagṛha of the brilliant palace, and tamed King Bimbisāra together with his son and retinue, eighty thousand gods, and many hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders of the region of Magadha, and accepted the Bamboo Grove. At that time the Blessed One was staying in Rājagṛha at the stūpa of Supratishthita.

Kāśyapa, beneath a certain tree, saw the Blessed One: beautiful, worthy of faith, with faculties at peace, with mind at peace, tamed and supremely tranquil in mind, seated steadfastly and resplendent like a pillar of gold. Having seen him, the thought arose: "Oh, I see the Teacher! Oh, I see an arhat! Oh, I see the Blessed One! Oh, I see the Sugata, the Well-Gone! Oh, I see the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha!" With this thought he held him in the highest regard, as his supreme guide, and fixed him in his mind. Reflecting with his entire mind, he went to where the Blessed One was, went up to him, and bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One with reverence. He then spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you are my Teacher, and I am a śrāvaka of the Blessed One. Venerable Blessed One, you are my Teacher — my Teacher! And I am a śrāvaka of the Blessed One — a śrāvaka!" When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed Kāśyapa with these words: "Kāśyapa, it is indeed so. Yes, it is so. Kāśyapa, I am your Teacher —"

you are my śrāvaka. Kāśyapa, I am your Teacher — your Teacher! And you are my śrāvaka — my śrāvaka!

Kāśyapa, there are those who, thinking with their entire mind yet without true knowledge, declare: 'I know all things.' Without truly seeing, they declare: 'I see all things.' Without being a Tathāgata, they declare: 'I am a Tathāgata.' Without being an arhat, they declare: 'I am an arhat.' And without being a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, they boastfully claim: 'I am a perfectly and fully awakened buddha.' Kāśyapa, the head of such a teacher would split into seven pieces. But Kāśyapa, because I truly know, I declare: 'I know all things.' Because I truly see, I declare: 'I see all things.' Because I am a Tathāgata, I declare: 'I am a Tathāgata.' And because I am a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, I openly proclaim: 'I am a perfectly and fully awakened buddha.'

I teach the Dharma to śrāvakas always with a basis of occasion, never without occasion; with definite emergence, never without definite emergence; with reliance, never without reliance; with purpose, never without purpose; with miraculous display, never without miraculous display.

Kāśyapa, therefore you should train in this way: you should listen to whatever Dharma, to whatever wholesome teaching, there may be. You should honor all of it, take it as your highest guide, treat it as supremely important, make your mind one-pointed, open your ears, and listen having reflected with your entire mind.

Kāśyapa, furthermore you should train in this way: you should dwell by observing the arising and passing away of the five appropriated aggregates (skandhas). You should dwell by observing the arising and ceasing of the six sense sources. You should dwell with your mind well and closely settled upon the four foundations of mindfulness. Dwelling with your mind well and closely settled upon the four foundations of mindfulness, you should cultivate the seven limbs of awakening and, having directly realized with the body and fully accomplished the eight liberations, you should dwell in them.

You should dwell with a far greater degree of moral shame and embarrassment in the presence of wise ones who share the holy life equally with your Teacher. You should always be endowed with mindfulness of your own body and not let it go, and you should dwell in the body without becoming separated from it. Thus, Kāśyapa, you should train.

Then the Blessed One, having thoroughly shown, thoroughly guided, thoroughly praised, and thoroughly gladdened Kāśyapa, rose from his seat and departed.

Thereupon the venerable Kāśyapa followed in the footsteps of the Blessed One and, thinking to lay out a seat for the Blessed One in the place where he dwelt, he spread out a great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets as a cushion.

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thoughts and reflections of the monk Kāśyapa, left the road and sat to one side.

Then the venerable Kāśyapa, quickly and with all haste, spread out the great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets and prepared a seat for the Blessed One. And he addressed him with these words: "Blessed One, out of compassion, please be seated on the prepared seat. Sugata, please be seated on the prepared seat. May this long be for my benefit, welfare, and happiness."

The Blessed One was seated on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he spoke to the venerable Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, your great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets is soft indeed. Kāśyapa, your great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets is supple."

When he had said this, the venerable Kāśyapa replied to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is indeed so. Sugata, it is indeed so. Reverend One, my great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets is soft. Reverend One, my great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets is supple. Blessed One, out of compassion, please accept the great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets."

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, take my robe — the charnel-ground cloth."

When he had said this, Kāśyapa replied to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please accept the great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets. Sugata, please accept the great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets. Reverend One, I shall take the Blessed One's robe, the charnel-ground cloth."

Then the Blessed One accepted the venerable Kāśyapa's great patchwork robe of a hundred thousand sheets, and with his own hands presented to him that charnel-ground cloth.

Then the venerable Kāśyapa, having received instruction, practiced as a trainee for eight days, living entirely on alms. On the ninth day he was a trainee no longer.

From that time forward, the venerable Kāśyapa became an arhat — free from all attachment in the three realms, his mind equable toward mud and gold alike, like the sky and the palm of the hand, like sandalwood that has been laid down, having torn open the enclosure of the door of ignorance, having attained knowledge, higher cognition, and individual perfect discernment, turned away from the gains and acquisitions of becoming and desire, and turned away from honor. The gods with Indra (Śakra) and their attendants came to paint his likeness, to make offerings to him, and to pay him homage.

At that time some people said: "How wonderful! Because the monk Kāśyapa has realized this great distinction, the name Great Kāśyapa — Mahākāśyapa — has arisen."

Then the Blessed One, gradually wandering through the districts, traveled to Rājagṛha and dwelt in the Bamboo Grove of Rājagṛha, the Kalandaka Grove. At that time in Rājagṛha there was a festival of meeting at the mountains, a festival of beauty. All the tīrthikas (non-Buddhists) without exception gathered there, and for a time even the naked ascetics went to Rājagṛha.

Then a brahmin's daughter of good character thought to herself: "Who will experience affliction like this for so long? Now that entry into Rājagṛha for alms-begging has arrived, this is the right moment for me." And so, with a mind aroused by affliction, finding her opportunity, she went to Rājagṛha having set her intention on begging.

The venerable Mahākāśyapa also, in the early morning, having dressed in his lower robe and taken up his Dharma robe and alms bowl, entered Rājagṛha for alms. He saw the brahmin's daughter of good character, that she had lost her healthy complexion and had become as she was. Having seen her, he said: "Sister, is the one who has undertaken the fully pure life well looked after?"

She replied: "Scion of a noble house, while I dwelt in my own home, that indeed was my pure life. But now I practice only unchaste conduct — there is no pure life."

He said: "Sister, in order to abide in the pure life, will you go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya?"

When he had said this —

The brahmin's daughter of good character spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Scion of a noble house, surely you have no reproach for me?"

Then, when the venerable Mahākāśyapa began to reflect, he who was of a nature to speak of faults saw that those who are of a faulty nature had applied her to what is not the holy Dharma. Recognizing that such a thing had come about, he spoke thus to the brahmin's daughter of good character: "Sister, do not be afraid. The teaching of the Blessed One is without foul smell and without evil. His śrāvakas do not seek even the pleasures of the gods — what need is there to speak of those of humans?"

He then entrusted her to a great female householder, and she had her go forth and receive full ordination. When she went out for alms, those who were deceitful, fraudulent, and corrupt spread the rumor: "She takes delight in not enjoying a form so lovely as this!"

Then on another occasion the venerable Mahākāśyapa, in the morning, having fastened his lower robe and taken up his Dharma robe and alms bowl, entered Rājagṛha for alms. The brahmin's daughter of good character also, in the morning, having fastened her lower robe and taken up her Dharma robe and alms bowl, entered Rājagṛha for alms. The venerable Mahākāśyapa saw the brahmin's daughter of good character. Having seen her, he said: "Sister, are you delighted in the teaching of the Blessed One?"

She replied: "I am delighted in the teaching of the Blessed One; there is not the slightest lack of delight. Yet this form has caused me harm, as a sheep causes harm with its fleece — wherever I go, people accost me."

The venerable Mahākāśyapa said: "Do not be distressed about alms. I shall give you, day by day, half of my own alms." He went for alms, and of what he collected half he consumed himself and half he gave to her.

When she was proceeding in this way, the monks of the group of six heard that when Mahākāśyapa had been a householder, he and this Bhadra had lived together in the same house for twelve years and yet had not once given rise in their minds to a thought of passionate attachment — and now, hearing this, they mocked him, saying: "Now he gives her half his alms!"

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa gave a mental exercise to the brahmin's daughter of good character, and through her effort, exertion, and striving she abandoned all afflictions and directly actualized arhatship.

After a time the venerable Mahākāśyapa heard the monks making these taunts. Having heard them, he spoke thus to the brahmin's daughter of good character: "Sister, what a spiritual friend should do I have already done. A deer does not rear a deer. Now go and cultivate, in the domain permitted by the Buddha, the qualities you have trained in your homeland, following your alms rounds." Having thus instructed her in this way, the venerable Mahākāśyapa took up the practice of equanimity.

At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru, relying on Devadatta as a companion in unwholesomeness, had killed the righteous Dharma-king his father, and was now sitting in lordship over the sovereignty of his father's kingdom. No sooner had he sat than remorse arose in his mind, and he entered a hall of grief. His grief could not be dispelled by many means. His ministers thought: "In the six great cities there are dancers, performers, comedians, acrobats, and —"

every type of musician that could be found, they would all be assembled. And so the ministers did exactly that. Before King Ajātaśatru, many different musicians played the sounds of musical instruments — lutes, flutes, clay drums, kettledrums, iron cymbals, and melodious instruments of every kind. They sang songs, performed dances, ran about, and leapt. Yet even so, they were unable to dispel the grief of King Ajātaśatru.

Then, at another time, the young brahmin woman Suvarṇā, in the early morning, clothed in an underskirt and robe, carrying her alms bowl, beautiful in all her conduct, entered Rājagṛha for alms. A minister of malicious mind caught sight of the brahmin girl Suvarṇā — fair of form, lovely to behold, beautiful, her body excelling even the colour of gold — and seeing her, thought to himself: "This one will dispel the king's grief." With this in mind, that minister seized the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, had her bathed in the baths befitting a king, adorned her with the finest perfumes, garlands of flowers, robes, and ornaments befitting a king, and presented her to King Ajātaśatru.

Now the brahmin girl Suvarṇā abided in a luminous state, certain that the karma she had formerly created and accumulated would without fail arise and be experienced — just as the shadows of mountains or mountain peaks descend and fall upon the ground below. In just that way, the brahmin girl Suvarṇā remained luminous, knowing with certainty that what she had formerly created and accumulated would without fail arise and be experienced. And so, before long, King Ajātaśatru, the moment he saw the brahmin girl, was seized by attachment and began to enjoy pleasure in her company.

Then on that very fifteenth-day observance ceremony (poṣadha), when inquiry was made, the brahmin girl Suvarṇā was nowhere to be seen among the assembly. The great Lady of Beings, the Great Gautamī, looking about, saw that the brahmin girl had grown faint and weakened. Perceiving that she was faint, weak, and ill at ease, the great Lady of Beings, Gautamī, said to Utpalāvarṇā: "Sister, look after the brahmin girl Suvarṇā."

Then Utpalāvarṇā, on that very fifteenth-day observance, went by means of supernatural power to where the house of Ajātaśatru was. Utpalāvarṇā entered through a window-opening and said these words to the brahmin girl Suvarṇā: "Sister, you have severed, abandoned, removed, and utterly relinquished the afflictions of the three realms that had been habitual since beginningless time — why have you not manifested these supernatural powers that are as tasteless as straw and common to all non-Buddhists?"

When she had spoken thus, the brahmin girl Suvarṇā said to Utpalāvarṇā: "Sister, I do not know the path of supernatural power."

Then Utpalāvarṇā taught the brahmin girl Suvarṇā the path of supernatural power. Thereupon the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, through the worldly path and in dependence upon the four meditative concentrations, fully accomplished supernatural power. Then the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, adorned with all her ornaments, went to where the nuns' rains-retreat dwelling was. A group of twelve nuns saw the brahmin girl Suvarṇā adorned with all her ornaments. Seeing her, they said to the great Lady of Beings Gautamī: "We do not observe the restoration ceremony together with a king's consort."

Then the great Lady of Beings Gautamī spoke these words to the brahmin girl Suvarṇā: "Sister, go now to the king's palace, return the garments and ornaments, obtain the king's permission, put on the ochre robes, and come back to us."

Then the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, heeding the words of the great Lady of Beings Gautamī, went to where King Ajātaśatru's palace was. At that time King Ajātaśatru had just awakened and, catching sight of the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, moved to embrace her. Thereupon the brahmin girl Suvarṇā rose up into the sky above. Then King Ajātaśatru saw the brahmin girl Suvarṇā soaring up into the sky above like a goose-king with wings outstretched. Seeing this, he was seized with fear and dread and amazement, and thought to himself: "Can she be a goddess? Or a nāga-woman? Or a gandharva-woman? Or a yakṣa-woman? Or a rākṣasī?" And he also spoke these verses:

Are you a goddess, or a nāga-woman,
a yakṣa-woman, rākṣasī, or gandharva-woman?
Or what manner of female spirit might you be?
Tell me, I ask — let your answer come to me.

When he had spoken thus, the brahmin girl Suvarṇā replied to King Ajātaśatru in these words:

I am no goddess, no nāga-woman,
no gandharva, yakṣa-woman, or rākṣasī.
O lord of men, I am a female hearer
who has accomplished the work of the Sugata.

Then King Ajātaśatru, upon hearing those words, felt pierced to the quick by a second arrow, as though he were a wild deer, and cried out, "Alas, alas! I have committed a great evil!" and spoke these verses as well:

Like one who has not yet reached the far shore of the ocean,
having not yet crossed even this one suffering,
now a second has drawn near —
and because an opportunity presented itself, many harms befall me.

So thinking, he fainted and fell to the ground, and after a time was revived by being sprinkled with water and roused. Then King Ajātaśatru recovered his composure and spoke these words to the brahmin girl Suvarṇā: "Alas, alas! Wandering as I do through saṃsāra, base and polluted, it would be most improper to become yet more base. Noble one, please descend, descend. I beg you to draw me, who has sunk into the river of mire that is wrongful conduct, up from the mud by the hand."

Then the brahmin girl Suvarṇā descended in order to guide him. Having descended, she arranged a seat and sat down. Then King Ajātaśatru, like a tree felled from its roots, prostrated with his head to the feet of the brahmin girl Suvarṇā and said to her: "Noble one, please have patience with those who are difficult to tame." The brahmin girl Suvarṇā replied: "Great king, I forgive you."

Then, after a short while, the brahmin girl Suvarṇā gave the garments and ornaments back to the king. The king in turn gave ochre robes to the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, prostrated at her feet, and also said: "Noble one, for as long as you live, I will provide you with robes, almsfood, a bed and seat, medicine for illness, and all requisites."

Then the brahmin girl Suvarṇā said to King Ajātaśatru: "O king, this was in all likelihood a fault of my own karma — it was not your fault. Why? Because the Blessed One has declared:

There is no place anywhere one can abide
where karma cannot reach —
not in the sky above, not within the ocean's depths,
not even by entering into the clefts of the mountains."

And further, another god declared:

Just as a shadow follows a person —
sitting when one sits, moving when one moves —
so too do virtue and non-virtue, like a shadow,
follow one always, as the awakened Blessed One has proclaimed without equal.

Then the brahmin girl Suvarṇā, in this way composing a heartfelt gathering of words for King Ajātaśatru, expounded the Dharma under many categories, in a thorough and correct manner. She caused him to grasp it correctly, praised him rightly, and filled him with genuine joy. Then she rose visibly into the sky above and returned to the nuns' rain-retreat dwelling.

Now, at this point the twelve groups said: "We shall not perform the restoration ceremony together with a nun who has fallen." When this was said, the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks in turn reported it to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, "Both assemblies of my Saṅgha will come to understand the meaning, and the foundation of training that I have established will be well-settled," convened both assemblies of the Saṅgha on account of this occurrence, this basis of discussion, this matter, and this occasion. The blessed buddhas act with full knowledge — they act knowingly, not unknowingly. They act at the right time, not at the wrong time. They act with purpose, not without purpose. This is the nature of the blessed buddhas: when something done lacks purpose, they ward it off, like warding off water with a water-scoop. And this is likewise the nature of the blessed buddhas: they know the right time for purposeful action. Therefore the Blessed One addressed the brahmin girl Suvarṇā and asked: "Nun, is it true that you acted in this way?" "Venerable One, I did not." "Nun, did you claim it as your own?" She replied as follows: "Venerable One, since I am by nature free from attachment, how could I ever claim it as my own?" The Blessed One then rebuked her, saying that what is unbecoming of the contemplative life, what is not in accordance with it, what is not proper, what is not fitting — that is not something one who has gone forth should do.

Then, having rebuked her repeatedly and under many headings, the Blessed One addressed both assemblies of the Saṅgha and declared: "Monks and nuns, therefore, for these ten benefits — in order to gather the Saṅgha together; in order to bring the Saṅgha to excellence; in order to bring the Saṅgha into harmony; in order that the Saṅgha may dwell in ease; in order to restrain those persons who are difficult to admonish; in order that those who are conscientious may dwell in comfort; in order that those who lack faith may come to have faith; in order that those who have faith may grow still further and flourish; in order to subdue the defilements of this very life; in order to turn back the defilements of future lives; in order to take up the holy life and uphold it; in order to bring the holy life to complete fulfillment; in order that the teaching may be harmonious; and in order that my teaching, having spread wide and brought benefit to the many, be correctly and completely proclaimed to gods and humans alike, and endure for a long time — with these purposes in view, a rule of training for the female hearers in the Vinaya is to be established. My female hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Furthermore, if any nun, while sharing the same training equally with other nuns, without having relinquished her training and without having shown its deterioration, engages in unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse — even if she were reborn together with one born in an animal realm —

That nun has incurred defeat and is not to remain in the community.

Now, regarding the phrase "any nun": there are four kinds of nun. There is the nun by name, the nun by pretension, the nun for the sake of begging, and the nun through the vanquishing of afflictions.

Who is a nun by name? She who is called a nun by her name, or addressed by that name, or designated by a second term, or referred to by an honorary title, or identified by recognition, by being called out to, by being labeled, by conventional usage as a nun, or as one belonging to the class of nuns, or as one who has become like a nun — she is called a nun by name.

Who is a nun by pretension? She who, though not a nun, claims "I am a nun," and abides in that claim deceptively, and who likewise affirms herself as a nun by asserting "I am indeed a nun" — she is called a nun by pretension.

Who is a nun for the sake of begging? She who sustains her livelihood by practicing begging in accordance with the Dharma — she is called a nun for the sake of begging.

Who is a nun through the vanquishing of afflictions? She who has abandoned, thoroughly understood, cut off at the root, and made groundless as a palmyra tree (Skt. tāla) felled at its crown, those defilements (Skt. āsrava) that defile utterly, that produce continued existence, that are accompanied by disease, whose karmic maturation is suffering, and that lead to birth, aging, and death in future lives — so that they have become incapable of arising again in the future — she is called a nun through the vanquishing of afflictions.

In the present context, the intention is that "nun" refers to one who has received full ordination, since it is not appropriate to apply the motion-and-four-fold-act of formal procedure to one who is immovable. Therefore the term "nun" is used here as well.

The phrase "together with other nuns" means: together with those others who are her companions in the holy life, following the same Dharma.

The phrase "sharing the same training equally" means: the training to be followed by a nun who received full ordination one hundred years ago applies equally to one who receives full ordination today; and the training undertaken by one who receives full ordination today applies equally to one ordained one hundred years ago. This equality consists in equality of moral discipline itself, equality of training itself, and equality in the very recitation of the Sūtra of Individual Liberation (Skt. prātimokṣa).
