Therefore the expression "sharing the same training equally" is used.

The phrase "having become" means: having continued in that way.

As for the phrase "without having relinquished her training" — what constitutes not having relinquished one's training? It is this: if a nun, overcome by rage and in the grip of anger, relinquishes her training, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If someone who is deranged, whose mind is disturbed, or who is overwhelmed by feelings relinquishes her training, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If she relinquishes her training in the presence of someone who is angry or in the grip of anger, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If a nun relinquishes her training in the presence of a foolish woman, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. Like that foolish woman, if she relinquishes her training in the presence of one who is mute, one who is dumb, one who is overcome by sleep, one who has entered meditative absorption, an image of a god, an image of a buddha, a non-human being, an apparition, or a being that has taken the form of an animal, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If a woman from the heartland uses the words of the borderlands to relinquish her training before a person of the heartland, and that person of the heartland does not understand what is being said in the language of the borderlands, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. Likewise, if a woman from the borderlands uses the words of the heartland to relinquish her training before a person of the borderlands, and that person of the borderlands does not understand what is being said in the language of the heartland, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training.

If a woman from the borderlands uses the words of the borderlands to relinquish her training before a person of the heartland, and that person of the heartland does not understand what is being said in the language of the borderlands, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If a woman from the heartland uses the words of the heartland to relinquish her training before a person of the borderlands, and that person of the borderlands does not understand what is being said in the language of the heartland, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If one relinquishes her training with the perception that a secluded place is not secluded, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If one relinquishes her training with the perception that a non-secluded place is secluded, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If one who is mentally deranged relinquishes her training before one who is mentally deranged, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. If one who wishes to relinquish her training does so without making it known to any nun who is sound of mind and dwelling nearby, it should be declared that she has not relinquished her training. This is what is called not having relinquished one's training.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the Third Fascicle. On the matter called "not having violated one's training."

There is the case of having violated one's training and not having relinquished it. There is the case of not having violated one's training and yet having relinquished it. There is the case of having violated one's training and having relinquished it. And there is the case of not having violated one's training and not having relinquished it.

What is the case of having violated one's training and yet not having relinquished it? It is as follows. A nun who wishes to leave, who is discontented, who wishes to wander about and does not seek the way of the contemplative life, or who is wearied by the way of the contemplative life, or who has become despondent, or who is in doubt, or who is reproachful — such a person approaches a nun and says: "Noble ones, the celibate life is difficult to practice. It is difficult to live in complete solitude. It is difficult to find delight in being alone. It is difficult to fully embrace dwelling in forest refuges, at the edges of forests, and in remote places. For as long as I live I shall have parted from the pleasures and sports of people. For as long as I live I shall sleep on a bed of grass, leaves, and fallen foliage. For as long as I live I shall have to look to others for support in others' homes. For as long as I live I shall have to go in need to others for robes, alms-food, a lodging place, medicines for the sick, and requisites. I do not think of my mother. I think of my father, brothers, and sisters. Please entrust me to good households." Speaking thus, uttering words, phrases, expressions, speech, statements, definitive words, verbal formulations, spoken words, verbal actions, and verbal communications — all of them expressing the wish to wander away — and yet at the same time saying, "I am not giving up my training," this is the case of having violated one's training without having relinquished it.

What is the case of not having violated one's training and yet having relinquished it? It is as follows. A nun who wishes to leave, who is discontented, who wishes to wander about and does not seek the way of the contemplative life, or who is wearied by the way of the contemplative life, or who has become despondent, or who is in doubt, or who is reproachful — such a person approaches a nun and says: "Noble ones, please attend to this. I, who am called such-and-such by name, hereby relinquish the training of a nun." If she speaks thus, it should be declared that she has relinquished her training. If she says, "I give up the Buddha, I give up the Dharma, I give up the Saṅgha, I give up my preceptor and my teacher" — or even if she says, "Please regard me as a female contemplative, please regard me as a laywoman, please regard me as a woman of loose character, as an eunuch, as one who has been expelled from the Saṅgha" —

— or who has killed her mother, killed her father, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṅgha, drawn blood from a Tathāgata with evil intent, who dwells by means of theft, who is a tīrthika, or who has entered the ranks of the tīrthikas — and who says: "I, one such as you, who live in accordance with the Dharma and walk the holy life, am content with this" — and who, wishing in this way to wander off, speaks such words, statements, utterances, expressions, definitive phrases, verbal formulations, vocal declarations, vocal actions, and vocal intimations, saying, "I hereby relinquish my training": it should be declared that she has relinquished her training. This is a case in which she has not violated her training and has relinquished it.

What then constitutes both violating one's training and relinquishing it? It is as follows. A nun who wishes to leave, who is displeased, who wants to wander off and does not wish to live the life of a female contemplative, or who is weary of the life of a female contemplative, or who has grown discouraged, or who is in doubt, or who is reproachful — such a person approaches a nun and says: "Noble ones, the holy life is hard to live. It is hard to dwell in complete solitude. It is hard to find joy in being alone. It is hard to endure dwelling in forest hermitages, in wood-edge retreats, and in remote border lodges. For as long as I live I shall be cut off from the joys and amusements that people enjoy. For as long as I live I shall make my bed of grass, leaves, and fallen foliage. For as long as I live I shall have to look to others in others' households, depending on their goodwill. For as long as I live I shall have to go seeking robes, alms-food, a seat and bedding, medicines for illness, and requisites from others in this way." "I do not remember my mother. I remember my father, my brothers, and my sisters. Please entrust me to good households." And then she says: "Please attend to this, you who possess the Dharma. I, who am called such-and-such by name, hereby relinquish my training. I give up the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, my preceptor, and my teacher." Or even if she says: "Please regard me as a female contemplative, please regard me as a laywoman, please regard me as a woman of loose character, as a eunuch, as one who has been expelled from the Saṅgha, as one who has killed her mother, killed her father, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṅgha, drawn blood from a Tathāgata with evil intent, who dwells by means of theft, who dwells separately, who ought not to remain, who is a tīrthika, or who has entered the ranks of the tīrthikas" — or says: "I, one such as you, who live in accordance with the Dharma and walk the holy life, am content with this" — and then, wishing to wander off in this way, she speaks the words and so forth, as stated in full just as in the first section above — then, one who speaks both sets of words in this manner has both violated her training and relinquished it.

What then constitutes neither violating one's training nor relinquishing it? Any case other than those forms described above is one in which she has neither violated her training nor relinquished it.

"Unchaste conduct" means the coming together of two with two. "Intercourse" — unchaste conduct, whatever it is, is also intercourse. The word "Dharma" here is used as a term for the Dharma in reference to what is not Dharma. "If one engages in it" means if one practices it further. "Even with one born into an animal existence, and together with such" means together with a bear, a monkey, and the like.

"Nun" refers to one in whom the substance of being a nun is present. What is the substance of being a nun? It is full ordination. What is full ordination? It is the performing of the act of a request together with a motion and three announcements; the examination itself; the thorough examination itself; the completing; the thoroughly completing; the acceptance of that individual by the assembly; the explicit acceptance; the non-reversal; the non-turning-back; the non-annulment itself; and whatever constitutes speech, words, conventional expression, utterance, declaration, definitive words, the path of words, verbal expression, verbal action, and verbal communication. The word "this" here is a phrase of close indication and comprehensive indication. "Has incurred defeat" means that it is the last, a downfall, inferior, a settling at the end, a severance, and a contradiction of the mind. Furthermore, whoever commits that downfall becomes immediately unfit to be a nun, unfit to be a contemplative, unfit to be a daughter of the Śākya clan, and has fallen away from the substance of being a nun: her state as a contemplative is ruined, degraded, broken, a downfall, a defeat, and her state as a contemplative is beyond restoration. It is just as when the top of a palm tree is cut off it can no longer turn green, and can no longer grow, increase, or expand: in the same way, when a nun has done such a thing, the passage up to "becomes immediately unfit to be a nun" follows as before. "She is not to be allowed to remain" means that the nuns are not to share with her the restoration ceremony, the invitation ceremony, a single request, a request together with a second announcement, a request together with a motion and three announcements, and she is not to be appointed by appointment among the twelve kinds of individuals; and therefore it is said "she is not to be allowed to remain."

Now, how does one incur the downfall? A summary verse:

Alone, and by means of the three bodily openings,
together with a human being and others,
inclining toward contact, striving,
causing intoxication, and being held by force.

If a nun practices the Dharma of intercourse, unchaste conduct, she incurs defeat. Furthermore, if any nun practices the Dharma of intercourse, unchaste conduct, with a human being by means of the three bodily openings — whether in the mouth, the passage for excrement, or the female organ — that nun has incurred defeat and is not to be allowed to remain. Just as she engages in the three bodily openings with a human being, so too if she engages with a non-human being or with one born into an animal existence, in all such cases she incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if any nun whose mind is inclined toward contact, who has fallen to contact, who having fallen there engages with a partially obstructed female organ in a partially obstructed manner, or with a partially obstructed organ in an unobstructed manner, or with an unobstructed organ in a partially obstructed manner, or with an unobstructed organ in an unobstructed manner, practices the Dharma of intercourse, unchaste conduct — in all such cases she incurs defeat.

Thus, here the same detailed explanation of the substance of the first defeat of a monk is to be presented, substituting "nun" throughout and elaborating accordingly. I have not written it out here because I fear excessive proliferation. The first defeat in brief is complete. As for the extensive treatment, it follows the individual liberation and analysis for monks.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the bamboo grove at Kalandaka in the Amra forest at Rājagṛha. At that time the monk Norchen, the former potter, was residing in a secluded corner of a hermitage in Rājagṛha. Then, when the monk Norchen, the former potter, had entered Rājagṛha for his alms round,

the cowherds, cattle-herders, grass-cutters, wood-cutters, those who live by working the roads, and those who live by working the byways of Rājagṛha had smashed and overturned the hermitage and carried off all the grass and wood. After that, beginning with "then the monk Norchen, the former potter, arrived," everything is to be recited just as before, in full, up to "five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas." Then, from "the Blessed One, the buddha, on account of this occurrence, this basis, this matter, and this occasion, convened the assembly of both Saṅghas," everything is to be recited in full up to "known by both Saṅghas, and I shall properly establish the foundation of training in the Vinaya." The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, act with full knowledge while feigning not to know — they act as if unknowing, but it is not that they do not know — all of this is to be recited in full, just as in the first defeat. Likewise, everything up to "the ten benefits" is to be recited just as in the first defeat.

Furthermore, whatever nun, whether dwelling in a village or dwelling in a hermitage of others, takes what is not given — that which falls under the category of theft — whatever the amount she takes without it being given, if she is thereupon seized by a king or a great minister, and it is said to her: "O nun, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are an idiot! You have stolen!" — and she is either killed, bound, or expelled — if a nun takes in that way what has not been given, that nun has incurred a defeat and is not to remain in the community.

Now, "whatever nun" refers to the four types of nun: the nun in name only, the nun by her own claim, the nun for the sake of receiving, and the nun through the defeat of afflictions. "Of others" means of men, women, or those of indeterminate sex. "Dwelling in a village" means residing within an enclosure. "Dwelling in a hermitage" means residing outside an enclosure. "What is not given" means that which has not been given by any man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex. "That which falls under the category of theft" means that what is not given also falls under the category of theft. "If she takes" means if she receives. "Whatever amount she takes without it being given" means five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas. "By a king" means by any man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex who has been consecrated with the royal consecration and invested with sovereignty — such a one is indeed a king, is of royal lineage, and has received the head-consecration. "By a great minister" means by those other than that: ministers, accountants, and those belonging to the higher nobility who sustain the royal administration by virtue of shared confidences, and who live in dependence upon the king and sustain themselves thereby. "Having been seized" means having been apprehended. "And it is said to her: 'O nun, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are an idiot! You have stolen!'" — these are words of reproach. "It is said" means it is declared, it is proclaimed. "Killed" means deprived of life. "Bound" means restrained by any of three kinds of bonds — those made of iron, those made of wood, or those made of grass. "Or expelled" means made to leave the territory, however that may be. "A nun" means one in whom the substance of nunhood is present. Beginning with "that one," the word "also" here is a close indication, and —

— the concluding term indicating what has been fully set forth — as well as "the motion," "the motion," and "two," and up to "the motion and the act of four": all of this is to be elaborated at length in exactly the manner of the first defeat. Now, as to how a transgression arises in this case:

In the general summary verse:

Oneself, space,
A cut in the earth, a mount, a boat,
The arising of autumn, water,
Theft, and seeking a site,
Footless, and a caṇḍāla,
And hanging last.

In the condensed summary:

Oneself, and the not-given,
Intention, and the fully seized,
Perception, and the fourth four —
The fifth made into two.

If a nun takes another's heavy belongings without their being given, by three causes, a defeat arises. What are the three? By oneself, by one who has been commissioned, and by one who has been dispatched.

How is it by oneself? By oneself stealing, by oneself entering into theft, and by oneself moving the object from place to place. That is how it is by oneself.

How is it by one who has been commissioned? Having commissioned another who then steals, having commissioned another who then enters into theft, and having commissioned another who then moves the object from place to place. That is how it is by one who has been commissioned.

How is it by one who has been dispatched? Having dispatched another who then steals, having dispatched another who then enters into theft, and having dispatched another who then moves the object from place to place. That is how it is by one who has been dispatched.

If a nun takes another's heavy belongings without their being given, by these three causes, a defeat arises.

Furthermore, if a nun takes another's heavy belongings without their being given, by three causes, a defeat arises. What are the three? The not-given, the heavy, and the moving from place to place.

How is "the not-given" defined? Whatever has not been given by a man, a woman, or a hermaphrodite — that is the not-given.

How is "the heavy" defined? Five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas — that is what constitutes the heavy.

How is "moving from place to place" defined? Taking something from the place where it was kept and depositing it in another place — that is what moving from place to place means.

If a nun takes another's heavy belongings without their being given, by these three causes, a defeat transgression arises.

Furthermore, if a nun takes another's heavy belongings without their being given, by three causes, a defeat arises. What are the three? The formation of intent, the making of effort, and the moving from place to place.

All of this — as expanded in the condensed verse — is to be set forth in exactly the manner in which it appears in the Prātimokṣa of monks. And wherever the word "monk" appears there, in this Prātimokṣa of nuns it is to be rendered as "nun."

The second defeat is complete.

In the general summary verse:

One who has servants, the warding off of beasts,
Oneself, and poison,
The reviving of a corpse — the last.

In the condensed summary:

One who has servants, and one who keeps,
One with a beak, and śīriṣika,
Alms bowls, and the Dharma robe,
One dwelling in the womb, and a merchant.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling while making his retreat beside a pleasant river, in a grove of torch trees. There the Blessed One taught the community of monks: "Monks, cultivate the perception of the unattractive. When the perception of the unattractive is practiced, cultivated, and developed, it yields great fruit and great benefit." Having taught the unattractive, he also spoke in praise of the cultivation of the unattractive, and so the monks began to cultivate the perception of the unattractive.

While the monks were cultivating the perception of the unattractive, they became weary of this decaying body, oppressed by disgust, seized by uncertainty, and given to self-reproach. Some drew weapons, some took poison, some bound themselves with rope, and some leapt into ravines.

In this way, some monks were even killing other monks. Then one monk, weary of this decaying body, oppressed by disgust, seized by uncertainty, and given to self-reproach, went to where Migalandika the ascetic-barber was staying. Having arrived, he said to Migalandika the ascetic-barber: "Come here, good man. Separate me from my life, and whatever alms-bowl and robe I have shall be yours."

Then Migalandika the ascetic-barber deprived that monk of his life, and carrying the bloodied sword, went to the bank of a pleasant river. He sat crouching on the bank of that pleasant river, washing the blood from the sword.

Then a deity belonging to the retinue of Māra, who was abiding above the current of that pleasant river, spoke these words to Migalandika the ascetic-barber: "Excellent, excellent, good man! In this way, you, who help virtuous and accomplished ascetics cross over what has not been crossed, free what has not been freed, give relief to those not yet relieved, and lead to complete nirvāṇa those not yet completely gone beyond sorrow — great merit shall accrue to you. And that their alms-bowls and robes should come to you — this too is a fine acquisition for you."

Then Migalandika the ascetic-barber came to hold, with great enthusiasm, the deeply evil view: "It is true that great merit accrues to me when I help virtuous and accomplished ascetics cross over what has not been crossed, free what has not been freed, give relief to those not yet relieved, and lead to complete nirvāṇa those not yet completely gone beyond sorrow. And that their alms-bowls and robes should come to me — this too is a fine acquisition for mine own."

Then Migalandika the ascetic-barber tucked a sharp sword under his arm and went wandering from garden to garden, from assembly hall to assembly hall, from house to house, from walkway to walkway, and along the byways. Whenever he saw a monk, he spoke these words: "Who among the virtuous and accomplished ascetics has not yet crossed over and wishes to cross, has not yet been freed and wishes to be freed, has not yet been relieved and wishes relief, has not yet completely passed beyond sorrow and wishes to completely pass beyond sorrow?"

Then a certain monk who was dwelling in weariness, disgust, uncertainty, and self-reproach on account of this festering body came forward and said to Migalandika the ascetic-barber: "Good man, I have not yet crossed over — release me. I have not yet been freed — free me. I have not yet been relieved — give me relief. I have not yet completely passed beyond sorrow — lead me to complete nirvāṇa."

Then Migalandika the ascetic-barber deprived that monk of his life. And in the same way he deprived two, three, and up to sixty monks of their lives.

At that time the monks became few in number, diminished, scattered, and the monastic Saṅgha grew thin. Then, on the very day of the fifteenth, the Blessed One was seated on a prepared seat at the center of the monastic Saṅgha for the restoration ceremony. The Blessed One looked out over the entire assembly and spoke these words to the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which the monks have now become few in number, diminished, scattered, and the monastic Saṅgha has grown thin?"

"Venerable sir, it is because the Blessed One taught the monks of the monastic Saṅgha the contemplation of the unattractive, instructing them in it and also speaking in praise of developing the unattractive — declaring that if one cultivates the unattractive, relies upon it, makes it familiar, and practices it repeatedly, the result will be great and the benefit will be great."

From the passage beginning "he taught the unattractive" up to "one must not kill" — and if one causes oneself or another to be killed — down to the passage ending with the training laid down on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, all of this is to be elaborated at length. And from that same point, drawing on it, the full analysis of the monk's rule is likewise to be given at length, just as it appears in the Monks' Code.

Then the Blessed One, by means of that very incident, that very occasion, that very matter, and that very circumstance, convened the assembly of both communities. And from the first defeat rule for monks, precisely as it stands, all is to be elaborated at length — up to the point where it is established that my hearers will understand this matter and that I will lay down the rule of training properly.

Furthermore, if a nun, with respect to a human being or to one who has human faculties, intentionally takes life with her own hand, or gives a weapon to that person, or procures a weapon-bearer for that person, or incites that person to die, or praises death to that person, saying such things as: "You, wretched one, what is the point of your living this evil, impure, and vile life? For you, death is better than life" — and if, through such intent of mind and such deliberation of mind, in many ways she incites that person to die or praises death to that person, and the one so incited subsequently dies — then that nun too has incurred defeat and is not to remain in the community.

Now, "a nun" refers to the four kinds of nun: the nun in name only, the nun who lays claim to the title, the nun who has entered for the sake of receiving alms, and the nun who has overcome the afflictions — just as in the first defeat rule, this is to be stated as before.

"A human being" refers to one in whose mother's womb the six faculties have been obtained: the faculty of the eye, the faculty of the ear, the faculty of the nose, the faculty of the tongue, the faculty of the body, and the faculty of the mind.

"One who has human faculties" refers to one in whose mother's womb these three faculties have been obtained: the faculty of the body, the faculty of the life force, and the faculty of the mind.

"Intentionally" means after having deliberated.

"With her own hand" means by means of her own hand.

"Takes life" means if life has been taken.

"Or gives a weapon to that person" refers to a sword, a razor, or a water-knife.

"Or procures a weapon-bearer for that person" means a man, a woman, or one of indeterminate sex.

"Or incites that person to die" — the person who is caused to seek death is of three kinds: one who is sick, one whose conduct is corrupt, and one whose conduct is pure.

As for one who is sick: suppose that nun — whether a monk or a nun — desires some robe, net, bowl, belt, or any requisite for the ascetic life from a sick monk or nun, and thinks: "As long as that person is alive I shall not obtain it. Let me go to that person and incite them to die." Having gone to that person, she speaks thus: "Venerable one, you are sick, you are suffering, you are gravely ill. As long as you live, venerable one, you will experience pain, agony, torment, burning heat, and misery" — and when she has said this...

And to that person she speaks thus: "What then am I to do? Come here. Abandon yourself. Destroy yourself. Allow yourself to be deprived of life." Having said this, if the sick person does abandon herself, or destroy herself, or allow herself to be deprived of life, the one who spoke incurs a root defeat.

If the sick person thinks: "She says such things, but still, a livelihood is hard to come by, and it is difficult to manage to kill oneself — so I will not abandon myself, I will not destroy myself, I will not allow myself to be deprived of life" — and accordingly does not abandon herself, does not destroy herself, and does not allow herself to be deprived of life, then by that earlier act of incitement to death a grave offense is nonetheless incurred.

If the sick person, moved by what was said to her, comes to feel remorse and thinks: "I am foolish, dull-witted, unclear in mind, and without understanding — I spoke words of doubt and reckless haste without having examined them one by one" — and goes to that nun and says: "I did indeed tell you to deprive yourself of life, but do not give up your own life. Why? Because if you are attended with suitable medicines individually prescribed, with agreeable food, and with proper nursing care, there is every prospect that before long you will become well, free of illness, and possessed of strength, and may go wherever you wish" — and if, having been turned back in this way, the sick person does not abandon herself, does not destroy herself, and does not allow herself to be deprived of life, still by that earlier act of incitement to death a grave offense is incurred.

If the sick person thinks: "She says such things, but who could endure sensations of the kind I am experiencing — pain, agony, torment, burning heat, wretchedness — and so I shall deprive myself of life" — and accordingly does abandon herself, or does destroy herself, or does allow herself to be deprived of life, then by that earlier act of incitement to death a grave offense is incurred. Such is the case with a sick person.

As for one whose conduct is corrupt: a nun desires some requisite for the ascetic life from a monk or a nun whose conduct is corrupt, and thinks: "As long as that person is alive I shall not obtain it. Let me go to that person and incite them to die" — and up to the point of actually going to that person, it proceeds as before.

Having gone to that person, she speaks thus: "You are one of corrupt conduct, a practitioner of evil Dharma, one who acts wrongly in body, who acts wrongly in speech and mind, who oozes from within like something rotten, who has heaped up defilements like grass, who ranges about everywhere like an unbridled donkey, who claims to be an ascetic without being one, who claims to practise the holy life without actually practising it. So long as you live, for as long as you continue to exist, demerit will grow greatly — and after that you will experience, among the beings of hell, sensations of extreme suffering, extreme agony, extreme torment, and intense burning heat

and experiences that are supremely disagreeable." When that was said, the other replied to him: "Then what am I to do?" At that point the first said to him: "Come here. Abandon yourself. Destroy yourself. Let yourself be deprived of life. If you die, these many such forms of demerit will not go on increasing, and you will not go on experiencing feelings of suffering so unbearable, so harsh, so hot, and so disagreeable." Having said that, if the other, upon hearing those words, abandons himself, or kills himself, or sets about depriving himself of life, that very act of having caused death constitutes a root downfall.

If, however, the other thinks: "He has indeed said this to me, yet life is difficult to find again, and it is hard to manage killing oneself — so I will not abandon myself, I will not kill myself, I will not set about depriving myself of life," and if, thinking thus, he neither abandons himself, nor kills himself, nor sets about depriving himself of life, then that earlier act of inducing him toward death is itself a grave offence.

If, upon hearing those words spoken to him, the other feels remorse and thinks: "I am foolish, stupid, dull, and unskilled; I spoke rashly and in confusion; I spoke words I had not considered," and he then goes to that person and says: "I did indeed say to you, 'Deprive yourself of life,' yet now I say to you: do not deprive yourself of life." And why? "Because if you were to please some spiritual friend, you could be lifted out of whatever impure conduct of body you have and established in virtuous bodily action; you could be lifted out of non-virtuous action of speech and mind and firmly established in virtuous action of speech and mind. If your conduct of body, speech, and mind were thus wholesome, there would come a time when, upon the breakup of this body, you would be born in a happy destiny, in the higher realms, among the gods of the celestial world." If, after saying all this, the other still neither abandons himself, nor kills himself, nor sets about depriving himself of life, that earlier act of inducing him toward death is itself a grave offence.

If the other thinks: "He has spoken thus to me, yet so long as I live, demerit will continue to arise in me in great abundance, and for as long as demerit keeps arising in me, I will experience suffering that is especially vast and especially long-lasting among the beings of hell — therefore I must certainly deprive myself of life. I will abandon myself, I will kill myself, I will deprive myself of life." And if, thinking thus, he does abandon himself, or kills himself, or deprives himself of life, that very earlier act of inducing him toward death constitutes a grave offence. That is how it stands for one who is without moral discipline.

Now, how does it stand for one who possesses moral discipline? In the following way. A nun who desires some article for the requisites of the ascetic life — just as described before — goes to a monk or nun who is endowed with good qualities, and says: "You are endowed with moral discipline, you are of wholesome Dharma, you are possessed of many excellent qualities. If you were to go to another region, the harvest there would be good and the higher realms would be all but assured —

— liberation is but a hand's breadth away, and the higher realms are assured by a silken thread alone; when this body breaks, rebirth among the gods will follow. Once you are born in the higher realms, you will be adorned with divine garments, necklaces, and bracelets upon your body; you will be satisfied in body by the nectar of the gods; you will experience the bliss of the gods."

If, when these words are said, that person replies, "Very well, but what am I to do?" — and the other then says, "Come here. Abandon your own life. Destroy your own life. Separate yourself from your life-force" — and if, in response to those words, that person does indeed separate from the life-force and dies, then through having caused death, the speaker incurs a root downfall (pārājika).

If, however, the one who possesses moral discipline thinks: "Although that person has spoken in this way, it is difficult to obtain a living one; self-destruction is difficult to accomplish. Therefore I will not abandon my own life. I will not kill myself. I will not separate myself from my life-force" — and accordingly does not abandon life, does not kill, does not separate from the life-force — even so, by reason of that very prior act of directing toward death, a grave offence arises.

If that person, having heard these words, becomes remorseful, goes to the other, and says: "Venerable one, know this: I was childish, foolish, confused, and unskilled. Out of uncertainty and rashness I spoke something unworthy. Do not abandon your own life. Do not kill yourself. Do not separate yourself from your life-force. Why so? Because the Venerable one is endowed with moral discipline, is of wholesome Dharma, is possessed of many excellent qualities. May you live long — and by living long, much merit will arise. For if you act in that way, you will for a long time experience great happiness among the gods" — and if, having been thus dissuaded, the other does not separate from the life-force and does not die, even so, by reason of that very prior act of directing toward death, a grave offence arises.

If the person who possesses moral discipline thinks: "Although that one has said these things, I am endowed with moral discipline and great learning, I am of wholesome Dharma and possessed of many excellent qualities; if I were to go to another region, the harvest there would be good; the higher realms are assured by a silken thread alone, liberation is but a hand's breadth away, and when this body breaks I will be reborn among the gods" — and thinking thus, does abandon the life, does kill, does separate from the life-force — then by that very prior act of directing toward death, a grave offence arises.

That is how it stands for one who possesses moral discipline. Therefore it is taught: "Has caused to be directed toward death."

As for what is said — "one may speak praise of death" — this means speaking praise of death in the presence of one who openly delights in dying. What is said, "O man!" and so forth are words of address. "What is the use of this sinful, impure, wretched life? O man, death is better for you than life" — these are words of disparagement. "Saying" means: while uttering these words. The rest is to be explained in full according to the first root downfall as set forth above.

As for "may not remain" — the nuns may not carry out with that person acts done with one motion, two motions, or four motions together with an invitation; the nuns may not appoint that person to any of the twelve offices. Therefore it is taught: "May not remain."

This, then, is to be stated in the Vinaya of the bhikṣuṇīs as the third root downfall. As for the rest, it is to be stated just as in the Vinaya of the monks. The third root downfall is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pool. At that time, five hundred fishermen were settled there beside a pleasant river, making their livelihood. Among them there were two groups called the Net-Casters and the Great-Net-Casters. Sometimes the Net-Casters would cast the net, and sometimes the Great-Net-Casters would cast it. When there were no fish to buy, the Net-Casters would cast the net; when there were fish to buy, the Great-Net-Casters would cast the net.

Now at a certain time a festival arose in Vaiśālī, and they set both nets together: two hundred and fifty cast the net of the Net-Casters, and two hundred and fifty cast the net of the Great-Net-Casters. Those who cast the net of the Net-Casters heaped up great mounds of fish, turtles, tortoises, young crocodiles, and many species of fish-eggs and the like — heaped up like great mounds of sesame, rice, thick rice porridge, pine seeds, and peas. Those who cast the Great Net drew into the pleasant river from the great ocean a vast crocodile-fish of enormous size, asleep like a great hare, and they began to haul it in. As they pulled, it awoke and charged at those two hundred and fifty fishermen along with their Great Net, heading upstream. Those fishermen called out to the other two hundred and fifty: "Friends! The Great Net and we ourselves are being carried off — come and turn it back!" Hearing that, the other two hundred and fifty fishermen also came and plunged in at that very spot, and they too were swept away.

Then someone standing on high ground nearby called out, and herders, cowherds, and others came and with great effort pulled it out — a crocodile-fish, piled up like a mountain, with eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes.

As a great crowd of people came and gathered there, six teachers who were not teachers and yet claimed to be teachers, who were not omniscient and yet claimed omniscience, also arrived at that time to watch the spectacle. Who were these six? They were: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gośāla's son, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra the Victorious, Ajita Keśakambala, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātaputra — these six who claimed to be teachers while not being teachers had also come at that time to witness the spectacle.

Meanwhile, the Blessed One, the Buddha — possessing nothing whatsoever of unknowing, unseeing, ignorance, or failure to comprehend, the Blessed One by nature living and dwelling in luminous presence, endowed with great compassion, engaged in benefiting others, unwavering in virtuous conduct, steadfast in diligence that overcomes all adversaries, solitary in his courage, solitary in his guardianship, without a second, not speaking in dualities, abiding in calm abiding and insight, illumining the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of discipline, having abandoned the three paths, free from attachment in all three realms, unfrightened and undaunted by the four fearlessnesses, having crossed the four rivers, well established in the ground of conduct of the four bases of miraculous power, long perfected in the four means of gathering beings, having abandoned the five limbs, having truly transcended the five destinies, fully completing the six perfections, endowed with the six limbs, dwelling in the six things that are to be constantly maintained, richly adorned with the flowers of the seven branches of awakening, and teaching the noble eightfold path —

skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, possessed of the ten powers, their renown spread and acclaimed in every one of the ten directions, supreme and distinguished above all who exercise sovereignty over a hundred worlds — it is the very nature of reality of such ones that, three times by day and three times by night, they survey the world with the eye of a buddha, perceiving: who has declined, who has progressed, who has come to harm, who has fallen into distress, who has met with harm and distress and misery; whose root of virtue has not yet been planted must have it planted; whose root of virtue has already been planted must have it brought to full ripening; whose root of virtue has fully ripened must have it brought to liberation; whoever is without the wealth of noble ones must be established in the lordship of noble wealth; whoever abides at a human fruit, whoever is to be trained by a buddha, whoever is to be trained by śrāvakas, whoever is to be trained by both buddhas and śrāvakas, whoever proceeds under the sway of attachment, whoever proceeds under the sway of aversion, whoever proceeds under the sway of delusion, whoever proceeds under the sway of attachment, aversion, and delusion together, whoever has been harmed by their transgressions, whoever is inclined toward the lower destinies, whoever is falling toward the lower destinies, whoever has fallen into the lower destinies — these I shall raise up from the lower destinies and firmly establish in higher states and in the fruit; whoever is sunk in the mire of harmful conduct, I shall draw out by the hand; and I shall make the world, adorned as it is with the arising of buddhas, bear abundant fruit — with such knowing and seeing, the Blessed One enters into contemplation.

Then it was further declared in verse:

The ocean's dwelling-place, the realm of sea-monsters,
may pass beyond its season and cease to be —
yet a buddha, with love for those to be trained,
does not pass beyond the season, nor ever fails.

Just as a mother, with her only beloved child,
thinks of that child and guards its very life,
so too the Tathāgata thinks of those to be trained
and guards their very lives with tender care.

With compassion riding through the stream of omniscient mind,
the mother-cow seeking her beloved calf is never weary —
to those fallen, diminished in saṃsāra and the lower destinies,
loving-kindness is like a mother-cow ever seeking her lost and cherished calf.

Thereupon the Blessed One's vision — that eye free from all obscuration, seeing through primordial wisdom, the buddha-eye — surveyed everything and contemplated: the beings of the fish and sea-monster class, those inclined toward the lower destinies, those falling toward the lower destinies, those who have already fallen into the lower destinies — though they did cultivate virtue in relation to former buddhas, they are now bereft of the arising of a buddha, and for many thousands of years have been experiencing suffering in the hells. Therefore, making use of this fish and sea-monster class, I shall draw forth a great assembly of those to be trained. He made evident and directly present the truth that sentient beings are the masters of their own karma. Thinking, therefore, "I shall go to the bank of a fair and lovely river," the Blessed One so resolved and proceeded.

The blessed buddhas, by the very nature of reality, are compassionate toward those beings who are to be trained. Therefore, from time to time they travel through the hells, roam through the animal realm, roam through the realm of hungry ghosts, roam through the realm of the gods, and journey through the various regions. From time to time they travel to mountains, to charnel grounds, to rivers, and to temples. It is with this purpose in mind that the blessed Buddha is said to travel to the river — from the point of "making a smile" up to the passage in which the Blessed One addresses the venerable Ānanda, declaring: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata intends to travel to the river; any of you who wishes to go to the river together with the Tathāgata, take up your robes'" — from here the opening subject-matter of the saffron-robed monks is to be extensively expounded. From the passage beginning "five hundred fishermen," the noble Śāriputra spoke in verse:

The Tathāgatas do not regard clan,
Lineage, or family with partiality;
They look with full discernment at the deeds
That have been done throughout the long, long past.

Up to and including that verse, and then up to the passage in which the offering is presented to the Blessed One and the Blessed One calls the monks forward with the words "Monks, come here," up through their full ordination by that call — and then what was further said:

When the Tathāgata uttered the call "Come here,"
They bore bodies still clothed in matted hair and bark garments;
Yet in an instant their sense faculties became perfectly calm,
And by the Buddha's intention their forms were covered over.

Up to and including that verse.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the Fourth Fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling together with the community of monks in Vaiśālī, in the city of Prabhāvatī. At that time there was a severe famine, the region was desolate, and alms-food was difficult for mendicants to obtain — from that passage up to and including the words "to say nothing of mendicants."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the monks: "Monks, at present there is a famine" — from that passage up to "alms-food is difficult for mendicants to obtain" — and then: "Monks, come here. According to what kind of invitation you receive, what kind of welcome is offered, and what kind of companionship is available, agree to spend the rains retreat right here in the vicinity of Vaiśālī. I too shall spend the rains retreat here in this very vicinity near Prabhāvatī together with my attendant monk, the venerable Ānanda. It would be improper if everything were made troublesome by begging for alms throughout the entire retreat" — from that passage up to: "Monks, go to wherever relatives are present by the banks of the pleasant river, and accept to spend the rains retreat by relying on the banks of the pleasant river."

From that passage up to the words "they proclaimed their qualities before the relatives."

The two assemblies — the gathering and the great gathering: the first is up to and including the words "the time of the rains retreat approach, on the middle day of the rains month."

Up to and including the passage about monks who had accepted to spend the rains retreat in the vicinity of the city of Vaiśālī and in the city of Prajñapti, having completed the rains retreat and returned — and up to "the venerable Ānanda welcomed them with words."

Those who came from the banks of the pleasant river were welcomed with words — from that passage up to "abounding in fat, hide, flesh, and blood" — and then from the venerable Ānanda's inquiry up to the words "by what was not proper."

He spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there are three kinds of thieves existing in the world — thieves, and great thieves. What are the three? Monks, first there is a thief who leads a band of a hundred or a band of a thousand, who marches at the head of a hundred or a thousand, who breaks into homes, who opens locked fastenings, who seizes property outright, who lies in wait on the road, who holds people without releasing them, who destroys roads, who steals from the royal treasury, who plunders villages, who destroys towns, who devastates entire regions — this, monks, is the first thief existing in the world, a thief and a great thief.

"There is yet another thief and great thief who does not lead a band of a hundred, nor a band of a thousand, who does not march at the head of a hundred or a thousand, who does not break into homes, who does not open locked fastenings" — and so on, as before — "yet who sells and sells again the Saṅgha's grass, wood, flowers, fruit, milk, or any other measured goods to sustain himself, and by doing so does not support the household: this is the second thief and great thief existing in the world.

"There is yet another thief and great thief who does not even have a retinue of five hundred —"

"— who does not even have a retinue of a thousand, who does not march at the head of a hundred or a thousand" — and so forth, as before — "who does not sell and sell again the Saṅgha's grass, wood, flowers, fruit, milk, or any other measured goods to sustain himself, and who does not support the household: yet who, though entirely without the supreme human quality, claims to possess it — this is the third thief and great thief existing in the world.

"Monks, a thief who has a retinue of a hundred, or a retinue of a thousand, who marches at the head of a hundred or a thousand and breaks into homes, as described before — such a one is the lesser kind. Among thieves, one who takes the Saṅgha's grass or wood" — and so forth as before — "is also the lesser kind. But one who claims a supreme human quality he does not possess — that one is the thief and great thief in the world together with its gods, its māras, its Brahmās, its ascetics (śrāmaṇas) and brahmins, and its beings both divine and human.

Here one who has not become an arhat
yet claims to himself the status of an arhat —
that one is a thief in the world with all its gods;
he is to be declared one of broken moral discipline.

Of corrupted wisdom, when the body has crumbled,
he will be born among the hell-beings.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this very occurrence, this very occasion, this very matter, and this very circumstance, convened the assembly of both communities, and — just as in the first case of defeat, from informing the female hearers so that all will know, up through 'I shall establish the training well' — the proclamation of the rule in full is to be given, in the same manner as the first defeat.

Furthermore, as for the phrase 'whatever nun' — it is as before, from 'among the four classes of nuns,' up through the point where, since the deed of a motion with four proclamations that is unshakable is not appropriate in this context, one should understand 'whatever full ordination constitutes the status of a fully ordained nun.'

As for 'not directly knowing' — what does she not directly know? The five aggregates: form and so forth.

As for 'not fully knowing' — what does she not fully know? Those same five aggregates: form and so forth.

As for 'the human quality' — these are the five hindrances.

As for 'the supreme' — it is the abandonment of those.

As for 'the ultimate' — it is nirvāṇa.

As for 'the noble' — these are the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Buddha's hearers.

As for 'the distinction attained' — these are the four fruits of the contemplative life; attaining them is what is called 'attaining the distinction.'

As for 'knowing' — it is knowing suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path.

As for 'seeing' — it is the knowledge that sees suffering, the origin, cessation, and the path.

As for 'abiding in contact' — these are the four meditative concentrations (dhyānas); in the noble discipline (Vinaya), 'abiding in contact' refers exclusively to contact with what is seen, the Dharma.

As for 'without' — it refers to that basis being absent.

As for 'while being without' — it refers to that very person.

As for 'I know this' — what does she know? She knows suffering.

She knows the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path. As for 'seeing' — what does she see? She sees gods, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, zombies, and corpse-reanimators.

As for 'having claimed' — it means having stated it. As for 'that transgression has occurred' — it refers to that very basis. As for 'wishing to become pure' — it means wishing to rise up. As for 'at some other time' — it means at a different occasion. As for 'whether asked' — it means asked by another. As for 'whether not asked' — it means that she herself feels remorse, regret, and dismay arising in her mind.

As for 'thus did the venerable one say, "What I did not know, I now know"' — this is through mental consciousness. As for 'and said, "I saw what I had not seen"' — this is through visual consciousness.

As for 'fabricated,' 'covered up,' and 'spoke falsely' — these are synonymous expressions for having spoken. As for 'if it is said' — it means if it is uttered. As for 'except for overweening pride' — it means with overweening pride set aside. As for 'nun' — it means one who possesses the essential qualities of a nun, as before. As for 'also' — this is a particle of proximate and comprehensive indication. The transgression is to be stated in the same manner as it was stated for the first case of defeat.

Now, how does one incur the transgression in this case? The summary verse:

Shifting perception, the wilderness, spreading one's mat in houses,
claiming one's own defining marks, and presenting oneself.

Furthermore, any nun who, having shifted her perception, tolerance, desire, understanding, thought, and view, says "I see gods" — she incurs defeat. Likewise with nāgas, yakṣas, and all the rest down to corpse-reanimators — saying "I see them" — she incurs defeat. In this way, the summary verse from the Vinaya of the monks, wherever the word 'monk' appears, is to be read and stated with 'monk' replaced by 'nun.'

The fourth case of defeat is complete.

The summary verse for the background story that follows:

Little desire, and both together,
fair complexion, brahmacarya, direct knowledge,
born wealthy, of high lineage,
and little desire — Kāśyapa.

The monks, having grown doubtful, asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to cut through all their doubts. They said: "Venerable Great Kāśyapa and the lovely Śersky — please look upon them both with their little desire." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now" — up to "in the time gone by as well." "These two, having performed and accumulated deeds" — from here it is to be expanded in full.

"Monks, in a time long past, in a certain royal palace, there was a farmer who rose early in the morning. He took his pickaxe and plough and set off to clear a field. He instructed his wife to bring food when the sun had risen. His wife took the food and was coming, when just at that moment a rhinoceros-like solitary buddha arrived. She bowed at his feet and rose, and he spoke" — up to here. Then, from "the solitary buddha sat in the sky" — she offered him alms food and made aspirational prayers. "Whatever transgression I committed, being under the power of all the afflictions" — from here to "may we both become those of little desire."

"Monks, the one who was the farmer at that time and place — he is this very Kāśyapa."

"Monks, the one who was the farmer's wife at that time and place — she is this very Śerkyabzangmo. Because these two, at that time, offered alms food to the solitary buddha and made aspirational prayers, both of them came to have little desire" — up to here.

"Therefore, monks, you should strive to abandon attachment. By doing so, you will come to develop an abundance of virtuous qualities. Monks, you should train in this way" — up to here.

Then, from "Furthermore, monks" as far as "What deed did the venerable Mahākāśyapa and the girl Bzangmo, daughter of Śerkya, perform, on account of which both of them went forth?" — up to there.

The Blessed One declared: "It was through the power of aspirational prayer. Where was this? Monks, long ago, in a time past, in a suburb outside a great city, there was a potter's workshop. At a time when no buddha was present in the world, a solitary buddha appeared — one who was compassionate toward the poor and destitute, and who was devoted to benefiting sentient beings. That solitary buddha went to the place where the potter's workshop was, and, having arrived, said to the potter: 'Good sir, if it is no inconvenience to you, let me stay in one corner of the workshop.' When he said this, the potter replied to the solitary buddha: 'Noble one, please dwell as comfortably as you like.' Then that solitary buddha spread a grass mat in one corner of the workshop and sat in cross-legged posture, his body coiled like a sleeping serpent-king.

Then a second solitary buddha also came" — up to "he obtained lodging from that potter and stayed in the second corner of the same workshop." "A third came and stayed in the third corner" — up to there. "Likewise a fourth came and stayed in the fourth corner" — up to there.

Then, as the sun set and the night deepened, those four solitary buddhas entered into meditative absorption on the fire element, and the potter, peering through a crack in the door, saw the entire workshop blazing, burning intensely, burning on all sides, the flames merging into one. He thought: "How remarkable that such worthy recipients have come and taken up residence in my workshop! This is a sign of my great power and of the merit I possess."

And again he spoke these words:

"O what wonder — worthy recipients have come!
Long indeed have I yearned to see this sight.
In this world and the world beyond,
I shall abide in happiness itself."

Those solitary buddhas too, wishing to cultivate roots of virtue for their patron, spent the night in meditative concentration (dhyāna), liberation, meditative absorption (samādhi), and meditative attainment, and then began to delight one another.

Then those solitary buddhas said to one of their number: "Who are you? Where are you from? Why, and in what manner, did you go forth?" When they asked him this, he replied to them: "Venerable ones, have you heard that in the land of Kaliṅga there arose a king called Karṇajalendhara?" They replied: "We have heard of him. Moreover, we have also heard that that king Karṇajalendhara is wealthy and of great dominion, and possesses many elephants." He said: "What you have all heard is true. Yet I, having seen the faults of royal sovereignty, went forth." They replied: "What fault did you see in royal sovereignty that led you to go forth?" He said:"

"If there is a fault, it is not a small one. What is it like? Listen, venerable ones. Once, while I was sitting on the roof of a fine upper palace chamber, a bird seized a piece of meat and flew up into the sky, whereupon many other birds attacked it for that very reason. The one that dropped the meat was freed, and the one that seized it was surrounded from all sides. In this way they snatched it back and forth from one another. As I watched this, clear and proper reflection arose in me: the one that takes hold is bound, while the one that lets go is free. Since I, enjoying the full prosperity of royal sovereignty, would inevitably come to fighting, quarreling, and warfare with the kings under the sun on account of it, I thought: enough of the pleasures of royal sovereignty. And so, finding that cause and that condition, I was decisively moved, and taking up residence in the forest of ascetic practice, I there actualized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."

He then spoke in verse:

When a bird carried off a piece of meat,
I watched as all the other birds gave chase and circled round.
Recognizing thus the nature of desire,
I chose to wander solitary, like a rhinoceros.

When they heard those words, they asked the second one how he had gone forth. The venerable ones asked him whether he had heard of a king named Gdong-ma-legs in the land of the Mithilas — up to the point where it says "while sitting on the roof of a fine upper palace chamber." The version continues: when he saw two bull elephants goring and wounding each other out of desire, clear and proper reflection arose in him, thinking: even these two beings born in the animal realm wound and injure each other on account of desire — up to the words "fighting, quarreling, disparaging, and warring with the kings under the sun," and then "he went forth and actualized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha." He then spoke in verse:

Seeing the stirring, the cunning, the ground and cause of desire,
watching them wound one another and drive each other away,
recognizing thus the nature of desire,
I chose to wander solitary, like a rhinoceros.

When they heard those words as well, they asked the third one: "Where are you from, and how did you go forth?" He replied: "I am from this very royal palace in the city of Vārāṇasī, under a king named Brahmadatta" — up to the point where it says "he came to possess many hundreds of elephant mounts."

They said to him: "What fault did you see in royal sovereignty? What flaw did you perceive in desire?"

He replied: "Listen. Once, when the winter season was past, its cold spell gone, and the spring season had arrived — when the blossoms on the trees bloomed beautifully, when the drone of bees in flight swayed the lovely crowns of flowers, when the fragrance of sandalwood drifted agreeably, when the call of the cuckoo rang out, when in the groves the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, and cuckoos filled the air — I went with the ladies of the harem to the pleasure garden. There I saw that the mango tree was in exceedingly full flower, and the ladies of the harem, seized by attachment to those blossoms, in an instant snapped off the branches and left them lying. At that I thought to myself: these outer things are beautiful when they are flourishing, and ugly when they are damaged.

I thought to myself that there could be no doubt about it — this is what it means to enjoy a kingdom in its full abundance — and so I went forth and directly realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. And then I spoke this verse:

When I saw the mango tree in glorious flower at its crown,
and saw those attached to its lovely form,
I understood in that way the qualities of desire,
and came to wander alone, like a rhinoceros.

The fourth person was then asked: "Who are you, and how did you go forth?" He replied, from the point where it was said that he came to be known as the naked king, Rulbuchul, when he slept in the lap of a woman — up to the point where he went up to the upper chamber of a fine mansion and lived there, enjoying pleasures. There, a queen of the Sāla clan, adorned with golden bracelets, was weaving. As she wove, a sound arose — and from that, up to the point described, I thought to myself: these outer things are without mind, and yet when they are struck repeatedly a sound comes forth — so what need is there to speak of my enjoying the full abundance of a kingdom? A kingdom alone will do. And so thinking that by abandoning the kingdom I had found a condition that let me see even small faults and flaws with clarity, I resolved with certainty, went forth, and directly realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. And then I spoke this verse:

The two golden bracelets on the wrists, gleaming bright,
well-hammered by the goldsmith's art —
hearing the striking, between me and another
living together under this one roof,
harsh and various words would break out, the mind thrown into turmoil.
I understood in that way the qualities of desire,
and came to wander alone, like a rhinoceros.

So it was that they sat, each speaking to the other in this way. Then the potter and his wife thought to themselves: these great and noble ones have abandoned even a vast kingdom of wide lineage and gone forth — why then do we, in this manner of beggar-like striving, pursue what is to be had from a household life with home and children and cook-pots and household implements, clinging to it with the perception of enjoyment? Why should we not go forth as well? And then they spoke this verse:

Abandoning the ground of village and surrounding lands and wealthy lineage,
if one walks through the human world with a mind free of attachment,
why should we go on manifestly pursuing what we have gained
through the manner of the destitute, carried away like something swept off by water?

And so it was that at dawn, when the night had ended and day broke, the potter's husband, with a devoted and reverent mind, invited those pratyekabuddhas and offered them alms — up to what is described — and they rose up into the sky above. Then the potter's husband uttered this aspiration: "Wonderful! By this wholesome root of giving what is to be given and of generating the awakening mind, may we never again be born in a poor man's house! May we too be so fortunate as to possess the Dharma of this kind! May we please this supremely excellent Teacher in this way, and never displease him!" Having said this, the two of them rejoiced greatly in the going forth.

Then for a time the potter, carrying a water jar, went to fetch water — up to what is described — and his wife, having been touched by this, turned back. From that point up to where the wife went forth is told; and she thought: "If I am not to be deceived, what shall I do now? These two children must be raised and nurtured." And so she raised and nurtured the two of them until they grew up. At that time the potter, with what was ripe and what was not yet ripe, and what was salt-brined,

tested the salted ones that were not yet brined. He also spoke these words in verse:

Just as one knows the ripe and the unripe,
and the salted and the unsalted alike,
since these two children have been born knowing this,
now is the time for me to go forth.

He then instructed the two children in this manner: "Dig the clay thus; sell the wares thus" — and so on up to what is described — and then he went forth. And from the passage beginning "seeing the potter going on alms round," the verse is spoken:

Just as one knows the ripe and the unripe,
and the salted and the unsalted alike,
since these two children have been born knowing this,
my dear wife has gone, and I shall go too.

The Blessed One declared: "Now, the potter of that time and that occasion is none other than Mahākāśyapa. The potter's wife is none other than the daughter of the householder, Bhadra of the merchant family. At that time too, they went forth with but slight disenchantment. Even now it is the same. What then should be done? By teaching the causes that lead to renunciation, one comes to possess such an accumulation of qualities. Monks should train just as Mahākāśyapa and Bhadra, the daughter of the householder, trained."

The summary verse reads:

Kāliṅga and the one with pendulous ears,
Mithilā and the one of comely face,
Kāśī and Brahmadatta,
sleeping on the breast and the naked ascetic.

Then, monks having arisen in doubt, in order to cut through all doubt, they addressed the Blessed One, the buddha, saying: "Blessed One, what karma did Bhadra of the householder's family perform and accumulate, such that by its ripening she came to be possessed of a beautiful and lovely form, pleasing to behold?" — up to what is described.

"Monks, long ago in a past time, in a certain royal palace there ruled a king" — and so on up to — "a wealthy merchant caravan leader, with great riches and vast possessions." Now, when he looked at the assembled multitude of people, he saw many hundreds and thousands of sentient beings with rough hands and feet, their bodies covered in sores, their heads disheveled, smeared with dust, their features sunken, wretched from heat and cold, afflicted with suffering. Others he saw clad in fine garments upon their bodies, adorned with distinctive ornaments, riding horses, elephants, men bearing litters, and chariots, endowed with the finest prosperity. Then he thought to himself: "These suffering beings have come to this condition through the karma of not having given in generosity. Even now, since they are unable to give generously, after dying and passing from here they will be reborn in whatever lowly destiny it may be — such is their situation. But those who are prosperous have come to be so through distinguished acts of generosity. I too will certainly, in another birth, give generosity, and thereby I shall obtain prosperity of this kind. And let me give, so that in other lifetimes I shall not fall into suffering." Having thought this, he went home and spoke to his wife as follows: "Bhadra, I am going to accumulate wealth for the world beyond and carry it away." She replied: "Very well, then let the mounts — the horses, the mares, and the donkeys — be prepared." He replied: "What use are these mounts? Ordinary wealth cannot be carried to the world beyond. Nevertheless, give generously, without ceasing, to the poor, the destitute, the blind, and to merchants who come to the house." She replied: "So shall I do."

At a time when no Blessed One, no buddha, had appeared in the world, a pratyekabuddha (solitary buddha) was to appear instead. This pratyekabuddha — gaunt and frail, wearing a tattered robe — had entered the royal palace precincts on his alms round, and there he stood at the gate of the merchant's house. Some male and female servants were coming out of that house to fetch water, and when they saw this gaunt and frail figure in his tattered robe, they thought: "The master has instructed us to give whatever is desired to anyone who is in suffering. We should show this noble mendicant the same kindness." And so they said to the venerable one: "Please enter this house; you will receive alms here."

He went in. But the merchant's wife, seeing him, thought: "He is just a gaunt and frail fellow in a tattered robe," and she gave him no alms. He departed. The servant women, having filled their water jars, returned to the house, and when they saw his alms bowl still empty, they asked him: "Did you not come to this house?" He replied: "I came, but I received no alms." They turned him around and brought him back, and they said to the mistress of the house: "Why was he not given alms?" She replied: "Because I had no faith in him." They said: "Did the master tell you to give only to those with good complexions, and only when you had faith?" She replied: "Since I have had no faith in him, what is the use of saying more?"

One of the servant women then thought: "If I take this monk back a second time and he is again turned away, a decision must be made right now as to how to send him off properly." So she said to the mistress: "Please give me a small measure of the finest milled grain from my own provisions." The mistress gave it, and the servant woman took a small measure of the day's ground flour and offered it to him. Then she thought further: "This noble one is being looked down upon because he wears a tattered robe; I shall offer him my own piece of cloth." And so she also offered him a length of white cloth.

The pratyekabuddha, for his part, thought: "This young woman will accomplish great merit." In order to arouse her faith, he soared up into the middle of the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings. The moment she saw this, her mind was filled with faith, and with a feeling of joy, delight, and elation, she knelt on the ground, bowed at his feet, and reflected: "However slight the disrespect shown to this noble one, it came from a poor complexion." And she made this aspiration: "Ah! By this root of virtue — the giving away of what is to be given as a gift — may I, in whatever birth I take and in whatever place I am born, be beautiful of form and fair of complexion, utterly lovely to behold. May I never be gaunt, and may I never have an ugly complexion."

Now at that very time a certain king was seated there, surrounded by a retinue of ministers and encircled by many hundreds and thousands of people, and the shadow of that pratyekabuddha fell upon him. He looked up and saw the pratyekabuddha — robed in his Dharma robe, holding a length of white cloth, his head shaved and his bowl black, moving through the sky in a manner at once singular and beautiful. The king thought: "A great person of this kind, who goes from place to place collecting alms individually through the land — such a one must be of great power and of benefit to others." And so he declared: "Whoever brings alms to him today shall today be given the finest gift in the city."

Now the merchant too was gathered in that very assembly, and he thought to himself —

"I gave orders at home that alms should be given to all who come seeking them — so without fail, alms will certainly be offered from my house. I shall go and check on that." With this thought he rose and walked quickly home.

His wife, too, had seen the pratyekabuddha's miraculous powers, and her mind had been filled with faith. She said to the maidservant: "The merit shall be mine. I will give you the finest food as your reward." But the maidservant replied: "You are the mistress, and you have power over my life — but not over my merit. I will not give it up." The wife flew into a rage, and in her fury, wrapped all around as she was, she struck the maidservant on the head with her wrist, bracelet and all. The bracelet struck true, and blood poured from the maidservant's head.

Then the merchant arrived home and asked what wrong had been done. The maidservant told him the whole story in full, and the merchant, in his anger, adorned the maidservant with all her ornaments, installed her as mistress of the household, and then went and reported the matter to the king.

The king said: "She is worthy to be mistress. You have done well. Had you not acted so, I myself would have stripped the other of her rank as maidservant. And yet I will bestow upon her the finest gift in the city."

Then the maidservant, having attained faith and found the conditions for it, gave generously to ascetics (śramaṇas), brahmins, and merchants. She accumulated merit, guarded her ethical conduct, and when the time of death came, she was reborn among the gods of the Thirty-Three. She appeared there endowed with an exquisite form, radiating light, splendor, and a vast luminous brilliance — and the entire assembly of gods was filled with wonder. The four divine lords and Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) were all struck with astonishment, and they began to say to one another: "She is mine! She is mine!"

Then Śakra spoke: "We are all tormented in mind by the fault of attachment (rāga), and so the one who composes the finest verse shall have her." And one of them recited:

Seized with yearning, deeply yearning,
I see no direction anywhere.
My mind has come to rest on her —
and so, my friends, this is what I desire.

The second said:

Alas, O lord of gods — how fortunate
is one who may recite a verse for this!
Like a drum struck at the face of battle,
just so has desire arisen in me.

The third said:

Though a great drum is beaten,
it grows weary here and there.
But like a great rushing river, unceasing —
just so has desire arisen in me.

The fourth said:

Though swept along by what is irresistible,
and caught, here and there, upon obstruction,
my eyes, like millstones ever-turning,
never cease to fix upon her.

Then Śakra said:

Since each of you has spoken a verse so well,
you are all happy — every one.
But as for me, I do not know
whether I shall live or die.

The others thought: "This being desires this divine maiden; it would not be right for her to pass away from this realm." And so they gave her to Śakra.

The Blessed One then declared: "She who was the maidservant at that time and in that age is none other than this very Bhadraṃkarā (Goodly One), daughter of the Śākyas — she who offered alms to the pratyekabuddha and presented him with a length of cloth; and it was by that cause that she came to possess a fair and beautiful form."

Then the monks addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable One, pray look upon this: a divine maiden caused the four divine lords and Śakra to fall into astonishment."

The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, it is no great wonder that she caused the four divine lords and Śakra to fall into astonishment. But monks, in a former time, listen well while I tell of how this same one caused four village libertines and a fifth, the most dissolute of all, to fall into astonishment." And he related at length how this divine maiden had been born in Jambudvīpa into a family of high lineage, great wealth, and abundant possessions, and had become one who pursued sensual pleasures. She was taken as wife by a merchant. When the four village libertines and the supremely dissolute fifth all caught sight of her, they were struck through with intense attachment and desire, and each separately sent go-betweens to her, and she received these advances. Yet since she was dependent on her husband, she would say to each, "Go away for now," and thus she kept their hearts in suspense.

Then one among them thought to himself: "Many days have now passed, and therefore I shall — " and so the story goes. He set an appointed time with her, saying, "I will come to you today." They asked him, "Where shall you come? Where shall we go?" He told them of a great nyagrodha tree not far from the city, rising high as the sky, with branches hanging down in abundance and leaves thick and dense, and said, "Go today and climb up into that tree," specifying each one's place. And while he sought an opportunity with the husband, he let slip to her that this was what he had in mind, whereupon she had him beaten and bound to a pillar.

Then she said to one of the others, "Go and climb that tree; sit up in the branch on the eastern side, and I will come to you shortly." He was delighted and did just as she said. And so the story continues: the second sat up in the branch on the southern side; the third sat up in the branch on the western side; and the fourth sat up in the branch on the northern side. The supremely dissolute one did likewise and sat up in the central branch of the tree.

They all remained there through the night, eagerly thinking she would arrive, but the woman never came, even until dawn. The night passed and morning came. When it grew light, the one sitting in the eastern branch sang out in verse:

The sun has risen in the east,
and farmers have already gone out from town;
may the nyagrodha tree bear witness
that the deceitful woman has not come.

The one in the southern branch replied:
The woman will come, will surely come;
she is not deceitful.
Yet may this very auspicious sun
rise just a little more quickly!
