The one in the eastern branch said, "Has even the rafter come?" The other replied, "Not yet."

Then the one in the western branch sang:
Because the sun has risen at the proper hour
and the farmers too have gone out from town,
not knowing the time myself,
I spent the whole night with eyes fixed, waiting.

Then the one in the northern branch spoke:
Not knowing the time here,
I have endured the night sitting through dawn.
Whoever becomes attached to another man's wife
will attain this fate — and worse besides.

Then the supremely dissolute one spoke:
You all are miserable because you sat waiting;
I at least will not grieve.
But I do grieve for the nyagrodha tree,
broken down blamelessly.

Just then the tree deity, seeing that these men had been deceived, laughed as before and said:

Mourn for yourselves, and likewise
for these four men;
those who are cut down
will spring up again in the last month of spring.

They, having abandoned all hope for the woman, climbed down and went each to his own home.

As for the woman, her husband set her free, and she, unseen, went to the place where the tree stood. When those men saw her, they said: "Why did you deceive us?" She then told them all that had come to pass.

Then they said to her: "You have come before our very eyes." She thought to herself: "I was born among five people — how could I possibly carry on in the manner of a dog?" And so she said to them: "Whichever one of you brings all the most beautiful flowers shall enjoy pleasure together with me."

Now within the enclosure of the royal palace there was a guard who watched over the king's lotuses. This guard, who cut off the ears and noses of intruders, kept watch there. The men went to that place thinking: "Though we may come back punished, still, if we speak that woman's praises and please her, she will give us flowers." Then one among them spoke to her in verse:

Just as bamboo and marsh reeds,
cut down and dug out, grow back again,
so may your nose grow back —
please bestow the flowers you seek.

The second said:
Just as kuśa grass and kāśa grass,
cut down and dug out, grow back again,
so may your nose grow back —
please bestow the lotuses you seek.

The third said:
Just as dūrvā grass and thorny plants,
cut down and dug out, grow back again,
so may your nose grow back —
please bestow the flowers you seek.

The fourth said:
Just as hair and beard,
shaved off, grow back again,
so may your nose grow back —
please bestow the flowers you seek.

The fifth said:
Every man who seeks lotuses from you
you call a fool.
Whether you give the lotuses or not,
your nose will never grow back.

The man thought: "The four men spoke to me with flattery, but the fifth man spoke truly and from the heart. I shall give the lotuses to him." He gave that man as many lotuses as he needed. That man, with a joyful, pleased, and delighted heart, took the lotuses and went to where the woman was, and enjoyed pleasure with her.

Afterward, the two of them reflected: "See how we have been utterly afflicted because of our desires. How shall we act so that the suffering of attachment may not arise?" At that time, no buddha, the Blessed One, had appeared in the world, but a pratyekabuddha had arisen in the world, and not very far from there stood a caitya of a pratyekabuddha. They offered those lotuses to it and made this aspiration: "Through this root of virtue born of fully relinquishing the nature of giving, in whatever births and in whatever lives we take birth henceforth, may our afflictions be diminished."

Now the man who received the lotuses at that time is this very Mahākāśyapa. The woman who was there at that time is this very Bhadrikā, the daughter of the Śākya clan. And through the karmic maturation of having offered those lotuses, she has become one of little attachment.

Then the monks again put a question to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what action did Bhadrikā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, perform and accumulate, so that a golden statue made from the gold of the Jambu River came to be outshone by her own radiance?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, I shall elaborate on the actions she performed and accumulated."

"Monks, in a past age ninety-one aeons ago, when the lifespan of beings was eighty thousand years, there appeared a perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Vipaśyin — a Blessed One, a Buddha. At the time when he had manifested perfect and complete awakening in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he came to the royal palace of King Bandhumān" — up to the passage that reads — "and entered the royal palace to partake fully of his meal."

When he arrived there, a girl happened to be sitting to one side, holding a fan with a handle made of gold from the Jambū River, fanning herself. The light of the Buddha caused the gold of the Jambū River to become dull and dim. The girl wondered, thinking: "Am I holding a fan with a handle made of iron?" — and doubt arose in her mind.

Then Vipaśyin finished his meal and departed, and she saw that the fan handle was indeed made of the finest gold from the Jambū River.

After three months had passed — up to the passage that reads — "he went on tour through the provinces."

Then King Bandhumān had an image made from the gold of the Jambū River. On a certain occasion that girl brought the golden image and, seeing that Vipaśyin's light had made it dim and dull, and that its color was no longer the same, she made an aspiration: "By the root of virtue arising from my complete and perfect act of giving" — up to the passage that reads — "may I come to have a body radiant in just such a way" — up to the passage that reads — "may I outshine others by my own radiance."

By the power of this aspiration as well, she pleased me and did not displease me.

"Monks, therefore one should act with devotion toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and one should make perfectly correct aspirations" — up to the passage that reads — "just as Bhadrikā, the daughter of the Śākya clan."

The Vinaya Analysis of Nuns, Fifth Section.

From the passage "Moreover" up to "monks, in a past time," and then up to "a certain king was reigning over a kingdom" — and from "a certain merchant" up to "outside the city was his pleasure grove, with a pond and many flowers, enclosed and shaded by trees, and adorned with excellent flowering and fruit-bearing trees of every kind."

"When a Blessed One Buddha does not appear in the world, a pratyekabuddha will arise in the world." — up to the passage that reads — "a certain pratyekabuddha fell ill" — up to — "and went to a physician." The physician said: "Enter the town" — up to — "and stay in the merchant's pleasure grove."

On a certain occasion the merchant saw him and provided him with all necessities — up to — "and he recovered from his illness."

"He passed into complete nirvāṇa" — up to — "and a reliquary stūpa was built over his remains."

On a certain occasion the merchant saw that the stūpa had become bare and whitish — up to the passage that reads — "and spoke to his wife."

She smeared it with saffron paste, scattered flowers upon it, and made this aspiration: "Alas! How wonderful! By the root of virtue from having served the noble one throughout his life, and from having built a stūpa after his passing into nirvāṇa and from making the perfect act of giving — may I be born into a household of wealth, great riches, and great prosperity. May I thoroughly realize such a Dharma as that which I have found. And may I please a Teacher even more supremely excellent than this, and may I never displease him."

Monks, the merchant who lived at that time was none other than the great Kāśyapa of this present day. The wife of the merchant at that time was none other than this very Bhadravadanā, the daughter of the householder Śreṇika — up to the passage beginning "smeared with turmeric paste, she became golden in complexion," and continuing through to "and thus, monks, should you train."

And again, monks — from the passage beginning "Monks, what had Bhadravadanā done that, while she and the great Kāśyapa shared the same bed for twelve years, no act of sexual union took place?" through to the end of that section. Then from "monks, those two had performed karma" through to "a king named Brahmadatta ruled in the city of Vārāṇasī." Then the passage: "At a certain time in that royal palace there dwelt a courtesan named Bhadravadanā, skilled in sixty-four arts, whose fee was not less than five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." Then from "at another time, five hundred companions of that royal palace took abundant food and drink" through to "and were led away by the prince." Then the passage: "At a certain time the companions made an offering of alms to a pratyekabuddha and made an aspiration," through to "she who was the courtesan at that time was this very Bhadravadanā, and the one who was Bhadravadanā the daughter of the householder Śreṇika at that time became her," and then "the five hundred companions were these very five hundred naked ones." Then through to "actions that are entirely white in character ripen into results entirely white, and actions that are entirely dark in character ripen into results entirely dark — this is how it should be understood."

Then, monks, doubts arose among the monks, and those monks presented all their doubts to the Buddha, the Blessed One — from that passage through to "even after attaining arhatship, he was tormented by King Ajātaśatru."

Monks, long ago, in the distant past, in this very Fortunate Aeon, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared a perfectly and fully enlightened buddha named Kāśyapa. He resided at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Forest of the Ṛṣipatana. At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was a wealthy merchant of great riches and great prosperity — up to the passage "and he was left without a son," and then "after his death, it will revert to the royal palace," so he thought. And the man spoke to him: "Your highness, the prince, please do not remain displeased in this way" — through to "if you take a second wife, you will not come to experience happiness." Then: "Toward the secondary wife he should hold the perception of a daughter" — through to "the first wife is dominant, and therefore one does not even make inquiries of the first wife." Then: "Why do I sit here like this?" — and she spoke to her husband: "Know that I am going for refuge and am going to take the bases of training." And he gave his consent. She went for refuge and undertook the bases of training.

Then that man fell into thought, and thought to himself: "This, then, is my field of merit." From that point, he began to offer flowers, fruits, and food first and foremost, and later to his secondary wife — up to that passage.

She thought to herself: "All the household duties, whatever they may be, I will do, while this one simply sleeps and eats" — from that passage through to the point where that man called the secondary wife in order to be intimate with her, and she spoke:

"Please be with the senior wife" — up to that statement.

From the passage "She undertook the bases of training": because affliction (kleśa) is exceedingly powerful, he went to the secondary wife's quarters and embraced her. She then said to him: "Were you not the one, O son of a noble family, who gave me leave to undertake the bases of training in just this way? What is happening now is not fitting." Yet he pressed himself upon her and acted in that manner — up to that passage.

Now, the one who at that time had become the secondary wife is this very girl Bzang mo, daughter of the Ser skya family. By the karmic maturation of the deed she had committed at that time — causing the senior wife to break her vows — even though she had attained the state of an arhat, she experienced seven days in the company of a natural enemy before her birth.

From the Blessed One: "What did she do, and for what reason was she declared foremost among those with swift direct knowledge, having attained the state of arhat?" — up to the passage: "She performed and accumulated this karma" — and then: the secondary wife, after becoming a widow and her husband having died, left the household. Under the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa she went forth into homelessness, and there she abided in the holy life of pure conduct for ten thousand years, guarding and protecting it fully. She became learned in the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases; learned in what is appropriate and what is not; and learned in dependent origination. Yet she did not penetrate wisdom to its ultimate limit. Nevertheless, at that time she made this aspiration: "May I please the Blessed One Kāśyapa — the one who prophesied the brahmin youth Uttara's complete awakening — and may I never displease him." Through this she did please him and did not displease him, and by the karmic maturation of her abiding in the holy life and fully maintaining it, she attained the state of an arhat.

Regarding that teaching: the nun under whom she had gone forth — she whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa had declared foremost among those with swift direct knowledge — at that time also made an aspiration: "Just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa declared my teacher foremost among those with swift direct knowledge, so too, when the brahmin youth Uttara attains complete awakening, may I likewise be declared foremost among those with swift direct knowledge." — up to the passage: "Monks, you should train accordingly."

Again, from the passage "Then the monks arose in doubt" to: "What did the venerable Mahā-Kāśyapa do and accumulate, such that by the karmic maturation of his karma he was born into a household of great wealth and extensive prosperity?" — and from there to the passage: "thirty villages on the border of that karma" — and then: eighty measures filled with golden barley, and nine hundred ninety-nine ploughshares — up to that passage.

"Monks, this is the karma he performed and accumulated" — from that point onward, to be elaborated fully.

"Monks, in a time long past, in a certain hermitage five hundred sages dwelt. At that time, since no buddha or Blessed One had appeared in the world, pratyekabuddhas — solitary buddhas — who bring benefit to the lowly and the destitute would appear in the world. Not far from that hermitage there also dwelt one such pratyekabuddha.

Each day the sages would rise early, leave a guardian sage behind, and go out in the four directions to gather firewood for the sacrificial fire and fruits to eat. On one such occasion, a certain sage who was passing by close to that pratyekabuddha again and again saw the pratyekabuddha seated there in cross-legged posture. When he turned back he saw him still seated in the same way, and he thought to himself:"

"This monk does not break his cross-legged posture during the day — where does he get his food, and how does he manage? I will ask him about it." Then he thought further: "If I go to him right now and ask, those sages will see me keeping company with a monk and will mock me. I will wait until it is my turn to guard the hermitage, and then ask him without embarrassment."

Then on another occasion the turn fell to that sage to guard the hermitage. When the other sages had gone out, he went to where the pratyekabuddha was staying, approached him, and asked: "Noble one, each day we go back and forth in search of food and fruit. Yet I have never once seen you unfolding your crossed legs or going out for alms. Do you eat joy?"

The pratyekabuddha replied: "I do not eat joy. When mealtime comes I go for alms, bring what I have collected back here, and eat."

The sage asked: "Where do you go for alms?"

The pratyekabuddha replied: "To the northern Unpleasant Sound."

"What is the Unpleasant Sound like?"

He replied: "It is a place where there is no possessiveness, where life is fixed in its span, where one goes in a distinguished manner, and even after death one continues to go in a distinguished manner. When one does not go to the northern Unpleasant Sound, one collects alms-food among the gods of the Thirty-Three."

The sage asked: "What are the gods of the Thirty-Three like?"

The pratyekabuddha replied: "They are radiant in color, abounding in happiness, dwelling in lofty mansions, long-lived, remaining for a great duration, dwelling for a very long time."

The sage thought: "This is truly a great being. Today I will offer him today's alms." And he said to the pratyekabuddha: "Noble one, today please accept alms from me, and may you look upon me with favor."

The pratyekabuddha said: "But you yourself have gone forth from the household life — how do you intend to give alms to me?"

The sage replied: "That is so, and yet I pray that you nevertheless grant me your benefit." And he spoke these verses:

You are glory and merit.
You are the supreme among those who teach the Dharma.
By your striving this world
Has become as though adorned on every side.

The pratyekabuddha consented. The sage, understanding from his silence that he had accepted, went back to his hermitage. Now he had earlier set aside a small measure of wild grain. He cleaned it, went to a nearby cowherd's settlement not far from the hermitage, obtained milk, cooked the grain in the milk, and when it was done he offered the alms-food to the pratyekabuddha. That venerable one, in order to bring benefit to the sage, accepted the alms, and then, to teach the Dharma through the medium of his body, soared up into the middle of the sky like a king of geese spreading his wings.

When the sage saw this he was filled with the highest faith, and with a mind of joy, delight, and gladness he placed his knees on the ground and made this aspiration prayer: "By this act of offering alms-food and giving it as a gift of generosity, may I never again be born as a hell-being, an animal, or a hungry ghost. May I always be born among the gods, and when I pass from there may I be born in the northern Unpleasant Sound, and from there may I be born among the gods again. And whatever assemblies of qualities that one has fully comprehended — may I too fully comprehend those. And may I satisfy and never displease a Teacher more supremely excellent than this one."

Monks, the one who at that time and on that occasion had become a sage — that was none other than the great Kāśyapa himself. And through the karmic maturation of the act of offering that small measure of grain at that time and on that occasion, he was born a thousand times in the northern Unpleasant Sound, and a thousand times he was born among the gods. And when he passed from among the gods, he was born into the brahmin caste. By the power of his aspiration prayer, he also satisfied me — a Teacher more supremely excellent than many tens of millions of pratyekabuddhas — and through this he attained that very accumulation of qualities.

Therefore, monks, show reverence to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; offer gifts; and accumulate merit. For if one acts in this way, one will come to possess just such an accumulation of qualities. Train yourselves, monks, just as Kāśyapa has done.

Then the monks, having grown uncertain, put this question to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, through what deeds performed and accumulated, and through the karmic maturation of those deeds, has the venerable great Kāśyapa gone forth in this way, abandoned all afflictions, and attained arhatship — and been declared by the Blessed One to be the foremost among those who speak of the qualities of having few desires, contentment, and cultivation?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, as for what deeds he performed and accumulated, let this be told in full. Monks, long ago, in a past age, in this very present aeon of excellence, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared a perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Kāśyapa — one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. Under his teaching, this one went forth into the holy life, and for the course of ten thousand years he dwelt in the holy life and fully guarded it. Yet though he did not generate the wisdom of final liberation, at the time of his death he made this aspiration prayer: 'May I not displease but rather satisfy the one whom the Blessed One Kāśyapa has prophesied saying: "Brahmin boy, your Teacher — in a future time, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will appear a perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Śākyamuni."'"

And furthermore, regarding the monk under whom this one went forth — that monk had been declared by the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa to be the foremost among those who speak of the qualities of few desires, contentment, and cultivation — and this one also made an aspiration prayer: "Just as the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa declared my preceptor to be the foremost among those who speak of the qualities of few desires, contentment, and cultivation, so too, when the brahmin boy the Teacher attains perfect awakening, may I likewise receive such a declaration."

Monks, through his abiding in the holy life at that time, he attained his fruit here in this life. Through having fully ripened his faculties at that time, he was here liberated. And through the aspiration prayer he made at that time, he was here given the declaration.

Therefore, monks, you should reverently receive scriptural transmissions and read them, and become skilled in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, occasions and non-occasions, and dependent origination. Likewise, make proper aspiration prayers, for by doing so your accumulation of qualities will grow. Train yourselves accordingly, monks.

Here ends the intermediate summary.

The farmer and the potter,
the merchant living by cloth,
the one who plasters stūpas with turmeric paste,
the courtesan and the grain-seller,
the wealthy and those of modest means —
these are the groups set forth.

Here now are the verses summarizing the eight rules of defeat. The summary:

Unchastity, theft,
taking life, and speaking falsehood,
keeping a doe, selling incense,
the woman with a lover, and born of a slave.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha. At the time when Utpalavarnā was engaged in the work of a courtesan in one of the six great cities, a brahmin became intensely attached to her in his mind and went to her, bringing her flowers, fruits, and tooth-cleaning sticks as tokens of service. Then Utpalavarnā said to that brahmin: "You are of high caste, and I am of low caste — why have you come here?" When she said this, the brahmin replied: "I wish to meet with you." She replied: "If you have some kārṣāpaṇas, we may meet later." Then the brahmin, having heard those words from Utpalavarnā, went out to the provinces to obtain kārṣāpaṇas.

Then, at another time, Utpalavarnā, relying on her spiritual friend, the venerable Maudgalyāyana the Great, abandoned the work of a courtesan and herself attained the state of an arhat. Now she was accustomed to sitting during the day in a dense forest grove, and so from that time forward Utpalavarnā went to sit during the day in a dense forest grove.

As for the brahmin, he took his kārṣāpaṇas and traveled from village to village, from town to town, from district to district, and through the environs of the royal palace, asking after her at every step, until at last he arrived at Śrāvastī. Then that brahmin went to the place where Utpalavarnā was staying, and upon arriving he made advances toward her, saying: "Here, please accept these kārṣāpaṇas." But she reflected and said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, I have abandoned that which is not the holy Dharma." When she said this, the brahmin replied to Utpalavarnā: "Even if you have abandoned it, I have not." Then Utpalavarnā said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, which part of my body have you become attached to in your mind?" He replied: "Your eyes." She then, by miraculous power, placed her eye in the palm of her hand and said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, if you desire it, take it." Then the brahmin, upon seeing the eye, became enraged and agitated, and struck the nun Utpalavarnā with a fist to the head and departed.

Thereupon Utpalavarnā immediately reported the matter to the nuns, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, women are weak in strength, prone to deceitfulness, frivolity, and trickery, and subject to desires of all kinds. Therefore, from this day forward nuns shall not dwell in forest hermitages." When the Blessed One had thus prohibited nuns from dwelling in forest hermitages, those who were living at crossroads, at four-way intersections, and at three-way junctions were also traversed by deceitful persons and others. After they had for a time been residing there, there was in Śrāvastī a faithful male lay practitioner named Sāgata, son of a hunter,

He was a man of virtuous intention and good character, endowed with the five bases of training. When he saw those nuns dwelling here and there in scattered places, he sought lodgings for them, went to them, and said, "Noble ones, please stay here as comfortably as you wish," and they did indeed take up residence there.

At that time, in the summer quarters of the nuns, there was a nun named Bhomā Gaṃgamo, who was beautiful in form, lovely, pleasing to behold, greatly given to attachment, and attractive to men.

Then on another occasion the duty-nun was appointed. The assembly of nuns, at the morning hour, dressed in their robes and lower garments, took up their Dharma-robes and begging bowls, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. At that point the nun Bhomā Gaṃgamo, pretending to be ill, turned back from that very place. Since she was attached to Sāgata, son of the hunter, who was staying there, she made a sign to him. He was unwilling, and she spoke these words to him: "When one desires something, those who do not desire it in the same way will in time come to be otherwise." Thereupon Sāgata, son of the hunter, said to Bhomā Gaṃgamo, "Sister, you have gone forth into renunciation, and I am a layman. Beyond that, you have attained the status of a royal consort through the king's grace. If the king were to learn that I had engaged in such misconduct, he would cause me to suffer the fate of the condemned this very night." Then Bhomā Gaṃgamo said to Sāgata, son of the hunter, "Son of a householder, do the king's great investigators follow us about wherever we go? If I am willing and you are willing, and we are together in that way, who would have cause to fear on my account?" Though she spoke thus, Sāgata, son of the hunter, would not comply.

Then the nun Bhomā Gaṃgamo thought to herself, "Shall I kill this body and die, or shall I take merely the contact of limb with limb as mine?" Having considered and reflected, she said to Sāgata, son of the hunter, "If the son of the householder is unwilling, then let there be contact of limb with limb only." She drew him into her arms, and from the knees upward and the eyes downward she brought about full contact, offering everything — and this very act of violation was perceived by the duty-nun.

The assembly of nuns, having collected alms in Śrāvastī, finished their meal, refused a further round of alms, and on their return went to the place where Sāgata, son of the hunter, was dwelling. Then the duty-nun said to them: "Oh, sisters, I fear that this Sāgata, son of the hunter, thinking he is providing us with a secluded dwelling for the sake of Dharma, has treated those who merely receive a touch of his head like the royal consorts of a king. Oh, sisters, those of you who still need to uphold moral discipline should go elsewhere from this day forward."

They asked her, "What has happened?" And she told the nuns the matter in full detail as it had occurred. The nuns then told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then thought, "My twofold assembly must understand this matter, and I shall properly establish a rule of training." With that in mind, and on account of this incident, this occasion, this matter, and these circumstances, he convened the twofold assembly.

Now, the blessed buddhas act with full knowledge and awareness — they act knowingly, not unknowingly; they act in timely fashion, not untimely; they act with purpose, not without purpose. The blessed buddhas are like this:

Acting without purpose is averted by the quality of flood-water. Now, the blessed buddhas are like this: they know the right time for purposeful action — and so the Blessed One, the Buddha, addressed the nun Sthulanandā, asking, "Nun, is it true that you have done this unseemly, unbecoming thing?" She replied, "Blessed One, I did it." The Blessed One, the Buddha, then rebuked her, saying that what is unbecoming for a contemplative, what is improper, what is contrary to proper conduct — that is not something a person who has gone forth should do.

Then, having rebuked her in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of nuns: "Nuns, it is for these ten benefits that I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for my female hearers. The ten are these: to unite the Saṅgha, to promote the Saṅgha's well-being, to bring harmony to the Saṅgha, to ensure the Saṅgha dwells in happiness, to restrain those individuals who are difficult to discipline, to enable those who are conscientious to dwell at ease, to generate faith in those who have none, to increase and expand the faith of those who already have it, to restrain the defilements of this present life, to ward off the defilements of future lives, to uphold the holy life, to bring the holy life to its full perfection, to harmonize the teaching, and so that my teaching — broad and beneficial to the many, rightly proclaimed to gods and humans alike — may endure for a long time."

Having seen this with clear vision, I shall establish for my female hearers a rule of training in the Vinaya. My female hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever nun, seized by passion, presses against a man who is likewise seized by passion — from the knee down, from the eye down — touching and fully touching, and indulges in that experience, that nun has incurred a defeat and must not remain in the community.

Now, the term "whatever nun" refers to Sthulanandā. "Seized by passion" means with attachment, with genuine clinging, with being enmeshed. "A man" means the son of a hunter, or any other man whatsoever. "Passion" means attachment, genuine clinging, being enmeshed. "From the knee down, from the eye down" means within that range. "Pressing and fully pressing" means touching and fully touching. "Indulges in that" means experiencing it through and through. "Nun" means one in whom the substance of a nun is present. What is the substance of a nun? Full ordination. What is full ordination? It is the act of performing the formal act with a motion and a corresponding resolution made three times, the deliberation, the complete deliberation, the bringing to a conclusion, the acceptance, the explicit acceptance — and this full ordination is expressed at the moment of ordination through speech, through words, through convention, through utterance, through expression, through definitive words, through the path of words, through verbal statement, through verbal action, through verbal declaration. The words "this" and "that" are particles of indication and comprehensive designation. "Has incurred a defeat" means she is final, downfallen, inferior, severed, defiled, discordant with the mind. And whoever commits that downfall — as soon as it is committed she becomes unfit to be a nun, unfit to be a daughter of the Śākyas; her conduct as a contemplative is ruined, weakened, broken, fallen, defeated, turned away — and her conduct as a contemplative is rendered irrecoverable. That is to say —

Just as a palmyra tree whose crown has been cut cannot turn green again, cannot grow and spread and flourish — in exactly that same way, whatever nun commits that transgression — "as soon as it is committed" — is as stated before. "She shall not remain" means that the other nuns shall not perform with her the restoration ceremony, the invitation ceremony, a formal act with a single request, a formal act with a request and motion, or a formal act with a request and three repetitions. Nor shall she be appointed to any of the twelve offices held by nuns.

How does one incur a defeat? The summary verse states:

With desire, touching a man who has desire —
from below the eyes down to above the knee —
fully giving such contact: a defeat.
If the man has no desire,
it becomes a grave offense.
What is given and what is withdrawn —
these become wrongdoing.

Furthermore, whatever nun, with desire, together with a man who has desire, touches, makes full contact, and experientially engages from below the eyes down to above the knee — she incurs a defeat.

Whatever nun, with desire, together with a man who has no desire, touches, makes full contact, and experientially engages from below the eyes down to above the knee — she incurs a grave offense.

Whatever nun, without desire, together with a man, touches, makes full contact, and experientially engages from below the eyes down to above the knee — she incurs a grave offense.

Whatever nun, with desire, together with a man who has desire, receives something given — making it her own — from as high as the armpits down, having made full contact and handed it over — she incurs a grave offense.

Whatever nun, without desire, together with a man who has desire, receives something given — making it her own — from as high as the armpits down, having made full contact and handed it over — she incurs wrongdoing.

Whatever nun, with desire, together with a man who has no desire, receives something given — making it her own — from as high as the armpits down, having made full contact and handed it over — she incurs wrongdoing.

Whatever nun, without desire, together with a man who has no desire, receives something given — making it her own — from as high as the armpits down, having made full contact and handed it over — she incurs wrongdoing.

The fifth defeat is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. At that time there was in Śrāvastī a young perfume-seller who was handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to look upon. He had taken a wife from among his own class, and together with her he sported, rejoiced, and lived in delight. Not long after he had taken her, the nun Sthūlanandā became attached to that young perfume-seller and went to him, saying: "Good-looking one, are you contented with your new bride?" He replied: "Noble one, if I am contented, what concern is that of yours? And if I am not contented, what concern is that of yours?" When he said this, Sthūlanandā said to the young perfume-seller: "I thought you and I might be able to do a certain small thing together. If even a little is not acceptable to you, then that is the end of it." The young perfume-seller then thought: "This nun has become infatuated." He went to her again and again, making signals, setting times, showing signs, and also engaging in flirtation, pressing close, and fondling. Then on another occasion the young perfume-seller came to Sthūlanandā, and she pulled him close and held him.

Then Sthūlanandā went outside the temple, washed her hands and feet, gave instructions to her pupils and attendants, and went to sit alone with the young perfume-seller in a secluded place. After a while, she allowed him to engage in sexual intercourse with her. At that moment, Sthūlanandā thought to herself: "Whatever standing I have above the other nuns — all of it is owed to my living in moral discipline, in the rules of training, and in the holy life. If I now commit such a misdeed and thereby bring disgrace to the order of nuns, who will come to ask me anything?" Having aroused this thought and reflected thus, Sthūlanandā said to the young perfume-seller: "Fair one, be off." Then the young perfume-seller thought: "Without any doubt, this is an uncomfortable situation." And so he too let go. Then Sthūlanandā, resting on her back, drew in her right leg and kicked the young perfume-seller once, breaking two of his ribs. The young perfume-seller then fled, vomiting blood as he went.

Then Sthūlanandā, sitting in the middle of the summer dwelling, cried out: "I have conquered Māra! I have conquered Māra!" When the nuns heard this, they said: "Sister, have you realized the fruit of stream-entry? Or the fruit of once-returning? Or the fruit of non-returning? Or have you realized the supreme fruit, arhatship? Or, at the least, have you planted a root of virtue in the teaching of the Buddha?" She replied: "None of these." They then said: "Then what kind of Māra have you conquered?" She spoke of it then among the many who were present.

Then the nuns said to Sthūlanandā: "You only just barely escaped meeting with a thorn. Had it been otherwise, you would have been expelled." Thereafter, though the many nuns said these things to Sthūlanandā, she showed neither pleasure nor displeasure. Showing neither pleasure nor displeasure, she rose from her seat and departed.

The many nuns then reported the matter to the monks at that time, and the monks in turn informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One then — from "this incident occurred, this was the occasion, this was the matter, and in this context" all the way through to "fully teaching for the benefit of the many, for gods and humans alike" — that whole preceding account is to be recited just as it was.

Furthermore, this is the rule of training to be promulgated for the female hearers in the Vinaya: If any nun who has become attached makes signals to an attached man, or sets a time, or shows signs, or engages in flirtation, pressing close, and fondling so as to bring a man who then comes within her grasp — and remains in a place from which, wherever a woman and man might go, she cannot drive him away — if in these eight respects a nun commits a transgression, immediately upon committing it she is no longer fit to be a nun and must not remain in the order.

Now, "any nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Who has become attached" means through attachment, through full clinging, through being thoroughly bound. "A man" means the young perfume-seller or anyone else whatsoever. "Attached" means attachment, full clinging, and being thoroughly bound. "Makes signals" means whenever she sees him in an open space, at a temple, or in some such prominent place. "Sets a time" means in the early morning, at midday,

"in the afternoon — come at that time" is what is said. "Displays a sign" means whenever he sees her not long after she has shaved her head, wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe. "Flirting and distraction" means making provocative gestures. "Sidling and jostling" means frolicking about in every direction. "Exposing the root" means making all manner of indecent noise. "Appropriates a man who has come" means she makes use of him carnally. "A place where a woman cannot properly stop a man from proceeding and there is no turning back" means a place where she comes under his power. "Positions her body" means her torso. "In these eight respects" means in whichever of those situations she has entered into. "A nun" means one who possesses the essential qualities of a nun. What are the essential qualities of a nun? Full ordination. What is full ordination? It is the performance of the formal act with a motion and three proclamations, the preliminary examination, the proper examination, the completion, the proper completion, the acknowledgment thereof, the assent, and the explicit declaration — as explained above. "If she commits a transgression" means if she acts beyond her limits. "Immediately upon" means in that very instant. The word "that," which is the term used for indicating proximity and full indication, begins from the phrase "the foremost of all" and continues up to "she must not be appointed to any of the twelve roles of a nun."

Now, how does a transgression arise? If a nun who is attached makes signals together with a man who is attached, a gross transgression arises. If she sets a time, a gross transgression arises. If she displays a sign, a gross transgression arises. If she flirts and distracts, a gross transgression arises. If she sidles and jostles, a gross transgression arises. If she makes indecent noise, a gross transgression arises. If she appropriates a man who has come, a gross transgression arises. If she positions her body in a place where a woman can stop a man from proceeding and there is a possibility of turning back, a gross transgression arises. If she positions her body in a place where a woman cannot properly stop a man from proceeding and there is no turning back, a defeat transgression arises. For one who is a first offender and the like, there is no fault.

This concludes the sixth defeat in the Vibhaṅga for Nuns.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the place where the Kalandakas reside, in Veṇuvana. At the time when the nun Priyā had fallen from her precepts, upon her falling from them her younger sister Priyamatī wept. The nuns said to her: "Dear Priyamatī, did not the Blessed One declare that whatever is assembled will come apart? Why then do you weep?" She spoke these words: "It is not because this my friend Priyā has fallen from this Dharma and Vinaya that I weep. Rather, I weep because even before this, she used to do such and such things." They said to her: "Did you know of this?" She replied: "I knew." They said: "Why then did you not tell us earlier?" She replied: "Because of affection for my younger sister." Then the many nuns said to the nun Priyamatī: "Sister, you have concealed a blameworthy matter" — and at that point the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nun, is it true that you acted in such a wrong, unseemly manner as this?"

She replied: "Blessed One, I did not." The Blessed One, the Buddha, rebuked her, saying that such conduct — improper for a renunciant, unsuitable and contrary to the monastic rule — was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Having rebuked her in many different ways, he then addressed the nuns: "Nuns, having seen ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for female hearers" — and what follows, concerning the establishment of the training rule, is to be recited in full.

Furthermore, whatever nun conceals with full awareness a transgression committed by a nun, and whenever that nun has died, lapsed, wandered away, or transferred — if at that time this nun were to say, "I knew beforehand that such and such transgressions had arisen in connection with that nun," then that nun herself, by reason of having willfully concealed a blameworthy matter, incurs a root defeat and must not remain in the order.

Now let the terms be explained. "Whatever nun" refers to one who is a friend or one who resembles such. "Nun" refers to Priyamatī. "Transgression" refers to any one of the eight root defeats. "With full awareness" means either she herself witnessed it, or another person had told her about it. "Conceals" means she covered it up. "Whenever that nun has died" means her life faculty has been cut off. "Has lapsed" means she has surrendered her training. "Has wandered away" means she has abandoned the district. "Has transferred" means she has come to rely on a dwelling of the tīrthikas. "At that time, this nun" refers to the friend. "Nuns of this" refers to those of this Dharma community. "I knew beforehand that such and such transgressions had arisen in connection with that nun" — here "transgression" means any one of the eight. "Were to say" means: if she so speaks. "Nun" refers to the one in whom the essential quality of a nun exists. What is the essential quality of a nun? Full ordination. What constitutes full ordination? Everything else is to be recited in full. "That" is a term of indication pointing to what has been stated and what has been stated in detail nearby. The passage extends up to "she must not be appointed among the twelve nuns." As for how this constitutes a transgression: if a nun knowingly conceals the blameworthy matter of a nun, in whatever way and in all cases she incurs a root defeat.

The seventh root defeat in the analysis of the nun's code is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, belonging to Prince Jeta. At that time there was residing at Śrāvastī a monk called Kṛtaka who was contentious, who would expose faults, who was divisive, who was quarrelsome, and who fomented disputes. The Saṅgha performed against him the act of formal banishment from the residence. The great female sovereign Gautamī heard that the monk Kṛtaka had had the act of formal banishment performed against him. Upon hearing this, she went to where the Blessed One was, went up to him, prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the great female sovereign Gautamī addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, if the Saṅgha has performed against some monk the act of banishment from the residence, how am I to conduct myself toward him?" The Blessed One declared: "If you encounter him, you need not bow but should rise from your seat." "Venerable One, this monk Kṛtaka is contentious, exposes faults, is divisive, quarrelsome, foments disputes, and has taken up dwelling together in close association with the nuns.

"If the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against him, how are we to conduct ourselves toward him?" The Blessed One declared: "You should observe the vow of one who is not worthy of being bowed to."

The Blessed One declared: "They did not understand." And so the Blessed One declared: "Having prepared the seats and struck the wooden signal board, properly inform the nuns with the words of the inquiry, and then, when the entire Saṅgha of nuns is gathered and in concord, let a nun make the motion and perform the act. It is to be done as follows. 'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. This monk Kṛtaka is contentious, exposes faults, is divisive, quarrelsome, foments disputes, and has taken up dwelling together in close association with the nuns; and the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against him. If the time is right for the Saṅgha of nuns, and if the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha of nuns proclaim to this monk Kṛtaka, who is contentious, exposes faults, is divisive, quarrelsome, foments disputes, and has taken up dwelling together in close association with the nuns, and against whom the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence, the vow of one who is not worthy of being bowed to. This is the motion.' The act is to be done as follows. 'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. This monk Kṛtaka is contentious, exposes faults, is divisive, quarrelsome, foments disputes, and has taken up dwelling together in close association with the nuns; and the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against him. The Saṅgha of nuns hereby proclaims to this monk Kṛtaka, who is contentious, exposes faults, is divisive, quarrelsome, foments disputes, and has taken up dwelling together in close association with the nuns, and against whom the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence, the vow of one who is not worthy of being bowed to. Those nuns who consent to the proclaiming of the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to upon this monk Kṛtaka should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.' The noble Saṅgha of nuns has consented and granted it, and so, by remaining silent, it is hereby accepted as such."

When the Saṅgha of monks had performed the act of banishment from the residence against the monk Kṛtaka, and the Saṅgha of nuns had also proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to, the monk Kṛtaka thought: "I have committed a fault, and so the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against me. But what fault have I committed against the Saṅgha of nuns that they should proclaim the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to upon me? I shall go to where the great female sovereign Gautamī is and ask about this matter." And so the monk Kṛtaka went to where the great female sovereign Gautamī was, and having arrived, he said to her: "Sister, I have committed a fault, and on account of that the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against me. But what fault have I committed against the Saṅgha of nuns that they should proclaim upon me the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to?"

"Nevertheless, there are some who speak ill of the nuns, and against those I, in anger and agitation, made them afraid, made them shrink and cower, and stirred up hostility. In this way, when I took the nuns' side, why do you proclaim upon me the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to?" When he had spoken these words, the great female sovereign Gautamī said to the monk Kṛtaka: "Venerable Kṛtaka, who allowed you to come and cause harm to the nuns' side? On top of that, the Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of banishment from the residence against you. And the Blessed One has also given command to proclaim the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to upon the nuns. Therefore we have proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to. Furthermore, Kṛtaka, hear me well. You are one who has gone forth from the Śākyan clan, from the Śākya lineage; you are endowed with the three collections of scripture and you are a Dharma speaker — and yet, being one so widely learned, will you act obstructively without seeking the Saṅgha's forgiveness?"

Then the monk Kṛtaka thought to himself: "This great female sovereign has spoken for my benefit, not against it. Just as a person who falls to the ground must rely on that very ground to rise again, so too, since I have committed a wrong against the Saṅgha, I shall go directly there, prostrate before the Saṅgha, demonstrate my reconciliation, remain within the boundary, and seek forgiveness." Then Kṛtaka thought further: "I shall go to where my mother and sisters are, and also ask the sisters." So Kṛtaka went to where the community of the Twelve Groups was, and having arrived, explained the whole matter to them in full.

Then the communities of the Twelve Groups spoke to Kṛtaka thus: "Noble Kṛtaka, do not prostrate before those who have gone forth from the many different castes, clans, and households. Do not demonstrate reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary and seek forgiveness. Why so? Because we will attend upon you in all matters you might wish to remember and inquire about — with alms bowl, with Dharma robes, with a strainer, with a cup, with a girdle, with medicines for illness timely allowed, those allowed for a watch, those allowed for seven days, and those allowed for one's entire lifetime — we will attend upon you in all these things, without your needing to trouble yourself with whatever you might wish to remember or ask about."

When they had spoken thus, the nuns told the monks, and the monks in turn informed the Blessed One.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga for Nuns. The Sixth Fascicle.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the nuns: "Nuns, you should approach the community of the Twelve Groups and proclaim to them as follows: 'Nuns, whichever monk has had the act of banishment from the residence performed against him by the Saṅgha of monks, and against whom the Saṅgha of nuns has also proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to — if that monk, his hair standing on end and his body's hairs risen, wishes to prostrate before the Saṅgha, intends to come forth, wishes to demonstrate reconciliation, wishes to remain within the boundary and seek forgiveness, and thereby wishes to abandon quarreling and fault-finding — knowing all this, you have gone to him and said: "Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not demonstrate reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary and seek forgiveness."'"

"We will not provide you with an alms bowl, robes, a strainer, a cup, a belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines that are allowable at the right time, medicines allowable for a period of hours, medicines allowable for seven days, medicines allowable for one's entire life, or services in connection with whatever needs may arise." These were the instructions they were told to give.

And when they had given those instructions, those nuns were told: "Sisters, whether the matter be virtuous or non-virtuous, do not say anything whatsoever to that monk" — and clinging to that very same position, holding it as supremely confirmed and firmly adhering to it, they kept designating it thereafter as: "This alone is true; everything else is false."

Then a great many nuns went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One in homage and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the great many nuns reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, whereupon the Blessed One declared to the nuns: "Nuns, open the proceeding against the twelve-group with a motion and a formal act with four readings. And the instruction should be given as follows, beginning with 'Having arranged the seating,' and the act should be performed by a single nun making the motion. The act is to be performed thus:

'May the noble Saṅgha of nuns hear me. These twelve-group members fight with monks, expose faults, cause divisions, dispute and quarrel, and have been dwelling in close and improper association with the nuns. The monks have performed the act of expulsion from the dwelling. The Saṅgha of nuns has likewise proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to. From this — his hair standing on end, his body's hairs risen — he wishes to prostrate before the Saṅgha, intends to come forth, wishes to demonstrate reconciliation, wishes to remain within the boundary and seek forgiveness. Against him, one went and said: "Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not demonstrate reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary and seek forgiveness. We will not provide you with an alms bowl, robes, a strainer, a cup, a belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable at the right time, medicines allowable for a period of hours, medicines allowable for seven days, medicines allowable for one's entire life, or services in connection with whatever needs may arise" — the nun who said this was admonished and instructed by the many nuns; and though admonished and instructed by the many nuns, she still clings to that very same position, holds it as supremely confirmed, firmly adheres to it, and keeps designating it thereafter as: "This alone is true; everything else is false." If it is the right time for the Saṅgha of nuns and they consent, the Saṅgha should approve of this. The Saṅgha of nuns shall perform the instruction of the twelve-group by means of a motion and a formal act with four readings.'

'Sisters, you fight with monks, expose faults, cause divisions, dispute and quarrel, and have been dwelling in close and improper association with the nuns. The monks have performed the act of expulsion from the dwelling. The Saṅgha of nuns has likewise proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to. From this — his hair standing on end, his body's hairs risen — he wishes to prostrate before the Saṅgha, intends to come forth, wishes to demonstrate reconciliation, wishes to show concordance.'"

— remaining within the boundary and wishing to seek forgiveness — went to meet her and spoke thus: "Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. We will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines that are allowable in season, allowable for a watch period, allowable for seven days, and allowable for life — and whatever else is needed we will provide in full, without your being troubled by this or that." Such was the basis for which, sisters, permission is given.

The motion is this, and the formal act is to be performed as follows. "May the noble Saṅgha of nuns hear me. These twelve groups of nuns — who fight with monks, expose faults, cause divisions, dispute and quarrel, who have been dwelling in close and improper association with the nuns, for whom the monks performed the act of expulsion from the dwelling, and for whom the Saṅgha of nuns likewise proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to — their hair standing on end, their body's hairs risen, wish to prostrate before the Saṅgha, intend to come forth, wish to demonstrate reconciliation, are remaining within the boundary, and wishing to seek forgiveness, went to meet her and spoke thus: 'Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. We will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable in season, allowable for a watch period, allowable for seven days, and allowable for life — and whatever else is needed we will provide in full, without your being troubled by this or that.' These nuns were then admonished by the assembly of nuns; yet even after being admonished by the assembly of nuns, they stubbornly and tenaciously clung to that very position, openly fixating upon it, saying, 'This alone is true; anything else is false.' Therefore, sisters, regarding these twelve groups of nuns — the nuns who fight with monks, expose faults, cause divisions, dispute and quarrel, who have been dwelling in close and improper association with the nuns, for whom the monks performed the act of expulsion from the dwelling, and for whom the Saṅgha of nuns proclaimed the vow of one not worthy of being bowed to — their hair standing on end, their body's hairs risen, who wish to prostrate before the Saṅgha, who intend to come forth, who wish to demonstrate reconciliation, who are remaining within the boundary, wishing to seek forgiveness, and who went to meet her and spoke thus: 'Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. We will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines,

fruit medicines — those allowable at the proper time, those allowable at a fixed hour, those allowable for seven days, and those allowable for the duration of one's life — and whatever else may be needed we will attend upon you with, free from any interference from whatever else may come up.' This is what was formally enjoined.

Concerning those who, among these twelve groups, consented to the enjoining by means of a motion and three readings of the formal act, they should say nothing. Those who did not consent should speak. This concludes the first recitation of the formal act.

For the second, the same matter is to be recited: 'Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me. These twelve groups of nuns engage in fighting, in fault-finding, in quarreling, in disputing, in wrangling. They have come to dwell together in extremely close intimacy with the nuns. They have undergone the formal act of removal from the residence by the monks. The nuns too have enjoined upon them a vow that is not worthy of reverence, their hair standing on end, their body's hairs risen, who wish to prostrate before the Saṅgha, who intend to come forth, who wish to demonstrate reconciliation, who are remaining within the boundary wishing to seek forgiveness, and who went to meet her and spoke thus: "Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. We will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable at the proper time, those allowable at a fixed hour, those allowable for seven days, and those allowable for the duration of one's life, and whatever else may be needed we will attend upon you with, free from any interference from whatever else may come up," — those nuns were admonished by many nuns and enjoined, and though admonished and enjoined by many nuns, they stubbornly clung to that very same position as supreme, adhering to it resolutely, and continued to assert: "This alone is true; all else is false." On account of this, the Saṅgha formally enjoined upon the twelve groups of nuns by means of a motion and three readings of the formal act.

Those among you, the venerable ones, who consent to the enjoining of these twelve groups of nuns by means of a motion and three readings of the formal act, should say nothing. Those who do not consent should speak. This concludes the second recitation of the formal act.

For the third, the same formal act is to be recited: 'Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me. These twelve groups of nuns engage in fighting, in fault-finding, in quarreling, in disputing, in wrangling. They have come to dwell together in extremely close intimacy with the nuns. They have undergone the formal act of removal from the residence by the monks. The nuns too have enjoined upon them a vow that is not worthy of reverence, their hair standing on end, their body's hairs risen, who wish to prostrate before the Saṅgha, who intend to come forth, who wish to demonstrate reconciliation, who are remaining within the boundary wishing to seek forgiveness, and who went to meet her and spoke thus: "Noble one, do not prostrate before the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. We will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable at the proper time, those allowable at a fixed hour, those allowable for seven days,

those allowable for one's entire lifetime, and whatever else one is engaged with, we shall attend upon you without leaving it undone."

When those nuns speak thus, many nuns approach them and give instruction, and even though many nuns approach those nuns and give instruction, those nuns nonetheless stubbornly hold fast to that very same basis of dispute, cling to it, and continue to designate it afterward as "this alone is true; all else is confused." Therefore the Saṅgha performs the act of admonition toward those groups of twelve nuns by means of a motion-and-three-proclamations procedure. "Venerable ones, those who are willing that the Saṅgha perform this act of admonition toward these groups of twelve nuns by means of a motion-and-three-proclamations procedure are to remain silent. Those who are not willing are to speak." The Saṅgha, having consented and agreed, has performed the act of admonition toward these groups of twelve nuns by means of a motion-and-three-proclamations procedure. Since no one has spoken, it is accordingly so upheld.

When the act of admonition by motion-and-three-proclamations is performed upon them, and those nuns nonetheless stubbornly hold fast to that very same basis of dispute, cling to it, and continue to designate it afterward as "this alone is true; all else is confused," the nuns speak to the monks. The monks, in turn, report the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, thinking "My female hearers will understand the matter, and I shall also establish the bases of training well," assembled the twofold Saṅgha on account of this occurrence, this occasion, this affair, and this circumstance, and proceeded through the steps from the assembling of the twofold Saṅgha to the laying down of the training rule.

Furthermore, if a nun, knowing full well that a monk upon whom the unified Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of suspension, and who is not worthy of being bowed down to by the Saṅgha of nuns either, is one upon whom a vow of restraint has been conveyed, and that this monk — though his hair has grown out and his body hair has risen — is bowing down to the Saṅgha, coming forth, showing reconciliation, remaining within the boundary seeking forgiveness, nonetheless speaks to her thus: "Noble one, do not bow down to the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. Rather than letting you continue your dispute, I myself will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable at the proper time, those allowable at a fixed hour, those allowable for seven days, those allowable for one's entire lifetime, and whatever else one is engaged with, without leaving it undone" — then the nuns say to that nun: "Sister, knowing full well that the monk upon whom the unified Saṅgha of monks has performed the act of suspension, and who is not worthy of being bowed down to by the Saṅgha of nuns either, is one upon whom a vow of restraint has been conveyed, and that this monk — though his hair has grown out and his body hair has risen — is bowing down to the Saṅgha, coming forth, showing reconciliation, remaining within the boundary seeking forgiveness, you nonetheless spoke thus: 'Noble one, do not bow down to the Saṅgha. Do not come forth. Do not show reconciliation. Do not remain within the boundary seeking forgiveness. Rather than letting you continue your dispute, we ourselves will attend upon you with alms bowl, Dharma robes, filter cloth, bowl stand, belt, things to remember, things to inquire about, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines allowable at the proper time, those allowable at a fixed hour, those allowable for seven days,

and whatever allowable for one's lifetime, and whatever task she is occupied with, that task we will attend to without interruption' — when she speaks such words, she follows in the wake of one who has been expelled from the residence, and for the purpose of creating discord, this instruction is to be given to her: 'Abandon such speech.' If the nuns give this instruction to that nun, and she abandons that ground of offense, then so much the better. If she does not abandon it, then for the purpose of having her abandon that ground of offense, the instruction and admonition should be given correctly up to a second and third time. If, when correctly instructed and admonished up to a second and third time, she abandons that ground of offense, then so much the better. If she does not abandon it, that nun incurs a defeat bringing about her expulsion from the residence, and she must not remain.

Now, as for the phrase 'moreover, whatever nun' — this refers to the group of twelve. As for 'whatever monk' — this refers to the one who creates strife, who causes discomfort, who is Gre-kye. As for 'the Saṅgha' — this is the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. As for 'the act of expulsion from the residence has been performed' — this is through the act of a motion with four readings. As for 'the nuns' Saṅgha' — this is the Saṅgha of nuns who are śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. As for 'admonishing the vow of one who is not worthy of homage' — this is through the act of a motion with two readings. As for 'that monk' — this is Gre-kye. 'Her hair standing on end, her body-hair bristling' up to 'does not make obeisance to the Saṅgha' — and as for 'knowingly' — this is either by seeing it herself or by it having been reported to her by another. Therefore, as for 'do not abandon the quarreling' — this has the meaning of 'do not bring it to peace.' As for 'if it is said' — this means 'if she says.' As for 'O noble one' — this refers to Gre-kye with hair standing on end and body-hair bristling. From 'do not make obeisance to the Saṅgha' up to 'do not abandon the quarreling' has the meaning of 'do not ask the Saṅgha for forgiveness.' From 'I will attend upon you with alms bowl and Dharma robes' and so forth up to 'will attend to you' — as for 'that nun' — this refers to the group of twelve. As for 'by the nuns' — this means by the nuns of this Dharma. As for 'this instruction is to be given' — this means she is to be spoken to in these words, and the instruction spoken with composure is to be given just as described previously. If the nuns give that instruction to that nun, and she abandons that ground of offense — that is good. If she does not abandon it, then for the purpose of having her abandon that ground of offense, the instruction and admonition are to be given correctly up to a second and third time — this means just as the instruction was given previously through a motion with four readings. As for 'when correctly instructed' — this means 'when correctly admonished.' As for how the transgression arises: to whatever degree a nun, from 'a monk who creates strife' through 'creating further strife, the Saṅgha having performed the act of expulsion from the residence, the nuns admonishing the vow of one not worthy of homage' — and knowingly speaks thus: 'I will attend upon you with the alms bowl' — this becomes a wrongdoing. With the Dharma robes also it becomes a wrongdoing. With the filter cloth also it becomes a wrongdoing. With the bowl stand also it becomes a wrongdoing. With the belt also it becomes a wrongdoing. 'Whatever task she is occupied with, that task I will attend to without interruption' — each and every one of these becomes a wrongdoing.

If, having accepted and then been instructed to relinquish that basis, one does so, that is good. If one does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises. If, before the words of the first motion have been completed, one relinquishes it, that is good. If one does not relinquish it and the words are completed, a grave offense arises. If, before the words of the second motion have been completed, one relinquishes it, that is good. If one does not relinquish it and the words are completed, a grave offense arises. Even before the words of the third motion are completed — if the proceeding has been conducted improperly by those in agreement, or conducted improperly by those in disagreement, or conducted properly by those in disagreement, but is conducted in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and what the Teacher has taught — there is no transgression. If the words of the third motion are also completed, and it has been conducted in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and what the Teacher has taught, yet one still does not relinquish that basis, then a defeat has arisen for that nun. For one who is a first offender and the like, there is no transgression.

This completes the eighth defeat as set out in the Analysis of the nuns' Vinaya (Skt. vibhaṅga).

In the context of the defeats, it was declared that twelve duties shall not be assigned to nuns. If someone asks what those twelve are, they should be told as follows: assigning a residence, assigning food, distributing porridge, distributing tooth-sticks, distributing small provisions, washing vessels, distributing cloth, distributing robes, washing the great rains-retreat linen, distributing the great rains-retreat cloth, giving assignments, and adornment.

In summary:

The one who makes objection, the groundless accusation,
the third — taking a partial share,
the fourth — making anything acceptable,
the fifth — freedom from attachment,
traveling by day and by night,
and being assigned beyond a river.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, a man named Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, was a person who mingled with the brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī, spoke pleasantly, exchanged friendly words, cultivated friendships, engaged minds, and was skilled at gaining entry into households. Those who wished to give their daughters in marriage to suitable parties would approach Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra and ask: "O Kṛṣṇa, is that young man capable, diligent, and enterprising? Can he provide abundant food and clothing for the daughter? Is he one who takes up even small tasks?" If he reported back that the young man was indeed capable at heart, diligent, enterprising, able to provide abundant food and clothing for the daughter, and one who takes up even small tasks, then they would give their daughters to such men. If he reported that the young man was in truth incapable, lazy, not enterprising, unable to provide abundant food and clothing for the daughter, and not one who takes up small tasks, then they would not give their daughters to such men. Likewise, those who sought daughters in marriage would also come to Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra and ask: "Mother, is that daughter capable, enterprising, and able to dwell in the home with care?" — and the rest should be stated in the same manner as for the young man. When they had given their daughters well through any such arrangement, they would say: "We have asked Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra, and the young man to whom we gave the daughter is capable, diligent, enterprising, able to provide abundant food and clothing for the daughter, and one who takes up even small tasks. Therefore all those who associate with Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra —"

— "who speak well of coming" — and they would praise all those who were admitted to the household, saying: "It will be like this for them as well." Likewise, whenever any of them had given a daughter in marriage badly, those people would say: "We asked Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra and gave the daughter, yet that young man is unskilled, lazy, incapable of achieving anything, unable to provide that daughter with abundant food and clothing, and not one who takes up even small tasks. Therefore all those who associate with Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra" — from "who speak well of coming" — "and all those who are admitted to the household, it will be like this for them too," and they would recite words of dispraise. What applies to the young man should be applied in the same way to the young woman. At that time, praise and dispraise of Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra arose simultaneously.

Now at that juncture, the twelve groups of nuns had taken speech from Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra, were acting as matchmakers, and were introducing people into households that were unsuitable, and they were insulting brahmins and householders. The monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, thinking, "The Saṅgha of my female śrāvakas will understand the matter, and I shall also establish the training rule well," convened the assembly of the community of nuns on account of this occurrence, this cause, this matter, and this juncture.

The blessed buddhas act with full knowledge: they act knowingly, not unknowingly; at the right time, not at the wrong time; with purpose, not without purpose. The blessed buddhas are such that acting without purpose is averted by them as one averts a debt. As for the blessed buddhas, because they know the right time for acting with purpose, the Blessed One, a buddha, asked the twelve groups of nuns: "Nuns, is it true that you have acted in such an improper and unseemly manner?" — "Blessed One, we have indeed done so."

The blessed Buddha then rebuked the twelve groups, saying: "That which is improper for a contemplative, unsuitable, and not in accordance with proper conduct is not something to be done by one who has gone forth." Then the Blessed One rebuked them in many ways. Having done so, he declared to the assembly of nuns:

"Nuns, therefore, I shall — for the ten benefits: 'In order to gather the Saṅgha,' and so forth — having fully examined this, establish a training rule in the Vinaya for female śrāvakas," and all of this up to the establishing of the training should be stated.

"Furthermore, whatever nun, using a woman's words toward a man or a man's words toward a woman, acts as a matchmaker — even if it is only for a single meeting — this very matter constitutes a transgression from the very first occurrence, and it carries a definitive outcome: one becomes subject to expiation with a remainder in the Saṅgha.

"'Whatever nun' refers to the twelve groups of nuns. 'Using a woman's words toward a man or a man's words toward a woman' means speaking words fitting for a woman to a man, or speaking words fitting for a man to a woman. 'As a wife' — the seven kinds of wife are: one given through water-libation, one bought with wealth, one obtained by capture, one who comes of her own will, one maintained with food and clothing, one who is a companion in a lower station —"

The seventh is one who meets occasionally.

As for what is meant by "a wife given through water-libation": a woman or a girl whom her parents have given to a man by pouring water of consecration, saying, "Let this one be your wife, the mistress of your household," and who then becomes his wife and mistress of the household, and whom he guards, guards closely, conceals, and conceals carefully so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others — she is called "a wife given through water-libation."

As for what is meant by "a wife bought with wealth": a woman or a girl whom a man has purchased from her parents with much or little wealth, saying, "Let this one be my wife, the mistress of my household," and who then becomes the mistress of his household, and whom he guards, guards closely, conceals, and conceals carefully so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others — she is called "a wife bought with wealth."

As for what is meant by "a wife obtained by capture": it is like this — a king arrays his fourfold army of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry, brings down those who have not submitted and crushes those who have submitted, and commands that they be brought under his dominion. At that time, a person, having made the king his standard of victory, seizes a woman or a girl, saying, "Let this one be my wife or the mistress of my household" — from that point up to "so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others toward mine" — she is called "one obtained by capture."
