Furthermore, another case of "one obtained by capture" is this: brigands who raid cities, raid villages, and raid regions, staking their own lives, sack cities, sack villages and regions, and seize a woman or a girl, saying, "Let this one be a wife and mistress of the household for us" — from that point up to "so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others toward mine" — she too is called "one obtained by capture."

As for what is meant by "a wife who comes of her own will": a woman or a girl who, out of her own faith, inclination, and arising affection, goes to a man and speaks these words: "O son of a lord, I shall be your queen and mistress of your household," and he in turn takes her as his wife and mistress of the household — from that point up to "so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others toward mine" — she is called "a wife who comes of her own will."

As for what is meant by "a wife maintained with food and clothing": a woman or a girl who goes to a man and speaks these words: "O son of a lord, give me clothing and food, and I shall be your wife and mistress of your household," and he in turn gives her clothing, and she becomes his wife and mistress of the household — from that point up to "so that she may not go about for the sake of the desires of others toward mine" — she is called "a wife maintained with food and clothing."

As for what is meant by "a wife who is a companion in a lower station": it is like this — a woman or a girl who brings whatever wealth she has, much or little, and goes to a man, saying, "O son of a lord, please take note: let us gather together your wealth and my wealth into one, and let us live together and enjoy what we desire, and whatever sons or daughters may come to us from us both — when the time comes and we die, let us make gifts and perform meritorious deeds —"

— and may the merit of this be dedicated so that our parents, wherever they have been reborn, may follow after them in that place — and having said this, the man took her as his wife and mistress of the household, and guarded her with the thought: "Let no other go about toward this woman of mine out of desire," guarding her closely, hiding her, and hiding her very thoroughly. She is called "a wife who is a companion in a lower station."

As for what is meant by "a wife met only for a time": it is like this — a woman or a girl whom a man approaches for a period of hire, giving her wages for that time, thinking, "Let me enjoy her company for just a while," and having guarded her for that span — she is called "a wife met only for a time."

These, then, are what are called the seven wives.

Now as for what is called "the ten female companions" — what are the ten? They are: one guarded by a mother, one guarded by a father, one guarded by a brother, one guarded by a sister, one guarded by a mother-in-law, one guarded by a father-in-law, one guarded by relatives, one guarded by clan, one guarded by lineage, and tenth, one who is undisturbed.

As for what is meant by "a female companion guarded by a mother": it is like this — when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, or he has been threatened by illness, or has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another region, or has been killed, or imprisoned, or expelled, or has gone forth into renunciation, or has died — and thereupon her mother thinks: "I will guard this one of mine so that no one may approach her uninvited and go about toward her by force out of desire," and guards her, guards her closely, hides her, and hides her very thoroughly — she is called "a female companion guarded by a mother."

As for what is meant by "a female companion guarded by a father": it is like this — when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, and so forth as set out at length up to and including his death, and thereupon her father thinks: "I will guard this one of mine so that no one may approach her uninvited and go about toward her by force out of desire," and guards her, guards her closely, hides her, and hides her very thoroughly — she is called "a female companion guarded by a father."

As for what is meant by "a female companion guarded by a brother": it is like this — when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, and so forth as before, up to and including the death of both parents, and thereupon her brother thinks: "I will guard this one of mine so that no one may approach her," and so on, "and go about toward her out of desire," and guards her up to that point — she is called "a female companion guarded by a brother." Just as the account of one guarded by a brother is given, so too should the account of one guarded by a sister be stated.

As for what is meant by "a female companion guarded by a mother-in-law": it is like this — when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, and so forth, up to and including the death of both parents and of her brother, her sister, the mother-in-law, and the father-in-law — and thereupon the mother-in-law speaks these words: "Just as I look after my own child, so too do I do the same for you; I will provide you with food and clothing, dear daughter-in-law, make you happy, let you remain in comfort" — and having said this, she thinks: "I will guard this one of mine so that no one may approach her uninvited and go about toward her by force out of desire," and guards her closely, hides her, and hides her very thoroughly — she is called "a female companion guarded by a mother-in-law." Just as the account of one guarded by a mother-in-law is given, so too should the account of one guarded by a father-in-law be stated.

As for what is meant by "a female companion guarded by relatives": it is like this — when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, and so forth, up to the death of both parents, of her brother, her sister, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law, she then resides in the presence of relatives,

And the relatives, thinking "We must guard this woman of ours so that no one, without proper inquiry, may have his way with her by force," guard her, guard her closely, hide her, and hide her very thoroughly. This is called "a female companion guarded by relatives." As for what "relatives" means: one should understand it to include the seven-generation patrilineal and matrilineal lineages.

What is meant by "a female companion guarded by clan"? It is like this: when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, and so forth, up to the death of both parents, of her brother, her sister, her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and her relatives, she then resides in the presence of those who share her own clan. And those people, thinking "We must guard this woman of ours so that no one, without proper inquiry, may have his way with her by force," guard her — up to that point. This is called "a female companion guarded by clan." As for what "clan" means: it refers to the brahmin clan, the kṣatriya clan, the vaiśya clan, and the śūdra clan.

What is meant by "a female companion guarded by lineage"? It is like this: when a woman or a young girl's husband has gone mad, or his mind has become disturbed, and so forth, up to the death of both parents, of her brother, her sister, her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and her relatives, she then resides in the presence of those who share her own lineage. And those people, thinking "We must guard this woman of ours so that no one, without proper inquiry, may have his way with her by force," guard her — up to that point. This is called "a female companion guarded by lineage." As for what "lineage" means: it refers to the lineage of Kuṇḍa, the lineage of Bharadvāja, the lineage of Śāṇḍilya, the lineage of Bhāradvāja, the lineage of Maudgalya, the lineage of Garga, and the lineage of Gautama.

What is meant by "a female companion who is unattached"? She is a fully ordained nun, a female probationer, a wandering mendicant woman, a woman who does not sleep with anyone other than her husband, or a woman who observes the Dharma as the basis of her practice and discipline. These, then, are called the ten female companions.

As for "acting as go-between": this means carrying a message. "Even for a moment" means even for the briefest instant. "This Dharma" refers to this matter that is not Dharma but is presented under the name of Dharma. "She incurs a downfall from the very first" means she incurs a downfall immediately. "With expulsion included" means with the element of rejection. "Saṅgha remainder" means that this transgression rests with both Saṅghas, is connected with both Saṅghas, and depends upon both Saṅghas; the transgression is lifted by both Saṅghas and not by an individual alone. Alternatively, these eight root defeats are final with no remainder, whereas this transgression does have a remainder — and for that reason it is called "Saṅgha remainder."

Now, as to how a transgression is incurred — the intermediate summary on acting as go-between:

A message carried by two nuns,
conduct, and what precedes it,
one's own or another's territory,
written message, hand-delivered — these concern the junior nun.

If a nun herself accepts a message she herself composed, carries it there herself, and brings the reply back herself, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun herself accepts a message she herself composed, carries it there herself, and has it brought back by a delegate, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun herself accepts a message she herself composed, has it carried there by a delegate, and

brings the reply back herself, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate, herself accepts it, herself carries the message there, and herself brings the reply back, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate, herself accepts it, herself carries the message there, and has the reply brought back by a delegate, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate, herself accepts it, has the message carried there by a delegate, and herself brings the reply back, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate, herself accepts it, has the message carried there by a delegate, and has the reply brought back by a delegate, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate of a delegate, herself accepts it, herself carries the message there, and herself brings the reply back, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate of a delegate, herself accepts it, herself carries the message there, and has the reply brought back by a delegate of a delegate, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate of a delegate, herself accepts it, has the message carried there by a delegate of a delegate, and herself brings the reply back, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If a nun accepts a message composed by a delegate of a delegate, herself accepts it, has the message carried there by a delegate of a delegate, and has the reply brought back by a delegate of a delegate, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties, both carry the message there, and both bring the reply back, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred for both.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties, and then one of them says, "For now, carry the message there on her behalf and bring the reply back," and that one then carries the message there and brings the reply back on the other's behalf, a Saṅgha-remainder transgression is incurred for both.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties, and then one of them says, "I will carry the message there but I will not bring the reply back," and then whichever of the two carries the message there and also brings the reply back incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression, while the one who carries the message there but does not bring the reply back incurs two gross offenses.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties, and then one of them says, "I will neither carry the message there nor bring the reply back," and then whichever of the two carries the message there and brings the reply back incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression, while the one who neither carries the message there nor brings the reply back incurs one gross offense.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties, and both carry the message there but neither brings the reply back, both incur two gross offenses each.

If two nuns both accept the message of both parties —

and both say, "We will neither carry the message there nor bring the reply back," then both incur one gross offense each.

When a single nun is traveling on the road together with one man and one woman, if the woman says to the nun, "Noble one, can you say to that man, 'You are the husband of this woman,' or 'You are her friend,' or 'Send word to her'?" — and if the nun accepts a message of that kind and carries it there, or brings the reply back, she incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression. Likewise, if the man says to the nun, "Noble one, can you say to that woman, 'You are the wife of this man,' or 'You are his friend,' or 'Send word to him'?" — and if the nun accepts a message of that kind and carries it there, or brings the reply back, she incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression.

What applies in the case of one nun, one woman, and one man is to be set out in full for two nuns, two women, and two men as well, and likewise for many nuns, many women, and many men. And just as it applies to those traveling on the road, it is also to be set out in full for those who are standing, sitting, and lying down.

Of two novice nuns — one walking ahead of the nun and one following behind — if the one walking ahead accepts the message and the one walking ahead both carries it there and brings the reply back, the one walking ahead incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression.

If the one walking ahead accepts the message and the one walking ahead carries it there while the one following behind brings the reply back, the one walking ahead incurs two gross offenses and the one following behind incurs one gross offense.

If the one walking ahead accepts the message and the one following behind carries it there while the one walking ahead brings the reply back, the one walking ahead incurs two gross offenses and the one following behind incurs one gross offense.

If the one walking ahead accepts the message and the one following behind both carries it there and brings the reply back, the one walking ahead incurs one gross offense and the one following behind incurs two gross offenses.

If the one following behind accepts the message and the one following behind both carries it there and brings the reply back, the one following behind incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression.

If the one following behind accepts the message and the one following behind carries it there while the one walking ahead brings the reply back, the one following behind incurs two gross offenses and the one walking ahead incurs one gross offense.

If the one following behind accepts the message and the one walking ahead carries it there, while the one following behind brings the reply back, the one following behind incurs two gross offenses and the one walking ahead incurs one gross offense.

If the one following behind accepts the message and the one walking ahead both carries it there and brings the reply back, the one following behind incurs one gross offense and the one walking ahead incurs two gross offenses.

Householders are of two kinds: the principal party and the non-principal party. The principal party is defined as one who is the master in giving a girl in marriage or in taking her away by force, and who, whether present in the royal palace and its environs or present in an assembly of legal proceedings, is someone whose word, even if false, is worthy of being taken as evidence. That is called the principal party.

The non-principal party is defined as one who is not the master in giving a girl in marriage or in taking her away by force, and who, whether present in the royal palace and its environs or present in an assembly of legal proceedings, is someone whose word, even if true, does not come to be worthy of being taken as evidence. That is called the non-principal party.

If a nun accepts a message from a principal party and carries it to the principal party and also brings the reply back from the principal party, she incurs a Saṅgha-remainder transgression.

If a nun accepts a message from a principal party and carries it to the principal party, but brings the reply back from a non-principal party, she incurs two gross offenses and one wrong-doing.

If a nun accepts a message from a principal party and carries it to a non-principal party, but brings the reply back to the principal party, she incurs two gross offenses and one wrong-doing.

If a nun accepts a message from a principal party and carries it to a non-principal party and brings the reply back from a non-principal party, she incurs one gross offense and two wrong-doings.

If a nun accepts a message from a non-principal party and carries it to the non-principal party and also brings the reply back from the non-principal party, she incurs three wrong-doings.

If a nun accepts a message from a non-principal party and carries it to a principal party, but brings the reply back from a non-principal party, she incurs one gross offense and two wrong-doings.

If a nun accepts a message from a non-principal party and carries it to a non-principal party, but brings the reply back to a principal party, she incurs one gross offense and two wrong-doings.

If a nun accepts a message from a non-principal party and carries it to a principal party and also brings the reply back from a non-principal party, she incurs two gross offenses and one wrong-doing.

There are three causes by which a message becomes the carrying of a reply but not the carrying of an outgoing message. What are the three? They are: by location, by sign, and by mark.

How is it by location? It is when she says: "Whenever you see me in a pleasure grove, or in a meeting place, or at some divine site, you shall know by that that the deed has been done." That is how it is by location.

How is it by sign?

It is when she says: "Whenever you see me in the morning, or at midday, or in the evening, you shall know by that that the deed has been done." That is how it is by sign.

How is it by mark? It is when she says: "Whenever you see me having recently shaved my head, or wearing a patched robe of reddish-yellow, or carrying a bowl with a lotus-leaf rim, or a bowl with an iron handle, or a bowl of clarified butter, or a bowl of grain oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl with a cover of raw sugar — whenever you see me thus, you shall know by that that the deed has been done." That is how it is by mark.

This is the seventh fascicle of the Analysis of the Nuns' Vinaya.

There are three causes by which a message becomes both the carrying of an outgoing message and the carrying of a reply. What are the three? They are: by word, by letter, and by hand-written document.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by word and also carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by word and carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by letter and also carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by location, by sign, or by mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by word and also carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by word and carries the reply by hand-written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by hand-written document and carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by hand-written document and also carries the reply by hand-written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by word and carries the outgoing message by hand-written document and carries the reply by location, by sign, or by mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and also carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by word and carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by word and also carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by location,

she carries the reply by location, sign, or mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and also carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by written document and carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by written document and also carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by letter and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by location, sign, or mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and also carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by word and carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by word and also carries the reply by word, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and carries the reply by location, sign, or mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and also carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by letter and carries the reply by written document, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by letter and also carries the reply by letter, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a nun accepts a commission by written document and carries the outgoing message by written document and carries the reply by location, sign, or mark, she incurs a Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

When the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — are combined, if it is during the time of fighting and the following conditions also apply: the fighting has not yet ceased, the grass has not been cut, the three pebbles have not been scattered, sand has been given but she has not been released, she has not been established as a witness that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed — if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as a single offense.

When the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — are combined, if it is after the time of fighting and the following conditions also apply: it is not during the time of fighting, the grass has not been cut, the three pebbles have not been scattered, sand has been given but she has not been released, she has not been established as a witness that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed — and all these are combined,

and if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as three offenses.

When a nun combines the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — beginning from those, up through the scattering of the three pebbles, together with: sand has been given but she has not been released, she has not been established as a witness that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed — and if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as three offenses and one grave offense.

When a nun combines the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — beginning from those, up through: sand has been given and she has been released, together with: she has not been established as a witness that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed — and if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as three offenses and two grave offenses.

When a nun combines the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — beginning from those, up through: she has been established as a witness that she is not a wife, together with: the bell has not been proclaimed — and if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as three offenses, three grave offenses, and one Saṅgha remainder.

When a nun combines the first three types of wife — one given with water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by abduction — beginning from those, up through: the bell has been proclaimed — and if all these are combined and they are in accord, it counts as three offenses, four grave offenses, and two Saṅgha remainders.

When a nun combines the other types of wife — those outside these three — during the time of fighting and after the time of fighting, and they are in accord, it counts in every case as a Saṅgha remainder.

If a nun goes to a layman's household and says: "Why do you not bring this young man into your home?" — that becomes a grave offense. If she says: "Why do you not send this grown girl away as a bride?" — that becomes a grave offense. If she says: "Why do you not send this young man to a weaver?" — that becomes a grave offense. If she says: "Why do you not lead this girl to a householder?" — that becomes a grave offense.

If a nun goes to a householder's home and says even this much: "Householder, why do you not settle those who serve you?" — that becomes an offense. Likewise with respect to a female householder, it also becomes an offense. For a first-time act and similar cases, there is no transgression.

Here ends the first Saṅgha remainder of the Analysis of the Nuns' code.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) was residing at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove. At that time, when a misdeed arose, there lived in that place a great warrior named Rājasena, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, of great enjoyment, whose domain of possessions was vast and extensive, who equaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled Vaiśravaṇa in riches, and who was abundantly furnished with gold and wealth. He took a wife from his own social rank and sported with her, rejoiced with her, and lived in delight with her. Yet though they sported together, rejoiced together, and lived in delight together, there was neither a son nor a daughter born to them. Having no son, he longed deeply for one, and for the sake of a son he made petition to many hundreds and thousands of gods — namely: to Brahmā, to Indra (Śakra), to the proximate gods, to Yama, to the Sun, to the malformed ones, to Kumāra the Ever-Young, to the Lord of Creatures, to Viṣṇu,

to the Lord of Power, to Śagā, to the All-Doer, to Revatī, to the God of Wind-Butter, to the God of Earth, to the God of Water, to the God of Fire, to the God of Wind, to the Guardian of the Regions, to the Noble-Born, to the Evil-Eyed, to the son of Vaiśravaṇa, to Precious Jewel, to Auspicious Fullness, to the Five-Honored, to the Five-Receivers, to the twenty-eight yakṣa generals, to the Robber-Woman attended by a retinue of five hundred, to the god of the pleasure garden, to the god of the forest, to the god of the crossroads, to the god of the triple junction, to the god who receives the torma offering, to the god born alongside, to the gods who are harmonious with the Dharma and who constantly attend, and to many other hundreds and thousands of gods besides.

Now there is a worldly saying to the effect that sons and daughters are born through the power of prayer to the gods. Yet this is not actually so. If it were, then, like a wheel-turning king, each such man would have a thousand sons. Rather, sons and daughters come to be born when six conditions are simultaneously present. What are those six? The parents must have accumulated the karma by which they would obtain a child; the child must have accumulated the karma by which it would obtain those parents; the mother must be in a fit state and have the right monthly season; the parents must be united in desire; and a gandharva (an intermediate being, a consciousness seeking rebirth) must be present nearby. Moreover, the gandharva must have entered with a mind that is either attached to both of those persons, or hostile to them — either frame of mind will do. When these six conditions are present together, sons and daughters are born.

So while that man was earnestly occupied with making petition to hundreds and thousands of gods, a being renowned for the great power of its meritorious karmic ripening — one who had planted roots of virtue before previous buddhas, who was in its final existence, who was seeking conduct befitting that stage, who had weakened its bonds, who had seized upon the provisions for liberation, who was turned toward nirvāṇa, who had turned away from saṃsāra, who had no concern for death and rebirth in any of the realms of existence, and who was holding its final body — passed away from the realm of the gods and entered the womb of that wife.

Now among women, some who are knowledgeable by nature know five things perfectly. They know when a man has become desirous and when a man has ceased to be desirous. They know the right time and the right monthly season. They know whether a being has entered the womb and also from whence that being has entered. And they know whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, the being rests leaning on the right side of the womb, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning on the left side.

Perceiving that the being who had entered her womb rested leaning to the right side, she understood that it would become a boy, and filled with delight, joy, and great happiness, she spoke to her husband: "Lord's son, I have a pleasing word to offer you." He replied: "Good woman, may you receive news pleasing to gods and men alike. What pleasing news is it?" She said: "Lord's son, a being has entered my womb, and just as my right side has been uncomfortable without being crushed, I know I have obtained a son."

Then Rājyadatta, who was counted among the great heroes, heard this and was filled with delight, joy, and great happiness; and with a face like a blooming lotus, he spoke these words of rejoicing: "Good woman, may that son of yours be born just as he is! May I see the face of the dear son for whom I have longed, the son I have thought of for so long a time, whose birth may be fulfilled just as I have wished, who is born in harmony with me and not in disharmony, who will carry out my affairs, who will nurse me in return when I have nursed him, and who will make use of my wealth and possessions,

who will cause my lineage and bloodline to endure for a long time to come; who will himself be wealthy, possessed of great riches, with vast and extensive holdings, so that my own lordship will not decline; and who, when we have died and passed our time, will on our behalf give gifts and make merit, and will follow us to whatever realm these two are born in" — and may he thus make the dedication of offerings. Knowing that a being had entered her womb, from that time forward he rejoiced in his wife, held her in great honor, and cherished her with love. He had her dwell without discomfort in an upper chamber, and he had her attended and cared for with whatever was needed for the cold in cold weather and for the warmth in warm weather — with food and drink prescribed by physicians, neither too cold nor too hot, neither too pungent nor too sharp, neither too salty nor too sour, neither too sweet nor too bitter, neither too oily nor too rough — food and drink entirely free from pungency, sharpness, saltiness, sourness, sweetness, bitterness, oiliness, and roughness. To nurture the being dwelling in the womb, he dressed his wife in robes of many varied colors, adorned her wrists with bracelets of gold, jewels, and pearls, and had her wear necklaces and pendants, armlets, shoulder ornaments, and earrings with rings. Her eyes were painted with eye salve, and her face was made beautiful with red lac marks. Her teeth were white as the flower of the kumuda lily, as silver, as snow, as pearls; her necklace was white as the jasmine flower, as the moon, as a swan, as cow's milk, as a conch, as a lotus root — pure and unstained; her waist was bound with a golden belt; and her feet were made beautiful with ankle ornaments. She was like a golden offering-pillar covered with flowers. Thus, through the merit accumulated and virtue performed by the being who had entered the womb, there arose in the upper chamber a harmonious and concordant retinue playing lutes, vihuelas, clay drums, great drums, and sweet-sounding musical instruments, and they played and made merry in that upper chamber just as divine daughters roam through a pleasure grove. They moved from one great, well-arranged couch to another, from small seat to small seat, without ever descending to the floor; and no one among them caused any unpleasant sound to arise. That household, too, grew and flourished with wealth, grain, sesame, gold, treasury stores, granaries, male servants, female servants, workers, those who live on dairy, bipeds, quadrupeds, and the like — just as the great ocean is daily filled by five hundred rivers, so did that household grow and flourish. After a time, the wives of the five hundred ministers counted among the great heroes also had beings enter their wombs. Then, when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and the boy born was handsome, pleasing to look upon, beautiful, fair in color like the stalk of a lotus flower, with a head like a parasol, long arms, prominent hips at birth, unbroken brow-lines meeting at the center, a high bridge of the nose, a throat like a lion, an upper torso like a lion, and long shoulders. On that very same day the sons of the five hundred great ministers counted among the great heroes were also born. Five hundred mares also foaled. Similarly, up through the one named Ratna, all should be related in full. His kinsmen gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — the third seven-day period — a birth-feast was held in the city.

All of this, up through the question "What shall the boy be named?" should be related in full. Among those present at the naming ceremony, some said: "He was born together with wealth, and moreover he is the son of one who counts among the great heroes; therefore let his name be given as Śūraputranandana — Son of the Hero, Wealth." Others said: "He was born into wealth in the same way, and his father too counts among the great heroes; let the boy's name therefore be given as Śūraputranandana." And so he was named Śūraputranandana. All of this, from that point up through "He was entrusted to eight nurses," and from "With milk, with curds, with clarified butter, with fresh butter" up through "He was nourished and raised" — all of it should be related in full.

A serving girl took him up on her shoulder and went out into the street. There a brahmin skilled in reading bodily marks saw him and spoke these words: "This two-footed one is a field of merit" — and all of this up through "He took him from his father" should be related. And from "Having anointed him with fine sesame oil and sweet-smelling unguents" up through "Having made offerings, he was escorted back home" — all of this likewise should be related in full.

When he had grown up, he was enrolled in the study of letters and arithmetic. All of this, from that point onward, including arithmetic, and as for others, he became sharp-minded and accomplished. In all the arts and occupational disciplines of the warrior class — riding elephants at the shoulder, riding horses, the techniques of the chariot, the techniques of the sword, techniques of hurling, of pushing backward, of pushing forward, of guiding with the iron hook, of casting the lasso, of hurling the single-pointed vajra, techniques of throwing the wheel, techniques of shooting great arrows, modes of grasping, modes of stepping, binding the topknot, cutting, hacking, striking, splitting, slashing, striking from a distance, striking with a ringing sound, pressing on vital points, striking so nothing escapes, and striking with great force — in all of these he became fully accomplished and perfected. In the four stances, the five throws, and all eighteen branches of knowledge he became supremely sharp-minded and accomplished.

His father also had three pleasure gardens made ready for him — a winter garden, a spring garden, and a summer garden. The winter garden was entirely warm. The spring garden was entirely cool. The summer garden was neither too warm nor too cold. The three circles of his wives — the chief, the middle, and the lesser — were also established. And there, on the roof of the upper palace, together with the female musicians, he took his pleasure with those who drew forth the sweet sounds of flutes, lutes, clay drums, wooden drums, iron cymbals, and melodious music — just as sentient beings who have accumulated merit and done wholesome deeds come to experience the fruits of their own merit.

Then at another time, his companions went out saying they had gone deer hunting. He asked them: "Friends, where have you come from?" They replied: "We went deer hunting." He asked: "What is this deer hunting?" They said: "One goes to a remote place, kills some deer, brings back the meat, and eats it — that is what one does." He said to them: "Those deer dwell in remote places, eating grass and drinking water — what harm have they done to you that you kill them?" They replied: "In truth, they have done us not the slightest harm. Nevertheless, we kill them for sport." He said: "Therefore, please do not take delight in this, and do not go along with it." They replied: "As it is, even though you do not wish to go, the idea of your not going is out of the question — that conduct is not good."

They thought to themselves: "If we do not bring him along, there may well come a time when we ourselves are not permitted to go" — and so it was up to that point.

Those companions went to find the parents of the youth Norgyé and said these words to them: "Father and Mother, since the young man is fierce and of great prowess, if the kings of the sun-realm beneath were to hear of this" — and so on up to — "and the queens of Śla too would be increased in number."

Then, as far as the passage that reads: "The father and mother went to him and the companions told him to do as they said" — and up to "Excellent!" — he, being respectful toward his parents and thinking: "I cannot turn back their words. Since my parents have instructed me, I must do as they say," he accepted the proposal.

Then the parents, realizing that their son intended to go, instructed the servants who lived in their own village and those who lived by selling milk curds: "Norgyé the youth is going to a remote place for game — you too should go along." And those, following the instruction, arrived on the second day; and Norgyé, accompanied by five hundred youths who were included in the company of hunters, along with the many people who lived by selling milk curds and numerous servants surrounding him on all sides, departed for the hunt.

Then his companions said to him: "Friend, will you go to drive the game, or will you sit in the blind?" He thought: "If I leave these people behind in the blind and I myself drive the game, once it has been driven together they will slaughter most of the animals. Rather, it would be better for me to sit in the blind." So he instructed those others to go and drive the game forward, and they were delighted and said: "Friend, we gladly agree." And they thought: "He has trained in four positions and five elevated places, so most of the game will be slain."

He sat in the blind holding a quiver filled with a thousand arrows. When those companions had driven together most of the animals from all sides, and those frightened deer came rushing toward the youth, the compassionate youth saw them as they arrived in their terror, and his heart became uneasy; he was seized with compassion, and at that moment he spoke these verses:

To give to all sentient beings
and to feel love for a single being —
the love felt for that one being alone
surpasses giving to all sentient beings.

The deer fled like the wind, and though some had been tormented by others and were scattered, he did not release a single arrow. Now, since all sentient beings share the one conventional consciousness of awareness, those animals thought: "This great noble one is compassionate," and so, feeling well-disposed toward him, they fled without fear.

Then Norgyé thought: "If some of my companions hear that I have not shot any arrows, they will be displeased." He then thought: "In order to prevent my mother from being scolded on my account, and in order to let people know that I am practiced in archery, I will shoot arrows." Having thought it through in this way — so that no harm would come to any sentient being — he shot his arrows with such skill that they went between the antlers, between the limbs, through the fur, and into the ears, and he let them fly. In this way he shot all those thousand arrows without causing harm to a single sentient being.

Then, when those deer had passed through and scattered, his companions came and sat with him in the blind —

They said among themselves: "Today we have surrounded nearly all the deer from every side, and this arrow-prince is skilled in the four stances and five modes of shooting. If many deer had been killed today, we could have carried off heavy loads — but in the end he has committed a single grave fault." Such were their thoughts.

When they approached him, they saw that he had not killed even one deer. Seeing this, they said to the arrow-prince: "Friend, where have those deer gone?"

He replied: "They fled and went away."

They said: "Did you not shoot your arrows?"

He replied: "I shot them — look, the quivers stand empty."

They thought to themselves: "For one of such renowned skill with the arrow — a reputation that is proven — not to know even one of the four modes, let alone all four, what more need be said?" And with that thought they began to mock and reproach his companions.

Then he came to his own home, went up to the roof of the upper palace chamber, rested his arms on the parapet, and turned inward in contemplation.

His parents came and spoke to him, saying — and the passage continues to the point where they ask: "Son, why did you not kill the deer?"

He replied: "Father and mother, do you hold me dear?"

"Son, you are most dear to us."

"If someone were to separate me from my life, what would become of you?"

They replied: "We would be in great pain and deep distress."

He said: "Then do you not also cherish your own lives?"

They said: "We cherish them most dearly."

"Then why do you set me to the task of taking the lives of others? And furthermore, have you not yourselves taught me this:

With love and compassion for all beings,
abandon killing, slaughter, and the binding of life.
Just as you cherish and protect your own life,
so too protect the lives of all others.

Did you not speak these very words?" — and the passage continues to that point.

Then those parents, having truly understood their son's resolve, said: "Son, in that case, go back up to the roof of the upper palace chamber and take your pleasure there with your circle of consorts."

Thereupon, from the roof of the upper palace chamber, the arrow-prince called out: "Whether you go on two feet or on none, whether you know medicine, spell-lore, or secret mantras — who among you is there that can liberate me completely from the wilderness of cyclic existence?"

At that time there were in the land the six teachers who were corrupt and who, though not omniscient, put on the proud display of omniscience — and so the passage continues from there.

He went into the presence of Kāśyapa and said: "What is your Dharma practice? What instructions do you give your disciples? What is the fruit of dwelling in the holy life under you, and what are its benefits?"

Kāśyapa replied: "Young man, my view is this, and I speak accordingly: There is no giving. There is no offering. There is no sacrificial fire. There is no good conduct. There is no bad conduct. There is no karmic maturation ripening from deeds of good or bad conduct. There is no this world. There is no world beyond. There is no mother. There is no father. There are no beings born by spontaneous generation. In this world there exist no arhats who have rightly gone forth and rightly entered in, who by their own direct knowledge have realized, accomplished, and thoroughly understood both this world and the world beyond, and who declare: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done.'"

— ending with the words "there are none who know anything beyond this present existence" — down to the passage concluding: "This teacher too has entered upon a wrong path; he pursues an evil path. The wise should abandon such a path, together with its dangers, exactly as it is" — and the verse that was spoken:

One who teaches wrong views and leads astray,
who is renowned for teaching what is inferior —
if his Dharma is of such a kind,
what indeed is his non-Dharma like?

— down through the passage concluding: "In the same way, those six teachers departed, struck like empty vessels."

It is the nature of reality of all blessed buddhas to survey the worlds three times by day and three times by night — six times in every day and night — with the buddha-eye, perceiving: who has come to ruin, who has come to suffering, who has come to misery, who has come to discomfort, who has come to suffering and misery and discomfort; those whose root of virtue has not yet been produced, they will cause it to be produced; those who have already produced it, they will cause it to grow; those whose root of virtue has not yet fully ripened, they will cause it to fully ripen; those whose root of virtue has already fully ripened, they will cleave it open with the sword of wisdom; who is to be tamed by a buddha, who is to be tamed by a śrāvaka, who is to be tamed by both a buddha and a śrāvaka; who is disposed toward aversion, who is disposed toward attachment, who is disposed toward delusion, who is disposed toward attachment and aversion and delusion; who has been harmed by whatever fault — those who lack the noble wealth will be established in lordship over the riches of the noble wealth; those who have sunk into the mire of misconduct, they will be drawn out by the hand; whoever is to be raised up from the lower realms will be established in the fruit of the higher realms and liberation. Thus the buddha-eye is directed in constant watchful regard.

And again it was spoken in verse:

The ocean may pass beyond its bounds,
the abode of makaras and sea creatures;
but a buddha, in love toward those to be tamed,
does not pass beyond the right time.

Then the Blessed One, with the buddha-eye — his unobscured eye of primordial wisdom — surveyed all and considered. He understood in his mind that Gyalbü Nor had in former times generated roots of virtue before the buddhas of the past, had offered aspirational prayers, had ripened results, and was like one who wished to cleave them open with the sword. The Blessed One then thought: "By what means will he be tamed? Will he be tamed by a śrāvaka, or will he be tamed by a buddha? Will he be tamed by conduct, or will he be tamed by the teaching of Dharma?" — and so the Blessed One considered. When the Blessed One considered "if he is to be tamed by conduct, by whose conduct will he be tamed?" — at that point the venerable Aśvajit went to the region of Śṛgālavati, and in that region a lotus grove was to be found in which insects dwelt.

Then the venerable Aśvajit, in the early morning — from the words "having put on his lower robe" — down through: Gyalbü Nor, sitting atop the roof of his upper mansion, saw the venerable Aśvajit walking, turning, flexing and extending his limbs, wearing his patched robe and dharma-robe and carrying his alms-bowl — a beautiful sight.

When Gyalbü Nor saw the venerable Aśvajit, he then spoke this verse:

Those who live by the Dharma of signs —
of these I have seen many here.
One who is peaceful and abides in peace —
such as this one I have never seen.

— down to the end of that passage.

From the words "he sent a man" — down through the passage concluding: "having observed his conduct and returned, he spoke to the youth."

Then the venerable Gyalbü Nor, urged on by his root of virtue and wishing to see — from that point down to what was done so that he would become truly delighted — he sat down, and said to him: "Are you a teacher, or are you a śrāvaka?" The venerable Aśvajit then spoke in verse. From the words "what is the difference between Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and a white mustard seed?" —

What is the difference between the ocean and a tiny puddle left by a cow's hoofprint? What is the difference between the vast net of the sun's rays and a firefly's glow? Such is the difference between a fully awakened buddha, that treasury of qualities, and a śrāvaka.

Down to the end of that verse.

From the words "he came before his two parents and made his entreaty" — down through the words "permission was not granted," and then through the passage ending "food was withheld for a full day," and then his parents came and said to him: "You do not know suffering — celibate practice is difficult to maintain. It is difficult to rejoice in solitude. It is difficult to live in isolated dwellings, in forest edges, and in remote wilderness. For as long as you live, you would have to dwell together with dangerous wild beasts. For as long as you live, you would have to remain far removed from the pleasures and amusements of people. Come, my son — stay here, give gifts, and enjoy the objects of desire."

Down to the end of that passage.

Then, from the words "having granted permission" — down through the passage ending "having properly developed bodily strength and power," and then down through the passage ending "a proclamation was made: all those who wish to go forth may do so today — for the father desired that the youth Nor go forth into homelessness."

Then those who were companions of Nor thought to themselves: "This youth Nor, though so young and so desirous of happiness, has given up the happiness of home life and has decisively gone forth into homelessness. What then should we do?" Reflecting thus, one of them spoke up clearly and said: "Enough of this — let us too go forth." And so the youth Nor, together with five hundred young men, went to where the venerable Aśvajit was staying. Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at the feet of Aśvajit and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the youth Nor said to the venerable Aśvajit: "Venerable one, please bestow upon us the going-forth and full ordination as monks in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. We shall practice the celibate life under you."

Then the venerable Aśvajit in due order gave the youth Nor the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him. He recited and meditated upon all three scriptural collections, and thereby became an arhat — free from attachment to the three realms, equal in regard to clay and gold, of a mind like unto space and like unto the palm of the hand, equal in regard to dung and sandalwood, having torn apart the shell of the egg of ignorance, having attained clear knowing, superknowledge, and the analytic knowledges, turning his back on becoming, on the gains and honors associated with desire, worthy of reverence, honor, and open praise from gods of every rank, both principal and attendant.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, established this as the regular custom: there are two great assemblies — at the middle month of the rains, at the time of performing the rains retreat, and on the fifteenth day of the middle month of autumn. Those who at the middle month of the rains, at the time of performing the rains retreat, received instruction and guidance, having passed the rains in towns, villages, districts, and royal residences — when the fifteenth day of the middle month of autumn arrived, they would recount what they had understood, and ask their seniors about it. Just as this was so for the Blessed One, the buddha, so too was it so for the great śrāvakas. Thus, when the venerable Aśvajit sent those who were his co-residents and attendants to pass the rains retreat in towns, villages, districts, and royal residences, and when on the fifteenth day of the middle month of autumn they came to where the venerable Aśvajit was staying,

the venerable Nandaka saw them. And seeing those who had lived the holy life, he went out to meet them and, speaking kind words, gladly welcomed them, and received their robes, staffs, begging bowls for rinsing the head, water-strainers, hats, sandals, and belts. Those monks then went to where their preceptor was staying, paid their respects, recounted what they had understood, and asked their seniors about it. And the venerable Nandaka saw those who were going to Rājagṛha to visit the Blessed One and to pay their respects to the Blessed One. Seeing them, he went to where their teacher was the same and their preceptor was the same, and said to them: "Where are you all going?" They replied: "We have already seen our preceptor; now we are going to see the Buddha, the Blessed One." Then the venerable Nandaka thought to himself: "If by relying on a preceptor and a spiritual friend I have seen the dharmakāya of the Blessed One, yet I have not seen his form body, then I too shall go to where the Blessed One is." Having thought this, Nandaka spoke to his preceptor as follows: "Preceptor, since by relying on a preceptor and a spiritual friend I have seen the dharmakāya of the Blessed One, yet have not seen his form body, I now wish to behold his form body." When he had said this, Aśvajit replied to Nandaka: "My son, Tathāgatas, arhats, and perfectly awakened buddhas are extremely rare to behold, like the udumbara flower. My son, go and behold the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha." Then the venerable Nandaka, given leave by his preceptor, arose and went together with those who shared the same preceptor to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma to many hundreds in his retinue. The Blessed One, from a great distance, saw Nandaka coming. Seeing him, the Blessed One said: "Nandaka, come here! Welcome! You have come at the right time." At that time the Blessed One then arranged the lodgings in a mixed manner: sūtra-holders together with sūtra-holders, Vinaya-holders together with sūtra-holders, sūtra-holders together with those who hold the Māmakā, Vinaya-holders together with sūtra-holders, Vinaya-holders together with those who hold the Māmakā — and in the same way all three-fold combinations were to be applied. Then the Blessed One thought: "This Nandaka, in regard to the buddhas of former times, made the aspiration prayer: 'May I become, for the Blessed One, the foremost in distributing lodgings and assigning food.'" And thereafter, up to that point, the Blessed One declared: "One who distributes lodgings and is endowed with five qualities should not be appointed if not yet appointed, and if already appointed should be dismissed. What are the five? One who goes by desire, one who goes by aversion, one who goes by delusion, one who goes by fear, and one who does not know which lodgings have been allocated and which have not. The virtuous counterpart is the opposite of these." Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, Nandaka is to be appointed as distributor of lodgings" — and then, having arranged the lodgings, the act is to be performed: "Noble members of the Saṅgha, please listen. If Nandaka is willing to serve as the Saṅgha's distributor of lodgings,

"If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it is agreeable, let the Saṅgha consent; and we will appoint Nandaka as distributor of lodgings for the Saṅgha" — up to that point is the motion. After that, the act is to be performed in the proper form.

Once Nandaka had been appointed as distributor of lodgings for the Saṅgha, he began to assign lodgings differently to different monks. He assigned those who mastered the sūtras together with other masters of the sūtras; those who mastered the Vinaya together with other masters of the Vinaya; those who mastered the Mātṛkā together with other masters of the Mātṛkā; those who were newcomers together with other newcomers; those who practised Yoga together with other practitioners of Yoga. Those who had attained the fruit of stream-entry he assigned together with those who were once-returners; those who had attained the fruit of once-returning he assigned together with the non-returners; and the non-returners he assigned together with the arhats. In this way he assigned lodgings, pairing monk with compatible monk, so that their conversations would be mutually beneficial, well-reasoned, and the side of virtue would increase.

At that time the venerable Nandaka distributed lodgings by means of his supernatural powers. To those who came earlier in the night he emitted light from one finger as he assigned lodgings. To those who came later in the night he emitted light from two fingers; and likewise from three, four, and five fingers in turn.

Then those monks thought: "This has been done by one who acts in accordance with the Dharma." What had not been understood became understood, and what had already been understood became understood in an even more distinguished way.

After this had been done, the reputation spread in all four directions that the venerable Nandaka distributed lodgings while displaying supernatural miraculous feats. At that time those who were astonished came by day to witness it for themselves, staying in the vicinity of the Grove of Light and waiting through sunset until night fell. To them as well the venerable one likewise displayed his supernatural miraculous feats and assigned lodgings.

Now in Rājagṛha there were donors and patrons who offered food to the Saṅgha in three grades. Some offered the finest; some offered the middling; some offered the inferior. Those households that offered the finest were known to the group of six monks in advance, so they went there alone. Where the middling was offered, their companions and attendants went. Where the inferior was offered, the ordinary monks were directed to go. At that time there was a householder named Supriya, who was regarded as the foremost among those who offered the finest. The group of six monks would go there one after another by turns: on the first day, Nanda and Upananda ate there; on the second day, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka; on the third day, Chanda and Udāyin. The householder asked them: "Noble ones, are there no other monks in the Grove of Light? How is it that none of you ever come to take a meal here at the invitation of others, yet you alone come again and again?" They said: "Householder, you do not know."

"Though there are monks in the Grove of Light, each day they engage in all manner of eating, drinking, and other indulgences. How could they eat the food you offer, fine as it is? We come solely to benefit you." Then the householder said: "Noble ones, if you noble ones do not act for my benefit, who else would do so?" He said this.

Then at another time a monk was making a tour southward in order to see the Blessed One, and traveling along he came in due course to the Grove of Light. That morning he had put on his robe, taken his alms bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to walk the alms round. As he was walking along the road, the householder Supriya saw him and thought: "This is someone I have not seen before." He spoke to him and said: "Venerable one, where have you come from?" He replied: "From the south." "Why?" "In order to see the Blessed One." "And where have you taken up residence?" He replied: "In the Grove of Light." "Why are you walking the alms round?" The monk replied: "Can one cut off eating?" "Venerable one, do the donors in the Grove of Light not presently offer the Saṅgha clean and plentiful food, drink, and various kinds of fine provisions?" The monk said: "Householder, if that were so, would I come to your locality for alms?" When the householder heard the monk's words, suspicion arose in him regarding the group of six: "They speak one way to me, yet this monk speaks otherwise." He escorted that monk, saying: "Please set your burden down a moment; if you will allow me to serve you your meal for today's worth, please accept me as your follower." And so he led the monk away with him.

The two monks appointed by the group of six also arrived. The householder made them comfortable, served them a great abundance of clean and excellent food and drink, and when the meal was finished the householder said to the two from the group of six: "Noble ones, you have been teaching me the Dharma, one lesson at a time, each day — yet today I have heard the Dharma from this monk who has never come before." The two then dedicated the merit of the offering and departed.

Then the householder Supriya sat before that monk and said to him: "Noble one, was the meal I served you today excellent, or was it poor?" He replied: "Donor, from the time I set out from the south until this very day, I have never eaten provisions of this quality." The householder said further: "Noble one, these monks constantly say to me that this food is poor — what sort of thing is that?" The monk replied: "They did that in order to ensure that no one else would come to this house." "Venerable one, why do other monks not come to this house?" "Householder, if others were to come here, what would an elephant do when sprinkled with water?" He thought to himself, "That is exactly so," and said to him: "Venerable one, it is a pleasure to meet you — now please speak a word of Dharma." And the monk, having given instruction through a discourse on the Dharma, departed.

Then the householder Supriya, on that occasion, addressed the monks and spoke thus: "I have laid out a meal's worth of provisions for the Saṅgha. If monks appointed by the Saṅgha come and make use of it, I will honor that pledge without breaking it. But if that is not the case, then leaving the things I have set out to be given as charity just where they are, I will not offer them house by house to individuals."

Then those monks thought to themselves: "What kind of transgression is this?" — and reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, Jyotishka should be appointed as the one to assign food." When the Saṅgha, by a motion-and-second act of the Saṅgha, had appointed the venerable Jyotishka as the food assigner, the venerable Jyotishka surveyed all the donor households to determine which ones offered superior provisions, which ones offered middling provisions, and which ones offered inferior provisions. Having made that survey, he appointed the elder monks to receive superior provisions, the middle-ranked monks to receive middling provisions, and the junior monks to receive inferior provisions. On the second day, the elders received the inferior provisions, the juniors received the middling provisions, and the middle-ranked received the superior. On the third day, the elders received the middling provisions, the middle-ranked received the inferior, and the juniors received the superior. In this manner he assigned the monks to their meals by rotation. As for monks who arrived unexpectedly, on the first day they were assigned to the superior provisions, on the second day to the middling, on the third day to the inferior, and on the fourth day they were made familiar with the layout of the streets and lanes. When the Saṅgha was thus arranged for meals in due sequence according to seniority, there was no jumping out of order.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, among my śrāvaka monks — those who apportion lodgings and those who assign food — this Jyotishka is the foremost."

At that time two monks, Mitra and Jātila, were traveling from region to region and arrived by stages at Rājagṛha. The venerable Jyotishka assigned those two their lodging and quarters as well. When morning came, Mitra and Jātila said: "Venerable ones, who is the food assigner?" A certain monk said to the two of them: "It is Jyotishka." The two of them then said to the venerable Jyotishka: "Jyotishka, please assign us our food."

So the venerable Jyotishka assigned those two, on the first day, to the households that offered superior provisions.

Then Mitra and Jātila, in the morning, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and made their way to the donor's house where they had been assigned. But that householder had lost his one beloved and pleasing son to death, and consumed by grief over the child's death, he had not prepared food for the monks. The two arrived unannounced, and the householder saw them. Seeing them, he asked the members of the household: "Has any food been set out for the monks?" They replied: "None at all." He thought to himself: "Already the death of my son is one disaster — why should I be saddled with a second?" Thinking thus, he offered them some poor quality food. The two ate it. Having eaten, they thought to themselves: "What we heard is one thing, and what we have experienced is another — we have ended up eating inferior food. Yet tomorrow we shall eat superior provisions." With that thought, on the second day the two were assigned to a household that offered middling provisions, and they went there — from this point forward...

...up to and including the words "the same fault occurred there." On the third day the two were assigned to go to a household of wicked patrons. Now, arhats do not engage their gnosis with deliberate intention, and since the two had eaten poor food repeatedly, their bodies became extremely weakened.

Then the two monks, Beloved Friend and Earth-Born, thought to themselves: "Alas, what suffering! Alas, how unbearable! The venerable Gyadbu Nor has deliberately had us eat inferior food three times in succession, leaving us utterly weak in body. We must find some way to steal food." So they resolved.

Now at that time the sister of the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born — a nun named Beloved Sister — was residing in Rājagṛha at the royal pleasure garden, in the nuns' rains retreat quarters. The nun Beloved Sister, becoming aware that the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born had departed, went to where they were. Arriving there, she prostrated with her head at the feet of the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born, and sat down to one side. While the nun Beloved Sister sat to one side, the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born would not converse with her, would not speak of how they had come, would not look at her, and would not glance at her at all.

Then the nun Beloved Sister spoke these words to the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born: "Noble ones, why will you not converse with me, not speak of how you have come, not look at me, not glance at me? Your sister — we two, your sister — have been made utterly weak in body by the venerable Gyadbu Nor, who three times in succession fed us inferior food. Have you just cast that aside? Noble ones, then what am I to do about it? Sister, come here. Go to where the Blessed One is, and say to him: 'Venerable one, thus it is — the noble Gyadbu Nor has engaged in unchaste conduct with me, and a defeat has occurred. That is unseemly and not in accordance with the rule.' And we two will tell the Blessed One: 'It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata — exactly as our sister has reported, so too do we confirm it.'"

When she had spoken thus, the nun Beloved Sister said to the two of them: "Noble ones, how could I slander a monk who is pure and without transgression with a matter that has no basis, accusing him of a fault entailing defeat? Sister, for as long as you do not say such a thing, for that long we two will not converse with you, will not speak of how we have come, will not look at you, will not glance at you."

Then the nun Beloved Sister sat for a short while without saying anything, and spoke these words to the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born: "Noble one, very well then — I shall do what is to be done. Sister, for that reason, stay here until we two have reached where the Blessed One is, and after that, you come."

Then the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, they prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Then the nun Beloved Sister, knowing that the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born had not been gone long, went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, she prostrated with her head at the two feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the nun Beloved Sister addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable One, it is unseemly and improper that the noble Beloved Friend has engaged in unchaste conduct with me and thereby incurred a defeat."

The two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, it is just as she says. Sugata, it is exactly so. We too affirm what our sister has reported."

At that time the venerable Beloved Friend was sitting right there in that assembly. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Beloved Friend:

"Beloved Friend, did you hear what was said?"

"Blessed One, I heard it."

"Beloved Friend, what is the truth of the matter for you?"

"As I truly am, the Blessed One knows. As I truly am, the Sugata knows."

The Blessed One declared: "Beloved Friend, if you remember, say 'I remember.' If you do not remember, say 'I do not remember.'"

"Blessed One, I do not remember. Sugata, I do not remember."

At that time the venerable Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa was sitting to one side behind the Blessed One, holding a yak-tail fan and fanning the Blessed One. Then the venerable Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable One, the nun Beloved Sister went to where the Blessed One was and said: 'Venerable One, it is unseemly and improper that the noble Beloved Friend has engaged in unchaste conduct with me and thereby incurred a defeat.' And the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born also said to the Blessed One: 'Blessed One, it is just as she says. Sugata, it is exactly so. We too affirm precisely what our sister has reported.' So what is there to say to the venerable Beloved Friend? Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa, that is why I asked him directly. Whatever he is willing to answer, let him answer accordingly."

"But if the nun Beloved Sister were to come to where I am and say: 'Venerable One, it is unseemly and improper that the noble Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa has engaged in unchaste conduct with me and thereby incurred a defeat,' and the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born were also to say: 'Blessed One, it is just as she says. Sugata, it is exactly so. We too affirm precisely what our sister has reported' — in that case, Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa, how would you respond?"

"Venerable One, I would say: 'I remember,' or I would say: 'I do not remember.'"

"For the moment, you foolish man — if even you would say as much, then why should the monk Beloved Friend, who is pure and without downfall, not speak up?"

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you should regard the monk Beloved Friend as one who possesses mindfulness. As for the nun Beloved Sister, since she has made her own admission, deal with her accordingly through formal procedure. As for the two monks Beloved Friend and Earth-Born — what did you see? How did you see it? Where did you see it? Where were you when you saw it? Investigate this thoroughly and question them carefully as to why they went there." Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and proceeded to the assembly hall for the midday rest. Shortly after the Blessed One had entered for the midday rest, the many monks, realizing it,

When they had been questioned and investigated thoroughly in this way, the two of them spoke as follows: "Venerable ones, the pārajika defeat for unchaste conduct has not come upon the venerable Beloved Friend. However, we — because the venerable Beloved Friend forced us to eat bad food three times in succession — became wracked with hunger and our bodies became utterly exhausted." And the two of them thought: "How terrible! How unbearable! Because the venerable Beloved Friend, acting deliberately, forced us to eat bad food three times in succession until our bodies were utterly exhausted, we thought to find some way to steal from him. What we said to the venerable Beloved Friend was said out of desire, out of aversion, out of delusion, and out of fear. The pārajika defeat for unchaste conduct has not come upon the venerable Beloved Friend. In this way, the venerable Beloved Friend is innocent and without transgression."

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, those two foolish men have, for the sake of a trifling material gain, knowingly spoken false words." And on that very occasion the Blessed One uttered two verses:

One who bears a body and speaks falsehood
has passed beyond the single Dharma,
and one who has rejected the world beyond —
there is no evil such a one will not commit.

Better to have eaten iron balls
blazing like tongues of flame
than, lacking discipline, without true restraint,
to eat the alms food of the land.

Then the gods dwelling in the midst of the sky cried out: "Alas! How unbearable is this gain and honor! Utterly unbearable!" And from that point on they said: "Whoever slanders a monk for the sake of a trifling material gain — that is wicked, wicked!"

Then, at that time, a monk recited this verse:

Because even Beloved Friend, blameless wanderer
through the three realms of existence,
was slandered —
what wise person in this world
would delight in cyclic existence?

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, if these three kinds of persons do not abandon their ways, they are bound for the lower realms, bound for hell. Which three? Monks, first there is the person who indulges in sensual pleasures and commits evil, unwholesome deeds. If that person does not abandon this, he is the first kind bound for the lower realms, bound for hell. Furthermore, monks, there is the person who holds the view and speaks thus: 'Sensual pleasures are pure; sensual pleasures are wholesome; sensual pleasures are to be enjoyed; there is no fault in sensual pleasures.' If that person does not abandon this, he is the second kind bound for the lower realms, bound for hell. Furthermore, monks, there is the person who himself engages in unchaste conduct and also falsely slanders others with a charge of unchaste conduct without any basis. If that person does not abandon this, he is the third kind bound for the lower realms, bound for hell."

Having spoken these words, the Blessed One, the Sugata, having said this,

The Teacher then spoke further, saying:

From the mouth of a person, when born,
An axe arises through the speaking of harsh words,
And by that very axe
One cuts oneself down.

Whoever praises what deserves blame
And blames what deserves praise —
From their mouth ruin is born,
And through that ruin they find no happiness.

One who wastes their own wealth through gambling —
That ruin is but a small thing.
But one who stirs up malice toward the Sugata —
That is a ruin very great indeed.

One who abides in the evil ground of blaming those whom the noble-minded revere:
To the number of a hundred millions, a thousand millions, a hundred thousand millions —
thirty-six and five, however many —
One goes, bursting in hell like a bubble.

When the Saṅgha rebukes a dear nun who has accepted discipline on her own, and a friend, one born of the earth, has been well and properly questioned, then the nuns who are of blameless natural character speak the praises of the monk Gyatbu Nor, while they speak dispraise of the dear nun. Then the sister of the dear nun, a nun named Dzawa Chenma, at the moment of speaking dispraise of the dear nun, with anger, agitation, and fierceness toward the nuns, basely accuses the nuns without any basis with a charge of a pārājika offence, and disparages the nuns.

At that time the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks in turn reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then had this occurrence, this context, this matter, and this occasion explained in full, from beginning to setting forth the rule of training.
