Furthermore, whichever nun, with anger and without having abandoned aversion, thinks "By any means let this one be separated from the chaste life," and without any basis — the three bases of what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected being absent — accuses a pure nun who has no downfall with a charge of a pārājika offence: even if she later disputes the charge, whether asked by others or not asked, that dispute too is without basis. And if it is said "The nun abides in aversion and spoke out of aversion" — this Dharma is a downfall from the very first offence, and the remainder to be dealt with is for the Saṅgha together with the formal procedure of expulsion.

Now, "whichever nun" refers to the dear one. "With anger" means with agitation, fierceness, ill-will, and dissatisfaction. "Without having abandoned aversion" means without having set aside agitation. "By any means let this one be separated from the chaste life" means "by any means let this one be separated from the conduct of a renunciant." "A pure nun who has no downfall" means one who has no downfall with respect to that particular ground. "Without any basis" means without the three bases: the basis of having seen, the basis of having heard, and the basis of having suspected. "A charge of a pārājika offence" means the charge of whichever of the eight applies. "With a charge of Dharma" means that what is not Dharma has been spoken under the name of Dharma. "From the accusation" means on account of having made the accusation. "At another time" means at a later occasion. "Whether asked" means by others. "Whether not asked" means when she herself, out of remorse — slight remorse, full remorse, or qualms arising in the mind — speaks. "That dispute too" refers to the four kinds of dispute: disputing out of remorse, disputing because of not being instructed, disputing on account of a downfall, and disputing on account of some matter. "Without any basis" means without the three bases being present. "The nun abides in aversion" means she desires to separate this one from the conduct of a renunciant. "Spoke out of aversion" means she desires still further to separate her from the conduct of a renunciant. "This Dharma" here means that what is not Dharma has been presented under the name of Dharma.

"Incurs a transgression from the very first" means she incurs a transgression immediately. "With a definite resolve to leave" means with firm intention. "The Saṅgha remains" means that this transgression depends upon both Saṅghas, is connected with both Saṅghas, and relies upon both Saṅghas; the transgression is to be lifted by both Saṅghas, not by any individual person. Alternatively, the eight defeats (pārājikas) leave no remainder, whereas this transgression does leave a remainder — and for that reason it is called "with remainder."

Now, how does a transgression come about? When one makes a false accusation against a pure person, a transgression is incurred through ten bases, but not through five bases. How does a transgression come about through the ten bases? When that person, with respect to something not seen, not heard, and not suspected, alters the perception and then alters the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and says, "I saw it myself," "I heard it myself," "I myself suspect it" — everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha. When one has heard something and then forgotten it, or has suspected something and then forgotten it, and yet alters the perception and then alters the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and says, "I heard it and did not forget it," "I suspected it and did not forget it" — everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha. When one believes what was heard and says, "I saw it myself"; when one does not believe what was heard and says, "I saw it myself"; when one doubts what was heard and says, "I saw it myself"; when one does not doubt what was heard and says, "I saw it myself"; when one has a suspicion and, on account of that suspicion, says, "I saw it myself" — in all these cases everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha. In this way a transgression is incurred through ten bases.

How is a transgression not incurred through five bases? When that person, with respect to something not seen, not heard, and not suspected, does not alter the perception, does not alter the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and yet says, "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspect it" — no transgression is incurred. When one has heard something and forgotten it, or has suspected something and forgotten it, and yet does not alter the perception, does not alter the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and says, "I heard it and did not forget it," "I suspected it and did not forget it" — no transgression is incurred. In this way a transgression is not incurred through five bases.

Just as, in the case of making a false accusation against a pure person, a transgression is incurred through ten bases and not through five bases, so too in the case of making a false accusation against someone pure who has been treated as impure, a transgression is incurred through ten bases and not through five bases. In the case of making a false accusation against an impure person, a transgression is incurred through eleven bases, but not through six bases.

How does a transgression come about through eleven bases? When that person, with respect to something not seen, not heard, and not suspected, alters the perception and then alters the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and says, "I saw it myself," "I heard it myself," "I myself suspect it" — everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha. When that person has seen something and then forgotten it, or has heard something and then forgotten it, or has suspected something and then forgotten it, and yet alters the perception and then alters the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, and the view, and says, "I saw it and did not forget it," "I heard it and did not forget it," "I suspected it and did not forget it" — everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha.

When one believes what one has heard and then says, "I saw it myself"; when one does not believe what one has heard and yet says, "I saw it myself"; when one suspects what one has heard and then says, "I saw it myself"; when one does not suspect what one has heard and yet says, "I saw it myself"; when one suspects what one has suspected and then says, "I saw it myself" — everything said becomes remainder for the Saṅgha. In this way, a transgression arises through eleven bases.

How does no transgression arise through six bases? When that person has not seen something, has not heard something, and does not suspect something, and yet does not alter the perception, the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, or the view, and says, "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspected it" — no transgression arises. When that person has seen something and has not forgotten it, has heard something and has not forgotten it, or has suspected something and has not forgotten it, and does not alter the perception, the acceptance, the intention, the understanding, the deliberation, or the view, and says, "I saw it and did not forget it," "I heard it and did not forget it," "I suspected it and did not forget it" — no transgression arises. In this way, no transgression arises through six bases.

Just as a transgression arises through eleven bases and does not arise through six bases in the case of making a false accusation against an impure person, so too in the case of making a false accusation against an impure person by representing them as pure, a transgression arises through eleven bases and does not arise through six bases.

The monks, having developed doubt, asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to resolve all their doubt — "What should be done?" — and the former narratives are to be set out at length up to that point. "Having done what can one make use of a dwelling, what constitutes begging for food, and yet one has attained the state of arhat and still has made a false accusation?" — this is to be set out at length as in the Rule for monks.

Here ends the second Remainder for the Saṅgha from the Rule for nuns.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing in Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. At the time when the nun of lotus-blue complexion, relying on the spiritual friend the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, had abandoned blameworthy deeds and attained the state of arhat, she would go each day, at all three times of day, to attend upon the Blessed One. The monks who had faith thereupon developed even greater faith upon observing that this great being, the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka, had set aside his own meditative absorptions, his liberations, and his meditative attainments in order to attend diligently to Dharma-related duties of service to the monks.

At that time, the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka was spending his days beside a pond called Walled-with-Stones, not far at all from Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha. Then the nun of lotus-blue complexion went to where the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka was, and having arrived she bowed her head to his two feet and sat down to one side. At that time the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka's patched monastic robe had been newly dyed a deep crimson, and the nun of lotus-blue complexion had only recently had her head shaved, so her hair had not yet grown long. Then his patched robe was carried off by the wind and became entangled around her head. At that time a deer also performed a deed improper for a male deer to do with a female deer. And also two close friends born of the same soil were washing their hands and feet at the Walled-with-Stones pond. When these two friends born of the same soil bowed to the feet of the nun of lotus-blue complexion and the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka —

the edge of the patched robe was carried off by the wind and became entangled around her head, and they also saw a deer performing with a female deer an act improper for a male deer to do. Having seen this, one friend said to the earth-born one: "Earth-born one, look at Nandakoṭinandaka and the lotus-blue one. At that time we had not found our match, but now we have found our match." Having said this, the two of them used that match to challenge the venerable Nandakoṭinandaka. The monks then said the following: "Are you two going to abandon gods and humans all at once and dwell alone in the hells?" The two replied, "If we have done no wrong, it is our own eyes that have done wrong" — and so on up to where the Blessed One said to the two of them: "What did you see? How did you see it? Where did you see it? Where were you when you saw it? You two, speak up properly: why did you go there? Inquire into it well." All of this is as before. The monks also questioned the two of them properly. When they were properly questioned and examined, the two said: "We saw a male deer and a female deer. We saw Nandakoṭinandaka and the lotus-blue one, and on the basis of that match we challenged him." At that point the monks reported to the Blessed One, and when the Blessed One laid down the training rule for the monks, the nuns used that match to challenge the lotus-blue one. Then the nuns told the monks about it, and the monks reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This being the case," proceeded through the laying down of the training rule, all as before.

Furthermore, if a nun who is angry and has not abandoned aversion thinks by any means to separate this one from the celibate life, and accuses a nun who is pure and free of any downfall — taking up, on the basis of a dispute that belongs to no other party, some matter that belongs to no other party, in a merely partial manner — and on the basis of that false accusation charges a nun who has not incurred a defeat with a matter of defeat, then even if later, whether questioned or not, that very dispute also belongs to no other party, and that dispute too is one in which a matter belonging to no other party has been taken up in a merely partial manner, and the nun, abiding in aversion, speaks out of aversion — in that case, already by this first act a downfall has occurred, and it is one entailing expulsion, and she is to be suspended from the Saṅgha.

Now, "a nun" refers to a female friend. "Who is angry" and the rest is as before. "A dispute" refers to the four kinds of disputes, as before. "Belonging to no other party" — "other" here refers to nirvāṇa, and "not belonging to it" refers to the eight factors that constitute a defeat. "In a merely partial manner" is like the case of the male deer and the female deer. "Matter" means that what is not Dharma is spoken of by the name of Dharma. "Takes up" means seizes upon it. "A nun who has not incurred a defeat" refers to the lotus-blue one. "A matter of defeat" means any one of the eight defeats. "On the basis of a false accusation" means on the basis of having leveled a false charge — and from there the entire training rule for baseless accusation is to be recited in full, exactly as before.

Now, as to how a downfall arises in this case: when a nun sees a nun who is about to incur a defeating downfall and comes to regard her as one who has no downfall, and having formed that perception, she then converts it — along with her patience, desire, and understanding —

— and her view, and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa (a Saṅgha-remainder offense) arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat, and having come to hold the view of Saṅghāvaśeṣa regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth up to that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat, and having come to hold the view of a transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat, and having come to hold the view of one requiring individual confession regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat, and having come to hold the view of a wrong deed regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of no transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of defeat regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of Saṅghāvaśeṣa regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of a transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of one requiring individual confession regarding that matter, she converts her perception, and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a Saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, and having come to hold the view of a wrong deed regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression of wrong doing, and having come to hold the view of no transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that is a wrong doing, and having come to hold the view of a defeat regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that is a wrong doing, and having come to hold the view of a Saṅghāvaśeṣa regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that is a wrong doing, and having come to hold the very view of a wrong doing regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that is a wrong doing, and having come to hold the view of a transgression requiring confession regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression that is a wrong doing, and having come to hold the view of a minor offense regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of no transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a defeat regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a Saṅghāvaśeṣa regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a wrong doing regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the very view of a transgression requiring confession regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a minor offense regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a minor offense, and having come to hold the view of no transgression regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a defeat regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a Saṅghāvaśeṣa regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of an offense requiring expiation regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a transgression requiring individual confession regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

When a nun sees a nun committing a transgression requiring confession, and having come to hold the view of a transgression requiring confession itself regarding that matter, she converts her perception — and so forth from that point — and declares "I have seen a nun committing a transgression that will lead to defeat," then a Saṅghāvaśeṣa arises.

This completes the third Saṅghāvaśeṣa from the Vinaya analysis for nuns.

The Blessed One was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the kingdom of Prince Jeta at Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Sthulanandā became attached to a young perfume-seller. She went to where that young perfume-seller was, approached him, and acted in such a way as to make him become attached to her as well. He, being attached, and out of that attachment, allowed her to take a small amount for herself. She went again and again, gave him a small amount, and received much in return at a high price.

Then the young perfume-seller thought to himself: "How long will I go on in this enjoyment?" Thereafter, at another time, the young perfume-seller said to Sthulanandā: "Noble lady, when will I be able to meet with you?" She replied: "You will meet with an elephant."

Then the nun who was following behind said to Sthulanandā: "Noble lady, does this man not know that you are attached to him?" She replied: "He knows." "Then why did you let the monks hear the occasion when the man, out of his attachment, allowed you to take a small amount for yourself?" Having heard this, the monks were told. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on the basis of this occurrence, and so forth through to the establishment of the training rule: "Whatever nun, being herself attached, takes even a small amount for herself from a man who is attached to her — this offense entails defeat from the very first instance, together with expulsion; it is a Saṅghāvaśeṣa."

"Whatever nun" refers to Sthulanandā. "Being attached" means being desirous, thoroughly desirous, and bound by passion. "A man who is attached to her" means one who is desirous, thoroughly desirous, and bound by passion — such as the young perfume-seller, or any other person of that kind. "Takes" means directly. "A small amount" means any of the five edibles or the five non-edibles. "Takes for herself" means receiving it and swallowing it down the throat.

The phrase "this rule" is expressed using the term Dharma for what is not Dharma. "From the very first instance entails a downfall" means it becomes a downfall from that very moment. "Together with expulsion" means that it is to be carried out with forfeiture. "Saṅghāvaśeṣa" means that this downfall depends on both Saṅghas, is connected to both Saṅghas, relies upon both Saṅghas, and arises from both Saṅghas rather than from an individual; furthermore, the eight other cases that entail defeat have no remainder, whereas this downfall does have a remainder — and for that reason it is called Saṅghāvaśeṣa.

As to how the downfall occurs: if a nun who is attached takes even a small amount from a man who is attached, it is a Saṅghāvaśeṣa. If an attached nun takes from an unattached man, it is a wrongdoing. If an unattached nun takes from an attached man, it is a serious offense. For a first offender and similar cases there is no downfall.

Here ends the fourth Saṅghāvaśeṣa from the Vibhaṅga of the nuns.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. At the time the Blessed One had laid down the training rule for the nuns, from that point forward the nuns never again engaged in buying and selling. They fell into poverty, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with mindfulness as your guide, you may buy." Then Sthulanandā said to Sthulanandita: "Now then, sister, first make yourself unattached, and once you have become unattached, receive a small amount from a man who is attached." She went and did exactly as described — taking a small amount from an attached man. Then Sthulanandita said to Sthulanandā: "Noble one, this man is attached." She replied: "Why is he attached?" While she was thus appropriating things in that way, the nuns said: "Why do you act like this?" She replied with such words as are fitting to the situation. The nuns then told the monks, and it continued up to the laying down of the training rule.

Whatever nun says to another nun: "Now then, sister, first make yourself unattached, and once you have become unattached, receive a small amount from a man who is attached" — this rule also entails a downfall from the very first instance, together with expulsion; it is a Saṅghāvaśeṣa. "Whatever nun" refers to Sthulanandā. "To a nun" refers to Sthulanandita. "First make yourself unattached" means: do not be desirous, do not be thoroughly desirous, do not let yourself be bound by passion. "From a man who is attached" means from one who is desirous, thoroughly desirous, and bound by passion. "Take a small amount for yourself" means: receive any of the five edibles or the five non-edibles and take them as your own — this is as in the previous rule. "Says" means utters these words.

As to how the downfall occurs: however much and to whatever degree a nun says to another nun, "Become unattached and then receive a small amount from an attached man and take it as your own" — in every case it becomes a Saṅghāvaśeṣa.

Here ends the fifth Saṅghāvaśeṣa from the Vibhaṅga of the nuns.

The Vibhaṅga of the Vinaya of the nuns, the ninth fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the kalandakas. At that time the nun Mitsemo, through her own consent, was taken by a man and made to live a household life, and he played with her, and children — both sons and daughters — were born.

Then at another time she fell ill, and her younger sister, a nun named Mitsemo, hearing that she had fallen ill, went alone to visit her, looked in on her, and returned.

After that, the sick nun said to her younger sister: "Noble one, even if I should die this very day, do not leave — remain here without departing." And so the younger sister stayed there. That very night the nun Mitsemo passed away. Then her husband began to mourn, and one of his friends said to him: "This is her younger sister, the one called Mitsemo — take her as your wife." So the husband said to Mitsemo: "Noble one, do not leave this house, for it belongs to you." But she replied: "May your house become a prison. May your house burn to ash." And saying that, she departed.

Then the nuns asked her: "Where did you spend last night?" She replied: "At the place where my younger sister passed away." They said to her: "If someone were to separate you from your vows, what would you do?" She replied: "If I had not remained silent, I would have been separated from my vows that very day." At that point the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and so on up to the laying down of the rule of training.

Furthermore, whatever nun stays outside alone at night — this matter too becomes a transgression from the very outset, and, involving an exit from it, it becomes a Saṅghāvaśeṣa. "Whatever nun" refers to the nun Mitsemo. "At night" means from the time the sun has set. "Alone" means without a second person. "Stays outside" means that she lets dawn break outside the summer retreat quarters. The rest is as before.

As for how the transgression arises: whatever nun stays outside alone at night — however that may come about — it becomes a Saṅghāvaśeṣa. If she stays outside together with a novice nun, it becomes a gross offense. If she stays outside together with a female trainee, it becomes a wrongdoing. If the nun who is accompanying her dies, becomes incapacitated, flees, or falls away, there is no transgression.

Here ends the sixth Saṅghāvaśeṣa from the Vibhaṅga of the nuns.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. At that time a nun named Pomgamo was preaching the Dharma alone in the homes of brahmin and householder families, going out each day as the sun set. When the sun went down she would return to the summer retreat quarters and say to the nuns: "Rub my back and waist." They asked her: "Noble one, where have you come from?" She replied: "From teaching the Dharma to brahmins and householders." They asked: "What nun accompanied you on your way back?" She replied: "I came back alone." They then said: "If someone were to separate you from your vows, what would you do?" She replied: "Did you not see that perfume seller's boy who jabbed me with a stick and broke two of my ribs?" They said:

"A water pot that is always submerged in water will never become hard and dry." Then the nuns spoke to the monks, and so on from that point up to and including the laying down of the training rule.

Furthermore, whatever nun remains outside alone during the daytime — this very offense constitutes an immediate downfall and requires expiation; it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's remainder. "Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "During the daytime" means from sunrise onward. "Alone" means without a second person. "Remains outside" means causing the sun to set somewhere other than the summer retreat quarters. The rest is as before.

As for how a transgression arises in that case: whatever nun remains outside alone during the daytime, under any circumstances whatsoever, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's remainder. If she remains outside together with a novice nun, it becomes a serious offense. If she remains outside together with a fully ordained nun, it is a transgression to be confessed. If the attendant nun accompanying her dies, falls ill, flees, or is brought down, there is no transgression.

The eighth Saṅgha's-remainder rule from the Analysis of the Nuns' Code is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī. Then Sthūlanandā sat alone at a crossroads where four great roads met, fully equipped with everything of like purpose, and set out on the road. She would go a league or a league and a half toward whichever great city she was heading for, and then turn back. And so, just as the sun was setting, she would return to the summer retreat quarters and say to the younger ones: "Rub my back. Rub my waist and ribs." They said to her: "Noble one, where have you been?" She replied: "Today I went to the roads of six great cities." They said: "With what attendant nun did you go?" She replied: "I went alone." They said: "If someone were to separate you from your vows, what would you do?" She replied: "If the sons of that perfume seller were to come and touch me, I would merely break their teeth with my black begging bowl." At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and so on from that point up to and including the laying down of the training rule.

Furthermore, whatever nun travels alone on a road outside — this very offense constitutes an immediate downfall and requires expiation; it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's remainder. "Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Alone" means without a second person. "Road" means a wilderness road. The rest is as before.

As for how a transgression arises in that case: whatever nun travels alone on a road outside, under any circumstances whatsoever, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's remainder. The rest is as before.

The eighth Saṅgha's-remainder rule from the Analysis of the Nuns' Code is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī. Then a number of nuns went wandering about and came to the bank of a river. Wishing to cross to the other side for some small purpose, they looked for a boat. They heard that on the far bank there was a boat moored to a stake. After a while the nuns caught sight of it, and they said: "If anyone among us knows how to swim, let her go and fetch the boat." At that time a nun named Kṛṣṇā, who had previously been a washerwoman, spoke up and said: "Noble ones, I will go and fetch the boat." Having said this, she tucked up her robes and entered the water.

But her former skill had faded, and her body had grown heavy, so that when she reached the middle of the river she sank down and touched the bottom. The nuns standing on the bank cried out, "Kṛṣṇā, swim! Kṛṣṇā, swim!" Exhausted, she managed to reach the bank, and at sunset she returned to the rains retreat quarters. The nuns asked whether she had crossed with some ease, and she told them in full what had happened. They then said to her: "Did you enter the water alone?" She replied: "Alone." They said: "If someone were to make you break your vow of discipline, what would you do?" — and at that point the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and so on up to the laying down of the training rule.

Furthermore, whichever nun swims alone to the far bank of a river incurs, from the very first instance, a transgression that entails expiation and is to be confessed before the Saṅgha. As for the phrase "whichever nun" — that refers to the nun Kṛṣṇā. "Alone" means without a second person. "Swims to the far bank of a river" means crosses over a river. The remaining terms are as before. How does a transgression arise in this case? Whichever nun swims alone to the far bank of a river incurs a Saṅgha expiation. If she crosses a stream, she incurs a grave offence. If she crosses a channel, she incurs a grave offence. If she crosses a rivulet, she incurs a minor offence. Here ends the ninth chapter of the Saṅgha Expiation section of the Nuns' Analysis.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time King Prasenajit had two men in his service: one called "Crusher of Armies by Might and Power," and another called "Noble Lineage." These two went before King Prasenajit, and whenever any mountain stronghold had rebelled, they would go there and do battle. When they went away on such campaigns, their wives would sport, make merry, and carouse with lewd women, flatterers, and deceivers. The men then thought: "We subdue rebellious mountain strongholds — can we not discipline our own wives? This is shameful and improper." And they resolved: "Whichever of our wives commits impropriety with another man shall have her head shaved and be cast out." Some among them said: "This law is far too harsh — let us petition the king." Then the general called Estimator, together with his troops, went to where King Prasenajit was, reported all of this to the king in full, and the king declared them not at fault. Now the daughter of General Estimator, whose name was Senā, had acted contrary to the rule, and when she did so, many women said: "If this one is not punished by the penalty, then we too shall break the rule." The soldiers heard this and reported it to Estimator. General Estimator thought: "I myself laid down this rule — how could it be right for me to rescind it?" So General Estimator dismissed Senā and ordered the soldiers to kill her. When Senā heard this, she went far, far away, and prostrating herself at the soldiers' feet, begged their forgiveness. They said: "We cannot condone such improper conduct as this —

"Nevertheless, so that looking to the soldiers shall not be in vain, her reply shall be given within seven days." She received her answer within those seven days, and while weeping she gave what was to be given. While she was making merit, the nun Phyar-mo asked Senā-mā, "Why are you weeping?" She said these words: "Her father has utterly abandoned her. Her mother has utterly abandoned her. Her husband has utterly abandoned her, and she will not be here in seven days." At this, Phyar-mo said, "Would you not wish to go forth right now?" and thereupon Senā-mā went forth from that place. Phyar-mo then took her away to a summer dwelling.

When the soldiers heard of this, they said: "Even if she hid in the gap between an ox's horns, she shall not be left alive." When Senā-mā's mother heard this, she was terrified and went to take refuge with the group of twelve. Those twelve said: "Sister, if the children of Buzanma come, ward them off with a black bowl used as a pestle." She thought to herself: "These crows of the group of twelve cannot protect me," and so she went to take refuge with the Great Lady of Beings, Gautamī. She told her: "Thus I was utterly abandoned by my father, utterly abandoned by my mother, utterly abandoned by the soldiers, ordered to be killed by the king, and cast off by my husband" — from this point up to "who ordained you?" — and then she went on to take refuge with the queen Phreṅ-ldan-ma.

Then Queen Phreṅ-ldan-ma interceded with the king on behalf of Senā-mā, daughter of Estimator, and the king agreed. The king went to where the soldiers were stationed and spoke these words: "This Senā-mā, daughter of Estimator, has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, has come to me for refuge, and has gone for refuge to you — do not kill her." They replied: "Your Majesty, shall we violate the rule?" He said: "Protect the rule itself well and in full; however, on this account you shall give something excellent." At that juncture, the nuns told this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, from the account of what occurred, the ground for the rule, the object of the rule, and the occasion — all the way through to the laying down of the training rule — declared as follows.

Whatever nun, knowing that a woman has been ordered killed by the king, abandoned by her husband, utterly cast off by her parents, and condemned to be killed by the soldiers, nevertheless admits her into the community — that matter from the very first moment becomes a transgression that entails expulsion and proceeds with a remainder, becoming a matter for the Saṅgha to decide.

Now, "whatever nun" refers to Phyar-mo. "A woman" refers to Senā-mā. "Ordered by the king" means that the king Śukla himself consented to it. "Abandoned by her husband" means by Senā-mā's husband. "Utterly cast off by her parents" means by Estimator and by Estimator's wife. "Condemned to be killed by the soldiers" means by the one who crushes the power of the mighty and by the one of good lineage. "Knowingly" means whether she herself knew or was told by another. "Admits into the community" means she causes her going forth and full ordination (upasaṃpadā) in this Dharma-Vinaya through the act of the four announcements.

The rest is as before.

As to how the transgression arises: if a nun causes a woman of such a kind to go forth in any way whatsoever, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha to decide.

The tenth chapter of the section on the rules for nuns, the Saṅghāvaśeṣa, is complete.

A summary verse:

When one procures a surety bond, causes one to seek forbearance,
Abandons the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
Speaks of desire, anger, and fear,
Dwells together with the two, sides with that person,
Causes a schism in the Saṅgha and sides with the schismatics,
And brings trouble to a household — these are the ten that cause distress to the mind.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. At that time in Śrāvastī there was a householder who was struck down by illness, yet he continued to give gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and the destitute, and to make merit. The nun Sthūlanandā heard of this. She then went to where that householder was, and having arrived, she gave him a Dharma teaching. After giving the Dharma teaching, she said this to the householder: "Good sir, women receive little, so please give something to me as well." He said this in reply: "Noble one, why did you not come sooner? I am nearly dead, and I have already sent everything to the next world." She said: "If you have a change of heart, you will live for a hundred years without any illness whatsoever." He said: "Noble one, are you willing to accept a surety bond?" She said: "Good sir, if you give it, then yes." Thereupon he gave it to her. She took the surety bond and went to another householder, and having arrived, she said to that householder: "Good sir, please read this a moment." He read it, and then said: "Noble one, do you have authority over this?" She replied: "I have authority over it; I shall present it." Then Sthūlanandā seized hold of that householder and said: "If you do not give this to me, I will hand you over to the royal court." And indeed he remained there under her grip. A friend of his arrived and asked him: "What is happening here?" He replied: "I have been seized over a debt I owe." "Who is it that you owe this debt to?" He replied: "It is a nun." The friend said: "Can you really find nothing else in the world to use, that you should take from a nun?" Then, because brahmins and householders were doing such things as taking surety bonds, they began to revile, criticize, and reproach, saying: "The conduct of the female renunciants among the sons of the Śākya is burnt up and destroyed." The nuns, hearing this, spoke to the monks. The monks, in turn, reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence having arisen," established a training rule through to its conclusion.

Furthermore, whatever nun procures a surety bond: this matter is also an offense from the very first instance, entailing expulsion from the community, and it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha to decide.

As for the phrase "whatever nun," this refers to Sthūlanandā. "Surety bond" means a pledge-document used to recover a debt. "Procures" means if she takes it. "This matter also" — here the word "matter" is applied to what is not truly a proper matter. The rest is as before.

As to how the transgression arises: if a nun procures a surety bond in any manner whatsoever, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha to decide. For one who entered through a minor pretext, and for a first offender and the like, there is no transgression.

The eleventh chapter of the section on the rules for nuns, the Saṅghāvaśeṣa, is complete.

The origin of this rule is in Śrāvastī. At that time in Śrāvastī there was a nun named Dundubhī who was quarrelsome, who caused strife, who picked fights, who delighted in disputes. Her daughter, named Dundubhikā, heard all of this and repeated everything back to her mother.

Because of this, those of the nuns' Saṅgha came running and began to fight and quarrel. Then, after the nuns' Saṅgha had investigated the matter, once the congregation had gone on alms round, the nuns' Saṅgha performed the act of suspension against the nun Dundubhikā in her absence, since she was not seen in the assembly.

Thereafter Dundubhikā wept and told her mother that the nuns' Saṅgha had performed the act of suspension against her in her absence. Her mother said to her, "They can also perform the act of expulsion from the three realms — watch!" Saying this, she went outside the boundary of the consecrated area, sought the nun's forbearance, and proceeded to live together with her, eat together with her, and sleep together with her in the same house.

The other nuns then said to Dundubhikā, "Why do you live together, eat together, and sleep in the same house with one who has been expelled?" She replied, "What do you mean, expelled? Is it not permitted to stay somewhere in another direction or locality?" The nuns said, "Seek the forbearance of the nuns' Saṅgha." She replied, "I myself performed the expulsion. Where and how did you nuns expel her?" The nuns said, "Outside the boundary." She replied, "Whether it is proper or not to expel someone outside the boundary — I have done it! As for seeking forbearance, that ought to be done properly. But what you have done was done out of desire. It was done out of aversion and delusion." On account of this, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks in turn reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then declared, "Nuns, you should summon the nun Dundubhikā, or anyone else similar to her, and admonish her." The nuns summoned and admonished that nun. But when summoned and admonished, she stubbornly clung to that very same position, grasped at it as supreme, and persisted in asserting, labeling with the designation: "This alone is true; anything else is false." Because of this, the nuns again spoke to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared, "The nuns should admonish the nun Dundubhikā through a motion and three proclamations. The admonishment is to be done as follows: having prepared the seats — so it is said — one nun makes the motion and performs the act. The act is performed in this manner:

'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, may you hear me. This nun Dundubhikā, while the nuns' Saṅgha performed against her an act of suspension in her absence because she was not seen, has nonetheless — knowingly, and after such an act of suspension was performed — lived together with the one against whom the act of suspension was performed, eaten together with her, and slept together with her in the same house. Then, when the nuns summoned and admonished her, she stubbornly clung to that very same position, grasped at it as supreme, and persisted in applying the designation: "This alone is true; anything else is false." If the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, may the Saṅgha approve this.' The admonishment of the nun Dundubhikā through a motion and three proclamations is performed. This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows:

'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, may you hear me. This nun Dundubhikā, knowing that the nuns' Saṅgha performed against a nun an act of suspension in her absence, has nonetheless lived together with the one against whom that act of suspension was performed, eaten together with her,

slept in the same dwelling, and when the nuns admonished her and instructed her on this matter, she held to that same ground obstinately, grasping it as supreme, and in applying the designation, "This alone is true; anything else is false," the noble Saṅgha of nuns has performed the act of admonishment toward that nun Dundubhikā through a motion and three proclamations. Those who consent to this may remain silent; those who do not consent may speak. This is the first proclamation of the act. The second and third are to be proclaimed in the same way. The Saṅgha having consented and approved by remaining silent, this is how it is held to be. From "through a motion and three proclamations she held to that same ground obstinately" and so forth, it is as before. From "thereupon the nuns" up to "bound by the training" it is as before.

Furthermore, if any nun, knowing that the harmonious Saṅgha of nuns has performed against some nun an act of suspension from her dwelling, goes out alone beyond the boundary and causes a request for consent to be made, this very act from its very beginning constitutes a transgression and incurs a residual matter requiring the Saṅgha as remainder.

Now, the phrase "if any nun" refers to the subject nun. The phrase "the Saṅgha of nuns" refers to the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's female disciples. The phrase "some nun against whom" refers to the object nun. The phrase "has performed an act of suspension from her dwelling" means through a motion and three proclamations. The phrase "knowing" means either by herself knowing it or because another person told her. The phrase "goes out alone" means she goes out by herself. The phrase "beyond the boundary" means she goes outside the circle of the boundary. The phrase "causes a request for consent to be made" means through a motion and three proclamations. The rest is as before.

As for how this becomes a transgression: if a nun, knowing that an act of suspension from her dwelling was performed against some nun, goes out beyond the boundary and causes a request for consent to be made, and then sits together with her, eats together with her, or sleeps in the same dwelling with her, in every such case this constitutes an offense. During the admonishment, if she abandons that ground, that is good. If she does not abandon it, there arises a grave offense. If, before the words of the first act are complete, she abandons it, that is good. If she does not abandon it and the words are completed, a grave offense arises. If, before the words of the second act are complete, she abandons it, that is good. If she does not abandon it and the words are completed, a grave offense arises. Even if the words of the third act are not yet complete, if it was performed invalidly through a concordant group acting contrary to Dharma, or through a discordant group acting contrary to Dharma, or through a discordant group acting in accord with Dharma, and if it was not done in accordance with what the Dharma prescribes, in accordance with what the Vinaya prescribes, or in accordance with what the Teacher taught, then there is no transgression. If the words of the third act are complete and it was done in accordance with what the Dharma prescribes, in accordance with what the Vinaya prescribes, and in accordance with what the Teacher taught, yet she still does not abandon that ground, then there arises a residual matter requiring the Saṅgha as remainder. If that nun, remaining right there on her seat, speaks these words, "Noble sisters, a residual matter has arisen for me," that is good. If she does not speak thus, it constitutes an offense. If she does not confess and disclose that transgression and thereafter participates in a motion, a motion with two proclamations, or a motion with three proclamations, in every case it constitutes an offense. For one who is being admonished for the first time, and so on, there is no transgression.

This completes the twelfth residual matter requiring the Saṅgha as remainder from the Analysis of Nuns' Rules.

The setting of the rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, at Śrāvastī, there was a nun by the name of Nagmо who had formerly been a tīrthika. While quarreling with the other nuns, she became angry and said: "These practitioners of the Śākya sons alone are held to possess moral discipline and virtue, yet there are other practitioners outside them who also possess moral discipline and virtue. By practicing the holy life in their presence, one has done all that needs to be done; I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha." Upon her saying these words, the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks in turn informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "O nuns, you are to restrain and admonish the nun Nagmo, and any others like her. The admonishment is to be carried out as follows: 'Nagmo, when quarreling you became angry and said: these practitioners of the Śākya sons alone are held to possess moral discipline and virtue, yet there are other practitioners outside them who also possess moral discipline and virtue, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha — do not say such things. Nagmo, abandon this view of yours, which has become a view of evil.'" So were the nuns to restrain and admonish her.

When the nuns did restrain and admonish her in this way, she clung firmly to that very ground, holding it fast and remaining attached to it, continuing to assert: "This is true; everything else is false." The nuns then reported the matter again to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "The nuns are to admonish the nun Nagmo by means of a motion with a fourfold proclamation. The procedure for this admonishment is as follows: Let seats be prepared" — and so on down to — "and let one nun make the motion and carry out the formal act." The formal act is to be performed thus:

"Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, may you hear me. This nun Nagmo, having quarreled together with the other nuns and become angry, said: 'These practitioners of the Śākya sons alone are held to possess moral discipline and virtue, yet there are other practitioners outside them who also possess moral discipline and virtue, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha.' And when the many nuns restrained and admonished her, she clung firmly to that very ground, holding it fast and remaining attached to it, asserting: 'This is true; everything else is false.' If this is the appropriate time for the Saṅgha, and if the Saṅgha approves, then let the Saṅgha grant consent: the Saṅgha shall admonish the nun Nagmo — who quarrels with the other nuns — by means of a motion with a fourfold proclamation. This is the motion.

The formal act is to be performed thus: Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, may you hear me. This nun Nagmo, having quarreled together with the other nuns and become angry, said: 'These practitioners of the Śākya sons alone are held to possess moral discipline and virtue, yet there are other practitioners outside them who also possess moral discipline and virtue, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha.' And when the many nuns restrained and admonished her, she clung firmly to that very ground, holding it fast and remaining attached to it, asserting: 'This is true; everything else is false.' Accordingly, the Saṅgha has performed the admonishment of the nun Nagmo — who quarrels with the other nuns — by a motion with a fourfold proclamation.

When the many nuns again restrained and admonished her —

clinging firmly to that very ground, holding it fast and remaining attached to it, asserting: 'This is true; everything else is false.' Accordingly, the noble Saṅgha of nuns has performed the admonishment of the nun Nagmo by a motion with a fourfold proclamation.

When the Saṅgha has performed the admonishment of the nun Nagmo by a motion with a fourfold proclamation, those who consent should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. This is the first proclamation of the motion. The second and third are likewise to be proclaimed with the same content — continuing up to: the Saṅgha has consented and approved, remaining silent in this way, and so it is understood to be accepted.

When she was admonished by the motion with the fourfold proclamation — continuing up to: clinging firmly to that very ground — it is as before.

At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared — from that point up to: including the training — what is to be trained in.

Furthermore, if a nun, while quarreling with the other nuns, becomes angry and says: 'Only these female renunciants (śramaṇas) who are disciples of the Śākyan possess moral discipline and virtue; other renunciants too who possess moral discipline and virtue exist, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha,' the other nuns are to admonish that nun as follows: 'Sister nun, while quarreling with the other nuns you became angry and said: "Only these female renunciants who are disciples of the Śākyan possess moral discipline and virtue; other renunciants too who possess moral discipline and virtue exist, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha." Sister nun, do not say this. Sister nun, abandon this kind of corrupt view.' The nuns are thus to admonish that nun. If she abandons that ground, well and good. If she does not abandon it, the nuns are to admonish her a second and a third time, saying: 'Sister nun, while quarreling with the other nuns you became angry and said: "Only these female renunciants who are disciples of the Śākyan possess moral discipline and virtue; other renunciants too who possess moral discipline and virtue exist, and by practicing the holy life in their presence one has done all that needs to be done — I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha." Sister nun, do not say this. Sister nun, abandon this kind of corrupt view.' If the nuns have duly admonished her a second and a third time and she still does not abandon that ground, then by that very fact this constitutes a transgression with expulsion from the very outset, together with what follows from it, and she becomes one who is no longer part of the Saṅgha.

Now the term 'a nun' refers to Nagmo. The phrase 'while quarreling' means while two sides have formed. 'Becomes angry' means having become displeased in mind. The phrase 'only these female renunciants who are disciples of the Śākyan' means these ones alone. 'Possess moral discipline and virtue' means possessing moral discipline as prescribed. 'Possess virtue' means possessing virtues such as learning and the like. 'Other renunciants too' means those outside of these. 'In their presence' means in the vicinity of those others.

The phrase 'only having practiced the holy life' means only having gone forth into renunciation. 'Will abandon the Buddha' means the foremost among two-footed beings. 'Will abandon the Dharma and the Saṅgha' means the foremost free from attachment, and the foremost among assemblies. The phrase 'to that nun who says so' means to Nagmo. 'By the nuns' means by those who hold this Dharma. 'Speaking thus' means taking up the matter and giving instruction just as the earlier formal instruction was given. 'If, upon being instructed, she abandons that basis, then so much the better' means that would be good. 'If she does not abandon it' refers to her having fallen into a sinful view. 'Upon giving correct instruction and correct guidance up to two and three times' means according to what was said in the motion and the fourfold formal act, as previously instructed.

Then, as for how the transgression arises: if a nun who is quarreling becomes angry and says, "Only these female renunciants who are disciples of the Śākyan possess moral discipline and virtue — but there are also other renunciants who possess moral discipline and virtue, so I shall only practice the holy life in their presence; I will abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha" — saying this is a transgression in every case. If, upon being instructed, she abandons that basis, then so much the better. If she does not abandon it, it becomes a grave offense. If, before the words of the first formal act are complete, she abandons it, then so much the better. If she does not abandon it and the words are completed, it becomes a grave offense. If, before the words of the second formal act are complete, she abandons it, then so much the better. If she does not abandon it and the words are completed, it becomes a grave offense. If the words of the third formal act are also not yet complete, and the matter has been conducted invalidly through agreement, or conducted invalidly through disagreement, or conducted as valid through disagreement, and it has not been done in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teaching of the Teacher, there is no transgression. If the words of the third formal act are also complete, and it has been done in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teaching of the Teacher, yet she still does not abandon that basis, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's remainder. That nun, while still seated in that very place, should speak words such as: "Noble ones, a Saṅgha's remainder has arisen for me" — if she does so, so much the better. If she does not speak thus, it becomes an offense. If, without having confessed and disclosed that transgression, she then participates in the motion, the motion-with-one-recitation, and the motion-with-three-recitations that follow immediately thereafter, it is a transgression in every case. For those performing the formal act for the first time and similar cases, there is no transgression.

The thirteenth Saṅgha's remainder from the Vibhaṅga for nuns is complete.

The basis for this rule is in Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Stubborn Gaiety was quarreling with another nun and took up a dispute. Having become embroiled in it, the nuns instructed her, saying, "Sister, do not quarrel." She became angry at them and said, "Because you give instruction to this one but not to others, you nuns go by desire, you go by aversion, you go by delusion, you go by fear." At that, the nuns told the monks about this, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Nuns, you should take up the matter of Stubborn Gaiety" — and from those words onward, "do not quarrel," one should take up the matter and give instruction. And when she has been taken up and instructed, on that very basis, firmly —

up to "she shall be instructed by a motion and three proclamations" — that is the extent of it. Now, regarding instruction by a motion and three proclamations: from the words "on that very basis, firmly" up to "together with the training" — that is the extent of it.

Furthermore, when a nun who is quarreling and persisting in it is told by the other nuns, "Sister, do not quarrel," and she becomes angry and says the following: "Because you speak to some who are quarreling but do not speak to others, some of the nuns here go by desire, go by aversion, go by delusion, go by fear" — to that nun who has spoken thus, the nuns shall say the following: "Do not say, 'Because you speak to some who are quarreling but do not speak to others, some of the nuns here go by desire, go by aversion, go by delusion, go by fear.' These nuns do not go by desire, do not go by aversion, do not go by delusion, do not go by fear. Therefore, abandon such a course as this, in which you speak words such as 'They go by desire, they go by aversion, they go by delusion, they go by fear.'" When the nuns have addressed that nun in this way, if she abandons the matter, that is excellent. But if she does not abandon it, she shall be properly instructed and properly admonished up to two and three times for the sake of abandoning it. If, upon being properly instructed and properly admonished up to two and three times, she abandons it, that is excellent. But if she does not abandon it, this very matter will become a transgression from the very first instance — a definite arising — and she is to be expelled from the Saṅgha.

Now the commentary: "Whatever nun" refers to Stubborn Gaiety. "Who is quarreling and persisting in it" refers to one who has taken up both sides. "The nuns" refers to those who hold this Dharma. "Sister, do not quarrel" means "do not take up both sides." "Became angry" means out of mental discomfort. "And said the following — 'Because you speak to some who are quarreling but not to others'" — up to "they go by fear" — "to that nun who has spoken thus" refers to Stubborn Gaiety. "The nuns" refers to those who hold this Dharma. "The following" means that one should instruct by taking up the matter exactly as the earlier instruction was given. When one has taken up the matter and given instruction, "if she abandons it, that is excellent" means that would be good. "But if she does not abandon it" refers to the words "they go by desire" and so forth. "Being properly instructed and properly admonished up to two and three times" means: having done so by means of the motion and three proclamations as described earlier. The rest is as before.

As for how the transgression arises: to whatever extent a nun says to the nuns, "They go by desire," that becomes a wrongdoing. If she says, "They go by aversion," that becomes a wrongdoing. If she says, "They go by delusion," that becomes a wrongdoing. If she says, "They go by fear," that becomes a wrongdoing. The remaining twelve items are to be stated as before.

The fourteenth category of "Saṅgha remainder" from the Analysis of the Nuns' Code is complete.

The opening occasion takes place in Vaiśālī. At that time, nuns who have death omens and those who have near-death omens were living together mingled with one another. While living thus intermingled, they would laugh, play, and engage in rough and rowdy bodily conduct.

Because these two were living together in extreme proximity, it became a matter of concern. The nuns grew worried, and when they instructed the two of them, saying, "Sisters, the two of you must not live together in such excessive closeness," the two continued to live together in exactly that way. At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks in turn reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must not live together in closeness. Why is that? Know that if you live together in closeness, wholesome qualities will not increase but will only diminish. Nuns, you must live apart from one another. Why is that? Know that if you live apart from one another, wholesome qualities will not diminish but will only increase." Even after the Blessed One had given this declaration, when the nuns then instructed the two saying, "Do not live together in closeness," the two continued to live together in closeness just as before. The nuns again spoke to the monks, and the monks again reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Nuns, you should summon any nun who has death omens, any nun who has near-death omens, and any others who are of a similar kind, and instruct them. The instruction should be given as follows: the nuns should say to those two, 'Do not live together in closeness; live apart from one another. Why is that? Know that if you live apart from one another, wholesome qualities will not diminish but will only increase.' That is how the instruction should be given."

When the two were then summoned and instructed in this way — from the phrase "with insistence upon that very basis" as far as "the other is delusion" — the nuns again spoke to the monks, and the monks again reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Nuns, you should instruct the nun with death omens and the nun with near-death omens by means of a formal act with a motion and four announcements. The instruction should be carried out as follows: seats are to be arranged," and so forth, "and one nun is to make the motion and perform the act. The act should be performed as follows:

'Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. These two — the nun with death omens and the nun with near-death omens — have been living together in extreme closeness. Many nuns have said to them: Sisters, the two of you must not live together in such excessive closeness; the two of you should not dwell together; sisters, the two of you should live apart from one another. Why is that? Because if the two of you live apart from one another, wholesome qualities will not diminish but will only increase.' When the nuns have thus summoned those two and instructed them — from 'with insistence upon that very basis' as far as 'the other is lying' — if the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha is agreed, let the Saṅgha grant its consent, and let the Saṅgha perform for the nun with death omens and the nun with near-death omens the act of instruction by means of a motion and four announcements. This is the motion."

The Analysis of the Nuns' Code, the tenth fascicle.

The act is to be performed as follows: the statement is to be recited three times in full. When the nuns have thus instructed those two by means of a formal act with a motion and four announcements — from the phrase "with insistence upon that very basis" as far as "this alone is true, the other is delusion" — the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with the words "this occurrence" and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, proceeded as follows.

Furthermore, whatever nuns are living together in community, and while living together in community they engage in laughing, playing, and rough physical horseplay — the other nuns are to address those nuns as follows: "Sisters, do not live together in community. Know that if you live together in community, the wholesome qualities will only decline and will not increase. Know that if you live separately, the wholesome qualities will only increase and will not decline."

If, when the nuns address those nuns in such words, they abandon that basis, then so much the better. But if they do not live separately and persist in living together in community, then in order to cause them to abandon that basis, the nuns are to admonish and instruct those nuns properly two and three times. If, when properly admonished and instructed two and three times, they abandon that basis, then so much the better. If they do not abandon it, this matter carries with it a definite consequence — it is a Saṅgha Remainder offense.

Now, the phrase "whatever nuns" refers to those facing death and those in proximate danger of death. "Living together in community" means seeking out one another's company — dwelling together sharing seats, beds, and food. "Laughing" means scoffing. "Playing" means sportive behavior. "Rough physical horseplay" means behaving in ways fitting for mockery. The phrase "those nuns" refers to those facing death and those in proximate danger of death. "The other nuns" refers to those who uphold this Dharma. "Are to address them as follows" means they are to speak in these words. The phrase "Sisters, do not live together in community; know that if you live together in community, the wholesome qualities will only decline and will not increase" means: since living together in community is not conducive to the side of virtue, you should each live separately and apart. If you live separately, the side of virtue will only increase.

The phrase "if the other nuns" refers to those who uphold this Dharma. The phrase "when they address those nuns in such words" means admonishing those facing death and those in proximate danger of death just as the admonition was set out above. "Then so much the better" means it is good if they do so. "But if they do not abandon that basis, in order to cause them to abandon that basis, they are to be properly admonished and instructed two and three times" means: just as the admonition was set out above, they are to be admonished and instructed by a formal act with a motion and four announcements. And this constitutes the proper admonition, and this constitutes the proper instruction.

The phrase "this matter also" employs the word "Dharma" with reference to what is not in conformity with Dharma. "Carries with it a definite consequence" means it carries with it that upon which one must rely. As for how a transgression comes about: from the moment one says so much as "Sisters, please do live separately" and they continue living in community — in every such instance an offense is incurred. If they do not heed the formal admonition, it becomes a grave offense. The remaining sequence is just as explained previously in the twelfth Saṅgha Remainder.

The Analysis of the Nuns' Code, the fifteenth fascicle, is complete.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. At that time, when the Blessed One had spoken those words, those nuns proceeded to live separately. But when they were living separately, Sthūlanandā said to them: "Why do you live separately? Come, live together with us. Did not the Blessed One declare that through establishing conversation one's wisdom increases? Know then that if you live together in community, the wholesome qualities will only increase and will not decline." At that time the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "O nuns, summon Sthūlanandā and reprove her. The reproof is to be given in this way: 'Sthūlanandā, while knowing full well that the wholesome qualities of those nuns who live separately will only increase and will not decline, do not say to them: "Come, live together with us. If you live together, the wholesome qualities will only increase and will not decline."'" — from that point up to the words "the rest is delusion."

At that time the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Let the nuns summon Sthūlanandā and, by the act of petition-with-four-proclamations, reprove her. The reproof is to be given in this way: after preparing a seat" — from that point up to "one nun having made the petition, the act is to be performed."

The act is to be performed as follows. "Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. Sthūlanandā went to the nuns who were living separately and said: 'O nuns, do not live separately; rather, come and live together with us. If you live together, know that the wholesome qualities will only increase and will not decline.' Thereupon, the many nuns, having summoned her and reproved her" — from that point, the basis remains the same, continuing with the words "insisted" up to "the rest is delusion." "If it is time for the noble Saṅgha and all agree, please grant it. What the noble Saṅgha does — reproving Sthūlanandā by the act of petition-with-four-proclamations — this is the petition. The act is to be performed as follows" — from that point, if the reproof by petition-with-four-proclamations is given three times, it is insisted upon as the supreme — from that point up to "the rest is delusion."

At that time the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, from the words "this occurrence" up to "established the training rule":

"Furthermore, whatever nun, knowing that certain nuns are living together, laughing, playing, and behaving in a coarse and disorderly manner with their bodies, goes to those who are living separately and says: 'Sisters, do not live separately; rather, come and live together with us. If you live together, know that the wholesome qualities will only increase and will not decline' — if the nuns say this to that nun, the nuns must say: 'You, who tell those living separately from those who are living together in laughter, play, and bodily coarseness, "Come and live with us and do not live separately" — do not say this.' And if, when the nuns have spoken those words, she abandons that basis, then good. If she does not abandon it, in order to get her to abandon it, she is to be reproved and admonished correctly two and three times. If, after being correctly reproved and admonished two and three times, she abandons it, then good. If she does not" — from "three times" up to "this Dharma too is accompanied by definite emergence and belongs to the remaining Saṅgha."

"Furthermore, whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Whatever nuns" refers to those on the verge of death and those in the vicinity of death. "Laughing" means giggling aloud. "Playing" means engaged in amusement. "Coarse and disorderly bodily conduct" means behavior fit to provoke laughter. "Knowing" means either by herself or because others have told her.

"Those who dwell separately" means each one dwelling apart. "If she says this" means when she speaks. "Sister, you" refers to those on the verge of death and those in the vicinity of death. "Not dwelling separately" means individually. "You should seek to mingle" means she should seek it out. "If you dwell mingled" means she should seek it out. "Know that wholesome qualities will only increase and not decline" means that the wholesome side will only increase and not decline. "To that nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "The nuns" refers to those belonging to this Dharma. "Should be told as follows" means she should be gathered and instructed just as the instruction was given before. "If she abandons that basis, then good" means it is well. "If she does not abandon it, in order that she abandon that basis, she should be correctly reproved and admonished two and three times" means this is done through a motion and a fourfold act of the Saṅgha, just as instructed before. How does a transgression arise in this matter? In whatever measure a nun, knowing that certain nuns are dwelling together, laughing, playing, and engaging in coarse and disorderly bodily conduct, then says to those who dwell separately, "Do not dwell separately; you should seek to mingle," in every such case she incurs an offense.

The sixteenth section on the remainder of the Saṅgha from the Differentiation of Nuns is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the kalandakas. At that time a terrible famine had come, and the forest mendicants found it very difficult to obtain food. There was a monk who had obtained supernormal powers. He was known by the name Jambū, meaning one who knows Jambudvīpa. He went to Jambudvīpa and filled his bowl with rose-apple shoots possessed of color, fragrance, and flavor, and carried them back. He himself enjoyed them fully and also shared them with those skilled practitioners who lived the holy life. Just as he did with the rose-apple shoots, so too he filled his bowl with the shoots of the bel tree, the āmalaka, and the kapittha, and carried them back. He himself enjoyed them fully and also shared them with those skilled in the holy life.
