Likewise, he went among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings, and he went among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and filled his bowl with ambrosia, and carried it back. He himself enjoyed it fully and also shared it with those skilled in the holy life. Likewise, he went to the northern continent of Uttarakuru and filled his bowl with rice gruel made from naturally growing, unplowed and unsown rice, and carried it back. He himself enjoyed it fully and also shared it with those skilled in the holy life. Likewise, he went to the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha and to the western continent of Aparagodānīya, and went to those lands that were prosperous, extensive, pleasant, fertile, and filled with many people and many inhabitants, and filled his bowl with pure, fine food and drink, possessed of color, fragrance, and flavor, and carried it back. He himself enjoyed it fully and also shared it with those skilled in the holy life.

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "Now a terrible famine has come, and the forest mendicants find it very difficult to obtain food." And Devadatta thought further:

"I too shall attain supernatural powers, and I too shall go to that place which, being named Jambu, is known as Jambudvīpa, and shall fill my bowl with the fruits of the jambu tree, possessed of color, fragrance, and flavor, and take it away. I myself shall fully enjoy it, and I shall also share it with those skilled in the holy life. Likewise, I shall go to those lands that are prosperous, extensive, pleasant, fertile, and filled with many people and many inhabitants, and fill my bowl with pure, fine food and drink, possessed of color, fragrance, and flavor, and take it away. I myself shall fully enjoy it, and I shall also share it with those skilled in the holy life."

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "Now I shall go to where the Blessed One is."

So Devadatta went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Devadatta spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please show me the path of supernatural powers. O Sugata, please show me the path of supernatural powers."

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that Devadatta's wish had become wicked, spoke thus to Devadatta: "Devadatta, strive for now in the higher moral discipline, and supernatural powers and further qualities will arise in you. Strive in the higher mind and in the higher wisdom, and supernatural powers and further qualities will arise in you."

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "The Blessed One will not show me the path of supernatural powers." Realizing this, Devadatta went to where the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya was, and having arrived, he said to Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya: "Elder, please show me the path of supernatural powers."

Then the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya examined the mind of the Blessed One and, perceiving that Devadatta's wish had become wicked, spoke thus to Devadatta: "Devadatta, attend to form as it truly is, and supernatural powers and further qualities will arise in you. Attend properly to consciousness, up through consciousness, and supernatural powers and further qualities will arise in you" — up to the point where it says: Devadatta accomplished supernatural powers on the basis of the ten powers of Kāśyapa, and having become one, became many.

Now, when his mind was fully absorbed, there arose in him this wicked wish of such a kind: "At the present time the Blessed One, worn out with age and exhaustion, lies down to advise the fourfold retinue. How wonderful it would be if the Blessed One were to entrust the community of monks to me, so that I might take full charge of the community of monks, while the Blessed One, with but a little mental effort, devotes himself to the practice of the yoga of dwelling in ease in the present life."

Thereupon Devadatta went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, at the present time, being worn out with age and exhaustion" — up to the point where it says — "while you devote yourself to the practice of the yoga of dwelling in ease in the present life."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to Devadatta: "O man of delusion! I would not entrust the community of monks even to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana, who are accomplished in the holy life — so what need is there to speak of entrusting it to you, a spit-swallower?"

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Devadatta rose in anger and resentment, bowed his head three times in formal acknowledgment, and departed — from the passage beginning "he bowed" up to "he departed from the presence of the Blessed One."

After that, Devadatta began to work at causing a schism in the community of monks. At that same time, a nun named Sthūlanandā also began to exert herself in causing a schism in the community of nuns, and the nuns were alarmed that she was embarking upon this effort. At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks in turn reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must confront Sthūlanandā and remonstrate with her. The remonstration is to be carried out as follows: 'Sthūlanandā, do not set about dividing the harmonious community of nuns. Do not take up a dispute for the purpose of division and persist in clinging to it. Sthūlanandā, be in harmony with the community. Do not break the harmony of the community. Rejoice together, do not quarrel, and be as water and milk blended into one, reciting in unison with a single purpose — and so illuminate the Teacher's teaching and dwell in the touch of ease. Sthūlanandā, abandon that very basis of causing schism in the community.' If, even after being thus confronted and remonstrated with, she insists on that very same basis, clings to it stubbornly as supreme, and keeps designating it as: 'This alone is true; everything else is confused' — then the nuns are to speak to that nun's companions as follows: 'Sisters, do not say anything at all to this nun, whether virtuous or unvirtuous, even the least thing. Why so? Because this nun is a speaker of Dharma and a speaker of Vinaya; she has properly taken up Dharma and Vinaya and clings to them, continually designating accordingly — this nun speaks knowingly, not from ignorance. Whatever she approves of and assents to, we too approve of and assent to.'"

Then a great number of nuns went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and said to him: "Blessed One, we have confronted and remonstrated with Sthūlanandā. But when we remonstrated with her, she persisted on that very same basis" — from the passage beginning "she insisted stubbornly" up to "everything else is confused." And her companions likewise said to those nuns — from the passage beginning "Sisters, do not say anything at all to this nun" up to "we too approve of and assent to."

The Blessed One then declared: "Nuns, you must confront those nuns and others of that same kind, and remonstrate with them. The remonstration is to be carried out as follows: 'Nun, knowing full well that a certain nun has entered upon the course of dividing the harmonious community and has taken up a dispute for the purpose of causing schism and is clinging to it, you nonetheless befriend her, align yourself with her views, and side with her discordant speech. Sisters, abandon this — following after one who would divide the community and speaking discordantly.' When the nuns are spoken to in this way, if they persist on that very same basis" — from the passage beginning "if" up to "that very same basis" and "everything else is confused."

At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks in turn reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must confront Sthūlanandā by means of a formal act of the fourfold procedure."

The procedure for the formal act of confrontation is to be conducted as follows, from the passage beginning "having prepared the seat" up to "one nun makes the motion and performs the act."

"Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. This nun Sthūlanandā has undertaken to divide the community of nuns, has taken up a quarrel for the sake of division, and persists in holding fast to it. When many nuns approached her and confronted her, even though many nuns approached and confronted her, she clung tenaciously to that very same basis, adhering to it with conviction, and continued to designate it with the words: 'This alone is true; everything else is false.' Therefore let the noble Saṅgha of sisters address Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act with these words: 'Sister Sthūlanandā, do not set yourself to divide the harmonious community; do not sit persisting in taking up a quarrel for the sake of division. Sister, be in harmony with the community. Let the community be harmonious and undivided — joyful together, without dispute, single in purpose, reciting together, blended like water and milk. Let it illuminate the Teacher's teaching, and you shall dwell in touch with ease. Sister Sthūlanandā, abandon this basis of yours that divides the community.' If it is timely and agreeable to the noble Saṅgha, let the noble Saṅgha consent. Let the noble Saṅgha address Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act: 'Sister Sthūlanandā, do not set yourself to divide the harmonious community; do not sit persisting in taking up a quarrel for the sake of division. Sister, be in harmony with the community. Let the community be harmonious and undivided — joyful together, without dispute, single in purpose, reciting together, blended like water and milk. Let it illuminate the Teacher's teaching, and you shall dwell in touch with ease. Sister Sthūlanandā, abandon this basis of yours that divides the community.' That is the motion."

The formal act is performed as follows.

"Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. This Sthūlanandā has undertaken to divide the community, has taken up a quarrel for the sake of division, persists in it and carries it through. When many nuns approached and confronted her, even though many nuns approached and confronted her, she clung tenaciously to that very same basis, adhering to it with conviction, and designated it with the words: 'This alone is true; everything else is false.' On account of this, the noble Saṅgha addresses Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act: 'Sister Sthūlanandā, do not set yourself to divide the harmonious community; do not sit persisting in taking up a quarrel for the sake of division. Sister, be in harmony with the community. Let the community be harmonious and undivided — joyful together, without dispute, single in purpose, reciting together, blended like water and milk. Let it illuminate the Teacher's teaching, and you shall dwell in touch with ease. Sister Sthūlanandā, abandon this basis of yours that divides the community.' When the noble Saṅgha has thus addressed Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act, those venerable ones who accept and consent to the noble Saṅgha addressing Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act are to remain silent; those who do not consent are to speak. This is the first recitation of the formal statement; it is likewise to be recited a second time and a third time. The noble Saṅgha has consented and approved; the noble Saṅgha has addressed Sthūlanandā through the motion and the fourfold formal act. Because no one has spoken, so it is upheld."

When she has been confronted in this way through the motion and the fourfold formal act, yet persists on that very same basis — from the passage "persists tenaciously" up to "this alone is true; everything else is false" — she fully confirms it. Her companion nuns then say to those other nuns: "Sisters, whether this nun has done something meritorious or something blameworthy, say nothing to her whatsoever. And why? Because this nun speaks the Dharma; she holds the Dharma and the Vinaya correctly and persists in sustaining that position. This nun speaks knowingly — she does not speak out of ignorance."

"Whatever this nun desires and approves of, that too we desire and approve of" — so saying, they spoke those words.

Then a great many nuns went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed their heads to the Blessed One's feet and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, we admonished Stubborn Delight and conducted the fourfold formal act against her, yet from the passage 'persists tenaciously' up to 'this alone is true; everything else is false,' she fully confirms it. And her companion nuns too said to the other nuns, 'Sisters, whether this nun has done something meritorious or something blameworthy, say nothing to her whatsoever' — from that passage up to 'that too we desire and approve of' — so they spoke."

The Blessed One declared: "You nuns must also admonish those nuns and conduct the formal act against them. The admonishment is to be carried out as follows: 'You nun — you who, knowingly, are befriending and supporting that nun who has taken up a genuine dispute with the aim of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha, who holds fast to it and persists in confirming it — do not take the side of those who speak discordantly. Do not say to the other nuns, "Sisters, whether this nun has done something meritorious or something blameworthy, say nothing to her whatsoever." And why? Because this nun speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya; she has correctly taken up the Dharma and the Vinaya and holds fast to it, persisting in confirming it. This nun speaks knowingly, not out of ignorance. Do not say, "Whatever this nun desires and approves of, that too we desire and approve of."

And why? Because these nuns do not speak the Dharma and do not speak the Vinaya; rather, these nuns speak what is not the Dharma and speak what is not the Vinaya. These nuns have correctly taken up what is not the Dharma and what is not the Vinaya, and they hold fast to it, persisting in confirming it. These nuns speak out of ignorance, not out of knowledge. Do not desire and approve of whatever these nuns desire and approve of.

Sisters, do not wish to divide the Saṅgha — instead, sisters, wish for the Saṅgha to remain in harmony. Let the Saṅgha be in harmony and undivided, rejoicing together and without quarrel, with one recitation and one purpose, blended like water and milk. Then, illuminating the Teacher's teaching, you will dwell in contact with happiness. Sisters, abandon this conduct of siding with those who divide the Saṅgha and speaking discordantly.'"

"If, even after they have been admonished in this way, those nuns — from the passage 'persist tenaciously' up to 'everything else is false' — still persist in confirming it, then the nuns are to inform the monks, and the monks are to report it to the Blessed One."

The Blessed One then declared: "You nun, you must conduct the formal act with admonishment and the fourfold procedure against those who are acting as companions and against any others of the same character. The admonishment is to be carried out as follows — from the passage 'having prepared the seats' up to 'one nun makes the motion and the act is performed.'

'Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. These partisans — these nuns who, wishing to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, have entered upon a dispute for the sake of division, have taken up a genuine quarrel aimed at division, and who, holding fast to it and persisting in confirming it, act as companions to her and take the side of those who speak discordantly —

If many nuns have prepared and admonished them, and those nuns continue to confirm their position from the passage 'on that very ground' up to 'all else is false,' then on that account the noble Saṅgha of sisters should, to those nuns who are acting as companions, carry out admonishment by means of a motion and three acts as follows.

The motion is this: 'Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. These nuns who act as companions — these nuns who, wishing to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, have entered upon a dispute for the sake of division, have taken up a genuine quarrel aimed at division, and who, holding fast to it and knowingly persisting in it, act as companions to her and take the side of those who speak discordantly — those nuns have been prepared and admonished by many nuns, and from the passage "on that very ground" up to "all else is false" they continue to confirm their position. If it is now the right time for the noble Saṅgha and the Saṅgha is pleased, let the noble Saṅgha give its consent. And let the noble Saṅgha admonish these nuns who act as companions, saying: Sister nuns, do not take the side of a nun who, wishing to divide the Saṅgha, has entered upon a dispute for the sake of dividing the Saṅgha, has genuinely taken up that quarrel, holds fast to it and knowingly persists in it, and who speaks discordantly. Sisters, abandon this — abandon taking the side of one who speaks discordantly in this way. Let the Saṅgha be harmonious and undivided, united in joy and without dispute, of one mind, reciting together, mingled like water and milk, and dwelling in touch with ease, illuminating the teaching of the Teacher.' This is the motion; the act is then performed with a motion and three repetitions.

The act is to be performed as follows: 'Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. These nuns who have taken sides — these nuns who, wishing to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, have entered upon a dispute for the sake of division, have genuinely taken up that quarrel, and knowingly hold fast to it while persisting in it, acting as companions to her and taking the side of those who speak discordantly — those nuns have been prepared and admonished by many nuns, and continue to confirm their position from the passage "on that very ground" up to "all else is false." On that account, the noble Saṅgha admonishes those sister nuns, saying: Do not take the side of a nun who, wishing to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, has entered upon a dispute for the sake of division, has genuinely taken up that quarrel, holds fast to it and knowingly persists in it, who acts as a companion to her and speaks discordantly. Sisters, abandon this — abandon taking the side of one who speaks discordantly in this schism of the Saṅgha.' This admonishment is performed by a motion and three acts.

Those among the noble Saṅgha of sisters who consent to the admonishment of these nuns by motion and three acts — let them be silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak. This is the first recitation of the act. In the same way it is to be recited a second and a third time.

The noble Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the noble Saṅgha has performed the admonishment of the nuns who act as companions by means of a motion and three acts. Since no one has spoken, it is accepted as such — up to and including this passage.

When those nuns have been admonished by a motion and three acts, and when those nuns continue to confirm from the passage 'on that very ground, by force' up to 'all else is false,' the nuns then reported this to the monks, and the monks in turn reported it to the Blessed One, whereupon the Blessed One, beginning from the account of what had occurred, proceeded to establish the training rule.

Furthermore, any nun who, wishing to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, has entered upon a dispute for the sake of division —

and has fully taken up the dispute and continues to hold firmly to it — those nuns shall address that nun as follows: "Noble sister, do not enter upon dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not, having fully taken up a dispute for the sake of division, hold to it and pursue it further. Noble sister, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. Let the Saṅgha not be divided. Rejoice together, without dispute, with one single aim; recite together; be like water and milk blended into one. Make the Teacher's teaching shine clearly, and you will dwell touching upon ease. Noble sister, abandon this very ground of yours that causes division in the Saṅgha." In this way she is to be admonished.

When those nuns admonish that nun in this way — if she relinquishes that ground, then that is well. If she does not relinquish it, in order to make her relinquish that ground she is to be admonished and instructed a second time and a third time in full. When she has been admonished and instructed a second time and a third time in full — if she relinquishes that ground, then that is well. If she does not relinquish it, then this very matter, on the third occasion, together with the announcement, constitutes the remainder for the Saṅgha.

Now as for "whatever nun" — this refers to Stomāgamoā, or any other who is similar to her. "Saṅgha" refers to the community of female śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. "Harmonious" means of one taste. "For the sake of division" means for the purpose of making it into two. "Has entered upon" means exerts herself. "For the purpose of causing division" — the grounds for division are fourteen: whether it is Dharma or not Dharma, Vinaya or not Vinaya, transgression or not transgression, one that has a remainder or one that has no remainder, grave or light, requiring confession or requiring restraint, contrary to the Vinaya, or something that will be declared an offence — whatever thing of these, having been well and thoroughly seized upon. "Dispute" refers to the four kinds of dispute, from "dispute" through to "dispute for the sake of action." "Having fully taken up and holding to it" means with attachment and clinging. "Those nuns shall address that nun" means those who belong to this Dharma. "She is to be admonished, having taken her aside" means admonishing just as was said before. "If that ground is relinquished" — that is the view. "If she relinquishes it, then that is well" means "then that is good." "If she does not relinquish it" — that is the view. "She is to be admonished and instructed a second time and a third time in full" means just as was said before through the motion and the three acts — this is the full instruction, this is the full teaching. "This very matter" employs the term "Dharma" for what is not Dharma. "On the third occasion, together with the announcement" means together with the recitation. All else is as before.

As to how a downfall arises in this matter: if a nun enters upon dividing the Saṅgha, whatever and however it may be, in every case it becomes a downfall of wrongdoing. When she has been admonished, if she relinquishes that ground, then that is well. If she does not relinquish it, it is a grave offence. The rest is to be stated just as before.

Here is completed the seventeenth remainder of the Saṅgha in the analysis of the rules for nuns.

Thereupon the Blessed One, while remaining in that very place, established the second rule of training. One nun, or two, or many — however many — who have become companions of that nun,

who speak in a discordant way, say to the other nuns: "Noble ones, do not speak anything at all to this nun, whether good or bad. Why is that? Because this nun speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya. This nun has taken up the Dharma and the Vinaya correctly, holds them firmly, and follows them in practice. This nun speaks with awareness and not without awareness. Whatever she approves of and consents to, we too approve of and consent to." If they say such words as these, the nuns should say to those nuns: "Noble ones, do not say such things as: 'This nun speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya; this nun has taken up the Dharma and the Vinaya correctly, holds them firmly, and follows them in practice; this nun speaks with awareness and not without awareness; whatever she approves of and consents to, we too approve of and consent to.' Why is that? Because this nun does not speak the Dharma and does not speak the Vinaya. Rather, this nun speaks what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Vinaya. This nun has taken up what is not the Dharma and what is not the Vinaya, holds them firmly, and follows them in practice. This nun speaks without awareness, and not with awareness. Do not approve of and consent to whatever she approves of and consents to. Do not divide the Saṅgha. Wish for harmony with the Saṅgha. Be harmonious with the Saṅgha. Let the Saṅgha be harmonious and undivided, rejoicing together and without dispute, dwelling in unity, reciting together, and blended like water and milk. Illuminating the Teacher's teaching, you will come to abide in the touch of happiness. You nuns, abandon this conduct of speaking in a discordant way, taking the side of one who would divide the Saṅgha." In this way the nuns should address those nuns.

When the nuns have thus addressed those nuns, if they relinquish that ground, then that is well. If they do not relinquish it, in order to induce them to relinquish that ground, they are to be admonished correctly up to a second and a third time, and correctly instructed. When they have been correctly admonished and correctly instructed up to a second and a third time, if they relinquish that ground, then that is well. If they do not relinquish it, this same rule, at the third time, together with the arising from it, is a grave offence against the remainder of the Saṅgha.

The phrase "of that nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. The phrase "who have become companions" refers to the twelve groups. The phrase "one" means just one. The phrase "two" means just two. The phrase "however many" means more than two is many. The phrase "to the nuns" means to those who observe this rule. The phrase "if they say such words as these" means when they speak thus. The phrase "noble ones" means you all. The phrase "to this nun" means to Sthūlanandā. The phrase "do not say anything at all" means "do not teach anything at all, whether much or little." The phrase "whether good" means "do not lead her to take up what is virtuous." The phrase "or bad" means "do not draw her out from what is non-virtuous." The phrase "because this nun speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya" means in accordance with how the Dharma is and in accordance with how conduct is. The phrase "this nun speaks with awareness and not without awareness" means she expresses things in terms of how she knows them and how she sees them. The phrase "whatever she approves of" means what she and we alike consent to.

The phrase "to those nuns" means to the twelve assemblies. The phrase "by the nuns" means by those who adhere to this Dharma. The phrase "this is to be declared" means that this is to be reported in these words. The phrase "in harmony" means with one voice. The phrase "the Saṅgha" means the Saṅgha of female hearers of the Tathāgata. The phrase "division" means that it becomes split in two. The phrase "to engage in" means to exert oneself. The phrase "of hers" means of Subhāgā. The phrase "having become an accomplice" means to bring something to completion. The phrase "siding with" means consenting with patience, desire, and mental intention. The phrase "speaking discordantly" means bringing about a state of disharmony. The phrase "to those nuns" means to the twelve assemblies. The phrase "by the nuns" means by those who adhere to this Dharma. The phrase "this is to be declared" means that this is to be reported in these words.

The phrase "Sister, abandon this behavior — this siding with one who speaks discordantly so as to divide the Saṅgha" means: "By many different approaches, do not seek to divide the Saṅgha." The phrase "if, when this has been declared, she abandons that basis, then that is good; if she does not abandon it, it is to be taken up and reported again" means as previously described in the declaration. The phrase "and if, upon taking it up and reporting it again, she abandons that basis, then that is good; if she does not abandon it, it is to be reported by the act of a motion with three resolutions" means as previously described in the declaration; this constitutes proper admonishment; this constitutes proper instruction. The phrase "this Dharma also" means that what is not Dharma is presented under the name of Dharma. The phrase "accompanied by formal disclosure at the third instance" means accompanied by the Teacher. The rest is as stated previously.

As for how a transgression arises in this context: if a nun enters into siding with schism in the Saṅgha — whatever form this takes — in all such cases it becomes a transgression of a wrongdoing. If she is taken up and reported again and she abandons that basis, then that is good; if she does not abandon it, a grave offense is incurred. The rest is to be stated as before.

The eighteenth rule among the remainder of the Saṅghāvaśeṣa offenses in the Analysis of the Nuns' Code is complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha), the Bhagavān, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, two monks by the names of Agalamgyo and Napso, together with reddish-yellow-robed monks, were dwelling there practicing and established in all the sinful Dharmas of those who bring disgrace upon households. These individuals would engage in chattering and amusing themselves together with women; they would sport about, make noise, laugh, play, and physically frolic with abandon. They would sit together with women on a single seat and lie together on a single bed; they would eat many kinds of food from a single vessel and drink many drinks from a single vessel. They would gather flowers, have others gather them, wear them as ear ornaments, and have others wear them as ear ornaments. They would weave garlands of flowers and have others weave them. They would beat time in dance, sing songs, and produce musical sounds, asking one another "Was the dancing well performed? Was the song well taken up? Was the musical sound well drawn out?" — all the way through running, leaping, and jumping. They would lay aside their robes and walk exposing their chests. They would leap like fish, crawl like tortoises, and also roll about on their backs. They would clap their hands, slap their shoulders, swing their thighs, and strike their bodies, while also producing from their mouths the sounds of drums and cymbals — ta and ha — as well as the sounds of the mṛdaṅga drum and the sounds of ordinary drums from their mouths; they would emit the cry of a bull-elephant, produce the sound of a buffalo, and bellow in the manner of a great elephant.

They would emit the cry of a peacock and produce the call of a cuckoo. They would stage mock battles with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and set those battles in motion. They would stage mock battles with armies of women, armies of men, armies of boys, and armies of girls, and set those battles in motion. They would stage the fighting of cocks, the fighting of rams, the fighting of quails, and the fighting of partridges — pitting cocks, rams, quails, and partridges against one another — and set those contests in motion. These and other things unbecoming of a renunciant they would do and cause others to do.

At that time the twelve groups of companions would laugh, play, and engage in rough and rowdy behavior with their bodies. While they dwelt in that conduct, in that manner of life, and on that path of behavior, monks of good character would not come to stay where those corrupt monks resided, and those who had already come would wish to leave. Even those with matted hair or shaved heads found it intolerable.

The brahmins and householders settled on Mount Reḍeri, witnessing their conduct, became displeased and lost faith, and thought to themselves that they would not give alms even to the genuine monks — let alone to those who had just arrived. At that time the venerable Ānanda, together with the elder monks, went to Mount Reḍeri and performed the act of expulsion against the two monks Gamaggo and Nabaso. At that very time, the twelve groups of nuns were likewise expelled for having brought disgrace upon households.

The companions and attendants who dwelt with those twelve groups of nuns then came to Śrāvastī, confessed what was to be confessed, and restrained what was to be restrained. Together with the nuns of upright conduct they undertook the rites of the restoration ceremony, the invitation ceremony, formal requests, the act of two requests, and the act of a request with four motions.

Thereupon the twelve groups thought: "We will go to seek the approval of the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of monks, and the Saṅgha of nuns." The twelve groups then set out, circling around toward Śrāvastī, and proceeding on their way they eventually arrived at Śrāvastī. When the nuns there saw the twelve groups of nuns approaching, they reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, these twelve groups have been expelled — how should we now proceed?" They said nothing aloud, but with a gesture of the hand pointed toward the last assembly hall. Those groups acted accordingly. Thereupon the companions and attendants of those groups also said nothing, spoke no words to anyone, and showed no sign of welcome to anyone. And those twelve groups said this to their companions and attendants who dwelt with them: "Sisters, what is there for us to say or proclaim or announce that you have not already said, proclaimed, and announced? For the senior nuns among the nuns to say nothing, to speak to no one — that is fitting for them. But you — why do you not speak?" Those attendants, keeping the nuns at a distance, said: "What you say is true, yet we ourselves have confessed what was to be confessed, restrained what was to be restrained, and undertaken all acts up to and including the act of a request with four motions."

Then those twelve groups of nuns said this to the elder nuns among the nuns: "Here there are some nuns who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear — and from what is precisely the same class of transgression, some nuns expel and others do not expel." Then the nuns said to the twelve groups of nuns: "Whom do you accuse of acting out of desire?" They replied: "The elder nuns among the nuns." At that point the nuns spoke to the monks. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you are to confront the twelve groups of nuns. And you nuns are to say this to the elder nuns among the nuns: 'Here there are some nuns who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear — and from what is precisely the same class of transgression, some nuns expel and others do not expel' — do not say that. And why not? These nuns do not act out of desire, out of aversion, out of delusion, or out of fear. Rather, it is you yourselves who are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct. Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that they corrupt households? Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that they practice wicked conduct? Sisters, let go of this manner of speaking — from the phrase 'acting out of desire' through to the phrase 'acting out of fear.' When confronting them and delivering the instruction, use the text beginning with 'on that very basis, persistently' through to 'the other is delusion.'"

At that point the nuns spoke to the monks again. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, the confrontation of the twelve groups of nuns by a request and a fourfold act is to be carried out as follows: seats are to be arranged, and then one nun makes the motion and the act is performed. 'Sisters, let the noble Saṅgha hear me. These twelve groups of nuns are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct. Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that they corrupt households? Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that they practice wicked conduct?' — up to and including 'fully learned that they practice wicked conduct.' The elder monks, at the stated time and place, have performed the act of expelling them, and they have been reproached before the nuns with the phrases running from 'acting out of desire' through to 'acting out of fear,' and many nuns have confronted them and delivered the instruction; and when confronting them and delivering the instruction, the text runs from 'on that very basis, persistently' through to 'the other is delusion.' If the time is right for the noble Saṅgha and they consent, let them grant approval. And let the noble Saṅgha confront the twelve groups of nuns by a request and a fourfold act. Sisters, do not say: 'Here there are some nuns who act out of desire' — down to 'who act out of fear.' Rather, it is you yourselves who are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct,' — from that point down to: 'Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that you practice wicked conduct?' Sisters, let go of this manner of speaking — the phrase 'acting out of desire,' and 'acting out of aversion,' and 'acting out of delusion,' and 'acting out of fear.' This is the motion."

The act shall be performed as follows. "Let the noble Saṅgha, sisters, hear me. These twelve groups of nuns are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct. Whether they saw, heard, or fully learned of this corruption of households — and whether they saw, heard, or fully learned of the practice of wicked conduct — the senior monks went to the boundary marker, performed the act of expulsion, and when those nuns then reproached them, saying 'acting out of desire' down to 'acting out of fear,' and when they were thereupon admonished by a large number of nuns — upon that admonishment, from the phrase 'be firm on this very ground' down to 'the other is delusion' — let the noble Saṅgha confront these twelve groups of nuns by a request and a fourfold act. Sisters, do not say: 'Here there are some nuns who act out of desire' — down to 'who act out of fear.' Rather, you yourselves are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct — from that point down to: 'Have you seen, heard, or fully learned that you practice wicked conduct? Sisters, let go of such language as the phrase "acting out of desire," and "acting out of aversion," and "acting out of delusion," and "acting out of fear."' Those among the noble Saṅgha who approve of confronting these twelve groups by a request and a fourfold act, let them remain silent. Those who do not approve, let them speak. This is the first recitation of the motion. In the same way let the matter be recited a second and a third time. The noble Saṅgha has approved and consented; the Saṅgha has confronted these twelve groups of nuns by a request and a fourfold act. Because no one has spoken, so it is held." Down to this point.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the eleventh fascicle.

Even though they were confronted by a request and a fourfold act, in the passage from "be firm on this very ground" down to "the other is delusion," the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" onward, proceeded to establish a training rule.

A large number of nuns were residing near a certain village or town, and they too had become corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct. Whether others had seen, heard, or fully learned of this corruption of households, or had seen, heard, or fully learned of their practice of wicked conduct — if so, the nuns were to address those nuns in these words: "Venerable sisters, you are corrupters of households and practitioners of wicked conduct. Have you seen, heard, or fully learned of your own corruption of households? Have you seen, heard, or fully learned of your own practice of wicked conduct? Venerable sisters, it is enough that you have resided in this place. From today, leave this place." Then, if those nuns said to the nuns: "Here there are some nuns who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear — yet among those guilty of exactly the same transgression, some nuns are expelled and others are not," the nuns were then to address those nuns with these words: "Venerable sisters, you have said: 'Here there are some nuns who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear,

yet among those guilty of exactly the same transgression, some nuns are expelled and others are not.' Do not say such a thing. Rather, venerable sisters, you yourselves are the ones who bring disgrace upon households and who engage in wicked conduct everywhere. Do you see, hear, or fully know that you bring disgrace upon households? Do you see, hear, or fully know that you engage in wicked conduct everywhere? Therefore, noble sisters, abandon this kind of verbal path of 'acting out of desire,' and of 'acting out of aversion,' and of 'acting out of delusion,' and of 'acting out of fear.'" When the nuns have addressed those nuns with these words, if they relinquish that basis, then so much the better. If they do not relinquish it — up to that point which reads "they are to be addressed properly a second and a third time, and instructed properly" — they are to be addressed properly a second and a third time and instructed properly, in order that they relinquish that basis. When they have been properly addressed and properly instructed a second and a third time: if they relinquish that basis, so much the better; if they do not relinquish it, then this matter too is fit to be resolved by a Saṅgha motion carried to a third proclamation. "Nuns" refers to those who belong to this Dharma. "Many" means more than two, that is, a great many. "In a town or in a village" means in a market town, or in the countryside, or in a mountain region. As for the phrase "those who bring disgrace upon households," "households" means the households of brahmins, of the royal class, and of householders. "Bringing disgrace" means: it is to be fully understood that disgrace is brought upon households by two causes — by association and by enjoyment. How is it by association? By laughing together, playing together, and engaging in bodily contact with women, boys, and girls, and dwelling right there in that place — that is the disgrace through association. How is it by enjoyment? By stripping flowers, fruits, or plants right within those same households — that is the disgrace through enjoyment. "See" means by means of visual consciousness. "Hear" means by means of auditory consciousness. "Fully know" means by means of the remaining collections of consciousness other than those. "Those nuns" refers to those belonging to the twelve groups. "The nuns" refers to those who belong to this Dharma. The phrase "with these words" means: when properly addressed with these very words. The phrase "venerable sisters, do not speak the words 'acting out of desire'" is a rebuke. "Of exactly the same transgression" means from among equivalent transgressions. "Some nuns are expelled" refers to the twelve groups. "Others are not expelled" refers to those dwelling together with them and their attendants. The phrase "the nuns are to address them with these words" means: from the words "venerable sisters, abandon the verbal path of acting out of desire" up through the words "and of acting out of fear" — they are to cast aside that verbal path. When the nuns have addressed those nuns with these words, "if they relinquish that basis, so much the better" means: that would be excellent. "If they do not relinquish it, they are to be addressed formally" means: it is to be done just as stated in the previous address. When they have been addressed formally and still do not relinquish that basis, "they are to be addressed by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations" — this likewise is to be done just as stated previously. "Properly addressed" is precisely that; "properly instructed" is precisely that. "This matter too" means: this non-Dharma is spoken of here by the name of Dharma. "Fit to be resolved by a third proclamation" includes the Teacher. The rest is as before. Then, as to how a transgression arises here:

If a nun says to even a small extent to another nun, "Here, some nuns go out of desire, some go out of aversion, some go out of delusion, and some go out of fear," she incurs a transgression of wrongdoing in every case. When she has been formally addressed and instructed, if she then relinquishes that basis, all is well. If she does not relinquish it, she falls into the heavier offense. The rest is to be stated just as above.

The nineteenth section of the Saṅgha remainder offenses from the Nuns' Vibhaṅga is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling in Kauśāmbī, in the Ghositārāma pleasure grove. At that time in Kauśāmbī a Śākyan daughter who had gone forth as a nun bore the name Dundā. A transgression had arisen in her case. Those who lived the holy life alongside her, those who wished her well, who wished her benefit, who wished her happiness, who wished to guide her, who wished her success and wellbeing, said to her: "Dundā, a transgression has arisen in you; please come forward to confess it." To this she replied: "Whether you have done good or ill, sisters, say nothing whatsoever to me about it. For you have all gone forth from families of various clans, various lineages, various bloodlines. Just as in the autumn season the dried leaves of the trees are gathered together by the wind and piled into one heap, so too you have gone forth from various clans, various lineages, various bloodlines. Yet it was said of me that my noble one has manifestly awakened to full awakening."

At that point the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you should formally address and instruct the nun Dundā, saying: 'Dundā, when nuns who wish you well, who wish you benefit, who wish you happiness, who wish to guide you, who wish you success and wellbeing, speak to you, do not make yourself one who is not to be spoken to — rather make yourself one who is open to being spoken to. And let the nuns speak to Dundā in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya; and you too, Dundā, speak to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. For it is in this way — by speaking to one another, by guiding and instructing one another, by lifting one another out of transgressions — that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, will grow. Dundā, see the end of the conduct of one who does not open herself to being spoken to.' You should address and instruct her thus."

When the nuns gave her this formal address and instruction, from the phrase "that very basis" through to "that is a lie" — all of that interval the nuns reported to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you are to address and instruct the nun Dundā by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations. The formal address is to be performed as follows: beginning from the words 'having prepared a seat,' a single nun is to make the motion and carry out the act. The act is as follows:

'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. The nun Dundā here, when those who live the holy life alongside her, those who seek her wellbeing, who seek her benefit, who seek her happiness, who seek to guide her, who seek her success and wellbeing, said to her, "Please come forward to confess your transgression," replied in this manner: "Sisters, whether you have done good or ill, say nothing whatsoever to me about it, and I likewise will say nothing to you, whether good or ill." '

When the nuns formally addressed and instructed her in great numbers with these words —

she stubbornly held to that very position, clung to it with attachment, and continued to designate it afterward as follows: "This alone is true; everything else is false." If it is fitting for the noble Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, then let the noble Saṅgha grant its approval. And let the nun Dundā be formally instructed by the Saṅgha with a resolution and three proclamations: "Dundā, when the nuns speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, do not treat yourself as one who is not to be addressed — rather, treat yourself as one who is to be addressed. And why? Because when the nuns speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, you in turn will be speaking to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. It is in this way — by speaking to one another, by guiding one another, by raising one another up from transgressions — that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, will grow." This is the motion.

The act is as follows:

Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. The nun Dundā here, when those who live the holy life alongside her, those who seek her wellbeing, who seek her benefit, who seek her happiness, who seek to guide her, who seek her success and wellbeing, said to her, "Please come forward to confess your transgression," replied in this manner: "Sisters, whether you have done good or ill, say nothing whatsoever to me about it, and I likewise will say nothing to you, whether good or ill." When the nuns formally addressed and instructed her in great numbers with these words, she stubbornly held to that very position, clung to it with attachment, and continued to designate it as follows: "This alone is true; everything else is false." For that reason, the noble Saṅgha formally instructs the nun Dundā with a resolution and three proclamations: "Dundā, when the nuns speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, do not treat yourself as one who is not to be addressed — rather, treat yourself as one who is to be addressed. And why? Because when the nuns speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, you in turn will be speaking to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. It is in this way — by speaking to one another, by guiding one another, by raising one another up from transgressions — that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, will grow."

Those nuns who consent to and approve of the formal instruction of the nun Dundā by means of a resolution and three proclamations, let them remain silent. Those who do not consent, let them speak.

This is the first recitation of the act. In the same way, this matter is repeated a second and a third time.

The Saṅgha having consented and granted approval, the Saṅgha has formally instructed the nun Dundā by means of a resolution and three proclamations. Since no one has spoken, it is hereby taken that the matter stands as thus accepted. The instruction by resolution and three proclamations is so established.

Now during the formal instruction by resolution and three proclamations — specifically the portion beginning with "she stubbornly held to that very position" and ending with "this alone is true; everything else is false" — the nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence," proceeded to set forth a training rule. There are some nuns who by nature are difficult to admonish; and the training rules belonging to the category of exhortation, along with those belonging to the category of sūtras of the Sugata, when the nuns speak in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya —

she makes herself unavailable to be spoken to. "Noble ones, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, say nothing at all to her. And she likewise, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, will say nothing at all to the noble ones. Noble ones, leave the path of words open to me — what would be accomplished by your speaking to me?" When this is said to that nun, the other nuns should speak to her as follows: "Noble one, do not make yourself unavailable to be spoken to regarding the training rules belonging to the category of exhortation and those belonging to the category of sūtras of the Sugata. Noble one, when the nuns speak in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, do not make yourself unavailable to be spoken to — rather, noble one, make yourself available to be spoken to, and to be spoken to alone. And when the noble ones speak to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, the noble one too should speak to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. Why is that? Because it is in this way — through one speaking to another, through one instructing and guiding another, through one lifting another out of transgressions — that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, will grow. Noble one, abandon that kind of conduct of making yourself unavailable to be spoken to." If the nuns speak thus to that nun and she abandons that basis, then well and good. If she does not abandon it, this matter is to be dealt with up to three times by the requisite portion of the Saṅgha. "Nun" means the petitioner. "One who is difficult to admonish" means one who does not receive in a straightforward and fitting manner the listening and following of harmonious verbal counsel, or who receives it in an antagonistic manner. "Exhortation" means that which is shown in the sūtra on individual liberation (Skt. prātimokṣa). "Sugata" means the Teacher. "Sūtra" means that which was spoken by the buddha or uttered by a śrāvaka — namely the eight training rules that constitute defeat, the twenty rules requiring a formal act of the Saṅgha, the thirty-three rules of abandonment, the one hundred and eighty rules entailing transgression, the eleven rules requiring individual confession, the many rules of training, the seven principles for settling disputes, the seventeen Vinaya bases, the minor rules, the small rules, the occasion for framing a rule, the Vinaya Mātṛkā, the extension of the Vinaya, the fifth Vinaya, the sixteenth Vinaya, the Brāhmaṇī's Daughter, and those included in the questions of the Nearby Retinue — all of these well composed together. "When the nuns speak in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya" means: whatever act accords with the Dharma as it is, with the Vinaya as it is, and with the teaching of the Teacher as it is. "When it is spoken" means: when it is applied in a gentle manner. "Making oneself unavailable to be spoken to" means: setting aside oneself as other than that instruction and teaching. "Sisters, say nothing at all to her" means: placing her in a state of elevated and extreme difficulty to admonish due to her own self-concern. "Whether it be wholesome" means: not placing her in virtue. "Whether it be unwholesome" means: not lifting her out of wrongdoing. "And she likewise will say nothing at all to the sisters" means: abandoning, out of her own self-concern, the elevated mutual instruction and guidance of one toward another. "Whether it be wholesome, she too to the sisters" means: not placing them in virtue. "Whether it be unwholesome, she too to the sisters" means: not lifting them out of wrongdoing. "Noble ones, leave it alone" means "let it go at a distance," and "what — do you?" means "have you been appointed by these reasons to guide me?" "To that nun" means to the petitioner. "The nuns" means those who hold this Dharma.

"In order to relinquish that basis" means: as before. "In that case, excellent" means: in that case it is good. "If she does not relinquish it" means: if, having been admonished and instructed, she is instructed as before. "In that case, if she relinquishes that basis" and so forth up to that point is as before. "In that case, excellent" means: in that case it is good. "If she does not relinquish it" means: if she is instructed by means of a motion with a fourth recitation, instructed as before. That proper instruction is precisely that.

"This Dharma too" means: this which is not Dharma is spoken under the name of Dharma. "Arising together with up to three recitations" means: what is fitting to arise. "With the Saṅgha as remainder" means: this transgression depends on the two assemblies of the Saṅgha; it relies on the two assemblies of the Saṅgha; it is the two assemblies of the Saṅgha that will lift one from that transgression — not an individual person. Moreover, while the eight defeats leave no remainder, this one has a remainder, and therefore it is called "with the Saṅgha as remainder."

How does one come to incur this as a transgression? When the nuns have spoken to a nun even the slightest amount, and she then says, "Sisters, say nothing at all to me!" — whenever she speaks thus, it becomes a wrongdoing in every instance. If, when admonished and instructed, she does not relinquish that basis, it is a grave offense. When the first recitation of the formal act is performed, if she relinquishes that basis, it is excellent in that case; if she does not relinquish it, it is grave. When the second recitation is performed, if she relinquishes it before the recitation is complete, it is excellent in that case; if she does not relinquish it, it is grave when the recitation is complete. While the third recitation is being performed, if before it is complete she acts in conformity with what is not Dharma, or acts in non-conformity with Dharma — that is, if she does not act in accordance with what the Dharma is, what the Vinaya is, and what the Teacher's teaching is — there is no transgression. When the fourth recitation is performed and completed, if she then acts in accordance with what the Dharma is, what the Vinaya is, and what the Teacher's teaching is, it becomes the Saṅgha remainder.

That nun, while remaining in her very seat, should declare: "Noble ones, I have incurred a Saṅgha-remainder transgression." If she declares it, that is excellent. If she does not declare it, and she goes on to confess a transgression and without having confessed it individually proceeds thereafter to undertake a motion, a motion with a second, and a motion with a fourth recitation, it becomes a wrongdoing in every instance. For one who is acting for the first time and so forth, there is no transgression.

The twentieth Saṅgha remainder is complete. The Saṅgha remainders from the Vinayavibhaṅga of the nuns are hereby concluded.

Summary verse:

Retaining robes for ten days, not parting from them,
not dispatching a non-relative in a month,
the upper robe and the lower robe together,
two hides, sending a messenger,
silk, fine wool, gold and silver,
and engaging in various trade.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, many robes of this kind came to the nuns: with one robe, some went to visit their abbesses and teachers; with another robe, some had prostrations performed in the temple; with another robe, some had saluting gestures made; with yet another robe, some had it sent along smeared with a coarse paste of liquid; with another robe, some had the latrine area and the urinal area wiped; with another robe, some had tooth-sticks thrown away; with another robe, some had the lodgings and utensils swept and put in order.

With another robe, some went into the village on alms-round. With another robe, some were seated in the row at mealtime. With another robe, some listened to the Dharma by day. With another robe, some listened to the Dharma by night. With another robe, some individually experienced the instructions and guidance given in the presence of the Teacher.

When nuns of lesser purpose were engaged in reproaching others in this regard, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this grounds for a rule, and this circumstance, convened the community of nuns and said: "This is done so that my female disciples may come to know, and so that the basis of training may be well established."

The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, deliberately inquire even while knowing: they inquire while knowing, not while not knowing; at the proper time, not at an improper time; purposefully, not without purpose. For the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, turn away the flood of wrongdoing. Therefore, it being purposeful, the Blessed One deliberately inquired of the nuns about this matter: "Nuns, is it true that robes of this kind, in such great number, have come to you?"

"Blessed One, it is so."

The Blessed One rebuked them with censure for being difficult to provide for, difficult to satisfy, having great desires, not knowing contentment, not possessing the virtue of refinement, and not knowing moderation. Then the Blessed One praised the nuns for being easy to provide for, easy to satisfy, having few desires, knowing contentment, possessing the virtue of refinement, and knowing moderation. And the Blessed One established the rule of training for the nuns:

"When a nun has accepted a robe and released her claim-mark, she may retain an extra robe beyond what is allowed for up to ten days. If she retains it beyond that, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment."

Now, what is meant by "has accepted a robe" encompasses four cases: there is accepting a robe without having released the claim-mark; there is releasing the claim-mark without having accepted the robe; there is both accepting the robe and releasing the claim-mark; and there is neither accepting the robe nor releasing the claim-mark.

What is the case of accepting a robe without having released the claim-mark? It is as follows: a nun has washed, spread out, spread flat, and turned over the robes, but the community of nuns has not yet released the claim-mark. That is the case of accepting a robe without having released the claim-mark.

What is the case of releasing the claim-mark without having accepted the robe? It is as follows: the community of nuns has released the claim-mark, but the nun has not yet washed, spread out, spread flat, and turned over the robes. That is the case of releasing the claim-mark without having accepted the robe.

What is the case of both accepting the robe and releasing the claim-mark? It is as follows: the nun has washed, spread out, spread flat, and turned over the robes, and the community of nuns has also released the claim-mark. That is the case of both accepting the robe and releasing the claim-mark.

What is the case of neither accepting the robe nor releasing the claim-mark? It is everything other than those cases just described.

"Nun" refers to those who belong to this Dharma. "Up to ten days" means ten daytime periods. "An extra robe beyond what is allowed" means more than the five that have been consecrated. "Without having been made allowable" means that it has not been made allowable in anyone's name whatsoever, and is being held as one's own.

"Is to be relinquished — an offense requiring expiation" means that one must relinquish that article and then confess the offense of expiation. "Offense" refers to falling into hell, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into an evil destiny, into a wretched rebirth — and therefore it is said to "occasion an offense."

Now, how does the transgression come about in this case? It is as follows. If a nun obtains a robe on the first day of the fortnight, that nun must, within those very ten days, either consecrate that robe, make it allowable, give it away, or bestow it upon another. If she neither consecrates it, nor makes it allowable, nor gives it away, nor bestows it upon another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation.

Just as with obtaining a robe on the first day, so too for obtaining it on the second day, the third day, and so on through within the tenth day: that nun must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the robe, make it allowable, or give it away. If she neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation.

If a nun obtains one robe on the first day and then obtains another on the following day, that nun must consecrate the earlier robe and either make the later one allowable or consecrate it. Alternatively, she may consecrate the later robe and make the earlier one allowable. If she neither consecrates nor makes allowable nor gives away, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation.

Similarly, if a nun obtains one robe on the ninth day and obtains another on the tenth day, that nun must consecrate the earlier robe and either make the later one allowable or give it away — and so on through: it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation.

If a nun obtains two robes on the first day and also obtains two on the second day, that nun must consecrate the earlier two robes and either make the later two allowable or give them away. If she neither makes them allowable nor gives them away, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation. If a nun obtains two robes on the ninth day and also obtains two on the tenth day — this is to be stated in full in the same way.

If a nun obtains a very great many robes on the first day and also obtains a very great many on the second day, that nun must consecrate the very great many earlier robes and either make the very great many later robes allowable or give them away. Alternatively, she may consecrate the very great many later robes and either make the very great many earlier robes allowable or give them away. If she neither consecrates, nor makes allowable, nor gives away, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation. If a nun obtains a very great many robes on the ninth day and also obtains a very great many on the tenth day — and so on in the same way through: it is an offense requiring relinquishment and expiation.

If a nun's robe has become subject to relinquishment, and without having relinquished it and separated from it, and without having confessed the offense, she obtains another robe, that too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the taint of the former one. If a nun's robe has become subject to relinquishment, and although she has relinquished it and separated from it, yet without having confessed the offense she obtains another robe, that too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the taint of the former one. If a nun's robe has become subject to relinquishment, and she has relinquished it and separated from it, yet without having confessed the offense she obtains another robe, that too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the taint of the former one.

If a nun's robe has become subject to relinquishment, and she has relinquished it and separated from it, and then confessed the offense and obtains another robe, there is no transgression. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensation, there is no transgression.

The first section on relinquishable offenses from the Nuns' Vibhaṅga is complete.

The case that gave rise to the rule occurred at Śrāvastī. Some nuns who had undertaken the rains retreat and completed it to the end obtained robes of the Dharma. They washed those robes, turned them, filled a bundle, tied them into a roll, and then went wandering through the countryside wearing their outer robes and lower robes. While they wandered through the countryside in this way, the robes were neither hidden nor stored away. The nuns who were resident in their lodging had much work to do with those robes, drying them and shaking them out, and they were occupied with much activity, so that recitation of scripture, reading, memorization, meditation, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding of mind were interrupted — all because nuns with little to attend to were being criticized. The nuns then spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence" and so on, proceeded through to laying down the training rule. The rule was: if a nun who has taken possession of a robe removes the marking thread and separates from any one of the five Dharma robes beyond the boundary, it is a relinquishable offense. Thus was the original training rule established.

Then, when the Blessed One was residing at Rājagṛha and had granted the elder Mahā-Kāśyapa permission not to be separated from his patched robe, he laid down the training rule once more. At that time the senior nuns came to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and prostrated with their heads at his two feet. They then addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, how are we to recite this training rule?" The Blessed One then spoke in praise of nuns who desire the training, who are respectful toward the training, and who are equipped with the means for the training, and he declared to the nuns: "The former rule is set aside. Since this is now the allowance, my female śrāvaka disciples shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: if a nun has taken possession of a robe and removes the marking thread, and then is separated from any one of the five Dharma robes for even a single night beyond the boundary, unless the Saṅgha has granted permission, it is a relinquishable offense."

As for "having taken possession of a robe," this is as explained above. As for "the five Dharma robes," these are the patched robe and the outer robe and so forth — any robe that has been duly consecrated as a Dharma robe. As for "separated beyond the boundary," this means when dawn breaks. As for "unless the Saṅgha has granted permission," this means setting aside the permission granted by the Saṅgha. As for "relinquishable offense," this is as explained above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? The summary verse on the bounds of transgression:

One house, two houses,
an assembly, a space enclosed by a fence,
the perimeter surrounding a pond,
a house, a shop, a market stall,
a rooftop, a thoroughfare, a battlefield,
an assembly of armies, a non-Buddhist chariot,
a boat, a pleasure garden,
a grove of trees — and what is asked.

What is a village of one house? What is a village of two houses? What is an assembly of houses? What is a village enclosed by a screen? What is a village enclosed by a wall? Likewise, what is a village enclosed by a moat, and what is a single outlying neighborhood of a village,

a single outlying neighborhood of a village with multiple neighborhoods, multiple villages with a single outlying neighborhood, and multiple villages with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods — what is a household with a single outlying neighborhood? What is a household with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods? What is a group of many households with a single outlying neighborhood, and a group of many households with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods? Likewise, there are shops with a single outlying neighborhood and shops with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many shops with a single outlying neighborhood and many shops with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are market stalls with a single outlying neighborhood and market stalls with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many market stalls with a single outlying neighborhood and many market stalls with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are rooftops with a single outlying neighborhood and rooftops with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many rooftops with a single outlying neighborhood and many rooftops with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are battlefields with a single outlying neighborhood and battlefields with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many battlefields with a single outlying neighborhood and many battlefields with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are armies assembled for battle with a single outlying neighborhood and armies assembled for battle with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many armies assembled for battle with a single outlying neighborhood and many armies assembled for battle with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are non-Buddhist households with a single outlying neighborhood and non-Buddhist households with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many non-Buddhist households with a single outlying neighborhood and many non-Buddhist households with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are the households of wanderers with a single outlying neighborhood and households of wanderers with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many such households with a single outlying neighborhood and many such households with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are chariots with a single outlying neighborhood and chariots with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many chariots with a single outlying neighborhood and many chariots with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are boats with a single outlying neighborhood and boats with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many boats with a single outlying neighborhood and many boats with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are pleasure gardens with a single outlying neighborhood and pleasure gardens with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many pleasure gardens with a single outlying neighborhood and many pleasure gardens with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. Likewise, there are groves of trees with a single outlying neighborhood and groves of trees with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods, many groves of trees with a single outlying neighborhood and many groves of trees with multiple separate outlying neighborhoods. This is the teaching on that transgression.

Now the explanation shall be given. What is a village of one house? The Blessed One declared: it is whatever settlement belongs to nomads, forest-dwellers, or to those whose livelihood depends on craftsmanship — such a settlement is a village of one house. Just as with a village of one house, so too with a village of two houses. What is a village that is an assembly of houses? It is whatever settlement has become the dwelling place of various leading persons among humans — this is called a village that is an assembly of houses. What is a village enclosed by a screen? It is whatever village is enclosed by a screen. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside, or the distance covered by a twelve-rung ladder placed against it, or the space that would be filled by a cartload of bamboo from the land of Magadha. If a nun leaves her robes inside and goes to the outlying neighborhood as dawn is breaking, there is no transgression. If she leaves her robes in the outlying neighborhood and goes inside as dawn breaks, there is likewise no transgression. But if she leaves her robes either inside or outside and goes elsewhere, and dawn breaks while she is there, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture. What is a village enclosed by a wall? It is whatever village is enclosed by a fence. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — or the distance to where one beats grain, where one threshes, where one eats, where boys play, or where people by nature possessed of modesty go to relieve themselves, or the distance a crow flies in one wing-beat as it alights — that is its outlying neighborhood.

If a nun leaves her robes inside and dawn breaks while she is in the outlying neighborhood, she incurs no transgression. If she leaves her robes in the outlying neighborhood and dawn breaks while she is inside, she incurs no transgression. If she leaves her robes inside or in the outlying neighborhood and dawn breaks while she is elsewhere, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village enclosed by a moat? It is whatever village is enclosed by a moat. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — as set out from the passage beginning "everything within" up to "where boys play" — or the distance to where the dust raised by cattle and sheep moving along is not stirred by the wind, or the distance a garland-bearer reaches by shaking a ceremonial cloth. That is its outlying neighborhood. The full rule, from the passage beginning "If a nun leaves her robes inside" down to "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture," applies here as well.

What is a village with a single outlying neighborhood? It is a village in which there is one park, one assembly ground, or one shrine of a deity. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — as stated from the passage beginning "everything within" up to "where boys play." The full rule, from "If a nun leaves her robes inside" down to "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture," applies here as well.

What is a village with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is a village in which there are many parks, assembly grounds, or shrines of deities. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? The gate.

If a nun has left her robes either inside or outside and dawn is about to break, and she is separated from the outlying neighborhood, she should remain at the gate until dawn breaks. If dawn breaks while she is elsewhere, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a collection of many villages with a single outlying neighborhood? It is the case of many villages in which there is one park, one assembly ground, or one shrine of a deity. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — as stated from the passage beginning "everything within" up through "if she causes dawn to break while elsewhere, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a collection of many villages with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is where those villages have many parks. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing whatsoever.

What is a household with a single outlying neighborhood? It is the household of one person, or a household whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — as stated from the passage beginning "everything within" up through "if she causes dawn to break while elsewhere, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a collection of many households with a single outlying neighborhood? It is the households of one person, or households whose family doors have been opened separately. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside — as stated from the passage beginning "everything within" up through "if she causes dawn to break while elsewhere, she incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."
