What is a collection of many households with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the households of different persons, or households whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing whatsoever.

What is a shop with a single outlying neighborhood? It is the shop of one person, or shops whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything within, together with one fathom outside, or the area where grain is piled, where it is threshed, where small measures are set out, and where weighing vessels are placed — that is its outlying neighborhood. The full rule, from the passage beginning "If a nun leaves her robes inside" down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture," applies here as well.

What is a collection of many shops with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the shops of different persons, or shops whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? The market storehouse.

What is a collection of many shops with a single shared outlying neighborhood? It is the shops of one person, or shops whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall — from the passage beginning "the full rule" down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a collection of many shops with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the shops of different persons, or shops whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing at all.

What is a market stall with a single outlying neighborhood? It is a market stall belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, as well as any place where their flat boards are laid out, where perfumes are woven in, where bundles are tied, where goods are made equal in measure — from that passage down through "whoever does it as a boy." As for a nun, from the passage beginning "a nun, within the outlying neighborhood, her robes" down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a market stall with a separate outlying neighborhood? It is a market stall belonging to different persons, or one whose family doors have been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is separate. What do they share in common? The sitting platform.

What is a collection of many market stalls with a single shared outlying neighborhood? It is the market stalls of one person, or of those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall — from the passage beginning "the full rule" down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a collection of many market stalls with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the market stalls of different persons, or of those whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing at all.

What is an upper-story dwelling with a single outlying neighborhood? It is this: an upper-story dwelling belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall. Everything else is as before.

What is an upper-story dwelling with a separate outlying neighborhood? It is this: an upper-story dwelling belonging to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? The staircase.

What is a collection of many upper-story dwellings with a single shared outlying neighborhood? It is this: upper-story dwellings belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing at all.

What is a lodging house with a single outlying neighborhood? It is this: a lodging house belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, as well as any place where bamboo is cut for them, where weaving is done, and where the doors of the canopies — from that passage down through "if one causes the dawn to break, it incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a lodging house with a separate outlying neighborhood? It is a lodging house belonging to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is separate. What do they share in common? The banner post.

What is a collection of many lodging houses with a single shared outlying neighborhood? It is the many lodging houses belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, as well as any place where bamboo is cut — from that passage down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a collection of many lodging houses with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the many lodging houses belonging to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately. What are their outlying neighborhoods? They are each separate. What do they share in common? Nothing at all.

What is a single threshing floor with one outlying neighborhood? It is the threshing floor belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, or any place where straw is stacked, where measuring vessels, sweepings, and weighing containers are placed and hoisted, and wherever the coarse husks blown off when grain is winnowed are carried by the wind without being swept back. That is its outlying neighborhood. For nuns, from "robes within the outlying neighborhood" onward, the rest is as before.

What is a single threshing floor with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the threshing floor belonging to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The interior of the threshing floor."

What is a collection of many threshing floors with one outlying neighborhood? It is the collection of threshing floors belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. The rest is as before.

What is a collection of many threshing floors with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever collection of threshing floors belongs to different persons — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

What is a granary with one outlying neighborhood? It is the granary belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, or any place where oxen are yoked and dung is deposited. The rest is as before.

What is a granary with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is the granary belonging to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately. As for its outlying neighborhood — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The gate."

What is a collection of many granaries with one outlying neighborhood? It is whichever collection of granaries belongs to one person — and so on as before.

What is a collection of many granaries with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever collection of granaries belongs to different persons — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

What is the household of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) with one outlying neighborhood? It is that of those who share one view, one forbearance, one intention, and one aspiration. What is their outlying neighborhood? It is any place where they perform fire oblations, and where they deposit grass, dung, the wood for fire-offerings, and ladles. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is everything inside, plus one fathom beyond the outer wall, or any place where cutting is done — and so on down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is the household of non-Buddhists with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is that of non-Buddhists who hold various views — and so on down through "various aspirations." Their outlying neighborhoods are each separate. What do they share in common? A divine abode.

What is a collection of many non-Buddhist households with one outlying neighborhood? It is to be stated just as in the first case.

What is a collection of many non-Buddhist households with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever non-Buddhist households belong to different persons — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

What is a carriage with one outlying neighborhood? It is the carriage belonging to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? Whether the carriage is moving or stationary, it is one fathom as its outlying neighborhood, or any place where oxen are yoked, where muñja grass is beaten, and where ropes are loaded — or wherever cutting is done — and so on down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a carriage with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever carriage belongs to different persons, or to those whose family doors have been opened separately — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The driver's seat."

What is a collection of many carriages with one outlying neighborhood? It is to be stated just as in the first case.

What is a collection of many carriages with separate outlying neighborhoods?

It is whichever boats belong to persons who are not separate — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the twelfth fascicle.

What is a boat with one outlying neighborhood? It is whichever boat belongs to one person, or to those whose family doors have not been opened separately. What is its outlying neighborhood? It is one fathom in the direction of travel, the place where stakes are driven and the boat is repaired, where muñja grass is beaten, where ropes are loaded, where outriggers are set — or wherever cutting is done — and so on down through "who does the work as a boy." A nun who keeps her robes inside — and so on down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a boat with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever boats belong to persons who are not separate — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The prow of the boat."

What is a collection of many boats with one outlying neighborhood? It is to be stated just as in the first case.

What is a collection of many boats with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever boats belong to persons who are not separate — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

What is a pleasure garden with one outlying neighborhood? It is whichever pleasure garden belongs to one person, or to those whose family doors have been opened. What is its outlying neighborhood? The place where green leaves are washed, where bundles are tossed, where garlands of flowers are strung — and so on down through "what is done by the boy servants." A nun who keeps her robes inside — and so on down through "when dawn breaks, incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a pleasure garden with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever pleasure garden does not belong to persons who are not separate — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The well."

What is a collection of many pleasure gardens with one outlying neighborhood? It is whichever pleasure garden does not belong to one person — and so on down through: it is to be stated just as in the first case.

What is a collection of many pleasure gardens with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is whichever of the many pleasure gardens do not belong to persons who are not separate — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

What is a tree with one outlying neighborhood? It is this: a tree whose branches and leaves join together so as to form a single dense canopy. What is its outlying neighborhood? The entirety of the interior, together with one fathom on the outside; or a space covered by the shadow of half a day cast by the sun on the last day of the month of the cold season, in which one may sit; or where withered leaves fall without being blown by the wind; or where drops of water fall when rain descends — that is its outlying neighborhood. A nun who keeps her robes inside — and so on down through "incurs a transgression entailing forfeiture."

What is a tree with separate outlying neighborhoods? It is this: a tree whose branches and leaves do not join together — and so on down through "what do they share in common? The trunk of the tree."

What is a collection of many trees with one outlying neighborhood? It is this: many trees whose branches and leaves do not join together, having separate shadows — and so on down through "what do they share in common? Nothing at all."

The venerable Upāli then put this question to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, what is the outlying neighborhood for nuns who have entered the residency? One fathom when walking, one fathom when standing, one fathom when sitting — it is a full circle all around."

"Venerable One, if nuns who have entered residency and are dwelling together entrust their robes to attendants and remain as they are — what is their outlying neighborhood?" The Blessed One declared:

Just as I have taught that when mango trees are planted at intervals of seven fathoms each among brahmin-born lineages, they become very richly endowed with blossoms, fruits, and branches — the spacing between such mango trees amounts to forty-nine fathoms.

Venerable One, if a nun sleeps at the boundary between two temple buildings, what is the boundary? So long as the corner of her robe does not separate from her, she does not become separated from her robe. At the moment when the corner of her robe does separate from her, she becomes separated from her robe, and the nun's robe is relinquished. From "not relinquished" onward, this is to be stated in the same way as before. The second offense entailing relinquishment is complete.

The narrative context is at Śrāvastī. At that time, nuns received many gains in cloth of this sort: someone, having obtained a piece of blue cloth, would not put it to use right away, thinking, "When I obtain cloth like this, I will take it up and keep it." And so she would set it aside in expectation. What applies to blue cloth is to be stated likewise for yellow, red, thick cloth, and thin cloth. At that time the nuns told the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, proceeding from "this occurred" through "laid down the training rule," declared:

If a nun has her robe period in hand, and when the cold season begins she wants to obtain a robe at an unseasonable time, that nun may accept such a cloth. Having accepted it, if she does not rise to use it, she should quickly store it away. If she has expectation of a robe, or if it serves to complete what is lacking, that nun may keep that cloth until the end of one month. If she keeps it beyond that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment.

"A nun who has her robe period in hand" is as before. "Obtained" means from another. As for "unseasonable cloth" — what is the season for cloth, and what is unseasonable cloth? In a place where the cold-season robe is spread out, the five months from the middle month of autumn through the last month of spring constitute the robe season. The remaining seven months are the unseasonable period. As for "any of the seven kinds of cloth" — what are those seven? They are: wool, cotton, a blend of wool and cotton, fine silk, muslin, Kautamba cloth, and sun-bleached cloth. "Wants" means if she seeks it with intent. "Having accepted it, if she does rise to use it, she should quickly store it away." "If she does not rise" refers to any of the five. "That nun may keep that cloth until the end of one month" means until the end of thirty days. As for "expectation of a robe" — what is expectation of a robe? It is the expectation that her mother will give it to her, or her father, or her brothers and sisters, or that she will obtain it at the time of the great quinquennial festival. "If it serves to complete what is lacking" means if it serves to complete that cloth.

"Beyond that" means past that point. "Keeps" means retains. "An offense entailing relinquishment" means, from "having relinquished that article" through "falling into the lower realms as a wrong downfall" — that is the range.

Now, how does a downfall arise? In summary verse:

With expectation and without expectation,
having deteriorated — three cases each —
with no completion, an interruption of the continuum,
and the two kinds of cloth themselves,
then five kinds of cloth,
two regarding rags from charnel grounds,
the measure of a patch cloth, and illness —

the sweat cloth, the bathing cloth itself, and also
the three-sided covering cloths,
and the outer wrap made last.

A nun, on the date itself, finds a blue cloth but does not put it to use, thinking, "When I find a cloth like this, then I will do it" — having expectation regarding a cloth, she sets it aside. Now, since she has expectation regarding a cloth, if on that very same date she finds one with expectation, that nun must consecrate, relinquish, or make proper that cloth within those ten days. If she does not consecrate it, does not make it proper, or does not relinquish it, when the dawn of the eleventh day rises, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

If a nun does not find a cloth on the date itself, nor on the second date, but on the ninth date finds one with expectation, that nun must consecrate, relinquish, or make proper that cloth within those ten days. If she does not consecrate it, does not make it proper, or does not relinquish it, when the dawn of the eleventh day rises, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

Furthermore, if a nun does not find a cloth on the date itself and does not find one on the second date, but on the twenty-ninth day finds one with expectation, that nun must consecrate, relinquish, or make proper that cloth within those thirty days. If she does not consecrate it, does not make it proper, or does not relinquish it, when the dawn of the thirtieth day rises, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

Just as it is for the blue cloth, so too it is the same for the yellow cloth, the thick cloth, and the fine cloth.

If a nun on the date finds a blue cloth and does not put it to use, thinking, "When I find a cloth like this, then I will do it" — having expectation regarding a cloth, she sets it aside — and if on that very same date she finds another one without expectation: from "that nun, within those ten days" through to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" — that is the range.

If a nun does not find one on the date itself, nor on the second date — from that point through "nor within the ninth and tenth" — from there through to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" — that is the range.

Furthermore, if a nun does not find one on the date itself — from that point through "if on the twenty-ninth day she finds one without expectation" — from there through to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" — that is the range.

Just as it is for the blue cloth, so the same applies through to the fine cloth.

If a nun on the date finds a blue cloth and does not put it to use, thinking, "When I find a cloth like this, then I will do it," having expectation regarding a cloth and setting it aside — and then her expectation regarding that cloth deteriorates, is postponed, or diminishes — and if on that very same date she finds another cloth without expectation: from that point through "likewise on the ninth date as well" through to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" — that is the range.

Furthermore, if a nun on the date finds another cloth — from that point through "on the twenty-ninth day" — through to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" — that is the range.

Just as it is for the blue cloth, so the same applies through to the fine cloth.

If a nun on the date finds a blue cloth and does not put it to use, thinking, "When I find a cloth like this, then I will do it," having expectation regarding a cloth and setting it aside — while her expectation regarding that cloth has not come to fulfillment —

without interruption — if on that very date she finds another cloth regarding which she has no expectation, and so forth — and likewise, "not on a date" through "through the ninth day" and through "on the twenty-ninth day" — all of this is to be stated in full. Just as it is for the blue cloth, so the same applies through to the fine cloth.

When her expectation regarding that cloth has been entirely and completely cut off without interruption, and on that very date she finds another cloth regarding which she has no expectation, and likewise, "not on a date" — from there through "the ninth day" — and likewise through "regarding the twenty-ninth day, without expectation" — all of this is to be stated in full. Just as it is for the blue cloth, so the same applies through to the fine cloth.

Cloth is of two kinds: newly woven, and cloth that has been used at one of the three seasons. Of these, newly woven cloth is cloth freshly woven by a weaver. Cloth used at one of the three seasons is cloth that has been put to use at any one of the three seasonal periods.

As for the five types of cloth — what are the five? Cloth with an owner, cloth without an owner, cloth taken from what has been cast away, charnel-ground cloth, and the fifth is rag cloth. Of these, cloth with an owner is cloth designated as a gift by a man, a woman, or a person of neither sex. Cloth without an owner is cloth for which no donor up to a person of neither sex can be identified, or alternatively, cloth found lying on the road. Cloth taken from what has been cast away is this: when someone near death has cloths held as canopies and is conveyed to the charnel ground, cloths are then taken from there and offered to the nuns — this is called cloth taken from what has been cast away. Charnel-ground cloth is whatever has been taken from a charnel ground that has no keeper. The fifth is rag cloth.

Furthermore, rag cloth is of five kinds — what are the five? Rag cloth from a main road, rag cloth from a riverbank, cloth cast away in a wilderness, tattered and rotted cloth, and the fifth is rag cloth itself. Furthermore, rag cloth is of five kinds: cloth eaten by calves, cloth eaten by crickets, cloth eaten by mice, cloth scorched by fire, and the fifth is cloth that has fallen to the ground.

If a nun finds newly woven cloth and is able to do so, she should make a patched garment from that cloth with a double layer, the border-strip also double-layered; the upper robe should be single-layered, and the lower robe likewise single-layered. Likewise, the sweat-cloth and the shoulder-protector are also to be single-layered.

If a nun unravels to the third layer in a double-layered patched garment made from newly woven cloth, the act of unraveling is a wrongdoing. If ten days have passed, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

If a nun, having made a double-layered patched garment from newly woven cloth, thinks "I will reinforce it differently" and pulls out one layer, the act of pulling out is a wrongdoing. If ten days have passed, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

If she forms the intention, "I will unravel it, wash it, turn it around, and reinforce this very same one," and then pulls a layer out, there is no transgression. If ten days have passed, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

Likewise, the same is to be stated for the border-strip.

If she unravels a layer in a single-layered upper robe, the unraveling is a wrongdoing. If ten days have passed, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

Just as it is for the upper robe, so the same is to be stated for the lower robe. This is to be stated through to the five Dharma robes — and for all of them it is to be stated that it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

When a nun obtains a robe acquired at the appointed time and is able to do so, she should patch it with four layers. A border-strip, an upper robe, and a lower robe should be patched with two layers. A perspiration cloth and a shoulder-covering for one with a broken shoulder are likewise.

When a nun pulls out a fifth layer from a four-layered patch, the pulling out is a wrongdoing. If ten days have passed, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment. The passage up to "if she unravels it" is as stated above. Likewise, the same is to be stated for the border-strip. The upper robe and lower robe are also the same. For the perspiration cloth and the shoulder-covering for one with a broken shoulder, the same is likewise to be stated.

From "the second layer," up to the point where it reads: if she unravels a third layer while already having unraveled one, the unraveling is a wrongdoing, and if ten days have passed it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

From "thinking, 'It has been worn; I will patch it elsewhere,'" up through: if she unravels it, it is a wrongdoing, and if ten days have passed it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

From "having unraveled and washed it and turned it inside out," up to: if she thinks, "I will patch this very same one," there is no transgression; and if ten days have passed it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

As for the stitches of rags picked up from a dust-heap, she may patch them as much as she wishes.

The venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable sir, what are the strip-widths of a patched robe?" The Blessed One declared: "There are nine strip-widths, Ānanda. What are the nine? The ninth, the eleventh, the thirteenth, the fifteenth, the seventeenth, the nineteenth, the twenty-first, the twenty-third, and the twenty-fifth."

These nine patched robes with such strip-widths are called patched robes, Ānanda. Of those nine, the ninth, the eleventh, and the thirteenth are to be kept folded into a third of a board's width. The fifteenth, the seventeenth, and the nineteenth are to be kept folded into a quarter of a board's width. The twenty-first, the twenty-third, and the twenty-fifth are to be kept folded into a fifth of a board's width. They are to be patched accordingly. Beyond that, they are merely scraps.

"Blessed One, what are the dimensions of a Dharma robe?" "There are three kinds, Ānanda: a large, a medium, and a small. As for the largest patched robe, its maximum length is five cubits and its width is three cubits. As for the smallest patched robe, its maximum length is two and a half cubits and its width is one and a half cubits. The medium is between the two."

Likewise there are three kinds for the upper robe, and three kinds for the lower robe. Similarly there are three kinds for the perspiration cloth and the shoulder-covering for one with a broken shoulder.

Furthermore, one further dimension for the lower robe is a length of five cubits and a width of one and a half cubits. Another dimension for the lower robe is a length of four cubits and a width of one and a half cubits. The minimum lower robe is that which covers the three joints. The minimum of things to be relinquished is enough to wrap around the entire cubit.

From "when a nun's robe has come to be relinquished," up to "it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment," is as stated at the beginning.

The third offense entailing relinquishment is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana) of Anāthapiṇḍada in Prince Jeta's park. At the time when the Blessed One, relying upon Ānanda, had received a meal from Anāthapiṇḍada who was not a relative and had established a training rule, monks were robbed by thieves, and relying upon the monks having been robbed by thieves, the Blessed One gave permission, as follows.

When the elder nuns heard of this, many of them went to where the Blessed One was, drew near, and bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, then sat to one side. Seated to one side, the many elder nuns addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what are we to do regarding this training rule?"

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke in praise of the nuns who desired training, who were respectful toward training, and who were furnished with the implements of training, and then declared to the community of nuns:

"Furthermore, whatever nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a robe outside of the permitted time — exceeding that limit — commits an offense entailing relinquishment. The permitted time is this: when a nun's robe has been stolen, or lost, or burned, or carried away by water, she may go to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and ask for a robe. That is the permitted time.

"Now, 'whatever nun' means one belonging to this Dharma. 'Who is not a relative' means that a maternal grandmother or paternal grandfather and their descendants down to seven generations are relatives; beyond that they are not relatives. 'A householder' means a man. 'A householder's wife' means a woman. 'Goes' means having gone. 'Begs' means, outside the permitted time, soliciting either oneself or causing another to solicit. 'The permitted time is this' means this is what is in accordance with the Dharma. 'The robe has been stolen' means thieves or deceivers have taken her robes away. 'Lost' means her robes have been lost or have gone astray. 'Carried away by water' means her robes have been carried away by water. 'Burned' means her robes have been burned by fire. 'Commits an offense entailing relinquishment' — and so forth, set forth at length.

"How does a transgression arise from this? It is determined by value, by color, and by cubit-measure.

"How by value? Whatever nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas or more — in the asking there is a wrongdoing (Skt. duṣkṛta); if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. If, however, she receives something of greater value, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated for ten kārṣāpaṇas and for twenty kārṣāpaṇas. Such, then, is determination by value.

"How by color? A nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a blue robe — in the asking there is a wrongdoing; if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. But if she receives a yellow one, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated at length for blue, for red, and for white.

"A nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a yellow robe — in the asking there is a wrongdoing; if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. But if she receives a blue one, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated for yellow, red, and white.

"A nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a red robe — in the asking there is a wrongdoing; if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. But if she receives a blue one, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated for yellow, red, and white.

"A nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a white robe — in the asking there is a wrongdoing;"

if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. But if she receives a blue one, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated for white, yellow, and red. Such, then, is the category of transgressions arising from color.

As for how transgressions arise from measure: if a nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and begs for a robe of five cubits, in the asking there is a wrongdoing, and if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment. If, having begged for a robe of five cubits, she receives one of six cubits, there is no transgression. Likewise this is to be stated for ten cubits and eleven cubits, and for twenty cubits and twenty-one cubits. Similarly, if she begs up to ten cubits and does not receive the cloth, or does not beg for cloth but receives up to a patched robe, there is no transgression.

The fourth offense entailing relinquishment is complete.

The narrative origin is at Śrāvastī. At that time in Śrāvastī, nuns who had been robbed by thieves arrived. Then the group of twelve — Gaṇḍā, Upagaṇḍā, and Sthūlagaṇḍā among them — went to the homes of brahmins and householders on those nuns' behalf and procured a great many robes. Having procured them and then proceeding to offer them, certain nuns of modest needs raised objections. The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon, beginning with "This has come about," proceeded to establish the training rule as follows: if a nun's robe is stolen, destroyed, burned, or carried away by water, she may go to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and beg for a robe. If to that nun a believing brahmin or householder offers a great many robes, that nun may accept from those robes no more than is sufficient for an upper robe together with an under robe. If she takes more than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment.

"Her robe is stolen" means that a thief or a deceiver has taken her robes away. "Begging" means doing so either personally or through another. "To that nun" means to the very nun in question. "Believing" means one who has faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha — one who has seen the truth and attained the fruit. "Brahmin" refers to a brahmin of pure lineage and so forth. "Householder" refers to one of a different class from that. "Repeatedly" means again and again. "A great many" means whatever among the seven types of robes is more than sufficient for one's needs. "Offers" means presents as a guest-gift. "If she wishes" means if she desires it for her own benefit. "That nun" means the one who desires it for her benefit.

Regarding "no more than is sufficient for an upper robe together with an under robe": there are two types of upper robe together with under robe — that of a laywoman with an under robe, and that of a fully ordained nun with an under robe. What constitutes a laywoman's upper garment together with lower garment? A large bolt of cloth of twelve cubits, and a small bolt of cloth of seven cubits, with its fastening — this is called a laywoman's upper garment together with lower garment. What constitutes a fully ordained nun's upper robe together with under robe? A patched robe of two layers for the outer robe, and a small bolt of cloth of five cubits with its fastening. "She may accept from those robes" means she may accept the upper robe together with the under robe from among them. "If she takes more than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment" is as stated above.

As to how a transgression arises in this case: if a nun has received a laywoman's upper garment together with lower garment, and the laywoman's upper garment together with

lower garment has been received, she should make that large bolt of cloth of twelve cubits into a patched robe of two layers. From the small bolt of cloth of seven cubits and the sash she should make the under robe. If it does not come to the full measure, she need not make up the remainder; and if there is excess, she need not give it away.

If a fully ordained nun receives a fully ordained nun's upper robe together with under robe, and takes the upper robe together with the under robe, she should make from that patched robe simply a patched robe. From the small bolt of cloth of five cubits and the sash she should make the under robe. If it does not come to the full measure, she must make up the remainder; and if there is excess, she must give it away.

If a fully ordained nun accepts from a layperson something less than the permitted amount, that act of acceptance is an offense of wrongdoing. Upon receiving it, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment. If a fully ordained nun accepts something less than the permitted amount, it is an offense of wrongdoing. If there is a surplus and it has not been given away, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment. For one who is acting for the first time, and similar cases, there is no transgression. The fifth transgression entailing relinquishment is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time there was a householder at Śrāvastī, wealthy and possessed of great wealth and extensive resources, who had a wife taken from an equal family, and he was in the habit of competing in wealth with the son of Vaiśravaṇa. At a certain later time, he entered into worldly dalliances with another woman, and his wife put a stop to this. When he did not desist despite her objection, stricken with grief over that wife of his, he took up pleasure with another man. As a result the household fell into ruin from both sides, and the two of them kept beating their maidservant without respite.

Then the nun Sthūlanandā in the morning took up her robe and alms bowl and went for alms in Śrāvastī. Going on her alms round in Śrāvastī, she came to the house of that householder. When she arrived, she taught the Dharma of mental liberation to the householder and the householder's wife, so that those bound by attachment might become free from attachment. The two of them looked at each other and said to Sthūlanandā: "Noble one, it is not I who am at fault — this fault belongs to this nobleman's son." The merchant said: "It is not so. She is not my fault; this fault belongs to the virtuous lady." Then Sthūlanandā placed both the householder, for having been with another's wife, and the householder's wife, for having been with another's man, under a training rule. As the two of them turned away from that unwholesome conduct, the household prospered, and the maidservant too was installed as the mistress of that household.

Thereafter the householder and his wife reflected: "Whatever good fortune and happiness we possess, whatever little we may have, all of it has come from the noble Sthūlanandā." The maidservant too reflected: "Whatever little comfort and ease of mind I now possess — all of that has come from the noble Sthūlanandā. Alas, I should make an offering to the noble Sthūlanandā." She then went outside and saw Sthūlanandā. Seeing her, she spoke these words: "Noble one, I will convey a pleasant message to you: the noble one will receive a large bolt of cloth from the nobleman's son."

Then Sthūlanandā went to that house and said to the householder and his wife: "Householder, please show me the large bolt of cloth that you wish to give to her." The householder then took the large bolt of cloth and gave it to Sthūlanandā. When Sthūlanandā saw that it was a very thick large bolt of cloth, she made a grimace and wrung her hands. The two of them said: "Noble one, what is the matter?" And she replied:

"Do you perhaps think this cloth is of good quality? Householder, if she were to distribute this among households, and someone were to ask her from whom she had received such cloth, what could she say in her embarrassment?" The two of them then said: "Noble one, we have only this; we have nothing else." She replied: "Householder, you should let her decide. What would she have you do?" And she said: "Householder, add a little more on top of the price you receive from selling this very large bolt of cloth, and it will turn into something far superior." The wife also said: "Noble son, please do as she says."

She then went to the market, fixed a date with a merchant, took a fine new large bolt of cloth on credit and draped it over the first. When the appointed time came and the merchant seized that trader while others were watching and began to reproach him, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, beginning with "this occurrence" and proceeding through to the laying down of the rule, established the following: if a nun, for the sake of a nun, approaches a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and solicits cloth-money, and then, without having previously invited that nun, generates even some conceptual thought and goes to her and says, "You, on my behalf, have solicited cloth-money — with that cloth-money please have the venerable ones buy such-and-such cloth and bring me suitable cloth at the right time," then, if the cloth is obtained because of the desire for something good, it is an offense requiring relinquishment.

"Nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Non-relative" is as before. "Cloth-money" means silver and gold. "Having solicited" means having assembled, in the sense of: "With this silver and gold that is my cloth-money." "Such-and-such" means: "From whichever of the seven types of cloth is appropriate, buy cloth of this kind." "This nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "When she comes" means upon her arrival. "Bring" means present or offer. "Cloth" refers to any of the seven types. "Suitable, at the right time" means at a time when it is fit for use.

"That nun" in the phrase refers to Sthūlanandā. "Without having previously invited" means without having previously arranged as a guest. "Generating even some conceptual thought" means giving rise to even a little bit of deliberation. "You, on my behalf" means presenting herself as the direct beneficiary. "If the cloth is obtained" means upon receiving it. "It is an offense requiring relinquishment" is as before.

Now, how does a transgression arise in regard to this? It arises with respect to price, color, and measure in cubits.

How does it arise with respect to price? If a nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and says, "Give cloth worth five kārṣāpaṇas," and cloth worth five kārṣāpaṇas is given, there is no transgression. But if she asks for more than that, there is a wrong act in the asking, and if the cloth is obtained, it is an offense requiring relinquishment.

In the same way, one should continue to state this up to cloth worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas. That is how transgression arises with respect to price.

How does it arise with respect to color? If a nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and says, "Give blue cloth," and blue cloth is given, there is no transgression. But if she takes yellow cloth instead, there is a wrong act in the asking, and if it is obtained, it is an offense requiring relinquishment. Just as with blue, so also with yellow, red, thick, and fine — the explanation proceeds as before. That is how transgression arises with respect to color.

How does transgression arise with respect to length? If a nun goes to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and says, "Give a large bolt of cloth five cubits long," and a large bolt of cloth five cubits long is given, there is no transgression. But if she takes more than that, there is a wrong act in the asking, and if it is obtained, it is an offense requiring relinquishment. The same applies up to twenty cubits. The sixth offense requiring relinquishment is complete.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. From that incident onward the training rule was established. A householder or a householder's wife who was not a relative had, each separately, pooled funds for cloth on behalf of a nun, thinking: "With the funds we have each pooled for cloth, let each of us buy such-and-such separate pieces of cloth, and when the nun called so-and-so arrives, let her be clothed by each of us in turn." Then, if that nun, without having been invited beforehand, were to give rise to just some thought of desire and go to them and say, "The funds for cloth that you, venerable ones, have each pooled on her behalf — with those separate cloth-funds, let each venerable one buy such-and-such a kind of cloth, and such-and-such a kind, and combining both together, at one time bestow on her a proper and excellent garment" — if a garment is completed out of desire for finery, it is an offense requiring relinquishment. The sequence of offenses is to be stated in conformity with this training rule just as in the preceding cases. However, the distinguishing feature here is this: from the phrase "each separately" — meaning "one by one" — up to the phrase "out of desire for finery," this section is to be treated as distinct. The seventh offense requiring relinquishment is complete.

The origin story is set in Rājagṛha. Since the Blessed One established certain training rules in common with monks, certain ones in common with nuns, and certain ones in common with both, here the Blessed One established one in common with both. At the time when the Blessed One in Rājagṛha, on account of the nun Nandā, established the training rule concerning the acceptance of kārṣāpaṇas, those nuns who desired training followed suit. Then the nun Nandā, when soliciting kārṣāpaṇas from kings, great ministers, brahmins, and householders, created an occasion for nuns of little ambition to censure her, and the nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared — and from that point onward the training rule was established — that if a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, a town-dweller, a country-dweller, a wealthy person, a merchant, or a caravan leader were to send funds for cloth by the hand of a messenger on behalf of a nun, and that messenger were to take those funds for cloth and go to that nun and say to her, "Noble lady, please be informed: these funds for cloth have been sent to you by such a one — a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, a town-dweller, a country-dweller, a wealthy person, a merchant, or a caravan leader. Noble lady, please be so kind as to accept these funds for cloth" — then that nun should say to that messenger the following: "Venerable messenger, nuns are not permitted to accept funds for cloth. When a proper garment is found at the proper time, she will accept it."

If that messenger then says to that nun, "Noble lady, does the noble lady have someone who looks after her affairs and carries out what is to be done for the noble ladies?" —

The nun who desires the robe should point out to those messengers the attendant of the monastery — whether a lay resident of the monastery or a lay practitioner who manages affairs — saying: "These messengers are to be looked after by the nuns."

Then that messenger should go to wherever that attendant is, and upon arriving should say to the attendant the following: "Venerable attendant, please take note. For the sake of such and such a nun, funds for cloth in this amount have been sent by a king" — and so on down through "caravan leader" — "and so, attendant, with these funds for cloth please purchase such and such cloth and such and such items, and when the proper garment is found at the proper time, let the nun named such and such come to you, and at the right time provide her with suitable cloth."

Then that messenger should instruct and inform that attendant thoroughly and correctly, and should go to wherever that nun is. Upon arriving, the messenger should say to her: "The one I have been shown as the attendant who manages affairs for the noble ladies — I have duly informed that person, and you should go to him. He will provide you with suitable cloth at the proper time."

Then the nun who desires the robe should also go to wherever that attendant is. Upon arriving, she should say: "Venerable attendant, I desire a robe. Venerable attendant, I desire a robe" — reminding him of this two or three times. Having gone two or three times and reminded him, if the robe is then obtained, that is good. If it is not obtained, she should remain silent on the matter until the limit of four, five, or six times. Having remained silent until the limit of four, five, or six times, if the robe is then obtained, that is good. If it is not obtained, then if she pursues efforts beyond that to procure the robe and does procure it, that constitutes a transgression entailing forfeiture. If it is not obtained at all, then that nun should go herself to the person from whom those funds for cloth came.

Alternatively, she may send word to the messenger who brought them: "You have sent funds for cloth on behalf of the nun named such and such, but those funds for cloth have not served that nun's purposes in any way. Please take notice, venerable ones, and do not let your own wealth go to waste." That is the proper procedure in such a case.

The phrase "for the sake of the nun" refers to the daughter of the Śākya clan, the female companion. "King" means one consecrated as lord from the head of the kṣatriya lineage — whether a woman, a man, or a person of indeterminate sex consecrated by royal consecration, that person is a king, is of the kṣatriya lineage, and is consecrated from the head. "Great minister" means one who carries out the affairs of a king and lives by employment in a confidential role. "Brahmin" means a brahmin of pure birth. "Householder" means a wealthy person. "Town-dweller" means a village resident. "Country-dweller" means one who lives in the countryside. "Wealthy person" means one rich in tens of millions in wealth. "Merchant" means one who wears a turban. "Caravan leader" means one who conducts organized caravans to other lands for profitable ends. "Through the hand of the messenger" refers to a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. "Funds for cloth" means gold and silver. "Sent" means dispatched. "That messenger" refers to a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. "Having taken those funds for cloth" means having carried them.

"That nun" refers to Nandā, the daughter of the Śākya clan. "Having gone" means having departed. "Said the following" means having spoken. "Noble one, please know" means: know that these funds for cloth were sent by the king. "Accept them" means receive them. "Having taken it to heart with care" means having taken it to heart with goodwill. "That nun" refers to Nandā. "That messenger" refers to a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. "Shall instruct as follows" means shall correctly convey these words. "Venerable one, the funds for cloth are not allowable for nuns to receive" means that the Blessed One has prohibited their being received, but the Blessed One has granted permission for cloth itself to be acceptable for them.

"If that messenger then says to that nun" means if he asks. "What serves as suitable service for the noble ones?" means what is the service that the noble ones are to receive. "A nun who wants cloth shall indicate a suitable service" — here, "one of the monastery" means one who makes things allowable. "Layman" means one who holds the five bases of training. "These are the ones who perform suitable service for nuns" means these are the ones through whom those nuns experience the receiving of service. "If that messenger is to go to wherever the service-giver is, and having arrived" means having gone there in order to make known what is needed.

"Make known the service. These funds for cloth" refers to the gold and silver sent by the king. "For the nun of such-and-such name" means for Nandā, the daughter of the Śākya clan. "Then that messenger" refers to a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. "Having thoroughly and correctly conveyed the message to the service-giver, whether one of the monastery or a layman" means by many different ways of expression. "That nun" refers to Nandā. "Is to go to that place and, having arrived" means having gone there. "Say the following: the service that was indicated as serving the noble ones — I have correctly indicated it; please come, and that person will provide you with cloth" — here "whichever of the seven" means any one of the seven allowable types. "Allowable" means fit for use. "A nun who wants cloth" means if she has come to seek cloth. "Having gone" means having departed. "Two times" means up to two times. "Three times" means up to three times. One should urge and remind. "If the matter is accomplished, then that is excellent" means that is good. "If it is not accomplished, one should remain silent without speaking to any side, up to the limit of four, five, or six times" — this is explained by means of the four ways of standing to one side and the six methods of urging.

What are the four ways of standing to one side? They are: the dwelling-place of sweepers, the sitting-place, which is the household where one habitually stays, the market-place, and the place at the end of a task.

The Vinaya Analysis of the Nuns — the Thirteenth Fascicle.

Now, "the dwelling-place of sweepers" refers to the dwellings of sweepers and potters. "The sitting-place" means the household — the place where one especially resides. "The market-place" means the shop and the market-stall. "The place at the end of a task" is threefold: the place at the end of the task of harvesting rice, of salt production, and of sugarcane — these are called the four ways of standing to one side.

What are the six methods of urging? They are as follows: if one asks "have you come?" — for that reason; if one says "it is good that you have come" — for that reason; and

"Sit on this seat" — for that reason; "accept this livelihood" — for that reason; "eat this food" — for that reason; "drink this drink" — for that reason: these are the six methods of urging.

If one speaks without pause, and urges in a situation where there is no opportunity, one should declare that the urging is not fully complete. If one urges in a situation where there is opportunity, one should declare that the urging is fully complete.

Thus, if one sits in silence in those places, "when the cloth is obtained" means: if it is acquired. "That is good" means: that is well. "If it is not obtained" means: if one does not receive it. "Having made further effort" means: with additional effort beyond that. "When the cloth is obtained" means: if it is received. "It constitutes a transgression involving forfeiture" means: having given up that thing — as before. "If it is not obtained" means: if one does not receive it. "That nun" means: the fellow practitioner. "From whatever direction those cloth-prices have come" means: from whatever source they have arrived. "Whether I myself should go there" means: oneself personally. "Or send a trustworthy messenger" means: one who, if sent, would accomplish that purpose. "Those cloth-prices that you sent on behalf of the nun called such-and-such have not accomplished any purpose for her" means: not even a small thing has been done. "Let it be known" means: venerable ones, do not let your own wealth be consumed in a way that is improper. "In that regard, this is the proper procedure" means: in that regard, this is the conforming rule. As for how a transgression arises in that regard: if the donor goes to the nun and says, "Noble one, please accept the cloth," then that nun should say to the donor, "I have renounced these things; give them directly to her." If the donor then says, "Noble one, please accept these; I wish to win her favour," and if the nun accepts without following this procedure, it becomes a transgression involving forfeiture in every case.

If a nun who has not been authorized by examination appropriates as her own any alms bowl, Dharma robes, or any other requisite for a monastic's livelihood whatsoever, it becomes a transgression involving forfeiture. This concludes the eighth transgression involving forfeiture.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One had prohibited woollen blankets of sheep's wool mixed with coarse fibre, twelve groups of nuns continued to make such blankets, induced others to make them, and criticized nuns of modest wants. The nuns then spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, from "this occurrence" onward, undertook the process through to the laying down of the training rule: "Moreover, should any nun make a blanket from fresh sheep's wool, it is a transgression involving forfeiture."

"Moreover, should any nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. Regarding the word "fresh": there are two kinds of freshness — fresh by being new, and fresh by being newly acquired. In this context, only freshness by being new is intended. "Sheep's wool" refers to the wool of sheep. Regarding "blanket": there are two kinds of blanket — one with lining and one without lining — and in this context both are intended. "Make" means by oneself or by another. "It is a transgression involving forfeiture" — as above.

As for how a transgression arises in that regard: through bundling, through unravelling, and through combining — when a nun bundles sheep's wool together, destroys it, or teases it apart,

as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. When a nun bundles loose sheep's wool together, destroys it, or teases it apart, as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. When a nun bundles a heap of sheep's wool together, destroys it, or teases it apart, as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. When a nun bundles together a bundle, loose wool, and a heap of sheep's wool, destroys them, or teases them apart, as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. When a nun bundles together loose wool, a heap, and a bundle of sheep's wool, destroys them, or teases them apart, as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. When a nun bundles together a heap, loose wool, and a bundle of sheep's wool, destroys them, or teases them apart, as long as she does not spin it, it is a wrongdoing. If she does spin it, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. If what has been made is found and used, there is no transgression.

The ninth transgression involving forfeiture is complete.

The origin story takes place in Rājagṛha. At the time when the Blessed One, drawing on the substance of the Jewel-Pinnacle Sūtra, established the training precept concerning the taking of gold and silver, the twelve groups were at that time taking gold and silver with their own hands, having others take it for them, and reviling nuns of few wants. On that occasion the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, from the account of what had occurred up to the establishment of the training precept, did so, and declared: "Furthermore, any nun who takes gold and silver with her own hand, or has it taken for her, incurs a transgression involving forfeiture."

"Furthermore, any nun" — as before. "With her own hand" means by herself. "Gold and silver" means silver and gold. "Takes" means by herself. "Has it taken for her" means by another. "A transgression involving forfeiture" — as above.

As for how a transgression arises in that regard, it does so through eight grounds: "Take this," "Take from here," "Take this much"; "Bring this," "Bring from here," "Bring this much"; "Put this down," "Put it down here," "Put down this much"; "Take that," "Take from there," "Take that much"; "Bring that," "Bring from there," "Bring that much"; "Put that down," "Put it down there," "Put down that much."

"Take this" refers to silver or gold. "Take from here" means from an iron vessel, an earthenware vessel, a bronze vessel, a tin vessel, or a basket. "Take this much" means a hundred or a thousand — if one instructs someone engaged in any suitable activity, or a person who is there as a contemplative, saying "take this," it is a wrongdoing; if it is taken, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. If, in the course of saying "Take this," "Take from here," or "Take this much," one instructs someone in a direction where it cannot be obtained, or a place where there is no novice nun, saying "take this," it is a wrongdoing; and if it is taken, it is likewise a wrongdoing — up to that point.

Furthermore, concerning a householder of the same locality, the Blessed One declared: "It may be accepted, provided it is kept by another trusted person." The manner of keeping it is as follows: one should address the noble one, saying: "Noble lady, please be aware —"

"I, who am called so-and-so, have come into possession of kārṣāpaṇas that are not allowable. I, who am called so-and-so, will render them allowable through the name of a donor, or through the name of a lay attendant, so-and-so, belonging to that donor, and will keep them on that very basis alone. From the time when I who had not yet rendered them allowable do render them allowable — from that moment, let it be recorded that I have rendered them allowable." That is how they are to be kept.

Here ends the tenth transgression involving forfeiture.

The occasion was in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the Group of Six, was laying down rules of training regarding the performance of various kinds of conduct involving explicitly named goods, the Group of Twelve likewise performed various kinds of such conduct, and nuns of little standing rebuked them. The matter was then brought before the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This having occurred," proceeded to lay down the rule of training. The rule is: "Whatever nun performs various kinds of conduct involving explicitly named goods — that is a transgression involving forfeiture."

The phrase "whatever nun" is as before. "Various kinds" means many types. "Involving explicitly named goods" means silver or gold. "If she conducts herself" means if she acts excessively in this way. "Transgression involving forfeiture" is as above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? There are four modes: engaging in trade, engaging in investment, distributing as loans, and distributing at interest.

Of these, engaging in trade is as follows: for the purpose of obtaining goods in the market, one engages in trade using a market stall or a cart, gathers people together, and says, "This item is yours; this one is mine" — for as long as one does not appropriate the gains for oneself, it is a wrongdoing; if one does appropriate the gains, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. Such is what is called engaging in trade.

How does one engage in investment? For the purpose of increasing gold gains from ten to eleven, one engages in investment using a stall for gold acquisition, going there for the sake of sealing agreements, going to find ink or witnesses. For as long as one does not appropriate the gains for oneself, it is a wrongdoing; if one does appropriate them, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. Such is what is called engaging in investment.

How does one distribute as loans? For the sake of obtaining new barley or grain at harvest time, one sends out grain or barley as a loan, measured by a measuring vessel, and then goes seeking those measuring vessels, small measures, bushels, weighing instruments, and people for that purpose. For as long as one does not appropriate the gains for oneself, it is a wrongdoing; if one does appropriate them, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. Such is what is called distributing as loans.

How does one distribute at interest? One distributes at interest through pearl interest, or distributes at interest through gold interest, and then goes seeking brokers, ink, and witnesses for that purpose. For as long as one does not appropriate the gains for oneself, it is a wrongdoing; if one does appropriate them, it is a transgression involving forfeiture. Such is what is called distributing at interest.

When the rule of training had been laid down in this way, it was not applied to what had been placed in perpetual endowments for stūpas and for the Saṅgha. The Blessed One then declared: "It may be applied." Then, when those responsible sent such funds to whoever they wished and those funds came to be wandering loose, the Blessed One declared:

"Do not send funds to the destitute, nor to remote and border regions, nor to those who are violent and given to evil deeds, nor ever to those who wield power."

This completes the eleventh rule of training subject to forfeiture.

The case arose at Śrāvastī. At that time the group of six nuns were engaged in various kinds of trade: they would buy in, they would send out, they would purchase, and they would sell. How did they buy in? Whenever there was scarcity at Śrāvastī and abundance in the surrounding regions, they would procure goods from those regions and bring them into Śrāvastī. Such is what is called buying in. How did they send out? Whenever the harvest was good at Śrāvastī and had failed in the surrounding regions, they would procure goods from Śrāvastī and send them out to those regions. Such is what is called sending out. How did they purchase? Whenever something was abundant, they would purchase it. Such is what is called purchasing. How did they sell? Whenever something was scarce, they would sell it. Such is what is called selling.

While they were engaged in trade, they would scold the nuns who were getting the worse of the bargain. The nuns then spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from the statement "This occurrence..." all the way through to the laying down of the rule of training: "Whatever nun engages in various kinds of trade incurs a transgression involving forfeiture." The phrase "whatever nun" is as before. As to how the transgression arises: if a nun purchases desiring gain and sells desiring gain, then in the act of purchasing she commits a wrongdoing, and in the act of selling she incurs a transgression involving forfeiture. If she purchases desiring gain and sells without desiring gain, then in the act of purchasing she commits a wrongdoing, but in the act of selling there is no transgression. If she purchases without desiring gain and sells desiring gain, then in the act of purchasing there is no transgression, but in the act of selling she incurs a transgression involving forfeiture. If she purchases without desiring gain and sells without desiring gain, there is no transgression in either act. Involvement in another region is to be purified through the earlier continuum.

Then the Saṅgha had provisions on hand, and donors came wishing to provide food. They searched for grain but found neither food nor drink. The Blessed One declared: "Give according to the price at which it was purchased." On some occasions what had been purchased when abundant later became scarce, and on other occasions what had been purchased when scarce later became abundant. The Blessed One declared: "Give it at the market price."

This completes the verse summary of the first rule of training subject to forfeiture.

The summary verse runs:

The alms-bowl, thread, and the returning thereof,
Recovering by force, and likewise what was examined,
Gain, medicine, and one day,
Exchanging, in season, and out of season.

The case arose at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One, on account of the group of six, had laid down the rule of training concerning keeping an alms-bowl without proper relation, the group of twelve nuns were carrying alms-bowls both without proper relation and without a companion. The nuns who dwelt in the proper manner then spoke thus to the group of twelve: "Sisters, has the Blessed One not laid down a rule of training?" The group of twelve replied to those nuns: "That rule of training belongs to the monks; it does not apply to the nuns." At that point the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with the words "This incident having arisen," performed all that is done up to the laying down of the rule of training. The rule is as follows: Whatever nun, while a usable alms-bowl without the five associations is available, out of desire for something better solicits another new alms-bowl, and upon obtaining that bowl abandons the original — that is an offense entailing relinquishment. That nun must offer the bowl to the community of nuns. Whichever bowl is last in the community of nuns, that one is to be given to that nun with the words: "Nun, you must not consecrate this bowl, nor give it away, nor donate it to another, but must use it gently and carefully until it breaks." That is the proper procedure.

Now the commentary on the rule follows. "Whatever nun" is as before. "An alms-bowl without the five associations" means one lacking any one of the five associations. "While available" means while it is still usable. "Solicits another new one" means solicits a second one instead. "Out of desire for something better" means out of desire for something superior, or else out of desire for what belongs to another. "Upon obtaining it" means upon receiving it. "An offense entailing relinquishment" is as before.

"That nun must offer the alms-bowl to the community of nuns" means she must give it over. "Whichever belongs to that community of nuns" means whichever bowl is last among the nuns' bowls. The community of nuns then must appoint a nun to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation. A nun possessing five qualities must not be appointed to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation even if she has not yet been appointed, and if she has already been appointed she must be removed. What are the five? Going by desire, going by aversion, going by delusion, going by fear, and not knowing which bowls have been distributed and which have not. Likewise, the reverse, the qualities of the white side, are to be applied in the same way.

Following that, by a motion and a second formal act of the assembly, a nun is to be appointed to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation. After the seat has been prepared, one nun makes the motion and the act is performed. It is to be done in this manner: "Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. If it please the noble Saṅgha, and if the time is right and the assembly consents, the Saṅgha of noble ones should appoint the nun named so-and-so to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation. This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows: 'Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. The nun named so-and-so wishes to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation to the noble Saṅgha. The noble Saṅgha appoints the nun named so-and-so to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation for the noble Saṅgha. Those among you, sisters, who consent to the appointment of the nun named so-and-so to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation, remain silent. Those who do not consent, speak.' The Saṅgha has consented and agreed, and the noble Saṅgha has therefore appointed the nun named so-and-so to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation. Since no one has spoken, it is held to be so."

Following that, the nun appointed to distribute alms-bowls without proper relation, at the time of the assembly gathering, is to address the Saṅgha, saying: "Tomorrow morning, at the time of distributing alms-bowls without proper relation, each of you please bring your own bowl." Then, when dawn breaks, the distributing nun, after preparing the seats,

should distribute the alms-bowls without proper relation, then stand before the senior nun of the assembly, recite the full praise of distributing alms-bowls without proper relation exactly as prescribed, and also say these words: "Venerable, please accept an alms-bowl." If the Saṅgha takes the senior nun's alms-bowl without proper relation, the Saṅgha is to give the senior nun's alms-bowl to the next most senior nun. The next most senior nun's alms-bowl is then to be given to the one after her, and so it continues in this way all the way down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha. If the senior nun of the Saṅgha does not accept the alms-bowl without proper relation and the distribution has already passed to the third in seniority, then if the senior nun of the Saṅgha requests one again, it is not to be given. Even if she requests a second time, it is not to be given. But if she requests a third time, it is to be given, and the transgression against the Vinaya is to be confessed. And so it continues likewise down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha. If no one has accepted an alms-bowl without proper relation, or if one bowl remains over, that very bowl is to be given to that person, and she is to be told to use it from that point on.

When the Blessed One declared this, not knowing how it was to be done, the Blessed One declared: "Rules of conduct are to be established for the nun who carries an alms-bowl without proper relation. A nun who carries an alms-bowl without proper relation, if she goes on alms-round, is to hold the alms-bowl without proper relation in her right hand and the consecrated bowl in her left hand. If she receives cooked wet rice, she is to accept it into the consecrated bowl. If she receives dry cooked rice, she is to accept it into the alms-bowl without proper relation. If she is about to place things into the alms-bowl vessel, the lower position is for the consecrated bowl and the upper position is for the alms-bowl without proper relation. If she is doing the washing up, the alms-bowl without proper relation comes first, and the consecrated bowl afterward. If the alms-bowl is to be placed on a bowl-stand, the alms-bowl without proper relation is to be set on top of the consecrated bowl. If work is to be done with the alms-bowl and there is a good kiln, the alms-bowl without proper relation is to be fired in it. If she is going on a journey, she is to give the consecrated bowl to co-residents and attendants to carry, while she herself carries the alms-bowl without proper relation. If there is no one to carry anything at all, the right armpit holds the alms-bowl without proper relation and the left holds the consecrated bowl."

If a nun who carries an alms-bowl without proper relation does not properly accept and use it in accordance with the rules of conduct as laid down, she incurs a serious offence. The last alms-bowl of the Saṅgha is not to be consecrated — it must not be consecrated, must not be given to anyone — but is to be kept carefully and slowly, gradually, for as long as it lasts until it finally breaks.

As to how a transgression arises in that connection: if a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with a single patch, and without mending it she seeks another while it is still serviceable, that is a wrongdoing. Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with two patches, and without mending it she seeks another while it is still serviceable, that is a wrongdoing. Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with three patches, and without mending it she seeks another while it is still serviceable, that is a wrongdoing. Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with four patches, and without mending it she seeks another while it is still serviceable, that is a wrongdoing.

Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with five patches, and without mending it she seeks another while it is still serviceable, that is a wrongdoing. Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with one patch, and she has it mended, yet while it is still serviceable she seeks another, that is a wrongdoing. Should she obtain one, she incurs a forfeiture offence. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with two patches, and she has it mended, yet while it is still serviceable — and so on through: that is a wrongdoing, and she incurs a forfeiture offence. Likewise, the case where three patches are appropriate, and likewise the case where four patches are appropriate, should be stated in the same way. If a nun's alms-bowl breaks and it is fit to be mended with five patches, whether she has it mended or not, there is no offence in seeking another bowl. There is likewise no offence for one who is a first offender and so forth. The thirteenth forfeiture offence is complete.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when, on account of Udāyin, the training rule concerning receiving thread from a non-relative was established, the nun Sthūlanandā received thread from non-relatives and also from relatives, and had a weaver who was not a relative — as well as weavers who were relatives — weave cloth. Nuns of few desires censured this, and the nuns then reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this has occurred," proceeded to establish the training rule. The rule is as follows: whatever nun receives thread from a householder or a householder's wife who is not her relative, and has a weaver who is not her relative weave cloth from it, that is a forfeiture offence. "Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "From one who is not a relative" means up to the seventh generation removed on the mother's side and the father's side. "Thread" means any of the seven kinds. "A weaver who is not a relative" means one who weaves cloth. "Cloth" means any of the seven kinds. "Has it woven" means having had it woven. "A forfeiture offence" is as before. How does the transgression arise? If a nun receives thread from a non-relative and, while requesting a weaver who is not a relative to weave cloth, that is a wrongdoing. If she has a weaver who is not a relative weave it and the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. If a nun receives thread from a non-relative and, while requesting either herself or a weaver who is not a relative to weave it, that is a wrongdoing. If she weaves it herself, that is also a wrongdoing. If she has a non-relative weave it and it is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. If a nun receives thread from a non-relative and requests a weaver who is a relative to weave the cloth, that is a wrongdoing. If she has a relative weaver weave it, there is no offence.
