If a nun receives thread from a non-relative and requests either herself or a relative to weave it, that is a wrongdoing. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing. If a relative weaves it, there is no offence. If a nun receives thread from a non-relative and requests either herself or a non-relative to weave it, that is a wrongdoing. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing. If she requests a relative to weave it, there is no offence. If she has a non-relative weave it and the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. If a nun receives thread from a relative and weaves it herself, and while requesting this there is no offence. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing.

If a nun receives thread from a relative and requests a non-relative to weave it, there is no offence in the requesting. If the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. If a nun receives thread from a relative and requests either herself or a relative to weave it, there is no offence in the requesting. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing. If she has a relative weave it, there is no offence. If a nun receives thread from a relative and either weaves it herself or requests a non-relative to weave it, there is no offence in the requesting. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing. If she has a non-relative weave it and the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. Furthermore, if any nun receives thread from a relative and requests a weaver who is a relative to weave it, there is no offence in the requesting, and there is likewise no offence in having the relative weave it. If a nun receives thread from a relative and either weaves it herself or requests a relative to weave it, there is no offence in the requesting. If she weaves it herself, that is a wrongdoing. If she has a relative weave it, there is no offence. If she has a non-relative weave it and the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence. For those acting for the first time and so forth, there is no offence. The fourteenth forfeiture offence is complete.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At that time, at Śrāvastī, the laywoman Sthūlanandā had inspired faith in a householder together with his retinue. That householder gave thread to a weaver on behalf of the nun Sthūlanandā. Sthūlanandā heard of this from a maidservant, and upon hearing it went to where that weaver was and spoke these words: "Weaver, for whom is this great bolt of woven cloth that you are weaving?" He replied: "I do not know." She then said: "It is for her," meaning herself, and said furthermore that for as long as he was able to do so, whether he provided her with food, or a mere meal, or the means to obtain food, the nuns of modest wants criticized this conduct. The nuns then spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning from the occasion of this incident and proceeding through the laying down of the training rule, ordained: if a householder or a householder's wife has a non-relative weaver weave cloth on behalf of a nun, and that nun — who had not previously been acquainted with that weaver — entertains some thought and goes to the weaver and says: "Venerable weaver, please know that this cloth is for her," meaning herself, and says, "Venerable one, please make this cloth wide in breadth, long in length, well-finished at the edges, and well-woven in texture. If you do so, she will repay you, the venerable weaver, with food, or a mere meal, or even just the smallest means of obtaining food" — and if that nun then gives that weaver even just a little food, or a mere meal, or the means to obtain food, and thereby obtains the cloth, and the cloth is completed, that is a forfeiture offence.

"Any nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "From a non-relative" means those who are not related within seven generations on either the mother's side or the father's side. "Householder" means a man. "Householder's wife" means a woman. "A weaver who is a non-relative" means one who weaves cloth. "Has cloth woven" means any one of the seven. "That nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Entertains some thought" means that some suspicion or doubt has arisen. "Goes to the weaver" means having gone there. "Spoke these words" means having spoken. "This cloth" means pointing out the cloth at hand. "Have it woven for her" means identifying herself. "The venerable weaver does it well" means the venerable weaver does it in a fine manner.

"You have woven this cloth" means whatever cloth was had woven. "Wide" means that it is broad in extent. "Long-hemmed" means that the hem is long. "Bound with a fringe" means without a knot. "Well-woven with a fine weave" means the weave is good and the edge-thread is short.

"If that is so, she should arrange for you a meal, or a light meal, or even a small amount of food" means the five kinds of staple food and the five kinds of non-staple food. "If that nun" means Sthūlanandā. "Should arrange even a little" means this: she gives a meal, or a light meal, or a small amount of food. "In order to get the cloth woven" means for the sake of obtaining the cloth. "When the cloth is finished" means when it has been obtained. "It is an offense entailing forfeiture" means as stated above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? From the point when a nun, in order to obtain cloth, goes begging in the homes of householders and gives the five kinds of staple and the five kinds of non-staple food to the weaver, up until the work is not yet completed, she has committed a wrong act. When it is completed, it is an offense entailing forfeiture.

The fifteenth offense entailing forfeiture is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

At that time, the twelve groups distributed robes and bowls among those who lived together with them and their attendants. Because women are by nature prone to anger, whenever those women quarreled and found fault with one another, those among them who lived together and the attendants would again snatch back the robes, or cause them to be snatched, and during this occasion nuns of few wants censured them. The nuns then reported this to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and so forth, established the training rule as follows.

Furthermore, whatever nun, having given robes to nuns, afterward becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of discontent says, "I shall not give you the robes, nun — give them back!" and either snatches them herself or has them snatched: that nun must return whatever remainder of the robe exists, and if she makes use of it, it is an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Whatever nun" means the twelve groups. "Nuns" means those who dwell together and the attendants. "Having given robes" means any one of the seven kinds. "Afterward" means at a different time. "Having become angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of discontent" means while the agitation has not subsided. "Snatches" means by her own hand. "Has them snatched" means through another person. "The nun should return that robe" means whatever remainder there is of any one of the seven kinds of robe. "She should return it" means she should give it back. "If she makes use of it" means for however long she continues to make use of it. "It is an offense entailing forfeiture" means as stated above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? It arises through bodily action, through verbal expression, or through both together. How does it arise through bodily action? By seizing it with the hand and snatching it away — for as long as the cloth does not leave one's grip, a wrong act is being committed. When it is released, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Such is the transgression arising through bodily action. How does it arise through verbal expression?

By verbal expression it arises thus: when one says the words "Nun, give back the cloth," a wrong act is being committed for as long as one does not release one's hold on the hem of the cloth. When it is released, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Such is the transgression arising through verbal expression. How does it arise through both together? By saying in words "Give back the cloth" and at the same time seizing it with the hand — a wrong act is being committed for as long as one does not release one's hold on the hem of the cloth. When it is released, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Such is the transgression arising through both together. When there is another purpose, or when it is done by means of a Vinaya instrument, there is no offense.

How is it done for another purpose? It is like this: when nuns and their attendants are traveling at an unsuitable time in frightening circumstances, and their preceptors and teachers, seeing that robbers are about to snatch their robes, take the robes from them saying, "This is not right" — such is the case of another purpose. How is it done by means of a Vinaya instrument? It is like this: when nuns and their attendants are keeping company with bad spiritual friends and traveling along with them, and one takes their robes from them so that they may travel instead with good spiritual friends — such is the case of a Vinaya instrument.

The sixteenth offense entailing forfeiture is complete.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the degraded kṣatriyas together with their retinues had been presented before the noble ones by Dharmadattā, and they received gifts and honors from King Prasenajit, they thought: "Everything that causes us to see the noble ones is owing to the noble spiritual friend, the noble Dharmadattā. What can we do to repay her? We who received these gifts and honors from the king through her — we should certainly offer them to Dharmadattā." Then the degraded kṣatriyas took those gifts, went to where Dharmadattā was, arrived there, bowed their heads at Dharmadattā's feet in homage, and offered her those gifts and honors.

Dharmadattā then thought: "Has anyone provided the Blessed One with medicine and almsfood for three months, I wonder?" And as she turned this thought over, she came to know that the Blessed One had been sustained by those very people. Then Dharmadattā spoke to those degraded kṣatriyas as follows: "Householders, today please provide the Blessed One with three months' worth of medicine and almsfood" — and so on down to "and all necessary requisites."

Then they went and provided all of this to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of hearers, and to Dharmadattā together with her retinue. Then the wives of those degraded kṣatriyas began to render service to those nuns. The degraded kṣatriyas also caused expensive and ordinary robes to be set aside for the monks and nuns. During the rains retreat, however, the king sent them away on a mission elsewhere, and Anāthapiṇḍada turned them back from that. After the rains had ended, the nuns made a sign indicating they desired robes, and the wives said: "Noble ones, we have already offered the value of the robes — the insects have eaten them." The nuns replied that the Blessed One had declared that gains accruing during the rains retreat should not be distributed during the rains period.

In that instance of not distributing because one wished to train, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this matter having arisen," proceeded to establish the training rule.

When a nun obtains a robe that has come from those seeking ordination (pravrajyā), within the period running from the last ten days of the last month of autumn up to the end of the rains, and if she desires a robe that has come from those seeking ordination, that nun may accept it. Having accepted it, she shall keep it until the time of the robe-giving. If she keeps it beyond that, it entails a forfeiture-transgression.

"Ten days" means that on the tenth day the invitation ceremony will take place. "Nun" means those who follow this Dharma. "Obtained" means from another. As for "a robe that has come from those seeking ordination," there are five kinds of robes that come from those seeking ordination. What are the five? One who has come, one who is about to depart, one who is sick, one who nurses the sick, and the robe-guardian nun. "Robe" means any of the seven. "If she desires" means if she seeks it for her own purpose. "She shall keep it until the time of the robe-giving" means until the invitation ceremony, which is ten days of the robe-giving period. "Beyond that" means more than that. "It entails a forfeiture-transgression" is as before.

Now how does a transgression arise in this regard? If a nun distributes within the rains period any gain whatsoever accrued during the rains period, or if she keeps it beyond the invitation ceremony, in all cases it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. However, if a nun has been appointed to store robes, there is no transgression. The seventeenth forfeiture-transgression is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of Ānanda, established the training rule regarding turning property of the Saṅgha into one's personal possession, the twelve groups of nuns, having taken gains received on behalf of the Saṅgha and converting them to personal use, were censuring those nuns who had fewer gains. In that instance, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this matter having arisen," proceeded to establish the training rule.

Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly takes for personal possession a gain that has been offered to the Saṅgha incurs a forfeiture-transgression.

"Whatever nun" means the twelve groups. "Knowingly" means it has been said either by herself or by another. "Of the Saṅgha" means the Saṅgha of the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. "Gain" means the two kinds of gain: gain of robes and gain of food; in this context it is understood to mean gain of robes. "That has been offered" means that has been given. "Takes for personal possession" means makes it her own. "It entails a forfeiture-transgression" is as before.

Now how does a transgression arise in this regard? As long as a nun who knowingly diverts a gain offered to the Saṅgha to a different individual has not yet personally appropriated the gain, it is a misdeed. When she personally appropriates it, it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. If a nun resides in different Saṅgha communities separately, and she diverts a gain offered to one community to the other community, as long as she has not personally appropriated the gain it is a misdeed. When she personally appropriates it, it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, if she diverts what was offered to the monks' Saṅgha to the nuns' Saṅgha, it is also as before.

Likewise, if she diverts to one Saṅgha community a gain that was offered to both Saṅgha communities together, it is a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, if she diverts to both Saṅgha communities together a gain that was offered to one Saṅgha community, it is also a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, the same applies beginning from the place designated for flowers at shrines, up to the place for the ceremonial vessel, as well as to the various gate sections and the like. Similarly, if she diverts to a bathhouse what was offered to a rest hall, and the same applies to a hearth room, to the Saṅgha's pleasure grove, to pillars, to beams, and to the ground itself — all of these are to be stated in the same way. Even if what was offered for one meal is diverted to a different meal, it is a misdeed. If, however, what was sought is not found, or if permission is granted, there is no fault. The twenty-eighth forfeiture-transgression is complete.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the fourteenth fascicle. The narrative setting is Rājagṛha. At the time when the Blessed One, while residing together with the son of Pilindavatsa and in reliance upon the personal attendants, established the rule of training concerning medicines common to both communities, the twelve groups of nuns received and ate those medicines, received them hastily, mixed what they had each received together with one another, combined them with powdered food until the portions could no longer be distinguished, and ate them both at proper times and at improper times. The nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with the words "This occurrence" and proceeding through to the establishment of the rule of training, acted as follows. Furthermore, the Blessed One permitted the following medicines to be individually used by sick nuns as appropriate for their respective conditions: ghee, sesame oil, honey, and the froth of molasses. A sick nun may use these by means of consecrated stored-goods for a period extending to the seventh day at most. If she uses them beyond that, it is a forfeiture-transgression.

Now, the phrase "the Blessed One" means the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha. The phrase "for sick nuns" means for those who are ill. The phrase "appropriate" means what is suitable. The phrase "for individual use" — meaning fitting medicines — includes the following: "ghee" means clarified butter; "sesame oil" means sesame oil itself; "honey" means that of bees; "the froth of molasses" means molasses. The phrase "to the end of seven days" means for seven days. The phrase "by means of consecrated stored-goods" means having been ritually consecrated. The phrase "for individual use" means to be consumed. The phrase "beyond that" means in excess of that. The phrase "it is a forfeiture-transgression" is as before.

Now, how does a transgression arise in this case? If a nun on the first day of the fortnight finds a medicinal substance for the sick, she should within seven days either consecrate it, give it away, or use it. If she neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor uses it, then when the dawn of the eighth day breaks, it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, as stated for the first day, the same is to be stated identically for each subsequent day up through the sixth day, just as before. If a nun finds a medicinal substance for the sick on the first day, and then on the second day finds another, she should either consecrate the earlier one, give it away, or

use the later one, or consecrate the later one, or use the earlier one. If she neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor uses it, then when the dawn of the eighth day breaks, it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, the case of finding two on the second day of the fortnight, and again finding two on the second day, is to be stated in full up through the sixth and seventh days. The full statement up through "a nun finds many medicinal substances for the sick on the first day of the fortnight" is also to be given in detail. Likewise, the case of finding many on the first day of the fortnight and finding others again on the second day is to be stated in full up to that point.

Now, whatever medicinal substances received from those sick persons have been mixed together with one another and have been mixed with food powder and minced — those are to be given to the novices of another monastery. Whatever medicinal substances received from those sick persons have not been mixed together with one another and have not been mixed with food powder and have not been minced — those are to be given to those who live the holy life, saying: "This medicinal substance has been held for one day; I will use it for six days." And so on in the same way, down to one day remaining.

If a nun has found a medicinal substance for the sick, and without having relinquished it, separated herself from it, or confessed the transgression, she finds another — that too becomes a forfeiture-transgression through the fault of the earlier one. Likewise, if she has relinquished it but has not separated herself from it and has not confessed the transgression, that too becomes a forfeiture-transgression. Likewise, if she has separated herself from it but has not confessed the transgression, that too becomes a forfeiture-transgression. If she has relinquished it, separated herself from it, and confessed the transgression, and then uses it, there is no transgression. And for those acting for the first time and so forth, there is no transgression. The nineteenth forfeiture-transgression is complete.

The background narrative takes place at Śrāvastī. At that time the group of twelve were finding bowls in excess and accumulating what they found, neither using them themselves, nor distributing them to the nuns who were present, nor giving them even to those who begged. When nuns who were content with little reproached them for this, those nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurred," established the training rule up to that point: a nun may keep an extra bowl for at most one day. If she keeps it beyond that, it becomes a forfeiture-transgression.

"One day" means one full day. "Nun" means a member of the group of twelve, or another who is similarly situated. "An extra bowl" means one beyond what has been consecrated. "If she keeps it beyond that" means more than that limit. "It becomes a forfeiture-transgression" is as before.

How does the transgression arise? If a nun keeps an extra bowl for more than one day, in every case it becomes a forfeiture-transgression. If she keeps a plain, unconsecrated bowl, there is no transgression. The twentieth forfeiture-transgression is complete.

The background narrative takes place at Śrāvastī. At that time a certain householder living in Śrāvastī took a wife of equal social standing, played with her as was fitting, and eventually she gave birth to a son, whom he named Kāmaka. Since desires are like salt water — never satisfying — he continued in his pleasures, and she gave birth to a daughter, whom he named Kāmikā. Then at another time the householder passed away. When the householder died, his wife, together with her two daughters and one son, went forth into renunciation.

Then the young monk Dunpa went from the monks' monastery to the nuns' monastery to visit his mother. He was wearing a robe dyed with fresh color, turned to a reddish-gold hue. When he arrived, his sister asked him: "Brother, whose robe is this?" He said, "It is mine." She said, "Please give it to me," but he did not give it, and she began to cry. Their mother asked, "Daughter, why are you crying?" She said, "I asked my brother for his robe and he would not give it to me." Then the mother said to the young monk Dunpa, "Son, give your sister the robe." He replied, "Would that not constitute some kind of transgression?" She said, "There is nothing wrong with it." So Dunpa gave the robe to his sister Dunma, and Dunma in turn gave her own robe to Dunpa.

Before many days had passed, Dunma had made the robe dirty. Dunpa, for his part, had washed his robe well and cared for it properly, and then he came again to visit his mother. Dunma said to her brother, "Brother, whose robe is this?" He replied, "Well, it was once yours — but it is now mine." She said, "Take this robe of mine in exchange and give me back my own robe." He did not give it. She then appealed to their mother, who said, "Son, give it to her." And he did.

Later the nuns said to the nun Dunma, "Your robe is always being washed and well cared for, so it looks as clean as a new residence." She then told the nuns what had occurred. The nuns said to her, "Why do you make a practice of exchanging robes with a leading member of a community of men?" She replied, "Whether it was proper to exchange or not, I exchanged it." Those nuns who were of few desires proceeded to rebuke her. Those nuns then told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One — and so the rule was established. "Whatever nun exchanges robes with a monk and then afterward says, 'Noble one, take this noble robe of yours and return my robe to me' — that is a forfeiture-transgression."

In this rule, "whatever nun" refers to Dunma, and "monk" refers to Dunpa. "Exchanges robes" refers to any one of the seven types. "Forfeiture-transgression" is as stated above. As for how the transgression occurs: however much and to whatever extent a nun engages in exchanging robes with a monk, it constitutes a forfeiture-transgression in every case.

The twenty-first forfeiture-transgression is complete.

The background narrative takes place at Śrāvastī. At that time the nun Bhomgamo, together with the nuns' Saṅgha, had just performed the spreading of the reed mat on the last day of the autumn month, and immediately said to the nuns: "Sisters, take up the reed mats — come here. Many achievements and much wellbeing will arise from taking up the reed mats." They replied, "We do not take up the reed mats at an improper time." She said, "If she is learned in the three baskets of scripture, surely she knows what the proper time is for taking up the reed mats, does she not?"

She did not listen to the words of those nuns and, at an improper time, took out the reed mats and divided the gains. Those nuns then took up their five robes and went wandering through the districts. The other nuns asked them: "Noble ones, did you complete the spreading of the reed mats?" They replied: "We ourselves did not know, but the noble Bhomgamo said, 'Since I am learned in the three baskets of scripture, I know the proper time for taking out the reed mats.'" The other nuns said, "And did you take out the reed mats?" When they replied that they had, those nuns of few desires began to criticize them. Those nuns then told the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. And so the training rule was established: Any nun who takes out the reed mats at an improper time incurs an offense of abandonment.

Now, "any nun" refers to Bhomgamo. "An improper time" — what is the proper time and what is the improper time for spreading the reed mats? From the last month of autumn through to the first month of spring is the proper time for spreading the reed mats. If the mats are taken out within that period, it counts as taking them out at an improper time. How does the transgression arise? Whenever a nun takes out those reed mats at an improper time, in every case it becomes an offense of abandonment. If, however, it is because thieves have taken the mats away, there is no transgression.

This concludes the twenty-second offense of abandonment.

The background narrative takes place at Śrāvastī. At that time Bhomgamo did not take out the reed mats at the proper time for doing so. The nuns said to her: "Noble one, the time has come to take out the reed mats — why do you not take them out?" She replied: "Since I am learned in the three baskets of scripture, I know the proper time for taking out the reed mats." Those nuns then passed the proper time for the reed mats and went wandering through the districts wearing their outer and lower robes. The other nuns asked them: "Sisters, why do you go wandering through the districts with your outer and lower robes on, having passed the time for taking out the reed mats?" They replied: "The noble Bhomgamo said she is learned in the three baskets of scripture — and yet she still has not taken out the reed mats." At that, the nuns of few desires began to criticize them. And so the training rule was established: Any nun who does not take out the reed mats at the proper time incurs an offense of abandonment.

Now, "any nun" again refers to Bhomgamo. "At the proper time" means taking out the reed mats on the fifteenth day of the first month of spring. "Incurs an offense of abandonment" is as explained above. How does the transgression arise? To whatever extent a nun fails to take out the reed mats at the proper time, in every case it becomes an offense of abandonment.

This concludes the twenty-third offense of abandonment.

Summary verse:

The first concerns what is openly marked, then each one individually,
And that which is repeatedly released,
Gaining other goods in place of robes,
And lodging, and the summer dwelling,
And gaining things for the sake of many people,
And soliciting on behalf of the Saṅgha,
And the heavy one of great value,
And the light one — that is the last.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was a goldsmith in Śrāvastī who took a wife from an equal family.

Then the husband, wishing to be intimate with his new bride, placed a gold earring there and went to sit apart. Now, Bhomā Gāmo went in the morning, having put on her under-robe and taken up her alms-bowl and outer robe, and came to the house where the goldsmith dwelt. On arriving, she wished the bride good health, and then spoke these words: "O lady of good features, please give alms." The bride brought out some flour, and when Bhomā Gāmo saw the flour she said: "It is not right that I should take flour from you before anyone else. The ignorant woman then showed the gold earring and said, 'Then give me this.'" The bride said neither "Take it" nor "Do not take it," and so she took it and departed.

Then that man did not find the gold earring. Not finding it, he set upon the bride and began to beat her. Those who stood around on either side said: "You have no complaint and no grievance — why do you beat this blameless woman with a stick? Has the nun perhaps taken the gold earring and gone?" Thereupon the goldsmith ran to where Bhomā Gāmo was. Now she too was skilled in distinguishing the footsteps of men and women, and so, startled, she put the gold earring in her mouth. When the man came close to her, Bhomā Gāmo spoke to him thus: "Son of Zanmo, do you not know that the king has granted her the status of a queen's consort? Do not touch her with your hand." He said, "You evil-headed woman," and then thrust his fist against her so that blood came from her mouth, beat her several times, and struck her again.

She came to the rainy-season dwelling with her eyes swollen, and the nuns there asked her: "Noble one, what has happened to you?" She, being angry, said: "Are you satisfied by others' misfortune?" Then she recounted the whole matter in detail to the nuns. From the point where "those nuns with few concerns began to reproach her" to the point where the matter was reported to the Blessed One, and then from where "the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence" to the point where "he laid down the training rule" — all of this proceeds as before.

And now: whatever nun solicits something openly marked is guilty of an offense of abandonment.

As to "whatever nun" — this means Bhomā Gāmo or any other who is similar to her. As to "solicits something openly marked" — this means gold or silver. As to "is guilty of an offense of abandonment" — this is as described above.

Now, how does the transgression arise in this case? Whatever nun solicits something openly marked for her own sake is guilty of an offense of abandonment. If she solicits gold, she is guilty of an offense of abandonment. And if any nun solicits whatever else is not permitted, that too is an offense of abandonment.

The twenty-fourth offense of abandonment is complete.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time Bhomā Gāmo was teaching pleasing and beautiful Dharma discourses to the wives of many householders in Śrāvastī. At that time the five Dharma robes of Bhomā Gāmo were worn out and her patched outer robe was threadbare. The wives of the householders then said to her: "Noble one, if you can teach the Dharma so well, why do you wander about with five old robes?" She replied: "Is it that, as with you, there are those who work on her behalf — husband and sons? Who is there to give to a nun?" At that they showed her their threads, saying: "We offer these threads of ours for weaving into cloth for the noble one's sake, and we present them to her." And she spoke as follows:

"Since you do not know how to make a nun's robe, she will weave it herself." With those words she took the thread and went to where a merchant's man was, and when she arrived she said to the merchant's man: "Good sir, for how much will you buy this thread, and for how much will you sell it?" He replied: "I will buy it for such-and-such a price and sell it for such-and-such a price." She then said: "Take this thread and give her the price for it." The merchant's man gave the price of the thread in kārṣāpaṇas.

Bhomā Gāmo then went to the summer quarters and, with those kārṣāpaṇas, had various food dishes prepared — dishes tossed together, well-tossed dishes, dishes garnished with fruit, dishes with a coating of oil, dishes with a coating of fruit, dishes of a hundred layers, and dishes with filled interiors. In this way she had eighteen and twenty kinds of food dishes prepared, and she consumed those kārṣāpaṇas in many fewer days than might be expected. After eating, she went again to the wives of the householders, and the wives of the householders said to Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, has the robe been woven?" She replied: "There is still the matter of the weaver's fee." They gave her the weaver's fee as well, and she ate that too. In the same way she also ate the fees for the fulling and for the dyeing.

Then the wives of the householders said to Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, why have you not yet sewn the robe?" She replied: "Rejoice!" They said: "Noble one, what have you done?" She said: "I have hidden it as a treasure." They said: "We, for our part, hide things as treasure for our children and our husbands. But you, noble one, are alone, like a munditā and like a cypress — for whose sake have you hidden a treasure?" She replied: "Do you think I dug a hole in the ground and buried a treasure? Rather, she made eighteen and twenty kinds of food dishes and tossed them from the hollow of her hand into her stomach, and from the stomach cast them down into the earth of the belly." They then said: "Noble one, we have children and we manage a household, yet even we do not desire food of this sort. Why is it that you, who have gone forth into homelessness, should enjoy food of such a kind?" At that she said: "This girl is a very young daughter of the Śākya clan who has mastered the three baskets of scripture, and she cannot survive on poor food." When the nuns heard this, the nuns proceeded to censure her — and so on up to the establishing of the training rule.

"Furthermore, whatever nun uses gains from robes belonging to others to dedicate to her own mouth — that is an offense requiring abandonment."

Now, "whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo or another who is similar to her. "Others" refers to other items. "Robe" refers to any of the seven kinds. "To her own mouth" means swallowing it into her stomach. "An offense requiring abandonment" is as stated above.

As for how a transgression arises in this case: however much gain from robes a nun dedicates to the mouth, it all becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

The twenty-fifth offense requiring abandonment is complete.

The setting is in Śrāvastī.

At that time Bhomā Gāmo became attached to a young perfume-seller, and she went to his shop and spoke as follows:

"Good-looking one, tie up a bundle of window-lattice strips." Just as she had entered into the tying, he said: "No, no — tie a bundle of long pepper. No, no — tie a bundle of cardamom. The woman is forgetful — tie a bundle of sugar. No, no — tie a bundle of fennel. No, no — tie a bundle of coarse cloth remnants." At the moment when she was undoing one thing and tying another, the young perfume-seller became angry and struck her with the bundle. Having struck her, he said these words: "You wretched scratcher of heads!" Then a nun who had been following along behind said to her: "Can your ability well demonstrate the three baskets of the Canon? Or does he think you a fool who has forgotten? Well, all the same, she takes the words as her own." He then said: "If one is struck by attachment and does not cry out, and does not burn like dry wood that has caught fire, that is truly astonishing." When this was said, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, and so forth up to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having tied a bundle and then repeatedly caused it to be untied, commits an offense requiring abandonment. Furthermore, whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "Having tied a bundle and tied it" means the bundle itself. "Having repeatedly caused it to be untied" means different occasions. "Commits an offense requiring abandonment" is as stated above. As for how a transgression arises in this case: however much a nun, with even slight attachment, ties and unties a bundle, all of it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

The twenty-sixth offense requiring abandonment is complete.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. Then Bhomā Gāmo, in the morning, put on her lower robe, took her alms-bowl and Dharma-robe, and went to the palace of Queen Mālinī. Queen Mālinī, from a considerable distance, saw Bhomā Gāmo coming. Seeing her, she had a seat prepared. Then Bhomā Gāmo sat down on the seat that had been arranged and, having sat, taught Dharma sweetly and pleasingly to Queen Mālinī. At that time the lower portion of Bhomā Gāmo's Dharma-robe was worn and the patched section was also threadbare. Then Queen Mālinī said these words to the nun Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, your Dharma-robes are worn out." She replied: "Your Majesty, do you mock me for my great belly? Or does she possess the wealth of Kāśī and Kośala? Moreover, Your Majesty, women are of meager gain." Then Queen Mālinī said these words to the nun Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, I will offer you five Dharma-robes." She replied: "You do not know how to sew nuns' Dharma-robes, but I myself will sew them." She then gave her large bolts of precious cloth as the material for five Dharma-robes. She took them, went to a merchant, and sold them, and so forth up to: she made eighteen sorts of food and twenty kinds of food, ate them, and went again, and so forth up to: she also ate the wages for dyeing and the wages for tailoring. Then Queen Mālinī said these words to Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, why have you not worn those Dharma-robes?" She replied: "Your Majesty, I have kept them hidden as a store — please rejoice in it." Then Queen Mālinī said these words to Bhomā Gāmo: "Though her wealth may be that of Kāśī and Kośala, still she would not use it as a store," and so forth, together with the eighteenth and

the twentieth, making eighteen and twenty kinds of food, eating them, and so forth up to: "I am a master of the Three Baskets." This is the conclusion of the section on monks and nuns of few concerns rebuking her, leading up to the laying down of a training rule.

Furthermore, whatever nun, for the sake of robes, consecrates other acquired goods to her own mouth, incurs a forfeitable transgression.

The phrase "whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "Other goods" means goods that had been dedicated to another purpose. "Gains relating to robes" means any one of the seven kinds. "To the mouth" means to swallow in secret. "Incurs a forfeitable transgression" is as above.

As to how the transgression arises: to whatever extent a nun consecrates other acquired goods to her mouth, she incurs a forfeitable transgression in every case.

This completes the twenty-seventh forfeitable transgression.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bed and furnishings of Bhomā Gāmo's rain-retreat dwelling had become worn and broken. The wives of brahmins and householders said to her: "Why have you not repaired the worn and broken furnishings?" She replied: "Does she have sons and household servants to do it for her?" They gave her many kārṣāpaṇas for the repair of the furnishings. And she made the eighteen and twenty kinds of food and ate them, and so forth to that point.

Again, having seen the worn and broken furnishings, and so forth up to where she said: "She is a master of the Three Baskets," the monks and nuns of few concerns rebuked her, and so forth up to the laying down of a training rule.

Furthermore, whatever nun consecrates gains from the rain-retreat dwelling to the eating of her own mouth, incurs a forfeitable transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "Gains from the dwelling" means the canopy, the hanging of curtains, or the hire thereof. "Incurs a forfeitable transgression" is as above.

As to how the transgression arises: to whatever extent a nun consecrates even a little of the gains from the rain-retreat dwelling to the mouth, she incurs a forfeitable transgression.

This completes the twenty-eighth forfeitable transgression.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, on the eighth and fifteenth days, very many wives of householders came to the rain-retreat dwelling to hear the Dharma, and that night rain fell, and all the rain-retreat dwellings began to drip. Then those wives of householders said these words to Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, why have you not repaired the rain-retreat dwelling?" She replied: "Does she have sons and household servants in her house?" They gave her kārṣāpaṇas for the repair of the rain-retreat dwelling, and she made the eighteen and twenty kinds of food and ate them, and so forth up to: again, having seen the dripping, and so forth to that point.

They said: "Noble one, have you not repaired the rain-retreat dwelling?" and so forth up to where she said: "She is a master of the Three Baskets." The monks and nuns of few concerns rebuked her, and the Blessed One declared — and so forth up to the laying down of a training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun consecrates gains obtained for repairing the rain-retreat dwelling to the eating of her own mouth, incurs a forfeitable transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "Rain-retreat dwelling" means the temple.

"Gains" refers to gold, silver, or anything else whatsoever. "Incurs a forfeitable transgression" is as above. How does the transgression arise? To whatever small extent a nun consecrates gains obtained for repairing the rain-retreat dwelling to the eating of her own mouth, she incurs a forfeitable transgression. The twenty-ninth forfeitable transgression is complete.

The context for the following rule is Śrāvastī. At that time a great many nuns arrived at Śrāvastī from a certain region, and on their behalf the wives of brahmins and householders presented many gains. Those wives said: "Noble one, please keep them in trust." The nun replied: "Add to them again and again, a little at a time." The wives gave again and again, and then they said: "Noble one, the time has come to hold what has been kept in trust." She replied: "The time for eating has not yet arrived." When those nuns departed for their own regions, she took from those gains and made categories of the eighteenth through the twentieth portions and ate them — and so forth up to: "She is a master of the Three Baskets." The nuns of few concerns rebuked her, the Blessed One declared — and so forth up to the laying down of a training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun collects gains on behalf of nuns who have arrived suddenly and eats them alone incurs a forfeitable transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "Nuns who have arrived suddenly" means the female śrāvaka disciples of the Blessed One. As for "gains," gains are of two kinds: gains in the form of food, and gains in the form of robes. In this context, gains in the form of food are intended. "Incurs a forfeitable transgression" is as above. How does the transgression arise? To whatever extent a nun eats alone gains that exist on behalf of nuns who have arrived suddenly, she incurs a forfeitable transgression in every such case. The thirtieth forfeitable transgression is complete.

The context for the following rule is Śrāvastī. Then, when nun Bhomā Gāmo was properly soliciting food gains on behalf of the community of nuns, the wives of brahmins and householders said to Bhomā Gāmo: "Noble one, why do you not seek gains in food for the community of nuns? Take these repeatedly, a little at a time." Having taken them repeatedly alone, and having stirred them properly and well — from the categories of the eighteenth through the twentieth portions — she ate them, and so forth up to: "Rejoice in it!" and "She is a master of the Three Baskets." The nuns of few concerns rebuked her — and so forth up to where the Blessed One laid down a training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun collects gains on behalf of the Saṅgha and consecrates them for eating by her own mouth incurs a forfeitable transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Bhomā Gāmo. "On behalf of the community of nuns" means on behalf of the community of nuns who are female śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgata. As for "gains," gains are of two kinds: gains in the form of food and gains in the form of robes. In this context, gains in the form of food are intended. "Collects" means from another party. "For eating by her own mouth" means for her own mouth's eating. "Consecrates" means swallowing it secretly. "Incurs a forfeitable transgression" is as above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? However much of the community of nuns' gains a nun consecrates for eating by her own mouth — in every case, that constitutes a forfeitable transgression.

The thirty-first forfeitable transgression is complete.

The origin narrative takes place in Śrāvastī. At that time, the king of the Licchavis had sent a precious woolen garment as a gift to King Prasenajit, and he gave it to his soldiers whose noble rank had declined. They in turn gave that precious woolen garment to Dharmadattā, saying, "The Teacher of the Dharma is our spiritual friend." She then draped the precious woolen garment over the rail of her robe-stand and set it there. Nandapriyā, having entered the dwelling, saw it and asked Dharmadattā, "Noble one, whose is this precious woolen garment?" She replied, "It is hers," meaning her own. Then Nandapriyā said: "The Blessed One has declared: 'Merit is something to be done; without merit made, suffering comes. In this world and the next, one who has made merit will rejoice.' This teaching has arrived right on time — through the merit you have made, you have come to be honored by gods and humans." Then Dharmadattā said to Nandapriyā, "If you wish, take it." She replied, "This has defeated a god," and with that, she took the precious woolen garment, divided it, draped each piece over her two arms, and wandered along the main roads and byways. When brahmins and householders saw her, they said: "Who is this? Is she the wife of some wealthy man, or of a merchant, or of a caravan leader?" Others said, "It is Nandapriyā." Those who looked and understood then said: "The wives of brahmins and householders wear heavy and costly garments — and these female renunciants, daughters of the Śākyas, also wear heavy and costly garments. What difference is there? What distinction of intention is there? What difference can be made?" And they criticized her, jeered at her, and gossiped about her.

In that connection, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," called Nandapriyā to account: "Nun, is it true that you did something so unbecoming?" "Blessed One, it is so." The buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked Nandapriyā, saying, "That which is contrary to the way of a female renunciant, inappropriate, and unbecoming — such a thing is not to be done by one who has gone forth." Then the Blessed One rebuked her in many ways, and addressed both communities of the Saṅgha: "Monks, a woman is like food: even when there are no fine garments, she is something desirable — how much more so when she is dressed in fine garments!" The Blessed One then reflected: "All the faults and misfortunes that have arisen have come from possessing heavy and costly garments," and so the Blessed One declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun possesses a heavy and costly garment incurs a forfeitable transgression."

"Whatever nun" refers to Nandapriyā. "Heavy" means a winter garment. "Costly" means worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas, or the worth exceeding twenty-five. "Possesses" means wears. "Forfeitable transgression" is as above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? However much a nun wears a heavy and costly garment — in every case, that constitutes a forfeitable transgression.

The thirty-second forfeitable transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, the king of the country of Kaliṅga sent a precious silk garment as a gift to King Prasenajit. He in turn gave it to certain soldiers of the warrior caste who had fallen on hard times. They then gave it to Dharmadattā, saying, "She is our good spiritual friend." She accepted it and folded it away in a bundle of Dharma-robes. When Śironandinī entered the dwelling and saw it, she said: "Noble one, Dharmadattā, whose is this?" Dharmadattā replied, "It belongs to her." Then Śironandinī said to Dharmadattā, "You have accumulated merit and are honored by gods and humans alike; you possess a spring garment just like this." Dharmadattā replied, "If you wish, take it." And so Śironandinī said, "I have no desire to be the ruin of a goddess." Then Dharmadattā gave the silk to Śironandinī. She put it on, and when she entered the marketplace wearing it, even though it covered her body, she appeared as though she were naked. Then brahmins and householders, seeing Śironandinī approaching from a considerable distance, said, "Who is this — the daughter of a wealthy man, a merchant, or a caravan leader coming our way?" Others said, "It is the nun Śironandinī." They looked at her and said, "This wearing of silk is altogether unbecoming for nuns," and they criticized her, made jeering gestures, and spoke ill of her. At that juncture, nuns of few desires criticized her conduct. The nuns then told the monks in full, and the monks informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One thereupon convened the assembly of both communities of the Saṅgha, so that this occurrence, this origin of the rule, and this occasion would be known by my female śrāvaka disciples, and so that I might properly establish a training rule. The blessed buddhas ask while knowing, not while unknowing — and so, knowing, he asked: "Nun, is it true that you have done something so unbecoming?" She said: "Reverend One, I have." The Blessed One rebuked her, saying to the nuns, "Nuns, a woman who is even well clothed is unbecoming — how much more so when she is not clothed at all?" Having rebuked her in many ways, the Blessed One then spoke to the nuns:

"Nuns, having seen ten genuine benefits, I institute training rules in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas — namely, for the proper unifying of the Saṅgha," and so forth up to "so that it may be rightly and well proclaimed among gods and humans."

And my female śrāvaka disciples shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: "Furthermore, whatever nun wears a precious and costly garment incurs a forfeitable transgression."

"Whatever nun" refers to Śironandinī. "Garment" refers to silk. "Precious and costly" means worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas, or worth twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas. "Forfeitable transgression" is as above.

Now, how does the transgression arise? If a nun wears silk — a forfeitable transgression. If she wears something variegated or something thin, in every case it constitutes a forfeitable transgression. For one who acts for the first time and the like, there is no transgression.

The thirty-third forfeitable transgression is complete.

The forfeitable transgressions of the Vinaya Analysis for Nuns are complete.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns. The fifteenth fascicle.

Now the transgressions proper are to be set forth. The summary verse is:

With full knowledge; and seed;
likewise the act of carrying;
striking the palms; with deliberate intent;
theft; and the great storehouse.

The summary verse:

Knowingly drawing out a fault;
slander; and expressions of weariness;
teaching Dharma to a man;
and nullifying a pleasant training.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana) of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī, the city of King Prasenajit. At that time, the groups of twelve nuns knowingly told lies to other nuns so as to elevate themselves, and they spoke disparagingly of nuns who were few in wants. The matter was reported to the Blessed One, and then the Blessed One, proceeding from the account of what had occurred and continuing through the establishing of the training, ordained: "To speak a deliberate lie is a transgression."

"Deliberately" means after having examined the matter. As for the phrase "to speak a lie," there are lies of eight kinds; there are lies of seven kinds; there are lies of six kinds; there are lies of five kinds; there are lies of four kinds; there are lies of three kinds; and there are lies of two kinds.

What are the eight kinds of lies? A groundless accusation of a root defeat; an accusation deserving a formal act of the Saṅgha; a transgression; a transgression requiring individual confession; a fault; a groundless accusation of having seen; of having heard; and of having suspected. These are the eight kinds of lies.

What are the seven kinds of lies? A groundless accusation of impaired moral discipline; of an impaired view; of an impaired ritual conduct; of an impaired livelihood; a groundless accusation of having seen; of having heard; and of having suspected. These are the seven kinds of lies.

What are the six kinds of lies? A nun who intends to speak falsely thinks, "I will speak a lie"; she thinks, "I am speaking a lie"; she thinks, "I have spoken a lie"; a groundless accusation of having seen; of having heard; and of having suspected. These are the six kinds of lies.

What are the five kinds of lies? A groundless accusation of a root defeat; an accusation deserving a formal act of the Saṅgha; a transgression; a transgression requiring individual confession; and a fault. These are the five kinds of lies.

What are the four kinds of lies? A groundless accusation of impaired moral discipline; of an impaired view; of an impaired ritual conduct; and of an impaired livelihood. These are the four kinds of lies.

What are the three kinds of lies? A groundless accusation of having seen; of having heard; and of having suspected. These are the three kinds of lies.

There are also another three kinds of lies: when intending to speak falsely, one thinks, "I will speak a lie"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a lie"; and having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken a lie." These are those three kinds of lies.

What are the two kinds of lies? While speaking falsely, one thinks, "I am speaking a lie"; and having spoken falsely, one thinks, "I have spoken a lie." These are the two kinds of lies.

There is no single solitary kind of lie standing alone. There are lies that result in a root defeat; there are lies that result in a formal act of the Saṅgha; and there are lies that result in a coarse transgression.

There are lies that result in a transgression, and there are lies that result in a serious wrong.

What is a lie that results in a root defeat? It is this: when a nun falsely claims superhuman qualities that she does not possess. This is a lie that results in a root defeat.

What is a lie that results in a formal act of the Saṅgha? It is this: when a nun, without any basis, accuses a pure nun of an offense entailing a root defeat. This is a lie that results in a formal act of the Saṅgha.

What is a lie that results in a coarse transgression? It is this: when a nun deliberately teaches within the Saṅgha that what is not Dharma is Dharma, that what is Dharma is not Dharma, that what is not Vinaya is Vinaya, and that what is Vinaya is not Vinaya. This is a lie that results in a coarse transgression.

What is a lie that results in a transgression? It is this: when a nun, knowing it to be false, speaks a lie before the assembly of the twelve classes of nuns and thereby satisfies them. This is a lie that results in a transgression.

What is a lie that results in a serious wrong? It is this: when, during the restoration ceremony on the fifteenth day, the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited and the question is asked, "Is the assembly pure in this matter?"— and a nun who is not pure remains silent and consents by saying nothing. This is a lie that results in a serious wrong. Apart from these four types, all other lies fall into the category of transgressions.

The term "transgression" means that one is burned, scorched, and cast down into the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, and the wretched realms of miserable rebirth. Now, how does one incur a transgression?

The summary verse:
Not having forgotten, and with doubt,
and perception combined with four kinds —
these are joined.

When one has not seen, not heard, not understood, and not cognized something, yet one alters one's perception, conviction, desire, reasoning, thought, and view, and says, "I have seen it, I have heard it, I have understood it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something but has forgotten it, or when one has heard, understood, or cognized something but has forgotten it, and then alters one's perception, conviction, desire, reasoning, thought, and view, and says, "I have seen it and have not forgotten; I have heard it, understood it, and cognized it and have not forgotten" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something oneself but is doubtful about it, or when one has heard, understood, or cognized something oneself but is doubtful about it, and then alters one's perception, conviction, desire, reasoning, thought, and view, and says, "I have seen it and am not doubtful; I have understood it, I have cognized it, and am not doubtful" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something but perceives it as not having seen it, or when one has heard, understood, or cognized something but perceives it as not having cognized it, and then alters one's perception, conviction, desire, reasoning, thought, and view, and says, "I have not seen it; she has not heard it; she has not understood it; she has not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has not seen something, yet from having heard, understood, and cognized it — altering one's perception and so forth — if one says, "I have not seen it, I have not heard it, I have not understood it, I have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has not heard something, yet from having seen, understood, and cognized it — altering one's perception and so forth — if one says, "I have heard it but not seen it; I have not discerned it; I have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has not understood something —

Although one has not understood something, yet from having seen, heard, and cognized it — altering one's perception and so forth — if one says, "I have understood it but have not heard it, I have not discerned it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has seen something and not forgotten it, and has heard, discerned, and cognized it and not forgotten it — yet altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I saw it and then forgot it; she heard it, discerned it, and cognized it and then forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has heard something and forgotten it, and has seen, discerned, and cognized it and forgotten it — yet altering one's account from that basis — if one says, "I heard it and did not forget it; I saw it, discerned it, and cognized it and did not forget it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has discerned something and not forgotten it, and has seen, heard, and cognized it and not forgotten it — yet altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I discerned it and then forgot it; I saw it, discerned it, and cognized it and then forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one has cognized something and not forgotten it, and has seen, heard, and discerned it and not forgotten it — yet altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I cognized it and then forgot it; she saw it, heard it, and discerned it and then forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one saw something and was uncertain about it, and was uncertain about having heard, discerned, and cognized it — yet altering one's account from that basis — if one says, "I saw it and am not uncertain; she heard it, discerned it, and cognized it and is not uncertain" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one heard something and was uncertain about it, and was uncertain about having seen, discerned, and cognized it — yet altering one's account from that basis — if one says, "I heard it and am not uncertain; she saw it, discerned it, and cognized it and is not uncertain" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one discerned something and was uncertain about it, and was uncertain about having seen, heard, and cognized it — yet altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I discerned it and am not uncertain; she saw it, heard it, and cognized it and is not uncertain" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Although one cognized something and was uncertain about it, and was uncertain about having seen, heard, and discerned it — yet altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I cognized it and am not uncertain; she saw it, heard it, and discerned it and is not uncertain" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives what one has seen as not having been seen, yet perceives what one has heard, discerned, and cognized as having been cognized — altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I have seen it but have not heard it, have not discerned it, and have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives what one has heard as not having been heard, yet perceives what one has seen, discerned, and cognized as having been cognized — altering one's account from that basis — if one says, "I have heard it but have not seen it, have not discerned it, and have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives what one has discerned as not having been discerned, yet perceives what one has seen, heard, and cognized as having been cognized — altering one's account from that basis — if one says, "She has discerned it but has not seen it, has not heard it, and has not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives what one has cognized as not having been cognized, yet perceives what one has seen, heard, and discerned as having been discerned — altering one's perception from that basis — if one says, "I have cognized it but have not seen it, have not heard it" —

— "I have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen, heard, discerned, and cognized something, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I have not seen it, I have not heard it, I have not contacted it, I have not cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something and not forgotten it, and has heard, discerned, and cognized something and not forgotten it, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I saw it and forgot it; I heard it and forgot it; I discerned it and forgot it; I cognized it and forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something and does not doubt it, and has heard, discerned, and cognized something and does not doubt it, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I saw it but now doubt it; I heard, discerned, and cognized it but now doubt it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives what one has seen as having been seen, and perceives what one has heard, discerned, and cognized as having been cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I have seen it, I have not heard it, I have not discerned it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has indeed seen something but has not heard it, not discerned it, and not cognized it, and from that basis one alters one's perception — and says, "I have not seen it, yet I have heard it, I have discerned it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has indeed heard something but has not seen it, not discerned it, and not cognized it, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I have not heard it, yet I have seen it, I have discerned it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has indeed discerned something but has not seen it, not heard it, and not cognized it, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I have not discerned it, yet I have seen it, I have heard it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has indeed cognized something but has not seen it, not heard it, and not discerned it, and from that basis one alters — and says, "I have not cognized it, yet I have seen it, I have heard it, I have discerned it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has seen something and not forgotten it, yet has forgotten what one has heard, discerned, and cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I have not seen it, yet I have heard it, I have discerned it, I have cognized it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has not forgotten what one has seen, not forgotten what one has heard, not forgotten what one has discerned, and not forgotten what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I saw it and forgot it; I heard it and forgot it; I discerned it and forgot it; I cognized it and forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has not forgotten what one has discerned, not forgotten what one has seen, not forgotten what one has heard, not forgotten what one has discerned, and not forgotten what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I discerned it and forgot it; I saw it and forgot it; I heard it and forgot it" —

"I cognized it and forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has not forgotten what one has cognized, not forgotten what one has seen, not forgotten what one has heard, and not forgotten what one has discerned, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I cognized it and forgot it; I saw it and forgot it; I heard it and forgot it; I discerned it and forgot it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has no doubt about what one has seen, no doubt about what one has heard, no doubt about what one has discerned, and no doubt about what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I saw it and I am in doubt; I heard it and I am in doubt; I discerned it and I am in doubt; I cognized it and I am in doubt" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has no doubt about what one has heard, no doubt about what one has seen, no doubt about what one has discerned, and no doubt about what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view, and says, "I heard it and I am in doubt; I saw it and I am in doubt; I discerned it and I am in doubt; I cognized it and I am in doubt" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has no doubt about what one has discerned, no doubt about what one has seen, no doubt about what one has heard, and no doubt about what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters and says, "I discerned it and I am in doubt; I saw it, I heard it, I cognized it, and I am in doubt" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one has no doubt about what one has cognized, and no doubt about what one has seen, heard, or discerned, and from that basis one alters and says, "I cognized it and I am in doubt; I saw it, I heard it, I discerned it, and I am in doubt" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives as seen what one has not seen, and perceives as cognized what one has heard, discerned, and cognized, and from that basis one alters and says, "I saw it but did not hear it; I did not discern it; I did not cognize it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives as heard what one has not heard, and perceives as seen, discerned, and cognized what one has seen, discerned, and cognized, and from that basis says, "I heard it but did not see it; I did not discern it; I did not cognize it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives as discerned what one has not discerned, perceives as seen what one has seen, perceives as heard what one has heard, and perceives as cognized what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters and says, "I discerned it but did not see it; I did not hear it; I did not cognize it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

When one perceives as cognized what one has cognized, and from that basis one alters one's perception, patience, wish, reasoning, deliberation, and view regarding what one has seen, what one has heard, and what one has discerned, and says, "I cognized it, but I did not see it; I did not hear it; I did not discern it" — everything one says in that way becomes a transgression.

Here ends the first category of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, groups of twelve nuns spoke thus in mocking speech, using the following nicknames to jeer at and taunt one another — calling each other by such names as Tall One, Hunched One, Tiny One, Droopy-lips, Big-head, and Scaly-hands — deriding one another by drawing attention to women's physical faults in speech and conduct. Those who were thus mocked through such speech and conduct, being taunted by reference to women's bodily flaws, came to experience much suffering and mental distress. They neglected their scriptural study, their recitation, their memorization, their practice of yoga,

mental application, and contemplative practice. This also proved an obstacle to those few who possessed genuine virtue in this Dharma and Vinaya. And when those nuns of little purpose took occasion to revile others in this way, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One addressed the nuns, saying: Nuns, from the point beginning "In a former time, in a certain land, there came to a householder farmer a young man" down to "and he won his heart" — tell that story in full. Then from "he gave that young man his daughter" down to "but the farmer, heeding his wife's words, gave her no longer" — tell that in full. Then from "he beat those oxen of his" down through "the two oxen then questioned that young man, and he replied, saying: 'From among you, let two of the finest oxen go to the king's palace; we will bear witness'" — and continuing down to "there was one who was widely known as Broken-horn, Stumpy-tail, Old Bony — but he proved unfit" — tell that story in full. Then from "the king with his retinue" down to "though a field of black lentils and beans was in perfect bloom, for seven days he did not eat, and when growth appeared he still ate nothing at all" — tell all of that.

Nuns, if even creatures reborn in the animal realm, when spoken of by reference to human defects as they go about their lives, are caused to take offense, what need is there to speak of those who have become human? Beginning from there, this previous cause and background is to be told in full.

Then again the Blessed One addressed the nuns: Nuns, in a former time there was a charioteer who had two female mules called Delightful and Dapple, and from this beginning — down to "there were two foals" — tell that story. Then: from those two fighting, one had its horn broken, and the other, raising its head, called out with a broken stub of horn, "This horn — " and so on — tell that story down through "when driven by the charioteer" to "it was altogether exhausted" — tell that in full. Then from "Delightful and Dapple spoke" down to "a double share was obtained" — tell all of that.

And then it was said in verse:

When the road is exceedingly rough,
and when the load is exceedingly heavy,
it is then that she who carries the load
is the one who is led by the nose.
When kind words are spoken to her,
even a heavy burden she will shed.

Tell that down to that verse.

Now, if even creatures reborn in the animal realm are caused to take offense when spoken of by reference to human defects, what need is there to speak of those who have become human? Therefore, nuns, speaking by reference to a woman's physical faults is a transgression. Whatever utterance, word, term, expression, voice, definitive statement, verbal path, verbal sound, linguistic conveyance, verbal act, or vocal articulation is expressed with the intention of speaking of a woman's physical faults — all of these constitute a transgression.

And how does a transgression arise? Here is the summary verse:

By lineage, by craft, by occupation,
by sign, within the five classes of downfall —
along with the minor afflictions,
reviling is the last.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Noble one, you have gone forth from a brahmin family — what good is the conduct of a renunciant? What good is the brahmin's holy conduct?" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — tell that story down through "it becomes a transgression."

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Noble one, you have gone forth from a kṣatriya family — what good is the conduct of a renunciant or the brahmin's holy conduct for you?" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression. When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Noble one, you have gone forth from a merchant family — what good is the conduct of a renunciant or the brahmin's holy conduct for you?" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression. When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Noble one, you have gone forth from a commoner family — what good is the conduct of a renunciant or the holy conduct for you?" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression. This is what is called reviling by lineage.

As for reviling by craft, here is the summary verse:

Brahmin, kṣatriya,
merchant, commoner, and craftsmen —
rope-makers, weavers, painters,
carpenters, blacksmiths, iron-workers,
cobblers, potters, basket-weavers,
wood-workers, bamboo-workers, and servants.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from a brahmin family, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in the brahmin manner of conduct, in deportment, in cleanliness, in all-round behavior, in taking up ashes, in taking up a water-vessel with a crow's bill spout, in taking up clay, in reciting praises, in calling out 'Hail!', in saying 'May you be victorious!', in all forms of recitation and chanting, in attendance at the proper times, in the Vedic science of correct explanation, in the Vedic science of sacrifice, in the Vedic science of poetry, in the Vedic science of the protection of existence, in performing sacrifice, in causing others to perform sacrifice, in reading, in causing others to read, in giving and in receiving alone — for a brahmin woman who is diligent in these six activities is a holy woman" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from a kṣatriya family, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in dancing, singing, playing the lute, playing the single-stringed lute, in what is called the bābhiṣke, in what is called the māṇikaprebane, in applying perfume, in grooming the head, in draping robes, and in cleaning" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from a merchant family, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in letters, in calculation, in numbers, and in finger-reckoning" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from a commoner family, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in spinning, in weaving, in the use of the loom and the loom-beam," and so forth down through "in carding, in combing, and in carrying loads" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from the rope-makers, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in silk, in great bolts of cloth, in garments, in silk strips, and in Mon silk" —

— whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from the thread-drawers, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in cording, in patterned weaving, in back-supports, in large round-woven interior work, in hat-making, and in basket-work" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the dyers, it becomes a transgression down through "stitched cloth, hats, garments that cover the five limbs, and padded robes," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the blacksmiths, it becomes a transgression down through "alms bowls, small alms bowls, weapons, needles, and awls," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the iron-smiths, it becomes a transgression down through "stirrups, small knives, cups, and razors," and so on.
