Likewise, when one has gone forth from the shoemakers, it becomes a transgression down through "shoes, sandals with straps cut away, lip-soled footwear, thin-soled footwear, and saddles," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the potters, it becomes a transgression down through "clay vessels, round pots, water jars, bowls, alms bowls, and small alms bowls," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the barbers, it becomes a transgression down through "shaving the face, shaving the armpits, trimming the nails, and cutting the hair," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the carpenters, it becomes a transgression down through "thrones, small seats, bed-frames, sitting chairs, door-fittings, and door-panels," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the bamboo-workers, it becomes a transgression down through "parasols, fans, mats, corner-poles, hanging screens, and small carrying-baskets," and so on.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from the servant class, your own tradition is as follows: you must train in massaging, in bathing service, in polishing, in going to the great chambers and coming back, and in receiving orders" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression. This is called an artisan transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from the brahmin class, your own tradition is as follows: you must perform the work of libation-ladles, copper vessels, fire offerings, burnt offering-wood, grass, fire, and water-carrying" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

When a nun approaches another nun and says, "Since you have gone forth from the warrior-noble class (kṣatriya), your own tradition is as follows: you must perform the work of the lute, the single-stringed lute, and the court entertainment" — whether the nun who is addressed has actually gone bald or not — it becomes a transgression.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the petty-noble class, it becomes a transgression down through "script and calculation," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the commoner class, it becomes a transgression down through "carrying away, grinding, and bearing loads," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the weavers — "a fine loom-shuttle, warp-thread, a bobbin, a reed, a reed-knife, thread,"

"the rice-press and the work of the stretching-cord" — it becomes a transgression down through that.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the embroiderers, it becomes a transgression down through "a loom-frame, a fine shuttle, a spool-needle, a comb-reed," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the tailors, it becomes a transgression down through "a mesh-knife, a needle, a thimble-ring, a thumb-guard," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the blacksmiths, it becomes a transgression down through "a bellows-tube, a whetstone, a knife, a small anvil, a great hammer, bellows, and a drying-scraper," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the potters, it becomes a transgression down through "a wheel, a stick, a wheel-support, a laying-board, a net-peg, and a water vessel," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the barbers, it becomes a transgression down through "scissors, a razor, a thorn-lancet, a nail-cutter, a mirror," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the woodworkers, it becomes a transgression down through "a chisel, a plane, a gouge, an axe, a large adze, a small adze, and a scraper," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the reed-workers, it becomes a transgression down through "a reed, a cord, a trimming-knife, dye, and a thorn-pin," and so on.

Likewise, when one has gone forth from the class of female servants, it becomes a transgression down through "a rope, a water-pot, grain-oil, massage, and bathing" — and this is what is called the category of occupations.

If a nun goes before another nun and says to her "you are a hunchback," it becomes a transgression. Likewise, if she says "you are stooped," "you are short," "you have elephant-feet," "you are pot-bellied," "you are mute," "you are a hunchback," "you are blind in one eye," "you have a wandering eye," "you have club-feet" — in every such case it becomes a transgression. This is what is called the category of physical marks.

If a nun goes before another nun and says to her "you are a leper," it becomes a transgression. Likewise, if she says such things as "you have scabs," "you have fine pimples," "you are exhausted and wasted," "you are withered," "you have mange," "you have a skin disease," "you have a festering sore," "you have foot-rot," "you have scrofula," "you have something disgusting," "you have fever," "you are wasted with consumption," "you have goitre," "you have difficulty breathing," "you have a dry mouth," "you are forgetful," "you suffer from hunger-trembling," "you have a pallid complexion," "you have a tumor," "you have a blood disease," "you have a bile disease," "you rupture at night" — if she utters these or any such words, in every case it becomes a transgression. This is what is called the category of diseases.

If a nun goes before another nun and says to her "you will incur a root defeat, you are one who owes a remainder to the Saṅgha" — it becomes a transgression. If she says "you are one who requires individual confession, you are one who has committed a fault" — in every such case it becomes exactly as the basis warrants.

If a nun goes before another nun and says to her "you are wrathful," "you are resentful," "you are concealing," "you are burning with envy," "you are jealous," "you are miserly," "you are deceitful," "you are one of cunning" — in every such case it becomes a transgression. This is what is called the category of secondary afflictions (upakleśas).

If a nun goes before another nun and says, in the act of insulting her, "womb" or "one possessed of a donkey's member" — whether or not the nun who is insulted has actually become bald, in every case it becomes a transgression. However, if many people share the same name, there is no transgression.

In that case as well, one should not speak without a specific object in mind, but should name someone by name for the sake of the purpose. For those who are beginners and the like there is no transgression. The second defeat-producing offense is complete.

The occasion for the third arose in Śrāvastī. At that time twelve groups of nuns were everywhere practicing slander: having heard from the Chuvī nuns, they reported it to the Phavī nuns; having heard from the Phavī nuns, they reported it to the Chuvī nuns. Because of this, those nuns were split into two factions and came to feel mutual pain and distress of mind, and their scriptural recitation, reading aloud, chanting, yoga, mental application, and inner calm abiding of the mind were all rendered empty and vacant. While things stood thus, nuns of few concerns began to criticize this conduct, and the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then declared to the nuns: "Nuns, do not practice slander one toward another." And why? "Nuns, in the past, in a certain dense forest, there was a pregnant lioness. Now it was their nature that when her cubs had nursed or were hungry, thinking 'it would be wrong for them to go without,' she would form a hunting party of flesh-eating animals alone in order to make that animal her food" — and she killed a cow and pursued it. That cow also had a calf that was drinking from the very teats of that same lioness. This continued until both had grown up. Then, at the time when death was approaching — from "how the two became great" up to "there are many things that divide the dear" — a fox spoke what was true and accurately. From "a fox divided the two" up to "those two separated each other from life." Then a deity spoke in verse:

By keeping company with evil people
one never comes to see what is good.
Look how a fox divided
the lioness and cow, supreme companions.

Nuns, even animals reborn in the animal realm, when they practiced slander, came to kill one another — how much more need one say of women, who are supremely prone to anger? One should recount this former story in full.

Furthermore, there is another former story. Nuns, in the past a lioness had given birth to a cub not long before, and had gone to forage in her own territory; weak and emaciated with hunger, she encountered, not very far away, a tigress that was also being driven along. While she was wandering in that famished state, she met a tigress and the tigress began to suckle her — from "thus it began" up to "they dwelt together in one place." The lion's name was Mchebzangs and the tiger's name was Dpungbzangs — from thus up to "a fox then began to create discord between those two." At last the lion spoke in verse:

For Mchebzangs, endowed with magnificent form,
with skill and with strength,
for Dpungbzangs to attack her
is not right.

Dpungbzangs replied:

For Dpungbzangs, endowed with magnificent form,
with skill and with strength,
for Mchebzangs to attack her
is not right.

From "those two questioned each other" up to "the fox was killed." Then a deity spoke in verse:

Do not abandon a friend on account of another's words.
What others say should be examined carefully.
Those who wish to divide look for an opening —
therefore one should not trust a slanderer.
A fox that spreads slander, that parts friends,
that fox born a male, whose carcass this is —

by killing it one rejoices in happiness. Nuns, those creatures who have gone to rebirth in the animal realm likewise cause much suffering and mental distress to one another through the constant practice of slander — how much more so women who are particularly wrathful. Therefore, nuns, one should not engage in slander. If one does, it is a transgression.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and proceeding up to the establishing of the rule, declared: if a nun speaks slander, it is a transgression.

The section beginning "Whoever is of slanderous intent" and continuing through "speech" and "words" is the same as before. The section continuing through "it is a transgression" — meaning "it constitutes a transgression" — is likewise the same as before.

Now, how does a transgression come about? A nun goes to the presence of a woman who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says the following: "Noble one, a certain senior nun has said this to you: 'What is the point of your practicing the conduct of a contemplative and the conduct of the celibate life? You have gone forth from the brahmin caste.'" If she speaks thus and proclaims her lineage, it is an offense. If she proclaims her clan, it is likewise an offense. In the same way, from "has gone forth from the warrior caste" through "it is an offense." In the same way, from "has gone forth from the noble caste" through "it is a transgression." In the same way, from "with regard to one who has gone forth from the commoner caste" through "it is a transgression" — this is what is meant by "lineage."

A nun goes to the presence of a woman who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says: "Noble one, a certain senior nun has said this to you: 'What is the point of your practicing the conduct of a contemplative and the conduct of the celibate life? You have gone forth from the brahmin caste, so you should train according to your own traditional system.'" If she speaks thus and proclaims her craft, it is an offense. In the same way, from "has gone forth from the warrior caste" through "it is an offense." In the same way, from "has gone forth from the noble caste" through "it is a transgression." In the same way, from "has gone forth from the commoner caste" through "it is a transgression." The intermediate rule is to be stated in full, as explained above.

As for this, the craftspeople are: the weaver, the dyer, the smith, the cobbler, the potter, the ditch-digger, the woodworker, the basket-weaver, and the maidservant. This is what is meant by "craft."

A nun goes to the presence of a nun who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says: "Noble one, a certain senior nun has said this to you: 'What is the point of your practicing the conduct of a contemplative and the conduct of the celibate life? You have gone forth from the brahmin caste, so you should do the work of your own traditional occupation.'" If she speaks thus and proclaims her occupation, it is an offense. In the same way, from "with regard to one who has gone forth from the warrior caste" through "it is an offense." In the same way, from "with regard to one who has gone forth from the noble caste" through "it is a transgression." In the same way, from "with regard to one who has gone forth from the commoner caste" through "it is a transgression." The intermediate rule is to be stated in full, just as explained above.

Lineage, craft, occupation,
mark, and illness — these are the five.
Transgression and minor affliction,
and abuse as the last.

The third group of transgressions is complete.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī.

At that time, those among the twelve groups who had settled a dispute said repeatedly and with displeasure: "This dispute has not been purified by the recitation; it must be purified by the recitation again. This dispute has not been properly examined; it must be properly examined again. This dispute has not been well adjudicated; it must be well adjudicated again. This dispute has not been settled; it must be settled again." Then those nuns, amid fighting, fault-finding, and dispute — having fallen into fault-finding — abandoned the recitation of scripture, study, oral recitation, yoga, mental application, and the inner calm abiding of the mind. When nuns of little virtue were being censured, the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This being the case," proceeded to establish the training rule. "Furthermore, if any nun, knowing that a dispute has been settled in accordance with Dharma by a harmonious Saṅgha, then stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression."

"Furthermore, if any nun" refers to the twelve groups. "Knowing" means by her own awareness. "In accordance with Dharma" means in accordance with the Vinaya as it is and the Teacher's dispensation as it is. "Dispute" refers to the four disputes: dispute arising from quarreling, dispute arising from censure, dispute arising from transgressions, and dispute arising from matters of procedure. "Settled in accordance with Dharma" refers to settlement by motion and by the four-part act. "Stirs up discontent over that act" means doing so with the intent to do it again.

How does a transgression arise in this? If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from quarreling as one that has arisen from quarreling, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified by the recitation, then stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If a nun has doubt about what has been purified by the recitation, it is a transgression. If a nun, perceiving what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified by the recitation, stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified by the recitation, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from quarreling as one that has arisen from censure, and perceiving it as having been purified by the recitation, stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If she perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified by the recitation, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from quarreling as one that has arisen from a transgression, and perceiving it as having been purified by the recitation, stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If she perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified by the recitation, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from quarreling as one that has arisen from a matter of procedure, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If she perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from censure as one that has arisen from quarreling, and perceiving it as having been purified by the recitation, stirs up discontent over that act, it is a transgression. If she has doubt about what has been purified by the recitation, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from censure as one that has arisen from a transgression, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression.

If she perceives what has been purified by the recitation as having not been purified by the recitation, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from censure as one that has arisen from a matter of business, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If she perceives what has been purified by the recitation as having not been purified, it is a wrong act. If she perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having not been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a transgression as one that has arisen from a quarrel, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has been purified by the recitation as having not been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a transgression as one that has arisen from censure, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a transgression as one that has arisen from a matter of business, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a matter of business as one that has arisen from a quarrel, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a matter of business as one that has arisen from censure, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

If a nun, perceiving a dispute that has arisen from a matter of business as one that has arisen from a transgression, and perceiving what has been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a transgression. If she has doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun perceives what has not been purified by the recitation as having been purified, it is a wrong act. If she has doubt, it is a wrong act.

There are five kinds of nuns. What are the five? The nun who is a permanent resident, the nun who performs the act, the nun who submits a motion, the nun who states her view, and fifth, the nun who has come accidentally. Who is the nun who is a permanent resident? She is one who knows the beginning, the middle, and the end of that dispute. Who is the nun who performs the act? She is one who has performed an act in that matter. Who is the nun who submits a motion? She is one who has herself submitted a motion in that matter. Who is the nun who states her view? She is one who has declared her own view in that matter, saying: "This I approve; this I do not approve; this I desire; this I do not desire." Who is the nun who has come accidentally? She is one who does not know the beginning, the middle, or the end of that matter. Of these, the first three — the permanent resident, the one who performs the act, and the one who submits a motion — if any of them stirs up discontent over what has been duly settled as a dispute according to the Dharma, it is a transgression. If either of the last two stirs up discontent, it is a wrong act. If the fault has been cleared by the recitation, there is no transgression. This completes the fourth transgression.

The Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns, the sixteenth fascicle. The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. At that time Sthūlanandā went on her alms round to such and such households of householders, and to the homes of brahmins and

those householders, teaching the Dharma to them alone, she disclosed to the men all the secrets of women, and all the great secrets of women. Those men then told their wives. Because women are jealous, from that time on, when the elder nuns went on their alms rounds, those women would gossip about them to the neighborhood, saying: "Who would think of giving alms to you, who go about creating disturbance in the world?" Sthūlanandā replied: "Come now, sisters, what fault have we committed that you scold us?" They answered: "The noble Sthūlanandā has been slandering us before our husbands." Those nuns did not obtain alms. When they failed to obtain alms, they were abused, spat upon, and gossiped about. At that juncture this was reported to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then reflected: "Whatever slight fault has arisen, all of it has come about through teaching the Dharma. Therefore the Dharma shall not be taught in that manner." When those nuns again set out for alms, the brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, please teach us the Dharma." The nuns replied: "The Blessed One has forbidden it." The brahmins and householders said: "Then also let our almsgiving be forbidden." When those nuns once again suffered from lack of alms, this was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore you shall teach the Dharma in five sentences." When the Blessed One had declared that they were to teach the Dharma in five sentences, those nuns did not know how. The Blessed One declared: "Householder, form is impermanent. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent." From that time when they began to teach the Dharma in five sentences, those brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, why do you not teach more Dharma?" The nuns replied: "Householders, the Blessed One has ordained exactly that much." The householders said: "Noble ones, are you really going to teach the Dharma at a mere peppercorn's worth?" Then those brahmins and householders said: "Just as little Dharma has been taught to us, just so little alms shall we give." Since those nuns were again suffering from lack of alms, this was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You shall teach the Dharma in six sentences." When the Blessed One had declared this and those nuns did not know how, the Blessed One declared: "Householder, the eye is impermanent. Householder, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are impermanent." When those nuns then began to teach the Dharma in six sentences, the group of twelve said: "Let us make what was five into six." Whereupon the group of twelve said: "If through the sixth sentence one has not drunk beer and has not eaten raw onions, what transgression is there?" Similarly, when they deliberately set out to teach a sixth, they would carry it past to a seventh. At that juncture this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be taught" — up to the point where they suffered from lack of alms — and the Blessed One declared: "One may teach the Dharma together with a man" — up to that point.

When that group of twelve went on their alms rounds, at those householders' homes they said to the householders: "Householder, listen to the Dharma." The others replied: "Noble ones, first please call the women together and seat them."

That group of twelve said the following: "Is this hen not a female? Is this female monkey not a female? Is this ewe not a female? Are these female cats not female?" — and by means of this they would get the men to consent and then teach them the Dharma.

Then the great female householder Gautamī, having dressed in her lower robe in the morning and taken her alms bowl and outer robe, entered her alms round, and went into those householders' homes to collect alms. The householders then said to her: "Noble one, please teach the Dharma. Go, bring the women together, and come back." One of those householders also said: "Is this hen not a female?" Then the great female householder Gautamī said to that householder: "Who is it that teaches Dharma to you in such a way?" They replied: "It is the group of twelve." She thought: "So this situation too has arisen among us" — and as the monks of few wants began to express their disapproval, and so on up to the Blessed One having been informed of what had occurred, a rule of training was established:

"Whatever nun teaches the Dharma to a man in sentences of five or six, without a woman present, incurs a transgression — with the exception of a learned woman."

"Whatever nun" refers to the group of twelve. "Sentences of five" refers to the five aggregates beginning with form, and so forth. "Sentences of six" refers to the six sense faculties beginning with the eye, and so forth. "With the exception of a learned woman" means that a learned woman is set aside. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above.

As to how a transgression arises: whatever nun deliberately teaches a man the Dharma in five sentences and carries it on to a sixth thereby incurs a transgression. In the same way — from the statement about the section above on through to the section on houses — in all those cases a transgression is incurred. Likewise, if she deliberately teaches in six sentences and carries it on to a seventh, she incurs a transgression. If she answers a question, there is no transgression. For beginners and the like, there is also no transgression. This completes the fifth transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time the group of twelve were inciting women who had not received full ordination, as well as men, boys, girls, and the like, to perform recitations of the Dharma. Then in that summer residence, just as arithmetic teachers in a counting school would do, there arose loud noise and great clamor, and the monks of few wants expressed their disapproval. Then from the Blessed One — and so on — a rule of training was established:

"Whatever nun incites persons who have not received full ordination to perform Dharma recitations incurs a transgression."

"Whatever nun" refers to the group of twelve. As to the phrase "persons who have not received full ordination": those who have received full ordination are of two kinds — monks and nuns. All the rest are those who have not received full ordination. "Inciting" means reciting in unison with identical words, or reciting with additional words, or with identical syllables, or with additional syllables.

"Identical words" means that for as long as one says "abandon all that is evil," the other likewise says "abandon all that is evil" — this is called identical words. "Additional words" means that before one has finished saying "abandon all that is evil," the other says "practice virtue in full abundance" — this is called additional words. "Identical syllables" means that for as long as one says the syllable "A," the other likewise says "A" — this is called identical syllables.

"Additional syllables" means that before one has finished saying the syllable "A," the other also says "A."

"Entering upon a Dharma recitation" means something spoken by a buddha or said by a śrāvaka.

"It constitutes a transgression" — this is as stated above. As to how a transgression arises in this case: however little it may be, if a nun faces and leads a person who has not received full ordination in a Dharma recitation, this constitutes a transgression in every instance.

If, however, one is stammering, speaking quickly, reciting from memory, or responding to a question that has been asked, there is no transgression.

The sixth transgression is complete.

The origin story took place in Śrāvastī. Because they had not abandoned their afflictions, and out of ignorance, certain transgressions arose, and because these nuns were causing earlier transgressions to proliferate, they were engaging in reverential conduct. Each morning they would rise early and pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they would sweep, dust, and wipe down the premises.

Those twelve groups sat and remained in a small space, subdued in spirit. A householder then arrived, and when those twelve groups saw the older nuns doing all of this, they thought: "These elderly nuns know what is precious and accumulate what is precious. These twelve groups do not know what is precious and do not accumulate what is precious."

Thereupon, when the twelve groups heard this from the householder, they spoke thus: "You should accumulate such precious things." Those nuns replied: "Why do these ones exert themselves in offering and reverence to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and so forth?" Those nuns then said: "Such and such transgressions arose." When the twelve groups heard this, they reflected: "If even the elderly nuns have come to such a condition, what will become of the younger ones?" The twelve groups, having understood the matter, asked the novices: "What are your preceptresses and teachers doing?" The novices replied: "They are making merit." Then the twelve groups said: "You too should make merit of this kind." The novice nuns asked: "What is it?" The twelve groups then said to those novice nuns: "Do you not in your hearts think that your preceptresses and teachers are devoted to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and so forth, calling this a good Dharma? Nevertheless, such and such transgressions have occurred."

When those nuns had arisen from those transgressions and then instructed the novices saying, "You novices should be purified by the fully ordained nuns," the novices replied: "Why don't you yourselves do it?" The elder nuns said: "It is not appropriate for us to do so." The novice nuns then said: "Is it appropriate for some and not for others?" The fully ordained nuns replied: "Who told you that?" When the novices said that it was the twelve groups who had told them, it was at that point that nuns of few words criticized them for this, and the matter was reported in full to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "It must not be said." Thus he made a prohibition.

Thereafter a nun named Ṛjū, wishing to make known to a great assembly of people certain improper behavior that was being practiced in households in just such a manner, reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "A nun is to be appointed to oversee households individually." Since it was not known precisely what the Blessed One had declared, the Blessed One then declared: "A nun endowed with five qualities is to be appointed to oversee households individually. What are the five? She does not go out of desire; she does not go out of aversion; she does not go out of delusion; she does not go out of fear; and she knows which households have been supervised and which have not." The appointment is to be carried out as follows. After the bedding has been laid out, beginning with the words, "Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me" — the motion proceeds thus: "The nun Ṛjū, whatever improper conduct is being practiced in the households such that a great assembly of people may come to lack faith, has made that known in just that way. She who is called such-and-such is willing to oversee the households individually on behalf of the nun Ṛjū. If the time is right and the noble Saṅgha consents, may the noble Saṅgha approve it, and may she who is called such-and-such be appointed to oversee the households on behalf of the nun Ṛjū. She who is called such-and-such will, on behalf of the nun Ṛjū, go to those households. Sisters, take the measure of what this nun Ṛjū, who is like a seed scorched, like a seed ruined, has taught. Let the great mistress of beings take the measure of what she has taught. Let Gautamī the thin, and Utpalavarṇā, and Dharmadattā, and the noble Śīlavatī take the measure." That is how she will carry out the supervision. This is the motion. The formal act is to proceed as follows: beginning with "Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me," and going as far as "The noble Saṅgha has consented and approved, and since nothing is said, this is so understood."

Then the nun Ṛjū heard that a nun had been appointed to oversee the households on her behalf. Upon hearing this, the nun Ṛjū went to where the nun appointed to oversee the households was staying, and said to her these words: "Sister, has the Saṅgha appointed you to oversee the households on her behalf?" That nun replied: "It has." Ṛjū then said: "Sister, do you believe that she has caused much loss of faith in the households in this way?" That nun replied: "I do believe it." Ṛjū then said: "Just as you believe one person, so too, in a similar way, she circled the intestines of your belly around the summer dwelling with a bowel." The nun was frightened, and reported the matter in full to the assembly of nuns at that time. The nuns reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The nuns should carry out only the motion." Since it was not known precisely what the Blessed One meant by "carry out only the motion," the Blessed One then declared: "After the bedding has been laid out, beginning with the words 'Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me,' the motion is to be as follows: 'The nun Ṛjū, whatever conduct is being practiced in households such that a great assembly of people may come to lack faith, has made that known in just that way. If the time is right and the noble Saṅgha consents, may the noble Saṅgha approve it.' Having then performed only the motion, whatever appears fitting to the nun Ṛjū, and in whichever place she sees fit, she herself shall say the following to the sisters: 'Sisters, take the measure of what this wicked nun, who like a scorched seed lacks the power to give rise to growth, has taught. Nevertheless, let the elder nuns, the elder nuns, take the measure of this teaching.'" This is the motion.

Having performed only the motion, the nuns shall make it known in whatever place there is a great assembly of people. It shall be proclaimed in that very place where faith was undermined, but it shall not be proclaimed elsewhere, for it would be inappropriate to die of hunger alone. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence," proceeded to lay down the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun discloses a transgression that entails defeat to those who have not received full ordination, except with the Saṅgha's permission, she commits an offense."

"Whatever nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. "Discloses" means speaks of it. "Except with the Saṅgha's permission" means setting aside cases in which the Saṅgha has granted permission. "Commits an offense" is as stated above.

As for how the transgression arises: if a nun sees that another nun has incurred a transgression entailing defeat, and she discloses it to one who has no knowledge of it, perceiving her as having no knowledge, she commits an offense. Likewise, if she is in doubt about one who has no knowledge, she commits an offense. If a nun sees that another nun has incurred a transgression entailing defeat, but perceives one who does have knowledge of it as not knowing, that is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she is in doubt about one who does have knowledge, that is a wrongdoing. As with a picture drawn on cloth — in a case where one has made it known exactly as one knows it, and in this way the entire world comes to know it — there is no offense. This completes the seventh section on offenses.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Monkey Pond. At that time a devastating famine arose in the wilderness region, making food exceedingly difficult to find. Thereupon a great many nuns went wandering through various districts and came to be deprived of alms. They then deliberated among themselves, saying, "Why should we not proclaim our own good qualities?" They said to one another: "Whether truthfully or not?" And they replied: "Truthfully." Then, having mutually proclaimed one another's good qualities truthfully, and since the world delights in good qualities, the people ensured that the nuns were no longer deprived of alms. When the time came, after wandering through the districts, those nuns went to Vaiśālī. The nuns who had been resident there, both the settled and the long-established, saw them and said, "Welcome, you who are endowed with the Buddha, endowed with the Dharma, endowed with the Saṅgha! Welcome, welcome! Have you been faring well?" They replied, "We have been faring well." "Reverend sisters, I trust you have not been deprived of alms?" They replied, "We have not." "Elder sisters, elder sisters, given that you were deprived of alms, what means did you employ that you were not?" They replied, "By proclaiming one another's good qualities." "And was it fitting for you to proclaim one another's superhuman qualities?" When they said "We proclaimed them," nuns of few wants made this an occasion for rebuke and reported it to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence," proceeded to lay down the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun truthfully discloses a superhuman quality to one who has not received full ordination commits an offense."

"Whatever nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. As for "to one who has not received full ordination," those who have received full ordination are two in number; all others are those without full ordination. "Truthfully" means that it actually exists. "Commits an offense" is as stated above.

As for how the transgression arises, the intermediate summary verse runs:

Seeing, perception, in wilderness,
and in households, seats spread out,
claiming one's own distinguishing marks,
and presenting oneself.

A nun with perception and —

— with perception, acceptance, desire, intelligence, reflection, and without altering her view, she says these words: "I have seen a god," and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Likewise, if she says the same of yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas (dri za), kiṃnaras (mi'am ci), great serpents, kumbhāṇḍas, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, and corpse-demons, and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

Likewise, from the statement "I will go in order to see the gods" through "to bodies that are corpses" — if it is true, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

If a god or similar being truly approaches her, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

Likewise, if she truly hears the voice of a god or similar being, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

If she converses and communicates with gods and comes to a definite conclusion about it, and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

Likewise, if a god in turn converses and communicates with her and comes to a definite conclusion about it, and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Even in the case of a flesh-eater in a charnel ground, if it is true, she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

If a nun, with perception, acceptance, desire, intelligence, reflection, and without altering her view, says these words: "I have attained the perception of impermanence," and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Likewise, if she claims the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of no-self in what is suffering, the perception of disenchantment with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of the drawbacks, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of impurity, the perception of bloating, the perception of discoloration, the perception of putrefaction, the perception of crimson decomposition, the perception of being eaten away, the perception of dismemberment, the perception of scattering, the perception of bones, and the perception of individually discerning emptiness — and if she claims from the first, second, third, and fourth meditative concentrations through to the eight liberations as meditative absorptions she has attained, and if it is true, she commits a transgression.

From the phrase "a nun, without altering her perception" up to the words "she says as follows": if many nuns are dwelling in a wilderness and the non-human beings there do not harm them, and she says, "If she too dwells there, they will not harm her," and if it is true, she commits a transgression. Likewise, the same is to be stated with regard to seats spread out and arranged in households.

From the phrase "a nun, without altering her perception" up to "she says as follows": if a nun, clinging to her own distinguishing marks and relying on the sign of calm abiding, suppresses the afflictions through worldly mental application and does not engage in sensory desire, ill will, and so forth — and if she says from "that one exists" up to "she herself as well," she commits a transgression.

If a nun, with perception, acceptance, desire, intelligence, reflection, and without altering her view, says, "There exists a nun who has seen a god," and if she does not then say "and that is she herself," she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

Likewise, the same applies to yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, great serpents, kumbhāṇḍas, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, and —

— and if she does not say "and that is she herself" regarding decomposing corpses, she commits an offense of wrongdoing. Even regarding a flesh-eater dwelling in a charnel ground, if she does not say "and that is she herself," she commits an offense of wrongdoing. In like manner, following this same sequence, one should recite the words of this rule.

Furthermore, from "whatever nun, without altering her perception" up to "the following," the meaning is this: whatever nun, holding her own characteristic mark and relying on the sign of calm abiding, by means of worldly mental application suppresses the afflictions and does not engage in attachment to desire, ill will, and so forth — and who says "There exists such a one," yet does not then say "and that is she herself" — she commits an offense of wrongdoing.

Here ends the eighth section on transgressions.

The original occasion was at Śrāvastī. At the time when the nun Dharmadattā had received full ordination and had seen the noble truths, she was diligent in attending properly to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma within her own rains-retreat dwelling. She was endowed with faith, was good, and possessed a virtuous intention, so there was nothing at all that she would not offer or give entirely to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or her fellow nun friends. Through giving in that way and through making such complete offerings, even her worn-out and patched robes were stripped away until she was left threadbare.

Thereupon it occurred to the community of nuns: "This nun Dharmadattā is endowed with faith, is good, and possessed of a virtuous intention; she has set aside meditative concentration, the liberations, meditative absorption, and the meditative attainments, and is diligent in attending properly to the nuns in accordance with the Dharma; and there is nothing at all that she does not offer or give entirely." — up to the phrase: "her robes were stripped away until she was left threadbare." The nuns then thought: "We should make up a large bolt of cloth and give it to Dharmadattā." Later, at another time, they obtained a large bolt of cloth and gave it to her.

She thereupon reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared that it had been given upon request. Then, having proceeded in this way, making ready a seat — up to: "Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, I ask that you hear me. This nun Dharmadattā is endowed with faith, is good, and possessed of a virtuous intention. There is nothing at all that she has not offered or given entirely to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or her fellow nun friends. Through making such complete offerings, even her five worn-out and patched robes were stripped away until she was left threadbare. If the time has come and the noble Saṅgha sees fit, may the noble Saṅgha please grant its consent, and may the noble Saṅgha bestow upon Dharmadattā this large bolt of cloth. This is the request."

When they had made this request and given the large bolt of cloth to Dharmadattā, twelve members of the group known as the Group of Twelve spoke to the remaining nuns: "Sisters, how could it ever come about that the gains of the Saṅgha accrue to the community of nuns, when the gains of the Saṅgha are being redirected in favor of individuals?" Upon this being said, the nuns of little discernment were displeased.

Then the Blessed One, beginning from "this occurrence," proceeded to establish a training rule. Furthermore, whatever nun previously having spoken approvingly afterward says to the nuns: "Sisters, the nuns, having acted for the sake of individuals, redirected what was the Saṅgha's gain toward a personal recipient" — she commits a transgression.

The phrase "whatever nun" refers to a member of the Group of Twelve.

The phrase "having previously spoken approvingly" means having expressed agreement. The phrase "afterward" means at a different time. The phrase "says thus" means when she speaks. The phrase "of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of female śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. As for the phrase "gains," gains are of two kinds: material gains and gains in robes. In this particular matter, the intended meaning is gains in robes. As for the phrase "for the sake of a friend," one may ask: whose friend is which? The co-resident's friend is the preceptress, and the preceptress's friend is the co-resident. The attendant's friend is the instructor, and the instructor's friend is the attendant. A companion's friend is likewise a companion. One who is spoken of with affection has likewise one who is spoken of with affection. One who dwells in the same place has likewise one who dwells in the same place. The phrase "to redirect" means when she diverts. The phrase "to an individual" means when she gives to a particular person. The phrase "she commits a transgression" is as stated above.

One may ask how a transgression arises in this case. Whatever nun, having previously spoken approvingly and afterward saying to the nuns, "Sisters, a nun, for the sake of a friend, is redirecting toward an individual what had been dedicated as the Saṅgha's gain" — in every such instance she commits a transgression. However, if what she says is simply true, there is no transgression.

The ninth transgression is complete.

The occasion for this rule was at Śrāvastī. At that time, when the Group of Twelve nuns were reciting the prātimokṣa sūtra (the sūtra of individual liberation) fortnightly, they said: "Sisters, of what use are these minor and most minute training rules — those rules concerning which both the underlying basis is evident, and the individual, the village, and the field are also evident — being extracted from the fortnightly recitation of the prātimokṣa sūtra?" Upon their saying this and censuring the nuns who held the training rules in high regard, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning from "this occurrence," proceeded to establish a training rule. Furthermore, whatever nun, when reciting the prātimokṣa sūtra fortnightly, says, "Noble sisters, of what use are these minor and most minute training rules — those that cause nuns to feel remorse, anxiety, discomfort, harm, and distress — being extracted from the fortnightly recitation of the prātimokṣa sūtra?" — she commits a transgression.

The phrase "whatever nun" refers to one from Somā's group, a nun fond of quarreling. The phrase "fortnightly" means every fortnight. The phrase "individual liberation" refers to what is drawn from the eight root defeats, the twenty rules requiring a meeting of the Saṅgha and more, the one hundred and eighty transgressions, the eleven rules requiring individual confession, the many training rules, the seven rules for settling disputes, the seventeen Vinaya bases, the minor rules, the fragments, the occasion narratives, the Vinaya Mātā, the supplement to the Vinaya, the fifth Vinaya, the sixteenth Vinaya, and what arises from the questions of the inner circle. The word "sūtra" means what is well composed. The phrase "reciting" means teaching fully. The phrase "says thus" means when she speaks. The phrase "sisters, of what use are these" refers to whatever nuns feel remorse, anxiety, discomfort, harm, and distress on account of rules concerning which the individual is evident along with the village, the field, and the underlying basis. The phrase "she commits a transgression" is as stated above. One may ask how a transgression arises in this case.

When a nun, while reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra every half-month, says to the nuns, "Sisters, of what use are these minor and extremely subtle rules of training on account of which the nuns fall into remorse?" — up to that point she commits a transgression. If she says "mental distress" or "mental discomfort," she commits a transgression. Likewise, if when reciting a sūtra that contains rules of training she belittles it, she commits a transgression. Likewise, if when reciting verses that contain rules of training she belittles them, in all cases it becomes an offense. If there has been a deterioration, or if it occurs within the nuns' Saṅgha, there is no transgression. Here ends the summary verse of the first set of transgressions.

The summary verse:

Tilling a field and entering a tilled field, speaking disparagingly,
and at the ear, the dwelling-place,
and the hanging objects — these make five.
Then high thrones and beds, their arising,
grasses, a great house,
and a single place — these are set out likewise.
The underlying basis is at Śrāvastī.

At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon a monk who was formerly a wood-carver, established the rule of training concerning the destruction of seed-collections and the dwellings of beings, there were twelve groups of nuns who were themselves cutting green grass and planting it in fields. The nuns of good conduct who were present said to them: "Sisters, the Blessed One has established such a rule of training — do not cut green grass, and do not cause it to be cut." Thereupon those twelve groups said to those nuns: "This rule of training belongs to the monks — it does not belong to the nuns." At that, nuns of few wishes reproached them, criticized them, and rebuked them; those nuns told the monks; the monks informed the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, from the words "this occurrence" onward, proceeded through to establishing the rule of training: if one destroys or causes to be destroyed a seed-collection or the dwelling of a being, one commits a transgression.

As for the phrase "seed-collection," seeds are of five kinds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, cutting-seeds, and grain-seeds, which are the fifth. Among these, root-seeds are: galangal, white hellebore, mustard, ginger, white aconite, and likewise any other such roots — whatever roots themselves become seeds. These are called root-seeds. What are stem-seeds? The kañcana tree, the pīṭala, the aśvattha (sacred fig), the udumbara (cluster fig), the nyagrodha (banyan), and likewise any other such stems — whatever stems themselves become seeds. These are called stem-seeds. What are joint-seeds? Sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, marsh-grass, kāśa grass, and likewise any other such jointed plants — whatever joints themselves become seeds. These are called joint-seeds. What are cutting-seeds? Ārdraka (fresh ginger), śārjaka, śeyab, yellow-flowered grass (Atis or similar), bhūdṛṃhaka, and likewise any other things that, when cut, become seeds. These are called cutting-seeds. What are grain-seeds? Barley, wheat, śāli rice, various legumes such as black lentils and the like, and likewise whatever else becomes a seed of seed. These are called grain-seeds, and they are the fifth.

Regarding what is called the abode of life-bearing organisms: "life-bearing organisms" refers to snakes, venomous snakes, tree-borers, wood-boring beetles, worms, flat insects, and sesame-husk eaters. Whatever tree serves as the dwelling of such organisms is called the abode of life-bearing organisms.

"Cuts" means doing so oneself. "Causes another to cut" means through someone else. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above.

As to how a transgression is incurred: if a nun perceives a root-seed as a root-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a root-seed as a root-seed and perceives it as green, and is doubtful about it, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a root-seed as a root-seed and perceives what is dry as moist, she incurs a wrongdoing. If a nun perceives a root-seed as a root-seed and is doubtful about what is dry, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a stem-seed as a stem-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a stem-seed as a stem-seed and perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a joint-seed as a joint-seed and perceives it as green, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a joint-seed as a joint-seed and perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a cutting-seed as a cutting-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a cutting-seed as a cutting-seed and perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a grain-seed as a grain-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a grain-seed as a grain-seed and perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a root-seed as a stem-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a root-seed as a stem-seed and perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun perceives a root-seed as a joint-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a root-seed as a joint-seed and perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing.

The same applies when root-seeds are taken for grain-seeds. If a nun perceives a stem-seed as a joint-seed and perceives it as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression.

If a nun perceives a stem-seed as a joint-seed and perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for root-seeds. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for grain-seeds. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for propagating-seeds.

If a nun perceives a joint-seed as a propagating-seed and perceives what is green as green, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If a nun perceives a joint-seed as a propagating-seed and perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when joint-seeds are taken for stem-seeds.

If a nun perceives a root-seed as a root-seed and perceives what is green as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when root-seeds are taken for stem-seeds. The same applies when root-seeds are taken for joint-seeds. The same applies when root-seeds are taken for propagating-seeds. The same applies when root-seeds are taken for grain-seeds.

If a nun perceives a stem-seed as a stem-seed and perceives what is green as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for joint-seeds. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for propagating-seeds. The same applies when stem-seeds are taken for grain-seeds.

If a nun perceives a joint-seed as a joint-seed and perceives what is green as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when joint-seeds are taken for root-seeds. The same applies when joint-seeds are taken for stem-seeds. The same applies when joint-seeds are taken for propagating-seeds. The same applies when joint-seeds are taken for grain-seeds.

If a nun perceives a propagating-seed as a propagating-seed and perceives what is green as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when propagating-seeds are taken for root-seeds. The same applies when propagating-seeds are taken for stem-seeds. The same applies when propagating-seeds are taken for joint-seeds. The same applies when propagating-seeds are taken for grain-seeds.

If a nun perceives a grain-seed as a grain-seed and perceives what is green as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a transgression. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green, and then cuts it or causes another to cut it, she incurs a wrongdoing. Similarly, if she is doubtful, she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies when grain-seeds are taken for root-seeds. The same applies when grain-seeds are taken for stem-seeds.

The same applies when grain-seeds are taken for joint-seeds. The same applies when grain-seeds are taken for propagating-seeds.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the Seventeenth Fascicle, the Intermediate Section.

The five kinds of root-seeds,
and the cutting of trees and grass likewise,
creeping grass, continuous growth, fish-scale shoots,
water-weeds, and blooming flowers.

If a nun, with the intention that seeds might be destroyed, pours the five kinds of seeds into a mortar, then beats them with a pestle, intending that the seeds be damaged and completely ruined, and through such forceful pounding the seeds are indeed damaged, she incurs a transgression. If they are not damaged, she incurs a wrongdoing.

Similarly, if she uses fire, a digging implement, a dibble, a planting stick, a stove, a fire-pit, a large fire-pit, earth, porridge, boiling water, or a bag full of cooked grain — and so on, saying "May the seeds be damaged, may they be completely ruined," together with a great lake, a great stream, and so on down to a small amount of water, excrement, brine, a transforming agent, and mixing with earth — if through any of these the seeds are indeed damaged, she incurs a transgression. If they are not damaged, she incurs a wrongdoing. That concludes this section.

If a nun, with a single act, cuts one tree or causes it to be cut, she incurs one wrongdoing and one transgression. Similarly, if with two acts she cuts one tree, she incurs two wrongdoings and one transgression. Similarly, if with many acts she cuts one tree, she incurs many wrongdoings and one transgression.

If a nun, with a single act, cuts two trees, she incurs one wrongdoing and two transgressions. Similarly, if with two acts she cuts two trees, she incurs two wrongdoings and two transgressions. If a nun, with many acts, cuts two trees, she incurs many wrongdoings and two transgressions.

If a nun, with a single act, cuts many trees, she incurs one wrongdoing and many transgressions. Similarly, if with two acts she cuts many trees, she incurs two wrongdoings and many transgressions. Similarly, if with many acts she cuts many trees, she incurs many wrongdoings and many transgressions.

If a nun perceives green grass as green and treads upon it, she incurs a transgression. If she causes another to tread upon it, she incurs a transgression. If she is doubtful about what is green and treads upon it, she incurs a transgression. If she causes another to tread upon it, she incurs a transgression. If she perceives what is dry as green and treads upon it, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she causes another to tread upon it, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she is doubtful about what is dry and treads upon it, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she causes another to tread upon it, she incurs a wrongdoing.

If a nun, with a single act, treads upon a single clump of grass, she incurs one wrongdoing and one transgression. Similarly, two should also be stated. Similarly, the same applies to treading upon two clumps of grass with many acts. Just as it was stated for trees, so too it should be stated in detail for many clumps of grass.

If a nun pulls out strands of grass from a tree, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she strips off the outer bark, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she strips off a secondary layer, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she strips off the inner bark, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she extracts the heartwood, she incurs a transgression. If she pares a dried leaf, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she breaks off a fresh leaf, she incurs a transgression. If she opens a flower bud, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she breaks an unopened bud, she incurs a transgression. If the fruit is ripe and she damages it, she incurs a wrongdoing. If the fruit is unripe and she damages it, she incurs a transgression. If she walks upon green grass, saying "May the grass be damaged, may the grass be completely ruined," she incurs a transgression.

The same applies to puddles and the like — she incurs a transgression. If she says, "May it be damaged, may it be completely ruined," and then drags a branch or tree limb, she incurs a transgression. If her intention is to drag it or to walk, she incurs no transgression. If she walks saying, "May the water puddle be damaged," she incurs a wrongdoing. The same applies to puddles and trees and the like. If her intention is to walk, she incurs no transgression. For as long as a fish scale has not been removed from the water, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she removes it, she incurs a transgression. If she extracts the seed element of something without a root, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she extracts fish eggs, spawn, or flesh, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she smears grey mud onto a water-pot, she incurs a wrongdoing. If she eats food that has grey mud on it, she incurs a wrongdoing. If, however, it has been made suitable, she incurs no transgression. Here ends the first portion of the second category of transgressions.

The context-setting narrative is at Rājagṛha. On the occasion when a nun named Mzaʼ-mo (Priyā) publicly reviled the venerable Gyad-bu-nor in front of the group of the Six, likewise a nun named Priyā reviled the venerable Gyad-bu-nor in front of the group of the Twelve. The elder nuns then spoke thus: "Priyā, do not revile the head of the retinue." Even though she was told this, she continued to revile. At that point the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, let the nun Priyā be subjected to the procedure for having reviled face-to-face. The procedure for subjecting her is to be carried out as follows: after the seating has been arranged" — and so on up to — "Sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please listen to me. This nun Priyā has reviled the venerable Gyad-bu-nor face-to-face. If the noble Saṅgha sees fit, and if it consents, let the noble Saṅgha grant that the nun Priyā be subjected to the procedure for face-to-face reviling." This is the motion. The formal act is to be recited in the same way.

However, on the occasion when she acted by reviling indirectly, the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, let the nun Priyā be subjected to the procedure for indirect reviling" — and so on up to: "This is the motion. The formal act is also to be recited."

On the occasion when she later did both — reviling indirectly and reviling face-to-face — the Blessed One declared: "Let the nun Priyā be subjected to the procedure for both kinds of reviling" — and so on up to the end. The motion and the formal act are both to be recited.

When, even after being told in this way, she continued to revile, and when nuns of little account began to censure her, this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This incident occurred," and so forth, up to "established the training rule": if one reviles or reviles indirectly, one incurs a transgression. "Reviling" means any speech, words, or utterances made with the intention to revile, and so forth — as explained above. As to how a transgression is incurred: if a nun who has been subjected to the procedure reviles the twelve nuns appointed by the Saṅgha who have not yet released their undertaking, she incurs a transgression. If she reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If she both reviles and reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If a nun who has been subjected to the procedure reviles the twelve nuns not appointed by the Saṅgha who have not yet released their undertaking, she incurs a transgression. If she reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If she both reviles and reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If a nun who has been subjected to the procedure reviles the twelve nuns not appointed by the Saṅgha who have not yet released their undertaking, she incurs a transgression. If she reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If she both reviles and reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression.

If a nun who has been subjected to the procedure reviles the twelve nuns appointed by the Saṅgha who have already released their undertaking, she incurs a transgression. If she reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If she both reviles and reviles them indirectly, she incurs a transgression. If a nun who has not been subjected to the procedure reviles the twelve nuns appointed by the Saṅgha who have not yet released their undertaking, she incurs a misdeed. If she reviles them indirectly, she incurs a misdeed. If she both reviles and reviles them indirectly, she incurs a misdeed. The remaining three cases are likewise to be set forth in full. The second rule of the second class of transgressions is complete.

The origin story is set in Kauśāmbī. There a certain nun named Dundumā incurred a transgression, and those who were practicing the holy life alongside her, wishing her benefit, wishing her welfare, wishing her comfort, wishing to reach her, and wishing her accomplishment and ease, said to her: "Sister, you have incurred a transgression; come and deal with it." But she broke the instruction of those nuns. At that juncture the nuns reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, the nun Dundumā is to be subjected to the procedure for breaking instruction. The procedure for subjecting her is as follows: having prepared a seat," and so on up to: "Noble Saṅgha, sisters, please listen to me. This nun Dundumā has incurred a transgression, and those who were practicing the holy life alongside her, wishing her benefit, wishing her cure, wishing her comfort, wishing to reach her, and wishing her accomplishment and ease, said to her: 'Dundumā, you have incurred a transgression; come and deal with it.' But she broke their instruction. If the noble Saṅgha's time has come and it consents, let the noble Saṅgha grant this: let the nun Dundumā be subjected to the procedure for breaking instruction." This is the motion. The act is to be performed in exactly the same way.

She then thought: "If I keep silent or if I say nothing, I will not be subjected to the procedure." For there is also a verse to this effect:

A person endowed with wisdom
should guard the four kinds of speech.
Within a forest, the top burns first —
look to what is caught when sound is drawn out.

Having thought thus, she said nothing, and so she broke the instruction of the nuns. The Blessed One then declared: "She is to be subjected to the procedure for breaking instruction by both motion and act."

Now, while she was being given the instruction yet was in the act of breaking it, certain nuns of few concerns criticized her, and the nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having related the incident beginning with the words "this occurrence," established a rule of training up to the following: if one breaks an instruction, one incurs a transgression.

"Breaking an instruction" means any speech, words, or utterance with the intention of breaking an instruction — and all the rest is as explained above. "Incurs a transgression" is likewise as explained above.

How does one come to incur a transgression in this matter? A nun goes to another nun and says: "Did you see a certain nun — one who shaved her head not long ago, wearing a patched robe of reddish-yellow, with a bowl covered by a leaf-lid, her bowl filled with butter, or filled with honey, or filled with milk, walking along?" And the other, replying to this, says: "I saw a nun walking on foot," giving a different answer to what was asked, and if this is done with the intention of breaking the instruction, she incurs a transgression.

A nun goes to another nun and says: "Did you see a certain nun who shaved her head not long ago —"

— wearing a patched robe of reddish-yellow, carrying a staff bound with an iron ring and bearing a bowl with a leaf-lid —"

and then all the rest is stated, and if this is done with the intention of breaking the instruction, she incurs a transgression — up to and including that point.

A nun goes to another nun and says: "Did you see, along this road, a layman carrying a load of sugarcane, or a load of reeds, or a load of bamboo, or a load of arrows, or a pot of butter, or oil, or honey, or a pot with a sugar-froth lid, walking along?" And the other, replying to this, says: "I saw a layman coming on foot, but not by reason of those other things" — giving a different answer to what was asked, and if this is done with the intention of breaking the instruction, she incurs a transgression.

A nun goes to another nun and says: "Did you see, along this road, laywomen going about dressed all in blue, or all in yellow, or all in red, or all in white?" And the other, replying to this, says: "I saw a laywoman going on foot" — giving a different answer to what was asked, and if this is done with the intention of breaking the instruction, she incurs a transgression.

If someone who has fled from an executioner is being pursued by that executioner, and the executioner goes to a nun and says: "Noble one, did you see a fugitive who has committed murder passing along this road?" — then the nun should speak to that executioner in a way that is fitting with respect to the act of killing. If it is a time of heat, she should say: "Good sir, rest a little while, drink some cool water" — and she should fan him with a fan. If it is a time of cold, she should say: "Good sir, go and warm yourself somewhere, rest a little while in a warm place." If the executioner says: "Let the fugitive go, I release him" — she should look up at the sky and say: "I see the sky." Likewise she should look at her fingernails and say: "I see my fingernails." If the executioner has already seized the person and says: "I am not inquiring about these things of mine — I am inquiring about a murder" — then that nun, contemplating with supreme conviction that all formations are empty, should say: "I do not see even the slightest thing."

A nun goes to another nun and questions her in this way; if the nun breaks the instruction by remaining completely silent, she incurs a transgression. However, if medicine has been placed in her mouth due to illness, or if she has been struck by an affliction of the mouth, there is no transgression.

This completes the third part of the second section on transgressions.

The setting of the following rule is in Śrāvastī. At a time when the Blessed One, having observed that the monks were residing in great numbers at lodgings without a roof or shelter, established a rule of training — and at that time, those nuns who were by nature well-conducted followed and practiced that same rule of training — the group of twelve nuns, without refraining from the unroofed lodgings, went outside the boundary. Then the elder nuns said to that group of twelve the following: "Sisters, has the Blessed One not established a rule of training?" They replied: "The rule of training that was established is for monks, not for nuns." When they said this, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared:

"The rule of training that I established is common to both."

The Blessed One thus established that one must not take lodgings without a roof. Then, at a later time, the nuns traveled together as a group of companions to a certain mountain cave. They found lodgings in that temple, and when on the following day they were vacating those lodgings, they became separated from their companions, and while traveling alone they were assaulted by bandits. The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should entrust the lodgings and then depart." Not knowing that the Blessed One had said this, the Blessed One then declared: "If one is staying in a temple, one should entrust it to a monk. If one is staying in a summer dwelling, one should entrust it to a nun." When they found it burdensome to entrust those lodgings to them, the Blessed One declared: "The entrusting of lodgings is fivefold. What are the five? Saying 'This is the temple'; saying 'Look to the temple'; saying 'This is the lodging'; saying 'Look to the lodging'; and the fifth is the locking of the door. Having done so, one may then depart."

Then the Blessed One, after praising to the nuns the wish to train and reverence for the training, spoke thus: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly leaves without having gathered up, or having had gathered up, or without having entrusted to a nun who is present, a throne of the Saṅgha, or a seat, or a cushion filled with cotton, or a mat, or bedding inserted in a frame, or a square cushion that she herself has placed without a roof covering — save for extraordinary circumstances, she commits a transgression."

"Whatever nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. "Of the Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of female hearers of the Tathāgata. "Temple" refers to a place that can accommodate the four activities. "Throne" refers to one for reclining. "Seat" refers to one for sitting. "Cushion filled with cotton" refers to one stuffed with tree-cotton. "Mat" refers to a mat. "Bedding inserted in a frame" refers to bedding fitted into a frame. "Square cushion" refers to a four-cornered one. "Without a roof covering" means open to the sky. "She herself has placed" means placed by herself. "Having had placed" means by another. "Without having gathered up" means by herself. "Without having had gathered up" means by another. "Departs without" means departing while abandoning the perimeter of the lodging.

What constitutes the perimeter of a lodging? The Blessed One declared: "Forty-nine arm-spans. If it is turned over, it is a transgression. If it is not turned over, it is a misdeed."

The venerable Upāli (the close attendant) asked the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable one, in how many ways may a lodging become turned over?" The close attendant said: "There are two. What are the two?
