Being turned over by rain, and being turned over by wind. What is being turned over by rain? If rain-water causes two layers of the lodging to become wet, it becomes a transgression. If not wet, it is a misdeed. This is called being turned over by rain. If wind causes two layers to be overturned, it becomes a transgression. If not overturned, it is a misdeed."

"If, while on the road, one remembers, one should arouse the intention and also say aloud: 'I have placed such a lodging in such a place; may the celibate practitioners inspect it.' And that transgression should thereupon be remedied according to the Dharma. If while on the road one sees a nun, one should entrust it even verbally, wherever one has gone, one should entrust it even verbally; and that transgression too should be remedied according to the Dharma."

"Without having entrusted to a nun who is present" means whichever nun happens to be there at that time.

"Except in such a case" means whatever would become an obstacle to her very life. "It is a transgression" is as above.

Now, how does a transgression come about? If a nun, to whatever small extent, places uncovered bedding — thrones, small seats, and cushions belonging to the Saṅgha in the Saṅgha's monastery, as stated from "thrones" onward — or has it placed there, and then departs without having gathered it up or caused it to be gathered, in all such cases it incurs a transgression. If a nun places uncovered bedding belonging to the Saṅgha in the Saṅgha's monastery, or has it placed there, and then enters the monastery and sets it properly within, thinking, "I shall establish mindfulness that has not been established, settle the mind that has not been settled, or liberate the mind that has not been liberated," and during the first half of the first session it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression. If it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if during the first session itself it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if during the first half of the middle session it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if during the middle session itself it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if during the first half of the last session it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if during the last session itself it comes about that she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if it comes about at the time of the first gleam of dawn, and she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if it does not come to sleep, it is a misdeed. Likewise with the last gleam of dawn; likewise at the time of the elephants being led out; likewise when the elephants have been led out; likewise when it becomes the time of sleeping by night; likewise when it becomes light; likewise at the moment of sunrise; likewise at the tip of the sun's rays; likewise in the early warmth of morning; likewise in the great heat of day; likewise when it has passed midday — in all these cases, if she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if she does not sleep, it is a misdeed.

The phrase "in the Saṅgha's monastery" and what follows up to "thinking, 'I shall liberate the mind that has not been liberated'" refers to her having entered for the purpose of setting it properly within. The phrase "from the third blowing of the conch" through "when it comes about at the time of sunset" — if she sleeps, that incurs a transgression; if she does not sleep, it is a misdeed.

The condensed verse summarizing the root text of the teacher is as follows:

Listening to Dharma, and likewise
eating food, and likewise entering a dwelling,
entrusting to the monastery,
the sick, and bedding —
these five are not to be entrusted,
and two persons sitting on a single throne.

Then it came about that the wives of brahmins and householders came in great numbers to the nuns' rains-retreat quarters, and those nuns passed the time with them in idle conversation and gossip. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, it is not fitting to engage in idle conversation and gossip. Instead, you should teach the Dharma." They then rose, and respectfully seating themselves in front, began to teach the Dharma. The Blessed One declared: "Teach the Dharma while seated, and offer seats to those laywomen as well." When the Blessed One had declared that the Dharma should be taught while seated, those nuns then arranged themselves in a long row. The Blessed One declared: "The two kinds of seats should be set out in a crescent shape or arranged in a square."

When the Blessed One declared that the Dharma should be taught, the nuns did not know who among them should teach. The Blessed One declared: "Whoever possesses the power of eloquence, let her teach."

Then it came about that the senior nuns lacked the power to speak well, and the younger nuns began to teach. When this happened, the senior nuns would go from their own seats down to where the younger ones sat in order to listen, and in doing so they became forgetful of their place. The Blessed One then declared: "A lion's throne for the Dharma-teacher should be set out, and she is to teach from the lion's throne."

When the Blessed One had declared that teaching should be done from the lion's throne, some nuns began to expound very long sūtras at great length, and the laywomen grew weary. The Blessed One then declared: "It is permitted to teach by counting a third part, then from a fifth down to a third part, and stopping when the Teacher's full proclamation has been recited."

When the laywomen were serving food and became busy, the nuns began to collect the vessels and utensils. The Blessed One declared: "Receive them." When the nuns had collected the seats, the Blessed One declared: "Receive them." Then when those laywomen invited the nuns as guests to their homes, the Blessed One declared: "Go there as well, and partake of what is offered."

Thereupon the laywomen said to the nuns: "Noble ones, why have you come without bringing your water vessels?" The Blessed One declared: "In that case too, jars, round vessels, seats, and the lion's throne should be brought along."

Now, there was a nun who was ill, and she said: "Sisters, I am going to die." The other nuns said: "But what of it?" She then said: "No one comes to ask after me when I am sick." The Blessed One therefore declared: "You should go and look in on the sick. If one does not go to visit the sick, it constitutes an offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that the sick should be visited, the gong was struck from then on, and the entire Saṅgha would set out to visit the sick nun. But when the sick nun saw the entire Saṅgha arriving, she thought: "Why has the entire Saṅgha come? Surely I am not about to die!" and she became frightened. The Blessed One then declared: "In that case, one or two should go."

When they went and found there were no seats, the Blessed One declared: "For the purpose of asking after the sick, seats are to be placed." But when they were placed, some thought: "The Blessed One has said that one should not abandon one's lodging without a cover." And since those nuns were guarding and staying right in that place, they were neglecting their duties to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the preceptors, and the teachers. The Blessed One therefore declared: "Entrust your duties to someone and then go."

So the nuns entrusted their duties to the sick nun. The Blessed One then declared, from the words "The Blessed One declared" through to "one should not abandon one's lodging without a cover on account of five conditions": those five conditions being old age, shamelessness, the presence of obstacles, the absence of remorse, and not having received full ordination — on account of these one should not abandon the lodging. If one does abandon it, it constitutes an offense.

When two nuns are sharing a single throne, which of them should fold it away? The Blessed One declared: "The more junior one." If both are of equal seniority, then if one is willing, she should do it alone.

This completes the fourth section of the second category of offenses.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

At the time when the Blessed One laid down the training rule concerning grass-mat seats on account of a monk who had come from the south, those nuns who were living in accordance with the precepts heard of it and put it into practice. The monks of the Group of Twelve, however, spread out grass-mat seats, had them spread out by others, and then neither folded them away themselves nor had them folded away. Then those nuns said to the monks of the Group of Twelve: "Dear brothers, has not the Blessed One laid down a training rule? Why do you not fold up the grass-mat seats?" Those monks replied: "That training rule was laid down for monks, not for nuns." At that point they were censuring the nuns of few wishes; and when the nuns told this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One — from "this incident having occurred" up through the laying down of the training — established the rule as follows:

Whatever nun spreads out a grass-mat seat or a leaf-mat seat in the Saṅgha's assembly hall, or has one spread out by another, and then neither folds it away herself nor has it folded away, and goes away without entrusting it to a nun who is present — except for such circumstances as are specified — it is an offense. "Whatever nun" is as stated above.

With respect to "a grass-mat seat or leaf-mat seat": "grass" means grass itself; "leaf" means leaves themselves. "Spreads out" means by oneself. "Has spread out" means by another. "Does not fold away" means by oneself. "Does not have folded away" means by another. "Goes away" means having departed from its vicinity.

What is the vicinity of a mat seat? The Blessed One declared: Forty-nine arm-lengths. If it becomes entangled, it is an offense. If it does not become entangled, it is a misdeed.

Upāli asked: In how many ways can a mat seat become entangled? Upāli, there are two ways: entanglement by wind, and entanglement by insects. What is entanglement by wind? Wind causes the mat seat to reverse its two layers — that constitutes an offense. If it does not reverse, it is a misdeed. This is called entanglement by wind. What is entanglement by insects? If insects cause the mat seat's two layers to be gnawed through — if gnawed through, it is an offense. If not gnawed through, it is a misdeed.

"If one remembers while walking on the road, it is a misdeed" — from there onward, it should be elaborated in full in accordance with the lodging section. "It is an offense" is as stated above.

How does the offense come about? Whenever a nun has spread out or had spread out a grass-mat seat or leaf-mat seat in the Saṅgha's assembly hall, and has neither folded it away nor had it folded away — for as long as she has departed from its vicinity, in every instance it constitutes an offense.

Furthermore, whatever nun spreads out or has spread out a grass-mat seat or a leaf-mat seat in the Saṅgha's assembly hall without a cover, then, having entered the assembly hall, has properly settled within herself the intention: "I shall establish mindfulness that had not been established, I shall place in equipoise a mind that had not been placed in equipoise, I shall liberate a mind that had not been liberated" — if, when half of the first session has passed and entanglement occurs, it is an offense. If entanglement does not occur, it is a misdeed. From "at the setting of the sun" up through "if entanglement occurs, it is an offense; if it does not occur, it is a misdeed," it should be elaborated in full in accordance with the lodging section.

As for those who had spread out mat seats by the roadside and had lain down and were now filled with remorse, the Blessed One declared: "They should roll them up."

If one does not roll them up, it becomes an offense with remainder.

Thereafter, when dyeing work was being done in the rains retreat dwelling, the nuns had spread out grass, and those who desired training gathered that grass together and threw it outside the rains retreat dwelling, while others were left without any. From that point, the Blessed One declared: "If someone says 'please take a little less,' one should not throw it away." This completes the sixth rule in the second category of offenses.

The setting for the following is at Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Stout Delight went wandering about after the summer rains retreat had ended. The young nuns then said to their preceptresses and instructresses: "Venerable ones, we too wish to go wandering." Those teachers asked: "Together with whom?" The young nuns replied: "With the venerable Stout Delight." The teachers said: "Do not go." "Why not?" "Because Stout Delight habitually keeps bad company." Even so, the young nuns went wandering with her. As they went wandering, they came to a certain forest grove. There, those young nuns gathered grass, laid out mats, and lay down. Stout Delight leapt into their midst, harmed and molested them, and then, having chased them off their seats, said: "Whoever cannot bear it, let them leave." The nuns then returned the following morning. The nun Stout Delight said to them: "I shall provide medicines and the like for your ailments." From that point up through "those young nuns reported the matter in full to their preceptresses and instructresses" is to be understood as described.

When the Blessed One was being informed of those nuns of few words being censured, the Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" onward, proceeded to establish the training rule:

"Whatever nun, knowing that other nuns are already seated, then makes use of that very fact as a condition, presses in afterward, and sits down on a seat — it is an offense. Whatever nun" refers to Stout Delight. "Knowingly" means having been told by herself or by another. "Already seated" means seated beforehand. "Presses in afterward" means forces her way in at once. "On a seat" means on a mat. "Sits down" means sits or reclines one's body. "Whoever cannot bear it" means whoever cannot fit. "Let them leave" means let them rise and go. "That very fact as a condition" means no other pretext. How does a transgression arise in this matter? However much and to whatever extent a nun, while knowing that nuns are already seated, presses in afterward and sits down so that whoever cannot bear it must leave — in every such case it becomes an offense. If one is ill, there is no transgression. If one is frightened, there is no transgression. This completes the sixth rule in the second category of offenses.

The setting for the following is at Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Stout Delight went wandering about together with her retinue, and arrived at Śrāvastī. It being the custom in the Blessed One's teaching that monks and nuns distribute lodgings, the nuns were distributing the lodgings in the nuns' rains retreat dwelling. A portion fell to Stout Delight, specifically an upper-story room. Lacking all heedfulness, she remained in that lodging. While residing there, she caused the roof timbers to crack by striking them with the legs of a chair —

— and a chair leg fell through, striking the head of a nun who was below. The nuns of little desire then censured her, and the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and so forth, proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Whatever nun presses down heavily upon a chair or a small chair whose legs protrude upward through the uppermost room above the hall of a monastic residence, and sits or lies there, it is an offense." As for "whatever nun," that refers to Stout Delight. As for "of the Saṅgha," that refers to the community of the Tathāgata's female hearers. As for "hall," that refers to a place that can accommodate the four modes of conduct. As for "above the hall," that refers to the upper story. As for "uppermost room," that refers to the dwelling room. As for "whose legs protrude," that refers to the feet of the chair sticking through. As for "sits," that refers to being seated. As for "lies," that refers to reclining the body. How does the offense arise? Whenever a nun sits or lies in the uppermost room of the upper story of the hall upon a chair or small chair with legs protruding through, in all cases it is an offense. However, if the floor is covered with planks, or covered with flat boards, or there are cross-beams, or flat pieces of wood, or small flat pieces of wood covering it, or it is sealed shut, or a foot-rest is inserted beneath — in such cases there is no offense.

This completes the seventh rule in the second category of offenses.

The setting for the following is at Śrāvastī. At that time, Stout Delight watered grass with water containing living creatures, and also watered soil with such water. The nuns said to her, "Sister, do not water grass or soil with water containing living creatures." She replied, saying, "What account has been given to her, and what has been entrusted to her? If one goes to the great ocean of the east, what is the harm? If one goes to the great oceans of the south and west, what is the harm?" The nuns of little desire censured her, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and so forth, proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Whatever nun waters grass, or soil, or earth with water containing living creatures, or causes another to do so, it is an offense." As for "whatever nun," that refers to Stout Delight. As for "containing living creatures," living creatures are of two kinds: those that are visible to the naked eye, and those that are caught by a strainer. As for "with water," that refers to watering with water, soil, mud, clay, or slurry. As for "waters," that refers to doing so oneself. As for "causes another to do so," that refers to having others do it. As for "it is an offense," this is as stated above. How does the offense arise? If a nun, perceiving water that contains living creatures as containing living creatures, waters with it herself or causes another to do so, it is an offense. Likewise, if she is in doubt, it is an offense. If a nun, perceiving water that does not contain living creatures as containing living creatures, waters with it herself or causes another to do so, it is a misdeed. Likewise, if she is in doubt, it is a misdeed. If a nun draws water and as many living creatures as die thereby correspond to that many offenses, and as many as do not die correspond to that many misdeeds. Likewise for diverting a stream, breaking irrigation channels for a field, and blocking and releasing water — in all such cases the basis determines the outcome accordingly.

This completes the eighth rule in the second category of offenses.

The Vinaya Exposition for Nuns, the eighteenth fascicle.

The setting for the following is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One declared:

Merit is the thing to be done;
when merit is not done, suffering follows.
In this world and in the next,
one who has made merit shall rejoice —

at that time,

those nuns set about constructing a residence hall, a fence, a gate-house, and the like. Then Bhomgamo thought to herself: "I have fallen away from such a great accumulation of merit," and in the early morning she tied on her waist-cloth, took up her bowl and robe, went to the home of a merchant's wife, and upon arriving spoke thus: "May the noble lady be free from illness." The householder's wife then spread a seat for Bhomgamo. Bhomgamo sat down on the seat that had been spread. Having sat, she extensively expounded the sūtra on the seven meritorious acts arising from material things, and in so doing inspired faith in the householder's wife and led her to make an opening. At that point she said to her: "Please give some materials for a temple." This is the account up to that point.

Then Bhomgamo began to build on that summer-retreat building — it had no window-openings and no water-outlet — something resembling a cuboid enclosure. At that, the other nuns said to Bhomgamo: "Did the Blessed One not declare that, for the gate-house and the permanent residence of the Blessed One, one should plaster it to a height of two or three courses? He declared that to the monks, not to the nuns." But she replied: "Even so, daughters of good family, sisters — since I am one who holds the three scriptural collections, I know how a temple ought to be built." And when she belittled the nuns of lesser learning, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, taking the incident that had occurred as his basis, proceeded through all the steps up to the laying down of the training rule, which reads: When a nun undertakes to build a large temple, she should survey the site with the intention that it will have a gate-house, permanent quarters, and a lit chamber, and then plaster it to a height of two or three courses. If she builds higher than that, it is an offense.

Now, as for the word "large": "large" is of two kinds — large with respect to what is to be given, and large with respect to measure. In this context it is understood to mean large with respect to what is to be given. "Temple" means a place that can accommodate the four deportments. "Undertakes to build" means either oneself or another. "Gate-house and permanent quarters" means with the perception of a gate-house, with the perception of a window-opening, and with the perception of a water-outlet. "Two or three courses of plastering" — "plastering" means daubing with clay; "courses" means layers; "should plaster it" means it is to be raised up. "Higher than that" means above that. "It is an offense" — as before. How does the transgression arise? However much a nun plasters beyond two or three courses, she incurs an offense for every bit of it. If the temple is built from stone, or if the owner of the temple is far away, there is no offense.

This completes the ninth rule in the second category of offenses.

The setting for the following is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the venerable Śāriputra was residing at a dwelling of the naked ascetics, and a householder's wife together with her retinue was firmly established in the fruit of stream-entry — relying on that very circumstance, twelve thousand two hundred sentient beings were caused to see the truth — taking the venerable Śāriputra as the basis and having carefully considered the matter, the Blessed One laid down a training rule. At that time, the twelve groups were sleeping together in a single dwelling and eating in a single dwelling, and they were also eating the last portion of the almsfood left over. At this the nuns who were of proper conduct spoke thus: "Sisters, did the Blessed One not lay down a training rule concerning the dwelling?"

They replied, saying: "The rule that the Blessed One laid down is for the monks, not for the nuns." And so it was that the nuns who were few in their concerns, who were given to reproach, reported the matter to the monks, and the monks in turn reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." proceeded through to the laying down of a training rule. "Whatever nun, being in good health, dwells in a single dwelling, shall eat almsfood one single time; if she eats more than that, it is a transgression." The phrase "sleeps in a single dwelling" means: sleeping in the dwelling of non-Buddhists. The phrase "whatever nun" refers to the twelve groups. The phrase "being in good health" means: excepting one who is ill. The phrase "shall eat almsfood one single time" means: it is not the last leftover portion. The phrase "more than that" means: going beyond that. The phrase "it is a transgression" is as stated above.

As to how a transgression arises in this regard: if a nun stays for however short a time in a single dwelling, or eats in a single dwelling while remaining there, she has committed an offense in that stay; and if she eats, it is a transgression. If she stays in a single dwelling but eats elsewhere, she has committed an offense in that stay; but in eating elsewhere there is no transgression. If she eats in a single dwelling but then goes to stay elsewhere, in eating in the single dwelling she incurs a transgression; but in going to stay elsewhere there is no transgression. If she goes to stay elsewhere and also eats elsewhere, there is no transgression in either regard.

Here ends the tenth rule under the second category of transgressions.

The summary verse:

Carrying a load, gathering, untimely acts,
placing without permission — these make the fifth.
Living creatures therein included,
and two who feign to be bedmates.
Naked, beyond two nights among soldiers,
and watching at an assembly.

The occasion for this rule was in Śrāvastī. At that time a certain householder took a wife of equal social standing, and he would play with that wife, enjoy her company, and sport with her in pleasure, until the time came when she gave birth to a daughter born with a birthmark on the right side. The narrative then continues through to where the story unfolds of a plan being laid to kill the wife, and a date being set. Many people accordingly made preparations on her account. Then, a certain friend and close companion, entering that house to seek alms, was addressed by the two of them in this manner: "Lady of fair marks, give us alms." She replied, saying: "I am in some distress." The two of them said: "What troubles you?" She replied: "The task has fallen to me of delivering the infant born with the right-side birthmark." The two of them said: "If our sister gives birth today, will we not receive alms today itself?" And with joyful, pleased, and greatly delighted minds, they gave a great quantity of alms. The two of them took the alms and departed.

After them, Stout Delight and Crown Delight arrived, and those two likewise took alms and departed. Then it came to pass that Joyful Victory and Near-Joyful-Victory saw Stout Delight and Crown Delight with their hands and begging bowls full. Seeing this, they said: "Sister, the infant born with the right-side birthmark is being delivered today — go now!" Then Joyful Victory and Near-Joyful-Victory also went to that very place to seek alms. In the same way, Companion of Victory and Guardian of Victory went; and likewise Virtuous One and Supremely Virtuous One; and likewise Beautiful Delight and Queen-Possessing One also went. All the preparations that had been made for the delivery of the infant with the right-side birthmark — every last thing — was given to the twelve groups.

While they were beginning to make further preparations, a certain close friend of the one known as the Wife-Killer said: "The girl with the right-side birthmark has many faults. The tooth-stick of the lac tree and..."

"Sleeping while showing the left side at night, drinking the midnight curd, and taking the right-side portion — and peace, too, departs from its place," he said. In this way he created an obstacle to that right-side woman's receiving her portion.

The brahmins and householders began to revile the conduct and the holy conduct of the renunciants, the sons of the Śākyas, saying: "Their renunciant conduct and their brahminical conduct are burned away, for they create obstacles to the girl's receiving her portion." On that occasion the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, beginning with the words "This has arisen..." and continuing up to the promulgation of the training rule, established the rule. Furthermore, when the nuns go out in great numbers to the houses, if faithful brahmins and householders happen to serve them abundantly with curds or oils, and if a nun so wishes, she may accept up to one bowl-load or up to three measures. If she takes more than that, it constitutes a transgression. Having received one bowl-load or three measures, she should go outside the house to the pleasure garden and share it with the nuns assembled there. That is the procedure in this matter.

Now, "nuns" refers to the twelve groups. "When going to the houses" means to the houses of brahmins and householders. "If faithful brahmins and householders" — "faithful" means those possessing faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha, up to and including those who have attained a fruit. "Abundantly" means sufficiently. "Serve" means when inviting as guests. "Curds" means powdered. "Oils" means carried. "If she wishes" means if she desires it. "One bowl-load or three" — "one bowl-load" means a large one. "Three" means small, medium, and large. Among these, "large" is the size of a small vessel of the Magadha country. "Small" is half of that small vessel. "Medium" is the middle one. Having received them, she should go outside the house to the pleasure garden and share with the nuns who are assembled in the monastery. "Those assembled there" means the nuns who are present there. "More than that" means exceeding that amount. "Constitutes a transgression" — as above. How does a transgression arise in this case? If a nun takes three large bowl-loads, it constitutes a transgression. If she takes two large and one medium, it constitutes a transgression. If she takes two medium and one large, it constitutes a transgression. However much a nun takes in excess of a single small vessel-measure, in every such case it constitutes a transgression. This completes the first part of the third group of transgressions.

The context is Rājagṛha. At the time when the Blessed One had prohibited the eating of communal food in connection with Devadatta, the nuns then argued that it was held in common by both. Thereafter, some became ill and were unable to sustain themselves on a single meal, and so the Blessed One declared: "When one is ill, it is the appropriate time — eat." Similarly, regarding those who had set out on a journey and had grown hungry and were unable to engage in virtuous activity, from that point up to "they should eat" — the same applies. Similarly, those performing labor may also eat. Similarly, those who have boarded a boat may also eat. Similarly, when many are assembled and provisions have arrived, the Blessed One declared: "They may eat." Similarly, a male wanderer (parivrājaka) or a female wanderer who has faith in the teaching of the Buddha — from what is received from them one may also eat. "Nuns, what is received from a wanderer who has faith in the teaching of the Buddha is rare," the Blessed One said.

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of the nuns' aspiration for the training, their respect for the training, and their devotion to the training as a resource, spoke these words:

Eating together outside of the permitted times constitutes a transgression. The permitted times are these: the time of illness, the time of work, the time of travel, when one has boarded a boat, when a great assembly has gathered, and the time of the ascetic's meal. "Eating together" means eating in a mixed gathering. "Outside of the permitted times" means, for example, when one has fallen ill and a single meal is not sufficient to sustain life. "The time of travel" means what is given by a donor to one who has set out on a journey. "Having boarded a boat" means alms given by a donor at the time of boarding a boat. "A great assembly has gathered" means food when many are assembled. "The time of the ascetic's meal" — here, one who has gone forth from the traditions outside this teaching is called an ascetic. "That is the permitted time" means that it is a circumstance in accordance with the rule.

How does a transgression arise in this? If a nun, perceiving herself to be within a boundary when she is within a boundary, eats together, it is a transgression. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun, perceiving herself to be within a boundary when she is outside a boundary, eats together, it is a wrongdoing. If she eats with doubt, it is a wrongdoing.

If a nunnery has both a main hall and cloisters, and some nuns eat in the main hall while others eat in the cloisters, those who are eating in the main hall must ask those eating in the cloisters, "Have you been satisfied with food?" If they eat without asking, it is a transgression for those in the main hall, and a wrongdoing for those in the cloisters. The same is to be said of dwelling quarters, gatehouse, and so forth. If they have been satisfied with food, even the smallest bit — a sip of plain water or a taste of salt — being offered is sufficient, and there is no transgression.

This completes the second rule under the third category of transgressions.

The occasion for the following rule was in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the group of seventeen, established the training rule concerning eating at an improper time, the group of twelve would eat at the proper time and also eat at improper times. The nuns then said, "Has the Blessed One not established a training rule concerning eating at improper times?" Those of the group of twelve replied, "He established it for the monks but not for the nuns." The nuns of few desires then reproached them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This has occurred," proceeded through to the formal establishment of the training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun eats or swallows solid or liquid food at an improper time commits a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to those of the group of twelve. As for "at an improper time," there are two kinds of improper time: the improper time after midday has passed, and the improper time before dawn has arisen. "Solid food" and "liquid food" refer to the five kinds of solid food and the five kinds of liquid food. "Eats or swallows" means if it is swallowed down the throat. "Transgression" is as explained above.

How does a transgression arise? If a nun, perceiving it to be an improper time when it is indeed an improper time, eats or swallows, it is a transgression. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, it is a transgression. If a nun, perceiving it to be an improper time when it is in fact a proper time, eats or swallows, it is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, it is a wrongdoing.

This completes the third rule under the third category of transgressions.

The occasion for the following rule was in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the case of Kālakāraka the dark one, established the training rule concerning stored food, the group of twelve, after going for alms, would separately set aside dry cooked rice, and separately set aside wet cooked rice, and whatever remained after use they would dry out and store away.

Whenever wind arose or famine struck, the group would wash those stores with water, cook them over fire, and consume them. The nuns who were concerned about minor matters criticized this, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurred," established the training rule up to the point of the formal promulgation. The rule is: whatever nun, having stored food, prepares it or eats it, commits a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to the group of twelve. As for "having stored food," there are two kinds of storing: receiving the earlier food and storing the later food, or receiving the later food and storing it beyond the proper time. As for "prepares it or eats it," this is as before. As for "commits a transgression," and what precedes, this is as in the sections above.

How does a transgression come about in this case? If a nun perceives stored food as stored and eats it, she commits a transgression. If she perceives unstored food as stored and eats it, it is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, it is a wrongdoing. If she stores robes, she commits a transgression. If she stores a bowl, she commits a transgression. If she stores a water vessel, she commits a transgression. If she stores a door-bolt, it is a wrongdoing. If she stores a bent key, it is a wrongdoing. If she stores a door-bolt pin, it is a wrongdoing.

This completes the fourth rule under the third category of transgressions.

The occasion for the following rule was in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the case of the great black monk of the charnel-ground ascetics, established the training rule concerning the acceptance of offerings, the nuns did not understand what the proper acceptance was and what was to be accepted. The nuns asked the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "There are five kinds of acceptance. What are the five? Accepting body-to-body contact, accepting with the body what is connected to the body, accepting what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, accepting with the body what is connected to the body through contact, and the fifth is the act of setting down the prescribed ceremony." As for what is referred to as an object of reproach — that they also lie down with their mothers — he declared: "Draw a circle on the ground there and receive the offering." When fruits were found and the nuns did not know how to accept them, the Blessed One declared: "There are five kinds of acceptance: a bowl, a throne, a low seat, a strainer, and a begging bowl — one accepts by touching these with the hand." When those items that have been accepted are stirred and if they are caught without falling they are themselves the accepted items. Even if they roll far away, one may accept them again. These items are to be rendered fit for use. Since the nuns did not know how many ways there were to render them fit for use, the Blessed One declared: "There are five ways of rendering fit for use. What are the five? Rendering fit by fire, rendering fit by a blade, rendering fit by a bird's beak, rendering fit by a fingernail, and the fifth is rendering fit by wilting. And further, there are five ways of rendering fit: by removing, by splitting, by cutting, by piercing, and the fifth is by eliminating the capacity for germination. For blue ones, this same method renders them fit." Later, when brahmins and householders wished to obtain some of those items, the Blessed One declared, since they had not been given: "Give them." When nuns, having set out on a journey, were staying in a remote forest place, they accepted offerings from forest lions, monkeys, bears, and the like. It was evident that they held them, and it was equally evident that they accepted from those animals. While they were on the road and encountered a shortage of water and tooth-cleaning sticks, the nuns reported the matter to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "With the exception of water and tooth-cleaning sticks, it is permitted." Then the Blessed One, having offered praise to the nuns for their desire for training, their reverence for training, and their use of requisites in training, spoke these words: "Furthermore, whatever nun, with the exception of water and tooth-cleaning sticks, eats swallowable food by mouth without it having been given, that is a transgression. As for 'whatever nun,' these are those who belong to this Dharma. As for 'without having been given,' that means it has not been given by anyone. As for 'by mouth,' that means eating it with the mouth. As for 'the rule,' it is as before. As for 'with the exception of water and tooth-cleaning sticks,' water and tooth-cleaning sticks are set aside. As for 'that is a transgression,' it is as stated above. Now, how does a transgression come about? If a nun, perceiving as given what has not been given by a nun, touches or eats it, that is a transgression. Likewise, if she eats it with doubt, that is a transgression. If a nun, perceiving as not given what has in fact been given by a nun, eats or touches it, that is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she eats it with doubt, that is a wrongdoing."

Intermediate summary verse:

The five instances of giving, and the fruit,
And likewise the five that are permissible,
And those from lions, monkeys, and bears —
These the Tathāgata permitted;
This is the intermediate summary.

The fifth item of the third category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion is Kauśāmbī. At that time there was water containing living creatures, and the nuns who were there said: "Sisters, do not use water containing living creatures." Those women replied: "Who are you to count and assign us our conduct? If we go to the great eastern ocean, what harm is there? If we go to the great southern, western, or northern ocean, what harm is there?" Nuns of few desires censured them, and the matter was then reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly uses water containing living creatures, that is a transgression. As for 'whatever nun,' these are those who are fully ordained and nearly fully ordained. As for 'water containing living creatures,' living creatures are of two kinds: those that are visible to the eye and those that are caught by a water-strainer. As for 'uses,' use is of two kinds: internal and external. External use consists of bathing, splashing, washing things such as clothes, soaking them, causing them to be dried, and having others perform such actions — this is called external use. Tooth-cleaning sticks are also included, as is drinking. As for 'that is a transgression,' it is as stated above. Now, how does a transgression come about? If a nun, perceiving water containing living creatures as water containing living creatures, uses it in either way, that is a transgression. Likewise, if she uses it with doubt, that is a transgression. If a nun, perceiving water without living creatures as water containing living creatures, and uses it in either way, that is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she uses it with doubt, that is a wrongdoing. In the same way, branches, leaves, fruits, and the like containing living creatures should also be explained."

The sixth item of the third category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion is Śrāvastī. At that time there was a young boy who sold perfume and incense, not yet taken in marriage and not yet of adult age, who was staying in a shop one evening to keep watch. In the middle of the night the shop door was closed and he departed for home, whereupon he was seen entering the domain of a woman called Bhadrā.

Seeing this, she thought, "Oh my, that boy is going home with desire in his mind," and so, having followed after him some distance, she entered the home of that young perfume merchant and sat down on a seat and remained there. Then the young merchant returned home and began to look for his wife, whereupon she said to him, "Noble lady, your mistress is sitting here." When the boy then saw Bhadrā, he began to disparage the nuns who had gone forth in the way of the Śākyan daughters, and to speak ill of their conduct as renunciants and their conduct of celibacy, saying: "How is it that even when one's own wife is alone with one in a private place, one cannot find the opportunity?" He mocked them in this way, and the matter of monks and nuns of few wants being reviled was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule. The rule is:

Whatever nun, knowingly, in a home where someone goes to seek out a man to lie with, pushes her way in by force and sits down on a seat, that is a transgression.

The words "whatever nun" refer to Bhadrā. The words "goes to seek out a man to lie with" mean that a woman goes to seek out a man for sexual intercourse. "In a home" means in the home of householders. "Pushes her way in" means abruptly, without leave. "Sits down" means if she sits down. "That is a transgression" is as explained above.

As for how the transgression arises: in whatever home where someone goes to seek out a man to lie with, if the nun pushes her way in by force and sits down on a seat, in all such cases it becomes a transgression.

The seventh item of the third category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion is Śrāvastī. Then Bhadrā, in the morning, having donned her lower robe and taken her outer Dharma robe and alms bowl, entered her round of almsgiving, and Bhadrā then saw that same young perfume merchant going home. Bhadrā thought to herself: "The Blessed One has established a training rule concerning sitting; as for me, I shall stand in the doorway." Thereupon the young perfume merchant saw her and began to revile her. From "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," the rule was established:

Whatever nun, knowingly, in a home where someone goes to seek out a man to lie with, in a private place with access to shelter, stands there, that is a transgression.

The words "whatever nun" refer to Bhadrā. The words "knowingly" mean either she herself knows it, or it was said to her by another. The remaining terms are as before.

As for how the transgression arises: in whatever home where someone goes to seek out a man to lie with, in a private place with access to shelter, if the nun stands there, in all such cases it becomes a transgression. If, however, she is frightened or there is an obstruction, there is no transgression.

The eighth item of the third category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion is Rājagṛha. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence on Ānanda, established the training rule concerning male and female naked wanderers, the twelve sects were preparing and serving food with their own hands and giving it to male and female naked wanderers and to male and female parivrājakas, and the matter of monks and nuns of few wants being reviled was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule:

Whatever nun, with her own hands, prepares and serves food and gives it to a male or female naked wanderer, or to a male or female wandering ascetic, that is a transgression.

The words "whatever nun" refer to the twelve sects. "Male naked wanderer" means one without clothing. "Female naked wanderer" likewise means one without clothing. Similarly, "wandering ascetic" (parivrājaka) refers to the Sāṃkhyas.

"Female wandering ascetic" is likewise the same. "With her own hands" means hand to hand. From "food and provisions" through "that is a transgression" is as before. How does a transgression come about? If a nun gives even so little as a morsel of food or provisions with her own hands to anyone from a naked wanderer through to a female wandering ascetic, that is a transgression. However, if the recipient is her father or mother, there is no transgression. If someone who has come to visit wishes to be given something, there is no transgression. If someone begs, one should say to them: "Place your begging bowl on the ground," and then speak accordingly. If they have placed it down, one may give. But if they have not placed it down, one should not give. This completes the ninth rule of the third section on transgressions.

The narrative setting is in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the group of six, established the training rule concerning watching troops on parade, the twelve sects then went to watch the troops on parade. This was the occasion when nuns of few wants expressed disapproval, and it was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule: Whatever nun goes to watch troops on parade, that is a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to the twelve sects. "Parade" means taking delight in troops. As for "troops," there are four kinds of troops: troops of one division, troops of two divisions, troops of three divisions, and troops of four divisions. Troops of one division are those of elephants. Troops of two divisions are those of elephants and cavalry. Troops of three divisions are those of elephants, cavalry, and chariots. Troops of four divisions are those of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. "To watch" means for the purpose of watching. "If she goes" means if she proceeds. "That is a transgression" is as before. How does a transgression come about? If a nun goes even a little way for the purpose of watching troops on parade, in every case it is a transgression. If she is sitting in the corridor of a rain-retreat dwelling, there is no transgression. This completes the tenth rule of the third section on transgressions.

The narrative setting is in Śrāvastī. At the time when brigands returned to King Prasenajit, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and others gave food, and the lay practitioners too were sent there by the king and went. After that, having requested permission from the Saṅgha, the group of six went. At that time the training rule on a limit of two days was established for the group of six. Then at another time, the twelve sects remained at the military encampment until the end of two days. When they came back, those nuns said the following: "Dear friends, dear companions, the plump companions have returned — welcome, welcome! From where did you come here, and where did you stay?" Those nuns replied: "We went to teach the Dharma to the troops on parade and stayed right there." Then those other nuns said: "Did the Blessed One not establish the training rule on the limit of two days?" They replied: "That rule was established for the monks, not for the nuns." This was the occasion when nuns of few wants expressed disapproval, and it was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule: If it happens that a nun must look upon troops on parade due to such a necessity, she may stay within that encampment for up to two days. If she remains beyond that, it is a transgression.

"A nun" refers to one of the twelve assemblies. "If such a necessity arises" means except when such a necessity has arisen. "Eager" means taking delight in the troops. The phrase "troops" through "four kinds" has already been explained. "At the limit of two days" means within two days. "Beyond that" means past that limit. "It is a transgression" is as explained above. How does the transgression come about? Whatever amount, even a little, beyond two days a nun remains within the camp, in every case it is a transgression.

The twelfth rule under the third category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion for the following took place in Śrāvastī. The passage beginning with "when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent word" and ending with "she remained within that camp up to the limit of two days" is as given. At that time, the Blessed One established for those nuns the training rule concerning the display of battle, the finest of victory banners. Then those twelve assemblies again went to see the display of battle, the finest of victory banners, and entered the finest of the troops. The nuns said: "Sisters, has a training rule not been established?" They replied: "That rule was established for the monks, not for the nuns." The nuns of few wants expressed disapproval, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule: Furthermore, if a nun who has remained two days within that camp then individually experiences seeing the display of battle, the finest of victory banners, the finest of the troops, and a marshaled formation of troops, it is a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to the twelve assemblies. Regarding "seeing a marshaled formation," "marshaled" refers to formations resembling the shape of a chariot, or the shape of a garuḍa's wings, or the face of a grain ear, or the shape of a lotus, or the shape of a half-moon. "Formation" refers to the finest of troops. "It is a transgression" is as before. How does the transgression come about? Whatever amount, even a little, a nun goes into the midst of a display of battle, in every case it is a transgression.

The twelfth rule of the third category of transgressions is complete.

The summary verse:

Striking and the palm of the hand,
washing, concealing, soliciting for alms,
accepting an ill abode, hiding at a house and at a fire,
desire and two nights,
interruption and vigilant awareness,
and two female novices who alter their complexion.

The occasion for the following took place in Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Sthūlanandā quarreled and brawled with other nuns, and pulled at their weak points. Since women are by nature prone to anger, being naturally enraged she became wrathful and violent, and struck the nuns with the back of a staff and with a whip. Nuns of few wants expressed disapproval, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule: Furthermore, if any nun, having become wrathful and violent and having given rise to displeasure, strikes a nun, it is a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Wrathful" means enveloped throughout by anger. "Having become violent" means being intensely seized by it. "Having given rise to displeasure" means having generated mental discomfort. "A nun" means one who belongs to this Dharma.

"Strikes" means striking with five fingers. "It is a transgression" is as above. As to how transgression arises in this case: if any nun, having become wrathful, strikes nuns with one finger, it is one transgression. Likewise, if she strikes with five fingers, it is five transgressions. Similarly, if she strikes with the hand, the fist, the head, the shoulder, the body, the elbow, the knee, the forearm, the foot, or the big toe, in every case it is a transgression. Likewise, if she strikes with a stick, a clod of earth, a pestle, and so forth, in every case it is a transgression. If she strikes with a broom, as many bristles of the broom as make contact, that many transgressions accrue; and as many as do not make contact, that many are lesser offenses. Likewise, if she strikes with a handful of peas, as many grains of the peas as make contact with the body, that many transgressions accrue; and as many as do not make contact, that many are lesser offenses. For a first offender and the like, there is no transgression. The first of the fourth transgressions is complete.

The narrative setting is in Śrāvastī. The preceding occurrence is the same, with this difference: the passage runs from "those very nuns" through "having raised the palm to strike." The occasion of the nuns of few wants expressing disapproval was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, from "this occurrence" through "the establishment of the training rule," established the rule: Furthermore, if any nun, having become wrathful and violent and having given rise to displeasure, raises her palm to strike a nun — even with the palm alone — it is a transgression. "Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. The rest is as before. The difference is this: "raises to strike" means having raised but not yet struck. "It is a transgression" is as above. As to how transgression arises: the sequence of transgressions is to be stated in precisely the same way. In every case, however slightly a nun raises her hand against a nun, it is a transgression. The second of the fourth transgressions is complete.

The Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns, the nineteenth fascicle.

The narrative setting is in Śrāvastī. Then the venerable Cāraka, early in the morning, having put on his robe, took up his bowl and outer robe and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having made his alms round in Śrāvastī, he went to the house where the woman Vedī lived. Vedī saw Cāraka coming from a great distance and said these words: "Cāraka has gone forth — what am I to do now?" Then Cāraka said to Vedī: "The bodhisattva renounced sixty thousand queens and went forth — you would not even be fit to wash their feet, so what does it matter?" She replied: "I too shall go forth." Then Cāraka said to Vedī: "Set your household affairs properly in order." She did so, and went with Cāraka to Rājagṛha, where they spent the rains retreat. Then Vedī went to the Jeta Grove, and a friend said to her: "What have you come for?" Vedī replied: "To go forth." The friend said: "Cāraka — a razor from the land of Kośala being blunt — has gone to the land of Magadha for a razor." Then Vedī thought to herself: "I have not yet gone forth, and yet I cannot remain as a householder either," and she sat there, her mind troubled inwardly. Then another wandering nun, having entrusted Vedī, the great mistress of people, to —

up to the words "she went forth." Then, after Cāraka had passed the three months of the rains retreat, he went to Śrāvastī, and when the nun Vedī heard that Cāraka had come, she went to where he was staying and knocked on the door of the dwelling. Cāraka then asked, "Who is there?" She said, "It is I, Vedī." Cāraka then said, "Come inside, householder's wife." She replied, "I am not a householder's wife — I am one who has gone forth." He then taunted her, saying, "And who gave you permission to go forth like that?" Vedī then asked Cāraka's forgiveness. After that, Cāraka began to teach her the Dharma, and as he did so, attachment arose in him. The Blessed One has said, "A man who knows the nature of a wise woman knows her attachment," and so Vedī, being startled, gave the sign of making water and fled. Cāraka was skilled in discerning the sound of footsteps, and realizing what had happened, he ran out after her, and as he brushed against her thigh, her lower robe became wet. Vedī, knowing that she was free of attachment, went to where Cāraka was and said to him, "Noble Cāraka, had I not acted as I did, both of us would certainly have fallen from the mode of life of ascetics." When she had said this, Cāraka said to Vedī, "Excellent! Excellent, Vedī! The Blessed One's saying, 'Whoever guards oneself guards others, and whoever guards others guards oneself,' has come home here — for in this way, Vedī, you have guarded yourself and have also guarded me." Vedī then said to Cāraka, "You have come weary from the road; give me your robes and I shall wash them." He gave them, and when Vedī saw them, remorse arose in her, and she lamented repeatedly: "I have acted with the inconstancy of a woman; I have acted with the inconstancy of an ascetic and a brahmin. As for these limbs of my body — is there anything here that Cāraka has not seen, not touched, that no one knows of?" And with those many lamentations, she poured filth into an open wound. Then Vedī washed Cāraka's robes and went to where the nuns were spending the rains retreat.

Then at another time Vedī became pregnant. The nuns, upon seeing the changed condition of Vedī's body — from this point, the nuns spoke to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen here arose from nuns washing, changing the color of, and ironing the robes of monks who are not their relatives." The Blessed One then, beginning with "Given this occurrence," proceeded to establish a rule of training: "Whatever nun washes, changes the color of, or irons the old robes of a monk who is not her relative, that is an offense entailing confession."

Now, "whatever nun" refers to Vedī. "Who is not a relative" means that a relative is one connected through up to seven generations of either the maternal or paternal line. "A monk" refers to one of this teaching. "Old" refers to robes that have been used during any of the three seasons — winter, spring, or summer. "Robes" means any of the seven types. "Washes" means even rinsing once with water. "Changes the color of" means even dipping once into dye. "Irons" means even pressing once with the palm of the hand. "An offense entailing confession" is as explained above.

Now, how does a transgression come about in this case? If a nun, with the perception that a monk is not a relative, washes the robes of a monk who is not a relative, that is an offense entailing confession. If she changes their color, that is an offense entailing confession. If she irons them, that is an offense entailing confession. Likewise, if she washes the robes of one who is not a relative while holding a doubtful mind about whether he is a relative, that is an offense entailing confession. If she changes their color, that is an offense entailing confession. If she irons them, that is an offense entailing confession. If a nun, with the perception that a monk who is actually a relative is not a relative, washes his robes, that is a wrong action. If she changes their color, that is a wrong action. If she irons them, that is a wrong action. Likewise, if she washes the robes of a relative while holding a doubtful mind, that is a wrong action. If she changes their color, that is a wrong action. If she irons them, that is a wrong action. With regard to a father, son, or brother, there is no transgression. This completes the third rule of the fourth set of offenses entailing confession.

The narrative context is in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the group of seventeen, had established for the monks a rule of training concerning concealment, the group of twelve then, with a mind bent on mischief, concealed the robes of the monks and disparaged nuns of few desires. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, proceeding from "this occurrence" through to the establishing of the rule of training, declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun conceals — or causes to be concealed — the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the strainer, the salt bag, or the girdle of a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, that is an offense entailing confession."

Now, "whatever nun" refers to the group of twelve. "A monk" means one of this teaching. "A nun" means a female śrāvaka of the Blessed One. "A female probationer" means one who is training in the training of a female probationer. "A male novice" means a young man who has gone forth. "A female novice" means a young woman who has gone forth. "Alms bowl" means one that has been consecrated and the like — even a single vessel qualifies. "Dharma robe" means any of the seven types. "Strainer" means a strainer proper. "Salt bag" means a vessel for salt. "Girdle" means a strap, a belt, or anything else of the kind — in short, whatever requisite for a nun's livelihood is concealed, except in such-and-such circumstances, is an offense entailing confession. "Except in such-and-such circumstances" means setting something aside for safekeeping in those circumstances. "An offense entailing confession" is as explained above.

Now, how does a transgression come about in this case? However much of a renunciant's requisites for livelihood a nun conceals — except in the prescribed circumstances — it is in every case an offense entailing confession. This completes the fourth rule of the fourth set of offenses entailing confession.

The narrative context is in Śrāvastī. At that time the Blessed One, on account of the group of six, had prohibited the solicitation of food, while permitting it for the sick. Thereafter those twelve nuns went to the homes of brahmins and householders, solicited food, and partook of it — both when they were ill and when they were not ill. When the nuns reported them, those twelve said: "That rule of training was established for monks, not for nuns." They then disparaged the nuns of few desires, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, proceeding from "this occurrence" through to the establishing of the rule of training, declared: "The foods permitted to be solicited by sick nuns are as follows: milk, yogurt, fresh butter, fish, meat, and dried meat. Furthermore, whatever nun who is not ill solicits such food for her own sake from the homes of others and accepts it or eats it, that is an offense entailing confession."

The phrase "those that are" refers to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha. The phrase "for the sick" refers to those who are afflicted by illness. The phrase "nuns" refers to the female hearers of the Tathāgata. The word "delicious" means that which is savory. The phrase "solid foods and soft foods" refers to the five solid foods and the five soft foods. The word "milk" means milk itself. The word "yogurt" means yogurt itself. The word "fresh butter" means butter. The word "meat" means meat itself. The word "fish" means fish itself. The phrase "dried meat" means meat that has been dried. The phrase "soliciting in this way from households" means doing so oneself. The phrase "causing another to solicit" means through someone else. The phrase "eats or accepts" means if one swallows so much as a single mouthful in secret. The phrase "it is an offense entailing confession" is as explained above. If one who is not ill solicits and eats while not being ill, there is a wrongdoing in the soliciting and an offense entailing confession in the eating. If one who is not ill solicits and eats while being ill, there is a wrongdoing in the soliciting but no offense entailing confession in the eating. Likewise, if one who is ill solicits and eats while not being ill, there is no offense in the soliciting but an offense entailing confession in the eating. Likewise, if one who is ill solicits and eats while being ill, there is no offense in either.

The fifth rule in the fourth chapter on offenses entailing confession is complete.

The occasion for the following took place in Śrāvastī. The members of the group of twelve committed offenses of bad conduct, concealing these from one another; they quarreled and exposed each other's faults, reproaching one another on the basis of those same matters. When the nuns of few desires heard of this, they expressed disapproval, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, proceeding from "this occurrence" through to the establishing of the rule of training, declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly conceals an offense of bad conduct committed by a nun is guilty of an offense entailing confession."

The phrase "whatever nun" refers to those in the group of twelve. The phrase "bad conduct" refers to two kinds of bad conduct: that which has come about through defeat and is raised by the entire community, and that which is raised by the majority of the Saṅgha. The phrase "conceals" means not speaking of it to others. The phrase "offense entailing confession" is as explained above. As for how an offense arises in such a case: if a nun sees that a fellow nun has committed an offense of bad conduct that brings about defeat, and she forms the intention to hide it for her, that constitutes an offense entailing confession. The same applies likewise for offenses raised by the majority of the Saṅgha, and likewise for offenses entailing confession, offenses entailing confession individually, and wrongdoings — in those cases it is a wrongdoing. If it has already become known, there is no offense.

The sixth rule in the fourth chapter on offenses entailing confession is complete.

The occasion for the following took place in Śrāvastī. The members of the group of twelve thought: "If these needle-workers with their black alms bowls were to expose us publicly before the nuns, what harm could we do to them?" Then Joyful-of-Fat and Joyful-of-Crown spoke up: "It would be better to expose them in return." And so those nuns summoned the elder nuns to crossroads, to triple-junctions, and to four-way junctions as guests, and then caused them to wander about without food for as long as there was nothing left to eat. The members of the group of twelve, meanwhile, went in pairs and in secret to the homes of brahmins and householders and ate their alms food. Later, when those elder nuns came to the rains-retreat residence and huddled together, their fellow residents and those nearby said to them: "Noble ones, could it be that today's meal is someone else's — is your food also provided by others?" They replied: "Who would have eaten today, one wonders?"

Those women said, "The gruel is cold and has gone stiff," and with those words they then spoke to the nuns, and this occasion of nuns with few desires reproaching them was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with the words "On this occasion," proceeded to lay down a training rule. Furthermore, whichever nun sought a pretext, thinking, "By all means I shall find a fault with this nun," and used that very intention as her grounds for saying to a nun, "Noble one, please enter these homes, and there let them give you as much food and provisions as you desire" — and then, without actually causing them to give her food and provisions as desired, subsequently said to her, "It is not pleasant for you and me to speak or sit together. Still, it is pleasant for me to speak or sit alone. If you say 'Go away,' that constitutes a transgression." Now, "whichever nun" refers to the group of twelve. "To a nun" refers to a female disciple of the Blessed One. "Saying such words" means speaking them. "Please enter these homes" means the homes of brahmins and householders. "Let them give you as much food and provisions as you desire" refers to the five kinds of provisions and the five kinds of food. "As much as you desire" means as much as one wishes to eat. "Without causing them to give her such, then saying 'It is not pleasant for you and me'" means it is not enjoyable to be together with you. "Speaking" refers to words. "Sitting" refers to being seated. "Seeking a pretext" means looking for an opportunity to rake up faults. "That constitutes a transgression" is as stated above. How does a transgression occur in this case? If a nun, to whatever small degree she is seeking a pretext, speaks such words, in every instance that constitutes a transgression. However, if there is a medical prescription, or if on that basis the Saṅgha's food supply has been cut off and the matter is an improper one, there is no transgression.

This completes the seventh rule in the fourth group of transgressions.

The narrative setting is Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence on the group of six, laid down the training rule that fire must not be lit in an unroofed place — with the exception of sick persons, for whom it had been permitted — the group of twelve then lit fire with their own hands, caused others to light it, and this occasion of nuns with few desires reproaching them was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with the words "On this occasion," proceeded to lay down a training rule. Furthermore, whichever nun, not being ill, desiring comfort for her own sake, lights a fire or causes one to be lit — that constitutes a transgression. Now, "whichever nun" refers to the group of twelve. "Not being ill" means except for one who is sick. "For her own sake" means for her own benefit. "Lights a fire" means kindling a fire herself. "By herself" means by her own hand. "Causes it to be lit" means through another person. "That constitutes a transgression" is as stated above. How does a transgression occur in this case? If a nun fills a fire vessel with fire not yet purified or received, doing so for the sake of fragrance, she must consecrate it with a time-formula. If she has not consecrated it, that constitutes a transgression. Likewise, if she applies fragrances for the sake of fragrance, she must consecrate it with the words "This is for the sake of the Buddha," as a time-formula. If she has not consecrated it, that constitutes a transgression. Similarly, if it is for the sake of an abbess and she has not consecrated it, that constitutes a transgression.

Likewise, if fire is lit for the sake of the Saṅgha, one must consecrate it with a time-formula for as long as what is needed has not yet been completed. If one does consecrate it, that is well. If one does not consecrate it, that constitutes a transgression. Even if one adds wood piece by piece, one must consecrate it each time with a time-formula. If one does consecrate it, that is well. If one does not consecrate it, that constitutes a transgression. Likewise, if one scatters or heaps up the fire, that too constitutes a transgression. If a nun takes a fire-wheel and spins the fire-wheel around, that constitutes a transgression — and so on up to: if one traces a design on a paint vessel, that constitutes a transgression. If a nun takes a paint vessel, and if she consecrates it with a time-formula, that is well. If she does not do so, that is an offense. If for the sake of a sick person she boils food in an uncovered vessel, and likewise if she performs work involving pigments or work involving alms bowls — in all such cases, if she has consecrated them with a time-formula, there is no transgression.

The eighth section of the fourth group of transgressions is complete.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the seventeen factions, established a rule of training that was fitting for a legitimate act of the Saṅgha, the nuns who were naturally well-behaved performed Saṅgha business in accordance with a legitimate act of the Saṅgha. At that time, those of the twelve factions, after having already consented to a legitimate act of the Saṅgha, withheld their consent, or gave it improperly, or said, "It was done by those in opposition, not by those in agreement," and when nuns of little sense began to scold them, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning from "This has occurred," established the rule of training up to and including its promulgation:

Furthermore, whatever nun, having already given her consent to a legitimate act of the Saṅgha, subsequently acts in a manner of retraction and says, "Give back my consent — I do not give it to you" — that constitutes a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to those of the twelve factions. "A legitimate act of the Saṅgha" refers to single-recitation acts, two-recitation acts, and four-recitation acts that are legitimate acts of the Saṅgha. "Having already given her consent" means having given her assent. "Subsequently" means at another time. "Acts in a manner of retraction" means that she has said, "I have not given my consent." "Constitutes a transgression" is as stated above.

How does a transgression occur in this case? Whenever a nun, to whatever small degree, having given her consent to a legitimate act of the Saṅgha, acts in a manner of retraction, in every such case a transgression occurs. However, if the retraction was truthful or if the consent was given improperly, there is no transgression.

The ninth section of the fourth group of transgressions is complete.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon a certain senior novice who had entered the order, established the rule: "One must not dwell together with an unordained person in all circumstances; if one does so, that constitutes a transgression" — and furthermore, concerning one who bore the name of a novice, permission was granted for up to two nights — then the twelve factions said: "Wherever it is two nights, let it become three; wherever it is three, let it become four." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the nuns, the Blessed One declared: "One must not dwell together. If one does so, that constitutes a transgression."

Then, when those nuns allowed novice nuns who had gone outside the boundary of the Saṅgha's meeting hall to go unaccompanied and unguarded, this matter was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not send them outside the boundary of the Saṅgha's meeting hall."

Nevertheless, the root case is to be abandoned. When that was done, there was a nun who gave food to a sick novice nun and then did not receive it back with her own hand, thinking she had not given it with her own hand, and then did not touch her again — and on that matter, from the phrase beginning thus, the Blessed One declared: "One must anoint her with one's own hand; one need not feel regret about that."

Then, when those sick novice nuns, being wearied from sitting at the time of the meal, and the nuns not providing seats for them — on that matter the Blessed One declared: "One must seat them together on a single seat and rely on that; one need not feel regret about that."

Then again, when evening came and those novice nuns were sent away and departed, and the sick one was thirsty through the night — on that matter the Blessed One declared: "One must stay with her through the night itself; one need not feel regret about that."

Likewise, when a nun herself is ill, novice nuns or attendants are to remain there, and may remain there even with a lamp lit; one need not feel regret about that.

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of the nuns who desire training, who are devoted to training, and who are equipped with the requisites for training, and the foregoing was established as a rule. This is a permission. Female hearers should also recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: "Whatever nun who has not received full ordination sleeps in the same dwelling for more than two nights — that constitutes a transgression."

The phrase "whatever nun" refers to the twelve factions. The phrase "has not received full ordination" — those who have received full ordination are of two kinds: monks and nuns; the rest have not received full ordination. The phrase "more than two nights" means when two nights have passed. In the phrase "sleeps in the same dwelling," there are four kinds of dwelling: one entirely roofed and entirely enclosed, one entirely roofed but mostly not enclosed, one mostly not roofed and mostly not enclosed, and one mostly roofed and mostly enclosed. "Entirely roofed and entirely enclosed" refers to a residence hall, a cloister with a surrounding gallery, or a multi-storied building. "Entirely roofed but mostly not enclosed" refers to a circular cloister or a sheltered passageway. "Mostly not roofed and mostly not enclosed" refers to a cloister with three sides open. "Mostly not roofed and mostly not enclosed" refers to a cloister with four sides open. The phrase "when dawn breaks" refers to whichever of the three dawns arises — the first, the middle, or the last. The phrase "constitutes a transgression" is as explained above. As for how the transgression arises: as soon as a nun sleeps in the same dwelling for a third night — that is, beyond two nights — together with one who has not received full ordination, she incurs a transgression in every case. The tenth of the fourth group of transgressions is complete.

The setting of the following rule is in Rājagṛha.
