At that time there occurred a case such as this: a nun who was at the point of death had come to hold a wrong view of a pernicious kind, saying that she understood how the Blessed One had taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed — and when this was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, go attend to the nun who is at the point of death and admonish her." When they went and admonished her, she seized upon that very basis with great tenacity, clinging to it resolutely and asserting, "This alone is true; all else is delusion" — and when the nuns reported this to the Blessed One,

The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must admonish the nun who is at the point of death by means of a formal act (karma) with motion and resolution fourfold. The admonishment is to be done as follows: beginning with 'Having prepared a seat,' and ending with 'One nun shall make the motion and perform the act.'"

The text of the act is as follows:

"Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In the case of this nun who is at the point of death, there has arisen a falling into a wrong view of a pernicious kind of this sort — namely, that she understands the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed by them. Many nuns have seized upon her and admonished her, but when they seized upon her and admonished her, she clung to that very basis with great tenacity, grasping it resolutely and continues to declare, 'This alone is true; all else is delusion.' If it seems timely and fitting to the noble Saṅgha, let the noble Saṅgha grant its consent. This is the noble Saṅgha's act of admonishing the nun who is at the point of death by means of a formal act with motion and resolution fourfold. This is the motion."

The act itself is then to be performed three times in the same way.

Now, when she was admonished by means of this formal act with motion and resolution fourfold, and she continued to say "This alone is true; all else is delusion," the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared:

"Nuns, since the nun who is at the point of death and has fallen into a pernicious wrong view cannot be made to give it up, you must also perform an act of expulsion against anyone whosoever who persists in a view consonant with hers. The act is to be performed as follows: beginning with 'Having prepared a seat,' and ending with 'One nun shall make the motion and perform the act.'"

The text of the act is as follows:

"Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In the case of this nun who is at the point of death, there has arisen a falling into a wrong view of a pernicious kind of this sort — namely, that she understands the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed by them. If it seems timely and fitting to the noble Saṅgha, let the noble Saṅgha grant its consent. This is the noble Saṅgha's act of expelling from the position of one who persists in being unable to relinquish the pernicious wrong view into which the nun who is at the point of death has fallen. For as long as the nun who is at the point of death who has fallen into a pernicious wrong view cannot be made to give it up, the nuns are not to converse with her, not to speak of her as one of good standing, not to receive her with individual rejoicing — and she is to be utterly condemned, as one condemns the daughter of an outcaste. This is the motion."

The act then proceeds: "Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In the case of this nun who is at the point of death, there has arisen a falling into a wrong view of a pernicious kind of this sort — namely, that she understands the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed by them. The Saṅgha has performed the act of expulsion, placing her in the position of one who persists in being unable to relinquish the pernicious wrong view into which the nun who is at the point of death has fallen."

For as long as the nun who is at the point of death persists in being unable to relinquish this pernicious wrong view into which she has fallen, the nuns shall not converse with her, shall not address her in a welcoming manner, and shall not take individual delight in her company; rather, they shall utterly despise and revile her as one would revile the daughter of an outcaste. Those sisters who consent to the act of expulsion — that of placing the nun who has fallen into the pernicious wrong view and who persists in being unable to relinquish it in the position of one who so persists — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent, let them speak. This is the first proclamation of the act; the same matter shall be proclaimed a second time.

Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In the case of this nun who is at the point of death, there has arisen a falling into a wrong view of a pernicious kind of this sort — namely, that she understands the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed by them. The Saṅgha has performed the act of expulsion, placing her in the position of one who persists in being unable to relinquish the pernicious wrong view into which the nun who is at the point of death has fallen. For as long as the nun who is at the point of death persists in being unable to relinquish this pernicious wrong view into which she has fallen, the nuns shall not converse with her, shall not address her in a welcoming manner, and shall not take individual delight in her company; rather, they shall utterly despise and revile her as one would revile the daughter of an outcaste. Those sisters who consent to the act of expulsion — that of placing the nun who has fallen into the pernicious wrong view and who persists in being unable to relinquish it in the position of one who so persists — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent, let them speak. This is the second proclamation of the act; the same matter shall be proclaimed a third time.

Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In the case of this nun who is at the point of death, there has arisen a falling into a wrong view of a pernicious kind of this sort — namely, that she understands the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that even if one practices the things the Blessed One taught as obstructions one will not be obstructed by them. The Saṅgha has performed the act of expulsion, placing her in the position of one who persists in being unable to relinquish the pernicious wrong view into which the nun who is at the point of death has fallen. For as long as the nun who is at the point of death persists in being unable to relinquish this pernicious wrong view into which she has fallen, the nuns shall not converse with her, shall not address her in a welcoming manner, and shall not take individual delight in her company; rather, they shall utterly despise and revile her as one would revile the daughter of an outcaste. This is the third proclamation of the act. The noble Saṅgha, having consented and agreed by remaining silent, so holds it to be.

Now although the act of expulsion placing her in that position had thus been performed, she stubbornly clung to that very same ground, adhered to it tenaciously, and continued to designate with that very declaration: "This alone is true; all else is delusion." At that juncture the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with the words "this occurrence," proceeded up to the laying down of a rule of training.

Furthermore, if any nun says, "I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in just such a way that what the Blessed One has declared to be an obstructing factor does not become an obstructing factor even when one practises it individually" — to that nun the nuns are to speak thus: "Sister, do not say, 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in just such a way that what the Blessed One has declared to be an obstructing factor does not become an obstructing factor even when one practises it individually.' Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. Sister, what are obstructing factors is precisely what the Blessed One has declared in many categories to be obstructing factors, and if one practises those individually they will indeed become obstructing factors. Sister, abandon this kind of wrong view that you have taken up." So they are to address her.

If that nun, when the nuns have spoken to her thus, abandons that position, then that is well. If she does not abandon it, she is to be admonished a second time and a third time, thoroughly and correctly. In order that she may abandon that position, if when she has been admonished thoroughly and correctly a second and third time she abandons it, that is well. If she does not abandon it, it constitutes a transgression.

Now the phrase "any nun" means one who is about to die. The phrase "says thus" means if she speaks. The phrase "I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One" refers to the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened Buddha. The phrase "what the Blessed One has declared to be an obstructing factor" refers to what obstructs the way of a contemplative — namely: the eight factors that entail defeat; twenty matters reserved for the Saṅgha; thirty-three abandonment transgressions; one hundred and eighty transgressions; eleven matters to be individually confessed; the many trainings; and the seven principles for settling disputes. These things that are not the Dharma, he has described using the name of Dharma. The phrase "even when one practises it individually" means even when one cultivates it earnestly. The phrase "does not become an obstructing factor" means does not become an obstruction to the way of a contemplative. The phrase "to that nun" refers to the one who is about to die. The phrase "the nuns" refers to those who belong to this Dharma community. The phrase "are to speak thus" means they are to say the following: "Sister, do not say, 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in just such a way that what the Blessed One has declared to be an obstructing factor does not become an obstructing factor even when one practises it individually'" — from that point up through the words "when admonishing her while she is held." If she abandons that position, then that is well. If she does not abandon it, she is to be instructed thoroughly a second and a third time, and admonished thoroughly — from there up through "she is to be admonished by the act of the motion and three proclamations" — which is the same as the previous admonition procedure. The "thorough admonition" is that very thing. The "thorough instruction" is that very thing. "It constitutes a transgression" is as above.

Now how does the transgression arise? To whatever extent a nun even slightly says, "I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in just that way," it becomes a wrong-doing in every instance. When, having been held and admonished, she abandons that position, then that is well. If she does not abandon it, it is a wrong-doing. When the first part of the act — the motion — is spoken, if she abandons it then that is well; if she does not abandon it, it is a wrong-doing.

When the second part of the act is being spoken, if she abandons that position before the speaking is complete, then that is well. If the speaking is complete and she still does not abandon it, it is a wrong-doing.

When the third part of the act is being spoken, before the speaking is complete: if those who are in discord act contrary to Dharma, or if those who are in discord are corrected as though contrary to Dharma, or if those who are in accord are corrected as though contrary to Dharma, or if it is not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Teacher's dispensation, and one acts accordingly, then there is no transgression. When it is in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Teacher's dispensation, and when the fourth part of the act is spoken to completion, it becomes a downfall-offense.

Here ends the eleventh section of the fourth downfall-offense.

The Vinaya Analysis of the Nuns. The Twentieth Fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Rājagṛha. At that time the twelve groups were conversing with a dying person, speaking of comings and goings, making free use of things, and sleeping in the same lodging. And nuns of little concern were criticizing them. This was reported to the Blessed One. Then, beginning with "This occurrence," the Blessed One established a training rule as follows:

"Whatever nun knowingly associates with a nun who has spoken in such a fashion, who has not acted in accordance with the Dharma and who has gone into a wicked view and has not abandoned it — conversing with her, speaking of her comings and goings, making free use of things, staying along with her, sleeping together in the same lodging — that is a downfall-offense."

"Whatever nun" refers to the twelve groups. "Who has not acted in accordance with the Dharma" means she has not been expelled by a formal act consisting of a motion and four proclamations. "Conversing with her" means providing her with scriptural recitation. "Speaking of her comings and goings" means reminding her of what she has forgotten. "Making free use of things" means appropriating acts of service and attendance for oneself. "Staying along with her" and "sleeping together in the same lodging" means being together with her until dawn breaks in four kinds of lodging. "A downfall-offense" is as above.

Now how does the transgression arise? To whatever slight extent a nun sleeps together in the same lodging with her, in every instance it becomes a downfall-offense. If she wishes to separate herself from that one who has gone into a wicked view, there is no transgression.

Here ends the twelfth section of the fourth downfall-offense.

The background story is set in Rājagṛha. The senior nun Spomgamo had two novice nuns, Mdzesma and Rgyelma. In those two there arose a wicked view of such a kind as this: that just as the Blessed One has declared that desires are obstructions, so even while individually relying upon those very things, no obstruction arises. They said, "Thus do we understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the nuns, the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must seize those two novice nuns, Mdzesma and Rgyelma, and admonish them."

When the two were seized and admonished, they tenaciously grasped that very basis, clung to it openly, and continued to designate those who held otherwise, saying, "This alone is true; the rest is confusion." When this was again reported to the Blessed One by the nuns, the Blessed One declared: "Nuns, you must admonish those two novice nuns by a formal act consisting of a motion and four proclamations." The admonition is to be performed as follows: after having arranged the seats — beginning from that point, give a proper and complete admonition in reply to the questioning of the nuns.

The two novice nuns were removed from the hearing range and placed within the seeing range, and then one nun made the motion and the act was performed. The act is as follows: "Reverend sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me. In regard to these two novice nuns there has arisen this kind of wrong and sinful view — namely, that while the Blessed One has declared that sense pleasures are an obstruction, they have claimed to understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma to the effect that even if one individually indulges in those very things that the Blessed One has declared to be an obstruction, they do not thereby become an obstruction. When the two were seized and admonished by a great many nuns, they tenaciously grasped that very basis, clung to it openly, and continued to designate those who held otherwise, saying, 'This alone is true; the rest is delusion.' If it is the right time and the noble Saṅgha approves, let the noble Saṅgha grant permission for this, and let the admonition of these two novice nuns, Sumanā and Jayā, be carried out by a formal act consisting of a motion and four proclamations." This is the motion.

The act is then to be performed as follows: "Reverend sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me. In regard to these two novice nuns, Sumanā and Jayā, there has arisen this kind of wrong and sinful view — namely, that while the Blessed One has declared that sense pleasures are an obstruction, they have claimed to understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma to the effect that even if one individually indulges in those very things that the Blessed One has declared to be an obstruction, they do not thereby become an obstruction. When the two were seized and admonished by a great many nuns, they tenaciously grasped that very basis, clung to it openly, and continued to designate those who held otherwise, saying, 'This alone is true; the rest is delusion.' The noble Saṅgha is performing the admonition of these two, Sumanā and Jayā, by a formal act consisting of a motion and four proclamations. Those reverend sisters who accept this, let them remain silent. Those who do not accept it, let them speak." This is the first proclamation of the act. In the same manner the second and third proclamations are also to be recited. From the words "The noble Saṅgha, having accepted and permitted" down to the words "as they say nothing, so it is here held to be" — that is the conclusion.

When, upon being admonished by means of the formal act consisting of a motion and four proclamations, the two still tenaciously grasped that very basis, clung to it openly, and continued to designate those who held otherwise, saying, "This alone is true; the rest is delusion," at that point the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns, perform the act of further censure against the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā. The act is to be performed as follows: after having arranged the seats, the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā are to be removed from the hearing range and placed within the seeing range, and then one nun makes the motion and the act is performed. The act is to be performed thus: Reverend sisters of the noble Saṅgha, please hear me. In regard to these two novice nuns, Sumanā and Jayā, there has arisen this kind of wrong and sinful view — namely, that while the Blessed One has declared that sense pleasures are an obstruction, they have claimed to understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma to the effect that even if one individually indulges in those very things that the Blessed One has declared to be an obstruction, they do not thereby become an obstruction. When the two were seized and admonished by a great many nuns, they tenaciously grasped that very basis, clung to it openly — and then the two novice nuns, Sumanā and Jayā, were seized and admonished by a great many nuns,

— admonishing the two of them beginning with the words "when the two were seized and admonished" down to the words "this alone is true; all else is delusion" — the Saṅgha admonished those two by means of a motion and a resolution with four recitations. When the two were admonished by the Saṅgha with a motion and a resolution with four recitations — beginning with the words "when the two were admonished by a motion and a resolution with four recitations" down to the words "this alone is true; all else is delusion" — since it is the proper time and if it pleases the noble Saṅgha, let the noble Saṅgha grant the following: that the noble Saṅgha perform the act of censure upon the two novice nuns, Sumanā and Jayā, declaring thus — "Sisters, from this day forward you shall not refer to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, as your Teacher; you shall not follow behind any person who practices pure conduct (brahmacarya) as a preceptor, in the manner of a wise master; and the permission formerly granted to other novice nuns to sleep in the same lodging as fully ordained nuns until the second night — that permission is henceforth revoked for you. You two deluded women, go elsewhere this very day." This is the motion. After that motion of censure has been performed upon those two, they shall be admonished to abandon that sinful view. If they abandon it, that is well. If they do not abandon it, the act shall then be performed. The act is as follows: "Sisters, let the noble Saṅgha hear me. To the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā there has arisen this deviation in the form of a sinful view — namely, that even if one individually indulges in those very things that the Blessed One has declared to be an obstruction, they do not thereby become an obstruction; that is how they claimed to understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma. When the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā were seized and admonished by a great many nuns — beginning with the words 'when the two were seized and admonished' down to 'this alone is true; all else is delusion' — and when those two were admonished by the Saṅgha with a motion and a resolution with four recitations, beginning with the words 'when the two were admonished by a motion and a resolution with four recitations' down to 'this alone is true; all else is delusion' — since the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā, who have gone astray into a sinful view and are unable to relinquish it, are to receive the act of censure: those who consent to the act of censure being performed upon those two shall remain silent; those who do not consent shall speak. This is the first proclamation of the act." After that, those two shall again be admonished. If they abandon it, that is well. If they do not, the same matter shall be proclaimed a second time. Beginning again with "Sisters, let the noble Saṅgha hear me," after the second proclamation has been made, they shall be admonished again. If they abandon it, that is well. If they do not, the same matter shall be proclaimed a third time. Beginning with "Sisters, let the noble Saṅgha hear me" — the noble Saṅgha, having consented and granted approval to performing the act of censure upon the novice nuns Sumanā and Jayā, who have gone astray into a sinful view and are unable to relinquish it — in that silence, so it is held. Thereupon, those two novice nuns, weeping, went to the presence of the preceptress and, having arrived, said to her: "Preceptress, the Saṅgha of fully ordained nuns has performed the act of censure upon us." Then Bhaddamukhā said to those two novice nuns: "For those upon whom the act of censure has been performed, are the three realms not all there? Are there no towns and provinces?" — and saying this, she went on conversing with those two upon whom the act of censure had been performed.

she walks with them, speaks with them, shares all manner of enjoyment with them, and sleeps in the same dwelling — in such a case, nuns of few desires censure her. This matter was then reported to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and so forth, proceeded to establish a training rule. He spoke to the novice nuns as follows, addressing that novice nun who had said: "In the way the Blessed One has declared that sensual pleasures are obstructions, yet even if one pursues them individually they do not become obstructions — that is how we understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma." The fully ordained nuns said to that novice nun: "Novice nun, do not say: 'In the way the Blessed One has declared that sensual pleasures are obstructions, yet even if one pursues them individually they do not become obstructions — that is how we understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma.' Do not denigrate the Blessed One. To have denigrated the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One never said anything of the sort. Novice nuns, sensual pleasures are obstructions precisely because they are obstructions. The Blessed One has declared in many ways that they are obstructions, and if one pursues them individually they become obstructions as well. Therefore, novice nuns, abandon such a course as this — this wandering into a sinful view." When the fully ordained nuns admonished that novice nun in these words: "If you relinquish that ground, so much the better. If you do not relinquish it, then for a second and third time you are to be properly instructed in order to lead you to relinquish that ground." When properly instructed a second and third time: "If you relinquish that ground, so much the better. If you do not relinquish it," then the fully ordained nuns are to say to that novice nun: "From this day forward, novice nun, you must not call the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, 'the Teacher.' You must no longer follow step by step after any of those who live the holy life and are learned. Novice nun, the permission that was granted to you — to sleep in the same dwelling as other fully ordained nuns for up to two nights — that too is henceforth withdrawn from you. Novice nuns, be gone." Thus they are to be addressed.

Furthermore, whatever fully ordained nun knowingly keeps close to such a censured novice nun, or teaches her, or shares all manner of enjoyment with her, or sleeps together with her in the same dwelling — she incurs a transgression.

The term "novice nun" refers to Mañjulā and Uttarā. The term "fully ordained nuns" refers to those who follow this Dharma. The phrase "saying this" means "when she speaks." The statement "In the way the Blessed One has declared that sensual pleasures are obstructions, yet even if one pursues them individually they do not become obstructions — that is how we understand the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma" means: even though one engages in them freely, they do not become an obstruction to the mode of the fully ordained nun. The phrase "to those two" refers to the novice nuns Mañjulā and Uttarā. "The fully ordained nuns" refers to those who follow this Dharma. The phrase "are to say thus" means: having assembled and admonished them, they admonish them exactly as stated before. "Properly instructing" means just that; "properly admonishing" means just that. When they have been thus followed up in that manner, if they relinquish that ground, so much the better; if they do not relinquish it, the act of censure is to be carried out — this is done as stated above. The phrase "whatever fully ordained nun" refers to Bhaddamukhā. The phrase "knowingly" means that it was declared either by herself or by others. The phrase "such a censured one" means: one upon whom the act of censure has been carried out. The term "novice nun" refers to Mañjulā and Uttarā.

"Provides accommodation" means that one gives lodging. "Provides instruction" means that one gives questioning. "Fully enjoys" means that one makes the honor one's own. From "dwells together, sleeps in the same place" through "constitutes an offense" — all this is as stated above. How does a transgression occur in this regard? To whatever slight degree a fully ordained nun knowingly provides accommodation to a novice nun who has been thus expelled, or provides instruction to her — from that point through "sleeps in the same place" — in every case it constitutes an offense.

The verse summary of the fourth offense is complete.

Summary verse:

Accepting dyed cloth, and at the half-month,
with deliberate intent, and remorse,
fat of the kaka bird, and at the waterside,
sleeping with a man — one must not whisper.
Giving cloth without a basis, on the road
one must not travel in the company of a man.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the Kalandakas. At the time when King Bimbisāra had established a festival for the nāga king Riwo and Yidong — those two — and then on another occasion, from the south, a great master of dance arrived and performed a dance-drama called "The Conduct of the Buddha," and received great acclaim from the faithful — from that point through "the six groups were put to shame" — all that passage is as given there. Then, following that, the account of how the six groups and the assembly of twelve groups of nuns combined dance gestures and performed a dance, from that passage through the occasion when the nuns of few wishes expressed their disapproval and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "All these faults that have arisen stem from those fully ordained nuns who wore the white garments worn by householders" — and then, from "the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence" through "established the training rule," the content is as follows: if a fully ordained nun obtains a new piece of cloth, she must change its color to any one of the three altered colors — blue, mud-color, or ochre.

If a fully ordained nun wears a new piece of cloth without having changed it to any one of the three altered colors, it constitutes an offense. As for the word "new," there are two senses of "new": new, and newly obtained — and in this context "newly obtained" is what is intended. "Cloth" refers to any of the seven kinds. "Fully ordained nun" refers to those who belong to this Dharma. "Without having changed it to any one of the three altered colors" means: without having changed the color. "Wears the new cloth" means: having put it on. "Constitutes an offense" is as stated above. How does a transgression occur in this regard? To whatever slight degree a fully ordained nun wears a new piece of cloth without having changed it to any one of the three altered colors, in every case it constitutes an offense. Even if only a bowl-sized piece has not been altered, it is still a misdeed.

The first part of the fifth offense is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the Blessed One, while at Vaiśālī, established the training rule regarding accepting with respect to the six groups, and at Śrāvastī permitted it with respect to Ānanda — then the twelve groups, while in the vicinity of a pleasure garden or outside its vicinity, wherever gems or things said to be gems were lying about, took them with their own hands, caused others to take them, and did not return them to their rightful owners; and the nuns of few wishes expressed their disapproval and reported it to the Blessed One. Then, from "the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence" —

He established the training rule up to that point. Furthermore, whatever nun takes with her own hand, or causes another to take, a gem or something said to be a gem — unless she is sitting within the pleasure garden or sitting within the dwelling-hall — commits a transgression. Whatever nun, while sitting within the pleasure garden or within the dwelling-hall, finds a gem or something said to be a gem, should think, "Whoever owns this, that very person shall come to take it," and with that thought as her motive she may take it and set it aside. That is the proper procedure for her in that case.

"Whatever nun" refers to the twelve groups. "A gem or something said to be a gem" refers to all implements used in battle and all implements of a pleasure garden. "Takes" means taking by herself. "Causes another to take" means through another person. "Sitting within the pleasure garden" means being in the grove. "Unless sitting within the dwelling-hall" means unless she is inside the temple.

"She should think, 'Whoever owns this, that very person shall come to take it,' and taking it with that very thought as her condition" — this means acting in accordance with that very intention. "Except at the proper time" means she should set it aside. "Commits a transgression" is as stated previously.

Now, how does a transgression arise in this regard? If a nun takes a gem, taking one that is perforated constitutes a transgression; taking one that is not perforated constitutes a misdeed. Just as with gems, so too with pearls, vajra-stones, lapis lazuli, conch-shells, crystal, coral, silver, precious stones, carnelians, and right-spiraling conch-shells: taking a perforated one constitutes a transgression; taking one that is not perforated constitutes a misdeed. Even taking a small gem bead constitutes a misdeed. Taking a necklace constitutes a transgression. Likewise, taking ornamental anklets, armlets, breast-ornaments, a single pendant-chain, and so forth constitutes a transgression. Even taking a necklace made of single gem-pieces constitutes a misdeed — and that is the extent of what is covered here.

If a nun takes a silver gem, if it bears a distinguishing mark, it constitutes a transgression; if it does not bear a distinguishing mark, it constitutes a misdeed. Even taking a worn sandal constitutes a misdeed.

If a nun takes a lute together with its strings and fittings, it constitutes a transgression; if without strings, it constitutes a misdeed. Likewise, taking a bāvabhīṣaka, a single-stringed lute, a small hand-drum, a large drum, a clay drum, or a paṭaha drum together with strings and fittings constitutes a transgression; without strings, a misdeed. Even taking a lute made of grass together with strings and fittings constitutes a transgression; without strings, a misdeed.

Likewise, taking a single-pointed vajra, a discus, a single-pointed weapon, a sword, a short lance, a great bow, a spear, a half-spear made of iron, an iron arrow, or a half-arrow made of iron that is fit for throwing constitutes a transgression; taking one that is not fit for throwing constitutes a misdeed. If a nun takes an arrow together with an arrowhead, it constitutes a transgression; without an arrowhead, a misdeed. Even taking a grass bow constitutes a misdeed.

If a nun takes an image of a buddha together with relics, it constitutes a transgression; if without relics, a misdeed. However, if she takes it with the perception of making an offering to the Teacher, and places it in the hands of a novice nun or one who is qualified, there is no transgression.

Summary verse:

Gems, necklaces, lutes,
conch-shells, bows and arrows,
and images together with relics —
these are here correctly enumerated.

The second section of the fifth category of transgressions is complete.

The occasion is at Rājagṛha. At that time, King Bimbisāra, when he was cold from the austerity waters, felt warmth, and when warm, felt cool — and there were three such sensations.

On the first occasion, the king himself bathed. On the second, it was for the queen. On the third, it was shared in common by all the world.

Then King Bimbisāra thought to himself: "I have already honored the Blessed One and the Śrāvaka Saṅgha abundantly in every way with all manner of provisions, yet I have not done so with the austerity waters for bathing. Therefore, I shall offer the austerity waters freely to the Blessed One, to the monks, and to the nuns." Having thought this, King Bimbisāra went to where the Blessed One was. Upon arriving, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Once seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed King Bimbisāra with a discourse in accordance with the Dharma — and here the text continues through to the point where the king rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Blessed One, together with the Śrāvaka community of nuns, I offer you the austerity waters for bathing. Where the Blessed One, together with the Śrāvaka Saṅgha, bathes — in the manner of a king of the royal caste consecrated by anointing — may the Blessed One together with the Śrāvaka Saṅgha please bathe there. And wherever the Tathāgata's Śrāvaka community of nuns bathe, accompanied by their retinue of attendants, may they bathe and use those facilities as they please."

The Blessed One said nothing, and thereby King Bimbisāra understood this as permission to provide the austerity waters for bathing. The text then continues from "Then, as much as the king..." through to "...and departed."

Thereupon the Twelve Groups heard that the Blessed One had accepted King Bimbisāra's invitation for the austerity-water bathing. Having heard this, those of the Twelve Groups went to where the queen of King Bimbisāra was performing her austerity-water bathing, in order to bathe themselves. At that time, the queen of King Bimbisāra wished to bathe and went to where the austerity water was — and the text continues from there through to the point where she found no opportunity on account of the Twelve Groups.

She then went and complained before the nuns, and the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "In that case, bathing is not to be done." Because they did not bathe, their bodies became quite malodorous, and when they went on alms rounds, laywomen said to them: "Something smells foul." Those nuns who were straightforward and honest by nature said: "That foul smell is from our bodies." The laywomen then said: "Have you not been bathing?" The nuns replied: "The Blessed One has prohibited bathing." When the nuns reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "In that case, you may bathe twice a fortnight."

Then, because of affliction by heat — the text continues from there through to where it is established that the three fortnights of summer are the hot season — you may bathe. Likewise, when the time of illness is established, you may bathe. Likewise the time of work, the time of travel, the time of wind and rain — when these are established, you may bathe.

Then those of the Twelve Groups, using the designation of the hot-season time, bathed at all times, and nuns of fewer concerns criticized them. The matter was then brought before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One began: "Since this matter has arisen..."

...and so he established the training rule. The Blessed One had declared "one may bathe at fortnightly intervals," and anyone who bathes more frequently than that, except at the permitted times, commits an offense. The permitted times are these: the last two fortnights of the cool season, the first month of the rains seasons, and these three fortnights together constitute the hot season. The remaining times are: the time of illness, the time of work, the time of travel, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of wind-with-rain — in these, bathing at that time is permitted.

As for the phrase "at fortnightly intervals," this means each half of the month. As for the word "bathe," bathing is of two kinds: consecration-bathing and immersion-bathing. The phrase "except at the permitted times" means that those times have been set aside. "In these, that is the permitted time" means: the remaining two fortnights of the cool season, and as for the first of the rains seasons — that means the first month, namely the beginning month of the rains, and these three fortnights together constitute the hot season. "The remaining is the time of illness" means: if one does not bathe, one will become ill. "The time of work, bathe" means: one has performed work and thereby become fatigued. "The time of travel, bathe" means: one has come by a road of half a league or one league and has thereby become fatigued. "The time of wind, bathe" means: one has been disturbed by wind — even so much as the corner of one's monastic robe being stirred by the wind. "The time of rain, bathe" means: two or three drops of rain have fallen on the body — that is the time of rain. "The time of wind-with-rain, bathe" means: one has been stirred by wind and also two or three drops of rain have fallen on the body. "Commits an offense" — this is as stated above.

Now, how does the offense come about? If a nun bathes with consecration-bathing, she must consecrate that time. If she has not consecrated it, then up to the point where the water reaches her navel it is a wrongdoing. If it goes beyond the navel, it is an offense entailing expiation. If a nun bathes with immersion-bathing, she must consecrate that time. If she has not consecrated it, then up to the point where the water reaches her navel it is a wrongdoing. If it goes beyond the navel, it is an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if having bathed with consecration-bathing she wishes to bathe with immersion-bathing, she must consecrate a different time. If she has not consecrated it, up to the navel it is a wrongdoing; if it goes beyond, it is an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if having bathed with immersion-bathing she wishes to bathe with consecration-bathing — from that point up to where the water reaches the navel it is a wrongdoing; if it goes beyond, it is an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if having bathed in warm water she wishes to bathe in cold water — from that point, it is a wrongdoing; if it goes beyond, it is an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if having bathed in cold water she wishes to bathe in warm water — from that point, it is a wrongdoing; if it goes beyond, it is an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if she wishes to bathe again in that very same manner, she must consecrate a different time.

If one splashes water on a person who has fainted, or if one wades across, or if one falls into water while jumping, or if one crosses a river or crosses a great lake and is submerged in the water — in these cases there is no offense.

This concludes the third of the fifth chapter on offenses entailing expiation.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, taking the case of Cāraka as occasion, established the training rule concerning deliberate generation of an animal rebirth, at that time those of the Twelve Groups, with deliberate intent...

...without deliberate intent, they kill living beings belonging to the animal realm, and they revile nuns of minor standing. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from the words "this occurrence" up through the establishing of the training rule, which reads: Moreover, whatever nun deliberately kills a living being belonging to the animal realm incurs an offense entailing expiation.

"Whatever nun" refers to those of the Twelve Groups. "Deliberately" means having considered the matter. "Belonging to the animal realm" means even so much as an ant. "Kills" means causes harm to its life. "Incurs an offense entailing expiation" is as stated above. As for how the transgression arises: however slight the intention, if a nun deliberately kills a living being belonging to the animal realm, she incurs an offense entailing expiation in all cases.

This concludes the fourth of the fifth chapter on offenses entailing expiation.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time those of the Twelve Groups, with deliberate intent, cause nuns to feel remorse, and they revile nuns of minor standing. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from the words "this occurrence" up through the establishing of the training rule, which reads: Moreover, whatever nun deliberately, using it as a means, causes a nun to feel remorse — thinking "I shall ensure that this one does not touch even the slightest thing, even for a moment" — incurs an offense entailing expiation.

"Whatever nun" refers to those of the Twelve Groups. "Deliberately" means having considered the matter. "Causes to feel remorse" means speech, words, and statements uttered with the intention of generating remorse, up to and including verbal expression. "Incurs an offense entailing expiation" is as stated above.

As for how the transgression arises: when a nun, with deliberate intent and with the thought of generating remorse, goes to another nun and says, "Sister, do you remember the great earthquake, or the great merchant ship, or the earthquake, or the moon being seized by Rāhu, or the sun being seized by Rāhu, or the fire at the horizon?" and that other nun replies, "I do not remember," and then the first says, "It is because what happened occurred at an earlier time. Sister, you received full ordination before you had reached the age of twenty, and since you have not received full ordination validly, you must receive full ordination again" — then whether or not remorse arises in that nun, whatever constitutes the causing of remorse incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if she says, "Sister, who is your preceptress?" and when told her name, she says, "That nun who is called the preceptress — the Saṅgha performed the act of removal from her seat" — then whether or not remorse arises in that nun, and so on, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if she says, "She is a person of corrupt conduct" — it incurs an offense entailing expiation, and so on.

Likewise, if she says, "Sister, where did you receive full ordination?" and when told the place, she says, "That place — the boundary was not properly demarcated, the boundary markers are not apparent within the maṇḍala, and the ordination was accomplished amid discord and conflict, not in harmony; therefore, sister, your ordination is not validly received" — and so on, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if a sister takes the robes of an ordaining preceptress or a teacher, or if, when it is said "She takes them thus," one says to her, "By taking them thus, you have incurred a transgression that will result in defeat" — and so on up to the concluding phrase, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if a sister teaches fully that all formations are impermanent, that all phenomena are without self, and that nirvāṇa is peace — or if, when it is said "She teaches thus," one says to her, "By speaking thus of the supreme teaching of a noble one, you have incurred a transgression that will result in defeat" — that too incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if a sister goes to some region, or when it is said "She goes thus," one says to her, "That region is one where violent people have settled; therefore you are about to incur a transgression that will result in defeat" — and so on, from the statement up to the phrase "it incurs an offense," it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

Likewise, if a sister eats meat, fish, dried meat, butter, milk, yogurt, or cream — or when it is said "She eats thus," one says to her, "If you eat such food, you will be afflicted with leprosy, small lesions, discolored patches of skin, spotted skin disease, itching, festering sores, body odor, nausea, pallor, wasting disease, a cough, breathlessness, and dryness — such forms of illness will come upon you" — then whether the nun feels regret or not, it incurs an offense entailing expiation. With a different purpose, or through the instrument of the Vinaya, there is no offense.

As for what is meant by "a different purpose": if a sister recalls a great king, or when it is said "She recalls him thus," one says, "That king has been gone a long time. Sister, you are twenty years old and are properly and fully ordained, so whatever anyone may say to you, do not feel regret" — and so likewise regarding a statement about a direction, and so on. Likewise, "Your preceptress is one endowed with moral discipline and is learned." And, "The place where you received full ordination — the boundary there is clearly demarcated and apparent within the maṇḍala." And, "You have eaten fish or meat," and so on up through cream: "If you have not eaten them, you are likely to become ill." Such cases as these constitute a different purpose.

As for what constitutes the instrument of the Vinaya: "Sister, surely you have not, with thieving intent, taken the robes of the preceptress or teachers?" And, "Surely you have not incurred a transgression?" And, "Surely you did not speak with the intention of uttering the words of a noble one's teaching?" And, "Did you go to that place? Surely you have not come into conflict with those living the celibate life? Surely you have not — surely you have not" — such as these constitute the instrument of the Vinaya.

The summary verse:

On birth-family and full ordination,
on the preceptress herself and the theft thereof,
on going and on speaking,
on a different purpose and the Vinaya's instrument.

The fifth section of the fifth offense-group is complete.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time, the twelve groups, with the intention of causing amusement, inserted their fingers into the armpits of nuns and tickled them, and in so doing they mocked nuns of few concerns. The matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded to establish the training rule: if one tickles with a finger, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

"With a finger" means: whatever is accompanied by the intention of tickling. "It incurs an offense" is as stated above.

As for how the offense is incurred: if a nun tickles with one finger, it incurs an offense entailing expiation. Likewise with two, and

likewise with three, four, and up to five fingers — these are the five ways of incurring the offense. If, however, one displays a mole or a dark mark, there is no offense. This completes the seventh rule under the fifth section on offenses entailing expiation.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the group of seventeen, had established the training rule concerning playing in water, the group of twelve thereupon entered the water and played in it, and induced others to play. The nuns then said to them: "Sisters, has the Blessed One not established a training rule concerning this?" The group replied: "That rule was established for monks; it was not established for nuns." The nuns of few concerns reproved them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded to establish the training rule: if one plays in water, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

"In water" means: whatever falls within the range of speech and words uttered by a nun with the intention of playing, up to and including what is understood as verbal communication. "It incurs an offense" is as stated above.

As for how the offense is incurred: there are nine bases. If a nun, with the intention of playing in water, wishes to enter the water, ties on a cloth, enters the water, and dives in — this incurs an offense entailing expiation. Similarly, causing oneself to rise up to the surface, going from the near bank to the far bank, or striving to swim against the current or with it — all of these incur an offense entailing expiation. Making the sound of a drum on the water also incurs an offense entailing expiation. Similarly, making sounds ranging from a beat on the water up to that of a single-faced clay drum — all of these incur an offense entailing expiation. If a nun scatters water on one another, it incurs an offense entailing expiation. If a nun delights in the water, it incurs an offense entailing expiation. If she causes another to delight in it, it incurs an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, playing, causing another to play, making merry, and causing another to make merry — all of these incur an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if through laughter and distracted excitement one stirs the water with the body, all of these incur an offense entailing expiation. Even striking the water in a pot with a bare finger incurs a minor offense. Likewise with a water vessel, meat broth, rice gruel, and soup. If a sick person, with the intention of playing, strikes soup or meat broth with a bare finger, there is no offense. This completes the seventh rule under the fifth section on offenses entailing expiation.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the venerable Anaṅgana, had established the training rule against lying in the same dwelling as a woman, the group of twelve then lay down together with men. The nuns said to the group of twelve: "Sisters, has the Blessed One not established a training rule against lying down together in the same place?" The group replied: "That rule was established for monks; it was not established for nuns." The nuns of few concerns reproved them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded to establish the training rule: furthermore, if any nun lies down together with a man in the same place, it incurs an offense entailing expiation.

"Any nun" refers to the group of twelve. "Together with a man" means: together with one who possesses male faculties. "Lies down in the same place" means: causes the dawn to break in any of four kinds of dwelling. "It incurs an offense" is as stated above.

As for how the offense is incurred: if a nun lies down on the ground floor of an upper-story building, and

a man is lying on the floor below, the nun must remove the stairs. If it is a staircase landing, she must block the door with a bolt and lie down below that landing. If she does not remove the stairs or does not block the door with a bolt, and simply lets down a hanging curtain and lies there, an offense is incurred.

Likewise, if a man lies in the space between floors and a nun lies on the floor above, an offense is incurred. And similarly, if a man lies in the upper story and a nun lies below, she must remove the stairs or block the door with a bolt. If she does not do so and lies there, an offense is incurred. Likewise, if a man is lying in the space between floors and a nun lies on the floor above, an offense is incurred as well. The same applies in the case of animal enclosures and the like: she must arrange a barrier of wood, planks, and lattice-work around the space, and if she does not do so, an offense is incurred. Whatever the situation, to whatever slight degree a nun lies in the same place together with a man, an offense is incurred in all such cases.

Here ends the eighth rule under the fifth class of offenses entailing expiation.

The Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns. The twenty-first fascicle.

The occasion for this rule arose in Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Sthūlanandā, with a mind of frivolous mockery, was frightening young nuns with ugly and frightful things, inciting them to be terrified, and deriding nuns of little learning. This was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded to establish the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun, with intent to terrify other nuns, frightens them or causes them to be frightened — even if with no more than a playful intention — an offense entailing expiation is incurred.

"Whatever nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Frightens them" means she herself does so. "Causes them to be frightened" means through another. "An offense is incurred" is as stated above.

As for how the offense is incurred: if any nun, with the intention of terrifying other nuns, approaches carrying ugly and frightful things — things dark and sooty in color, repulsive in appearance, resembling charred stumps of wood — and says such words as: "Yakṣas (yakṣas), hungry ghosts (pretas), flesh-eaters, spirits, kumbhāṇḍas, corpse-like beings, and rotting creatures of such forms as these will come to you and kill you; you will be deprived of your life" — whether the nun is actually terrified or not, an offense is incurred.

Similarly, when one produces sounds such as those of lions, tigers, and wolves, and likewise the various sounds of hungry ghosts and flesh-eaters, and so forth, an offense is incurred.

Similarly, when one produces various smells such as those of vomit, urine, of goats, and of shaggy goats, and likewise the various smells of hungry ghosts and the like, and so forth, an offense is incurred.

Similarly, when one produces various tactile sensations using wood, planks, lattice-work, and fans, and likewise the various touches associated with hungry ghosts and the like, and so forth, an offense is incurred.

When a nun, with the intention of terrifying another nun, displays pleasing forms such as: a great sāla tree of the warrior caste, a great sāla tree of the brahmin caste, a great sāla tree of the householder caste, or forms such as those of gods, gandharvas (gandharvas), kiṃnaras (kiṃnaras), great serpent kings (nāgas), and

whether the nun is terrified or not, an offense is incurred.

Similarly, when one produces pleasing sounds — such as those of a lute, iron cymbals, a drum, and exceedingly melodious instruments — an offense is incurred, from the words "sounds of this kind, such as those of gods," and so forth, down to "an offense is incurred."

Similarly, when one produces pleasing fragrances — such as those of aloeswood, sandalwood, bdellium resin, and camphor — an offense is incurred, from the words "fragrances of this kind, such as those of gods," and so forth, down to "an offense is incurred."

Similarly, when one produces pleasing tactile sensations — such as those of silk, cotton cloth, woolen garments, brocade, and cloth of fine muslin — an offense is incurred, from the words "tactile sensations of this kind, such as those of gods," and so forth, down to "an offense is incurred."

The ninth section of the fifth offense-group is complete.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. At that time, Stomāgāmā had a large retinue, and because she ate and drank in great quantity, dust had soiled her robes and rendered them unfit for use. Being unable to wash and rinse those robes herself, she gave them to her attendants and co-residents as a permanent gift. They washed and rinsed those robes, folded them up, placed them inside their bundles, and then entrusted them back into her hands before setting out on a journey. When they had set out on their journey, she, thinking she would reclaim them, made use of the robes. Having soiled them once again with defilement, she placed them back inside those very same bundles. When they returned and saw that those robes had been made dirty, they began to reproach her, and in that context the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "this occurrence," and so forth, proceeded to lay down a training rule: "Furthermore, if any nun gives robes to another nun and then, without having reclaimed them from her, makes use of them, an offense is incurred."

The phrase "any nun" refers to Stomāgāmā. The phrase "robes" refers to any of the seven types of allowable robe. The phrase "without having reclaimed them" means without having taken them back in hand. The phrase "an offense is incurred" is as before.

How does the offense arise? Whenever a nun gives robes of any size whatsoever to another and then uses them without having reclaimed them, an offense is incurred in every instance. If, however, the recipient is an intimate friend and would be glad to hear of it, there is no offense.

The tenth section of the fifth offense-group is complete.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. At that time, the twelve-fold group was quarreling with nuns and raking up their faults, and, overcome with anger and aversion, they groundlessly brought the matter before the formal Saṅgha against the nuns, and they were reproaching nuns of few concerns. In that context, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "this occurrence," and so forth, proceeded to lay down a training rule: "Furthermore, if any nun, having become angry and displeased, groundlessly imputes to a blameless nun — one who has no offense — a matter warranting formal Saṅgha action, an offense is incurred."

The phrase "any nun" refers to the twelve-fold group. The phrase "having become angry" is as before. The phrase "formal Saṅgha action" refers to any matter involving twenty or more. The phrase "an offense is incurred" is as before.

How does the offense arise? When a nun sees a formal Saṅgha offense occur with regard to another nun, and from that nun's having arrived at the view that no offense occurred, she shifts her perception, her patience, her wish, her reasoning, her thought, and her view, and says, "I saw the offense warranting formal Saṅgha action occur with regard to that nun" — then an offense is incurred. When a nun sees a formal Saṅgha offense occur with regard to another nun, and

from that nun's having arrived at the view that a transgression is warranted regarding her, she shifts her perception, her patience, her wish, her reasoning, her thought, and her view, and says, "I saw the offense warranting formal Saṅgha action occur with regard to that nun" — then an offense is incurred. When a nun sees a formal Saṅgha offense occur with regard to another nun, and from that nun's having arrived at the view that individual confession is required regarding her, she shifts her perception, her patience, her wish, her reasoning, her thought, and her view, and says, "I saw the offense warranting formal Saṅgha action occur with regard to that nun" — then an offense is incurred. When a nun sees a formal Saṅgha offense occur with regard to another nun, and from that nun's having arrived at the view that a misdeed is involved regarding her, she shifts her perception, her patience, her wish, her reasoning, her thought, and her view, and says, "I saw the offense warranting formal Saṅgha action occur with regard to that nun" — then an offense is incurred.

In the same sequential manner, the rule concerning the slightest trace of the formal Saṅgha offense is to be elaborated in full in just the same way. However, if a nun, even from some small degree of anger, aversion, and displeasure, makes a groundless accusation of a formal Saṅgha offense against another, an offense is incurred in every case.

Here ends the eleventh section of the fifth chapter on offenses.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At that time a young man from the town of Campā had recently taken a wife. Not long afterward, he became angry with his own wife and set off back to Campā. At that time the nun Sthūlanandā was sitting by the road and, seeing that young man, spoke to him: "Good sir, where are you going?" He replied: "I am going to Campā." Thereupon Sthūlanandā set out together with him. The wife of the Campā man was sitting on the upper floor of the house, and she saw her husband going down the road in the company of a certain nun, as if setting out on a journey. Seeing this, she cried out in a loud voice that her husband had run off with a nun. Then a great many men from Campā beat Sthūlanandā, leaving her with a swollen eye, and she went to the retreat residence. When the nuns asked her what had happened, she told them everything at length. The nuns of few wants rebuked her, and the matter was brought before the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, proceeding from the phrase "This incident occurred" up through the establishment of the rule, proclaimed: "If any nun travels down a road from village to village unaccompanied by a woman, in the company of a man — even as far as a single village — an offense is incurred."

"If any nun" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Unaccompanied by a woman, in the company of a man" means in a place where there is no woman. "Travels down a road" means going along a wilderness path. "Even as far as a single village" means going from village to village. "An offense is incurred" is as before.

How does the offense arise? Whenever a nun goes from village to village unaccompanied by a woman, in the company of a man, having traveled half a league, she has committed a misdeed. For each league, an offense is incurred.

Here ends the twelfth section of the fifth chapter on offenses.

Summary verse:

Not with a thief, not with twenty,
not digging, traveling, and the training;
listening, rising, disrespect,
drinking ale, wandering at wrong hours.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At that time Sthūlanandā set out from Rājagṛha together with a group of ivory merchants heading to Śrāvastī. When the road diverged and they entered a ravine, the ivory merchants caught up with her, and there too Sthūlanandā was beaten. She gradually made her way to Śrāvastī, and

The nuns said to her, "It is good that you have come, noble one." When the ivory merchants asked whether she had not been harmed, she told them the whole story of what had happened. The nuns then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered it: all those misdeeds had arisen because a certain nun had traveled the road together with thieves who shared a common purpose. He then proceeded from "this occurrence" through the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, should any nun set out upon a road together with thieves who share a common purpose, it is an offense." As for "furthermore" and "any," these refer to Sthūlanandā. "Thieves who share a common purpose" means merchants who deal in stolen ivory, or thieves. "Upon a road" means setting out and traveling on a road through a wilderness. "It is an offense" is as stated above. How does the offense arise? From the very moment a nun sets out even a little way along the road together with thieves who share a common purpose, it is an offense. For every half-league, it becomes a misdeed. For every full league, it is an offense.

Here ends the first of the sixth group of offenses.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At that time Sthūlanandā, wishing to have attendants, gave full ordination as a nun to a woman who had not yet reached the age of twenty. The nuns said to her, "Sister, did the Blessed One not establish a training rule? That rule was laid down for monks, she replied, not for nuns." The nuns who were modest censured her, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from "this occurrence" through the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, should any nun confer full ordination as a nun upon a candidate who has not yet reached the age of twenty, through a formal act with a motion and three announcements, that nun's ordination is not valid, and those who performed it shall be censured with a transgression. This is certain in that case. This is in accordance with the Dharma in that case." As for "it is an offense," it is as stated above. How does the offense arise? If the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty and perceives herself as not having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I have not reached twenty," then if the nuns confer full ordination upon her as a nun, those nuns shall be associating and sharing benefits with one who from the very outset was not fully ordained, and they shall also incur a transgression. The community of nuns, moreover, becomes thereby seriously compromised. If the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty and perceives herself as not having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I do not know and cannot remember whether I have reached the age of twenty — I am of two minds about it," then if the nuns confer full ordination upon her as a nun, those nuns shall be associating and sharing benefits with one who from the very outset was not fully ordained, and they shall also incur a transgression. The community of nuns, moreover, becomes thereby seriously compromised. If the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty and perceives herself as not having reached twenty, and she too neither knows, nor remembers, nor is certain about it, and the nuns neither ask anything of her nor receive any answer from her, and yet the nuns confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then the Blessed One declared:

The nuns shall be associating and sharing benefits with that nun who received full ordination under those circumstances, and they shall also incur a transgression. The community of nuns, moreover, becomes thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty but perceives herself as having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I have reached twenty," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then those nuns shall be associating and sharing benefits with that nun who received full ordination under those circumstances, yet they shall not incur a transgression, and the community of nuns shall not be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty but perceives herself as having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I know and remember clearly that I have reached twenty, and I have no doubt about it," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then those nuns shall be associating and sharing benefits with that nun who received full ordination under those circumstances, yet they shall not incur a transgression, and the community of nuns shall not be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has reached the age of twenty but perceives herself as not having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I have not reached twenty," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then those nuns shall consider that nun as fully and properly ordained from the very outset, and they shall not incur a transgression by associating and sharing benefits with her, but the community of nuns shall be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has reached the age of twenty but perceives herself as not having reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I know and remember clearly that I have not reached twenty, and I do have doubt about it," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then those nuns shall consider that nun as fully and properly ordained from the very outset, and they shall not incur a transgression by associating and sharing benefits with her, but the community of nuns shall be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has reached the age of twenty yet neither knows, nor remembers, nor is certain about it, and the nuns neither ask anything of her nor receive any answer from her, and yet the nuns confer full ordination upon her as a nun, then those nuns shall consider that nun as fully and properly ordained from the very outset, and they shall not incur a transgression by associating and sharing benefits with her, but the community of nuns shall be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has fully reached the age of twenty and perceives herself as having fully reached twenty, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I have reached twenty," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, the Blessed One declared: those nuns shall consider that nun as fully and properly ordained from the very outset, and they shall not incur a transgression by associating and sharing benefits with her, and the community of nuns shall not be thereby seriously compromised.

If the candidate has reached the age of twenty and perceives herself as having reached twenty, and knows and remembers clearly and has no doubt about it, and the nuns ask her, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and she replies, "I know and remember clearly that I have reached twenty, and I have no doubt about it," and the nuns then confer full ordination upon her as a nun, the Blessed One declared:

Nuns, that nun shall be properly ordained from the very outset, and they shall not incur a transgression by associating and sharing benefits with her, and the community of nuns shall not be thereby seriously compromised.

Nuns, among these four cases of nuns, those in the first category are the ones who are disturbed from the outset, and they are worthy of reproof because they have not been properly ordained from the very beginning. As for the nun in that case who does not know, does not remember, and is in doubt — she must be made to know, made to remember, and must abandon her doubt and uncertainty. When she has come to know, has come to remember, and has abandoned her doubt and uncertainty, then if all the conditions are complete, she is ordained just as she was ordained. If they are not complete, she must either move her seniority date or be fully ordained again. If she neither moves her seniority date nor is fully ordained again, and she goes on to participate two or three times in the restoration ceremony together with nuns who are abiding in their proper standing, then, nuns, she is dwelling by stealth and that nun is worthy of reproof.

Nuns, in that case, a nun who has not yet reached twenty and is fully ordained with the perception that she has reached twenty, and her relatives arrive and speak as follows: "Is there one called so-and-so?" and the others reply, "She is fully ordained." And the relatives then say, "She has not reached twenty" — upon hearing those words, the Blessed One declared: The months in the womb and the remaining months after birth should also be counted. If then all is complete, well and good. If it is not complete, she must either move her seniority date or be fully ordained again. If she neither moves her seniority date nor is fully ordained again — from that point up to the statement "she is worthy of reproof," the same applies as above.

Nuns, in that case, a nun who has reached eighteen is fully ordained with the perception that she has reached twenty, and if she can recover the recollection of two years, she is ordained just as she was ordained — because, nuns, going forth and full ordination in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya and the status of nunhood are difficult to obtain. If she can recover only the recollection of one year, the months in the womb and the remaining months after birth should also be counted. If then all is complete, well and good. If it is not complete — from that point up to "she is worthy of reproof," the same applies as above.

Nuns, in that case, a nun who has reached nineteen is fully ordained with the perception that she has reached twenty, and if she can recover the recollection of one year, she is ordained just as she was ordained — because, nuns, going forth and full ordination in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya and the status of nunhood are difficult to obtain. If she can recover the recollection of less than a year, the months in the womb and the remaining months after birth should also be counted. If then all is complete, well and good. If it is not complete, she must either move her seniority date or be fully ordained again — from that point up to "she is worthy of reproof," the same applies as above.

This concludes the second part of the sixth offense.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in reliance on the group of six, had established the training rule against digging the earth with one's own hands, the group of twelve then dug the earth with their own hands and caused others to dig it, and nuns who cared little for such matters censured them. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from the words "this occurrence" up through the establishing of the training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun digs the earth or causes it to be dug commits a transgression. "Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. As for "earth," there are two kinds of earth: earth that is by nature alive, and earth that is not by nature alive. "By nature alive" means earth that has become animate through three months of rainfall soaking it — this is called earth that is by nature alive. What is earth that is not by nature alive? Earth that has not become animate because rain has not fallen upon it — this is called earth that is not by nature alive. "Digs" means by oneself. "Causes to be dug" means through another. "Commits a transgression" is as stated above.

How does the transgression arise in each case? If a nun digs earth that is by nature alive, she commits a transgression in the act of digging. If she digs earth that is not by nature alive, she commits a misdeed. If a nun drives a stake into the earth, she commits a transgression. If she pulls it out, she commits a misdeed. If a nun squeezes out moisture from earth, and if the earth element is very abundant while the moisture element is very thin, she commits a transgression. If the moisture element is very thick while the earth element is very thin, she commits a misdeed. Likewise, if the heavy element is very abundant while the earth element is very small, she commits a misdeed. If a nun squeezes sand mixed with earth out of earth, and if the earth element is very thick while the sand element is very thin, she commits a transgression. If the sand element is very abundant while the earth element is very thin, she commits a misdeed. If she presses down on loose, uncompacted earth to compact it, she commits a transgression. If the earth is already compacted, she commits a misdeed. If she breaks down an uncompacted wall, she commits a transgression. If the wall is already compacted, she commits a misdeed. If she drives a stake into a wall, she commits a transgression. If she pulls it out, she commits a misdeed. If she stops up an unfired, uncompacted water channel, she commits a transgression. If it is already compacted, she commits a misdeed. Even if she merely scrapes off the surface, she commits a misdeed. If she drives a stake into mud, or prods it with a small stake, she commits a misdeed. If she stirs it, she commits a misdeed. If she drives a stake next to an old stake, she commits a misdeed. If she draws a line on the earth, she commits a misdeed. However, if she merely traces a calculation with the back of her hand, there is no transgression.

This concludes the third part of the sixth transgression.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in reliance on the group of six, had established the training rule against accepting invitations for four months, the group of twelve then accepted invitations for five and six months as their own prerogative. The nuns then said to them: "Did not the Blessed One establish the training rule permitting invitations for four months?" They replied: "That was established for monks, not for nuns." This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from the words "this occurrence" through the establishing of the training rule:

A nun may accept invitations for four months. If she exceeds that, it is a transgression, except for a proper occasion. The proper occasions are these: an individual invitation, a repeated invitation, a special invitation, and a standing invitation. "Four months" means four months. "Exceeding that" means seeking additional invitations. "Except for a proper occasion" means when a time has been established. "Individual" means one by one, separately. "Repeated" means again and again. "Special" means as much as is fitting. "Standing" means continuously. "These are proper occasions" means these are in conformity with the Dharma. "Commits a transgression" is as stated above.
