How does the transgression arise? If a nun accepts an invitation for a meal in the households of householders and solicits something beyond what was offered, she commits a transgression.

Likewise, the section beginning with "if invited as a guest by a householder and solicits alms" extends through to "she commits a transgression in all such cases." The section beginning with "for alms" through "if she solicits a householder" constitutes an offense requiring confession. However, if she is ill, or if she obtains alms and then solicits a householder, or if it is a convenient occasion, there is no transgression. This completes the fourth rule of the sixth group of rules entailing a transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. The Blessed One had established some rules of training that applied to nuns alone, some that were shared with monks, and some that were common to both. On one occasion, when the Blessed One had established a rule of training common to both, he sent monks to the nuns' rains retreat residence. When the monks gave instruction to the nuns, those nuns in turn passed the instruction on to other nuns. Those nuns then relayed the instruction to the members of the twelve groups, who responded by saying, "We are ignorant, confused, unclear, and unskilled. We will not train in the precepts according to your words," adding, "We will go and ask others — nuns who hold the sūtras, nuns who hold the Vinaya, and nuns who hold the Mātṛkā."

When they said this and began to disparage the nuns of lesser knowledge, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from the words "this incident occurred" through to establishing a rule of training. The rule runs as follows: if a nun, when instructed by other nuns saying, "Noble one, you should train in this precept," responds to those nuns by saying, "I am ignorant, confused, unclear, and unskilled — I will not train in the precepts on the basis of your words," and adds, "We will go and ask other nuns — those who hold the sūtras, those who hold the Vinaya, those who hold the Mātṛkā," she commits a transgression. A nun who wishes to know fully should train in that precept, and she should also inquire of nuns who hold the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā — that is the proper procedure for her.

Now, "whatever" refers to the members of the twelve groups. "When instructed by nuns" refers to those of this Dharma community. "You should train in this precept" extends from "the eight rules resulting in defeat" through to "the seven rules for the settlement of disputes." "Ignorant" means one who does not hold the sūtras, does not hold the Vinaya, does not hold the Mātṛkā — such a one is called ignorant. "Unskilled" means unskilled in the sūtras, unskilled in the Vinaya, unskilled in the Mātṛkā — such a one is called unskilled. "Unclear" means unclear regarding the sūtras, unclear regarding the Vinaya, unclear regarding the Mātṛkā — such a one is called unclear. The phrase "I will go and ask other nuns who hold the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā" extends through to "one who is clear regarding the sūtras, clear regarding the Vinaya, clear regarding the Mātṛkā." "A nun who wishes to know fully" means one who wishes to train. "She should also train in that precept" refers to the nuns in whose training she is to engage. "She commits a transgression" is as stated above.

How does the transgression arise? Whenever a nun, upon being instructed by the nuns, responds even slightly by saying "ignorant," she commits a transgression. If she says "confused," she commits a transgression. If she says "unclear," she commits a transgression. If she says "unskilled," she commits a transgression. This completes the fifth rule of the sixth group of rules entailing a transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time, members of the twelve groups, having stationed themselves at the doorway of the nuns' quarters to listen with their ears to a quarrel that had broken out among the nuns, heard whatever they could and then went about spreading to one side what they had heard from the other,

and spreading to the other side what they had heard from the first — and thereby quarreling, fault-finding, disputing, and divisiveness arose in the Saṅgha, and nuns of lesser standing were being reviled. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from "this incident having occurred" through to the establishing of the training rule.

Furthermore, if any nun, knowing that a quarrel, fault-finding, divisiveness, or disputing has arisen and is ongoing among the nuns, should think, "I will listen to what those nuns say and then describe it accordingly to the other party," and should sit listening with her ears while saying nothing, she commits a transgression. As for "any" — this refers to the twelve groups. "Should sit listening with her ears" means that she remains at the doorway wishing to hear. "She commits a transgression" is as above.

How does the transgression come about? If a nun is inside and another is coming in from outside, that nun should make a sound, make noise with her footsteps, or clap her hands. If she does not do so — or if she neither hears the sound nor understands the meaning — she has committed a misdeed. If she does hear the sound and also understands the meaning, she commits a transgression. Likewise, wherever she may be sitting, she commits a transgression. However, if she thinks, "If I hear, I will bring about peace," there is no transgression. This completes the sixth rule of the sixth group of rules entailing a transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time, members of the twelve groups, during a formal Dharma deliberation of the nuns' Saṅgha, rose from their seats without saying a word and departed. This was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "They must not depart." After they had fallen ill, the Blessed One declared, "They may inform the nuns present and then depart." The Blessed One then proceeded through the training for nuns from "those wishing to train" up to "with requisites removed."

Furthermore, the female hearers (śrāvikās) are to recite this basis of training in the Vinaya as follows: If any nun, during a formal Dharma deliberation of the Saṅgha, rises from her seat without saying a word and departs without informing the nuns present — except in circumstances such as those — she commits a transgression.

As for "any" — this refers to the twelve groups. "A formal Dharma deliberation" refers to such formal acts as: a motion alone, a motion with a second proclamation, or a motion with a fourth proclamation. "Without saying a word, rises" means she falls completely silent. "Without informing the nuns present" means without making her intention known. "Except in circumstances such as those" means an exceptional circumstance has been set down. "She commits a transgression" is as above.

How does the transgression come about? If a nun, at any point during a formal Dharma deliberation — even the slightest part of it — rises and departs without saying a word, from that point through to "without understanding the meaning" is a misdeed. If she does not hear the sound but understands the meaning, she commits a transgression. This completes the seventh rule of the sixth group of rules entailing a transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time, Stout Nandā together with her retinue showed disrespect toward the Buddha, disrespect toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and was reviling nuns of lesser standing. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded from "this incident having occurred" through to the establishing of the training rule: if one behaves disrespectfully, she commits a transgression.

As for "if one behaves disrespectfully" — there are two kinds of disrespect: toward the Saṅgha and toward an individual. "She commits a transgression" is as above. How does the transgression come about?

When the Saṅgha's steward instructs a nun to vacate a lodging and she does not comply, she commits a transgression. However, if she makes a request with the perception that the instruction is improper in terms of the Dharma, and does not comply on that basis, there is no transgression. Likewise, instructions such as "go" or "speak" — all such cases of this kind result in a transgression. This applies to disrespect toward the Saṅgha.

As for disrespect toward an individual: if the abbess or the preceptress instructs her to vacate a lodging and she does not comply, she incurs a wrong-doing. If told to go and she does not go, she incurs a wrong-doing. If told to speak and she speaks, she incurs a wrong-doing. If told to speak and she does not speak, she incurs a wrong-doing. In short, she incurs a wrong-doing in all such cases. However, if she makes a request with the perception that the instruction is improper in terms of the Dharma, there is no transgression. This completes the eighth section of the sixth chapter on transgressions.

The background occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the Venerable Legsong, established the training rule concerning wandering at improper times due to heedlessness — at that time the communities of nuns thought to themselves: "How are we to uphold this training rule?" With that in mind, the community of nuns went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One, then stood to one side. Having stood to one side, a great many nuns addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, how are nuns to observe the training rule regarding grain-beer and prepared beer?"

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of the nuns' desire to train, their reverence for the training, and their equipping themselves with the means for training, declared the following: "If one drinks grain-beer or prepared beer, she commits a transgression. What is called grain-beer is beer mixed with fermented grain-mash or mixed with food. What is called prepared beer is beer made from winter brew, sugar-cane brew, or other such substances mixed together. What is called drinking is swallowing it down the throat. What is called committing a transgression is as above."

How does the transgression come about? If a nun drinks, or causes another to drink, something that has the color of beer, the smell of beer, or the taste of beer, she commits a transgression. If it is prepared beer, she commits a transgression. If it is blended beer, she commits a transgression. If it merely has the color of beer, she incurs a wrong-doing. If it has the smell of beer, she incurs a wrong-doing. If it has the taste of beer, she incurs a wrong-doing. If she consumes the sediment, she incurs a wrong-doing. However, if on account of leprosy it is applied to the limbs as a medicinal rinse, or poured into the mouth and held there on account of a mouth ailment, or used as a boiling preparation, there is no transgression. This completes the ninth section of the sixth chapter on transgressions.

The background occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, on account of the Venerable Charka, established the training rule concerning wandering at improper times — at that time the twelve groups were wandering in the village both at proper times and at improper times. The nuns said to them: "Sisters, did not the Blessed One establish a training rule against wandering at improper times?" Those persons replied: "That rule applies to monks; it does not apply to nuns." Upon hearing this, the nuns presented the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, nuns must understand this and go accordingly." Then a certain nun went to a householder's home with her alms bowl and

left her outer robe there — at which point she heard that the householder's house had caught fire. That nun thought to herself: "The Blessed One said that nuns must understand and go accordingly when a nun is present." So, for as long as it took to make herself understood to a nun, her alms bowl and outer robe were burned. The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning from "desiring the training" and continuing through "one who is equipped with the requisites for training" — the former part being the rule as established, and this being the permitted allowance — declared that the female hearers (śrāvikās) should recite this rule of Vinaya training as follows: "Furthermore, whatever nun goes to the village at an improper time without having made herself understood to a nun who is present — except in such a circumstance as that — commits an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to a nun of this Dharma community. Regarding "at an improper time" — what is an improper time, and what is a proper time? From the time past midday until the break of dawn: this is an improper time. The remainder is a proper time. "Goes to the village" means to the homes of householders. "Commits an offense entailing expiation" is as explained above. As for how the offense arises: whatever nun goes at an improper time with the perception that it is an improper time commits an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if she is in doubt, she commits an offense entailing expiation. If she goes at a proper time with the perception that it is improper, she commits a minor offense. Likewise, if she is in doubt, she commits a minor offense.

Here ends the complete verse summary of the sixth offense entailing expiation.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the twenty-second fascicle.

Verse summary: The cause, the royal palace, the measurement of eight finger-breadths of bone for the first time, the low seat spread out, the border, and the robe of the Sugata.

The original account is set in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the nun Gāmā put on her lower robe in the morning, took her outer robe and alms bowl, and went together with a novice nun who was following along behind her to the home of a certain donor. She taught her the Dharma in accordance with her needs, inspired her with faith, and had her prepare food for the community of nuns. The next morning, the community of nuns put on their lower robes, took their alms bowls and outer robes, and went to the place where that householder had directed them — and this passage continues up to "they sat only when seats had been spread."

Now the nun Gāmā had many duties and much to accomplish, and so she missed the time of the gong. The nuns said to that householder: "Householder, be so kind as to serve the community of nuns at their proper time." He replied: "Noble ones, I had not intended not to invite you; it is Gāmā who knows the matter of the food offering" — and this passage continues up to the point where the few-wishing nuns expressed disapproval. They then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Nuns must not wander from house to house at the time of the prior meal and at the time of the later meal."

Then, when those who were serving or providing food had their community service and community provisioning disrupted, the Blessed One declared: "For the prior meal, two houses; for the later meal, three houses."

Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "desiring the training" and continuing through "equipped with the requisites for training," having spoken the praise, declared the following: "Furthermore, whatever nun who has been invited to a house with food goes from house to house to householders at the time of the prior meal and the time of the later meal without having made herself understood to the householder who is present commits an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to Gāmā. "A house with food" means a house with a feast prepared.

"To houses" means invited as a guest to the houses of householders. "The prior meal" means the morning time. "The later meal" means the afternoon time. "Commits an offense entailing expiation" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: whatever nun has been invited as a guest to a house with food, if during the prior meal she goes to two houses and then intentionally proceeds to a third house, she commits an offense entailing expiation. If during the later meal she goes to three houses and then intentionally proceeds to a fourth house, she commits an offense entailing expiation. If she has made herself understood to a member of the householder's family, there is no transgression. The first of the seven offenses entailing expiation is complete.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the group of six, had established the rule of training regarding fixed doors, the group of twelve said that this was a training rule for monks and declined to practice in accordance with that rule. The nuns then appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, for nuns also, until night has passed and dawn has not yet broken." At the time when King Prasenajit instructed the householder Gāṅgā that he wished his daughter to see the nuns, the householder Gāṅgā requested the monk Śāriputra to bring the nun Śrīmatī in order to instruct her and sent her to the royal palace, and the Blessed One also gave permission. Then on another occasion, when the daughter of Gāṅgā again wished to see the nuns, the householder Gāṅgā made a request to the Great Mistress of People, but she declined, saying that there were ten dangers in entering the royal palace. After that, King Prasenajit made his appeal. Then the Great Mistress of People reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Gautamī, the word of the six is not to be listened to in even one instance. Which six? The teacher, the preceptor, a king consecrated from the crown of the royal lineage, the Saṅgha, the senior member of the Saṅgha, and a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha." Having given this additional instruction, he entered the royal palace. At the time when the Great Mistress of People entered the royal palace, the group of twelve said to one another: "If we too were to go, today itself we would be carrying what is improper and unbecoming for the manner of a renunciant." The Blessed One then, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through "established the rule of training," declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun, before night has passed and before the three dawns have broken, crosses or stands beyond the fixed door or the boundary around the fixed door of a king consecrated from the crown of the royal lineage without having gathered up jewels or things called jewels — except in such circumstances — commits an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. "A king consecrated from the crown of the royal lineage" means that whether a woman, a man, or a person of intermediate sex has been consecrated as king, that one is a king, is of the royal lineage, and has been consecrated from the crown. "Before night has passed" means before night has turned to day. "Before dawn has broken" — "the three dawns," as before. "Without having gathered up jewels or things called jewels" means without having collected them.

As for what is called "a closed gate," there are three kinds of closed gates. What are the three? The closed gate of a city, the closed gate of a royal palace, and the closed gate of the queen's residential quarters. "Commits an offense entailing expiation" is as above. How does the transgression come about? If any nun, when dawn has not yet broken, with the perception that dawn has not yet broken, passes beyond a closed gate, she commits an offense entailing expiation. Likewise, if she is in doubt, she commits an offense entailing expiation. If any nun, when dawn has broken, has the perception that dawn has not broken, that is an offense of wrong-doing. Likewise, if she is in doubt, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If, however, she happens to come between a king, a queen, and a minister, there is no offense. This completes the second rule of the seventh category of offenses entailing expiation.

The ruling occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, nuns of the twelve groups said the following: "Noble sisters, we have only now come to know that this particular Dharma is included in the sūtra and summarized in the sūtra." When the nuns knew that those nuns had been present at two or three sessions of the restoration ceremony before — to say nothing of many times — the nuns therefore instructed that sister, saying: "Do not speak thus." And when those nuns were told, "What we have said is indeed so," this was the occasion for nuns of few wants to criticize them. The nuns then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and proceeding through to the laying down of the training rule, enacted the following: if any nun, at the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, says, "Noble sisters, only now have we come to know that this particular Dharma is included in the sūtra and summarized in the sūtra," and if the nuns know that she was previously present at two or three sessions of the restoration ceremony — to say nothing of many times — then she should be addressed thus: "Noble sister, ignorance is no excuse. Over and above causing the offense that arose to be dealt with according to the rule, you have not gained anything, noble sister — you have not gained what is to be gained, but you have gained a fault, in that you do not listen to the Dharma with reverence when the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited, you do not do so treating it as supreme, you do not do so taking it to heart, you do not do so with one-pointed ear inclined to listen, and you do not do so listening to the Dharma with your whole mind." That is the rebuke that is to be administered to her, and this constitutes an offense entailing expiation.

"Whatever" refers to the twelve groups. "Fortnightly" means twice a month. "During the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra" refers to the span from "the eight cases of defeat" through to "the seven rules for settling disputes." "Is to be recited in order" means to be recited in proper sequence. "Commits an offense entailing expiation" is as above. How does the transgression come about? Whenever a nun, at any point during the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, says "this particular Dharma is included in the sūtra," she commits an offense entailing expiation. If she says "summarized in the sūtra," she commits an offense entailing expiation. If the quorum is not assembled, or if one is otherwise absent from the formal act, there is no offense. This completes the third rule of the seventh category of offenses entailing expiation.

The ruling occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, at Śrāvastī there dwelt a certain Nirgrantha (a naked wanderer) hearer of the Dharma named Vāsomukha, who was a cowherd. A certain alms-beggar inspired him with faith in the teaching of the Buddha, and then had him offer needles to the Saṅgha of both communities. Thereupon the twelve groups had the needles, bones, and

horns made into needle-cases of various comb-like shapes. He had eaten his own food and done the work of others, and before long he was reduced to poverty.

Then the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), upon seeing the craft of needle-making, said the following: "When we had faith in it, we prospered; but when we came to have faith in the śramaṇī disciples of the Śākya sons, we became destitute." The nuns heard them say this. Having heard it, they reported the matter to the Blessed One on that occasion. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This incident arose," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: Any nun who has a needle-case made from tooth, bone, or horn — having broken it, there is an offense entailing expiation. The phrase "any" refers to the twelve groups. "Tooth" means tooth itself. "Bone" means bone itself. "Made from horn" means horn itself. As for the term "needle-case," there are two kinds of needle-cases: those with a stopper and those resembling a tube. "Does" refers to doing it oneself. "Has done" refers to having another do it. "There is an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

How does the offense arise in this case? To whatever extent a nun makes or has another make even a small needle-case of tooth, or bone, or horn — in every instance there is an offense entailing expiation. One before whom such a needle-case is being fitted together should ask whether it has been broken. If one has it fitted together without asking, that transgression too remains unconfessed, and for the one before whom it is being fitted together there is also a misdeed.

This completes the fourth rule of the seventh category of offenses entailing expiation.

The ruling occasion is at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One, on account of the six groups, had laid down the training rule that the measure of couches and chairs be eight finger-breadths of the Sugata (the Well-Gone One, the Buddha), the twelve groups then had couches and chairs made that exceeded the prescribed measure. The nuns said to them, "Sisters, did not the Blessed One lay down a training rule?" Those monks replied, "He laid it down for the monks — not for the nuns." Nuns who had few wishes then complained, and they reported the matter to the Blessed One on that occasion. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This incident arose," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: When a nun has a couch or chair made for the Saṅgha, she should have it made to the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata, excluding the insertion of the legs. If she has it made beyond that measure, having cut it, there is an offense entailing expiation.

The phrase "of the Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of the female śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. "Nun" refers to the twelve groups. "Couch" refers to a bed. "Chair" means a chair itself. "Of the Sugata" refers to the Teacher. As for the eight finger-breadths of the Sugata: that amounts to one standard cubit of a proportionate hand. "Excluding the insertion of the legs" means setting that aside. "If made beyond that" means if it is made in excess of that. "There is an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

How does the offense arise in this case? To whatever extent a nun makes anything even slightly in excess of the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata, in every instance there is an offense entailing expiation. The phrase "before whom it is being fitted together" is as before.

This completes the fifth rule of the seventh category of offenses entailing expiation.

The ruling occasion is at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One, on account of the monks and

had appointed the nuns to arrange the furnishings of the lodgings, at another time, when the nuns were arranging the lodgings, the group of twelve thereafter spread cotton-wool on the Saṅgha's beds and small chairs, and then others gathered it up and took it away. When nuns of few desires rebuked them for this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, established the rule of training up to that point.

"Furthermore, whatever nun stuffs or has stuffed cotton-wool into a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha — when it is gathered up, there is an offense entailing expiation."

As for the phrase "whatever nun" — this refers to the group of twelve. "Belonging to the Saṅgha" means belonging to the Saṅgha of female śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. "Bed" means a sleeping-bed. "Chair" means a small chair. As for the term "cotton-wool," there are five kinds of cotton-wool. What are the five? Cotton-wool from the arka plant, cotton-wool from the śalmalī tree, cotton-wool from the kaśa grass, wool from sheep, and fifth, cotton-wool from the śana plant. The phrase "stuffs or has stuffed — there is an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

How does the offense arise in this case? To whatever extent even a little of what is called a bed or chair of the Saṅgha is stuffed, in every instance there is an offense entailing expiation. Nevertheless, one must ask the one before whom it is being fitted whether it has been gathered up or not; the rest is as before.

This completes the sixth rule of the seventh category of offenses entailing expiation.

The ruling occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time many straps arose among the nuns in this manner: thinking "This strap is far too long," a nun would discard it and have another made; thinking "This strap is far too short," she would discard it and have another made; and likewise some were far too wide, others far too narrow. Because they acted in this way there was much work, and because there was much work, the recitation of the texts, the reading, the chanting, the yoga, the mental application, and the inner calm abiding of the mind were all being abandoned. When nuns of few desires rebuked them for this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, established the rule of training:

"When a nun makes a strap, she is to have it made according to the standard measure. The standard measure for a strap is this: in depth, one and a half of the Sugata's spans plus a span; in width, half a span plus a span. If made more than one span in height, she should unravel it. If made in excess of that, after unraveling there is an offense entailing expiation."

"Strap" means a strap. "Nun" means one who belongs to this Dharma. "Makes" means by herself. "Has made" means by another. "In depth" means however much liquid it can hold. As for "one span of the Sugata," the Sugata is the Teacher. Whatever constitutes one span of the Sugata corresponds to one standard cubit and a half plus a span; and whatever constitutes three spans of the Sugata corresponds to one standard cubit, one cubit, a half, and five. "In width, half a span plus a span" means one standard cubit, a span, and six finger-breadths. "In excess of that" means beyond that measure. "Makes" means by herself. "Has made" means by another. "There is an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

How does the offense arise in this case? To whatever extent a nun makes or has another make a strap even slightly in excess of one and a half spans plus five, in every instance after unraveling there is an offense entailing expiation. As for the phrase beginning "before whom the offense is being incurred" — the sequence of the offense is as before.

If a finished one is found, the finished one itself may be used. This completes the eighth rule of the seventh section on offenses entailing expiation.

The case setting is Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One had declared that monks and nuns should wear a robe for covering the shoulder, those nuns did not know what kind it should be or what its measure should be. The Blessed One then declared: "It shall be four Sugata-heights in height and one height in width." At the time when the Blessed One declared this measure, the group of twelve made theirs in excess of the measure, and those nuns of few wants rebuked them; this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "this occurrence" through to the laying down of the training rule, declared: "A nun who makes a robe for covering the shoulder shall have it made according to the measure." The measure of the robe for covering the shoulder is this: four Sugata-heights in height, and one Sugata-height in width. If she makes it in excess of that, after trimming it down there is an offense entailing expiation.

"Robe for covering the shoulder" means a robe for the sick. "Nun" means one who belongs to this Dharma. "Makes" means by herself. "Has another make it" means by another. "Four Sugata-heights in height" means six standard cubits, which is the measure of that Sugata's cubit. "Sugata" means the Teacher. "One Sugata-height in width" means three standard cubits. "In excess of that" means beyond that. "Makes" means by herself. "Has another make it" means by another. "After trimming" means after cutting it level. "There is an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

How does the offense arise in this case? To whatever extent a nun has another make a robe for covering the shoulder even slightly in excess of six cubits, in every instance after trimming there is an offense entailing expiation. As for the phrase beginning "before whom the offense is being incurred," the sequence is as before. This completes the ninth rule of the seventh section on offenses entailing expiation.

The case setting is Śrāvastī. At the time when Ānanda had a robe of the Sugata's prescribed measure made, and the Blessed One had prohibited this, Śobhā the female lay practitioner, upon seeing Ānanda, also had a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe, and having distributed it she went to the rains-retreat lodging of the nuns and, with some pieces of cloth of the Sugata's Dharma robe measure, tucked some under her armpits, draped some over her shoulders, spread some over her body, and sat there in a slovenly manner. The nuns said to her: "Noble lady, where are you going, having taken your bowl and Dharma robe?" She replied: "I am not going anywhere having taken my bowl and Dharma robe. Nevertheless, I did have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe." They then said to her: "Sister, did not the Blessed One prohibit this?" She replied: "He gave that prohibition to the monks, not to the nuns." Those nuns of few wants rebuked her, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "this occurrence" through to the laying down of the training rule, declared: "Moreover, whatever nun has another make a Dharma robe to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe, or has one made in excess of the Sugata's Dharma robe, after trimming there is an offense entailing expiation." The measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe is this:

In length, ten Sugata-cubits; in width, six Sugata-cubits. That is the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe.

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda.

"Has one made to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe" means: has a robe made to the measure of the Buddha's Dharma robe.

"In excess of" means: beyond that measure.

"That is the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe" is an enumeration of the categories.

"In length" refers to the length in question.

"Ten cubits" refers to ten Sugata-cubits, which equal fifteen standard cubits.

"Six cubits in width" — that equals nine standard cubits.

"An offense entailing expiation" — as stated above.

As for how the offense arises: whenever a nun, even to the slightest degree, has a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe, or has one made in excess of the Sugata's Dharma robe — in all such cases, after trimming, there is an offense entailing expiation.

The phrase "before whom she presents herself" and what follows arises as stated above.

The summary verse of the seventh section on offenses entailing expiation is now complete.

The mnemonic summary verse reads:

Garlic, nakedness, and one who has taken refuge,
whispering in the ear, a dark room, sitting there beforehand,
the rains retreat, twelve years within,
great desire, one who is young in the vows.

The further summary verse reads:

Garlic, hoeing and weeding the hair,
inserting two finger-joints,
striking with the palm — these are prohibited.
The origin story took place in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a terrible famine arose, and it was difficult for wandering mendicants in the forest to obtain food — so it is told up to the point: "There was a man who had a garlic garden, and many green herbs grew there." The nuns then asked that man for green herbs, and he said: "Please just take whatever you need — but do not pull up those garlic plants." Each day the man went to the nuns' rains-retreat residence bringing green herbs. Then Stout Ānanda asked the other nuns: "Sisters, where did you get these green herbs?" — and from that point the account continues until Stout Ānanda also went to the garlic garden and pulled up both the green herbs and the garlic together. The owner of the garlic, becoming alarmed, then sold the garlic garden to another person, and having done so said to the nuns: "Noble ladies, I have sold it to someone else — please ask that person for the green herbs." The new owner, however, placed a young boy as a watchman, allowing whatever else to be taken freely, but when the nuns came to pull green herbs, Stout Ānanda kept pulling out garlic as well. The boy tried to stop Stout Ānanda from pulling the garlic, and Stout Ānanda struck the boy. The boy told his father, and the next day the boy hid inside the garlic garden. Stout Ānanda came again and, as she was pulling garlic, the boy stopped her — and then, as it continues, the householder himself struck Stout Ānanda. She returned to the rains-retreat residence with her eye swollen shut, and when the nuns asked what had happened she told the whole story in full. The nuns of few wants rebuked her, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "this occurrence" through to the laying down of the training rule, declared: "Moreover, whatever nun eats garlic commits an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda.
"Garlic" refers to the bulb.
"Eats" means: swallows it covertly.
"An offense entailing expiation" — as stated above.

Now, how does one incur a transgression in this matter? The training rule was established as follows: a nun who eats even the slightest amount of garlic in any form whatsoever incurs a transgression. After this rule was laid down, there was a certain sick nun who consulted a physician, and the physician recommended garlic. The nun said: "Good sir, the physician — I am now as good as dead." The physician replied: "What is wrong?" She said: "The Blessed One has prohibited it." The physician said: "Your Teacher is compassionate; he will allow it." Thereupon the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "On a physician's prescription, there is no transgression for a sick person" — from that point through to: "Garlic, asafoetida (kiyū), and the like may all be used." The nuns then became uncertain, and in order to resolve all their uncertainties they appealed to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, look at how the nun Stout Ānanda, overcome by excessive attachment, was beaten on account of garlic." The Blessed One declared: "O monks, this is not only the case now; in times past as well, she was made to suffer wrongfully through excessive attachment. Listen!" — from that point through to: "In the city of Vārāṇasī there arose a king named Brahmadatta." Now, at one point a thief had broken into the royal palace — from that point through to: "having forgotten a silver bracelet at the child's door and left it behind, and then the thief, thinking to go back and retrieve it" — from that point through to: "he was seized by the king's guards and made to suffer wrongfully." Then a deity at that time spoke in verse:

When one is overcome by excessive attachment,
even what has been accomplished is lost.
One goes back seeking it again —
just as with the thief's bracelet, so it is.

"O monks, listen further to how one was utterly deprived of riches through excessive attachment alone. O monks, long ago in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a householder" — from that point through to: "a daughter was born to him, and after dying he was reborn as a king of geese who by his nature remembered his former life" — from that point through to: "each day he would bring jewels for the sake of the girl." Then the girl thought: "I will catch the king of geese and take the jewels too." But he fled and never returned. Then a deity spoke in verse:

Do not be excessively attached;
attachment contrary to the Dharma is sinful.
Through the thought of catching the king of geese,
one is utterly deprived of jewels.

O monks, what do you think? The thief and the girl of that time — they were none other than this very Stout Ānanda. From that time forward she became one of excessive attachment alone, and even now she is one of excessive attachment alone. Therefore one should not be excessively attached. O monks, train yourselves accordingly.

Here ends the first of the eight offenses entailing expiation.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time Stout Ānanda was performing the hair removal of the underarm region and washing that area, and she showed this to the wives of brahmins and householders, saying: "Look at how this spotted with sesame seeds appears." They said: "Noble lady, we do this to please our husbands — but what purpose does it serve you? Whom will you please? This is not fitting for one who has gone forth into renunciation." From that point through to: when the nuns of few wants rebuked her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," established the training rule up to its conclusion: "Furthermore, whatever nun performs hair removal in the region of the private parts incurs an offense entailing expiation in every case."

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "The region of the private parts" refers to the secret place. "Performs hair removal" means shaving or pulling out hair. "Incurs an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

As for how the transgression arises: however slight the hair removal a nun performs in the region of the private parts, she incurs an offense entailing expiation in every case. If it is done on account of a wound, there is no transgression.

This completes the second of the eight offenses entailing expiation.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time Stout Ānanda inserted her hand into the private place and washed it until the affliction was pacified, and thereby the private place became swollen. She kept crystal and sandalwood paste and the like nearby, and she told this to her companions and attendants. They said to her: "What is wrong with you?" She then related the matter in full, and it was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore nuns must not wash in that manner." But because they did not wash at all, a foul odor arose.

Then on another occasion, when the great lady Gautamī was teaching the Dharma to many wives of householders, they said to one another: "There is a foul smell." Then, since the great lady Gautamī was by nature straightforward, she said: "Sisters, that foul smell is hers." They said: "Why do you not wash?" The great lady Gautamī replied: "The Blessed One has forbidden it" — and so forth, until the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Therefore one should wash using two finger-joints." But in time that very practice came to be a cause of wrongdoing.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," established the training rule up to its conclusion: "Furthermore, whatever nun, when washing, inserts beyond two finger-joints, incurs an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "When washing" means having taken up water. "Inserts beyond two finger-joints" means more than that distance. "Incurs an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

As for how the transgression arises: however slightly a nun, when washing, inserts beyond two finger-joints, she incurs an offense entailing expiation in every case.

This completes the third of the eight offenses entailing expiation.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time Stout Ānanda, overcome by affliction, struck the private area with her palm until she was satisfied and the place became swollen. When the desire had subsided, she cried out in distress. Then, when her companions and attendants asked her about it, she related the matter in full, and when nuns of few wants rebuked her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," established the training rule up to its conclusion: "Furthermore, whatever nun strikes the female organ with her palm incurs an offense entailing expiation."

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "Strikes the female organ with her palm" means slapping the female mark with the palm. "Incurs an offense entailing expiation" is as above.

As for how the transgression arises: however slightly a nun strikes the female organ with her palm, she incurs an offense entailing expiation in every case.

The summary verses for the eighth class of offenses entailing expiation are now complete.

The summary verse reads:

One must not boil oneself naked,
nor scatter water about,
nor discard blue-green dung,
nor discard it behind a wall.

The founding occasion was at Śrāvastī.

The people of the city delighted in gardens and pleasure groves, and would frequent them regularly. Whenever they went into the pleasure groves, the stirrer would prepare the marinade. The householders therefore sent word ahead to the stirrer: "Come early tomorrow morning." Since she had not yet arrived, Stout Ānanda rose in the morning, put on her lower robe, took her Dharma robe and alms bowl, entered the alms-round district, and went into one householder's home, where she said: "Good lady, please give me alms." The householder's wife replied: "Noble one, I am not feeling well." Stout Ānanda said: "Why are you unwell?" The wife then explained the matter in full, whereupon Stout Ānanda said: "Why do you not stir it yourself?" She replied: "Noble one, I do not know how to do it." Stout Ānanda then said to the householder's wife: "Are you also someone whose work and that of your husband is all of one kind?" The wife replied: "Noble one, does your reverence know about it?" Stout Ānanda said: "Is there any craft or task in which she has not made herself skilled?"

Then the householder's wife said to Stout Ānanda: "Noble one, I now entreat you: please release the marinade and give it to me." Stout Ānanda replied: "Who then will give her alms?" The householder's wife said: "For that reason, I will offer to the nun who follows after me, I will offer to the preceptress, I will offer to the abbess, and I will offer even to the keeper of the residence." At those words, Stout Ānanda set her alms bowl and Dharma robe to one side, changed into different clothing, and — from there onward — washed the fermentation pot, scrubbed it, fired it, filled it with butter, and stirred it as the sequence required: first a gentle stir, then a thorough stir, then a stir to draw out the essence, and so on — yielding a frothy stage, a full-bodied stage, a skimming stage, a hundredfold-refined stage, and what resembles the form of a small creature. She cooked batches of all these kinds, and the smell from it pervaded half the town.

Then the people sitting in that half of the town came and asked: "Did the stirrer come to your home?" She replied: "She did not come. Nevertheless, the noble Stout Ānanda is doing the stirring." They too came and made their requests, and Stout Ānanda said: "Who then will give her alms?" They said: "We will offer to the residence keeper." And in like manner Stout Ānanda cooked all the marinades for half the city. Having cooked them, she took up the alms she had been offered, carried the load, and went to the rain-season dwelling.

Afterward the stirrer arrived and went door to door saying: "Housewives and ladies, please send out your marinades to be cooked." They replied: "They have already been cooked." The dyer asked: "By whom?" They replied: "By Stout Ānanda," and so the whole of the half-town came to know of it. At that, the dyer said: "The conduct of the mendicants who are sons of the Śākyan and their brahminical conduct are a sham — for this is how they cut short their livelihood!" and she began to revile them.

The nuns who were of few desires expressed their disapproval, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows: "Furthermore, whatever nun stirs up raw materials shall incur a transgression."

"Whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "Stirs up raw materials" means stirs up what has been prepared. "Shall incur a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however small the amount of raw material a nun stirs up, in every case she incurs a transgression.

Then a matter arose in the Saṅgha, and the Blessed One declared: "For the sake of the Saṅgha, one may sit in a secluded place and cook — there is no transgression." This concludes the first rule of the ninth group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time a certain householder, together with his wife, went forth from home into homelessness, and he went to the rains retreat dwelling to visit the nuns. While he was there, in the morning a nun was drinking some thick gruel, and another nun was standing before him holding a water vessel. Then that monk laughed and said: "When I was a householder, you used to stand before me like that." At that, she flung the water vessel at his head and said: "If you truly proclaim your own virtues, do you then enter into her faults?" and she fled. At that the nuns said: "Why did you pour water over the head of the chief of the assembly?" and the nuns of few desires expressed their disapproval. The matter was then reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows: "Furthermore, whatever nun pours water shall incur a transgression."

"Whatever" refers to a member of this Dharma community. "Chief of the assembly" means the foremost of the assembly. "Pours water" means with water. "Shall incur a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however small the amount of water a nun pours over the chief of the assembly, in every case she incurs a transgression. However, if one sprinkles water on the face of someone who has fainted, there is no transgression. This concludes the second rule of the ninth group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. Not far from the rains retreat dwelling there was a blue pool, and at that pool a brahmin was instructing five hundred brahmin boys in the secret words of the brahmins. Then those brahmin boys saw Stout Ānanda entering their domain, and they shouted at her. Now, Stout Ānanda had eaten a medicine that caused her to have diarrhea, and she had a great bout of it; she wiped herself and went up to the edge of the blue pool, and her discharge polluted the entire blue pool.

Then the brahmin boys came again and sat down. They said: "Sons of Kutsā, sons of Vatsā, sons of Bharadvāja — there is the stench of vomit!" And indeed their hands, feet, and clothes became fouled with the excrement. Since brahmins are desirous of purity, those brahmin boys sat there in great discomfort.

Then again, when Stout Ānanda returned from the alms round, she saw the brahmin boys sitting there in discomfort and said: "Ho there, brahmin boys! Have you done much harm?" Then she laughed and said: "You have been dealt with accordingly" — and so she reviled them. The nuns then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun discards excrement into green grass commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "Into green grass" means onto green vegetation. "Discards excrement" means foul matter. "Commits a transgression" is as above. As for how a transgression arises: whenever a nun thinks even slightly, "I am discarding this into green grass," and then discards excrement, in every such case she commits a transgression. This concludes the third rule of the ninth group of transgressions.

The Vinaya Analysis of the Nuns. The twenty-third fascicle. The occasion arose at Śrāvastī.

Stout Ānanda, having eaten and drunk in great quantity, was taken short in the night and placed a bronze chamber-pot and urinated into it. Now there was a man associated with the Great Elephant Trunk, named Palskyed, who had been punished with a fine by King Prasenajit. In the early morning hours he was passing from a place near the nuns' summer quarters on his way to the royal palace, when Stout Ānanda, without checking, threw out the bronze pot filled with urine, and it landed on his head. He then thought: "Will this be auspicious for me today, or inauspicious?" And so it came about that the keeper of the rhinoceros caused King Palskyed to show forbearance, and accordingly the king gave him an elephant named White Lotus, and restored to him his estate and authority as well.

Palskyed then took a large bolt of fine cloth and went to the nuns' summer quarters. When Stout Ānanda heard of this she became frightened. Then Palskyed spoke these words: "The one who, in the early morning hours, poured urine on me — that urine is something that brings auspicious joy. Therefore, today I wish to present a large bolt of fine cloth to the one who did so. Which nun was she?" Then Stout Ānanda said: "It was I." And he presented her with a large bolt of fine cloth.

Now when Stout Ānanda got into a quarrel with the other nuns, one of them said: "Even vomit is not equivalent to you." Then, reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "One must not discard without checking. If one discards, that is a transgression."

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun, without checking, discards excrement or urine commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "Without checking" means without having examined. "Discards excrement or urine" means if one throws it out. "Commits a transgression" is as above. As for how a transgression arises: whenever a nun, even slightly, discards excrement or urine without checking, in every such case she commits a transgression. However, if it is an empty building or a ruined wall, there is no transgression. This concludes the verse summary of the ninth group of transgressions.

The summary verse:

One must not sit alone with a man
in a place of shelter together with a nun,
nor with a man without cover,
nor with two who are not monks,
dwelling in solitude.

The occasion arose at Śrāvastī. Then, when Stout Ānanda was conversing with a man together in a sheltered place, brahmin wives and householders' wives said: "She signals in such a way and then will engage in misconduct at night." When nuns of few desires condemned her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun, alone, sits in seclusion with a single man in a sheltered place commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. "Together with a man" means with a male person.

The phrase "alone" means that no third person is present, whether a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex.

Regarding the phrase "in a sheltered and secluded place," there are three kinds of shelter: shelter provided by a wall, shelter provided by a screen, and shelter provided by a curtain.

The phrase "sits" means conversing.

The phrase "commits a transgression" is as before.

How does the transgression come about? Whatever the extent to which a nun sits together with a man in a sheltered and secluded place, in every case she commits a transgression.

Here ends the first rule of the tenth group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At the time when Carka and Bema had gone forth, Carka went to the residence where the nuns were on their rains retreat, and sat together with Bema in a sheltered and secluded place. When nuns of few desires condemned her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "this occurrence" and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun, alone, sits together with a single monk in a sheltered and secluded place commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Bema. "Alone, together with a single monk" means with Carka, in a place where no third person is present, whether a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. The remainder, down through "in a sheltered and secluded place," is as before.

The phrase "sits" means conversing.

The phrase "commits a transgression" is as before.

How does the transgression come about? Whatever the extent to which a nun sits together with a monk in a sheltered and secluded place, in every case she commits a transgression. If a companion is present, there is no transgression.

Here ends the second rule of the tenth group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. Stout Ānanda sat alone with a man in an unsheltered place and used words of coded allusion, saying "game of theft." The Blessed One, beginning from that point and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun, alone, sits together with a single man in an open and unsheltered place in seclusion commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. The rest is as before.

The phrase "unsheltered" means in the open.

The phrase "sits in seclusion" means conversing, and this is the distinguishing feature.

The phrase "commits a transgression" is as before.

How does the transgression come about? Whatever the extent to which a nun sits together with a man in an open and unsheltered place, in every case she commits a transgression. If a companion is present, there is no transgression.

Here ends the third rule of the tenth group of transgressions.

Likewise, beginning from the occasion of Bema and Carka sitting together in seclusion in an unsheltered place, and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule, the Blessed One did so as follows:

Furthermore, whatever nun, alone, sits together with a single monk in an unsheltered and secluded place commits a transgression. The phrase "whatever" refers to Bema. The monk is Carka. The rest is as it arises from what precedes.

The phrase "commits a transgression" is as before.

How does the transgression come about? Whatever the extent to which a nun, and so forth, is as before. If a companion is present, there is no transgression.

Here ends the fourth rule of the tenth group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. When Stout Ānanda made a signal to a man, he spoke to her thus: "Noble one, you have gone forth, and I am a layman within the household. If someone were to come to know this, both of us would be blamed." She replied: "What are you thinking? Must one come with conches blowing and kettledrums beating? Even so, come to the dwelling room of the rains residence." Thereupon that man came to the dwelling room. Then Stout Ānanda seated that man on a throne in a sheltered place and spoke as follows:

She said, "I am going to wash the abbess's feet," and departed. That man then made a request to the abbess and also received a scriptural recitation. He also engaged in conversation that brought scriptural recitations to the novices. In doing so much activity and accomplishing so many things, he forgot about the man altogether. Then he washed his feet outside the shrine hall, entered the dwelling room, and sat down upon the throne. At that point the man also began to stir. As he stirred and lifted the throne covering, she shouted, "A thief! A thief!" and called out an alarm. Thereupon that man talked back and fled. The nuns were scandalized, and in that state of scandal they began to reproach her, whereupon the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This being the occasion," proceeded through to the establishment of the rule of training: "Furthermore, if any nun who is alone, without a companion nun, spends the night in a dwelling room where there are no nuns, she commits a transgression." The phrase "any" refers to Stout Ānanda. The phrase "alone, without a companion, spends the night in a nun's dwelling room" means if she sleeps there. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises in this case: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun sleeps alone in a dwelling room without a companion, in every instance she commits a transgression.

Here ends the verse summary of the tenth group of transgressions.

The verse summary is as follows:

Whispering into ears — two cases —
and for oneself, claims of high station,
taking an oath in the celibate life,
and not speaking of a fault one has seen.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. When Stout Ānanda whispered in the ear of a certain man, brahmins and householders said: "She went forth for the sake of the Dharma, yet she whispers in the ear of one who lives in the household, and one who lives in the household whispers back to her — what difference is there between the two? What is the intention? What distinction is there?" And they mocked her. The nuns of few desires, in that state of reproach, reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This being the occasion," proceeded through to the establishment of the rule of training: "Furthermore, if any nun whispers in the ear of a man, she commits a transgression." The phrase "any" refers to Stout Ānanda. The phrase "whispers in the ear" means speaks words into the ear. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun whispers into the ear of a man, in every instance she commits a transgression.

Here ends the first rule of the eleventh group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. In the same way, when Ched-ma whispering in the ear of Char-ka — up to the point where the nuns of few desires reproved her — that matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This being the occasion," proceeded through to the establishment of the rule of training: "Furthermore, if any nun whispers in the ear together with a monk, she commits a transgression." The phrase "any" refers to Ched-ma. The phrase "monk" refers to Char-ka. The phrase "whispers in the ear together" means speaks words into the ear. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun whispers in the ear of a monk, in every instance she commits a transgression.

Here ends the second rule of the eleventh group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, when Stout Ānanda fell into a dispute with the nuns, she would bring up certain quarrels in conversation, and in doing so she would take the side of her own party,

the nuns of few wants censured them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and so forth, proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, in a state of agitation, strikes herself commits a transgression."

The phrase "whatever" refers to Stout Ānanda. The phrase "strikes herself" means she beats upon her own body. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun strikes her own body, in every instance she commits a transgression.

Here ends the third rule of the eleventh group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, whatever quarrel arose among the members of the Twelve Groups, wherever it arose, they would swear oaths by the Buddha in every case. They swore oaths by the Dharma, by the Saṅgha, by those who dwell in the holy life, by the preceptress, and by the teacher. The nuns of few wants censured them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and so forth, proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun swears an oath by the holy life commits a transgression."

The phrase "whatever" refers to the members of the Twelve Groups. The phrase "by the holy life" means swearing an oath by moral discipline. The phrase "swears an oath" means she does so in order to make herself believed. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun swears an oath by the Buddha, she commits a transgression. By the Dharma, she commits a transgression. By the Saṅgha, she commits a transgression. By those who dwell in the holy life, she commits a transgression. By the preceptress and the teacher, in every instance she commits a transgression.

Here ends the fourth rule of the eleventh group of transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, the members of the Twelve Groups got into a dispute with the nuns. When the dispute arose, they would bring up charges against the nuns. Whenever they were unable to prevail, they would bring up charges against the nuns on the basis of having seen a fault, bring up charges on the basis of having heard of a fault, and bring up charges on the basis of suspecting a fault. The nuns of few wants censured them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with "this occurrence" and so forth, proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun brings up charges against nuns on the basis of having seen a fault, having heard of a fault, or suspecting a fault commits a transgression."

The phrase "whatever" refers to the members of the Twelve Groups. The phrase "against nuns" means against the practitioners of this Dharma. "Brings up charges on the basis of having seen a fault commits a transgression." The phrase "brings up charges without having investigated on the basis of having heard of a fault or suspecting a fault" means she reviles them. The phrase "commits a transgression" is as above. As to how the transgression arises: however much and to whatever slight degree a nun brings up charges on the basis of having seen a fault, she commits a transgression. On the basis of having heard of a fault, she commits a transgression. On the basis of suspecting a fault, she commits a transgression.

Here ends the verse summary of the eleventh group of transgressions.

The verse summary reads:

In darkness, with lac sealed tight,
and going forth without entrustment,
spreading out a layman's seat —
upon that seat one must not lie.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, when the nuns were wandering through the countryside, they came to a certain mountain district. There they obtained a lodging from a certain householder, and that evening, while they were staying in that place, it happened that in the middle of the night rain fell, and the nuns pressed their way into a recess at the back of the dwelling to shelter from it. Now there was already a man in that recess who had entered before them. That man seized a nun and violated her.

As soon as the nuns made their request and were released, they returned to Śrāvastī, and there, in the interval during which they gave a full account of the matter to the other nuns, those nuns reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "This misfortune that has arisen has come about through nuns taking up lodging in a dwelling without having inspected it." Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with the words "This incident," proceeded to establish a training rule. It runs thus: "Furthermore, whichever nun takes up lodging in a dwelling without having inspected it commits a transgression." The phrase "whichever" refers to those within this Dharma. "Without having inspected" means without having made an inquiry. "Takes up lodging" means sleeping in the home of a householder. "Commits a transgression" is as before. As to how the transgression arises: whenever a nun sleeps even a little while in a householder's dwelling, in a dark recess, without having inspected it, in every such case she commits a transgression.

This is the first of the twelfth set of transgressions. It is complete.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At that time, Stout-and-Joyful went to the dwelling of a woman whose husband had gone abroad, and asked her: "Until that time, how do you relieve your affliction? You have gone forth into homelessness — what need is there to ask?" — up to the words "with a leather strap (Skt. carmabandha)." Then, as soon as Stout-and-Joyful went to the noble queen Phreng-ldan-ma and asked her: "Your Majesty, if your august belly grows large and you must travel to another region, how do you relieve your affliction?" — and the queen replied in these words: "You have gone forth, so why ask?" — down to the words "with a leather strap it is." Then, as soon as Stout-and-Joyful went to the maker of leather straps and, having purchased a leather strap, came to the summer dwelling, and at night bound it to the heel of her foot and relieved her affliction — at which point a fire broke out in the summer dwelling — and, as Stout-and-Joyful awoke startled, looked about, and came tumbling down the stairs naked and shivering, and there arose the sound of her crying out, a great crowd of people burst into laughter. It is said that they declared: "Ask your mother! Ask your sister! Ask your daughter!" — up to that point.

Now, when certain nuns of few concerns censured her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, beginning with the words "This incident," proceeded to establish a training rule. It runs thus: "Furthermore, whichever nun keeps a leather strap commits a transgression." The phrase "whichever" refers to Stout-and-Joyful. "Kept" means fashioned from leather. "By herself" means on her own. "Commits a transgression" is as before. As to how the transgression arises: whenever a nun carries even a little leather strap, in every such case she commits a transgression.

The monks grew doubtful, whereupon — from that point down to the words "Venerable One, look upon how Stout-and-Joyful made a great crowd of people burst into laughter."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is not only in the present that Stout-and-Joyful has made a great crowd of people burst into laughter — in a time gone by she did so as well. Monks, hear this." "Monks, long ago in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta was ruling his kingdom. There was a brahmin who took as wife the daughter of a brahmin from a provincial region" — down to "that brahmin's daughter could not please that brahmin" — and so, in order to convey her to a weaver's house, the girl mounted a donkey,

As she set out for the home of that girl's father, and from "when the girl asked, he spoke" down to "when the girl asked, the brahmin, just as customarily described, began to lie down with her" — and since the brahmin was one who desired cleanliness and was going to fetch water, at that moment a hen startled the donkey with the sound of her flapping wings, causing it to bolt. The donkey bolted, and in that very same attire she was carried from that city through a great crowd of people, who all burst into laughter.

Then that brahmin spoke this verse at that time:

A hen's wings beat and flapped,
the donkey started up in fright.
Because of what this woman did,
I too am shamed and mortified.

"Monks, what do you think? That brahmin's daughter — she is none other than this very Stout-and-Joyful" — and so on down to "then as now."

Here ends the second section of the twelfth chapter on offenses.

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī.

Then the wives of brahmins and householders, a great many of them, petitioned the noble Stout-and-Joyful, saying, "Noble one, please teach us the Dharma." She said to them, "Prepare a seat." They arranged a seat for her. She sat down right there on that prepared seat, looked toward a long wall, took hold of a lengthy sūtra, and launched into an explanation.

The brahmins and the wives of the householders then thought to themselves, "The task of nuns consists solely in reading and reciting — if we stay, our household duties will fall into disarray," and so they departed. The nun who was attending behind her said, "Noble one, to whom are you teaching the Dharma?" She replied, "To the brahmins and the wives of the householders." "They have grown weary and departed." — And with that, Stout-and-Joyful too set down her seat and left.

Those who had not been given the seat stole it. And when the brahmins and the wives of the householders began to reproach her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, from "this occurrence" down to "laid down a training rule," pronounced: Any nun who, while teaching the Dharma, abandons a seat without handing it over to a householder and departs commits an offense.

"Any" refers to Stout-and-Joyful. "Without handing it over" means without handing it to its owner. "Departs" means if she goes away. "Commits an offense" — as explained above. As for how the offense comes about: however slight the movement by which a nun departs without handing the seat over to its owner, it constitutes an offense throughout.

Here ends the third section of the twelfth chapter on offenses.

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī.

Now, in the central country it was the custom at the homes of brahmins and householders that the seats that had been arranged were not to be contaminated, and so a certain brahmin, after arranging a seat there, placed a guardian woman beside it. Stout-and-Joyful entered that house for the sake of alms and said, "Fair one, give alms." The woman replied, "Noble one, I am guarding the seat." She said to her, "Let the guard keep watch for you — you go and bring back the alms." That woman then entered inside to collect the alms, and Stout-and-Joyful sat down on the brahmin's seat. When the brahmin arrived and saw Stout-and-Joyful sitting on that seat, he began to berate her — and at that the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, from "this occurrence" down to "laid down a training rule," pronounced: Any nun who, without permission, sits down on a seat inside a house commits an offense.

Now, "whoever" refers to Stout-and-Joyful. "Without permission" means without having checked with the householder. "Sitting on a householder's seat inside a house" means having sat down there. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does the transgression occur? However long a nun sits, even for a moment, on a householder's seat inside a house without permission, in every instance she commits an offense. The fourth rule of the twelfth set of offenses is complete.

The occasion for the next rule was at Śrāvastī. A large number of nuns were wandering through the countryside, and they took up lodging for the night in the house of a rope-maker, spreading their bedding inside. Afterward, when the lamps were extinguished, the householder arrived and neither saw nor heard the nuns who were there. Then, when the householder went to lie with his wife, an indecent sound was made — and a young nun who had gone forth heard it and told others what had happened. The householder then said to his wife, "Who said that?" She replied, "It was a nun." When the householder heard this he became angry and said, "Why are you granting lodging to those who create disturbances in the world?" In his anger he drove them out at midnight. The nuns made an appeal, and from that point the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, from "this occurrence" down to "laid down a training rule," pronounced: Any nun who, without having checked with the householder, takes up lodging for the night inside a house commits an offense.

"Whoever" refers to a nun belonging to this same discipline. "Without having checked with the householder of the rope-maker's house" means in the rope-maker's house. "Takes up lodging for the night" means intending to sleep there. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does the transgression occur? However long a nun, without having checked with the householder, intends to spend the night inside a house, in every instance she commits an offense. The verse summary of the twelfth set of offenses is complete.

The summary verse reads:

Knowing that others were seated there before,
attending to the sick,
not being expelled from a rains-retreat dwelling,
and not sharing a single bed or chair.

The occasion for the next rule was at Śrāvastī. At that time Stout-and-Joyful was wandering through the countryside and entered a certain householder's dwelling. Some nuns who had already been staying there had not shown her the courtesies due a guest. She then used a stratagem to drive them out of that house, and nuns of few desires complained about her conduct. The matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, from "this occurrence" down to "laid down a training rule," pronounced: Any nun who, knowing full well that nuns had been residing in a place from before, arrives there at a later time and drives them out of the house commits an offense.

"Whoever" refers to Stout-and-Joyful. "Who had been residing from before" means who had been staying there from the outset. "Knowing full well" means whether she knows this herself or has been told by another. "Nuns" refers to those of this same discipline. "Arrives there at a later time" means on a different occasion. "Drives them out of the house" means from the lodging. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does the transgression occur? However often a nun drives out nuns who had been residing there from before, in every instance she commits an offense. The first rule of the thirteenth set of offenses is complete.

The occasion for the next rule was at Śrāvastī.

At that time, Stomhagimon had set aside those who dwelled with her and her attendants, and did not care for them when they were ill. Because they were without a protector and were suffering in an improper manner, this was reported to the Blessed One on the occasion when the nuns of little standing were speaking in reproach. The Blessed One then, beginning from "this occurrence," and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Furthermore, whatever nun sets aside those who dwell with her and her attendants, and when they are ill does not care for them, commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to Stomhagimon. "Sets aside those who dwell with her and her attendants" means having sent them away after they had gone forth. "When ill" means when afflicted by sickness. "Does not care for them" means with root medicines and the like. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does the transgression occur? However often a nun, having set aside even a small number of those in her retinue, does not care for them when they are ill, in every instance she commits an offense. The second rule of the thirteenth set of offenses is complete.

The occasion for the next rule was at Śrāvastī.

Then Stomhagimon thought: "Which nun shall I drive out of this rains-retreat dwelling?" And she reflected: "This great mistress of beings is one who renounces with a great retinue.
