This Dharma-giver, too, is one who recites scripture with a great retinue. But this lean Gautamī is of little standing, with a retinue of little standing. I shall drive out the small Gautamī." So she thought. Then, in the morning, Stomhagimon raised conversation about food, and in the morning distributed loin-cloths completely and went off, all of them departing. As for lean Gautamī, she had engaged those nuns in wholesome activities. Then lean Gautamī thought: "Now I ought to teach the Dharma to Stomhagimon as well." So lean Gautamī began to teach Dharma to Stomhagimon, saying: "Sister, are you only thinking about food? Is it not for the sake of what is wholesome?" Then Stomhagimon thought: "I have waited a long time and now I have found my opportunity." And she reviled her with the words "flesh-eater of her own child, deranged one, one fit for the charnel ground," and during that very rains retreat drove her out of the rains-retreat dwelling. When the nuns of little standing were reproaching her for this, it was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning from "this occurrence," and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having become enraged, agitated, and wrathful, drives a nun out of a rains-retreat dwelling, commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to Stomhagimon. "Enraged, agitated, and wrathful" means abiding in a state thoroughly bound up with anger. "A nun" refers to lean Gautamī. "Out of a rains-retreat dwelling" means from the dwelling. "Drives out" means expels. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does the transgression occur? Whether by bodily action, by verbal declaration, or by both together — it arises just as is stated in the offenses involving abandonment. The third rule of the thirteenth set of offenses is complete.

The occasion for the next rule was at Śrāvastī.

At that time, one near death and one approaching death were sleeping on the same seat. While those two were lying on the one seat, behaving in a manner resembling a man and a woman lying down together — laughing, being distracted, and rubbing their bodies roughly against each other — this was reported to the Blessed One when the nuns of little standing were ridiculing them. The Blessed One then, beginning from "this occurrence," and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Furthermore, whatever nun sleeps on the same seat together with a nun, commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to one near death and one approaching death.

"On the one seat" means on the one bed. "Commits an offense" is as before. How does a transgression come about in this case? However much a nun lies together with a nun on the one seat, in every instance she commits an offense.

Then again, when the nuns were wandering and going about, they found large couches and each took one for sleeping, while the rest were made to suffer. The laywomen then said this: "Noble ones, all of these couches are available for your use — why do you each sleep separately?" The nuns replied that the Blessed One had prohibited it. This was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, out of proper shame and modesty, place a dividing barrier — such as a stick or a begging bowl strap and so forth — in between, and each one wrapping her own body in her own robe, she may then lie down. In this there is no need for remorse." The fourth of the thirteenth offenses is complete.

Similarly, what follows regarding a hammock is to be stated in full. Having established the training rule up to that point, the text continues: "Furthermore, whatever nun sleeps with a nun on the same hammock without a barrier between them commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to one near death and one approaching death. "Hammock" means something suspended tier upon tier. "Without a barrier between them" means allowing the body to make bodily contact on one's own side. "Sleeps" means staying through the night. "Commits an offense" is as before. How does a transgression come about in this case? However much a nun lies with a nun on a hammock without a barrier between them, in every instance she commits an offense — as it is stated in the root text. The summary verse of the thirteenth set of offenses is complete.

The summary verse: One must not travel during the rains retreat; traveling after the rains retreat is concluded, and the two — the region of suspicion and the hamlet — temples come last. The origin of this rule is in Śrāvastī.

At that time Bhagūmati, together with her retinue, was wandering and going about during the rains retreat. The nuns questioned those nuns: "Sisters, why do you wander and travel about during the rains retreat?" They replied: "The noble Bhagūmati says that she knows the three collections of scripture and declares that the time for traveling has not yet come." The nuns of little standing criticized them, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning from "this occurrence," and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Furthermore, whatever nun wanders and travels about during the rains retreat commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to Bhagūmati. "During the rains retreat" means before the invitation ceremony has been performed. "Travels about" means going to a village, a town, a district, or a royal palace. "Commits an offense" is as before. How does a transgression come about? However much a nun wanders and travels about during the rains retreat, she commits an offense. The first of the fourteenth set of offenses is complete.

The origin of this rule too is in Śrāvastī. The nuns then said to Bhagūmati: "Noble one, the invitation ceremony has been performed — you may now travel." She replied: "She knows the three collections of scripture, and declares that the time for traveling has not yet come." Those nuns said to the other nuns: "Sisters, the invitation ceremony has already been performed — why are you not traveling?" They replied: "The noble Bhagūmati says that she knows the three collections and declares that the time for traveling has not yet come." The nuns of little standing criticized them, and this was reported to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," proceeded to lay down a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having completed the rains retreat, wanders and does not set out, commits an offense." "Furthermore, whatever" refers to Bhagūmati. "Having completed the rains retreat, wanders and does not set out" means after the invitation ceremony has been performed. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does an offense arise in this case? However much a nun wanders and does not set out after the invitation ceremony has been performed, in every instance she commits an offense. Even from one meditation hut to another she must go forth.

This concludes the second rule among the fourteenth offenses.

The occasion for the next rule is in Rājagṛha. At that time an announcement was made by Ajātaśatru: "Let no one go to Vaiśālī." The nuns then set out from Rājagṛha traveling toward Vaiśālī. As they were going, robbers harassed them along the road. At that point the nuns reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a nun must not travel through a district that is known to be dangerous." Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," proceeded to lay down a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun travels through a dangerous road into an inner district, commits an offense." "Furthermore, whatever" refers to one of the same kind. "A dangerous road" means a road known to be fearful. "Inner district" means one that is mutually hostile to another. "Travels" means wandering through it. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does an offense arise? However much a nun travels and goes between two mutually hostile districts, she commits an offense.

This concludes the third rule among the fourteenth offenses.

The occasion for the next rule is in Vaiśālī. Beginning with "The people of Vaiśālī made an announcement: 'Let no one go to Rājagṛha,'" the text proceeds to the laying down of a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun travels through a dangerous road into an outer district, commits an offense." The transgression is to be applied in conformity with the preceding rules.

This concludes the fourth rule among the fourteenth offenses.

The occasion for the next rule is in Rājagṛha. At that time Bhagūmati went to a shrine and engaged in disputes with the shrine keepers and also with others who were disputing there. After the sun had set she returned to the meditation hut saying, "My back and waist are aching," whereupon they asked her: "Where did you go?" She replied: "She settled the disputes at the shrine." They then said: "And the female renunciant who accompanied you?" She said that she had gone alone. At that point nuns of little standing criticized her, and this was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "On account of this occurrence," proceeded to lay down a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun goes to a shrine and engages in dispute, commits an offense." "Furthermore, whatever" refers to Bhagūmati. "Shrine" refers to the shrine of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). "Goes to" means having entered. "Engages in dispute" means engages in quarreling. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does an offense arise? However much a nun goes to a shrine and disputes with non-Buddhists, in every instance she commits an offense.

This concludes the fifth rule among the fourteenth offenses.

The occasion for the next rule is in Śrāvastī. At the time when visiting shrines was prohibited, there was going to a painter's house for the purpose of viewing it, and —

— and going to a dancer's house for the purpose of viewing it, nuns of little ambition criticized her. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun goes to a painter's house or a dancer's house for the purpose of viewing it commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to Bhagūmati. "A painter's house or a dancer's house" refers to whatever households are not ones into which nuns should enter. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does an offense arise? However much a nun goes, even a little, to a painter's house or a dancer's house for the purpose of viewing it, in every instance she commits an offense.

This concludes the verse summary of the fourteenth offenses.

The Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns, the twenty-fourth section.

The summary verse:

Not having reached twelve years,
having reached twelve years but not having been instructed,
having served in a household for twelve years —
yet even so, if not appointed by the Saṅgha.

The occasion is in Śrāvastī. The group of twelve then asked the monks: "After how many years do you take full ordination?" The monks replied: "After ten years." The group of twelve then said to the monks: "We too take full ordination after ten years, and you too take full ordination after ten years — so what is the difference between you and us? What is the intention? What is the distinction?" When they said this, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, it is permitted. A nun shall take full ordination after she has completed twelve years." Then Bhagūmati gave full ordination to someone who had not yet completed twelve years, and nuns of little ambition criticized her. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun gives full ordination to one who has not completed twelve years commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to Bhagūmati. "Who has not completed twelve years" refers to one who has not yet completed the twelve years required for full ordination. "Gives full ordination" means causes her to enter the assembly. "Commits an offense" is as explained above. How does an offense arise? However much a nun causes even one who has not completed twelve years to enter the assembly, in every instance she commits an offense.

This concludes the first rule among the fifteenth offenses.

The occasion is in Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One had declared that one who had not completed twelve years should not be admitted to the assembly, they were nonetheless admitting them indiscriminately — and those who were childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled were also being admitted to the assembly, so that they remained untamed and unpurified. The nuns reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Whoever wishes to admit someone to the assembly should request the vow of admitting to the assembly from the Saṅgha." The request is to be made as follows: having prepared the seating arrangement, and having struck the gong, with a response to the question, one fully informs the nuns in the assembly. That nun, sitting at the end of the senior nuns, bows to the assembly of nuns, and with palms pressed together, speaks these words: "Noble Saṅgha, sisters, please hear me.

"I, the nun called such-and-such, request from the noble Saṅgha the vow of admitting to the assembly. I, the nun called such-and-such, have come before the noble Saṅgha and request the vow of admitting to the assembly. May the noble Saṅgha, out of compassionate regard, grant to me, the nun called such-and-such, the vow of admitting to the assembly." This is to be repeated in the same way a second and a third time.

After that, a single nun makes the formal request and performs the act. The request is to be made as follows: "Noble Saṅgha, sisters, please hear me. This nun called such-and-such has come before the noble Saṅgha and requests the vow of admitting to the assembly. If the time is right for the noble Saṅgha and it is agreeable, may the noble Saṅgha give its consent, and in this way may the noble Saṅgha grant to the nun called such-and-such the vow of admitting to the assembly. This is the request."

The formal act is to be performed as follows: "Noble Saṅgha, sisters, please hear me. This nun called such-and-such has come before the noble Saṅgha and has requested the vow of admitting to the assembly. The noble Saṅgha is granting to the nun called such-and-such the vow of admitting to the assembly. Those among the noble Saṅgha who consent to the noble Saṅgha granting to the nun called such-and-such the vow of admitting to the assembly, let them remain silent. Those who do not consent, let them speak. The noble Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the noble Saṅgha has granted to the nun called such-and-such the vow of admitting to the assembly. Because no one has spoken, it is held to be so."

Then, when Sthūlanandā admitted someone to the assembly without the Saṅgha's approval, the nuns of few desires took occasion to censure her and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurred," proceeded to establish the training rule, as follows: "Furthermore, if any nun admits someone to the assembly without having requested from the Saṅgha the vow of admitting a nun to the assembly, she commits an offense."

The term "furthermore" refers to Sthūlanandā. "From the Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of female hearers (śrāvakas) of the Tathāgata. "The vow of admitting to the assembly" refers to the act performed by the request and the twofold motion. "Without having requested" means without having received it. "Admits someone to the assembly" means grants the going forth (pravrajyā), full ordination (upasaṃpadā), or a residence. "She commits an offense" is as explained above. As for how the offense arises: to whatever extent a nun admits someone to the assembly without having requested the vow of admitting to the assembly, in all such cases she commits an offense.

This completes the second of the fifteen offenses.

The locus of the rule is Śrāvastī. Then there arrived women who had kept house for twelve years, and after they went forth they were kept waiting for twenty years before receiving full ordination. They said: "For what reason are we not receiving full ordination?" The nuns replied: "You have not yet become accustomed to the life." Those women then said: "Noble sisters, when we were still living as householders, we held the mind of a woman who could be married, and the mind of a woman of the household, and in like manner we performed many household duties — will this not please the assembly of nuns?" When they said this, the nuns reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

Therefore, granting permission, he declared: "If a woman has kept the ways of the household for twelve years, she may receive full ordination."

When the Blessed One had declared that a woman who has kept the ways of the household for twelve years may receive full ordination, there arose at that time the case of Sthūlanandā giving full ordination to women who had not yet completed twelve years, and nuns of lesser standing rebuking her for this; and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One performed all the acts beginning with "this occurrence" up through the laying down of the training rule, as follows:

"Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly gives full ordination to a woman who has not kept the ways of the household for twelve years commits a transgression."

"Furthermore, whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Knowingly" means either by herself knowing or having been told by another. "Kept the ways of the household" means having dwelt in the ways of household life. "Twelve years" means for twelve full years. "Not completed twelve years" means having completed only eleven years. "Gives full ordination" refers to the actual act of ordaining as a nun. "Commits a transgression" is as explained above.

As for how a transgression comes about: a nun commits a transgression to whatever extent she gives full ordination to a woman who has not completed twelve years.

This concludes the third of the fifteenth group of offenses.

The origin story takes place in Śrāvastī.

At a certain time, a deluded man — a person of high birth but a companion of unwholesome friends, a son of the mother of suffering — reviled the Śākyas. At that time, a great many Śākya women, tormented by grief over their husbands and sons, went forth into the renunciant life. When they had gone forth thus tormented by grief over husbands and sons, they were at that time not tormented by mental afflictions. But when their grief subsided, they then became tormented by mental afflictions.

The Śākya women then spoke at that time with Sthūlanandā, and Sthūlanandā said: "I am now in the state of old age — what can I do? But you are beautiful, pleasing to behold, and lovely. Now each of you should know your own situation: enjoy yourselves with wealthy men, merchants, and caravan leaders. Be glad. Live in enjoyment and pleasure."

Thereupon those women went to Gautamī the Slim, and they told her in full what Sthūlanandā had advised them. And she spoke thus: "Sisters, let us set aside for now the sufferings of the world beyond. Listen to what she herself has experienced as suffering in this very world: the death of a husband, separation from a son, being struck down by one's own father and mother, eating the flesh of one's child, being driven to the charnel ground, mental disturbance, and being seized by madness — if one experiences only suffering, and nothing but suffering, in this very world, what need is there even to speak of the world beyond? Sisters, do not do such a thing." And Gautamī the Slim thus turned those many Śākya women away from non-virtue and directed their minds toward virtue. When they then said, "Sthūlanandā has cast us back into an impure pit," the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Therefore, granting permission: give them the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years. Let them train in these for two years and come to delight in them."

When the Blessed One had declared the six dharmas and

the vow of training in the six harmonious dharmas, they did not know how to confer it. So the Blessed One declared: "Prepare a seat, strike the gong" — and with those words as the opening, he gave full instructions to the nuns in response to their question.

The woman who has kept a household for twelve years and has reached the end of her seniority sits at the foot of her elder, joins her palms, and speaks these words: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters be pleased to hear me. I, called such-and-such, request full ordination from the preceptress called such-and-such. I, called such-and-such, request from the noble Saṅgha the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years through the preceptress called such-and-such. May the noble Saṅgha, out of compassion, out of close compassion, be pleased to confer upon me, called such-and-such, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years." This is to be recited in the same way a second and a third time.

After that, she is moved from the range of hearing to the range of sight, and one nun makes the motion, and the formal act is performed as follows: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters be pleased to hear me. This woman called such-and-such, who has kept a household for twelve years, requests from the noble Saṅgha, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years. If it seems right to the noble Saṅgha and they consent, may the noble Saṅgha grant it. In this way, may the noble Saṅgha confer upon this one called such-and-such, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years." This is the motion.

The formal act is performed as follows: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters be pleased to hear me. This woman called such-and-such, who has kept a household for twelve years, requests from the noble Saṅgha, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years. The noble Saṅgha confers upon this one called such-and-such, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years. Those members of the noble Saṅgha who consent to the conferral of the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years upon this one called such-and-such, through the preceptress called such-and-such, are to remain silent. Those who do not consent are to speak." The noble Saṅgha having consented and approved, the noble Saṅgha has conferred upon this one called such-and-such, through the preceptress called such-and-such, the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas for two years. The silence is so recorded, and it is held to be so.

When the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six harmonious dharmas had been conferred upon them for two years, and they had come to delight in that training, the Blessed One then declared: "After that, confer upon them the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya."

When the Blessed One had declared, "Confer the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya," they again did not know how to do so. The Blessed One declared: "Prepare a seat" — and with those words as the opening, he gave full instructions to the nuns in response to their question. The woman who has kept a household for twelve years, having reached the end of her seniority, sits at the foot of her elder, joins her palms before the assembly of nuns, and speaks.

She shall speak these words: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters please hear me. I, who am called such-and-such, wish to receive full ordination from the preceptress called such-and-such. I, who am called such-and-such, request that the preceptress called such-and-such, out of compassion, taking me near with compassion, please confer upon me, called such-and-such, the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya from the noble Saṅgha." This is to be repeated in the same way a second and third time.

After that, one nun shall make the formal request, and the act shall be performed. The formal request is as follows: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters please hear me. This person called such-and-such seeks full ordination from the preceptress called such-and-such. This person called such-and-such requests the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya from the noble Saṅgha, through the preceptress called such-and-such. If it is the right time and the noble Saṅgha is willing, may the noble Saṅgha grant its permission, and may the noble Saṅgha bestow upon the person called such-and-such the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya through the preceptress called such-and-such." This is the formal request.

The formal act is to be performed as follows: "May the noble Saṅgha of sisters please hear me. This person called such-and-such seeks full ordination from the preceptress called such-and-such. This person called such-and-such requests the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya from the noble Saṅgha through the preceptress called such-and-such. The noble Saṅgha is now conferring upon this person called such-and-such the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya through the preceptress called such-and-such. Those members of the noble Saṅgha who consent to conferring upon the person called such-and-such the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya through the preceptress called such-and-such shall remain silent; those who do not consent shall speak." The noble Saṅgha has consented and granted permission, and the noble Saṅgha has conferred upon the person called such-and-such the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya through the preceptress called such-and-such. Since no one has spoken, it is so held to be.

In this way, when the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya has been conferred upon any suitable candidate by the assembly of nuns, that nun may then be granted full ordination at will, and there is no cause for regret in this regard.

Then, again, when some probationary women (śikṣamāṇās) who had kept a household for twelve years sought the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya and full ordination without having made the request, and nuns of lesser diligence were criticizing them, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with the account of what had occurred and proceeding through to the laying down of the training rule, declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun, being a woman who has kept a household for twelve years, seeks the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya and full ordination without having made the request, commits a transgression."

Now, the phrase "furthermore, whatever" refers to a probationary woman. "Having kept a household for twelve years" means one who has lived in a household for twelve years. "The vow of abiding near the brahmacarya" refers to the rite proceeding by formal request and by a twofold act. "Without having made the request" means without having sought it. "Seeks full ordination" refers to the rite proceeding by formal request and a fourfold act. "Commits a transgression" is as explained above.

As to how the transgression arises: whenever a nun grants the vow of abiding near the brahmacarya and full ordination to a woman who has kept a household for twelve years without that woman having made the request, a transgression is committed in every instance.

The summary verse for the fifteenth transgression is complete.

The summary verse reads:

Granting the vow to one of great desire,
a pregnant woman, a trainee,
one set aside who is not being helped,
and the last — one to be expelled.

The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

At that time, the nun Sthūlanandā placed the disciples of one of great desire and neither held them, nor taught them, nor gave them guidance, so that they remained untamed, unquieted, unconcealed, and unguarded; and because nuns of little benefit were being disparaged, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then performed the acts beginning with "This has occurred" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, if any nun sets aside disciples of one of great desire and does not care for them in accordance with them, she commits a transgression."

"Furthermore, any" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Of great desire" means one who does not know sufficiency. "Disciples" means those who live together with her and those who are nearby. "Sets aside" means having taken on. "Does not care for them in accordance with them" means does not look after them. "Commits a transgression" is as explained above.

As to how the transgression arises: whenever a nun places even the slightest number of disciples of one of great desire, a transgression is committed in every instance.

The first of the sixteenth transgressions is complete.

The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

At that time, certain nuns who had been dwelling in a natural setting were eager to place disciples of one of great desire. Those nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "That nun should request the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire from the community of nuns." The nuns, not knowing that the Blessed One had said this, received further instruction from the Blessed One beginning with "Having prepared the seat" — the Blessed One explained it to the nuns in full through the form of questions and answers — so that nun, having prostrated in order of seniority, facing the community of nuns wherever they are assembled, joined her palms and, bowing down, spoke these words:

"I request the noble community of sisters to hear me. I, the nun called so-and-so, request the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire from the noble community. May the noble community, out of compassion, embrace me with compassion. Please, noble community, grant me, called so-and-so, the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire."

This is to be repeated a second and third time. After that, one nun makes the formal request and performs the act. The act is as follows:

"I request the noble community of sisters to hear me. This one, called so-and-so, requests the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire from the noble community. If it is the right time for the noble community and it consents, may the noble community grant it; and may the noble community bestow upon the one called so-and-so the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire." This is the formal request. The act is performed as follows:

"I request the noble community of sisters to hear me. This one, called so-and-so, requests the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire from the noble community. The noble community bestows upon the one called so-and-so the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire. Those who consent to bestowing upon the one called so-and-so the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak."

The noble community has consented and granted this.

The noble community of sisters has bestowed upon the one called so-and-so the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire. Because no one has spoken, it is held to be so.

In this way, whatever nun has received the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire may place disciples of one of great desire according to her own preference. She should have no regret in this matter.

Thereafter, Sthulanandā placed disciples of one of great desire without having requested the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire from the community. When nuns who had few desires censured her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun places disciples of one of great desire without having requested from the community the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'The vow of one of great desire' means by the act of a formal request and a twofold motion. 'Without having requested from the community the vow of placing disciples of one of great desire' — whether she causes someone to go forth, or grants full ordination, or bestows a residence as she pleases — this constitutes a transgression, as stated above. As to how the transgression arises: to whatever slight degree a nun places disciples of one of great desire without having requested the vow of one of great desire, a transgression arises in every instance."

This concludes the second of the sixteen transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Thereafter, Sthulanandā caused a pregnant woman to go forth. When brahmins and the wives of householders saw this, they spoke disparagingly, saying, "These nuns practice the holy life as frauds, mere pretenders." The matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly causes a pregnant woman to go forth commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'Pregnant woman' means one who carries a sentient being within her. 'Woman' means a woman. 'To go forth' means within this Dharma and Vinaya. 'Commits a transgression' is as stated above. As to how the transgression arises: to whatever slight degree a nun causes a pregnant woman to go forth, a transgression arises in every instance."

This concludes the third of the sixteen transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Thereafter, Sthulanandā caused someone to go forth and then did not train her. The nuns said to her, "You have received her into your circle — why do you not train her?" She replied, "She should train right here. If she does not train, she should train right here." The matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun causes someone to go forth and then does not train her commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'Having caused to go forth' means within this Dharma and Vinaya. 'Does not train her' means in the trainings of a nun. 'Commits a transgression' is as stated above. As to how the transgression arises: to whatever slight degree a nun causes someone to go forth and then does not train her, a transgression arises in every instance."

This concludes the fourth of the sixteen transgressions.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Thereafter, Sthulanandā, having caused someone to go forth, did not impart instructions, did not teach, and did not render any benefit. When nuns who had few desires censured her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having caused someone to go forth, renders no benefit, commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'Having caused to go forth' means within this Dharma and Vinaya.

"Renders no benefit" refers to the alms bowl, the monastic robe, the bowl bag, the staff, the belt, recitation of scripture, reading, oral recitation, yoga, and mental application. "Commits a transgression" — this is as stated above. How does the transgression come about? In every case, however little a nun has gone forth into the retinue and renders no benefit, a transgression is incurred. The fifth of the sixteenth transgressions is complete.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter, Sthulanandā caused the wife of someone who had gone abroad to go forth. At a later time, that woman's husband returned, and the woman heard that her husband had come home. Having heard this, she went to where Sthulanandā was and said to her: "Noble one, my husband has come; please send me away to another place for a while." But she did not send her away. Then the husband came, seized her, and said: "Who gave permission for her to go forth? If you, noble one, had sent her away at that very moment, she would not have been caught by the husband." When nuns who had few desires censured this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having caused someone to go forth, does not send her away, commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'Having caused to go forth' means within this Dharma and Vinaya. 'Does not send her away' means to another place. 'Commits a transgression' — this is as stated above." How does the transgression come about? In every case, however little a nun has kept someone in the retinue and does not send her away, a transgression is incurred. The verse summary of the sixteenth transgression is complete.

The summary verse: not yet having reached twenty years of age; having reached it but not made a request; a fierce woman tormented by grief; not having trained in the six dharmas.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter, nuns were conferring full ordination on young women who had not yet reached the age of twenty, and the Blessed One declared: "One who has not yet reached the age of twenty must not be given full ordination." Thereafter, Sthulanandā was conferring full ordination on women who had not yet reached the age of twenty, and when nuns who had few desires censured her, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," performed all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun confers full ordination on a young woman who has not yet reached the age of twenty commits a transgression. As for 'whatever' — this refers to Sthulanandā. 'Who has not yet reached the age of twenty' means one in whom twenty years are not complete. 'Confers full ordination' means through a motion and a fourfold act. 'Commits a transgression' — this is as stated above." How does the transgression come about? In every case, however much a nun confers full ordination on a young woman who has not yet reached the age of twenty, a transgression is incurred in each instance. The first of the seventeenth transgressions is complete.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter those nuns said to the monks: "You yourselves confer full ordination after reaching the age of twenty — should we not also confer full ordination after reaching the age of twenty? What distinction is there between you and us? What difference in intention? What difference in what is to be done?" When this was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted: when a young woman has reached the age of twenty, she shall train for two years in the six dharmas and

the vow of training in the six concordant dharmas. When the Blessed One declared, "When a young woman has reached the age of twenty, she shall for two years train in the six dharmas and the vow of training in the six concordant dharmas," the great progenitress Gautamī heard this and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, she prostrated with her head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. As she sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, correctly showed, and gladdened the great progenitress Gautamī with a Dharma-endowed discourse — and so forth up to: "He said nothing further."

Then the great progenitress Gautamī, understanding that the Blessed One's words had come to an end, rose from her seat, arranged her outer robe over one shoulder, turned to face the Blessed One, joined her palms together in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, it would be fitting for you to grant me something excellent. Sugata, it would be fitting for you to grant me something excellent."

"Gautamī, what excellent thing do you request?"

She spoke thus: "Venerable One, if those who have been householders for twelve years, and those young women who have reached the age of twenty, have obtained the going forth, and if it proves very burdensome to give them for two years the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six concordant dharmas — then, if the Blessed One would permit it, might you grant the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six concordant dharmas to those who have been householders for ten years and to young women who have reached the age of eighteen? Were this done, both groups would be complete."

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted. Confer for two years the vow of training in the six dharmas and the six concordant dharmas on those who have been householders for ten years, and on young women who have reached the age of eighteen. That said, once a householder of ten years standing, or a young woman of eighteen years of age, has completed the two-year training in the six dharmas and the six concordant dharmas, thereafter the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity shall be conferred upon her."

Now when the Blessed One declared, "Confer the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity on a young woman who has reached the age of twenty," those nuns did not know the procedure. The Blessed One declared: "Having prepared a seat" — and so forth up to: — the young woman who has reached the age of twenty shall, beginning from the side of her elder, make obeisance with joined hands. She shall prostrate with joined palms before the community of nuns and speak these words: "Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. I, a young woman of twenty years of age, called so-and-so, request from the Saṅgha, with the preceptress called so-and-so, the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity. May the noble Saṅgha, out of compassion, taking me under compassionate care, grant me, the young woman of twenty called so-and-so, the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity, with the preceptress called so-and-so." This shall be recited two and three times in succession.

After that, one nun shall make a motion and perform the formal act. The formal act is as follows: "Noble sisters of the Saṅgha, please hear me. This person called so-and-so, who has not yet reached the age of twenty, requests from the Saṅgha, through the preceptress called so-and-so, the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity. If it is the proper time for the noble Saṅgha, and if the Saṅgha consents, may the noble Saṅgha grant it.

The noble Saṅgha has conferred upon the young woman called so-and-so, who has reached the age of twenty, through the preceptress called so-and-so, the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity." This is the motion. The formal act shall likewise be recited in full.

Now, the occasion on which nuns of little concern reproached Sthūlanandā for conferring full ordination upon a young woman who had reached the age of twenty without first requesting the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and continuing through to the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Moreover, whatever nun confers full ordination upon a young woman who has reached the age of twenty without her having requested the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity commits an offense."

As for the analysis: "whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Young woman" refers to a woman who has gone forth as a novice. "Who has reached the age of twenty" refers to one whose twentieth year is complete. "The vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity" refers to what is obtained by means of the motion and the twofold formal act. "Without having requested" means without having requested it from the Saṅgha. "Confers full ordination" refers to the motion and the fourfold formal act. "Commits an offense" is as stated above. As for how the offense is incurred: to whatever extent a nun confers full ordination upon a young woman who has reached the age of twenty as a fully ordained nun without that young woman having requested the vow of dwelling in the practice of chastity, in all such cases she commits an offense. This completes the second of the seventeen offenses.

The setting for this next rule is Śrāvastī. On one occasion, Sthūlanandā, having put on her lower robe in the morning and entered the alms-round district, saw a woman on a main road quarreling with some other women, and Sthūlanandā saw that this woman, in her rage, had her hair standing on end. Then Sthūlanandā thought to herself: "I have found a companion who could become my partner in quarreling." She then spoke these words to the woman: "Sister, why do you not go forth into renunciation?" The woman replied: "I am extremely hot-tempered — who would ordain me?" Then Sthūlanandā said: "I will ordain you" — and so she ordained her and conferred full ordination upon her.

On a later occasion, when a quarrel arose between that woman and some nuns, the woman's companion was mentally restrained and said nothing at all. Then Sthūlanandā said to that nun: "Since I ordained you and conferred full ordination upon you for this very purpose, why are you now sitting there as if you had entered the fourth meditative absorption? Be my ally in this quarrel!" The woman replied: "I know what constitutes wrongdoing for laywomen, but I do not know what constitutes wrongdoing for these nuns." Then Sthūlanandā said: "I will show you their faults — for now, this great mistress of creatures is a self-initiated one; this blue-lotus-hued one has sold herself in six great cities; and this gaunt Gautamī has eaten the flesh of her own child and gone to the charnel ground in a state of mental derangement."

Then, on yet another occasion when a quarrel arose with the nuns, the extremely hot-tempered nun, having had her faults publicly proclaimed by Sthūlanandā, began to revile and berate the nuns. On seeing this, the great mistress of creatures spoke these words:

Those by whom this extremely hot-tempered one was ordained said: "It is Sthūlanandā." When this was said, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to "the laying down of a training rule," and declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly ordains a hot-tempered woman commits an offense." As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthūlanandā. "Knowingly" means either by herself or having been informed by another. "A hot-tempered woman" means one who is wrathful and quarrelsome. "Ordains" means within this Dharma-Vinaya. "Commits an offense" is as stated above. How does the transgression occur? To whatever extent a nun knowingly ordains even any hot-tempered woman, in every case she commits an offense. The third of the seventeenth class of offenses is complete.

The Vinaya Analysis of Nuns. The twenty-fifth fascicle. The basis of the case is at Śrāvastī.

Then one morning Sthūlanandā, having put on her lower robe, taken her alms-bowl and outer robe, and entered her alms-round district — up to the point where it says "Sthūlanandā ordained a woman afflicted with grief" — that woman rose before dawn, weeping and crying out: "My son! My daughter! Show yourself to me at least in a dream!" She lamented and wailed, beat her breast, and tore her hair in anguish. Then the great mistress of creatures, upon hearing this sound, spoke these words: "Who ordained this one afflicted with grief?" They replied: "It was Sthūlanandā." When this was said, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to "the laying down of a training rule," and declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun knowingly ordains a woman afflicted with grief commits an offense." As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthūlanandā. "Knowingly" means either by herself or having been informed by another. "Afflicted with grief" means separated from beloved relatives and one's own people. "Ordains" means within this Dharma-Vinaya. "Commits an offense" is as stated above. How does the transgression occur? To whatever extent a nun knowingly ordains even any woman afflicted with grief, in every case she commits an offense. The fourth of the seventeenth class of offenses is complete.

The basis of the case is at Śrāvastī. At a time when the nuns had ordained these women in the way described, those women did not know how to live alongside others or how their attendants were to be fully ordained. The Blessed One then declared: "Give to a woman who has been a householder for ten years, or to a girl who has reached the age of eighteen, the vow of training in the six rules and the six concordant rules for a period of two years." As they did not know what those six rules were and what those six concordant rules were, the Blessed One declared:

She should not travel alone on the road.
She should not cross to the far bank of a river.
She should not touch a man.
She should not sit together with a man.
She should not act as a go-between.
She should not conceal a wrongdoing.
These are called the six rules.

What are the six concordant rules? She should not grasp at gold or silver. She should not perform the act of shaving bodily hair. She should not dig in the earth. She should not cut green grass. She should not eat food that has not been received by hand. She should not eat food that has been set aside and stored. These six are called the six concordant rules.

Having trained in these for two years, full ordination into the vow of dwelling in pure conduct shall then be given.

After that, full ordination shall be given. But then it happened that a female trainee gave full ordination to someone who had not, for two years, requested the six rules and the six concordant rules, and monks of little understanding criticized this. The matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "this incident," proceeded to establish a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, knowingly, gives full ordination to someone who has not trained for two years in the six rules and the six concordant rules, commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to a female trainee. "Knowingly" means that she herself is aware, or that it has been told to her by another. "The six rules and the six concordant rules" are as already taught. "Without having trained for two years" refers to this training that is required to become a trainee nun. "Commits an offense" is as stated above. How does the transgression arise? However much, even a little, a nun gives full ordination without having requested the vow of training in the six rules and the six concordant rules for two years, in every case she commits an offense. This completes the verse summary of the seventeenth offense.

The verse summary is as follows:

Training, and one year,
assembly, the five with the mole,
the house-slot, the twenty-five, the shoulder,
and the housewife.
Without having opened the occasion, to ask,
and not to go alone to relieve oneself.

Summary verse:
The six rules, and having trained,
not permitted by the householder,
if one has given cloth to me,
afterward you are not my trainee.
The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then it happened that a female trainee, having trained together with companions and attendants for two years in the six rules and the six concordant rules, was not given full ordination by them. The nuns said to her, "Noble one, you have trained — why are you not given full ordination?" She replied, "They say to me that this female trainee is being given full ordination without having trained, and thinking that it all depends entirely on my teacher, her mind is thus." This matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "this incident," proceeded to establish a training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, knowingly, having trained for two years in the six rules and the six concordant rules in the proper cycle, does not give full ordination, commits an offense." "Whatever" refers to a female trainee. "Knowingly" means that she herself is aware, or that it has been told to her by another. "Having trained" refers to the training that is required to become a trainee nun. "Does not give full ordination" means through the request and the fourfold act. "Commits an offense" is as stated above. How does the transgression arise? However much, even a little, a nun knowingly, having trained for two years and going beyond that, does not give full ordination — in every case she commits an offense. This completes the first of the eighteenth offenses. The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then it happened that a female trainee, having put on her lower robe in the morning and entered the home of a certain householder, found a woman there quarreling with her husband. The woman said to her, "What is the matter — why are you so troubled?" That woman then explained the situation at length. Thereupon the female trainee said to the woman, "Why do you not go forth into homelessness?" The woman replied:

"Who would give me ordination?" The female trainee said to her, "You should do so," and shortly thereafter she gave her the going-forth.

After that, the husband came home and asked his wife, "Where has my wife gone?" She replied, "Somāgavatī has given her the going-forth." The householder then went to where Somāgavatī was and said to her, "Noble one, who gave this attendant of mine the going-forth?" Somāgavatī replied, "She did." The householder then said, "Noble one, is it fitting that you gave the going-forth without the husband's permission?" and after saying this, the householder departed having reproached her.

When nuns of few wishes were criticizing this conduct, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, proceeded to establish the rule of training: "Furthermore, if any nun knowingly gives the going-forth to a woman without the husband's permission, she commits an offense."

The term "furthermore, any" refers to a female trainee. "Knowingly" means either she herself knows or it has been stated by another. "Without the husband's permission" means without his having given leave. "Gives the going-forth" means into this Dharma and discipline. "Commits an offense" is as above. As to how the offense is incurred: in every case to whatever degree a nun gives the going-forth to a woman without the husband's permission, she commits an offense. This completes the second of the eighteenth offenses. The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then a female trainee said to Somāgavatī, "Noble one, please give me full ordination." She replied, "If you give me a robe, I will give you full ordination afterward." When nuns of few wishes were criticizing this conduct, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, proceeded to establish the rule of training: "Furthermore, if any nun, when a nun has spoken thus — saying 'If you give her a robe, I will afterward give you full ordination' — she commits an offense."

The term "furthermore, any" refers to a female trainee. "When a nun has spoken thus" means having spoken in this way. "If you give her a robe" refers to whichever of the seven robes it may be. "If you give" means if you have offered it. "Afterward" means at another time. "Full ordination" means into the status of a fully ordained nun. "Commits an offense" is as above. As to how the offense is incurred: in every case, to whatever degree a nun has spoken in this way — saying "If you give her a robe, I will afterward give you full ordination" — in every instance she commits an offense. This completes the third of the eighteenth offenses. The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then a woman went to where the aged Gautamī was and said to her, "Noble one, if you give me the going-forth, I wish to go forth." She replied, "Abandon your household affairs, and thereafter it will not be difficult." The wife of the householder then abandoned her household affairs and came, but the aged Gautamī did not give her the going-forth. When that woman said, "Now I am neither a householder nor one who has gone forth," the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, proceeded to establish the rule of training:

Furthermore, whatever nun says to a laywoman, "Abandon your household affairs, and thereafter it will not be difficult for you," and then, when she comes, does not give her the going-forth — that is a transgression.

Now, "whatever" refers to the aged Gautamī. "Laywoman" refers to a householder's wife. "Abandon your household affairs, and thereafter it will not be difficult for you" — this was said to one who was to go forth. "Thereafter does not give her" — means within this Dharma and Vinaya. "That is a transgression" — as explained above.

As for how the transgression occurs: however much, to even the slightest degree, a nun says, "Abandon your household affairs, and thereafter it will not be difficult," and then, when she comes, does not give her the going-forth — in every such case it is a transgression.

Thus ends the verse summary of the eighteenth transgression.

The mnemonic verse:

Prohibited year by year,
not the seventh day-loan,
half-month and half-month instruction,
the restoration ceremony without monks,
the rains retreat not without monks —
one who has done the rains retreat should perform the invitation ceremony.
The setting is in Śrāvastī.

Then the probationer (śikṣamāṇā) gave the going-forth each year, and later, when it came time to call out their names, she called them as "first year," "second year," and so on up to "fifth year." Then the nuns said to her, "Noble one, do you not know their names?" She replied, "Who could know so many names?" The nuns of few desires criticized her on that occasion and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, proceeded to establish the rule of training:

Furthermore, whatever nun gives the going-forth each and every year — that is a transgression.

"Whatever" refers to the probationer. "Each and every year" means year after year. "Gives the going-forth" means confers ordination. "That is a transgression" — as explained above.

As for how the transgression occurs: however much, to even the slightest degree, a nun gives the going-forth year after year — in every such case it is a transgression.

Thus ends the first of the nineteenth set of transgressions.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. Then the probationer, having taken on the intention of the earlier fortnight, proceeded also to observe the restoration ceremony of the later fortnight. The nuns said to her, "Noble one, why do you do that?" She replied, "I am one who knows the three collections of scripture, so I know what to do." The nuns of few desires criticized her on that occasion and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence" and so forth, proceeded to establish the rule of training:

Furthermore, whatever nun observes the restoration ceremony with an intention she has already used — that is a transgression.

"Whatever" refers to the probationer. "Already used" means already spent. "Intention" means the mental resolution. "Observes the restoration ceremony — that is a transgression" — as explained above.

As for how the transgression occurs: however much, to even the slightest degree, a nun observes the individual liberation with an intention she has already used — in every such case it is a transgression.

Thus ends the second of the nineteenth set of transgressions.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had declared that a nun who takes on the intention of the fortnight should go before the community of nuns and should receive from the monks the designation of the date together with instruction and guidance and should put these into practice, —

However, when those belonging to the twelve groups did not put the instruction and guidance into practice, the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" all the way through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, while observing the fortnight, does not put the instruction and guidance into practice, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to those of the twelve groups. As for "observing the fortnight" — this means observing the half-month. As for "does not put the instruction and guidance into practice" — this means not carrying it out together with the community of nuns. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as explained above.

As for how the transgression occurs: however much, to even the slightest degree, a nun observes the fortnight without putting the instruction and guidance into practice — in every such case it is a transgression.

Thus ends the third of the nineteenth set of transgressions.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. While the nuns were going about on their rounds, they came to the summer dwelling of a certain nun, and there those nuns performed the restoration ceremony (poṣadha) in a place without monks. Then, continuing on their rounds gradually, they arrived at Śrāvastī. When they came to the summer dwelling, the nuns said: "Welcome, you who have the Buddha, you who have the Dharma, you who have the Saṅgha. Where did you perform the restoration ceremony?" The others replied: "In some pleasant place." Then the nuns there said to those nuns: "Why did you perform the restoration ceremony in a place without monks?" — and when this was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun performs the restoration ceremony in a place without monks, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to those who hold to this Dharma. As for "a place without monks" — this means a place where no monks are present. As for "the restoration ceremony" — this means observing the individual liberation. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as explained above.

As for how the transgression occurs: however much, to even the slightest degree, a nun performs the restoration ceremony in a place without monks — in every such case it is a transgression.

Thus ends the fourth of the nineteenth set of transgressions.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had declared that a nun must not commit to the rains retreat in a place without monks, a group of nuns then came from a certain region and committed to the rains retreat in a place without monks. After completing the rains retreat they went to Śrāvastī, and as soon as they arrived the nuns asked: "Where did you spend the rains retreat?" They replied: "In some pleasant place." The nuns then asked them: "Were there monks present, or were there none?" When they replied "There were no monks," the nuns of few desires criticized them — and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun commits to the rains retreat in a place without monks, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to those who hold to this Dharma. As for "without monks" — this means a place where no monks are present. As for "place" — this means a place where all activities are openly conducted. As for "commits to the rains retreat" — this means making a formal commitment for three months.

As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun commits even the slightest bit to the rains retreat in a place without monks, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The fifth rule of the nineteenth set of transgressions is complete.

The narrative origin is in Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had declared that nuns who had completed the rains retreat should perform the invitation ceremony before both assemblies, those nuns then said the following to Sthulanandā: "Noble one, having performed the invitation ceremony before both assemblies, come here." She replied: "I will not go there. Why? For the moment she is a master of the three collections of scripture, and she knows how to perform the invitation ceremony — but one must offer a ceremonial whisk, a fan, and many small fans to the assembly of monks, so you all go today. I will not go there." This matter was then reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun, having completed the rains retreat, does not perform the invitation ceremony before both assemblies, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "having completed the rains retreat" — this means having gone through the full three months. As for "before both assemblies" — this means before the assembly of monks and the assembly of nuns. As for "does not perform the invitation ceremony" — this refers to what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun, having completed the rains retreat, fails even in the slightest to perform the invitation ceremony before both assemblies, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The verse summary of the nineteenth set of transgressions is complete.

Summary verse:

Not causing strife in the assembly,
disagreeable speech and miserliness — five;
not eating after departing,
and not accepting what has been cooked.

The narrative origin is in Śrāvastī. When Sthulanandā caused strife in the assembly, those dwelling together with her and the attendants said: "Noble one, it is not right for a nun to cause strife in the assembly." She replied: "Whether it is right or not, I have caused strife." Nuns who had few desires criticized her, and this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun causes strife in the assembly, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "in the assembly" — this means in the assembly of nuns. As for "causes strife" — this means having made a breach. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun causes even the slightest strife in the assembly, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The first rule of the twentieth set of transgressions is complete.

The narrative origin is in Śrāvastī. When Sthulanandā reviled the assembly of nuns with abusive terms such as "housewife," "prostitute," and "donkey-woman," the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon proceeded from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun reviles the assembly, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "the assembly" — this means the assembly of nuns. As for "reviles" — this means reviling with words befitting a laywoman. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun reviles the assembly even in the slightest, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The second rule of the twentieth set of transgressions is complete.

Then Sthulanandā gave lodging in a summer dwelling to some visiting nuns, and those nuns came to have abundant gain and honor. When she, out of miserliness, drove them away, the nuns said to her: "Noble one, surely miserliness has not harmed you?" She replied in these words: "Just as one in the cold is threatened by the cold, and one in the heat is threatened by the heat, shall this summer dwelling, built by me with great hardship, be given as an opportunity to these smooth-tongued ones?" Those nuns of few wishes, who censured this conduct, reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, proceeding from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun is miserly toward a lodging, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "toward a lodging" — this means toward a borrowed dwelling. As for "miserly" — this means being unwilling to share it with others. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun is even slightly miserly toward a lodging, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The third rule of the twentieth set of transgressions is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

Then the nuns would go to the homes of brahmins and householders and recite praises of the great lady Mahāprajāpatī: "The great lady Mahāprajāpatī is endowed with merit, the mother of the Buddha, and the Blessed One himself has declared her foremost among the senior queens. Utpalavarṇā, who has the blue-lotus complexion, has been declared foremost among those possessing supernatural powers. Gautamī the Lean has been declared foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya. Dharmadinnā has been declared foremost among those who analyze the sūtras."

Then Sthulanandā, hearing those words, said: "Ho! You daughters of those who eat the leftovers of others — this great lady Mahāprajāpatī ordained herself; she has neither a preceptor nor an instructor. Utpalavarṇā of the blue-lotus complexion is a prostitute. Gautamī the Lean ate the flesh of her own son. And yet you recite praises of these women!" She reviled them in this way. Those nuns then said to her: "Noble one, surely miserliness toward praise has not harmed you?" She replied in these words: "She herself has gone forth from the Śākya clan, she is a master of the Three Baskets — if she speaks praises of those who are unworthy of praise, and does not speak them of her, why should it harm her?" Those nuns of few wishes, who censured this conduct, reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, proceeding from "this occurrence" through to the establishment of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun is miserly toward praise, it is a transgression."

As for "whatever" — this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "praise" — this means being miserly and envious when the scriptural learning and realization of others is spoken of. As for "it is a transgression" — this is as before. How does the transgression come about? However much a nun, when the genuine and accurate praises of another are rightly spoken, is miserly toward that praise, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The fourth rule of the twentieth set of transgressions is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

Then Sthulanandā said this to the nuns: "Sisters, do not go to that household anymore." They replied: "Why do you say this?" She answered: "She herself, by great effort, taught the Dharma to that household and brought them to faith." The nuns then said to her: "Noble one, surely miserliness toward a household has not harmed you?"

When she said those words, the nuns of few wants rebuked her, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," and so forth, established the training rule: "Furthermore, if any nun is miserly toward a household, it is a transgression."

"Furthermore, any nun" refers to Sthulanandā. "Toward a household" means toward the household of a brahmin or householder. "Is miserly" means if she generates jealousy. "It is a transgression" is as before. As for how the transgression arises: however much a nun is even slightly miserly toward a household, in every instance it becomes a transgression. The fifth rule of the twentieth set of transgressions is complete.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

Then Sthulanandā, while giving instructions to the nuns, said: "Sisters, brahmins given to holding things in contempt will strike you with fists and flat blows and split your skulls — it is not fitting; do not go for alms as early as before." Having thus turned the others back, she herself divided her lower robe, took up her bowl and Dharma robe, and set out on her alms round. A brahmin given to holding things in contempt saw her, seized her, and struck her on the ear with his fist and the flat of his hand, such that her eyes were dazed and swollen. She then went into the summer dwelling, and the nuns said to her: "Noble one, who struck you?" She told them the whole story at length. The nuns then said to her: "Noble one, surely miserliness toward material gain has not harmed you?" When she said those words, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence," and so forth, established the training rule: "Furthermore, if any nun is miserly toward material gain, it is a transgression."

"Furthermore, any nun" refers to Sthulanandā. As for "is miserly toward material gain," material gain is of two kinds: gain in the form of food and gain in the form of clothing; in this context it is gain in the form of food that is intended. "Generates jealousy" means if she generates envy. "It is a transgression" is as before. As for how the transgression arises: however much a nun is even slightly miserly toward material gain, in every instance it becomes a transgression.

Now the preceding story is as follows. The monks, having arisen in doubt, requested the Blessed One, the buddha, to cut through all their doubts. They said: "Venerable one, behold how Sthulanandā teaches others and does not practice herself." The Blessed One declared: "Just as in the past, too, Sthulanandā taught others and did not practice herself, and through that improper conduct she came to suffer. Monks, once upon a time, in a past age, on a great road, there was a large herd of mountain does. Then someone said to the mountain does: 'Sisters, you have fallen ill with bile disease — it is not fitting; do not eat sesame.' Having thus instructed them, that one herself, by the roadside where carts were coming, was eating and eating sesame, and a cartwheel severed her head. Then a god at that moment spoke these verses:

She who teaches others
yet does not practice herself,
she who is ruled by craving —
this mountain doe has been crushed by the wheel.

Monks, know this: the mountain doe in that story was none other than this very Sthulanandā. And even then she taught others and did not practice herself, and through improper conduct came to suffer.

And even now she teaches others and does not practice herself, and through improper conduct she has come to suffer.

Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: whatever is compatible, practice it yourself first, and then teach it to others as well. Monks, you should train accordingly.

The sixth rule of the twentieth group of offenses is complete.

The origin is at Śrāvastī.

Now Sthulanandā was dwelling together with a companion, and the attendants recited a scriptural text. She then said to them: "For now, dye her vessel, and buy sugar and sesame." Having said this, she left them there without giving them a scriptural transmission. They then said: "Noble lady, do you not hold the Dharma in miserly regard?" She replied: "O daughters of gluttons! Because she pleased the six groups of monks with a bit of sesame in order to obtain a scriptural transmission — her hand developed mange; when she sought forbearance, her head was shaved; when she knelt and asked for the teaching, her tongue was split. Why then would I not be stingy?" When nuns of few desires censured this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, beginning with the establishment of the context, proceeded to lay down the training rule: "Furthermore, any nun who is stingy with regard to the Dharma commits an offense."

As for "furthermore, any": this refers to Sthulanandā. As for "stingy with regard to the Dharma": Dharma here means what has been taught by the Buddha or spoken by a śrāvaka. As for "commits an offense": this is as stated above.

How does one incur a transgression? However little a nun withholds the Dharma out of stinginess, in every such case she commits an offense.

A summary verse on the five kinds of stinginess:

Regarding dwelling, regarding praise, regarding household,
regarding gain itself, and regarding Dharma.

The seventh rule of the twentieth group of offenses is complete.

The origin is at Śrāvastī.

Now the twelve groups ate their meal in one place and then went to eat again in another. When nuns of few desires censured this practice of eating what had been set aside and what had not been set aside, the matter was reported to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, beginning with the establishment of the context, proceeded to lay down the training rule: "Furthermore, any nun who, having eaten and having made a formal setting-aside, then arranges or eats food that has been prepared or cooked commits an offense."

As for "furthermore, any": this refers to the twelve groups. As for "having eaten and set aside in one place, having violated proper conduct": this is to have eaten in one place and then broken the rules of decorum. As for "prepared food and cooked food": prepared food refers to five kinds of prepared food, and cooked food refers to five kinds of cooked food. As for "arranges or eats": this means swallowing a morsel secretly. As for "commits an offense": this is as stated above.

How does one incur a transgression in this? If a nun, perceiving what has been set aside as set aside, nevertheless arranges or eats it, she commits an offense. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, she commits an offense. If a nun perceives what has not been set aside as though it had been set aside and arranges or eats it, she commits a wrong deed. Likewise, if she eats with doubt, she commits a wrong deed.

The eighth rule of the twentieth group of offenses is complete.

The origin is at Śrāvastī.

Now Sthulanandā, in the early morning, put on her lower robe, took up her alms bowl and outer robe, and went out for alms. She entered the home of a certain householder. The householder's wife had just given birth to a son and did not know herself how to wash the infant. Then Sthulanandā said: "Noble lady, give alms." The woman replied: "Noble lady, my heart is not at ease." Sthulanandā said: "Why? No one has washed the boy for me." Sthulanandā then said: "Why did you not ask to have him washed?"

Sthulanandā said: "Are you also someone who, like your husband, does only one kind of work?" The woman replied: "Noble lady, does she have some skill?" Sthulanandā said: "Is there any craft or any work in which she is not skilled?" The woman then said: "Noble lady, please bathe my boy." Then Sthulanandā said: "But who will give her alms?" The woman replied: "I will give alms to the renunciant women who follow behind me, and I will give to the abbess and the monastery's caretaker."
