Thereupon Sthulanandā set down her alms bowl, changed her robes, took up the infant, and rocked him for a little while. Then she rubbed him all over with cleansing substances beneath the navel, washed him with warm water, applied eye medicine to his eyes, drew dots with a clay paste, trimmed his hair, anointed him with honey and butter oil, placed him in a cradle, rocked him, and instructed the woman: "You must bathe him like this every single day." She then had the alms loaded up and went to the rains retreat dwelling. When the householder came home, he said to his wife: "Good woman, it was well done that you bathed the boy today." From the passage beginning "How excellent!" up to the passage "Sthulanandā bathed him, and a very great quantity of alms was offered" — that is the account of the matter.

Then, on another occasion, the great prioress Gautamī, in the early morning, put on her lower robe, took up her alms bowl and outer robe, and entered that same householder's home to seek alms. She said: "Lady of good marks, please give alms." The woman replied: "Noble lady, please bathe my boy." Then the great prioress said: "Sister, she bathed a bodhisattva; she has not bathed any other boy. Sister, surely you do not think that in order to offer a gift to a nun who is endowed with moral discipline you would incur an action that leads to becoming a slave and the like? Be that as it may, sister, where did you ever see or hear of a nun bathing a boy?" The woman replied: "Noble lady, Sthulanandā bathed him." The great prioress then said: "This very thing has now also occurred among us." With those words, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, from the passage beginning "This incident occurred" up to the laying down of the training rule, established the rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun picks up a child commits an offense." As for the terms: "whichever" refers to Sthulanandā; "child" refers to an infant; "picks up" means plays with; "commits an offense" is as before. How does the offense come about? Whichever nun picks up any child whatsoever commits an offense in every case.

The verse summary of the twentieth group of offenses is complete.

The verse summary runs:
Bathing cloths, the matter of their use,
robes, the washing thereof,
patched garments and their exchange,
and giving Dharma robes to a novice.
The origin is at Śrāvastī.

Now the twelfth group: a great many householders' wives came together to bathe. Then Sthulanandā pointed out that her mass of pubic hair, being very dark and neatly curled, sat like the fruit of a black chickpea. The nuns reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with permission granted, a nun may keep a bathing cloth."

At the time when the Blessed One had declared that nuns should keep a bathing cloth, Sthulanandā was unconcerned and indifferent, and when nuns of few desires censured her for this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun bathes without a bathing cloth commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Sthulanandā. "Bathing cloth" means a cloth for bathing, and "without" means in the absence of it. As for "bathes," there are two kinds of bathing: immersive bathing and consecration bathing. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? Whenever a nun performs either of the two kinds of bathing even to the slightest degree without keeping a bathing cloth for that bathing, a transgression occurs in every case.

The first of the twenty-first group of offenses is complete.

The origin is at Śrāvastī. Then Sthulanandā sent robes soiled by impurity to a laundress to be washed, and when brahmins and householders complained, saying "She will make our robes impure as well," the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun sends robes to a laundress commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Sthulanandā. "Laundress" means a laywoman. "Robes" means any of the seven kinds. "Sends to be washed" means sending them to be laundered and cleaned. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? Whenever a nun sends even slightly impurity-soiled robes to be washed, a transgression occurs in every case.

The second of the twenty-first group of offenses is complete.

The Vinaya Analysis for Nuns, the twenty-sixth section.

The origin is at Śrāvastī. Because women are forgetful, the nuns had forgotten which of their Dharma robes had been consecrated and which had not, and not knowing which had been consecrated and which had not, the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, from this day forward, nuns shall experience the consecration of the Dharma robe on the fifteenth day of each fortnight." Then Sthulanandā, not performing the consecration of the Dharma robe on the fifteenth day of each fortnight, was addressed by the nuns: "Noble one, why do you not perform the consecration of the Dharma robe on the fifteenth of the fortnight?" She replied: "If I can remember the three scriptural collections, why would I fail to remember the consecration of the Dharma robe?" When nuns of few desires censured her for this, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun does not perform the consecration of the Dharma robe at the half-month commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Sthulanandā. "Half-month" means the half of the month. "Dharma robe" means any of the seven kinds. "Consecration" means that the consecration is to be remembered and carried out. "Does not perform" means not practicing the training of the Teacher. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about?

To whatever small extent a nun does not practice the consecration of the Dharma robe on each and every fifteenth day, she commits a transgression in every case. The third rule of the twenty-first transgression is complete.

The occasion for the next rule is in Rājagṛha. At the time when Sthulanandā accepted a dance-teacher's costume in exchange, gave it as a Dharma robe, and the recipient distributed it and performed a dance there — whereupon the group of six nuns exposed her on the spot. The group of six then heard of this, went to Sthulanandā, met her, and beat her until her eye swelled and was injured. She went into the rains-retreat dwelling. The nuns said to her: "Who beat you?" She spoke these words: "My brothers beat me — do not be displeased on my account." The nuns said: "Why did she speak at length on that occasion?" And at the occasion when nuns of few wants rebuked her, this was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun gives a Dharma robe of a renunciant to a laywomen commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Sthulanandā. "Laywoman" means one who dwells in a household. "A Dharma robe of a renunciant" means an ochre robe. "Gives" means giving it away. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever small extent a nun gives a Dharma robe of a renunciant to a laywoman, she commits a transgression in every case. The verse summary of the twenty-first transgression is complete.

The summary verse is as follows:

The menstrual cloth, the assembly's menstrual cloth,
The self-initiative of the poor,
What is to be given as a stiff extension,
And the robes that are to be distributed.

The occasion for the next rule is in Śrāvastī. Women, being propelled by karma from former lives, came to have a monthly flow, and the nuns began to drip with menstrual discharge month by month. The Blessed One declared: "A menstrual cloth is to be worn." At the very time when the Blessed One declared, "A menstrual cloth is to be worn," while they were wearing them and moving about, the cloths fell off. The Blessed One declared: "They are to be fastened with a cord." Furthermore, Sthulanandā, having no sense of shame, gave hers away while blood was dripping and went out for alms-gathering. Brahmins and householders seeing her asked: "Noble lady, what is this blood dripping from you?" She said: "Ask mother. Ask sister. Ask daughter." Those people then cried out, gossiped, and spoke reproachfully, saying: "This will make all our households impure." At the occasion of their reproach, the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," proceeded through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun does not wear a menstrual cloth commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Sthulanandā. "Menstrual cloth" means that which conceals the discomfort of women. "Does not wear" means not making it her own. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever small extent a nun does not wear a menstrual cloth, she commits a transgression in every case. The first rule of the twenty-second transgression is complete.

The occasion for the next rule is in Śrāvastī. The queen Mālavatī heard that the Blessed One had permitted the menstrual cloth for the nuns, and she thought: "How wonderful — I shall offer menstrual cloths to the entire community of nuns." Sthulanandā then went to wherever queen Mālavatī was, and having arrived, said to her:

"Your Majesty, the Blessed One has permitted menstrual cloths for the nuns." Queen Mālavatī then directed her household attendants, and they placed chests of various cloths in front of her. Queen Mālavatī then said to Sthulanandā: "Noble one, distribute these cloths as menstrual cloths to the entire community of nuns." Sthulanandā then took all those cloths for herself. Another nun went to wherever queen Mālavatī was, and having arrived, said to her: "Your Majesty, please give me a menstrual cloth as well." Queen Mālavatī then said to that nun: "Noble one, I have entrusted all the menstrual cloths for the entire community of nuns into the hands of Sthulanandā." Now, to whatever extent Sthulanandā had been asked and had not given, and nuns of modest means were speaking in complaint, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "This occurrence" up through the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Whatever nun makes her own, for a single individual, a menstrual cloth belonging to a community that has menstrual cloths, commits a transgression." As for "whatever" — that is Sthulanandā. "That has menstrual cloths" — that is a community of women with this need. "The community's menstrual cloth" — that which is held in common by the community of nuns. "For a single individual" — meaning for one person alone. "Makes her own" — means appropriates it for herself. "Commits a transgression" — is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever small extent a nun appropriates for a single individual a menstrual cloth belonging to a community that has menstrual cloths, she commits a transgression in every case. The second part of the twenty-second transgression is complete.

The occasion for the next rule is in Śrāvastī. At that time there was a householder who was ill and in severe pain. Sthulanandā went to wherever that householder was, and having arrived, said to him: "Good sir, the time has come for rhubarb — give me some rhubarb." He replied: "Noble one, I am destitute and have nothing at all." Sthulanandā then said: "She will vouch for you — good sir, take a loan from the shop and repay it later." Sthulanandā then caused that poor, wretched man to rejoice with his little bit of rhubarb, took it, and went to her dwelling for the rains retreat. Later, a merchant seized that householder and said: "Do not go anywhere until you have paid the kārṣāpaṇas." His companions then said to the householder: "What are you doing here?" He said: "I have been seized by creditors." They asked: "Why have you been seized by creditors?" He explained the matter in full, and they then said: "The śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan have merely words of renunciation and of the holy life — for they cause even a sick man to rejoice and take from him." This criticism was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "This occurrence" up through the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Whatever nun causes a wretched person to present rhubarb or causes them to rejoice and take it on loan commits a transgression." As for "whatever" — that is Sthulanandā. "A wretched person" — that is the sick man. "Causes to present rhubarb" — that refers to the Saṅgha's robe-cloth. "Causes to rejoice and take it on loan" — means causing someone to take a loan. "Commits a transgression" — is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about?

To whatever slight extent a nun causes a wretched person to rejoice in rhubarb, in every case that becomes a transgression. The twenty-second transgression, third section, is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then, in that place, very many nuns who had been robbed by a thief where rhubarb had been stored gathered together and said, "If the Blessed One would permit it, let us retrieve the rhubarb." At that time the matter was reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "It is permitted. The rhubarb may be retrieved." Not understanding what the Blessed One had said, the Blessed One then declared, beginning with the words "Having arranged the beds and furnishings," through the response to the question, that the nuns should be properly informed. Following that, one nun should make a motion and a formal act should be performed. The formal act is to be done thus:

"Let the noble Saṅgha of sisters hear me. In this place there are very many nuns who have been robbed by a thief. If the time is right for the noble Saṅgha and they are agreeable, may the noble Saṅgha grant permission. And in this way, may the noble Saṅgha cause the rhubarb to be retrieved on behalf of the very many nuns who have been robbed by a thief." This is the motion. In the same way the formal act too should be stated in full.

Then, from the point where Sthulanandā did not take the opportunity to retrieve the rhubarb, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One then, from the words "This occurrence," up through the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Whatever nun does not take the opportunity to retrieve rhubarb commits a transgression." As for "whatever" — that is Sthulanandā. "Rhubarb" — that is the Saṅgha's robe-cloth. "Does not take the opportunity to retrieve it" — means not contributing one's share. "Commits a transgression" — is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever slight extent a nun together with the Saṅgha does not take the opportunity to retrieve rhubarb, in every case that becomes a transgression. The twenty-second transgression, fourth section, is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had declared, "Having retrieved the rhubarb, whatever gains in cloth there may be from it shall be divided," then Sthulanandā did not take the opportunity to divide the gains in cloth from the rhubarb. At that time the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, from the words "This occurrence," up through the laying down of the training rule, established the following: "Whatever nun does not take the opportunity to divide the gains from rhubarb commits a transgression." As for "whatever" — that is Sthulanandā. "The gains from rhubarb to be divided" — means dividing the cloth. "Does not take the opportunity" — means not joining in. "Commits a transgression" — is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever slight extent a nun does not take the opportunity to divide the gains in cloth, in every case that becomes a transgression. If she herself does not wish to receive a share, there is no transgression. The versified summary of the twenty-second transgression is complete.

The summary verse is:
"Come here and be calmed,
should be sent after entrusting;
a spell not to be accepted or installed,
and food not to be sold."

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then, when the nuns were residing together,

the novices were quarreling with one another, and Stomā Gāmī lent support to one side, thereby causing the quarrel to grow very large. The nuns then said: "Noble one, come here — we will calm this quarrel." But Stomā Gāmī replied: "Why are you seeking to interfere? For the time being, I am going to keep quarreling, not calm things down." The nuns of few desires then reproached her, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon, beginning with "This occurrence…" and proceeding through to the laying down of the training, established the rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun has the power to calm a quarrel and does not do so commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Stomā Gāmī. "Has the power" means is endowed with the ability. "A quarrel" means a dispute. "To calm" means to bring fully to peace. "Does not do so" means does not stop it. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? To whatever slight extent a nun is able to calm a quarrel and a dispute, and has the power to do so, and yet does not calm it — in every case that becomes a transgression. The first of the twenty-third transgressions is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then Stomā Gāmī locked the door of the rains-retreat residence, took the key, and went off wandering through the countryside. While she was away, a fire broke out in that residence. When the nuns wished to break the door open, they could not find the key, and as a result they were burned in the fire. The nuns of few desires then reproached her, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon, beginning with "This occurrence…" and proceeding through to the laying down of the training, established the rule: "Furthermore, whichever nun goes off wandering through the countryside without entrusting the rains-retreat residence commits a transgression."

"Whichever" refers to Stomā Gāmī. "The rains-retreat residence" means the monastery. "Without entrusting" means without handing the key over to the nuns. "Goes off wandering through the countryside" means going beyond the boundary. "Commits a transgression" is as before. Now, how does a transgression come about? If a nun, perceiving herself to be within the boundary while she is indeed within the boundary, goes beyond the boundary without having handed the key to the nuns, she commits a transgression. Likewise, if she is in doubt, she commits a transgression. If a nun perceives herself to be outside the boundary while she is actually within it, and goes beyond the boundary without having handed the key to the nuns, she commits a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she is in doubt, she commits a wrongdoing. The second of the twenty-third transgressions is complete.

The basis of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then Stomā Gāmī, overcome by desire and wishing for a man, went to a young incense-seller and said to him: "Good-looking one, can you recite a spell?" He replied that he could. Stomā Gāmī then said: "Come now, recite it." He recited: "Sar phu, bi si ri phu, si ri bi svāhā." Stomā Gāmī told him to repeat it again and again. When he became angry, he insulted her, calling her a bad woman. A novice nun who was following behind then said: "If you cannot even retain two words, how could you ever have mastered the Three Baskets (Skt. tripiṭaka)?" He replied: "She had already memorized the first recitation, but was simply keeping the words to herself."

The novice nun who was following behind then said: "Noble one, it is remarkable that you are not inflamed by desire!" At that point the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who recites a spell learned from a layperson incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Stomā Gāmī. "From a layperson" means from one who dwells in a household. "Spell" means something that dispels. "Recites" means to master it fully. "Incurs a transgression" is as explained above. As for how the transgression arises: however little a nun recites a spell learned from a layperson, in every case she incurs a transgression. The third rule of the twenty-third group of transgressions is complete.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. Stomā Gāmī then had a man recite a spell, saying: "Kye nang rje si ri phu, bi si ri phu, si ri bi si ri phu svāhā — hold that!" She had him recite it two and three times. The man then said: "Noble one, I have mastered it completely." Stomā Gāmī again said: "Recite it again and again." The man became angry and said: "You bad, shaven-headed woman — you are not worth looking at, and there is simply no spell here at all!" The novice nun who was following behind said: "Noble one, why do you act in such a way?" Stomā Gāmī replied: "I am simply keeping the words for myself." The novice nun who was following behind then said: "Noble one, it is truly remarkable that you are not tainted by affliction!" At that point the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who has a man recite a spell incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Stomā Gāmī. "A man" means a human male. "Spell" here is used in the sense of a spell for something that is not really a spell. "Has recite" means has him recite it aloud. "Incurs a transgression" is as explained above. As for how the transgression arises: however little a nun has a man recite a spell, in every case she incurs a transgression. The fourth rule of the twenty-third group of transgressions is complete.

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. Stomā Gāmī obtained a large quantity of alms food. Whatever was good among the alms she ate herself, and whatever was poor — such as flour, husked grain, and the like — she sold. Then on another occasion Stomā Gāmī went outside on some errand. A flour-seller came to her and went to the great lady Gautamī, saying to her: "Noble one, do you have any flour?" The great lady Gautamī replied: "Good-looking one, is she surrounded by flour shops?" The man said: "Noble one, it is nuns who sell flour." She said: "Good-looking one, which nun is it who sells flour?" The man replied: "It is Stomā Gāmī." The great lady Gautamī then said to that very man: "This same occurrence has now befallen us as well," and the nuns of few desires reproached her. At that point the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who sells food incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Stomā Gāmī.

The word "food" refers to flour and similar things. The phrase "if she sells" means if she accepts payment. The phrase "incurs a transgression" is as above.

As to how the transgression comes about: for however much food a nun sells, for as long as she has not yet received the payment, she has committed a wrong action. When she receives the payment, she incurs a transgression.

This concludes the verse summary of the twenty-third transgression.

The summary verse reads:

She must not keep watch over a household's door,
Nor set a seat to grow,
Nor lay on thread,
And she must not hold an umbrella or sandals.

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī.

Now, Stomā Gāmī set down her robe in the morning, took her bowl and monastic robe, and went to a certain householder's home for alms. There she said to the wife of that householder: "Good-looking one, please give alms." The woman replied: "Noble one, I am unhappy in my heart." Stomā Gāmī said: "What, have all your calves drunk their fill of milk today?" The woman replied: "Noble one, I keep watch over the household's door but get no wages." Stomā Gāmī then said: "And are you too doing the same work as a needle?" The wife of the householder said: "Noble one, is there something you yourself are skilled at?" Stomā Gāmī replied: "What craft or work is there in which she is not skilled?"

The householder's wife then said to Stomā Gāmī: "Noble one, please keep watch over my household's door." She replied: "Who will give her alms?" The householder's wife spoke further, from "the duty" through to "and also maintaining the house."

Then Stomā Gāmī set her bowl aside to one edge, changed into clean robes, swept the entire house thoroughly clean, dusted it well, arranged the bedding, cleaned and set out the iron vessels, the silver vessels, and the gold vessels, and made the entire house beautiful. Then she took up her alms bowl and went to the summer house.

When the householder returned and saw this, he said: "Good woman, today you have cleaned and swept the house so well." The woman replied, saying: "Noble one Stomā Gāmī did it — I did not." He said: "Give her alms every day, and she shall keep watch over your household's door."

Then on another occasion the great lady Gautamī came to that house for alms, and the wife of that householder said to the great lady Gautamī: "Noble one, please keep watch over my household's door and give it your care." She replied: "Sister, when she was a laywoman she did not even keep watch over the door of a clean household, so should she now do so after going forth into renunciation? Nevertheless, sister, speaking to you who are endowed with moral discipline in this way accumulates much demerit and sows the seed of becoming a servant. And moreover, who has ever seen or heard of someone who has gone forth keeping watch over a household's door?" The woman replied: "It is Stomā Gāmī, noble one."

The great lady Gautamī then said to that very woman: "This same occurrence has now befallen us as well," and the nuns of few desires reproached her. At that point the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who keeps watch over a household's door incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Stomā Gāmī.

The phrase "keeping watch over a household's door" means performing the duties of one's own household. The phrase "incurs a transgression" is as above. As to how a transgression comes about: however much and to whatever degree a nun keeps watch over a household's door, in every instance she incurs a transgression. This completes the first of the twenty-fourth transgressions.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time, the nun Stomā Gāmī, when leading the nuns in recitation of scripture, had the nuns sit down on cushions the following morning and announced, "Take your things and go off somewhere pleasant." The nuns then rebuked her, saying: "You have had the nuns sit on cushions and experience discomfort, and in doing so you accumulate much that is not merit." The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who, from among the nuns, causes seats to be experienced — that is, has them sat upon — incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Stomā Gāmī. The phrase "from among the nuns" refers to this very order. The word "from" refers to the act. The word "seats" refers to small chairs. The phrase "causes to be sat upon" means has them carried off afterward. The phrase "experience" means appropriating them for herself. The phrase "incurs a transgression" is as above. As to how a transgression comes about: however much and to whatever degree a nun causes seats belonging to the nuns to be experienced — that is, appropriated — in every instance she incurs a transgression. However, if she is old and unable to manage without support, or if she is ill and is teaching the Dharma, there is no transgression. This completes the second of the twenty-fourth transgressions.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time the nun Tsugga'mo, having put on her lower robe in the morning and taken up her bowl and outer robe, entered a householder's home for alms and said to the householder's wife: "Good woman, please give alms." The woman replied: "Noble one, I am burdened with spinning thread and feel weary." Tsugga'mo then said: "You go, bring the alms, and come back," and the woman placed the alms in the bowl and sent it off. Then on another occasion, the great lady Prajāpatī entered that same home for alms and said: "Sister, please give alms." The householder's wife replied: "Noble one, please spin one skein of thread, and in the meantime I will go and fetch the alms." The great lady Prajāpatī said: "Sister, even when I was a householder I never carried a load — how much less so now that I have gone forth?" And with that, the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and proceeding through the establishment of the training rule, laid down the following: Any nun whatsoever who carries thread incurs a transgression. The phrase "any whatsoever" refers to Tsugga'mo. The word "thread" refers to any of the seven kinds. The phrase "carries" means makes it into a bundle. The phrase "incurs a transgression" is as above. As to how a transgression comes about: however much and to whatever degree a nun carries thread, in every instance she incurs a transgression. However, if it is for her own individual hermitage — for a strainer, a whisk, or a sash — there is no transgression. This completes the third of the twenty-fourth transgressions.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time the nun Tsugga'mo put on leather shoes and carried a parasol while going about for alms. Many people laughed, and brahmins and householders mocked her. This was then reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..."

...and thus instituted the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun carries a parasol or leather shoes incurs a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Tsugga'mo. "A parasol" means shelter from the heat. "Leather shoes" means footwear. "Carries" means by herself. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above.

How does the transgression come about? However much and to whatever degree a nun carries a parasol or leather shoes, in every instance she incurs a transgression. If she wears leather shoes in order to guard her sleeping place in a summer residence, there is no transgression.

This completes the verse summary of the twenty-fourth transgression.

The verse summary is as follows:

A wound arising at the shoulder,
a nun who is a prostitute,
a nun, a female trainee,
and a novice nun should not massage.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time a wound appeared on Tsugga'mo's shoulder, and a physician bound it. Once it had been bound, she said afterward: "This Bhadra has bound it far too tightly." When it was loosened, she said: "It is far too loose." In this way he continued binding and loosening it. Then the physician said: "Even if you do not heal, that is of no great consequence; the wound too will simply not recover," and he left. The nuns said: "Noble one, why do you behave in this way?" She replied: "She knows what is tight and what is loose — the mere act of touching is something to keep for oneself." The nuns then said: "It is astonishing that, even in those circumstances, when desire arose in you, you were not set thoroughly ablaze by it, like dry wood." This was then reported by the nuns to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence...," then instituted the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun repeatedly has a layman bind and release a wound that has appeared on her shoulder incurs a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Tsugga'mo. "A wound appearing on the shoulder" means a wound. "Repeatedly" means many times. "Has a layman bind and release it" refers to a householder. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above.

How does the transgression come about? However much and to whatever degree a nun has a man bind or release a wound that has arisen, in every instance she incurs a transgression. However, if it is the wound itself — that is, if she has it bound while keeping in mind a son, a brother, or a father — there is no transgression.

This completes the first of the twenty-fifth transgressions.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. At that time Bombagamo ordained a woman who was a prostitute. Then her former clients — the sinister one, the rough one, and the wanton one — came seeking that prostitute. When they heard that Bombagamo had ordained her, they thought: "Well, something good has been done — now we need not provide her food and clothing. All the same, we may still enjoy her company." They went to that place and began uttering improper words, while nuns who cared about the matter were distressed. This was then reported by the nuns to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence...," then instituted the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun knowingly ordains a female prostitute incurs a transgression.

"Whatever nun" refers to Bombagamo. "Knowingly" means either by herself recognizing this or having been told by another.

"Female prostitute" means one who is available to all. "Ordains" refers to ordination within this Dharma and Vinaya. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun ordains even a slight amount of a female prostitute, in every case she incurs a transgression. If she has the woman transferred to another district and then ordains her, there is no transgression. The twenty-fifth transgression, second section, is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter, Bombagamo had nuns massage her, and the nuns said: "What is the use of pleasing this one who frequents charnel grounds?" She then said words to the effect: "This will make the skin glow and become bright, and will captivate the hearts of merchants and weavers." This was reported by the nuns to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence...," then instituted the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun has nuns massage her incurs a transgression. "Whatever nun" refers to Bombagamo. "Nuns" means those who are in accord with this Dharma. "Has massage her own body" means having the body massaged. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight massage of her own body, in every case she incurs a transgression. The twenty-fifth transgression, third section, is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter, Bombagamo thought: "The Blessed One has said that nuns should not receive massage. So I shall have trainee nuns massage me." Accordingly she had trainee nuns massage her body, and nuns of few desires spoke disapprovingly. This was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence...," then instituted the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun has trainee nuns massage her incurs a transgression. "Whatever nun" refers to Bombagamo. "Trainee nun" means one who is training in the precepts that will lead to her becoming a trainee nun within this Dharma and Vinaya. "Has massage her own body" means having the body massaged. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight massage of her own body by a trainee nun, in every case she incurs a transgression. The twenty-fifth transgression, fourth section, is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Likewise, the same should be stated in full with respect to novice nuns as well, down to the institution of the training rule: furthermore, whatever nun has novice nuns massage her incurs a transgression. "Whatever nun" refers to Bombagamo. "Novice nun" means a female novice. "Has massage her own body" means having the body massaged. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight massage of her own body by a novice nun, in every case she incurs a transgression. The verse summary of the twenty-fifth transgressions is complete.

The summary verse:

She may not have a laywoman give massage,
nor likewise one who wanders everywhere.
Perfume applied with sesame paste,
and wiping with a cleansing substance.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Thereafter, Bombagamo thought: the Blessed One has prohibited massage as far down as novice nuns —

thinking, "I shall have a laywoman give me a massage," she had a laywoman give her a massage — from that point, through to where the nuns reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," established the training rule up to and including its promulgation:

Moreover, whichever nun has a laywoman give her a massage incurs a transgression.

"Whichever" refers to Bombagamo. "Laywoman" means one who dwells in a household. "Has her give a massage" means has her perform rubbing and kneading of the body. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight massage given by a laywoman, in every case she incurs a transgression. However, if one is ill and cannot endure the discomfort, or if it is her mother, her son, her daughter, or her brother-in-law who gives the massage, there is no transgression. The first part of the twenty-sixth transgression is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Likewise, the case of one who wanders everywhere is to be explained at length, from that point through to the establishment of the training rule:

Moreover, whichever nun has a wandering woman give her a massage incurs a transgression.

"Whichever" refers to Bombagamo. "A wandering woman" means a female renunciant of the Sāṃkhya school. "Has her give a massage to herself" means has her perform rubbing of the body. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight massage given by a wandering woman to herself, in every case she incurs a transgression. The second part of the twenty-sixth transgression is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Then Bombagamo was applying perfume, and the nuns said, "Noble one, what are you doing?" She replied with these words: "I am making the body fragrant." They said to her: "This body is foul-smelling by nature — for whom are you making it fragrant?" — and they continued speaking up to the point of saying: "When seen by someone with desire, it will become stained by that desire." The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence," established the training rule up to and including its promulgation:

Moreover, whichever nun applies perfume incurs a transgression.

"Whichever" refers to Bombagamo. "Applies perfume" means using sandalwood, turushka incense, and the like — fragrant substances. "Applies" means applying it herself or having another apply it. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun herself applies perfume or has it applied, in every case she incurs a transgression. The third part of the twenty-sixth transgression is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had prohibited applying perfume, from that point, the case of wiping with sesame paste is likewise to be explained, from there through to the establishment of the training rule:

Moreover, whichever nun has sesame paste rubbed on her incurs a transgression.

"Whichever" refers to Bombagamo. "Has sesame paste rubbed on her throughout" means has the pressed residue of sesame rubbed upon the body. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight amount of sesame paste rubbed on her, in every case she incurs a transgression. The fourth part of the twenty-sixth transgression is complete.

The origin of the next rule is at Śrāvastī. Then, when the twelve groups of monks were wiping the dirt from their bodies with a cleansing substance, this very act became an occasion for criticism, and the nuns of modest desires blamed them. The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This being the origin," proceeded through to "Let the training rule be laid down," and declared: "Furthermore, whichever nun uses a cleansing substance to wipe the body incurs a transgression." "Whichever" refers to the twelve groups. "Cleansing substance" refers to what is used to wipe away the dirt of the body and cleanse it. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun has even a slight amount of a cleansing substance applied to wipe the body, in every case she incurs a transgression. The verse summary of the twenty-sixth transgression is complete.

The Vinaya (monastic discipline) of the nuns, the analysis of the twenty-seventh bundle. The summary verse:

Questioning without prior occasion,
wearing the adornments of householders,
bathing while joined hand in hand,
dance, song, and music — these are not permitted.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then Stomāgāmā went to the assembly hall and questioned a monk without first making a request for the occasion, and when that monk was unable to resolve that question and became embarrassed, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This being the origin," proceeded through to "Let the training rule be laid down," and declared: "Furthermore, whichever nun questions a monk without prior occasion incurs a transgression." "Whichever" refers to Stomāgāmā. "A monk" refers to the head of the assembly. "Without prior occasion" means without having made a request. "Questioning" means asking about what was spoken by a buddha or said by a śrāvaka. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun questions a monk even slightly without prior occasion, in every case she incurs a transgression. The first part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then one morning Stomāgāmā put on her lower robe, took her bowl and her dharma robe, and went for alms at the house of a wealthy man. There, the servants of those household women had set down the ornaments beside the vessels for bodily adornments while they were dressing their hair. Thereupon Stomāgāmā, seeing a necklace, a string of ornamental beads, an armband, and the like, took them up and wore them. Those women said, "Noble one, what are you doing?" She replied, "Does it not look lovely to adorn her body with ornaments?" They responded, "What beauty is there in someone who has undertaken a different manner of life — one of going forth?" And while those women were thus reproaching her, the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This being the origin," proceeded through to "Let the training rule be laid down," and declared: "Furthermore, whichever nun wears the ornaments of householders incurs a transgression." "Whichever" refers to Stomāgāmā. "The ornaments of householders" refers to necklaces, strings of ornamental beads, armbands, and the like. "Wears" means puts them on as adornment. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun wears even a slight amount of the ornaments of householders, in every case she incurs a transgression. The second part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then the twelve groups of monks, holding hands with many wives of brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī, were bathing in the flowing river Ajiravatī, poking one another with their fingers, making one another laugh, engaging in play, romping about, joking and cavorting—

and exposing the coarseness and nakedness of the body—the monks of little concern criticized them, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and so forth, established a training rule up to the point of its full formulation: "Furthermore, whatever nun bathes while clasping hands shall incur a transgression."

"Whatever" refers to the twelve groups. "Clasping hands" means with hands joined together. As for "bathing," there are two kinds of bathing: the bathing of consecration, and the bathing of immersion. Here the intent is the bathing of immersion. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun bathes by immersion while clasping hands, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The third part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

At that time in Śrāvastī there were two groups of entertainers. One was a group of entertainers of the warrior caste (kṣatriya), and the other was a group of brahmin entertainers. The kṣatriya entertainers were accomplished in the arts of war, while the brahmin entertainers were accomplished in the arts of dance. Whenever the two groups competed against each other in a contest of martial skill, the kṣatriya group would win; and whenever they competed in dance, the brahmin group would win.

Then the kṣatriya entertainers thought to themselves: "From whom among us could we learn dance?" And they thought: "The noble Bhomā (Stomā) has gone forth from the Śākya clan and is accomplished in all crafts and all forms of work." With that in mind, they went to where Bhomā was and said to her: "Noble one, do you know even a little of the art of dance?" She replied: "Is there any craft or form of work in which I am not accomplished?" They said: "For now, grant us a fee that we will arrange, and teach us dance." She said: "Turn your hands thus, turn your waist thus, place your feet thus"—and so on, up to the point where she had the kṣatriya entertainers trained in dance.

Then those kṣatriya entertainers defeated the brahmin entertainers through dance. The brahmin entertainers then asked: "Who taught you?" When the others said it was Bhomā, the brahmins criticized, scorned, and reviled them, saying: "The conduct of the renunciants who are sons of the Śākyans, and their brahma-conduct (brahmacarya), is burned up—for they instruct others even in dance like this." The nuns then reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, beginning with "This occurrence..." and so forth, established a training rule up to the point of its full formulation: "Furthermore, whatever nun teaches dance shall incur a transgression."

"Whatever" refers to Bhomā. "Dance" means the moving of hands and feet. "Teaches" means gives instruction in it. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun teaches dance, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The fourth part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One had enacted the prohibition "One must not teach dance," shortly thereafter Bhomā went to an assembly of entertainers and performed dance for them—and beginning with that account, the Blessed One again established a training rule up to the point of its full formulation:

Furthermore, whatever nun teaches dance incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. "Teaches dance" means gives instruction in it. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun teaches dance, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The fifth part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

"From going to watch dance" up to the point of the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun goes to watch dance incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. "Goes to watch dance" means going out of a desire to see the spectacle. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun goes to watch dance, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The sixth part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

At the time when two groups of companions gathered together and a group of brahmin companions went to where Bhomā was for the purpose of song — from that account up to the point where they said, "Noble one, teach us song as well" — beginning with "The group of six" and so forth, and the terms Śeṣaghoṣā and Kaiśikā and the earthly ones having been trained extensively in the seven musical notes — the Blessed One established a training rule up to its full formulation: whatever nun gives instruction in song incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. "Song" means vocalization, that which is brought forth by the voice. "Gives instruction in it" means teaches it. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun gives instruction in song, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The seventh part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Likewise, from "teaching song" up to the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun teaches song incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. The sequence of transgressions is to be applied in correspondence with what was said above. This is the eighth part of the twenty-seventh transgression.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Likewise, from "going to watch song" up to the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun goes to watch song incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. The sequence of transgressions is to be applied in correspondence with what was said above. This is the ninth part of the twenty-seventh transgression.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

From the account of groups of the kṣatriya class going to where Bhomā was for the purpose of music, and upon arriving saying: "Noble one, teach us music — the vīṇā, the flute, the clay drum, the single-stringed vīṇā, the bābhiṣaka, the iron cymbals, and such things of most melodious sound — the seven notes" — from that account up to the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun gives instruction in music incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Bhomā. "Gives instruction in it" means in sounds possessed of the quality of sensual pleasure. "Incurs a transgression" is as above. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun gives instruction in music, even the slightest amount, in every case she incurs a transgression. The tenth part of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Likewise, from "teaching music" up to the full formulation of the training rule:

Furthermore, whatever nun performs music incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Sbom Dga' mo. The sequence of the transgression is to be understood as corresponding to the preceding ones in the same way. This is the eleventh part of the twenty-seventh transgression.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Likewise, from "going to watch music" up to the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun goes to watch music incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Sbom Dga' mo. The sequence of the transgression is to be understood as corresponding to the preceding ones in the same way. The verse summary of the twenty-seventh transgression is complete.

The summary verse is as follows:

From the dwellings where monks are present,
one must not go alone to defecate.
Crystal combs, fine-toothed combs,
bundles of grass, and hair-nets — these one must not keep.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then Gtsug Dga' mo said to a man: "Come here; do such-and-such." She signaled for him to come to the summer residence. That night the man came to the summer residence, and she placed him in the latrine area. He performed many acts and accomplished many things. Then she went to the latrine area, entered it, and said to the man: "This place is unclean — go elsewhere." He replied: "Where shall I go?" Gtsug Dga' mo said: "To your own house." Then the man said: "How shall I go?" Gtsug Dga' mo said: "Well then — ride upon her shoulder!" Thereupon he mounted her shoulder. Then Gtsug Dga' mo thought to herself: "Whatever standing I have before the community of nuns rests entirely on my moral discipline. If I, being a nun, were to break something of importance, how could I utter even a single word? Just as it is said: 'The pure one overawes the world; the impure one does not overawe the world.'" Reflecting thus, Gtsug Dga' mo became angry and cried out: "A noble woman is being abducted by a thief!" The man leapt from her shoulder to the ground and said: "What a vile, scheming woman — she herself gave the signal and now cries that a thief is abducting her!" When the nuns of modest needs heard this and began to criticize, the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning from "This incident occurred" and proceeding up to the full formulation of the training rule, declared: whatever nun goes alone to a latrine area incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to Gtsug Dga' mo. "Alone" means without a second person. "Goes to a latrine area" means goes to a place for defecating. "Incurs a transgression" is as before. As for how the transgression comes about: however much a nun goes even the slightest distance alone to a latrine area, in every case she incurs a transgression. This is the first part of the twenty-eighth transgression.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then the nuns of the group of twelve were using crystal combs to groom and arrange their hair, and other nuns said to them: "Sisters, what are you doing?" They replied: "We are growing our hair out untangled." The nuns said: "What you are doing like that is not growing hair — it is growing afflictions." When the nuns reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One then, beginning from "This incident occurred" and proceeding up to the full formulation of the training rule, declared: whatever nun removes hair with a crystal comb incurs a transgression.

"Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. "Crystal comb" means by the root of the virāṇa plant. "Removes hair" means grooming the hair of the head. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above. How does the transgression arise? However little a nun removes hair with a crystal comb, she incurs a transgression in every instance. This is the second rule within the twenty-eighth set of transgressions.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One had prohibited removing hair with a crystal comb, there was then the matter of removing hair with a tooth-comb, and this was reported to the Blessed One, beginning from "This incident occurred" up through the full formulation of the training rule: whatever nun removes hair with a tooth-comb incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. "With a tooth-comb" means with a tooth-comb. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above. As for how the transgression arises — that too proceeds as stated above. This is the third rule within the twenty-eighth set of transgressions.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Again, the matter of removing hair with a bundle of grass was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, beginning from "This incident occurred" up through the full formulation of the training rule, declared: whatever nun removes hair with a bundle of grass incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. "With a bundle of grass" means with a bundle of stalks rubbed together. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above. As for how the transgression arises, that proceeds as stated above. This is the fourth rule within the twenty-eighth set of transgressions.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Again, the matter of removing hair both with a tooth-comb and with a bundle of grass was taken up, and from that point the Blessed One, beginning from the relevant formulation up through the full training rule, declared: whatever nun removes hair with a tooth-comb and with a bundle of grass incurs a transgression. "Whatever" refers to the group of twelve. "With a tooth-comb and with a bundle of grass" means with both together. "Incurs a transgression" is as stated above. As for how the transgression arises, that too proceeds as stated above. This is the fifth rule within the twenty-eighth set of transgressions.

The origin of the rule is at Śrāvastī. Then the nun Sthūlanandā thought to herself: "I have given away everything I ever acquired. For now, let me at least obtain a mirror for myself." With that thought, she acquired a set of ornaments belonging to a musician, a garment belonging to a musician, and a pair of shoes belonging to a musician, and from a dancer she obtained a mirror. Sthūlanandā then put on all the ornaments, displayed the sign indicating the presence of a prostitute, and sat in a certain place. A man came and asked her: "What is your fee for a day?" She said: "Five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." The man replied: "That is far too much." She then said: "First look at this fine form. When you have seen how I conduct myself and are pleased, you may negotiate further on this matter." The man then gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. She told him to come inside. But then Sthūlanandā thought: "Whatever I do in my capacity as a nun is all merely a matter of moral discipline and religious conduct. If I were to do this thing as a nun, it would be breaking the moral discipline — and once a vessel is shattered, who will ever ask after it again?" With that reflection, Sthūlanandā removed the musician's ornaments and fled.

The man, startled, ran after Sthūlanandā and grabbed her by the wig. The wig came off and remained in the man's hand, and he cried out: "Foul bald-headed woman!"

Then Sthūlanandā said to the man: "Young man, do you not know that King Prasenajit has placed the nuns under royal protection? If anyone were to lay a hand on one of them, that hand would be cut off at the wrist." He replied: "A foul bald-headed woman like you is not one of those who are protected. Those who are protected are the Great Mistress of Beings, Gautamī the Slender, the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned One, Dharmadattā, Bhadravatī, and Śyāmā — not a bald-headed woman like you."

This incident occasioned criticism of nuns who had little sense of propriety, and the matter was reported to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then proceeded, from "This occurrence…" through to the laying down of the training rule: "Furthermore, whatever nun takes up a wig commits a transgression."

"Furthermore, whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. "Takes up a wig" refers to a dancer's wig. "Commits a transgression" is as explained above. As for how the transgression arises: however slight the contact a nun makes with a wig, in every such case a transgression is incurred.

Here ends the summary verse of the twenty-eighth transgression, the Pācittiya.

Here ends the full set of transgressions from the Vibhaṅga of the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya.

Now the individually confessable offenses are to be recited. The summary verse of the rules for individual confession is as follows:

Milk, curd, butter,
Clarified butter, grain oil, molasses,
Honey, fish, and meat,
Dried meat — these are the appointed items.
The origin story is set in Śrāvastī.

At that time the group of twelve women, out of craving for fine food, took milk from other people's households and consumed it. Because they were roaming about looking for milk, they lost their scriptural transmission, their recitation, their study, their yogic practice, their mental application, and their inner calm abiding. This was reported to the Blessed One, who declared: "It is not to be taken." Later, when the same fault arose in connection with purchasing it, the Blessed One declared: "It is not to be bought." When the same fault arose in connection with asking for it from relatives, the Blessed One declared: "It is not to be requested."

At a certain point there was a sick nun, and a physician prescribed that she take milk. She replied: "Noble sir, she is already as good as dead." The physician asked: "Why?" She answered: "The Blessed One has prohibited it." The physician said: "Your Teacher is compassionate — he will grant permission." On that occasion the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "When prescribed by a physician, it may be used as medicine."

Thereafter Sthūlanandā, whether sick or not sick, took milk from other households and consumed it. This was reported to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, proceeding from "This occurrence…" through to the laying down of the training rule, declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun, when not ill, for her own sake—"

goes to households, requests milk, and consumes it by drinking or eating, that nun shall go to the summer hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession."

"Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. "For her own sake" means for her own body. "When not ill" means when she has not been struck down by illness. "Households" means the houses of brahmins and householders. As for the word "milk," there are five kinds of milk: cow's milk, buffalo's milk, camel's milk, goat's milk, and fifth, sheep's milk. "Having requested" means having asked. "Consumes it by drinking or eating" means swallowing a gulp, even just a mouthful. "That nun" means whatever nun this may be. "Having gone to the summer hall" means to the temple. "Before the nuns" means before those who observe this same Dharma. "Shall confess" means shall disclose it openly. "An improper matter unworthy of a noble one" means that which is not to be done by a nun. "Improper" means it will become an occasion for attachment. "I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it" means one must confess it definitively. "This is a matter for confession" means it must absolutely be disclosed.

As for how a transgression arises in this matter: however much milk a nun requests, all of it becomes an offense of wrongdoing. Upon obtaining it, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Upon using it, it becomes a matter for confession. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is deranged, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is overcome by pain.

This concludes the first confessable offense in the Vinaya analysis of the nuns.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. At the time when the Blessed One had prohibited milk for the nuns, proceeding from "Then, requesting curds" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun, when not ill, for her own sake, goes to households and requests curds and consumes it by drinking or eating — that nun shall go to the summer hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: 'Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession.' 'Whatever' refers to Sthūlanandā." The remaining sequence of transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. Where "the five milks" appears there, one should here expand it as "the five curds." This is the second confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Likewise, proceeding from "requesting fresh butter" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared: "Furthermore, whatever nun, when not ill, for her own sake, goes to households and requests fresh butter and consumes it by drinking or eating — that nun shall go to the summer hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: 'Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession.' 'Whatever' refers to Sthūlanandā" — up to "as for fresh butter, there are five kinds." The remaining sequence of transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the third confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Then, proceeding from "requesting clarified butter" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared:

Furthermore, whatever nun, not being ill, requests clarified butter from households for her own sake and consumes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā — up to "as for clarified butter, there are five kinds." The remaining sequence of transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the fourth confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Then, proceeding from "requesting sesame oil" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared:

Furthermore, whatever nun, not being ill, requests sesame oil from households for her own sake and consumes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā — up to "as for sesame oil, it is the expressed essence of sesame seeds." The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the fifth confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Then, proceeding from "requesting raw sugar" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared:

Furthermore, whatever nun, not being ill, requests raw sugar from households for her own sake and consumes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā — up to "as for raw sugar, it is of sugar." The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the sixth confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Then, proceeding from "requesting honey" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared:

Furthermore, whatever nun, not being ill, requests honey from households for her own sake and consumes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā — up to "as for honey, it is the milk of bees." The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the seventh confessable offense.

The locus of origin is Śrāvastī. Then, proceeding from "requesting fish and meat" up through to the laying down of the training rule, he declared:

Furthermore, whatever nun, not being ill, requests fish and meat from households for her own sake and consumes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā — up to "as for fish and meat, it is that which moves in water and so forth." The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the eighth confessable offense.

The occasion for this arose in Śrāvastī. The rule was established from "then, requesting meat" up through the laying down of the training. Furthermore, whatever nun, when not ill, requests meat from households for her own sake and then distributes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. From that point up to "meat" refers to the milk of cattle and so forth. The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the ninth confessable offense.

The occasion for this arose in Śrāvastī. The rule was established from "then, requesting dried meat" up through the laying down of the training. Furthermore, whatever nun, when not ill, requests dried meat from households for her own sake and then distributes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: "Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession." "Whatever" refers to Sthūlanandā. From that point up to "dried meat" means that which is dried meat. The remaining sequence of other transgressions is to be applied in conformity with the foregoing as it stands. This is the tenth confessable offense.

The occasion for this arose in Śrāvastī. The background runs from "when General Siṃha saw the Truths" up through "the Blessed One having spoken, the Saṅgha granted the vow of training." Then the twelve groups entered that household and received alms. After that the nuns said to them: "Sisters, did the Blessed One not grant the vow of training with respect to that household?" Those men replied: "It was granted to the monks, but not to the nuns." Thereupon, the nuns of few desires rebuked them and reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One established the rule from "this occurrence" up through the laying down of the training: "Nuns, those households for which the Saṅgha has established a training rule are households under a vow of training. Whatever nun, without having been invited beforehand, goes to households designated as 'training households' — households known as such — and with her own hand takes what is to be distributed and eaten, and then distributes or eats it — that nun must go to the assembly hall and confess before the nuns this offense which is an improper matter unworthy of a noble one, saying: 'Sisters, I have committed this offense that is to be confessed — I confess it. This is a matter for confession.'"

"Whatever" refers to the twelve groups. "Of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas. "Households known as training households" means those of persons who have seen the Truths. "Under a vow of training" means so designated by a formal motion and twofold act. "Without having been invited beforehand" means without having been summoned as a guest. "Goes" means having gone. "With her own hand" means by herself. "What is to be distributed and what is to be eaten" refers to the five things to be distributed and the five things to be eaten. "Takes and distributes or eats" means swallowing bite by bite in secret. "That nun" means whichever nun she happens to be. "The assembly hall" means the temple. "Before the nuns" means before those who hold this Dharma. "Shall confess" means shall disclose. "An improper matter unworthy of a noble one" means something a nun ought not do. "Improper" means something that leads to attachment.

"A matter requiring individual confession has arisen; I acknowledge that matter as one requiring individual confession" means making a definite disclosure. "This matter is one requiring individual confession" means that it must without fail be confessed.

Now, how does a transgression arise in this regard? It arises in the range from "however many of the households known as training-places with vows of training, where the nun has not previously been uninvited" up to "if she takes or eats, in every case it becomes a matter requiring individual confession." If she was invited from the very beginning, or if she was given permission to relax the vow of training, there is no transgression.

Here ends the eleventh matter requiring individual confession.

Here ends the section on matters requiring individual confession from the Analysis of the Nuns' Vinaya.

Now the trainings shall be set forth. The summary verse for the trainings is as follows:

Wearing the robe well, not covering the head,
leaping and moving the body,
sitting, and the feet —
these are fully collected in the assembly.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at the hermitage of Kuñjakā the sage, in Śrāvastī. At that time, the Great Progenitress Gautamī Śākyamuni, her head shaved and robed in ochre, went and traveled toward Śrāvastī together with approximately five hundred women. Traveling gradually along the way, she arrived at the hermitage of Kuñjakā the sage in Śrāvastī. Now, at the time when the Blessed One, in dependence upon the Great Progenitress Gautamī, had given permission for nuns to go forth and receive full ordination in this Dharma and Vinaya, those nuns, not knowing how they should wear their robes, spoke to the monks. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The robe shall be worn rounded, neither too high nor too low."

When the Blessed One had thus spoken, the Great Progenitress and the other nuns who were there in their natural state put on their robes and lower garments. Then on another occasion a group of twelve nuns wore their lower garments hitched up very high, and the other nuns said to them: "Why do you wear your lower garments so high?" They replied: "We were accustomed to it when we were householders." The Blessed One thereupon declared: "One shall not wear the robe or the lower garment hitched up too high, nor shall one wear them trailing too low." Thus he established this as a rule of training.

When those nuns put on their lower garments they folded them back at the sides, and the other nuns said to them: "Why do you fold your lower garments back at the sides?" They replied: "That is how laywomen wear them." The other nuns said to them: "Are you then laywomen?" On that occasion the nuns reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in wearing the lower garment and the robe rounded — neither hitched up too high nor trailing too low."

The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

Then the group of twelve wore their robes like an elephant's trunk, and the other nuns said to them: "Sisters, why do you wear your robe like an elephant's trunk?" They replied: "Wealthy people, merchants, and caravan leaders wear them this way." The Blessed One then declared:

"You shall train in wearing the robe and the lower garment not like an elephant's trunk, not folded like a palm leaf, not like a grain spike, not like the hood of a serpent, and not like the nine folds of a serpent's hood."

The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

Then the group of twelve went to households with their shoulders bared, and the other nuns said to them: "Sisters, why do you walk about with your shoulders bared?" They replied: "So that when the lustful catch sight of them, their hearts will be broken." At that the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in entering a household with the robes well fastened and properly worn."

When entering households they went about making loud noise and great clamor, and the Blessed One declared: "You shall enter in a composed and subdued manner."

Then they went about glancing to either side, and the Blessed One declared: "You shall enter a household without letting the eyes wander."

Then they went about without looking forward at all, and the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in entering a household and sitting down with the robes well fastened and properly worn, moving in a composed and subdued manner, with eyes not wandering, looking only as far ahead as the length of a yoke."

Then when the group of twelve went about with their heads covered, the other nuns asked them why they did so. They replied: "When we were formerly daughters-in-law of weavers' families, this is how one behaved in the household." The others said: "Are you still daughters-in-law of weavers? Whatever is done in ignorance of that will be abandoned, and you too shall train in the training." At that the Blessed One declared: "You shall not enter a household with the head covered."

This is the twenty-eighth fascicle, the last, of the Analysis of the Nuns' Vinaya.

Then when the group of twelve went about swinging their arms like a pair of logs as they walked, the other nuns asked: "Why do you walk like that?" They replied: "That is how daughters-in-law of weavers' families walk." The others said: "Are you daughters-in-law of weavers?" The group of twelve said: "Whatever is done in ignorance of that will be abandoned, and you too shall train in the training." At that the Blessed One declared: "You shall enter that household without swinging the arms."

Then when the group of twelve walked with their robes slung over one shoulder in the manner of cowherds, the Blessed One declared: "You shall enter a household without slinging the robe over one shoulder."

Then when the group of twelve, imitating the way boys walk in a children's school, tucked their upper robes up high as they went into households, the Blessed One declared: "You shall enter a household without tucking the upper robe up high."

Then when the group of twelve slung their robes over both shoulders as they entered households and said: "This is how servants walk," the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in entering a household and sitting down without covering the head, without swinging the arms, without slinging the robe over one shoulder, without tucking the upper robe up high, and without slinging it over both shoulders."

Then when the group of twelve went about laughing loudly in households, saying: "This is how the lustful walk" —

the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way."
