Then when the group of twelve crouched down and went along saying: "This is how one walks artificially," and entered households crouching — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not enter a household walking in that way." Then when the group of twelve dragged their feet along the ground and entered households by shuffling their feet, saying: "This is how they walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way." Then when the group of twelve crept about stealthily and entered households by sliding along, saying: "This is how householders walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way." Then when the group of twelve leaned on a staff and entered households saying: "This is how the wealthy and merchants walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in entering a household and sitting down without stomping the feet, without leaping, without shuffling the feet, without sliding, and without leaning on a staff." Then when the group of twelve swayed their bodies and entered households saying: "This is how elephants walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not enter a household swaying the body in that way." Then when the group of twelve waved their arms and entered households saying: "This is how the wealthy and merchants walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way." Then when the group of twelve turned their heads from side to side and entered households saying: "This is how thoroughbred animals walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way." Then when the group of twelve clasped their hands together and entered households saying: "This is how those of supple manner walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not walk about in that way." Then when the group of twelve walked shoulder to shoulder into households saying: "This is how close companions walk" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall train in entering a household and sitting down without swaying the body, without waving the arms, without turning the head, without clasping the hands, and without pressing the shoulders together."

Then when the group of twelve sat down on seats in the homes of brahmins and householders without having been invited, and those hosts expressed displeasure — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit down uninvited." When the Blessed One established this as a rule of training, instructing that one should lean against the doorpost and examine the seat carefully before sitting down, then the group of twelve again sat down in households without examining the seat — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit down in that way." When the Blessed One established as a rule of training for novices that one should lean against the doorpost and not press down with the full weight of the body, then the group of twelve again sat in households pressing down with the full weight of their bodies — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit in that way." Then when the group of twelve sat inside dwellings with their legs crossed, saying: "This is how those of supple manner sit" — from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit in that way." Then when the group of twelve sat inside households with their thighs crossed, saying: "This is how the wealthy and merchants sit" — from that point the Blessed One declared:

"You shall train yourselves thus: when sitting inside a household, you shall do so only when invited, having properly inspected the seat, without pressing down with the full weight of the body, without crossing the legs, and without crossing the thighs."

Then the group of twelve sat in households with their haunches touching and resting against each other, saying: "This is how the dancers sit" — and from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit in that way."

Then the group of twelve, saying: "This is how the deep thinkers sit," placed one knee upon the other and sat thus — and from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit in that way."

Then the group of twelve sat with their feet tucked up, and when the wives of brahmins and householders came and paid reverence at their feet, the monks spread their feet apart, and those women, touching their heads to the ground, reproached them — and from that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit with your feet tucked up."

Then the group of twelve sat inside households with their feet stretched out, and when the wives of brahmins and householders came and paid reverence at their feet, the group of twelve spoke to them only a partial blessing, saying merely: "May you be free from illness," whereupon those women said: "Why do you not say the full words 'May you be free from illness'?" And the group of twelve said to them: "You have paid reverence to one foot — pay reverence now to the other foot as well" — and the women reproached them for this. From that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall not sit with your feet stretched out."

Then the group of twelve sat inside households with their feet excessively bent back, and when the wives of brahmins and householders came to pay reverence, those women reproached them — and from that point the Blessed One declared:

"You shall train yourselves thus: when sitting inside a household, you shall not place haunch against haunch, you shall not place knee upon knee, you shall not tuck your feet up, and you shall not stretch your feet out."

A summary verse:
Receiving properly, the uninvited,
tiptoeing, splitting grain,
with the hand, and with the mouth speaking,
not stooping — and not standing.

The Blessed One was dwelling in the land of Bharga, in the Frightful Mountain Forest of the Crocodile Child-slayer, in the deer park. At that time Prince Bodhi had a magnificent white-lotus palace with plastered walls built on Crocodile Child-slayer Mountain, and there he invited the Blessed One, together with the monks and nuns.

Now the retinue of the young Prince Bodhi were of no faith, and they hurled lumps of food violently, breaking the hands and bowls of the nuns.

Then, in another part of that place, the group of twelve gathered together, and they said among themselves: "Dear Joyful, Dear Rejoicer, Dear Plump One — let us teach these children of the child-slayer woman a lesson!" And so when the food came, they seized their bowls and tilted them back, and those cooked rice portions fell to the ground — whereupon nuns of little standing reproached them. From that point the Blessed One declared: "You shall receive food properly."

In the same way, having been invited to a certain household — and so forth up to: — however many portions of cooked rice and vegetables one has let fall from the bowl to the ground, that same amount one shall now accept — and the Blessed One declared: "You shall receive food without exceeding the brim or cutting short at the lip."

In Śrāvastī, a householder had invited them to his home — and so forth up to the point of the invitation — and when cooked rice and vegetables were being distributed in equal measure to those in the group of twelve, they kept calling out for more —

The Blessed One declared: "One shall eat cooked rice mixed together with vegetables in equal measure."

In the same way, having been invited to a certain household — and so forth up to that point — there was then a case where the cooked rice was plentiful but the vegetables were very scarce, and they would cover the vegetables over with cooked rice in order to ask for more. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not cover the vegetables with cooked rice."

In the same way, in another instance — and so forth up to that point — the vegetables were plentiful but the cooked rice was scarce, and out of desire for more, they covered the cooked rice with vegetables. The Blessed One declared: "One shall train in the following: to take food properly and eat it; to eat without stopping midway; to eat in equal measure with one's vegetables; and, out of desire for more, neither to cover the vegetables with cooked rice nor to cover the cooked rice with vegetables."

Then the group of twelve, even before the appointed meal had arrived, began receiving the bowl — and so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not receive it."

Then in the front row before a certain Sthūlanandā, an elderly nun who had been expelled was sitting with her mouth gaping open. Sthūlanandā threw a lump of food into that gaping mouth. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not sit with one's mouth gaping open, having not yet taken a morsel."

Then the group of twelve, while eating their meal, were making noise. The nuns said: "Sisters, what do you think you are doing behaving like that?" and those women replied: "When one forgets a word, one speaks it out thus," — and so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not speak with one's mouth full of a morsel of food."

Then the group of twelve were putting two or three grains of cooked rice at a time into their mouths — and so forth up to the point where they said: "Those who cannot read, eat like this." The Blessed One declared: "One's morsels shall not be too small."

Then the group of twelve were putting excessively large morsels into their mouths — and so forth up to the point where they said: "Those who are hungry, eat like this." The Blessed One declared: "One shall train in the following: not to receive the bowl even before the appointed meal has arrived; not to sit with one's mouth gaping open having not yet chewed one's morsel; not to speak with one's mouth full of a morsel; and to make one's morsels proper — neither too small nor too large."

And so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve were making a smacking sound while eating, and the nuns said to them: "What do you think you are doing behaving like that?" and those women replied: "Children eat like this," — and so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall eat without making a smacking sound," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve were making a slurping sound while eating — and so forth up to the point where they said: "Those who are ill and cannot read, eat like this." The Blessed One declared: "One shall not eat in that manner," — and so forth up to that point.

On one occasion, when the community of nuns had been invited as guests to a certain householder's home, that householder served abundant cooked rice but only a small amount of vegetables. Intending to make sport of him, the nuns ate making a loud smacking sound. The householder was embarrassed and said: "Noble ones, I did wish to offer plain cooked rice, but alas, there is only a little sauce available." The Blessed One declared: "One shall eat without making a smacking sound," — and so forth up to that point.

In the same way, when a certain householder invited them as guests, that householder was poor, and in the winter season he served cold food. Intending to make sport of him, they ate while blowing on it and making a "phu phu" sound.

The householder then became embarrassed and said: "Noble ones, I did wish to offer something, but my means are poor and there was nothing I could do." From that point, the Blessed One declared: "One shall eat food without making a 'phu phu' sound," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve, while wandering through the countryside and going about, arrived at the house of a farmer. There they shook out their robes, washed their feet and hands, and sat down to eat. At that moment, some naked ascetics (Jainas) arrived at the neighboring house and likewise sat down to eat. The group of twelve, intending to make sport of them, piled food up into the shape of a stūpa and planted a tent-pole as the spire, then said to those naked ascetics: "This is a stūpa of your Teacher." They then broke off pieces from that stūpa and ate them, all the while chanting in unison: "This is the stūpa of the Fully Accomplished One!" At that, the naked ascetics felt pain and distress, and began to weep, saying: "Today it seems our Teacher has passed beyond his time." The Blessed One declared: "One shall train not to make a 'tsug tsug' sound, not to make a 'hu hu' sound, not to make a 'balchag balchag' sound, not to make a 'phu phu' sound, and not to eat food having fashioned it to resemble a stūpa."

Then the group of twelve spread food out on a flat board and, picking up one grain at a time, placed it in their mouths. The nuns said to them: "Why do you eat like that?" They replied: "When birds pick up scattered offerings, they do it just like this." From that, the Blessed One declared: "One shall not pick through food grain by grain," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve was invited as guests to a house, and the host served them ordinary cooked food. They praised that food lavishly. When another host served them fine food, they found fault with it. From that, the Blessed One declared: "One shall not praise or find fault with food."

Then the group of twelve, while eating, were seen to transfer morsels of food from cheek to cheek as they ate. When it was said: "That is how sick people eat," the Blessed One declared: "One shall not shift morsels from cheek to cheek," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve were seen to bite food in half, rest it on the tip of the tongue, display it to one another, and then swallow it again. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not stick out the tongue over food," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve were seen to break a morsel of food into three parts: placing one part in the mouth, a second in the hand, and a third in the alms bowl. The Blessed One declared: "One shall train to eat food without picking through it grain by grain, without praising or finding fault, without shifting morsels from cheek to cheek, without sticking out the tongue, and without splitting off stray portions," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve were seen to lick their hands while food was still present. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not lick the hands," — and so forth up to that point. Likewise, they were seen to scrape their alms bowls. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not scrape the alms bowl," — and so forth up to that point.

Then Sthūlanandā put food in her mouth and shook her hands. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not shake the hands," — and so forth up to that point.

Then the group of twelve was invited as guests to a house, and Sthūlanandā, finding some flour there —

— she lifted up her alms bowl and said, "This alms bowl of mine has been taken — hand it back, hand it back!" And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not lift up the alms bowl," — and so forth up to that point.

Then a certain householder invited the community of nuns to his home as guests, and he prepared an abundance of side dishes and foods. Among the group of twelve there was an elderly nun who had gone forth. The householder first served the community of nuns with clarified butter and flour, and then the group of twelve took a great deal of flour. The householder then served from the older end of the twenty-eight varieties of porridge, and when the elderly nun who had gone forth looked to one side — wherever the elder was seated — the group of twelve threw lumps of food in front of that elderly nun who had gone forth and said, "It is said that showers of precious gems fall from the king upon those younger than I; so you, being endowed with merit, have received a shower of food." And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall train to eat one's food with the perception of an alms bowl, not licking the hands, not scraping the alms bowl, not shaking the hands, and not lifting up the alms bowl," — and so forth up to that point.

Then when the group of twelve looked into the alms bowls of their fellow nuns, they began to complain, saying, "Much has been served there, and little has been served to us." And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One who wishes to complain shall not look into the alms bowls of fellow nuns," — and so forth up to that point.

Then, when the group of twelve, with hands sticky from food, took hold of a water vessel, the stickiness of food caused flies to buzz around it, and the householders who saw this censured them. And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not take hold of a water vessel with hands sticky from food," — and so forth up to that point.

Then again a certain householder invited the community of nuns as guests. In the assembly, between the congregation and a companion nun, there sat a nun wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe. One of the group of twelve poured the rinsing water from her alms bowl over her and said, "Wretched, wicked woman — do you alone have a patched robe?" — and so complained. And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not throw the rinsing water of one's alms bowl at another," — and so forth up to that point.

Now, at the time when a prohibition was made at the hill of Kumāraghāta (the hill where children are slaughtered), at the White Lotus mansion, against pouring food-rinsing water inside a house — on account of another householder this was subsequently permitted, with the ruling that one may pour it inside after asking the householder who is present.

Then again, the group of twelve began pouring it inside houses without asking. And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not pour food-rinsing water inside a house without first asking the householder who is present," — and so forth up to that point.

At Śrāvastī, the son of a certain brahmin, his mind disturbed, went to Śrāvastī and happened to brush against the water in a monk's alms bowl, whereupon his mind was restored. Then another brahmin's son whose mind was disturbed — and that brahmin, having heard of this from the first brahmin, went to the nuns' rain-season residence, and asked how much Sthūlanandā had fetched the alms-bowl water — she filled the alms bowl with the remains of the community's food and gave it to him. The brahmin thought, "The death of my son is indeed not something to be wished for" — and did not accept it. And so forth up to that point. The Blessed One declared:

One should train not to look with lustful intent so as to slander fellow nuns, not to hold a water vessel that has been soiled with food by hand, not to sprinkle food-soiled water on a fellow nun, not to pour food-soiled water inside a house without asking the householder, and not to pour the leftover food into the alms bowl and discard it — up to that point.

Then the group of twelve nuns began placing their alms bowls on ground that had no foundation beneath it, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not place them so." Then the group of twelve nuns placed their alms bowls at the edge of a precipice, and the bowls fell and shattered, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not place an alms bowl at the edge of a precipice" — up to that point. They then began placing them at the bank of a stream, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not place them at the bank of a stream" — up to that point. They began placing them in the middle of a path, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not place them in the middle of a path" — up to that point. When they began polishing their alms bowls with a heavy wet mixture of sand, before long the bowls became pale and worn, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must train not to place an alms bowl on ground that has no firm foundation beneath it, not to place it at the edge of a precipice, not to place it at the bank of a stream, not to place it in the middle of a path, and not to polish an alms bowl with a heavy wet mixture of sand" — up to that point.

Then it happened that a young woman was standing to wash an alms bowl, and the nuns said to her: "Sister, stand and wash the alms bowl." When she replied, "What will come of this?" the bowl fell from her hands and broke. Then they said to her, "This is what will come of it," whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not wash an alms bowl while standing" — up to that point. In the same way, when they began drying one while standing, the Blessed One declared: "One must not dry an alms bowl while standing" — up to that point. When they began wiping one while standing, the Blessed One declared: "One must not wipe an alms bowl while standing" — up to that point. When they began putting an alms bowl into its case while standing, the Blessed One declared: "One must not put an alms bowl into its case while standing" — up to that point. When they then began taking an alms bowl out of its case while standing, the Blessed One declared: "One must train not to wash, dry, wipe, put into its case, or take out of its case an alms bowl while standing" — up to that point.

The summary verse:

Not while standing, not improperly, not with the head uncovered,
not with the arm akimbo like an elephant's shoulder;
one must not urinate on grass or in water,
nor fill a tree — not even a little.

Then the group of twelve nuns began teaching the Dharma while standing to those who were seated, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. Then when sick persons came, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach the Dharma to the sick" — up to that point. When they began teaching in the same manner to those who were seated or lying down, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill" — up to that point. When they began walking ahead of others and then turning back to follow behind them and teach the Dharma, the Blessed One declared:

"One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill while standing to one who is seated or lying down, nor to one on a lower seat while sitting on a higher seat, nor by following behind one who is walking ahead, nor by walking along the roadside while teaching the Dharma to one who is not ill and is traveling on the road — one must train accordingly" — up to that point.

Then the group of twelve nuns began teaching the Dharma to those with their heads covered, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When those with eye ailments came, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach the Dharma to those with eye ailments." Likewise, "One must not teach it to those who are not ill" — up to that point. When workers came, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it" — up to that point. Likewise, when they began teaching Dharma to those with a wound on one side, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill" — up to that point. When they began teaching Dharma to those making a neighing sound like a horse, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill" — up to that point. When they began teaching Dharma to those with their arms folded behind their necks, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When those with their arms folded behind their necks came, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill, to one with their head covered, nor to one not vomiting, nor to one without a wound, nor to one without a wound on both shoulders, nor to one who is not ill and has their arms folded behind their neck — one must train in not teaching the Dharma thus" — up to that point.

Then the group of twelve nuns began teaching the Dharma to those riding elephants, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. Then those riding elephants set out for battle, and they said: "Noble one, please teach the Dharma." The nuns said: "Dismount and I will teach the Dharma." Those riders said: "The enemies who would destroy us are pressing at our rear" — up to that point, and the Blessed One declared: "Declare them to be ill and teach the Dharma" — up to that point. Likewise, one should also speak to those riding horses and those who have mounted chariots. Then, those riding on a person's shoulders or head — one must not teach the Dharma — up to that point. When one among them became ill, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach" — up to that point. When they began teaching Dharma to those wearing high shoes, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to one who is not ill and is riding an elephant, nor to one riding a horse, nor to one mounted in a chariot, nor to one riding on a person — one must train in not teaching the Dharma to one who is not ill and is wearing high shoes" — up to that point.

Then the group of twelve nuns began teaching the Dharma to those with their hair piled up in a topknot, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When a king came, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it" — up to that point. Likewise, when those with their heads bound in a turban came, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When great ministers or sick persons came, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it" — up to that point. Likewise, when those with their heads bound in a garland came, "One must not teach it so" — up to that point, and the Blessed One declared:

"One may teach it to the sick" — up to that point. Likewise, when those with their heads bound in a turban came, "One must not teach it so" — up to that point, and the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it to a merchant or to the sick" — up to that point. Then again, when those wearing hats came, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When sick persons came, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to a healthy person with hair in a topknot, nor to one with a turban on the head, nor to one with a garland bound about the head, nor to one with a turban bound on the head, and one must train not to teach the Dharma to a healthy person wearing a hat" — up to that point.

Then, when the group of twelve were teaching the Dharma while carrying weapons in hand — "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. When one who is setting out for battle becomes sick, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it" — up to that point. Likewise, when those carrying a parasol came — "One must not teach it so" — up to that point, and the Blessed One declared: "One may teach it to the sick" — up to that point. Likewise, when one came carrying a staff in hand — "One must not teach it so" — up to that point. Then, if it is a sick person or an aged person who cannot survive without a staff, the Blessed One declared: "One may teach the Dharma to such persons" — up to that point. Likewise, when one came carrying a sword in hand — "One must not teach it so" — up to that point, and the rest is as above.

Likewise, when those wearing the five pieces of armor came, the Blessed One declared: "One must not teach the Dharma to a healthy person carrying a weapon in hand, nor to one carrying a parasol in hand, nor to one carrying a staff in hand, nor to one carrying a sword in hand, nor to one carrying war armor in hand, and one must train not to teach the Dharma to one wearing the five pieces of armor" — up to that point.

Then, when the group of twelve were standing and relieving themselves — "One must not do so" — up to that point. When a sick person is unable to sit, the Blessed One declared: "If one is sick, it is permitted."

Then, when Sthūlanandā (the Stout Delightful One) came to the Śakyan settlement, she saw someone guarding her own pleasure garden, and that person said: "If you had not gone forth into renunciation, what would you be to me?" And the other replied: "You would be my mistress." Sthūlanandā said: "Then why do you not provide me with vegetables and flowers as I need them?" The garden-keeper replied: "At that time, when you provided me with food and clothing as I needed them, I in turn served you. Now you have gone forth and I am a householder — how am I to serve you?" Thereupon Sthūlanandā took a purgative medicine, placed a pot, and poured into it a great quantity of her own excrement and urine, and when it was likewise filled with vomit she took the pot and a broom and went to the pleasure garden, where she scattered all those vegetables and the flowering trees with filth. The foul smell brought foxes and dogs rushing there. The next day the garden-keeper saw those vegetables in that condition and became distressed, and Sthūlanandā said to him: "Garden-keeper, how is your pleasure garden — fragrant and full of lush greens?" He replied: "Noble lady, this is your doing," and she mocked him, saying: "Yes, that is how you have been repaid." Up to that point, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not discharge excrement and urine onto green grass" — up to that point, and "If one is sick, it is permitted" — up to that point.

In the same way, from "one must not spit" up to "It is not to be done," the Blessed One declared: "If one is sick, it is permitted" — up to that point. In the same way, the same is to be said regarding mucus. From "one who discharges vomit and phlegm" up to the Blessed One's declaration: "One must train to refrain from discharging excrement and urine while standing upright when not ill, and from discharging excrement, urine, spittle, mucus, vomit, and phlegm onto ground where there is green grass when not ill" — up to that point.

In the same way, just as was said above in the foundation-story of Sthūlanandā regarding the garden-keeper and the nun Sthūlanandā, the same is to be said regarding the cook. From "after taking a purgative medicine" up to "she rendered the vessel filled with filth, the basin for beating, and the vessel for washing clothes unfit" — up to that point. Then when that cook was washing clothes, he saw those garments stained with various multicolored dyes and smeared with foul matter — up to that point. Then Sthūlanandā came and said these words: "Housewife, why have the garments turned pale?" He replied: "Noble lady, surely this is not your doing?" And when Sthūlanandā said: "Yes, that is how you have been repaid," she was reproached — up to the Blessed One's declaration: "One must not discharge excrement, urine, or spit into water" — up to that point. When sick ones were doing so in that very place, the Blessed One declared: "It is permitted." In the same way, from "spittle, mucus, vomit, and phlegm" — if one is sick, "it is permitted" — up to that point.

At the time when the Blessed One, while in Śrāvastī, laid down the rule concerning the duty-master regarding climbing trees, Sthūlanandā climbed a tree for some particular purpose. The nuns said to her: "Sister, did not the Blessed One lay down this rule?" She replied: "He laid it down for the monks; not for the nuns." From that point up to the Blessed One's declaration: "One must train to refrain from discharging excrement, urine, spittle, mucus, vomit, and phlegm into water when not ill, and from climbing trees to a height greater than the stature of a man, except in cases of necessity" — up to that point.

The many trainings are complete. The many trainings from the Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns are complete.

Now the procedures for the resolution of disputes are to be stated. In summary:

Direct evidence and recollection,
the verdict of one who is not insane, and its essential nature,
the spreading of many sticks of grass,
the formal acknowledgment, and the spreading of grass.

For one who is fit to be disciplined by direct evidence, the settlement by direct evidence is given. For one who is fit to be disciplined by recollection, the settlement by recollection is given. For one who is fit to be disciplined as one who is not insane, the settlement as one who is not insane is given. For one who is fit to be sent to seek the essential nature of the matter, that procedure is given. For one who is fit to have many sticks of grass spread, that procedure is given. For one who is fit to make a formal acknowledgment, that procedure is given. For one who is fit for what is like the spreading of grass, that procedure is given. One must train so that those who have fallen into dispute are disciplined, calmed, and thoroughly pacified in accordance with these seven principles for the resolution of disputes, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teaching of the Teacher.

The seven principles for the resolution of disputes are complete. The seven principles for the resolution of disputes from the Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns are complete.

Eight defeats, the Saṅgha remainder twenty,
likewise abandonments thirty-three,
and further, offenses requiring expiation one hundred and eighty,
and those requiring individual confession, eleven —

The garland of trainings is supreme
and the one who brings peace accords with the monk.
Patience, the holy austerity, is indeed patience —
nirvāṇa is supreme, so the Buddha has declared.
One who has gone forth and harms others,
who injures others, is no true renunciant.

Where one with eyes exists to overcome the far shore,
even as the humble do in the fitting way,
the wise, in this living world,
should entirely abandon evils.
One should not slander, nor do harm;
one should restrain oneself through the prātimokṣa.
One should know the measure in food;
one should dwell in a remote and solitary place.
One should rightly apply oneself to the higher mind.
This is the teaching of the Buddha.

Just as a bee upon a flower
takes the nectar without harming the colour or the scent
and flies away,
so should the Sage move through a village.

One should examine what is fitting and unfitting for oneself —
not the discordant acts of others,
not what others have or have not done.
One should be heedful with regard to the higher mind
and train in the grounds of restraint of the Sage.
One who is ever mindful of full tranquillity
is a protector who is free from sorrow.

Through generosity, merit greatly increases.
Through good restraint, one does not become an enemy and the like.
Endowed with virtue, one abandons evil.
Through the exhaustion of the afflictions, one passes beyond sorrow.

Commit no evil whatsoever;
accomplish virtue in full abundance;
tame your own mind completely —
this is the teaching of the Buddha.

Excellent is the restraint of body;
excellent is the restraint of speech;
excellent too is the restraint of mind;
restraint in all things is excellent.
The monk who is restrained in all these ways
is thoroughly liberated from all suffering.

Guarding one's speech, perfectly restraining one's mind,
and not committing non-virtuous acts with the body —
having thoroughly purified these three pathways of action,
one will attain the path proclaimed by the sage.

The All-Seeing Buddha, whose crown-protrusion protects all;
the Destroyer of Cyclic Existence, the Golden Sage, Kāśyapa;
Śākyamuni, Gautama, God of gods,
the supreme guide of the untamed, who is beyond compare;
the Protector of the World, the supreme Saviour —
these seven heroic Buddhas,
the prātimokṣa of each of the famous ones,
has been extensively set forth here.

Toward this, the Buddhas, and whoever —
and also the disciples of the Buddhas — show reverence.
Those who have come to hold it with reverence,
may they attain the unconditioned.

One should compose oneself and bring it forth;
one should enter into the teaching of the Buddha.
Like a great elephant attacking a house of reeds,
one should defeat the host of the lord of death.

Whoever with full heedfulness
will practise in this Dharma and Vinaya
will, having thoroughly abandoned the cycle of birth,
make suffering come to its final end.

The Analysis of the Vinaya for Nuns, together with the Prātimokṣa, is complete.

This was translated by the Kashmirian abbot Sarvajñadeva, Dharmākara, and the Indian abbot Vidyākaraprabha, together with the Tibetan translator the monk Palgyilhunpo. It was then edited and established by the Indian abbot Vidyākaraprabha and the great Tibetan editor-translator the monk Paltsegs.

Earlier, it was corrected by Ānanda and Śākyapal; the impurities of those two earlier corrections were cleared away. A third correction was made by the learned master of Nartang, and it was thus excellently purified upon this earth.

The fourth part of the Vinaya is present here.

Translator's notes

The verse section beginning "Blissful is the arising of buddhas" closely parallels known Udānavarga and Dhammapada material, particularly the "Sukha" chapter. The Tibetan here renders a Sanskrit Gāthā collection embedded in the Vinaya narrative.

The term rendered "leans to the far shore" and "leans to the near shore" translates ཕར་འཛིན and མར་འཛིན literally. These are somewhat elliptical and may refer to those oriented toward liberation (the far shore) versus those still engaged with worldly virtue (the near shore); the exact doctrinal referent is context-dependent and the rendering remains faithful to the Tibetan.

The list of deity names presents several figures whose identification required interpretive choices. Upendra is an epithet of Viṣṇu as younger brother of Indra; Karmāntaka refers to a deity of all actions; Pañcārṣika and Pañcaika are yakṣa commanders; Hārītī is the yakṣa mother figure often rendered "Hārītī" in Sanskrit. The sentence concluding the passage is deliberately left unfinished in the Tibetan, as the narrative continues into the next section. The term rendered here as "sacred trees" translates a word literally meaning "approach-banks" or "fording places" (a loan of the Sanskrit tīrtha in its sense of sacred site or tree-shrine); in this context it refers to sacred trees or tree-shrines associated with divine residence, consistent with the narrative's repeated mention of tree-deities.

The gandharva (dri za, literally "scent-eater") appearing as the fifth condition refers to the being in the intermediate state between death and rebirth, who must be present at conception — a standard Abhidharma account of the three conditions for conception: parental union, the mother's fertile period, and the presence of a gandharva. The five-crested hairstyle described for Brahmā's youthful form is a standard iconographic detail in the Sanskrit and Tibetan narrative tradition; no special doctrinal uncertainty attaches to it.

The list of epithets applied to Brahmā — Brahmā, Great Brahmā, Sovereign, Creator, Projector, Emanator, Supreme, Supremely Exalted, far shore of the world — is a standard polemical catalogue found in Buddhist critiques of the Brahmanical creator-god theology. The passage's dramatic irony turns on Brahmā's secret admission that he neither created the world nor was created by it, directly undermining each of these epithets.

The four great kings are the guardians of the four directions: Dhṛtarāṣṭra (East), Virūḍhaka (South), Virūpākṣa (West), and Vaiśravaṇa (North). The Tibetan text names Virūḍhaka and Vaiśravaṇa explicitly; the other two are implied by the group of four. The passage describes the bodhisattva's descent from Tuṣita (here rendered as the Tuṣita heaven based on context, though the Tibetan reads Dgaʼ ldan, literally "Joyful," the standard Tibetan rendering of Tuṣita) as a white elephant into Queen Māyā's womb, which is the classical account of Śākyamuni's final rebirth. The epithet "son of the earth-guardian" as a comparison for the elephant is unusual and may refer to a mythological elephant associated with the earth deity.

The phrase rendered as "raise the Dharma stūpa" translates a Tibetan term literally meaning "Dharma offering-pillar" or "pillar of Dharma worship"; it may refer metaphorically to establishing the teaching rather than a physical monument, but the image is intentionally grand. The final sentence is somewhat compressed and its precise meaning is debated. The phrase rendered "extending the lineage of kings by playing games with the great king Padma" reflects a passage about a brahmin possibly engaging in competitive or social interactions with a royal patron to establish dynastic or lineage continuity. The exact nature of "playing games" here may refer to a courtly or competitive context; the Tibetan is not fully explicit, and the broader narrative context would clarify the intended sense. The "golden barleycorns" planted at the outset is an unusual idiom; it appears to refer to a ritual or auspicious agricultural act connected with the birth rite, possibly a symbolic sowing done with gold-colored grain as a merit-making gesture for the birth of a son.

The eighteen branches of knowledge listed here correspond to a classical brahminic curriculum. Several items in the list — such as "the science of falling into water," "the science of swallowing," "the science of casting far into the world," and "the sixty-section Tantra" — are not standard Sanskrit equivalents easily identified from the Tibetan alone; the renderings given are literal translations of the Tibetan and may reflect unusual or specialized technical traditions. These are noted for scholarly attention but do not affect the doctrinal sense of the passage. The Jambū River gold (Jambūnadī gold) is a legendary gold of supreme quality said to flow from beneath the Jambū tree at the center of Jambudvīpa; it is a stock Indian literary image for the finest, most lustrous gold, here made explicit by the narrative conceit of casting a statue from it. This explains why the father considers such a standard impossibly high. The name "Śerśkya" is a rendering of the Tibetan "སེར་སྐྱ་" which literally means something like "yellow-tawny" or "golden-pale." It functions here as a brahmin family name. The translation retains it as a proper name rather than rendering it semantically, since it serves as a patronymic for the daughter Bhadra throughout the narrative.

The passage breaks mid-sentence at its end, corresponding to an incomplete source segment. The translation faithfully reflects this. The name "Bzangmo" (meaning "the good one" or "the fair one") is rendered as a proper name throughout rather than translated, as it functions as a personal name in the narrative. Similarly, "Śerśkya" is kept as the brahmin's name. The city name "Kapila" likely refers to Kapilavastu, the city associated with the Śākya clan.

The plant name "mālūta" is a best reconstruction of the Tibetan transliteration; the exact botanical identification is uncertain but it is a flowering tree used as a colour-reference simile. "Tamarind" renders "tin ti li ka," a standard Indic plant loanword. "Round cakes" renders "bal po se'u," a type of confection; the precise preparation is uncertain but the term is a loanword from Sanskrit or Prakrit culinary vocabulary. The phrase rendered as "eighty bushels of refined gold grain" (gser gyi nas sbyang brgyad bcu) is unusual — it appears to be a measure of refined gold reckoned in the unit of a bushel (nās), possibly a Sanskritic loan. The exact meaning of the accounting detail about King Padmachenpo's gold is somewhat obscure in context; the rendering follows the most natural syntactic reading.

The verse quoted by the brahmin boys appears to be a gnomic saying about things that travel unimpeded. The translation renders it as closely as possible to the Tibetan; the precise doctrinal or literary source is not identified here. The phrase rendered "leaf-bundle" translates a term that in this context likely refers to a mendicant's alms-bowl or a bundle associated with begging rounds; the Tibetan "lo ma'i phur ma" literally means "a bundle of leaves," possibly a leaf-bowl used for receiving alms, which was common practice. This is a minor lexical uncertainty with no doctrinal consequence. The name rendered consistently as "Bhaṅgamā" (Tib. བཟང་མོ) in the preceding passage was rendered as "the good girl" or "good woman" — here the Tibetan continues to use བཟང་མོ as both a name and an epithet (meaning "good one" or "Bhaṅgamā"); I have kept it as a name per the continuity of the narrative, treating it as a proper noun, while also retaining the vocative sense where context demands.

The verse rendered as camphor: ཕུ་ཤེལ (pusher / pushe) likely corresponds to Sanskrit puṣkara or puṣpacandana; the term may indicate a fragrant tree-resin or camphor-type substance. The rendering "camphor" is an approximation; the precise aromatic is uncertain but does not affect the doctrinal content.

The final sentence — "a teaching that is not wholesome" (དམ་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཆོས) — is rendered literally. In context it likely means the parents have arranged the situation in a way that invites transgression of the young couple's vow of celibacy, which Nyagrodha-born regards as a spiritually harmful act, hence "not wholesome" or perhaps "not virtuous." The doctrinal valence is that of akuśala-dharma, a morally unwholesome matter. The final line is incomplete in the source text as given; the verse breaks off mid-sentence. The rendering preserves this break faithfully rather than supplying content not present in the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "one possessed of the horn-mark" translates the Tibetan term for an ascetic bearing the distinctive horn-tuft, a conventional figure for a great brahminic or ascetic practitioner; the imagery is of a renowned ascetic whose power is destroyed by the touch of a woman.

The phrase "for the sake of warming ourselves" renders a somewhat condensed Tibetan expression suggesting a pretext (sharing warmth) that Bhadrā uses as cover for the practical necessity of sharing the single bed; this reading follows the narrative context. The verse beginning "A small monkey" is a gnomic utterance whose precise referent is not entirely clear from context. It appears to be a saying about contentment with little and the danger of craving for more; "delusion seizes the remainder" echoes the standard Buddhist analysis of how greed and bewilderment attend accumulation. The rendering follows the most natural syntactic reading of the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "verbal spears" is a free but defensible rendering of "ཁའི་མདུང་ཐུང་གིས་འདེབས་པ," literally "stabbing with short spears of the mouth," a vivid idiom for sharp, wounding speech used in quarreling. The phrase rendered "as far as the city's outskirts" translates "ཐེ་གི་ཙམ་གྱི་བར་དུ," where "ཐེ་གི་ཙམ" is a measure of distance, likely meaning the outer boundary or a short distance outside; the exact extent is not specified in the text and the rendering "city's outskirts" captures the general sense.

The repeated verse at the opening of this passage is identical to the verse closing the preceding passage, indicating that it belongs to Sgyug-mo's speech and is here attributed to the new speaker within the continuing narrative frame. The passage compresses a well-known narrative of the Buddha's life, moving from the bodhisattva's renunciation through awakening and the early period of conversion. The names Gayā and Gayābala render the two women who offered milk-rice; in some versions this figure is a single woman named Sujātā, but the Tibetan here explicitly names two women, consistent with certain Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya recensions. The milk porridge "reduced sixteen times" refers to a specific preparation method described in Vinaya literature. The town called "Senānī" renders the Tibetan "dmag ldan gyi grong," literally "the village of the army-possessing one," a standard translation of the Sanskrit Senānīgāma. The stūpa name rendered "Supratishthita" translates "bu mnams kyi mchod rten," literally the stūpa of Supratishthita, consistent with Mūlasarvāstivāda accounts. The ending of the passage is mid-sentence in the source, and the translation preserves that break faithfully. The phrase rendered "with a basis of occasion, never without occasion" and the parallel formulations that follow represent a set of technical conditions for legitimate Dharma teaching. The Tibetan terms གླེང་གཞི་དང་བཅས་པ, ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་དང་བཅས་པ, རྟོན་པ་དང་བཅས་པ, རྟུན་པ་དང་བཅས་པ, and ཆོ་འཕྲུལ་དང་བཅས་པ refer respectively to teaching that has a proper occasion or pretext, that leads to definite emergence from cyclic existence, that has something to rely upon, that has a suitable purpose or receptive basis, and that is accompanied by miraculous display. These are standard conditions in Vinaya-related contexts for authentic and legitimate teaching. The rendering is interpretive where the terms admit of variation. The phrase rendered "festival of meeting at the mountains, a festival of beauty" translates two compound terms that appear to describe a local seasonal or religious gathering. The precise nature of this festival is uncertain from the text alone; the rendering follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan.

The epithet "scion of a noble house" renders a conventional honorific address used when speaking to a woman of brahmin background.

The charnel-ground cloth exchange between the Blessed One and Kāśyapa is a celebrated episode reflecting the depth of their spiritual kinship; the Tibetan carefully uses honorific verb forms throughout to distinguish speech directed to the Blessed One from that of ordinary exchange. The epithet "མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ" (literally "the enemy born from the mother," i.e., one born as his mother's foe) is the standard Tibetan rendering of Ajātaśatru (Sanskrit ajātaśatru, "whose enemy is not yet born" or by folk etymology "enemy not yet born"), referring to the prince who murdered his father Bimbisāra. The text does not name him explicitly at this point but the epithet is unambiguous.

The phrase "རི་དགས་ཀྱིས་རི་དགས་མི་གསོས་" rendered as "a deer does not rear a deer" is a proverbial expression meaning that one should now stand on one's own — a wild creature is not nursed by its own kind once grown. The intended sense is that Mahākāśyapa has completed his role as spiritual guide and she must now be self-sufficient. The phrase rendered "Lady of Beings" translates སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, a high honorific title for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's aunt and the first fully ordained nun. The compound literally means "great mistress of living beings," functioning as a formal title rather than a descriptive epithet.

The description of karma as "luminous" renders the Tibetan འོད་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རྣམ་པར་གནས, meaning she abided as if radiant or bright — the sense being that the impending karmic result was clearly and inevitably present, like a light that cannot be hidden. This is an unusual metaphor and the precise doctrinal valence is not entirely standard. The verse spoken by King Ajātaśatru comparing himself to one who has not yet reached the far shore of an ocean is somewhat elliptical. The reading adopted here understands him to mean: he had not yet fully crossed the ocean of saṃsāric suffering, and now a second wave of transgression has come upon him. This is a plausible contextual interpretation; the Tibetan is grammatically compressed.

The final verse is a well-known canonical gāthā on the inescapability of karma, found with minor variants in several Pāli and Sanskrit sources (cf. Dhammapada 127); its citation here by Suvarṇā is theologically significant, as she exculpates the king while affirming that the encounter was shaped by her own past karma. The passage contains the standard Vinaya phrasing for what will become a pārājika rule for nuns. The final sentence is deliberately left open-ended in the Tibetan, as it introduces the rule whose full wording continues in the following passage. The phrase rendered "even if she were reborn together with one born in an animal realm" is a vivid idiomatic expression conveying the extreme gravity of the offense — that even such a degraded rebirth companion would not excuse the act. The twelve groups mentioned are the standard "group of twelve nuns" (dvādaśavargīyā bhikṣuṇī) who are the habitual troublemakers in Vinaya narratives, parallel to the group of six monks. The terms "heartland" and "borderlands" render the Tibetan technical distinction between a central region where the full Saṅgha is established and an outlying region where it is not, a distinction that carries legal weight in the Vinaya. The point here is that relinquishment of training requires a witness who genuinely comprehends what is being said; if comprehension fails due to a language barrier, the relinquishment is invalid.

The phrase rendered "motion-and-four-fold-act of formal procedure" refers to the standard Vinaya legal act (Skt. jñapticaturthakarman) consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations; its use indicates full legal standing within the Saṅgha. The term rendered "mentally deranged" translates the Tibetan ཅ་ཅོ་ཅན, which literally refers to someone who babbles or is incoherent, typically understood in the Vinaya context as a person whose mental incapacity renders their verbal acts legally ineffective.

The list of verbal expressions near the end of the first main case — words, phrases, expressions, speech, and so on — is a standard Vinaya formula enumerating different modes of verbal communication to ensure comprehensive legal coverage; it is rendered in full as it appears in the text.

The phrase rendered "woman of loose character" translates za ma, a term in Tibetan Vinaya literature denoting a woman of disreputable conduct; ma ning refers to a person of indeterminate sex or a eunuch; and dge slong sun phyung ba refers to a nun who has been expelled or whose status has been annulled. These three, together with the preceding categories, form a list of degraded or irregular statuses whose verbal invocation may serve as a form of relinquishing the training. The phrase rendered "the coming together of two with two" is a canonical Vinaya technical definition of sexual intercourse, referring to the joining of the two sex organs of two beings. This formulaic expression appears consistently in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya contexts.

The sentence about "mother" and "father" — "I do not remember my mother; I remember my father, my brothers, and my sisters" — is slightly elliptical in the Tibetan. The sense appears to be that the speaker is expressing homesickness and a desire to return to family and household life, offered as motivation for relinquishing training; the asymmetry regarding the mother may reflect a textual lacuna or scribal irregularity in this transmission. The term rendered as "motion and three announcements" reflects the standard Vinaya formula for formal acts of the assembly: one motion followed by three readings of the announcement, constituting a fourfold act. The passage on "partially obstructed" and "unobstructed" refers to a technical Vinaya analysis of anatomical conditions during the act, which is standard in commentarial literature on this rule. The name "Norchen" is a Tibetan rendering of a proper name; the underlying Sanskrit equivalent is not specified in the text. The passage is a Vinaya commentary expanding the second pārājika (defeat) rule for nuns, treating theft. The text operates as a cross-reference scaffold, directing the reader to recite whole sections verbatim from the parallel monk's rule, then provides the nun-specific analytical glosses. The term "māṣaka" is a unit of weight and monetary value used in Vinaya contexts to set the threshold for a pārājika theft offense; it is left in Sanskrit as a technical term of art. The phrase rendered "those of indeterminate sex" translates a term referring to persons of a third biological category recognized in Vinaya literature, sometimes called "pandaka" or "hermaphrodite" in older scholarship; the rendering chosen here is neutral and contextually appropriate. The final sentence breaks off mid-analysis, reflecting that the source passage itself is a continuous commentary that continues beyond the excerpt provided. The term rendered "one who has been commissioned" versus "one who has been dispatched" translates two distinct Tibetan expressions referring to a proxy acting under prior agreement versus one simply sent on an errand; the legal distinction matters for assigning culpability in Vinaya analysis but both result in defeat if the theft is completed.

The phrase "śīriṣika" in the condensed summary is a proper technical Vinaya term referring to a specific type of benefactor or donor category; it is left in Sanskrit as its exact meaning in this context requires fuller Vinaya commentary to unpack.

The five māṣakas is the standard threshold weight of value above which theft constitutes a defeat offense, corresponding to the ancient Indian monetary measure; it is equivalent here to the threshold established in the monks' Prātimokṣa. The name rendered here as "Migalandika the ascetic-barber" translates the Tibetan "ri dgas zlog dge sbyong sbed." This is an unusual compound: "ri dgas zlog" can mean "deer-repeller" or possibly be a proper name; "dge sbyong sbed" means "barber of ascetics" or "one who shaves ascetics." The traditional identification of this figure as Migalandika the barber — known from the Pāli parallel in the Suttavibhaṅga — supports this rendering. The precise Tibetan form may reflect a name that was transliterated and then partially translated or corrupted in transmission. The passage is a Vinaya canonical text, specifically from the section elaborating the third pārājika rule for nuns, which concerns killing a human being. The Tibetan follows the standard commentarial format found in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya vibhaṅga, analyzing the rule's constituent terms one by one. The phrase rendered "water-knife" translates Tibetan chu gri, which likely corresponds to a blade used for cutting in water or a specific surgical or barber's instrument; its precise identification is uncertain but it appears alongside sword and razor as a class of edged weapon. The terms "nun in name only," "nun who lays claim to the title," and so forth follow the standard fourfold classification of bhikṣuṇī found in this Vinaya tradition. The phrase rendered "oozes from within like something rotten" translates a stock Vinaya formula of abuse; the image is of interior moral putrefaction leaking outward. The "donkey" comparison renders "lung bong ltar kun du spyod pa," where lung bong is a wild ass or donkey; the point is uncontrolled, shameless wandering. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, cutting off during the description of hell; no text has been omitted — this is where the supplied Tibetan ends. The closing sentence is incomplete in the supplied Tibetan — it breaks off mid-thought. The translation reproduces it as far as the text goes, ending with the phrase about the higher realms being "all but assured," which renders the idiomatic Tibetan image of the higher realms being "cut off only by a silk curtain," meaning they are so close as to be nearly within reach. This vivid idiom has been rendered with equivalent sense rather than literally, to serve the oral listener. The phrase rendered "liberation is but a hand's breadth away" and "the higher realms are assured by a silken thread alone" are idiomatic Tibetan expressions conveying that liberation or a higher rebirth is tantalizingly close and well within reach. The image of a veil or screen for liberation and a silken thread for the higher realms is preserved as closely as English idiom allows.

The phrase "acts done with one motion, two motions, or four motions together with an invitation" refers to the formal categories of Vinaya procedural motions: a single-motion act, a two-motion act, and a four-motion act with invitation — the standard Vinaya legislative procedures for communal acts of the Saṅgha. The six named teachers are the canonical six non-Buddhist masters of ancient India known from Pāli sources as the six teachers of rival sects. The Tibetan renderings are phonetic approximations of their Indian names: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gośāla, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambala, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātaputra (the last being the Jain teacher Mahāvīra). Some of the Tibetan phonetic forms are partially unclear, but the identification of this group as a whole is not in doubt.

The passage ends mid-sentence with a long string of epithets describing the Blessed One; the syntax continues into the following passage and is left open accordingly. The passage "the nine successive meditative absorptions" renders the standard list of nine successive attainments (anupūrvasamāpatti): the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the cessation of perception and feeling.

The verse lines "the mother-cow seeking her beloved calf" and "like a mother-cow who has lost her cherished calf" render a traditional simile (the bereaved cow seeking her lost calf) used in Buddhist literature for compassionate, tireless seeking. The Tibetan ba bzho n ("mother-cow" or "nursing cow") and beu ("calf") are central to this image.

The closing section shifts into what appears to be a commentarial framing passage — explaining the narrative setting of a sūtra and indicating which portion is to be "extensively expounded." This is characteristic of an exegetical text (a vyākhyāna or ṭīkā) that is unpacking a root sūtra narrative. The reference to "the opening subject-matter of the saffron-robed monks" (ser skya'i gleng gzhi) indicates the formal occasion (nidāna) or frame story of the relevant discourse. The city name rendered "Prabhāvatī" corresponds to the Tibetan "འོད་མ་ཅན" literally "possessing light" and is identified as a locality near Vaiśālī in Vinaya literature. The city name "Prajñapti" renders the Tibetan "སྤོང་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གྲོང་ཁྱེར," literally "the city of elimination or designation," which may correspond to a different Sanskrit toponym in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya; the exact Sanskrit equivalent is not fully certain from the Tibetan alone. The phrase rendered "the supreme human quality" translates a technical term meaning the highest or most excellent quality attainable by a human being, specifically referring to supramundane attainments such as meditative absorptions and the noble fruits. Falsely claiming such attainments constitutes the fourth pārājika for nuns in the Vinaya.

The line "abiding in contact refers exclusively to what is seen, the Dharma" reflects a Vinaya commentarial gloss specifying that the phrase "abiding in contact" in this rule applies only to direct experiential contact with the Dharma as seen — i.e., the truths realized on the path of seeing — rather than any broader sense of meditative contact. The list of non-human beings includes several terms requiring comment. "Garuḍa" renders nam mkha' lding, the great sky-soaring bird of Indian mythology. "Gandharva" renders dri za, literally "scent-eaters." "Kinnara" renders mi'am ci, the half-human celestial musicians. "Kumbhāṇḍa" renders grul bum, a class of spirits. "Zombie" renders srul po and "corpse-reanimator" renders lus srul po — these are classes of lesser spirits associated with corpses; the precise distinction between the two terms is not entirely transparent in the canonical commentarial tradition, and the renderings are approximate.

The name "Śersky" for ser skya bzang mo is uncertain; this appears to be the name of a nun, literally meaning something like "the excellent tawny-yellow one" or a personal name. The identity and story are not elaborated in the passage and the rendering keeps the apparent name. The name Śerkyabzangmo is left as a Tibetan proper name, as the preceding passage established it in that form. The name Karṇajalendhara, rendered from the Tibetan རྣ་ལག་ཅན, literally means "the one with ear-ornaments" or "ear-lobed"; this is a plausible Indic royal name and is reconstructed accordingly. The transition structure of this passage alternates between abbreviated narrative summaries enclosed in quotation formulae and direct narration — a common feature of sūtra prose that has been preserved faithfully. The passage is a redactional summary section in which the compiler abbreviates parallel stories for the second and third pratyekabuddha narratives by saying "up to the point where it says such-and-such," indicating that the same full text applies with only minor variations. This is a standard Vinaya literary device and has been rendered transparently in the translation so the listener can follow the structure. The name "Gdong-ma-legs" in the second narrative is a Tibetan rendering left in transliterated form here since the Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain in this context. The phrase rendered "queen of the Sāla clan" translates སླས་ཀྱི་བཙུན་མོ, where སླས may be a clan or dynastic name rather than a common noun; the reading is not entirely certain but a proper name seems most likely in context.

The narrative is structured as a frame story in which multiple pratyekabuddhas recount their own going-forth, with verses attributed to each. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end as it does in the source passage. The passage is a narrative summary interspersed with direct quotation, characteristic of Vinaya storytelling, and the referential abbreviation phrases such as "up to what is described" and "from the passage beginning" reflect the source text's own internal cross-references to a fuller narrative version elsewhere. The summary verse listing "Kāliṅga," "the one with pendulous ears," "Mithilā," and so on is a mnemonic colophon listing the topics of adjacent stories in the same textual section; the Tibetan terms are rendered into their most likely Sanskrit equivalents or descriptive English where no proper name is apparent. The final sentence breaks off mid-thought in the Tibetan, as this is a continuous narrative passage. The translation faithfully reflects that the merchant's thought is left incomplete at the passage boundary. The name translated here as Bhadraṃkarā follows the standard reconstruction for the Tibetan "Bzang mo." The exact Sanskrit form of this character's name may vary by recension; the Tibetan simply gives "bzang mo," meaning "the good one" or "the fair one," and the reading here is inferential.

The phrase rendered "like millstones ever-turning" for "phye ma leb ltar" (literally "like a flat millstone") carries the sense of eyes that are wide, fixed, and unblinking — an image of helpless, open-mouthed fixation. This is a somewhat unusual simile and its precise nuance is debated. The phrase rendered "the supremely dissolute one" translates མཆོག་ཏུ་བཀྲབས་པ, literally "the supremely/utterly libertine one," the fifth figure distinguished from the four village libertines. The term བཀྲབས་པ denotes a dissolute rake or libertine; the rendering is consistent with the preceding passage.

The final verse spoken by the tree deity is genuinely terse and slightly ambiguous. The image of being "cut down" and "springing up again in the last month of spring" likely refers to the nyagrodha tree's branches that were broken by the men sitting on them, with the deity lamenting the tree while wryly predicting the men's continued foolishness — though it may also carry a karmic resonance about their future rebirths. The phrase rendered "a guard who cut off the ears and noses of intruders" reflects the Tibetan idiom for a punishing royal garden-warden; the mutilation is the penalty for unauthorized entry, not a description of the guard's own appearance.

The fifth man's verse turns on the key insight that flattery is useless — the nose will not regenerate regardless — and his sincerity distinguishes him as the deserving recipient, which is the narrative's moral pivot.

"Bhadrikā, the daughter of the Śākya clan" renders སེར་སྐྱའི་བུ་མོ་བཟང་མོ; སེར་སྐྱ is the Tibetan rendering of Śākya, and བཟང་མོ (Bhadrikā) is her name. The passage is a formulaic summary-by-reference text, citing earlier passages of the same canonical narrative by their opening and closing phrases rather than quoting them in full. This is standard Vinaya redactional style. The connective phrase rendered "up to the passage that reads" represents the Tibetan convention of indicating abridged quotation, and its function has been made transparent in the translation without using the Tibetan technical marker.

The name Vipaśyin (Tibetan: Rnam par gzigs) is the first of the seven buddhas of antiquity. "Bandhumān" (Tibetan: Gnyen ldan) is his father's name, well attested in canonical sources. The passage is a lengthy editorial abbreviation — a common redactorial device in Buddhist canonical texts whereby a scribe or editor signals that long passages already narrated earlier in the same text are to be understood as repeated here, marking only the opening and closing phrases of each section. The translation accordingly renders each abbreviated segment as a summary reference in the third person, faithful to the Tibetan structure. The names Bhadravadanā and Śreṇika follow standard scholarly conventions for this text. The phrase "མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲས་ཞག་བདུན་དུ་སྤྱད་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ" is rendered "she experienced seven days in the company of a natural enemy before her birth." The term "མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ" (literally "enemy before birth" or "innate enemy") is a somewhat unusual expression here; it likely refers to a hostile situation or oppressive relationship she endured at birth or in the womb-period, and the precise narrative context is not given in this excerpt. This is noted as a point of genuine uncertainty.

The name "བླ་མ" in "བྲམ་ཟེའི་ཁྱེའུ་བླ་མ" is rendered as the proper name "Uttara" following Indic conventions for this story cycle, where the brahmin youth Uttara (Skt. Uttara) is a recognized figure associated with the prophecy under Kāśyapa Buddha. If a different identification is intended by the redactor, this should be checked against the fuller text. The "northern Unpleasant Sound" renders Uttarakuru, the northern continent of classical Buddhist cosmology, whose Tibetan name is a calque of the Sanskrit. It is here glossed in the pratyekabuddha's description as a place without possessiveness, with a fixed lifespan, and with a distinguished mode of existence — standard Abhidharma attributes of Uttarakuru. The somewhat unusual framing ("when one does not go to Uttarakuru, one collects alms among the Thirty-Three") likely means the pratyekabuddha alternates between the two destinations depending on the occasion; the Tibetan syntax is compressed but this reading is the most coherent. The phrase rendered "occasions and non-occasions" translates གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ, literally "the possible and the impossible" or "what is feasible and what is not" — a standard Abhidharma category referring to the analysis of what can and cannot occur given conditions. This is a recognized doctrinal term pair and the rendering reflects its technical sense.

The expression ཕུང་པོ་དང་ཁམས་དང་སྐྱེ་མཆེད together constitutes the classic triad of aggregates, elements, and sense bases — the standard analytical categories of Abhidharma scholasticism — and is rendered accordingly. Utpalavarnā is the standard Sanskrit name for the Tibetan ཨུཏྤ་ལའི་མདོག (literally "hue of the blue lotus"), a well-known arhat nun in the early canonical literature; the name is kept in Sanskrit throughout.

The term kārṣāpaṇa (Tibetan transcription ཀཱར་ཥཱ་པ་ཎ) is an Indian coin of silver or copper, standard currency in the Vinaya narratives; left in Sanskrit for clarity.

The verse couplet at the opening enumerates certain social classes or occupations connected to the preceding Vinaya section; the final verse summarizing the eight defeats is a mnemonic gāthā. The eighth item, "born of a slave" (གྲེ་ལས་སྐྱེས), refers in Vinaya context to a rule involving a woman born of servile status — the precise referent will be clarified in the fuller commentary. The term rendered "duty-nun" translates the Tibetan office of dge skos ma, the female equivalent of the karma-dāna, the monk appointed to oversee the practical affairs of the assembly. The rendering "duty-nun" is a functional gloss; no single established English equivalent exists across all traditions.

The passage "contact of limb with limb" renders yan lag dang yan lag tsam reg pa, a technical euphemism used in Vinaya literature to describe a degree of physical contact that falls short of full sexual intercourse but nonetheless constitutes a transgression. The doctrinal and legal weight of this distinction is significant in the monastic code.

The sentence ending "the blessed buddhas are like this" appears to be a rhetorical introduction whose continuation falls in the next passage; it is left open accordingly. The phrase rendered "from the knee down, from the eye down" reflects the Tibetan "mig man chad pus mo yan chad," which specifies a body-contact zone between the knee and the eye — a standard Vinaya formulation delimiting the area of prohibited contact. The phrasing sounds paradoxical in English because it gives two opposite limits; both bounds together define the range, meaning the body between those two points. This is a fixed technical formula in the Vinaya's analysis of the pārājika rule.

The opening sentence about "flood-water" is an abbreviated continuation of the preceding list of contrasting qualities of the blessed buddhas; the Tibetan is elliptical and the full sense depends on context from the prior passage. The nun named here is Sthūlanandā — her Tibetan name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ means literally "Fat-and-Joyful," which is the standard Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit Sthūlanandā. She is a well-known figure in Vinaya narratives.

The anatomical boundary "from below the eyes down to above the knee" is the standard Vinaya formula for the zone of bodily contact that triggers this rule; the translation follows the text's own logic rather than attempting medical precision.

The term rendered "grave offense" for སྦོམ་པོ is the Vinaya technical category thullaccaya (Sanskrit sthūlātyaya), a serious but non-defeating infraction; "wrongdoing" renders ཉེས་བྱས (duṣkṛta / dukkṛta), the lightest category of Vinaya offense.

The phrase rendered "from as high as the armpits down" for འཕྲལ་བ་ཡན་ཆད is uncertain in its precise anatomical reference; the Pāli parallels suggest the armpit as the upper boundary for the second set of rules concerning receiving objects. The passage enumerates eight categories of behavior that constitute the offense, but the Tibetan text breaks off mid-enumeration at the point of explaining "sets a time," continuing through the remainder of the rule's analytical commentary. This is a direct excerpt from the Mūlasarvāstivāda Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya and the technical legal analysis that follows the narrative. The term rendered "pressing close and fondling" translates the same three-term Tibetan phrase used in the preceding passage, maintaining consistency. The phrase rendered "she cannot drive him away" translates a stock Vinaya formula indicating the irreversibility of the situation once the man has entered. The term rendered "sidling and jostling" for གཞོགས་སྟེགས and "exposing the root" for རྩ་བ་ཧྲལ are technical Vinaya terms whose precise physical referent is debated in the commentarial tradition; the renderings given follow the contextual gloss provided within the passage itself. The phrase "foremost of all" and "the twelve roles of a nun" refer to standard Vinaya enumerations whose full content is supplied by the surrounding text not included here. The name translated as "Priyā" renders མཛའ་མོ and "Priyamatī" renders མཛའ་ཅན་མ, both being approximate Sanskrit back-formations from the Tibetan meaning "the dear one" and "she who has affection" respectively. The name rendered "Kṛtaka" reconstructs the Tibetan གྲེ་སྐྱེས, which is an unusual form. The Sanskrit underlying it is uncertain; "Kṛtaka" is a plausible reconstruction but the reading remains tentative.

The title སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི is the great Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, here rendered as "the great female sovereign Gautamī" following the literal Tibetan, though the Sanskrit title Mahāprajāpatī ("great sovereign of beings") is implied. The wooden signal board renders the Indic term gaṇḍī, the wooden sounding board used in monasteries to summon the community, here left as a functional description rather than a transliterated term since the passage is intended for audio narration. The procedural formula for the monastic act follows the standard karmavācanā pattern of motion and announcement found in Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "his hair standing on end and his body's hairs risen" translates a Tibetan idiom for deep remorse and agitation — literally "hair of the head erect, body-hairs risen" — which in this Vinaya context signals the monk's genuine contrition and readiness to make amends.

The "community of the Twelve Groups" refers to a notorious group of twelve monks frequently cited in Vinaya narratives as causing disciplinary problems; their counterpart among the nuns is implied here in the address. The passage contains a long formal Vinaya legal formula being recited first as instruction and then as the actual motion and act. The list of medicines follows a standard Vinaya fourfold categorization: timely medicines (to be taken at mealtimes), medicines allowable within a period (yāmika, i.e., within a watch of the night), seven-day medicines, and lifetime medicines. The rendering of the motion formula attempts to capture the technical repetition characteristic of Vinaya procedure. The phrase rendered "things to remember" and "things to inquire about" translates dran par bya ba and dri bar bya ba, which in Vinaya contexts refer to memoranda or reminders and items one may ask about from a teacher; the precise referents are contextually specific to monastic practice but the translation preserves the sense adequately. The passage describes a formal Vinaya proceeding — specifically a saṅghakamma (formal act of the Saṅgha) against twelve groups of nuns who, even after being admonished, refused to relent and clung to their position. The list of allowable medicines and provisions represents standard Vinaya categories: those permitted at mealtime, during a watch period, for seven days, and for the duration of one's life. The text breaks off mid-sentence in the final repetition of the formal motion, which is characteristic of the Tibetan canonical Vinaya's use of abbreviated formulaic repetition — the full reading would complete the list with "fruit medicines" and continue with the remaining clauses as in the prior iterations. The passage is part of a formal Vinaya procedural text describing a羯磨 (karma / formal Saṅgha act) being performed against a group of problematic nuns. The phrase rendered "things to remember, things to inquire about" (དྲན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། དྲི་བར་བྱ་བ) likely refers to mnemonic aids and questioning items used in formal Vinaya proceedings, though their precise identity in this context is not entirely clear from the text alone. The four categories of medicines — timely, fixed-hour, seven-day, and life-long — are standard Vinaya classifications for permissible medicinal substances. The phrase rendered "things to remember, things to inquire about" (Tibetan: dran par bya ba dang, dri bar bya ba) refers to a standard list of items brought as attendants' courtesies; the exact referents are conventional and may include reminders and questions pertaining to the suspended monk's needs or status. The translation follows the same convention as the preceding passage for consistency. The name rendered here as Gre-kye (spelled gre skyes) appears to be a proper name or epithet for the monk in question who is the subject of the expulsion proceedings.
