The exact identity or meaning of this name is uncertain from context alone; it may be a phonetic rendering of a Prakrit or Sanskrit name. This is a straightforward Vinaya commentary passage and the terminological pattern of "motion with four readings" (gsol ba dang bzhi'i las) refers to the standard formal Saṅgha act (Skt. jñapticaturthakarman) consisting of one motion and three readings of the resolution. "Motion with two readings" (gsol ba dang las gnyis) likewise refers to a jñaptidvitīyakarman. The summary verse near the middle of the passage is a mnemonic condensing the twelve prohibited duties for nuns into brief headings. The referents of several items in the verse (such as "the one who makes objection," "the groundless accusation," and the numerical entries) follow the standard Vinaya enumerative format and point back to specific categories described in the preceding and subsequent Vinaya rules rather than being self-explanatory in isolation. This is normal for such closing gāthās in the Vinaya Vibhaṅga.

The passage ends mid-sentence, cutting off the narrative about Kṛṣṇa son of Mṛgādhāra; the translation renders it faithfully to the point of truncation. The phrase rendered "carries a definitive outcome: one becomes subject to expiation with a remainder in the Saṅgha" translates a technical Vinaya term for a saṅghāvaśeṣa or saṅghādisheṣa offence (one of the most serious class of transgressions short of a root defeat), combined with the qualifier that the transgression occurs from the very first act. The Tibetan "ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་དང་བཅས་པ་སྟེ་དགེ་འདུན་ལྷག་མར་འགྱུར་རོ" confirms this classification.

The enumeration of the seven types of wife breaks off mid-sentence in the source; the passage is clearly incomplete as transmitted in this segment. The phrase rendered "companion in a lower station" follows the standard commentarial understanding of the final type of wife, whose defining characteristic is a shared-wealth companionate union entered into from a position of relative social equality or inferiority; the passage is mid-sentence at the cut-off point, as the definition continues beyond the supplied text.

The repeated formula "from that point up to" is a condensing device standard in Vinaya literature, indicating that the full protective formula already quoted in the preceding categories is to be understood as applying again in full; this is preserved in the translation. The phrase rendered "a wife who is a companion in a lower station" and "a wife met only for a time" continues the preceding passage's enumeration of the seven wives. The Tibetan term "ཐང་འགའ་འཕྲད་པ" literally means "encountered / met for a certain time or occasion," which I have rendered as "met only for a time," consistent with the hired-companion context the passage immediately goes on to describe.

The ten female companions (མཛའ་ན་མོ་བཅུ) enumerated here include several roles defined by who guards the woman in her husband's absence. The terms "སྒྱུག་མོ" and "གྱོས་པོ" are here rendered "mother-in-law" and "father-in-law" respectively, which is the standard reading in this domestic legal context. The passage for "guarded by a father-in-law" is explicitly abbreviated in the Tibetan itself with a cross-reference to the preceding account, and the translation reflects this. The gotra names listed — Kuṇḍa, Bharadvāja, Śāṇḍilya, Bhāradvāja, Maudgalya, Garga, Gautama — are Brahminical clan lineages (gotras) well-attested in Sanskrit literature. The Tibetan renderings are phonetic approximations of Sanskrit originals; the identification of "Kuṅsa" (ཀུང་ས) with Kuṇḍa and "Bādsa" (བད་ས) with Bharadvāja involves some uncertainty in the precise Sanskrit equivalents, but the gotra context is clear.

The term rendered "female probationer" (དཔྱོད་པ་མ) corresponds to the Skt. śikṣamāṇā, a woman undergoing a two-year probationary period before full ordination, and "wandering mendicant woman" (ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུ་མོ) to Skt. parivrājikā. The phrase rendered "delegate of a delegate" renders the Tibetan construction meaning one who was appointed by a delegate rather than by the nun herself, indicating a second remove of delegation. The legal analysis here follows the standard Vinaya permutational method, systematically working through every combination of who composed, carried, and retrieved the message. The "gross offense" renders a term for a serious but sub-full transgression, distinct from the Saṅgha-remainder which is the gravest class short of defeat. The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the continuity instruction. The text shifts here from nuns (dge slong ma) to novice nuns (dge sbyong ma), a distinct Vinaya category of female renunciants below full ordination. The parallel case structure — who accepts the message, who carries it forward, who brings the reply back — is the organizing logic of this entire section, and the permutation matrix is followed precisely as given in the Tibetan. The final permutation (the one following behind accepts, the one walking ahead carries it there, and the one following behind brings the reply back) is implied by the text's closing case but the Tibetan as given ends at the case translated above; no text has been added beyond what is present. The distinction between "gross offense" and "wrong-doing" reflects two different levels of transgression in the Vinaya for nuns: the gross offense is a thullaccaya-level offense, and the wrong-doing is a duṣkṛta. The text ends mid-sentence with the question about sign-based messages, as the passage breaks off there. The term rendered "Saṅghāvaśeṣa offense" translates དགེ་འདུན་ལྷག་མར་འགྱུར་རོ, literally "it becomes a remainder for the Saṅgha," which is the standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit saṃghāvaśeṣa, the second category of offense in the Vinaya, requiring formal communal rehabilitation. The text distinguishes throughout between སྤྲིང་ཡིག (letter, a written message sent via a messenger) and ལག་ཡིག (hand-written document, a document carried directly). The passage appears to break off mid-sentence at the end of the supplied Tibetan, so the translation ends accordingly. The repetition of one case within the "word commission" series appears to be a scribal redundancy in the source text. The passage contains two distinct terminological series that require clarification. First, the text distinguishes སྤྲིང་ཡིག (rendered "letter") from ལག་ཡིག (rendered "written document"); both denote written communications but appear as distinct categories within the Vinaya's exhaustive permutation system. Second, the concluding section shifts to a different rule entirely, concerning categories of wives and the procedural conditions under which offenses are counted. The terms རྡེའུ་གསུམ་གྱིས་མ་གཏོར་བ ("the three pebbles have not been scattered"), རྩྭ་མ་བཅད་པ ("the grass has not been cut"), བྱེ་རྒྱ་བྱིན་ནས་མ་བཏང་བ ("sand has been given but she has not been released"), and དྲིལ་མ་བསྒྲགས་པ ("the bell has not been proclaimed") are technical Vinaya procedural markers whose precise ritual significance depends on the fuller commentarial context; they are rendered literally here. The term rendered "grave offense" throughout is a technical Vinaya category distinct from a "Saṅgha remainder" (saṃghāvaśeṣa); the Tibetan ཉེས་པ་སྦོམ་པོ literally means a "heavy offense" or thullaccaya in Pali usage, an intermediate category below a pārājika root defeat but above a minor transgression.

The name རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ rendered as "Vaiśravaṇa" refers to Kubera, the god of wealth, son of Viśravas, used here as a hyperbolic comparison for extreme affluence.

The phrase ལུས་ངན་པོ likely refers to the Kumbhāṇḍas or a class of inauspicious beings; however in this ritual enumeration context it may simply denote a class of minor gods associated with the body. The translation "malformed ones" is provisional. The list appears to be a conventional enumeration of deities petitioned in popular religious practice and corresponds to similar lists found in Sanskrit narrative literature. The names in the opening list — Śagā, All-Doer, Revatī, God of Wind-Butter, the Evil-Eyed, Noble-Born, Precious Jewel, Auspicious Fullness, the Five-Honored, the Five-Receivers, and the Robber-Woman with five hundred — are obscure folk or local divine figures attested in early Indian Buddhist literature. Their identifications are uncertain in some cases; the renderings given follow transparent semantic translation of the Tibetan. The twenty-eight yakṣa generals is a standard number in the Vinaya and related literature. The term rendered "God of Wind-Butter" is an unusual compound and may refer to a deity associated with ritual butter-lamp offerings combined with wind; its precise identity is uncertain. The name Rājyadatta for the husband is inferred from the Tibetan "རྒྱལ་སྡེས" which appears to be a proper name in context. The passage lists food qualities negated in the prescribed diet. The list is quite long and the terms overlap; the translation renders them as faithfully as possible to the sequence in the Tibetan. The phrase "similarly, up through the one named Ratna, all should be related in full" reflects a standard textual abbreviation device common in sūtra literature, indicating that a parallel account follows which the scribe has condensed. The reconstruction of the musical instruments is based on standard Tibetan organological terminology: "lute" for glingbu (transverse flute is also possible; the term can denote a stringed or wind instrument depending on context), "vihuela" or "lute" for piwang, "clay drum" for rdza rnga, and "great drum" for rnga bo che. The name rendered here as Śūraputranandana follows the sense of the Tibetan "gyad bu nor" literally meaning "hero's-son wealth/treasure." The Tibetan text is clearly abbreviating a longer narrative with formulaic markers indicating where passages from a fuller version should be inserted; the translation renders this structural device as explicit prose instruction, consistent with the preceding passage's treatment. The "four stances, five throws, and eighteen branches of knowledge" are standard formulaic enumerations of warrior and scholarly arts in classical Indian literature and their specific contents are not enumerated in this passage. The phrase "kings of the sun-realm beneath" renders ཉི་འོག་གི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རྣམས, literally "kings beneath the sun," likely an epithet for rulers of terrestrial kingdoms as opposed to celestial realms. The passage appears to be excerpted with formulaic connective phrases ("and so on up to," "and up to") that are part of the source text's own redactional structure, indicating this is a commentary or summary text that quotes and paraphrases a longer narrative in blocks. The identity of "Śla" (སླས) in the phrase "queens of Śla" is uncertain; it may refer to a specific kingdom or clan name in the narrative's underlying story. The verse on compassion versus generosity reflects a well-known Mahāyāna doctrinal position that compassion is the highest of virtues. The six teachers named here are the six well-known heterodox teachers (tīrthikas) of the Buddha's day — Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalī, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta — and the speech placed in "Kāśyapa's" mouth corresponds closely to the views attributed to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa in Pāli and Sanskrit sources, denying moral causation entirely. The passage rendered "arrow-prince" translates gyad bu nor, a proper name or title meaning something like "Jewel of the Archer-Warriors"; it has been kept consistent with the preceding passage. The text is a narrative excerpt from a vinaya or biographical sūtra context, likely the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya or a related narrative. The name rendered "Gyalbü Nor" (རྒྱལ་བུ་ནོར) literally means "Prince Wealth" or "the royal son Dhana"; this appears to be the figure known in Sanskrit sources as Kumāraka-Dhana or similar. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied in the passage itself, so the Tibetan form is retained consistently.

The phrase rendered "struck like empty vessels" for སྣོད་སྟོང་པ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྡབས་ཏེ་སོང་ངོ corresponds to a standard idiom for dismissal or departure in disgrace — like empty pots being struck and found hollow. This is the contextually apt reading.

The region name སྡིག་བྱུང is a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Śṛgālavati (a locality name); this identification is tentative but standard in the relevant vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "equal in regard to clay and gold" and "equal in regard to dung and sandalwood" are standard formulaic descriptions of an arhat's equanimity — indifference to what is base or precious, foul or fragrant. The image of "tearing apart the shell of the egg of ignorance" is a classical metaphor for breakthrough to arhatship. The "analytic knowledges" renders so so yang dag par rig pa, corresponding to the Sanskrit pratisamvid, the four discriminating awarenesses of an arhat. The "two great assemblies" passage describes the Poṣadha and Pravāraṇā ceremonies; the translation renders the institutional sense without inserting the Sanskrit technical names into the body, as the Tibetan itself does not use them explicitly here. The passage refers to "those who hold the Māmakā" — the Tibetan reads "མ་མོ་འཛིན་པ་" which could refer to a specific textual collection, possibly the Mātṛkā (Skt. mātṛkā), meaning the Abhidharma matrix texts or a specific canonical category. The rendering as "Māmakā" is a placeholder; this is a genuinely uncertain technical term and may refer to the Mātṛkā-holders (those who master the Abhidharma summaries). A specialist reader should be aware of this ambiguity.

The mixing of lodging assignments by category (sūtra-holders, Vinaya-holders, and the third group) follows a recognized Vinaya procedure for cross-assigning practitioners of different textual specializations; the text is noting that all permutations of three groups are to be applied, not just the pairs listed explicitly. The text rendered as "masters of the Mātṛkā" refers to monks who specialize in the Abhidharma matrices or numerical lists, a recognized scholarly category in Vinaya literature. The group of six monks named — Nanda, Upananda, Aśvaka, Punarvasuka, Chanda, and Udāyin — are the canonical "group of six" bad monks whose misconduct occasions many Vinaya rules; the Tibetan here uses descriptive terms rather than proper names for the first four pairs, and the names given are reconstructed from the standard list. The Tibetan for the householder's name, "dge bzang," literally means "virtuous and good" and corresponds to Sanskrit Supriya or a similar honorific; this rendering is provisional. The elephant simile — "if others were to come here, what would an elephant do when sprinkled with water?" — is an idiomatic expression whose precise meaning is somewhat elliptical. The sense appears to be that an elephant, when sprinkled, shakes off the water and moves on unperturbed, suggesting that the group of six, if other monks appeared at the house, would simply disregard or override the situation. Some uncertainty remains about the exact nuance of this colloquial image in context. The names གྱད་བུ་ནོར, མཛའ་བོ, and ས་ལས་སྐྱེས correspond to Sanskrit Jyotishka (or Jyotiṣka), Mitra, and Jātila respectively; these are standard identifications in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narrative context. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the passage with "from this point forward," indicating a deliberate continuation marker in the source and not a translation gap. The phrase rendered "would not converse, would not speak of how they had come, would not look, would not glance" reflects a stock Vinaya formula for deliberate social ostracism used as monastic pressure; the fourfold phrasing is formulaic and intentional.

The names "Beloved Friend" and "Earth-Born" render dge slong mdzaʼ bo and sa las skyes respectively, and "Beloved Sister" renders dge slong ma mdzaʼ mo. "Gyadbu Nor" is a personal name left untranslated as it appears to be a proper name without transparent doctrinal content. The phrase rendered "deal with her accordingly through formal procedure" translates a term indicating the formal monastic process of adjudicating a case where a confession has been made; the Tibetan indicates she should be "pressed" or "held to" her own admission, which in Vinaya context means proceeding with a formal inquiry or sanction based on her self-incrimination.

The closing sentence is incomplete in the source passage as given; the translation trails off as the Tibetan does, mid-sentence, indicating this is a continuous excerpt. The phrase rendered "forced us to eat bad food three times in succession" involves a compressed Tibetan idiom. The sense appears to be that Beloved Friend compelled the two witnesses to eat inferior or spoiled food repeatedly, causing them physical distress severe enough to motivate false testimony. The precise nature of this coercion is not elaborated in the passage. The verse section presents significant interpretive difficulty. The lines referring to "thirty-six and five, however many" are a numerical formula found in Buddhist canonical verse about the gravity of slandering the noble Saṅgha; the precise referent of the numbers is a matter of traditional commentary and is rendered as literally as the metre allows.

The proper names "Gyatbu Nor" and "Dzawa Chenma" in the prose narrative section appear to be Tibetan renderings of Indian monastic names that are unclear in this form. The passage seems to describe a concrete Vinaya case-narrative involving a named monk and a named nun; without the broader Vinaya context it is not possible to identify these individuals with certainty. The rendering follows the Tibetan syllables as closely as possible.

The phrase "one born of the earth" renders a term that in this Vinaya narrative context may designate a particular category of person eligible to serve as a legal reference-witness; the precise technical sense would require consultation of the broader Vinaya commentary. The term rendered throughout as "remainder for the Saṅgha" translates "དགེ་འདུན་ལྷག་མ" (Saṅgha-remainder), which in Vinaya technical usage denotes a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression — a downfall that, unlike a pārājika, is not final expulsion but requires a formal Saṅgha procedure for rehabilitation. The phrase "becomes remainder for the Saṅgha" preserves this technical sense while remaining natural to the ear.

The distinction between eleven and ten bases for impure versus pure persons reflects standard Vinaya casuistry: the additional base arises because in the case of an impure person there is a third category of direct perception (having actually seen the misconduct) that can itself be forgotten and then falsely claimed as remembered, whereas against a pure person no such direct perception exists. The phrase rendered "two close friends born of the same soil" translates "མཛའ་བོ་དང་ས་ལས་སྐྱེས" literally as "friends and earth-born," which may be a compound designating two individuals with a particular relationship — perhaps blood-brothers or village companions. The exact social or kinship sense is not fully transparent from the Tibetan alone; the rendering is contextually plausible but tentative.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, indicating the text continues beyond this extract. The phrase rendered "belongs to no other party" translates the technical Vinaya term gzhan gyi cha ma yin pa, referring to the legal concept that nirvāṇa is the only truly "other" referent, and thus the eight pārājika factors constitute what does not belong to that other sphere. This is a specialized Vinaya hermeneutic that the commentary unpacks in the gloss section, and the translation follows the commentary's own explanation closely.

The phrase "she then converts it — along with her patience, desire, and understanding" reflects the beginning of a longer technical analysis of the mental factors involved in a formal accusation; the passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source text provided. The text systematically enumerates permutations of misidentification: the witnessing nun observes an actual transgression of a given category, then misdescribes it as a defeat-level offense. Five categories of offense appear as both what is observed and as the misdescribed view: no transgression, defeat, Saṅghāvaśeṣa, a general transgression requiring individual confession, and a wrong deed. The passage is a legal matrix typical of Vinaya casuistry. The term rendered "wrong deed" represents a minor offense category. "Individual confession" renders the standard pratideśanīya class. The phrase "and so forth from that point" represents the formulaic abbreviation in the Tibetan signaling that the full set of mental factors listed earlier — patience, desire, and understanding — is to be understood as applying throughout. The fivefold classification of offenses appearing throughout this passage corresponds to a standard Vinaya taxonomy: no transgression, defeat (pārājika), Saṅghāvaśeṣa, wrong doing (duṣkṛta), transgression requiring confession (deśanīya), and minor offense (durbhāṣita). The term rendered "wrong doing" (Tib. ལྟུང་བྱེད) corresponds to Sanskrit duṣkṛta, and "transgression requiring confession" (སོ་སོར་བཤགས་པར་བྱ་བ) to Sanskrit deśanīya; "minor offense" (ཉེས་བྱས) corresponds to Sanskrit durbhāṣita. These are technical Vinaya categories and the renderings follow standard Vinaya scholarship. The exchange between the young perfume-seller and Sthulanandā — "When will I meet with you?" answered by "You will meet with an elephant" — is a cutting pun in the Vinaya narrative tradition. Sthulanandā's name literally means "greatly delighted" and is also a common Tibetan term for a female elephant. Her reply thus mockingly deflects the man's desire by exploiting the double meaning of her own name, a recognized literary device in Pali and Sanskrit Vinaya parallels.

The phrase rendered "any of the five edibles or the five non-edibles" reflects a standard Vinaya technical category. The precise items in each group vary slightly by tradition; no single rendering resolves this without importing one tradition's list over another's. The name rendered "Sthulanandā" and "Sthulanandita" follows the established nun characters of the Vinaya; the Tibetan reads Sbom dga' mo and Gtsug dga' mo respectively, which are the standard Tibetan translations of these Sanskrit names. The rendering of "Mitsemo" for the nun མཛའ་མོ (mdza' mo, "beloved") follows the convention of treating this as a proper name in context; alternatively it could be rendered simply as "the nun Beloved" or left as a transliteration. The phrase "the five edibles and the five non-edibles" follows Vinaya technical usage established in the preceding passage. The remark that "this is as in the previous rule" is a condensed cross-reference (Tib. snga ma bzhin) signaling that the analysis of this phrase has already been given fully above. The phrase rendered "involving an exit from it" translates a technical Vinaya formula (here ngyes par 'byung ba dang bcas pa, literally "with a definite arising/exit") that denotes the formal procedure of raising the matter before the Saṅgha; in Vinaya technical language this distinguishes a Saṅghāvaśeṣa from a pārājika, which has no such rehabilitative procedure. The standard rendering in Tibetan Vinaya scholarship is "with expiation" or "with a way out," meaning the offender is not permanently expelled but must undergo formal rehabilitation before the Saṅgha.

The name rendered "Pomgamo" ( སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ) is a Tibetan name meaning something like "Joyful and Stout" or similar; no Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable here with certainty, so it is left as transliterated Tibetan.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as this is the limit of the submitted text. The eighth rule is given the same ordinal number twice in this passage, which is unusual and may reflect a scribal or textual anomaly in the source. The passage as a whole is a section of Vinaya commentary providing the origin story, rule formulation, and analytical breakdown for successive rules in the Bhikṣuṇī Vibhaṅga. The term rendered "Saṅgha's remainder" translates the technical Vinaya term saṅghāvaśeṣa, a category of offense requiring formal proceedings before the monastic community. "Sthūlanandā" is the Tibetan sbom dga' mo rendered back into Sanskrit throughout, as this is a well-attested proper name in the Vinaya literature. The nun's name "Kṛṣṇā" is reconstructed from nag mo, meaning "black one," understood here as a personal name rather than a description. The term rendered "Saṅgha expiation" translates the Vinaya category of offence requiring confession and expiation before the full Saṅgha, corresponding to Sanskrit saṃghāvaśeṣa. The Tibetan "དགེ་འདུན་ལྷག་མར་འགྱུར་རོ" literally means "there remains a Saṅgha remainder," the standard formula for this class of offence. The rendering follows standard Vinaya usage.

The name "སྡེ་ཅན་མ" literally means "she who has a retinue" or "she of the regiment," here rendered as the proper name Senā, which is its Sanskrit equivalent and the likely original. The phrase rendered "something excellent" for མཆོག་ཞིག་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ is somewhat compressed in the original; it appears to mean a special gift or reward given to the soldiers in lieu of executing the penalty, as a way of honouring their service without carrying out the death sentence.

The expression rendered "the one who crushes the power of the mighty and the one of good lineage" for མཐུ་སྟོབས་རྡུལ་དུ་རློག་པ་དང་རིགས་བཟང་པོ་ལའོ appears to denote two specific military officers by epithet or title rather than by name; the precise referents are not entirely clear from context alone. The term rendered "surety bond" translates the Tibetan "ཆགས་རྒྱ" which in this legal context denotes a written pledge or bond used to secure a debt. The narrative makes clear it functions as a financial instrument that the nun exploits to coerce repayment, which is the basis for the offense. The name "Sthūlanandā" is the standard Sanskrit equivalent of the Tibetan "སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ," a well-attested nun who figures in several Vinaya origin stories. The phrase rendered "outside the boundary of the consecrated area" translates "mtshams kyi phyi rol," referring to the sīmā, the formally consecrated boundary within which Vinaya acts are valid. The exchange between Dundubhikā and the nuns turns on a deliberate sophism: she claims to have "expelled" the nun herself by escorting her outside the sīmā and seeking her forbearance, thereby declaring the Saṅgha's formal act null. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the formal proclamation; this is a function of the passage boundary, not a corruption. The technical phrase rendered throughout as "a residual matter requiring the Saṅgha as remainder" translates the Vinaya term saṅghāvaśeṣa (Tibetan: dge 'dun lhag ma), which denotes an offense of the second category of the nuns' Prātimokṣa, a saṃghātiśeṣa, requiring formal rehabilitation before the Saṅgha. The rendering "Saṅgha as remainder" preserves the literal meaning of the technical term.

The passage enumerates procedural categories of valid and invalid formal Saṅgha acts: an act performed by a concordant group (mthun pa) or discordant group (mi mthun pa), and whether it accords with Dharma or not. These reflect standard Vinaya analysis of the conditions under which a karmavācanā is legally binding. The name "Nagmo" renders the Tibetan personal name that literally means "dark one" or "black one." It appears to be the Tibetan translation of a Sanskrit name, possibly Kṛṣṇā. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the passage, as it continues into the next section. The formal act is presented in its standard Vinaya formula with deliberate repetition, which has been rendered faithfully throughout. The phrase rendered "holy life" translates the Tibetan for brahmacarya, meaning specifically the celibate religious life; the nun Nagmo's statement implies she would seek to practice celibacy with non-Buddhist renunciants rather than in the Buddha's community, which is the doctrinal gravity of the offense. The phrase rendered as "a transgression with expulsion from the very outset, together with what follows from it, and she becomes one who is no longer part of the Saṅgha" translates a dense Vinaya formula. The term rendered "expulsion" is the word for defeat, that is, a root downfall entailing permanent exclusion from the Saṅgha. The phrase "from the very outset" indicates that the offense is incurred at the moment of the third admonishment without further deliberation. The Tibetan formula "Saṅgha lhag mar gyur ro" literally means she becomes a remainder beyond the Saṅgha, a standard Vinaya idiom for complete exclusion. The passage transitions here mid-sentence at the end, breaking off after "on that very basis, firmly," which corresponds to the opening of the next procedural rubric. This is a natural continuation point in the Vinaya commentary format and requires no emendation. The phrase rendered "she is to be expelled from the Saṅgha" translates "dge 'dun lhag mar 'gyur ro," literally "she becomes a remainder of the Saṅgha," which is the standard Tibetan formulation for the saṃghāvaśeṣa ("Saṅgha remainder") offense — a formal ecclesiastical offense requiring Saṅgha action, not simple expulsion. The term is kept close to the technical sense here, but a fuller gloss would be: this constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the second gravest category of nuns' offenses, requiring a formal Saṅgha procedure for rehabilitation.

The phrase "death omens and near-death omens" refers to premonitory signs of impending death recognized in the Vinaya and Indian medical tradition; the precise nature of these signs is not elaborated in this passage. The phrases "from 'with insistence upon that very basis' as far as 'the other is delusion'" and similar formulaic cross-references throughout this passage are standard Vinaya shorthand pointing to passages given in full earlier in the text that are here abbreviated; the translation preserves their character as cross-references rather than attempting to supply the omitted text. The phrase rendered "a formal act with a motion and four announcements" translates the technical Vinaya term for a羯磨 (karman) consisting of one motion (ñatti) followed by three announcements, which together constitute four total proclamations — the standard procedure for a solemn Saṅgha resolution. The phrase rendered "those facing death and those in proximate danger of death" translates a technical Vinaya category. The Tibetan terms literally mean "sign of death" and "near sign of death," and in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya context they function as a classification of offenders rather than a description of their mortal condition; this unusual usage may reflect an underlying Sanskrit technical term for categories of monastics subject to a particular disciplinary status.

The name Sthūlanandā is reconstructed from the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོས, which literally means "Delight of the Stout One" or "Stout Delight," corresponding to the well-known Mūlasarvāstivāda nun Sthūlanandā, a recurring figure in Vinaya narratives known for her irregular conduct. The text throughout follows the standard Vinaya formulaic style of summarizing repeated procedural passages with abbreviated references, indicating that this is an extract from a larger continuous canonical text. The phrase rendered "act of petition-with-four-proclamations" translates the standard Vinaya technical expression for a formal saṅgha act initiated by a motion followed by three proclamations. The phrase "those on the verge of death and those in the vicinity of death" for the two categories of nuns designated by "whatever nuns" is a gloss embedded in the canonical commentary section at the close; it is a standard Vinaya exegetical device and the exact import of these categories in this specific context may depend on a fuller lemma not present in this excerpt. The name rendered here as Devadatta translates the Tibetan "lhas byin," which is the standard Tibetan equivalent of the Sanskrit Devadatta. The passage enters a new sūtra-style narrative section after the Vinaya commentary ends, and the transition is abrupt in the source text.

The term "Uttarakuru" is rendered from "byang gi sgra mi snyan gyi gling," which literally means "the northern continent of Unpleasant Sound," the standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Uttarakuru. "Pūrvavideha" is from "shar gyi lus 'phags" and "Aparagodānīya" from "nub kyi ba lang spyod," these being the standard Tibetan names for the eastern and western cosmic continents in traditional Buddhist cosmology. The phrase rendered "spit-swallower" translates the Tibetan "mchil ma 'thung ba ro," which is an extremely derogatory epithet. The precise idiomatic force is difficult to render; it conveys someone utterly base and contemptible, lower even than one who drinks spittle. The translation preserves the insult's sharpness as it stands in the text.

The passage "from the ten powers of Kāśyapa" is a somewhat condensed reference. The Tibetan reads "'Od srungs stobs bcu pa," which refers to Mahākāśyapa and his ten powers, indicating that Devadatta's supernormal attainments were modeled on or derived through the instruction associated with Kāśyapa. The translation renders this plainly.

The phrase "up to the point where it says" reflects an ellipsis in the Tibetan original, where the compiler signals that a fuller passage is being abbreviated by reference to a marker phrase. The phrase rendered "bowed his head three times in formal acknowledgment" translates a conventional expression indicating that Devadatta performed the triple salutation gesture — a formulaic departure rite — before leaving in anger. The triple bow here is a mark of formal respect even in the context of resentment, consistent with Vinaya narrative convention.

Sthūlanandā is a well-known nun in the Vinaya literature, frequently appearing as a problematic figure. Her name is kept in Sanskrit as is standard in Vinaya translation.

The closing "formal act of the fourfold procedure" refers to the standard Vinaya羯磨 (karma, formal ecclesiastical act) requiring three proclamations and a final motion — here applied to the confrontation of Sthūlanandā by the nuns' community. This is the technical "act in four parts" (Skt. caturvargakarman). The phrase rendered as "blended like water and milk" reflects a stock canonical simile for communal harmony, standard throughout the Vinaya literature. The name rendered in the preceding passage as "Stubborn Delight" follows the established rendering of སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ; the Tibetan here gives སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ and is treated consistently. The passage ends mid-sentence in the formal act proclamation, which reflects the structure of the source text; the translation preserves this open ending without artificial closure. The phrase rendered as "mingled like water and milk" is a classical Indian simile for harmonious unity, well established in Vinaya literature. The expression "from the passage … up to …" indicates a scribal convention of abbreviation, referring the reader back to full formulas given earlier in the text rather than repeating them in full. The passage ending mid-sentence is faithful to the source, which breaks off there in the excerpt provided. The term rendered "Stomāgamoā" in the phrase explaining "whatever nun" is the Tibetan Sbom dga' mo, a proper name likely corresponding to a Sanskrit name such as Sthūlanandā or similar; the exact Sanskrit reconstruction is uncertain but the reference is to a named individual used as the paradigm case, as is standard in Vinaya rule analysis. The phrase rendered "twelve groups" translates a term that in the Tibetan Vinaya tradition refers to the group of twelve nuns associated with Sthūlanandā, a well-known group of habitual offenders in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narrative. This is a stock reference and does not require further gloss in the body.

The phrase "together with the arising from it" renders a compound indicating that the grave offence (saṅghāvaśeṣa, here "grave offence against the remainder of the Saṅgha") is incurred at the completion of the third formal admonition, including the act of admonition itself that brings it about. This is standard Vinaya procedural language. The two names rendered as "Agalamgyo" and "Napso" are phonetic transcriptions of Tibetan syllables that appear to represent non-Tibetan personal names; their Sanskrit originals are uncertain and no standard identification is available.

The term rendered as "Subhāgā" in the phrase "of hers means of Subhāgā" follows the preceding passage's context where that nun was named; however the Tibetan here gives only a general term equivalent to "the plump and cheerful one," which in context is an epithet used for that particular nun. This is a minor point of identification rather than a genuine doctrinal uncertainty. The place name rendered "Mount Reḍeri" is a transliteration of the Tibetan "re lde ri," a toponym not readily identifiable with a well-known Sanskrit equivalent; the reading is uncertain but is consistent with the preceding passage's context. The two monk names "Gamaggo" and "Nabaso" follow the rendering established in the preceding passage ("འགྲོ་མགྱོགས" and "ནབ་སོ"); these appear to be Pali-influenced prakrit names, and the Sanskrit equivalents are uncertain. The repeated elliptical passages — "from 'on that very basis, persistently' through to 'the other is delusion'" — refer to a standard formulaic block of text used in the formal reprimand procedure that the Tibetan text treats as understood from context, citing only the opening and closing phrases of the inset. This is a normal Vinaya drafting convention; the full formula would have been recited in practice. The fourfold act referred to throughout is the standard Vinaya procedure of one motion followed by three proclamations. The phrase rendered "went to the boundary marker" translates a term referring to the sīmā boundary used for formal Vinaya acts; the precise procedural detail is preserved in the narration. The passage contains a complex layering of embedded speech and procedural recitation typical of Vinaya legislative texts; the translation follows the internal logic of the fourfold act formula throughout. The final sentence "Then, as to how a transgression arises here" is the opening of the next analytical section, left in the translation as it belongs to the continuous expository flow of the Vinaya commentary. The phrase rendered "including the Teacher" for "སྟོན་པ་དང་བཅས་པ" is a standard Vinaya formula indicating that the formal act requires the presence of the presiding authority or that the count of proclamations includes the motion itself — the precise technical referent may vary by commentarial tradition, but the rendering follows standard usage. The nun's name appears as འདུན་མ (Dundā or Iṣṭā; the Tibetan rendering is phonetic). The Pali parallel gives her name as Caṇḍakāḷī; the Sanskrit Mūlasarvāstivāda recension represented here uses a form transliterated as འདུན་མ, which may correspond to a Sanskrit name such as Dundā or possibly Iṣṭā. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain.

The phrase ཕུ་ནུ་མོ ("sisters," literally "elder and younger sisters") is rendered simply as "sisters" throughout, as is conventional in the Vinaya address to fellow nuns.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source; the translation reflects this open conclusion. The phrase rendered "the category of exhortation" translates "གདོན་པར་གཏོགས་པ་བསླབ་པའི་གཞི་རྣམས," which refers to training rules classified under the heading of admonishment or rebuke (formal censure procedures). The exact technical subclassification within the Vinaya is a matter of specialist concern but does not affect the general sense of the passage.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, as this is a continuous excerpt; the translation reflects this open ending faithfully. The long list of Vinaya textual categories midway through the passage presents genuine uncertainty regarding precise identification of several titles. Terms such as "the fifth Vinaya," "the sixteenth Vinaya," the "Vinaya Mātṛkā," the "Brāhmaṇī's Daughter," and the "questions of the Nearby Retinue" are technical designations for specific canonical Vinaya texts or sections whose exact referents vary across traditions and are not always determinable from the Tibetan alone. They are rendered here by their most literal, transparent equivalents. The phrase rendered "with a coarse paste of liquid" reflects a term that likely refers to a thick or greasy application smeared for some cleaning or treating purpose; the exact substance is not entirely transparent from the text, though this rendering follows the most natural philological reading.

The summary verse is a mnemonic listing the topics of the preceding Saṅgha-remainder rules; "silk" and "fine wool" are approximate renderings of the specific textile terms, which in the Vinaya tradition refer to particular luxury fabrics regulated by the rules. The term rendered "claim-mark" or "released the claim-mark" translates སྲ་བརྐྱང་, a technical Vinaya term referring to the formal act by which the community formally releases or seals the designation of a robe. This is a specialized procedural term in the nuns' Vinaya context; the exact ritual mechanics are complex, and "releasing the claim-mark" follows the most plausible contextual reading. Some editions and commentaries may differ slightly in how this act is described.

The phrase "five that have been consecrated" for བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ་ལྔ refers to the standard allowable set of five robes that have been formally sanctioned or dedicated; this is a technical Vinaya detail specific to the nuns' code. The three-fold sequence at the close — covering the cases of not relinquishing and not separating, relinquishing but not separating (or vice versa), and relinquishing and separating — yet all three ending identically with the taint carrying over, is notable. The Tibetan text as it stands presents these three as separate scenarios with the same outcome: any robe newly acquired while the offense remains unconfessed inherits the contamination of the unrectified prior offense, regardless of what physical steps have or have not been taken with the robe itself. This reflects standard Vinaya logic that physical relinquishment of the article does not alone expiate the offense; formal confession before the community is also required. The term rendered "marking thread" translates the Tibetan for a structural thread used to mark or maintain the seam of a robe; the precise technical referent is a securing or stiffening cord that is removed when the robe is put into active use, a detail found in Vinaya commentaries.

The phrase rendered "pleasure garden" translates a term literally meaning an enclosure of joy, equivalent to Sanskrit ārāma, a park or garden.

The final portion of the passage is the beginning of an extended definitional analysis in verse-and-prose format listing the various types of settlement and space relevant to determining what constitutes "beyond the boundary"; the text breaks off mid-enumeration. The term rendered "outlying neighborhood" throughout is ཉེན་ཀོར, a Vinaya technical term denoting the defined boundary zone surrounding a settlement, household, or other locus relevant to determining transgression in matters such as the robe-separation rule. It corresponds roughly to Sanskrit sīmā in some contexts but here functions specifically as a spatial buffer zone. The rendering "outlying neighborhood" is conventional in this Vinaya context.

The phrase ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུའི་ཁྱིམ, rendered "households of wanderers," likely refers to peripatetic or itinerant non-monastic ascetics, distinct from the tīrthika households mentioned just before; the exact reference is mildly uncertain but the general sense is clear. The phrase rendered "garland-bearer reaches by shaking a ceremonial cloth" translates a passage that is technically difficult. The Tibetan reads literally something like "the distance a garland-carrier arrives at by shaking a thrown ceremonial cloth," and the precise meaning of this boundary-marker in its Vinaya context is uncertain. It appears to be a traditional measure of distance parallel to the crow's wing-beat mentioned in the preceding section.

The distinction between households "whose family doors have not been opened separately" versus "whose family doors have been opened separately" reflects a Vinaya technical distinction between a single undivided household unit and one that has been formally partitioned among family members. The same distinction applies to the shop sections. The term rendered "lodging house" translates ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུའི་ཁྱིམ, literally "a house for wandering about everywhere" or "a house for going all around," which in the Vinaya context refers to an inn or lodging establishment where travelers stay — hence "lodging house." Some editions render this as "tavern" or "inn," but "lodging house" captures the itinerant character of its clientele most precisely.

The phrase སྤུན་སྒོ་བྱེ་བ and its negative counterpart སྤུན་སྒོ་མ་བྱེ་བ, rendered here as "family doors have been opened separately" and "family doors have not been opened separately," is a technical Vinaya expression for whether a household has been formally divided into separate domestic units. The image is of a partition door between adjacent family quarters being opened or kept shut to determine whether premises constitute one or multiple distinct dwelling units for the purposes of robe-boundary rules.

The phrase དྲི་དག་འཐག་པར་བྱེད་པ in the context of market stalls is rendered "where perfumes are woven in." This may refer to the interweaving or infusing of fragrances into goods — a genuine philological uncertainty, as འཐག་པ normally means "to weave" but in a market context may indicate some other form of processing aromatic materials. The term rendered "granary" translates a compound meaning a place where grain is gathered or stored, specifically one associated with yoked oxen and dung-disposal, consistent with a large agricultural storage facility. The distinction between the simple threshing floor and the granary reflects Vinaya categories of communal property boundaries relevant to the rules on keeping robes within one's outlying neighborhood.

The phrase "divine abode" as the shared element for non-Buddhist households likely refers to a shared shrine or sacred space dedicated to a deity, which would be the common ground uniting otherwise separately bounded sectarian establishments. The phrase rendered "family doors have been opened" versus "family doors have not been opened separately" reflects the distinction between households sharing a single domestic unit versus those maintaining separate household thresholds — a technical Vinaya criterion for determining common versus distinct outlying neighborhoods. The Tibetan སྤུན་སྒོ་བྱེ་བ and སྤུན་སྒོ་མ་བྱེ་བ are contrasted pairs; I have rendered them accordingly by context.

The term ཉེན་ཀོར, rendered throughout as "outlying neighborhood," is the Tibetan for the Sanskrit upacāra, the zone surrounding a defined space within which certain Vinaya rules regarding robes apply.

The passage ends mid-sentence with "The Blessed One declared," as the Tibetan breaks off before recording the answer — this appears to be a genuine textual caesura at the fascicle boundary or a deliberate suspension pending the next section. The phrase rendered as "cold-season robe period" translates the Tibetan institution of spreading out the winter robe, a recognized Vinaya season. The five-month and seven-month divisions of the cloth season follow standard Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya reckoning and are preserved as given.

The final summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā enumerating subcases of the downfall; it is deliberately elliptical and its full exposition would follow in the commentary. The translation renders it faithfully as verse, preserving its telegraphic style.

"Kautamba cloth" is a textile term of uncertain identification in the Vinaya literature; it may refer to a coarse hemp or bark-fiber cloth. This is noted as a genuinely uncertain identification. The passage is a Vinaya commentary systematically working through cases of cloth acquisition by nuns, cross-referencing a root rule about ten-day and thirty-day periods. The enumerated terms "date itself" (ཚེས་ཉིད), "date two" (ཚེས་གཉིས), "date nine" (ཚེས་དགུ), and "day twenty-nine" (ཞག་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་དགུ) refer to days within the kathina or robe-allowance period; the reckoning assumes a thirty-day framework in which the final day triggers the downfall if no action is taken. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation likewise ends there. The verse lines at the opening (sweat cloth, bathing cloth, etc.) are summary verses continuing from the preceding section. The term rendered "border-strip" (གདིང་བ) refers to the decorative or reinforcing strip along the edge of a sewn garment; its precise technical form varies by Vinaya tradition, but "border-strip" is the most neutral and accurate rendering here.

The phrase "cloth used at one of the three seasons" (དུས་ཚིགས་གསུམ) refers to the three seasonal divisions of the monastic year recognized in the Vinaya — the precise calendrical boundaries differ slightly by tradition but the tripartite structure is standard.

The expression "person of neither sex" (མ་ནིང) renders the term for a person who is neither clearly male nor female (Sanskrit: paṇḍaka or napuṃsaka in some contexts); its inclusion here as a category of potential donor reflects standard Vinaya enumeration. The term "ཉེ་བ་འཁོར" rendered as "Ānanda" throughout this section requires explanation. Literally meaning "intimate attendant" or "companion," it here designates Ānanda specifically as the Buddha's personal attendant who poses questions. This is consistent with Vinaya literary convention.

The measurement "གླེགས་བུ་ཕྱེད་དང་གསུམ་པ" and related terms present a genuine difficulty. I have rendered these as fractional subdivisions of a "board's width," referring to a standard folding-board used for robes. The exact physical referent of "གླེགས་བུ་" as a unit in this context is uncertain, but "board" is the most consistent rendering given monastic material culture.

The counting sequence for strip-widths — ninth, eleventh, thirteenth, and so on through twenty-fifth — reflects a technical Vinaya classification of robe configurations by their number of strips, counted in odd numbers. Only strips above the eighth qualify as a true "patched robe." The phrase rendered "if she receives something of greater value, there is no transgression" reflects a standard Vinaya principle: if the donor spontaneously gives more than what was solicited, the solicitation offense does not apply to the excess. The logic runs that the transgression is tied to the specific object solicited, not to whatever the donor freely chooses to give beyond it.

The color-by-color analysis is a standard Vinaya matrix: each color is stated as the solicited item, and receiving a different color incurs no transgression, because the object of the illicit request was not obtained. The text appears to be cut off mid-sentence at the white-robe case; the expected conclusion ("if she receives it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment; if she receives another color, there is no transgression") would follow in the next portion of the passage. The names Gaṇḍā, Upagaṇḍā, and Sthūlagaṇḍā are given as བཅུ་གཉིས་སྡེ་དགའ་མོ་དང་། ཉེ་དགའ་མོ་དང་། སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ. The first term བཅུ་གཉིས་སྡེ means "the group of twelve," and དགའ་མོ, ཉེ་དགའ་མོ, and སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ are Tibetan renderings of the Sanskrit names Gaṇḍā, Upagaṇḍā, and Sthūlagaṇḍā — members of the notorious group of twelve nuns in the Vinaya narratives. The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the original; the translation reflects this. The name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ་ is rendered throughout as Sthūlanandā, the well-known nun whose Sanskrit name means "the stout joyful one." This is the standard identification in Vinaya literature.

The phrase ཁྱིམ་བདག་གི་ཆུང་མ་དེ་ཡང་གཞན་གྱི་སྐྱེས་པ་དང་བསླབ་པའི་གཞི་འཛིན་དུ་བཅུག་གོ is somewhat compressed; it appears to mean that Sthūlanandā brought both parties under a precept or training rule regarding their respective transgressions, which is the reading adopted here. The phrase rendered "fine new large bolt of cloth on credit" translates a reading where Sthūlanandā effectively pawns or pledges the original cloth to obtain a better one on a delayed-payment basis. The syntax here is somewhat compressed and the exact commercial arrangement is slightly ambiguous, but the general sense — that she incurs a debt — is clear from context and from the merchant's subsequent seizure of the trader.

The seven types of cloth referred to are the canonical set of permitted robes in the Vinaya tradition: made from linen, cotton, silk, wool, coarse hemp, fine hemp, or a blend. This list is left implicit in the text and simply glossed as "the seven types." The nun's name "Nandā" appears here as "ཉེ་དགའ་མོ" — literally "she of rejoicing," which is a standard rendering of the name Nandā in Tibetan canonical Vinaya texts. The male counterpart "ཉེ་དགའ" earlier in the same sentence likewise refers to the monk Nanda. Both are rendered by their Sanskrit names here for clarity. The phrase rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates the Tibetan term for a third category of person recognized in Vinaya literature alongside male and female — traditionally a eunuch or a person of ambiguous sex. The exact referent across Vinaya contexts varies.

The phrase "remains silent on the matter" renders the Tibetan idiom of not speaking to any side, indicating a prescribed passive waiting posture during repeated visits, a standard Vinaya technique for allowable persistence without active solicitation. The term rendered "one of the monastery" translates a Tibetan word meaning literally "one who makes suitable or allowable" and refers to a monastery-affiliated lay steward who handles financial transactions on behalf of the nuns, since the nuns cannot directly receive money. This is a technical Vinaya figure, sometimes called a "kappiya-kāraka" in Pali sources.

The passage breaks mid-sentence in the source text at the sixth method of urging, indicating this is a continuous excerpt cut off at that point. The phrase rendered "woollen blankets of sheep's wool mixed with coarse fibre" interprets "mon dar gyi gding ba" (where "mon dar" is glossed in the text itself as "sheep's wool" and "gding ba" as "blanket"); the compound may refer specifically to a type of thick blanket or felt made from raw sheep's wool, and the precise material character remains somewhat uncertain from the Tibetan alone. The text enumerates all permutations of the three items "bundle" (ཆུན་པོ), "loose wool" or "strands" (འདའ་བ), and "heap" (ཕུང་པོ) in a formulaic Vinaya style, working through combinations systematically. The translation renders each permutation faithfully as it appears.

The phrase གཞི་བཅྭ་བརྒྱད, rendered "eight grounds," refers to the eight formulas that generate the transgression; the text then enumerates them in groups of three with minor variations, producing sets of nine instructions total, which the commentary condenses under the heading of eight grounds. This apparent discrepancy is a known feature of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya commentary style and is not an error in the translation.

The final sentence "Noble lady, please be aware —" is the beginning of a formula for the keeping of gold and silver through a lay trustee; the passage breaks off here as the translation covers only the provided portion. The phrase rendered "explicitly named goods" translates mngon mtshan can, literally "that which has a visible name or mark," referring to precious metals and currency that are identifiable as such by name and appearance — gold and silver. This is a standard Vinaya category for prohibited valuables.

The four economic activities listed — trade, investment, grain loans, and interest-bearing distribution — correspond to a classic fourfold scheme in Vinaya literature describing prohibited financial conduct for monastics. The term rendered "distributing at interest" uses the term skyed, which in this context means lending at interest or usury.

The closing sentence is clearly interrupted mid-passage; the translation follows the Tibetan faithfully to that point. The verse at the opening ("Do not send funds to the destitute...") is in a condensed rule-verse format and functions as a prohibition summarizing the conditions under which placement of funds is not permitted; it likely reflects a lost or embedded canonical verse within the Vinaya text.

The phrase rendered "involvement in another region is to be purified through the earlier continuum" reflects a technical Vinaya formula about karmic continuity across transactions in different jurisdictions; its precise procedural sense is tied to the broader Vinaya commentary tradition and remains somewhat opaque without the surrounding commentary.

"Group of six" and "group of twelve" refer to the notorious factions of monks and nuns respectively who appear throughout the Vinaya as negative exemplars. The phrase rendered "the five associations" refers to the five conditions under which an alms-bowl is considered to stand in proper relation to its owner — a technical Vinaya term. The precise content of these five is not spelled out in this passage but would be clarified by the surrounding Vinaya commentary.

The formula "motion and a second formal act" renders the standard Vinaya procedural term for a one-motion, one-proclamation formal act of the Saṅgha, as distinct from a one-motion, three-proclamation act. The term rendered throughout as "alms-bowl without proper relation" translates the Tibetan lhung bzed 'brel pa med pa, a technical Vinaya expression denoting an alms-bowl not formally affiliated or matched to a particular nun through the standard allocation procedure — in contrast to the byin gyis brlabs pa, rendered as "consecrated bowl," which denotes one that has been formally blessed and assigned. The precise English equivalents for these two technical categories are difficult; the rendering above follows the logic of the preceding passage for consistency. Some translators render byin gyis brlabs pa here as "the approved bowl" or "the allocated bowl" rather than "consecrated bowl," since in this Vinaya context the blessing at issue is the formal Saṅgha allocation rather than a ritual consecration per se. This is a genuine ambiguity worth noting for scholarly purposes.

The closing section on forfeiture offences (thob na spang ba'i ltung byed) corresponds to the Pāli nissaggiya pācittiya category, a standard Vinaya penalty class involving forfeiture of the wrongly acquired item and confession. The passage contains a series of dense casuistic permutations typical of Vinaya literature. The term rendered "first offender" translates a phrase indicating one who commits an act without prior knowledge of the rule, a standard Vinaya exemption category. The nun's name Sthūlanandā is a Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan Sbom dga' mo, a well-known figure in the bhikṣuṇī Vinaya narratives. The phrase "any of the seven kinds" for both thread and cloth refers to the standard Vinaya enumeration of seven types of textile materials; the specific list is not given in this passage but is understood from the commentarial tradition. The phrase rendered "up to the seventh generation removed" on both the mother's and father's side reflects the standard Vinaya definition of "relative" used throughout this literature. The phrase rendered "well-finished at the edges" translates a term referring to the selvedge or border of the cloth; the precise technical weaving term is uncertain but the general sense of a properly finished cloth edge is clear. The list "food, or a mere meal, or the means to obtain food" reflects a standard Vinaya triad distinguishing a full meal, a token amount, and the wherewithal to procure food; the distinctions are doctrinal and formulaic rather than requiring further gloss. The phrase rendered "bound with a fringe" for "ཐར་གྱིས་ཞག་པ" is somewhat uncertain in its precise technical meaning; it appears to describe the finishing of a cloth edge, possibly indicating a fringe-knotted border. The rendering follows the gloss "without a knot," which may indicate a particular style of cloth edge without tied fringe-knots, but the exact weaving terminology is not fully transparent. The phrase rendered "Anāthapiṇḍada turned them back from that" translates a compressed construction where Anāthapiṇḍada (literally "the Giver of Food to the Unprotected," a well-known lay patron) intervenes to prevent the kṣatriyas from being sent away by the king during the rains, so that their rains-retreat support obligations could be fulfilled. The syntax is slightly elliptical in the Tibetan and this reading follows the most natural narrative logic.

The closing sentence represents the nuns citing a Vinaya rule that rains-retreat requisites should not be redistributed within the rains period itself — the precise formulation is given only in summary here, as the full rule is presumably quoted in an adjacent passage. The term rendered "those seeking ordination" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning those who have gone forth in search of ordination or training; in this Vinaya context it refers specifically to postulants or candidates for ordination whose robes become the source of the gain described. The precise referent of "those seeking ordination" for the five categories is a technical Vinaya matter that commentators address at length; the five categories listed correspond to standard Vinaya classifications of persons whose robe-offerings may be received outside the normal schedule.

The phrase rendered "last ten days of the last month of autumn" reflects the Tibetan idiom for the specific period in the monastic calendar leading up to the end of the rains retreat, during which the robe-distribution season begins. The term rendered "fascicle" for བམ་པོ reflects the Sanskrit piṭaka-division unit (Skt. aṣṭaka / bambha), a textual fascicle or section-bundle in the Vinaya commentary tradition.

The phrase གསོག་འཇོག་གི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱིས་, rendered here as "by means of consecrated stored-goods," is a technical Vinaya term referring to the formal act of consecrating items kept in storage so that they may be legitimately retained and used — sometimes rendered "use as a stored requisite after consecration." The gloss in the text itself confirms this reading: བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་ནས་སོ, "having been ritually consecrated."

The name Pilindavatsa (Tib. པི་ལིན་དའི་བུ) is the son of Pilinda, a well-known disciple of the Buddha who appears frequently in Vinaya narratives; the Tibetan literally means "son of Pilinda." The phrase rendered "those who live the holy life" translates a term meaning those observing celibate or brahmacharya-equivalent conduct, likely referring to nuns in good standing as distinct from novices mentioned in the prior sentence.

The names Kāmaka and Kāmikā are reconstructed from the Tibetan འདུན་པ and འདུན་མ, which literally mean "the desirous one" (masculine and feminine forms). The remark that "desires are like salt water" is a stock canonical simile explaining the name.

The closing sentence says the householder's wife and "the three women" (མ་སྨད་གསུམ) went forth — that is, the mother and two daughters (three females in total). The rendering "wife, together with her two daughters and one son" is a slight adjustment: the Tibetan མ་སྨད་གསུམ more precisely means "mother and the younger ones, three in total," which likely refers to the mother and her two daughters, the son not being mentioned as going forth here. This is a consequential ambiguity worth noting. The names Dunpa and Dunma are the monk and nun rendered from the Tibetan personal names meaning roughly "the desirous one" (masculine and feminine forms respectively), consistent with the preceding narrative where the brother is Kāmaka and the sister is Kāmikā. These are the same characters rendered here in their Tibetan monastic-name forms, or possibly new monastic names; the text does not make this explicit.

The phrase "spreading of the reed mat" and "taking up the reed mats" refers to the ritual act of laying out and then removing the ceremonial grass or rush mat associated with the pravāraṇā (invitation ceremony) at the close of the rains retreat. The precise ritual action is somewhat technical and the translation follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan. The summary verse is a mnemonic enumeration of the preceding offense categories. The individual items in the verse are terse headings referring back to specific rules; the translation renders them as faithfully as possible given the compressed form. The phrase rendered "the heavy one of great value and the light one" refers to robe-cloth of great and lesser worth, contrasting two of the rules.

The term rendered throughout as "reed mats" follows the Tibetan consistently; in some Vinaya traditions this refers to felt or woven sitting mats spread out for the community during specific seasons, and the seasonal regulation described here — from the last month of autumn to the first month of spring — governs when such mats may be spread and when they must be put away or brought out. The name rendered throughout as "Bhomā Gāmo" appears in Tibetan as སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, a name that does not correspond to any widely standardized Sanskrit equivalent in available sources; it is retained as a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan. The episode describing how she put the earring in her mouth, the ensuing beating, and her arrival at the rainy-season dwelling with swollen eyes follows a formulaic narrative pattern common to the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins, and the abbreviation markers in the text indicate that the standard procedural passages are to be supplied from context rather than written out in full, a convention reflected in the translation. The terms translated as "dishes tossed together," "well-tossed," "of a hundred layers," and "with filled interiors" render a list of culinary descriptions in the Tibetan that appears to be a technical or semi-formulaic enumeration. The exact culinary referents of some items in this list are uncertain; the rendering follows the most plausible literal reading of each term. The phrase rendered "tossed from the hollow of her hand into her stomach" is Bhomā Gāmo's sardonic self-description of eating rather than literally burying treasure — a piece of dark humor the text makes explicit. The name rendered "Bhomā Gāmo" in the preceding passage is carried forward here for consistency, though the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ in this passage more naturally represents a name reconstructible as something like "Sthūlanadī" or a Prākṛt equivalent; the established rendering from the preceding passage is maintained. The name བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ, "Queen Mālinī," means literally "the garland-bearing queen" and corresponds to the Sanskrit Mālinī. The phrase བཞིན་བཟངས, rendered "good-looking one," functions as a form of address. The reference to "eighteen sorts of food" and "twenty kinds" reflects standard Vinaya lists of food categories; the passage breaks off at the end mid-enumeration, consistent with the source text. The term rendered as "temple" for the final gloss on "rain-retreat dwelling" reflects the Tibetan gtsug lag khang, which literally means a shrine hall or temple. In this Vinaya context it refers to a communal dwelling or assembly hall used during the rains retreat, and the gloss is the text's own clarification equating the two terms.

The term kārṣāpaṇa is a standard Indian copper or mixed-metal coin; it is left in Sanskrit as a proper monetary unit with no clean English equivalent. The phrase rendered "swallowing it secretly" translates a term meaning to consecrate or bless to one's own consumption while concealing the act — the sense here is that she secretly diverts to her own use what was gathered for the community; the verb carries the connotation of a covert appropriation rather than a ritual blessing, despite sharing vocabulary with "consecrate."

The repeated phrase about "categories of the eighteenth through the twentieth" likely refers to a classificatory scheme in the full Vinaya text that has been abbreviated here; the precise referent is internal to the larger text and not reconstructable from this passage alone. The phrase rendered "This has defeated a god" translates an idiom that appears to mean the garment is so splendid it surpasses even divine finery; the exact idiomatic force is somewhat opaque in context but this reading is standard in Vinaya commentary.

The identification of proper names here requires care: "Gtsug dga' mo" is rendered as Nandapriyā and "Chos sbyin" as Dharmadattā, following standard Sanskrit equivalents for these Tibetan names in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition.

The simile "a woman is like food" is a direct rendering of the Tibetan and reflects a conventional rhetorical device in Vinaya literature used to justify restrictive rules; it is not an independent doctrinal position. In the preceding passage, the rule concerned a "heavy and costly garment" (a winter garment), whereas this thirty-third rule concerns silk specifically. The Tibetan phrase translated "she appeared as though she were naked" literally says "her body's covering appeared like that of a naked person," conveying that the silk was so sheer as to be effectively transparent — an important doctrinal point about the garment's unsuitability. The name Śironandinī renders Tibetan Gtsug dga' mo (literally "she who delights in the crown"), and Dharmadattā renders Chos sbyin. The phrase rendered "I have no desire to be the ruin of a goddess" is Śironandinī's polite refusal of the offer, apparently playing on the word lha (god or divine lady) in reference to Dharmadattā's honored status; the exact nuance is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The summary verses at the opening are mnemonic verses listing topics to come in this fifteenth fascicle of the Bhikṣuṇī-vibhaṅga. Their items such as "seed," "the great storehouse," and "carrying" are abbreviated headings for rules that follow later in the text and are not explained in this passage; they are rendered literally as they stand.

The phrase rendered "groups of twelve nuns" reflects the Tibetan "dge slong ma bcu gnyis sde," referring to the notorious faction of twelve nuns frequently mentioned in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya as instigators of new rules.

"Formal act of the Saṅgha" renders "dge 'dun lhag ma," literally "a Saṅgha remainder," a technical Vinaya term for an offense requiring a formal transaction of the Saṅgha as part of its resolution. "Transgression requiring individual confession" renders "so sor bshags par bya ba," the class of offenses confessed before a single monk or nun rather than before the full assembly. The passage contains a highly technical and somewhat compressed Vinaya analysis of false speech as it applies to fully ordained nuns. The "twelve classes of nuns" is a standard Vinaya category referring to the twelve groups defined by their ordination and disciplinary status. The fourfold perceptual analysis that follows — not seen, not heard, not understood, not cognized — is a standard Vinaya formula for exhaustive enumeration of epistemic modes relevant to false declaration; the text runs through permutations of these four in combination with states of forgetting, doubt, and misperception. The summary verse is terse and likely serves as a mnemonic for what follows in the prose. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the final line, corresponding to the passage ending mid-analysis. The text alternates between first-person statements attributed to the speaker ("I") and third-person statements attributed to another person ("she"), following a pattern typical of Vinaya casuistry where testimony about oneself and about another party are treated in parallel. The switching between first and third person is present in the Tibetan and has been preserved faithfully. The final sentence is left incomplete as the Tibetan itself breaks off mid-enumeration, consistent with a passage that continues in the next section. The five mental terms that recur throughout — perception, patience, wish, reasoning, and deliberation — render the Tibetan sequence འདུ་ཤེས, བཟོད་པ, འདོད་པ, བློ་གྲོས, and རྟོག་པ respectively. In this Vinaya context these are not the technical doctrinal terms for their usual philosophical referents but rather terms for the successive mental acts or stances involved in formulating a false statement: perceiving the situation, accepting or acquiescing to it, intending to speak, exercising judgment, and deliberating. The sixth, view, refers to the specific framing one adopts. This usage is standard in Vinaya analysis of the false-speech pārājika and its related transgressions.

The passage appears to be a systematic matrix enumerating all combinations of seeing, hearing, discerning, and cognizing that, when falsely reported after altering one's account, constitute a transgression. The text ends mid-series and will continue in the next passage. The phrase rendered "I am in doubt" translates the Tibetan idiom literally meaning "doubt ate me" or "doubt consumed me," which is idiomatic for experiencing doubt or uncertainty about something. The rendering captures the sense naturally for a listening audience without losing the force of the expression.

The list of nicknames at the end of the passage presents some uncertainty: the terms are colloquial epithets for physical characteristics, and the renderings given are approximations. "Scaly-hands" for lag zha mo is the most uncertain of these, as the term may refer to rough or cracked skin rather than scales as such; the general sense of a physical defect of the hands is clear. The passage contains a series of abbreviated story references delivered in the typical Vinaya narrative style, where only the opening and closing phrases of each tale are cited and the audience is instructed to "fill in" the full narrative from memory or a known source. The stories themselves — involving a farmer, oxen with names like Broken-horn and Stumpy-tail, and the two mules Delightful and Dapple — are standard Vinaya illustrative tales (avadāna-style). The phrase rendered "went bald" reflects a Vinaya technical context in which a nun is described as having shaved her head, which in the mocking speech implies she has lost her brahmin identity; the ambiguity of whether she had or had not actually done so is deliberate in the rule formulation. The terms bābhiṣke and māṇikaprebane are transliterations of Indic words (likely Sanskrit or Prakrit) for specific musical instruments or performance arts associated with the kṣatriya class; their precise identification is uncertain and they are rendered phonetically as in the Tibetan.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, breaking off after the list of textiles associated with rope-makers; this appears to be a deliberate textual cut in the material provided for translation. The term rendered "thread-drawers" for སྐུད་རིས་མཁན is uncertain; it may refer to embroiderers or fine thread-workers rather than thread-drawers strictly speaking. The choice reflects the trade context.

The term བའི་ལྕི་བ, rendered "water-carrying," is uncertain; it may refer to carrying water vessels for ritual use, which fits the brahmin context.

The term བབྷིས་ཀེ, transliterated as "court entertainment," is a phonetic rendering of an Indic term (possibly Sanskrit vābhiṣeka or a related word) whose precise meaning in this context is uncertain; it appears to denote some form of royal or courtly performance associated with the warrior-noble class. The phrase rendered "you are one who owes a remainder to the Saṅgha" translates a technical Vinaya term referring to a nun who has committed a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense — one that requires the Saṅgha's involvement to resolve — as distinct from a root defeat (pārājika). The phrase "exactly as the basis warrants" in the confession passage means the gravity of the transgression follows whatever the underlying rule specifies.

The final insulting terms in the last paragraph are anatomical slang used as abuse; the rendering follows the plain sense of the Tibetan without euphemism, consistent with the Vinaya's own direct style of legal enumeration. The text as it stands is a Vinaya narrative interspersed with abbreviated back-references to a longer canonical story; the phrases "from X up to Y" are standard Tibetan Vinaya editorial contractions pointing to passages given in full elsewhere in the text. I have rendered them as such rather than inventing content. The lion and tiger names Mchebzangs and Dpungbzangs are left in transliterated form as they are proper names in the story whose Sanskrit equivalents are not recoverable from context. The final verse breaks off mid-sentence, as it does in the Tibetan; this is the end of the supplied passage. The text is a canonical Vinaya rule passage for nuns, proceeding in the highly formulaic and repetitive style typical of Vinaya literature. The four social castes referenced — brahmin, warrior (kṣatriya), noble, and commoner (vaiśya/śūdra) — are rendered as "brahmin," "warrior," "noble," and "commoner" following the documentary register of the passage. The term translated "noble caste" renders rje'u rigs, which in Tibetan Vinaya typically corresponds to the vaiśya class, though some traditions equate it differently; this is a minor classificatory uncertainty without doctrinal consequence. The closing verse summarizes a fivefold scheme of slanderous offenses structured around lineage, craft, occupation, distinguishing mark, and illness — a standard Vinaya enumeration for this rule category. The term rendered "recitation" throughout is the Tibetan word for the poṣadha confession ceremony's formal recitation procedure by which a dispute or transgression is formally declared purified through the saṅgha's communal recitation. The phrase "stirs up discontent over that act" renders the technical Vinaya expression for re-agitating a case already lawfully closed by saṅgha procedure. The "twelve groups" refers to the notorious group of twelve nuns who appear repeatedly in the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya narratives as instigators of misbehavior. The fourfold classification of disputes follows standard Vinaya taxonomy: disputes arising from quarreling, from censure, from transgressions, and from matters of procedure. The final line breaks off mid-sentence, as this is a transitional passage leading into a new origin story. The rendering reflects the abrupt ending of the supplied text. The term rendered "stirs up discontent" throughout corresponds to the Tibetan idiom for expressing dissatisfaction or opposition regarding a completed legal procedure, consistent with the preceding passage's established rendering. The five categories of nuns described here are standard Vinaya classifications used in determining culpability in communal legal proceedings. The phrase rendered "at a mere peppercorn's worth" translates a Tibetan expression for something of trifling value; the underlying simile is a small commercial measure.
