The doctrinal content here concerns the gradual promulgation of rules governing how nuns may teach the Dharma to laypeople, specifically the rule permitting teaching only up to a fixed number of sentences in the presence of men, ultimately resolved by allowing a nun to teach Dharma to a man when another person is present. The term rendered "inciting to perform Dharma recitations" translates a compound meaning to lead or prompt someone in choral or antiphonal recitation of Dharma texts. The specific pedagogical context — comparing the noise to an arithmetic school — makes clear this involves communal, loud recitation rather than private instruction, which is why the comparison to a counting school is used.

The phrase "sentences of five" and "sentences of six" is a Vinaya technical classification: five-sentence Dharma teaching refers to teaching organized around the five aggregates, and six-sentence teaching refers to teaching organized around the six sense bases. This is confirmed by the commentary's own gloss in the passage. The phrase rendered "sitting in a small space, subdued in spirit" translates a somewhat compressed Tibetan idiom; the sense is that the twelve groups were chastened and kept a low profile after the incident. The name དྲང་མོ, "Ṛjū," means "the Straight One" or "the Upright One" in Sanskrit; it is here treated as a proper name. The passage attributed to Ṛjū in the confrontation scene — rendered "she circled the intestines of your belly around the summer dwelling with a bowel" — is almost certainly a garbled or deliberately obscure insult. The Tibetan phrase "ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་ལྟོ་དྲལ་ལ་རྒྱུ་མས་དབྱར་ཁང་འཁོར་བར་བསྐོར་རོ" is syntactically strained and may be a graphic anatomical slur whose exact meaning is difficult to recover. The rendering here is as literal as the text allows; the intended meaning was clearly threatening and obscene.

The phrase "ས་བོན་ཚིག་པ་ལྟ་བུ / ས་བོན་ཉམས་པ་ལྟ་བུ" — "like a scorched seed, like a ruined seed" — is a standard Vinaya metaphor for a person so morally or spiritually degraded as to be incapable of producing any good fruit, comparable to a seed that cannot germinate. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, breaking off at "A nun with perception and." The translation reflects this exactly. The intermediate summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā listing categories relevant to how this offense arises; its items will be unpacked in the continuation. The phrase rendered "superhuman quality" for མིའི་ཆོས་བླ་མ (literally "a quality surpassing the human") is the standard Vinaya term for attainments such as meditative absorptions, spiritual powers, and similar realizations — the term corresponds to Sanskrit uttarimanuṣyadharma. The list of perceptions of a decomposing corpse — bloating, discoloration, putrefaction, crimson coloration, being eaten, dismemberment, scattering, and bones — corresponds to the classical set of cemetery contemplations (aśubhabhāvanā) found in Vinaya and meditation literature. The rendering follows standard doctrinal enumeration.

The phrase rendered "without altering her view" (lta ba ma bsgyur bar) indicates that the nun's assertion is made in full sincerity, without hedging or retracting her position — a key condition for the offense to arise. The phrase rendered "the Group of Twelve" translates སྦོམ་དགའ་མོས་བཅུ་གཉིས་སྡེ, which refers to a specific group of twelve nuns who are recurrent troublemakers in Vinaya narratives, paralleling the Pāli "Dvādaśavārgika" group; the name is a technical Vinaya designation rather than a literal description of their character.

The phrase "ཆོས་གོས་ལྔ་རྙིངས་ཤིང་སྣམ་སྦྱར་" refers literally to "five worn-out and patched Dharma-robes," meaning the full set of monastic robes, rendered here as "five worn-out and patched robes" for clarity; the earlier occurrence lacks the numeral "five" and has been rendered accordingly. The list of Vinaya textual categories near the end — "the minor rules, the fragments, the occasion narratives, the Vinaya Mātā, the supplement to the Vinaya, the fifth Vinaya, the sixteenth Vinaya, and what arises from the questions of the inner circle" — reflects a specific enumeration of Vinaya sub-texts whose precise identification varies across traditions and scholarship. The rendering follows the plain sense of the Tibetan terms as category labels rather than attempting identification with specific surviving texts, which remains an open question in Vinaya scholarship. The botanical identifications in the seed taxonomy are approximate. Several of the plant names are Tibetan transcriptions of Sanskrit terms that have multiple possible referents. "Shan yab" and "rtsa mkhris" in the cutting-seeds section are particularly uncertain; "bhu drin ka" (bhūdṛṃhaka) is a technical Vinaya plant name of disputed identification. The standard Vinaya commentarial tradition treats this fivefold seed classification as a legal category for purposes of the precept against damaging vegetation, not as a botanical taxonomy, so precise botanical identification is secondary to the legal principle. The Tibetan term འབྱུང་པོ here does not mean the usual "elemental spirit" or "ghost" but rather refers to organisms or living creatures that inhabit trees and plants — effectively plant-dwelling creatures in the Vinaya sense. The term is rendered "life-bearing organisms" to capture its technical Vinaya usage, which classifies certain trees as off-limits because they are inhabited by such beings.

The term སྔོན་པོ, literally "blue" or "green," is here a Vinaya technical term meaning "green" in the sense of "living, not yet dried out" — i.e., still viable as a seed or still alive. This is the relevant distinction for the offence: cutting something green and viable versus something already dry.

The graduated scheme of offences — full transgression versus mere wrongdoing — follows the standard Vinaya matrix: full perception plus green condition equals full transgression; misperception or dry condition reduces the offence to a wrongdoing. The five seed categories rendered here follow the established terminology of the preceding passage: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, propagating-seed, and grain-seed. The term rendered "propagating-seed" translates འགས་པའི་ས་བོན, literally "a seed that has split or sprouted," referring to seeds that propagate by division or germination; this rendering is conventional in Vinaya translations for this category. The term ས་བོན་གྱི་ས་བོན, literally "seed of seeds," is rendered "grain-seed" for consistency with the preceding passage, though some translators render it simply as "true seed" or "seed-proper." The passage contains a list of implements and substances used to damage seeds. Some terms in this list are Vinaya-technical and their precise referents are uncertain: "ཞུགས་ལིང་" (here rendered "dibble" or planting stick) and "སླ་ང་" (rendered "planting stick") are obscure agricultural tools, and the rendering is tentative. "འབྲས་ཁུར་ལྡུགས་པ་" is rendered "a bag full of cooked grain," though it could refer to a heavy load of grain placed upon seeds. The overall doctrinal and legal structure is clear in each case.

The counting logic for wrongdoings and transgressions in the section on cutting trees follows Vinaya analysis whereby the number of preparatory acts (སྦྱོར་བ) determines wrongdoings, while the number of plants cut determines transgressions. This is standard Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya accounting. The personal names Mzaʼ-mo and Gyad-bu-nor are preserved from the Tibetan without Sanskrit equivalents, as the Sanskrit originals are not determinable with confidence from this context alone. Mzaʼ-mo may correspond to Sanskrit Priyā, which is used in the translation; Gyad-bu-nor's Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain. The passage contains apparent repetition of the same triplet of offense combinations across three similar case-groupings, which appears to be authentic textual repetition in the Vinaya casuistic style rather than scribal error. The verse attributed to Dundumā's inner reasoning is cryptic and possibly proverbial. The image of the treetop burning first and of sound "catching" something is somewhat obscure. The rendering preserves the sense that speaking first or making oneself conspicuous leads to being caught; the verse may be a folk saying adapted to the narrative context.

The name "Dundumā" does not appear explicitly in the Tibetan as given but is implied by the narrative structure and context consistent with parallel Vinaya passages; the Tibetan uses the pronoun "she" and "that nun." The passage about the executioner and the fugitive is a remarkable casuistic section on how a nun may deflect a question without lying outright. The instruction to look at the sky and say "I see the sky," or to look at her fingernails, is a recognized Vinaya device for speaking truthfully while withholding harmful information. The phrase rendered "contemplating with supreme conviction that all formations are empty" is a doctrinal injunction invoking emptiness as the basis for saying "I see nothing" — this is not mere evasion but a meditative affirmation. The rendering is faithful to the Tibetan. The passage "བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཤེས་ནས" is slightly awkward — it appears to indicate that when the nuns did not know the Blessed One's earlier instruction (to entrust lodgings before departing), the Blessed One issued a clarifying second declaration. This is rendered accordingly.

The questioner addressed as "ཉེ་བ་འཁོར་" is literally "close attendant" — in Vinaya contexts this is conventionally Upāli, the foremost disciple in Vinaya matters, and has been identified as such, though the Tibetan does not name him explicitly here. The passage enumerates a precise sequence of time-periods within a day, from the three sessions of the night through multiple gradations of morning and daylight, each constituting a distinct unit for assessing transgression or misdeed. The term rendered "sleeps" throughout is literally "comes to sleep" or "falling into torpor" in context, indicating that the offence arises from actually falling asleep on the communal bedding rather than merely lying down. The phrase "ཕན་ཕུན་དུ་གྱུར་ན" literally means "if it has come to mutual benefit" but in this Vinaya context is a technical idiom meaning the occurrence of sleep or torpor, consistent with parallel Vinaya passages; it is rendered accordingly throughout. The condensed verse is a later mnemonic summary of the preceding rules. The passage "counting a third part, then from a fifth down to a third part, and stopping when the Teacher's full proclamation has been recited" is a compressed and technically obscure instruction about the permitted length of Dharma teaching. The Tibetan reads: cha gsum pa dang / lnga pa nas cha gsum pa dang / ston pa yongs su bsgrags pa la tshar bsrang ste smra bar gnang. This appears to describe proportional fractions of a text that may be taught — one third, then from one fifth up to one third — with the ceiling being the full canonical proclamation of the Teacher. The exact procedural import is uncertain, and commentarial guidance would be needed for a precise determination; it has been rendered here as literally as readability permits.

The phrase rendered "round vessels" for ril ba (literally "balls" or "round things") likely refers to small round containers or bowls carried by nuns; the exact referent is uncertain. The phrase rendered "entangled" or "entanglement" translates a term that in other Vinaya contexts refers to a mat becoming disarranged, overturned, or its layers displaced — here the two cases (wind reversing layers, insects gnawing through) make clear this concerns structural disruption of the mat. The word "ཕན་ཕུན་དུ་གྱུར་པ" literally means something like "turned upside-down" or "become reversed/disordered"; "entangled" follows the probable underlying Sanskrit usage in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya contexts, though "disordered" or "displaced" would be equally defensible.

The final sentence about nuns settling their minds in the assembly hall, with the meditation formula, is presented in the Vinaya as a legitimate reason for remaining inside — explaining why the exception "without a cover" and the meditation purpose could affect the ruling. This doctrinal nuance is preserved in the translation. The name rendered "Stout Delight" translates the Tibetan Sbom dga' mo, corresponding to Sanskrit Sthūlanandā, a notorious nun frequently appearing in Vinaya narratives. Some editions might romanize her name differently, but the rendering is consistent with the character known from parallel Sanskrit and Pali Vinaya texts.

The phrase rendered "offense with remainder" in the opening line refers to a thullaccaya-class offense in Vinaya taxonomy, a level below a root defeat but more serious than a simple misdeed. The line "What account has been given to her, and what has been entrusted to her?" renders a colloquial expression of dismissiveness — Stout Delight is sarcastically rejecting the nuns' authority over her, as if to say "Who appointed them to lecture me?" The ocean references that follow appear to be proverbial expressions of indifference: "what does it matter where the water ends up?"

The transition at the end is a verse opening that leads into the next narrative section; the translation preserves the sūtra-style suspension, as the Tibetan breaks off mid-scene. The name rendered "Bhomgamo" transliterates the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ. The Sanskrit form of this name is not given in the text; it may be a phonetic rendering or a Tibetan coinage, and no emendation has been introduced.

The phrase སྐབས་འབྱེད་དུ་བཅུག་གོ is rendered "led her to make an opening," meaning she persuaded the householder's wife to make a donation or create an occasion for giving. The exact idiom carries a sense of inducing someone to open themselves to generosity or to create the conditions for a meritorious act.

The expression བུ་ཟན་གྱི་བུ་མོ is a term of address. It is rendered "daughters of good family, sisters" in keeping with its honorific yet collegial tone within the monastic context; it literally means something like "daughters of good lineage." The proper names of the nuns appearing in this passage — Stout Delight, Crown Delight, Joyful Victory, Near-Joyful-Victory, Companion of Victory, Guardian of Victory, Virtuous One, Supremely Virtuous One, Beautiful Delight, and Queen-Possessing One — are rendered as close semantic translations of the Tibetan. These are clearly the same named members of the twelve groups appearing throughout the Vinaya narrative, and their Tibetan names are translated rather than transliterated since no established Sanskrit equivalents are determinable from this text alone.

The term rendered "the one known as the Wife-Killer" reflects a Tibetan phrase that appears to be an epithet for a character introduced earlier in the broader narrative context, referring to the husband or an associate who planned to kill his wife; the passage ends abruptly mid-sentence, so the final clause about the lac-tree tooth-stick is left open. The term rendered "right-side portion" and "right-side woman" follows the preceding passage's established usage of གཡས་ཞར་མ, which refers to the woman identified by a right-side birthmark. The text here is Vinaya commentary (likely the Bhikṣuṇī Vibhaṅga of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya), with the characteristic interweaving of rule, word-by-word gloss, and narrative occasion. The phrase ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུ is a parivrājaka, a non-Buddhist wandering ascetic, and ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུ་མོ its feminine form; these are rendered as "wanderer" with the Sanskrit gloss on first use. The remark that such a person's offerings are "rare" reflects a standard Vinaya concern about receiving from non-Buddhists. The figure translated as "Kālakāraka the dark one" renders the Tibetan name ནག་པོ་འཆར་ཀ, a transcription of what appears to be a personal name — likely Sanskrit Kālaka or similar — whose precise reconstruction is uncertain but the sense "the dark one" for ནག་པོ is clear. This is a named individual used as the occasion for the Vinaya rule that follows. The five kinds of "acceptance" described in this passage reflect a highly technical Vinaya discussion about the physical modes by which a nun may legitimately receive an object from another person's hands. The Tibetan formulation of the five categories is grammatically compressed and internally technical; the rendering given here follows the most natural doctrinal reading. Some commentarial sources elaborate these categories differently, and the precise distinctions between the five modes remain a point of Vinaya specialization.

The phrase rendered "great black monk of the charnel-ground ascetics" refers to a monk who practiced the ascetic discipline of dwelling in charnel grounds; his case had prompted the earlier rule on the acceptance of food. The epithet "great black one" may be a personal characteristic or a symbolic designation; without further context it is treated as a descriptive epithet.

The phrase about "lying down with their mothers" is a laconic and somewhat enigmatic reference; it appears to be a statement reported as an objection or criticism, and the Blessed One's response redirects to the proper ritual procedure. The precise narrative context is unclear from this passage alone. The phrase rendered "not yet taken in marriage and not yet of adult age" translates a compound indicating a young, unmarried minor — the precise age intended is not specified in the text.

The name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ is transliterated phonetically as Bhadrā in the translation, though the Tibetan spelling suggests a slightly different form; the exact Sanskrit equivalent is not fully certain from this passage alone. The term rendered "parivrājaka" — here glossed as "wandering ascetic" — appears as two forms: male and female. The Tibetan gloss equates "kun du rgyu" with the Sāṃkhya school (grangs can, literally "those with enumeration"), which is a recognized polemical identification in Vinaya literature, where the Sāṃkhya philosophers are sometimes classed as a type of wandering ascetic. This is standard and not an error, but it is worth noting for the specialist.

The phrase rendered "noble lady, your mistress is sitting here" is spoken by the nun Bhadrā to the young merchant. The Tibetan syntax is somewhat compressed; the reading adopted understands Bhadrā to be announcing her own presence by a form of self-reference, which is consistent with the narrative context. The phrase rendered "plump companions" translates a term of address that may carry an affectionate or slightly teasing tone among the nuns; the exact nuance is uncertain, but the sense of physical robustness after living among troops seems intended. The term "group of six" and "twelve sects" are technical Vinaya designations for particular sets of monks and nuns known for lax conduct; these are kept as standard renderings consistent with the preceding passage. "Anāthapiṇḍada" is the famous lay patron householder, here called "the householder who gives food to the protectorless," rendered by his well-known Sanskrit name. The summary verse is a mnemonic listing the topics of the preceding rules in compressed form; it is not itself a teaching passage, and several items in it remain terse. The term rendered "pulling at their weak points" translates a phrase meaning to probe or expose faults or vulnerabilities, a standard idiom in Vinaya contexts for conduct that undermines another's reputation or causes them distress. The Sthūlanandā who appears here is the same notorious nun recurring throughout the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narratives. The phrase "finest of victory banners" renders a military idiom for the paramount or most distinguished standard, here used to describe the spectacle of an army's display. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the passage, as it continues into the next fascicle division. The name rendered "Cāraka" (Tib. 'Char ka) is a monk's name; "Vedī" (Tib. Sbed ma) is the laywoman. The phrase "bodhisattva" here refers to the future Śākyamuni in a previous life, a standard Vinaya narrative device. The item "གསེག་མ" (gseg ma) translated as "clod of earth" could also refer to a fragment of tile or pottery; the translation "clod of earth" reflects the most common Vinaya parallel but a reader should be aware of the ambiguity. The phrase rendered "ironing" for འཆག་པ is a significant interpretive choice: the term literally means to press or smooth, and in Vinaya contexts refers to smoothing or pressing cloth — here rendered as "ironing" for clarity in English, though the implement is of course not a modern iron. Some translators render it "smoothing" or "pressing."

The episode of Vedī pouring filth into a wound is obscure and the Tibetan is terse; the most plausible reading is that she inflicted a wound on herself as an act of self-punishment or mortification, but the syntax does not make the target entirely explicit. This is noted as a genuinely uncertain passage. The phrase rendered "except in such-and-such circumstances" translates a Tibetan idiom literally meaning "having set aside in those circumstances" — the commentary is clarifying that storing an item for legitimate safekeeping does not constitute concealment and thus incurs no offense. The distinction between storage and concealment is doctrinally significant in Vinaya analysis. The phrase rendered "needle-workers with their black alms bowls" translates a term that appears to designate a specific group of ascetics or craftspeople used here as a taunt or comparison; the exact identity of this group is uncertain in context, but the Tibetan is rendered literally.

The sentence "Who would have eaten today, one wonders?" reflects the elder nuns' ironic or bewildered response, implying they themselves have gone without food while the group of twelve ate secretly. The phrase rendered "consecrate it with a time-formula" translates a technical Vinaya procedure in which a specific formula of words is pronounced to authorize a borderline use; "dus byin gyis brlab" literally means "to consecrate / bless by means of a time-occasion," indicating the utterance of a permissive declaration tied to a specific sanctioned purpose or moment. The precise wording of such formulae varies across Vinaya traditions; the rendering here reflects the general Tibetan Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya usage.

The phrase "bshos ma bkum grang" in the opening line is rendered as "the gruel is cold and has gone stiff" — a colloquial taunt; "bkum" can mean pressed down, congealed, or gone stiff, which fits the context of cold porridge left uneaten. The term rendered "fire-wheel" refers to spinning fire in a circular motion, likely a ritual or decorative practice that is here prohibited without the appropriate consecration formula.

The phrase "seventeen factions" and "twelve factions" refer to particular disruptive groups within the monastic community known from the Vinaya literature — the seventeen being associated with the followers of Aśvajit and Punarvasu, and the twelve being a related group. These are standard Vinaya designations and require no further gloss.

The single-, two-, and four-recitation acts refer to the formal categories of Saṅgha legal procedure (Skt. karmavācanā): a one-motion act, a one-motion-and-two-recitation act, and a one-motion-and-three-recitation act respectively — the standard Vinaya classification of formal Saṅgha transactions by the number of their ritual announcements. The fourfold classification of dwelling types by degree of roofing and enclosure reflects a standard Vinaya taxonomic scheme for determining whether a shared sleeping space constitutes "the same dwelling." The terms rendered as "entirely roofed and entirely enclosed" and so forth are technical descriptions of architectural types used to adjudicate transgression. The "three dawns" likely refers to the classical Indian tripartite division of the pre-dawn period, any one of which suffices to mark the passage of a night for legal purposes.

The phrase rendered "wrong view of a pernicious kind" translates a construction indicating a view that is both heretical and morally dangerous, associated with approaching death in a spiritually harmful state of mind. The specific content — that practicing what the Blessed One called obstructions would not actually obstruct — is a classic antinomian misreading, likely a denial of the principle of karmic obstruction. The phrase rendered "formal act with motion and resolution fourfold" reflects the standard Vinaya procedure of one motion followed by three proclamations of the resolution, making four utterances in all. The abbreviated formula "beginning with 'Having prepared a seat,' ending with 'One nun shall make the motion and perform the act'" is a standard Vinaya textual convention signaling that a full procedural template already given elsewhere in the text is to be inserted here; the translation conveys this as the text does, without inventing the missing material.

The term rendered "act of expulsion" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning a formal act that removes someone from standing within the community on account of her persisting in a specified wrong position; it is not a root defeat (pārājika) but a disciplinary suspension or censure action targeting anyone who holds the same view as the dying nun.

The image of "the daughter of an outcaste" renders a standard Vinaya phrase for the most extreme social contempt, used here rhetorically to indicate that the community is to treat her as utterly beyond the pale of respectful association. The phrase rendered "daughter of an outcaste" translates a term for a woman of the caṇḍāla caste, the lowest social group in the Indian context, used here as the strongest available simile for total social disgrace and ostracism. The phrase "beginning with the words 'this occurrence'" and "up to the laying down of a rule of training" is a standard Vinaya abbreviation formula indicating that the full narrative of the Buddha's response and the formal promulgation of the rule is understood to follow but is not reproduced at this point in the text. The phrase rendered "one who is about to die" translates a technical Vinaya term of analysis indicating the subject described by "any nun" in the rule — the commentary here is unpacking the rule clause by clause in scholastic fashion, and the rendering follows standard Vinaya commentarial convention. The precise doctrinal force of this gloss ("about to die" or "mortal" in the sense of "subject to death, i.e., a human being") is a standard Vinaya hermeneutic marker, not a comment on the specific nun's situation.

The enumeration of Vinaya categories — eight defeats, twenty saṅghāvaśeṣa matters, thirty-three pāyattika offences requiring abandonment, one hundred and eighty pāyattika, eleven matters for individual confession, the many trainings, and seven principles for settling disputes — reflects the standard Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa structure; the numbers given here are those of the Tibetan Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition and differ from those of other Vinaya traditions. The proper name "Spomgamo" and the two novice names "Mdzesma" and "Rgyelma" are rendered from Tibetan as they appear; the first is a senior nun's name and the latter two are her novice pupils. Their Sanskrit equivalents, if any existed, are not recoverable from context.

The phrase rendered "scriptural recitation" for the term translated literally as "providing lung" refers to the formal transmission of a text by oral reading, a recognized category in Vinaya contexts. The act described here moves through two successive stages of formal procedure: first a straightforward admonition by motion and four proclamations, and then, when that fails, a further formal act of censure. The Tibetan term rendered "further censure" is bsnyil ba'i las, a technical Vinaya category corresponding to the Pali tajjanīyakamma, a formal act of reprimand; it is distinct from the earlier admonition and implies a more consequential disciplinary measure. The names Sumanā and Jayā are reconstructed from the Tibetan mDzes ma and rGyal ma, which are direct semantic translations of those Sanskrit names. The phrase rendered "this alone is true; all else is delusion" is a formulaic refrain in Vinaya proceedings indicating the tenacious adherence to the wrong view; the Tibetan literally reads "this alone is true; the other is delusion," meaning the accused party insists their position is correct and all else is confusion.

The name "Bhaddamukhā" (Tibetan: Sbom dga' mo) corresponds to the abbess or senior preceptress figure who responds to the two novices after the act of censure. The name is reconstructed from the Tibetan phonetic rendering and the Pāli parallel.

The phrase "are the three realms not all there? Are there no towns and provinces?" is Bhaddamukhā's sarcastic and dismissive remark, implying that since the novices have been censured and expelled from the community's normal fellowship, the whole wide world lies open to them — a form of mocking reproach rather than sympathy. The novice nuns are identified in the commentary as Mañjulā and Uttarā — these are the Tibetan renderings Mdzesma and Rgyalma, meaning "the Beautiful One" and "the Victorious One" respectively, and are consistent proper names used throughout this Vinaya passage. The name Bhaddamukhā (Tibetan Sbom dgaʼ mo) for the preceptress also appears in the commentary gloss and has been rendered consistently with the preceding passage.

The opening clause connects directly to the preceding passage's account of Bhaddamukhā's conduct — the subject shifts mid-sentence from her behavior with the censured novices to a formal report to the Blessed One, then to the laying down of the training rule and its commentary. This is standard Vinaya sūtra-vibhaṅga structure. The "six groups" refers to the notorious group of six monks, and the "twelve groups" to their nun counterparts, standard characters in Vinaya narrative. The bird name translated "kaka bird" renders the Tibetan ga ga, likely a species of bird whose fat was used in certain applications; the exact species is uncertain but the term is retained descriptively. The two nāga kings named Riwo and Yidong are local Tibetan renderings of Sanskrit nāga-king names that remain unidentified with certainty in this context. The verse summary is a mnemonic condensing preceding rules and is rendered as verse accordingly. The passage lists numerous categories of objects with fine graduated distinctions between full transgressions and lesser misdeeds, contingent on features such as whether an object is perforated, strung, fitted, or marked. The rendering "perforated" for "ཕུག་པ" (literally "having a hole") follows the standard Vinaya commentarial understanding that perforated gems are finished, valued ornaments, and thus the graver offense applies to them. The term "bāvabhīṣaka" is a transliteration of what appears to be a Sanskrit loanword for a type of musical instrument; its exact identification is uncertain in the tradition. "ཀོ་ལྷམ་བཅོས་བུ" is rendered "worn sandal" following the sense of a repaired or used sandal of minimal value. The final lines introducing the new occasion — King Bimbisāra's three sensations of warmth and cold during austerity-water practice — are clearly the opening of the next narrative section. The phrase rendered "the Twelve Groups" refers to a stock designation in Vinaya narratives for a group of trouble-making monks or nuns. The king's silence functioning as consent is a standard narrative convention in Vinaya texts indicating tacit permission. The "three sensations" at the beginning (cold, warm, and common-to-all) relate to the three designated purposes of the austerity water described in the preceding passage. The term rendered "consecration-bathing" (dbang bskur ba'i khrus) and "immersion-bathing" ('jug pa'i khrus) describe two technical categories of bathing in the Vinaya context. The first likely refers to a ritual or ceremonial bath, the second to full-body immersion. The precise technical distinction is not fully transparent from context alone, but these renderings follow the literal Tibetan.

The phrase "the time of wind-with-rain" (rdzi char dus) is a compound that literally means something like "the time of wind-rain together"; it is rendered to reflect its dual nature as established by the preceding definitions.

The individual "Cāraka" ('char ka) is a figure whose name appears in this Vinaya narrative context; the reading and identity are not entirely certain from the Tibetan alone. The passage lists a series of false or misleading statements made to a nun with the deliberate intent of inducing regret or doubt about the validity of her ordination. The examples given include questioning the validity of her ordination on grounds of age, the disqualification of her preceptress, alleged misconduct, and defects in the ordination site or ceremony. The phrase rendered "fire at the horizon" renders phyogs tshig pa, literally "burning of the directions," which could refer to a great conflagration visible on the horizon, used here as a memorable shared event the speaker asks about to test the target's memory and thereby undermine her confidence in her own ordination date. The list of diseases in the middle passage is technical and archaic. The rendering follows the sequence as closely as possible, though some terms admit of more than one interpretation in classical Tibetan medical literature. The identification of "spotted skin disease" and "festering sores" are approximations of terms that may correspond to specific Ayurvedic categories not perfectly recoverable from context alone. This is noted for scholarly awareness but does not affect the doctrinal content of the passage. The venerable "Ma Agsagpa" is rendered as Anaṅgana following the Tibetan phonetic equivalent of the Sanskrit name; this is the monk whose case prompted the original rule about lying with women. The identification is based on standard Vinaya context, though the Tibetan here reads simply ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་མ་འགགས་པ, which literally means "the venerable Anaṅgana" — an unusual personal name worth flagging for the specialist. The terms translated as "space between floors" and "upper story" reflect a multi-storied building context standard in Vinaya architecture descriptions. The Tibetan distinguishes bar khang (intermediate floor or mezzanine level) from steng khang (upper story proper).

Sthūlanandā is the notorious nun who appears repeatedly in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya as the instigator of various offenses; her name is left in Sanskrit as is standard in this textual tradition.

The list of frightening beings — kumbhāṇḍa, lus srul po (corpse-like being), and srul po (rotting creature) — presents some classificatory difficulty; the rendering follows the most natural reading of a graduated list of increasingly grotesque spirit-beings found in similar Vinaya enumerations. The term rendered "bdellium resin" translates du ru ska, which corresponds to Sanskrit guggulu; some scholars render it simply "gugul." The rendering "formally entrusted" for btsol is paraphrased as context demands.

The phrase "twelve-fold group" renders bcu gnyis sde, referring to the notorious group of twelve monks or nuns frequently cited in Vinaya narratives as the instigators of rule-promulgations.

The phrase "twenty or more" for nyi shu po gang yang rung ba reflects the standard Vinaya quorum required for formal Saṅgha transactions of the highest gravity. The summary verse is a mnemonic condensing the subjects of the preceding rules in the fifth chapter; the renderings follow the content of the rules as translated in this and the preceding passage.

The term rendered "ivory merchants" translates a compound meaning merchants who split or deal in ivory or dice-bone; "ivory merchants" is the most natural reading in context, though the compound could also refer to bone-carvers or dice-makers. This does not affect the narrative. The phrase rendered "formal act with a motion and three announcements" translates the standard Vinaya term for the fourfold act (ñatticatuttha-kamma in Pāli; Skt. jñaptikāryaka), here specified as "ñatti and four" (གསོལ་བ་དང་བཞིའི་ལས). This is the standard quorum-based procedure for conferring full ordination in the Vinaya.

The phrase "seriously compromised" renders འགལ་ཚབས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ, literally "becomes one with a grave fault/violation," referring to the canonical notion that an invalid ordination performed within a community renders that community's acts legally defective. The passage presents a systematic matrix of cases varying three factors: whether the candidate actually is twenty, whether she perceives herself to be twenty, and whether she explicitly knows, remembers, and is certain. The Tibetan breaks mid-sentence at the end, continuing into the next passage. The rendering preserves the legal-formulaic repetition characteristic of Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "I have no doubt about it" translates literally "she does not eat doubt," a Tibetan idiom for certainty, and its antonym "she does eat doubt" means "she is uncertain or doubtful"; these are rendered idiomatically throughout. The phrase rendered "move her seniority date" translates a technical Vinaya term meaning to advance or transfer one's standing date of ordination, a recognized canonical remedy when the original ordination is found technically defective. The text's logic of counting womb-months reflects the Indian convention that gestation counts toward age, so a candidate may be credited months of pre-natal existence to make up a shortfall in the twenty-year requirement. The "group of six" and "group of twelve" are standard Vinaya designations for named sets of habitually wayward monks and nuns respectively, whose transgressions regularly occasion the laying down of new rules. The distinction between earth "by nature alive" and "not by nature alive" reflects the Vinaya concern for not harming living organisms within the soil. The three-month period corresponds to the monsoon season, during which the soil is held to teem with life. The technical rules about stakes, walls, moisture, sand, and compaction all turn on whether the action disturbs genuinely animate earth or not, determining whether the offense is a full transgression or the lesser category of misdeed.

The phrase rendered "traces a calculation with the back of the hand" is a recognized exception in the commentarial tradition, likely referring to a nun using the back of her hand to make a quick mark for counting or measuring purposes, which is not considered true digging. The term "Mātṛkā" renders མ་མོ་འཛིན་པ, literally "holders of the Mātṛkā." The Mātṛkā is an early doctrinal matrix or compendium, sometimes identified with the Abhidharma or its precursor lists; this is the standard reading in Vinaya contexts. The twelve groups refers to a set of notoriously undisciplined monks and nuns recurrently mentioned in Vinaya literature as the occasion for rules being promulgated. The phrase rendered "Stout Nandā" translates Tibetan Sbom dga' mo, a nun's name meaning something like "Plump Nandā" or "Fat Nandā." This is likely a rendering of Sanskrit Sthūlanandā, a well-known figure in Vinaya literature; the gloss is consistent with that identification.

The formal Saṅgha acts described — motion alone, motion with a second, motion with a fourth proclamation — render the standard Vinaya categories of ñatti, ñatti-dutiya-kamma, and ñatti-catuttha-kamma (Sanskrit: jñapti, jñapti-dvitīya-karman, jñapti-caturtha-karman). The phrase rendered "equipped themselves with the means for training" translates a somewhat compressed Tibetan idiom referring to gathering or taking up the requisites or implements of training; the sense is that the nuns came prepared and earnest in their commitment.

The Venerable "Legsong" (Tibetan: legs 'ongs) and "Charka" (Tibetan: 'char ka) are names of monks whose conduct prompted the respective training rules; no Sanskrit equivalents are recoverable with certainty from this context alone.

The passage ends mid-sentence, as the source text breaks off at that point. The phrase rendered as "made herself understood to a nun who is present" translates a Tibetan idiom indicating that she had first informed or notified a nun who was staying behind, so that her absence would be known — a technical requirement of the rule. The same idiom recurs in the second rule about householders, where it means informing the hosting householder.

The term translated as "prior meal" and "later meal" refers to the morning meal and the midday meal respectively, the two permissible meal times in Vinaya practice. The "Great Mistress of People" renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, which is an epithet of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's aunt and the first Buddhist nun. The context confirms this identification clearly.

The phrase "the three dawns" alludes to a technical Vinaya distinction among three stages of dawn recognized in the commentarial tradition; the text treats this as already explained in a prior passage ("as before"). The name "Vāsomukha" is a reconstruction from the Tibetan "ba so mkhan" (lit. "one who tends cattle / a cowherd"); Tibetan biographical epithets of this kind sometimes encode Sanskrit names imperfectly, and the exact Sanskrit form is uncertain. The term "Nirgrantha hearer of the Dharma" renders the Tibetan "gcer bu pa'i nyan thos chos," indicating a follower of the Nirgrantha (Jain) tradition who was a lay hearer, here contrasted with a Buddhist monastic. The phrase rendered "needles" for "kha ral" is a plausible reading in context of monastic requisites, though the term can also denote razors or blades; given the context of offering requisites to the Saṅgha, "needles" is the most likely referent. The phrase rendered "needle-cases of various comb-like shapes" reflects Tibetan describing objects made from horn fashioned in the shape of combs or similar implements; the exact referent of the compound is somewhat ambiguous in the Vinaya context but the general sense is clear. The term translated "stopper" for སྦུ་བུ་ཅན and "tube" for ཆང་བ་ལྟ་བུ describes the two structural varieties of needle-case; the precise technical distinction between these two forms is a minor point of material culture that does not affect the legal ruling. The passage contains technical measurements for a monastic strap or sling. The term rendered "strap" translates གདིང་བ, which likely refers to a carrying-strap or sling-strap used in monastic contexts. The measurement formulas involving Sugata-spans, standard cubits, and finger-breadths are internally consistent within the Vinaya measurement system, but the precise rendering of phrases like "one and a half of the Sugata's spans plus a span" reflects a somewhat compressed and formulaic original. The five types of cotton-wool listed use Sanskrit plant names preserved in Tibetan transliteration: arka (Calotropis gigantea), śalmalī (silk-cotton tree), kaśa (a type of grass), and śana (hemp or a similar fiber plant). The term rendered "robe for covering the shoulder" translates a Tibetan term for a garment covering the side or armpit area, used especially in illness — likely a sickbed robe or similar covering garment in Vinaya context. The identification "robe for the sick" follows standard Vinaya commentarial usage.

The name Śobhā is a reconstructed reading for the female lay practitioner described as "Sbom dga' mo" (literally "Joyful-and-plump" or "Plump-Śobhā"); this may be a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit personal name not yet fully recovered here. The name rendered "Stout Ānanda" translates the Tibetan sbom dga' mo, a nun's name. The first element sbom means "stout, fat, thick," and dga' mo is a feminized form of Ānanda ("joyful one"). Some editions render this nun's name differently; here the literal sense is preserved consistently with the preceding passage.

The phrase "fifteen standard cubits" and "nine standard cubits" render the commentary's conversion of Sugata-cubits into ordinary cubit measurements, where one Sugata-cubit equals one and a half standard cubits. The text refers to "kiyū" as an accompanying substance listed alongside garlic; this likely corresponds to a pungent plant such as asafoetida or a related allium, and "asafoetida" is given as the best approximation for a listening audience, though the exact botanical referent is uncertain.

The passage alternates between summarizing the narrative frame and quoting the canonical text directly, using the Vinaya formulaic style of "from this point through to that point" to indicate larger stretches that are not reproduced here. The translation follows this structure faithfully, rendering the formulaic bridging phrases as prose. The phrase rendered "the great lady Gautamī" translates a title indicating Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the first nun, the Buddha's maternal aunt and foster mother. This is consistent with her role elsewhere in the Vinaya as a spokeswoman for the nuns' community.

The expression rendered "two finger-joints" as the permitted measure for washing is a standard Vinaya anatomical limit; it refers to the length of two phalanges of a finger, a conventional maximum depth. The cooking terminology in the Vinaya narrative is a detailed technical sequence describing stages of preparing a churned butter or rendered fat marinade. The terms rendered as "gentle stir," "thorough stir," "stir to draw out the essence," "frothy stage," "full-bodied stage," "skimming stage," "hundredfold-refined stage," and "what resembles the form of a small creature" correspond to Tibetan technical culinary terms whose exact sequence in classical Indian cooking practice is not fully recoverable; the rendering is interpretive and follows the most plausible contextual reading.

The phrase rendered "residence keeper" translates khang skyong ma, the nun appointed to care for the nuns' dwelling. The phrase rendered "stirring up raw materials" refers to a Vinaya prohibition against nuns engaging in certain forms of food preparation, specifically stirring or processing uncooked or raw substances. The precise nature of the "raw material" (Tibetan rjen pa) in the context of the preceding narrative about marinades is preserved consistently.

The expression "beginning with 'this occurrence' and continuing through to the promulgation of the training rule" is a standard Vinaya formulaic abbreviation indicating that the full procedural narrative is condensed; the translated rendering reflects this convention.

The names Kutsā, Vatsā, and Bharadvāja are brahminical clan or gotra names addressed to the brahmin boys and are rendered here as Sanskrit equivalents of the Tibetan phonetic transcriptions. The name rendered "Palskyed" transliterates the Tibetan དཔལ་སྐྱེད. This is likely a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit name such as Śrījāta or similar; no Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable with certainty from context.

The phrase rendered "the keeper of the rhinoceros" translates རི་དགས་འཛིན, literally "holder of the wild animal," here most naturally understood as an official responsible for a rhinoceros or large animal in royal service; its precise institutional role is unclear from this context alone.

The summary verse at the center of the passage condenses the rules of the preceding section; its terse, elliptical grammar makes fully fluent rendering difficult without expanding slightly, which has been done conservatively here. The term rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates a term referring to individuals who are neither male nor female in the Vinaya's threefold classification; this is the standard technical usage in monastic law.

The names Carka and Bema represent the two nuns central to the narrative of these rules. Carka is a monk, and Bema is a nun, as clarified by the text's own analysis.

The phrase "words of coded allusion" renders an idiomatic expression meaning veiled or suggestive language used as a signal; the specific phrase "game of theft" appears to be a euphemism for illicit liaison. The names Ched-ma and Char-ka are rendered phonetically from the Tibetan spellings སྦེད་མ and འཆར་ཀ respectively. These appear to be proper names of specific nuns and monks in the narrative and their Sanskrit equivalents, if any existed, are not recoverable from context alone. The final sentence describes a sexual assault. The Tibetan reads literally that the man "seized" the nun and "impregnated her" or "ejaculated upon her." The verb བཏབ from ཁུས་བཏབ indicates seminal emission / violation; this is a technical legal detail establishing the circumstances for the rule that follows. The translation "violated her" conveys the meaning accurately and appropriately for the narrative context without clinical intrusion into the spoken rendering.

The verse summary at the end of the eleventh group appears to belong to a different twelfth group section that follows immediately; it may summarize rules of the twelfth group rather than recapitulate the eleventh. This is a common structural feature in Vinaya texts where the verse summary precedes the rules it epitomizes, and the section break may be slightly displaced in the manuscript. The term rendered "leather strap" (Skt. carmabandha in Sanskrit, transliterated into Tibetan as rgya skyegs) refers in this Vinaya context to a leather band used as a masturbatory implement. The text handles the matter obliquely and the Tibetan commentary likewise uses euphemistic phrasing ("relieves her affliction," i.e. sexual frustration). This is consistent with the Vinaya narrative style when dealing with sexual misconduct cases.

The name "Stout-and-Joyful" renders the Tibetan Sbom dga' mo, which appears to be a character-name unique to this Vinaya narrative. "Phreng-ldan-ma" is left as a transliteration as it is a proper name of a queen in this narrative whose Sanskrit equivalent is not recoverable from context. The phrase rendered "without permission" translates literally as "without it having been given," meaning without the owner's consent to occupy it. The same formula is used in the preceding rule, and the parallel structure is intentional in the Vinaya text.

The repeated formula "from this occurrence down to laid down a training rule" is a standard Vinaya abbreviation indicating that the narrative framework for promulgating the rule is being condensed; it is faithfully rendered as such rather than expanded. The phrase rendered "courtesies due a guest" translates a term meaning worldly or social proprieties, here specifically the customary welcome and hospitality owed to a visiting monastic. The summary verse is a mnemonic condensing the topics of the twelfth section; its four items correspond to the rules just enumerated in that section. The name rendered throughout as "Stomhagimon" is a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name not fully recoverable from this passage alone; it is kept consistent with established convention for this text. The epithet "lean Gautamī" (Gautamī the thin) refers to a specific nun identified by this description; "Gautamī" is her clan name. The phrase "near death" and "approaching death" render Tibetan terms that appear to be technical designations for specific categories of individuals; their precise identity is not fully clarified in this excerpt and may refer to nuns in particular states or stages. The expression "flesh-eater of her own child" is a severe verbal abuse formula found in Vinaya literature; it is rendered literally as it appears. The final rule's word analysis is cut off in the source at the point where "whatever" begins to be explained, indicating the passage continues beyond the excerpt provided. The term translated as "Bhagūmati" renders the Tibetan "སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ," which is a Tibetan back-formation from a Sanskrit name; the most plausible reconstruction is Bhagūmatī or a related form. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain but the name clearly refers to a particular nun throughout this passage.

The phrase "tier upon tier" for the hammock gloss reflects a suspended, layered structure; the Tibetan "སྟེང་རིམ་དུ་གདིང་བ" describes something hung or slung in layers or tiers, which may indicate a multi-level suspended sleeping structure rather than a simple hammock in the modern sense. The phrase rendered "inner district" and "outer district" reflects a distinction between neighboring hostile territories and more distant ones respectively; the exact administrative or geographical sense is difficult to pin down precisely from context alone, but the general sense of mutually antagonistic regions is clear from the commentary.

The term rendered "shrine" throughout is lha khang, literally "god-house" or "temple," here specified in the commentary as referring to non-Buddhist shrines or temples belonging to tīrthikas. The term rendered "group of twelve" refers to a notorious group of twelve nuns frequently mentioned in the Vinaya literature as instigators of occasions for new rules, corresponding to the group of six monks. The Tibetan "bcu gnyis sde" literally means "the party of twelve."

The phrase rendered "nuns of little ambition" translates "don nyung ba'i dge slong ma," a standard Vinaya idiom indicating conscientious nuns who are content with little and who therefore notice and object to misconduct. The term rendered throughout as "admitting to the assembly" translates a technical Vinaya procedure for formally installing a candidate within the Saṅgha, distinct from the going forth and full ordination, though related to them. The Tibetan phrase ལྟུང་བྱེད་བཅྭ་ལྔ་པའི་གཉིས་པ indicates this is the second rule in a collection of fifteen offenses in this Vinaya section. Sthūlanandā is a well-known transgressor figure in the Vinaya narratives; the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ is the standard rendering of her name. The final sentence of the passage breaks off at the Blessed One's declaration, which is to be continued in the next passage. The phrase rendered "son of the mother of suffering" translates a compressed Tibetan expression meaning a man who is an associate of suffering's source, i.e., rooted in delusion and bad companionship. The exact syntactic sense is somewhat compressed in the original; the rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading.

"Sthūlanandā" is the standard Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan name rendered phonetically as Sbom dga' mo, literally "Stout Joyful One," a well-known problematic nun in the Vinaya literature.

"Gautamī the Slim" renders Gautamī skems mo, i.e., the lean or emaciated Gautamī, to distinguish her from Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. The phrase rendered "abiding near the brahmacarya" translates the technical Vinaya category of the śikṣamāṇā, the probationary status of a woman candidate training under near-observance of the full celibate life before full ordination. The Tibetan ཚངས་པར་སྤྱད་པ་ཉེ་བར་གནས་པའི་སྡོམ་པ literally means "the vow of dwelling near/adjacent to the brahmacarya practice," which corresponds to the śikṣamāṇā vow. This is a distinct stage from the six-dharma training that precedes it and from full ordination that follows. The phrase rendered "rite proceeding by formal request and a twofold act" and "rite proceeding by formal request and a fourfold act" follows Vinaya technical usage: conferral of the brahmacarya vow requires a single motion plus one confirming vote (hence twofold), while full ordination requires a single motion plus three confirming votes (hence fourfold). This distinction is doctrinally significant and shapes the legal analysis in the commentary. The term rendered throughout as "disciples of one of great desire" translates a compound meaning the circle or retinue of a nun characterized by great desire — that is, Sthūlanandā's disciples. The rendering "placing disciples" for the vow refers specifically to the act of taking on and accepting responsibility for the retinue of such a nun. The phrase "dwelling in a natural setting" renders a term for nuns who lived apart from the main community rather than in a monastic residence. The repeated phrase rendered "performs all the steps up to and including the laying down of the training rule" translates a formulaic abbreviation indicating that the Buddha went through the standard narrative sequence of expressing approval, addressing the assembly, and then formally promulgating the rule. This is a conventional Vinaya abbreviation and is rendered here in its standard expanded sense.

The name Sthulanandā transliterates སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, literally "fat joyful one," a nun who appears repeatedly in Vinaya narratives as the protagonist of rule-generating incidents. The name is kept in its Sanskrit reconstructed form throughout for consistency. The term rendered "sends her away" or "send away" translates the Tibetan verb "bkar ba," meaning to dispatch or send someone off to another location. The context makes clear the nun was supposed to be removed from the premises before the husband arrived. The phrase "caught by the husband" renders a somewhat compressed idiom; the situation implies the husband physically reclaimed or seized his wife. The phrase rendered "great progenitress Gautamī" translates Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's maternal aunt and the first Buddhist nun. The Tibetan uses the title skye dgu'i bdag mo chen mo, literally "great lady-sovereign of living beings," which is a rendering of Mahāprajāpatī.

The phrase "beginning from the side of her elder" renders rgan pa'i mtha' nas, indicating that the act of making obeisance proceeds starting from the most senior member of the assembly. Sthūlanandā is the standard rendering of སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ་, a famously ill-behaved nun repeatedly named in Vinaya narrative literature; the Tibetan is a calque of the Sanskrit name meaning "Big Joy."

The three insults Sthūlanandā levels at her fellow nuns — "great mistress of creatures is a self-initiated one," "blue-lotus-hued one has sold herself in six great cities," and "gaunt Gautamī has eaten her child's flesh" — are stock epithets from Vinaya narrative that identify three specific nuns by allusive nicknames. The rendering follows the Tibetan literally; the doctrinal background (that these were real past deeds being disclosed as slander) is a matter for fuller commentary. The Tibetan phrase rendered "act of shaving bodily hair" literally means "the work of hair," which in Vinaya context refers to the depilatory or shaving practices reserved for fully ordained members; the rendering follows standard Vinaya commentarial usage.

The term rendered "go-between" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning to act as an intermediary in amorous or marital negotiations, a standard Vinaya category. The verse summary (verse of abbreviation) in this section is a condensed mnemonic listing the subjects of the rules in this grouping. The individual items in the summary verses are formulaic headings rather than complete sentences, and their referents become clear only in conjunction with the full rule narratives. The rendering preserves their compressed, list-like quality.

The phrase rendered "in the proper cycle" translates འཁོར་ལོ་གཉིས་སུ, literally "in the two cycles," a technical expression for completing two full annual periods of training; the nuance is that the two years must constitute proper, completed training periods.

The text breaks off mid-narrative with the woman's response beginning but not yet given in the passage provided. The "aged Gautamī" renders Gautamī Ṭhemmo, the honorific title given to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in the Tibetan Vinaya tradition. In this narrative context she appears to be a named character distinct from the great Mahāprajāpatī, or the name is used for a senior nun of the Gautama clan; the Tibetan is unambiguous in using the name as a proper noun.

The "seven robes" refers to the standard set of monastic robes (the lower robe, upper robe, great robe, and accompanying cloths) enumerated in the Vinaya; the exact count varies by tradition but the Tibetan here specifies "the seven, whichever it may be." The term rendered as "probationer" throughout is śikṣamāṇā, a woman in the two-year probationary training period between novice and full ordination. The Tibetan "sbom dga' mo" is the rendering of this term and is treated consistently.

The phrase "intention of the fortnight" (bca' lnga'i 'dun pa) refers to the formal resolution or mental act undertaken at the start of a fortnightly restoration ceremony. "Already used" (zhag lon pas) indicates that this resolution has been expended in the first fortnight and cannot validly carry over to the second.

The mnemonic verse is a condensed summary verse listing rule topics; it is rendered as verse accordingly. Some headings within it are abrupt by design, as they are pneumonic cues rather than full sentences. The phrase rendered "you who have the Buddha, you who have the Dharma, you who have the Saṅgha" is a formulaic greeting conveying that the arriving nuns carry the Three Jewels with them; it is a standard expression of welcome in Vinaya literature.

The expression "from this occurrence through to the establishment of the training rule" is a standard Vinaya abbreviation indicating that the full narrative preamble — inquiry, rebuke, assembly, and formal promulgation — is implied but not spelled out. The terms rendered "ceremonial whisk," "fan," and "small fans" reflect objects offered as a customary gift to the monks' assembly at the conclusion of the invitation ceremony. The precise identification of these implements involves some philological uncertainty, but the general referent is clear from the Vinaya context.

The word rendered "strife" or "causing strife in the assembly" translates a term meaning to expel or cast out from the assembly — that is, to cause a formal schism or rupture in communal proceedings. "Causing strife" is the conventional English Vinaya rendering; the underlying act is more precisely one of divisive disruption leading to exclusion. The phrase rendered "daughters of those who eat the leftovers of others" is a compound insult whose Tibetan is literally "daughters of the woman who eats the remnants" (bu zan mo'i bu mo dag). This is a derogatory expression likely playing on low social status. The reading is straightforward but the exact social referent of the insult is culturally specific.

The remark about Sthulanandā speaking in the third person about herself in the passage regarding praise is grammatically awkward in the Tibetan and the referents shift; the translation follows the most plausible doctrinal reading, in which Sthulanandā means that she herself is the one who deserves praise, being a member of the Śākya clan and a master of the Three Baskets. The term rendered "flat blow" or "strike with the flat of the hand" translates "thal lcag," which some traditions gloss as a blow with an open hand or with a flat implement; the precise meaning is somewhat uncertain but the general sense of a striking blow is clear.

The phrase "brahmins given to holding things in contempt" renders the Tibetan "bram ze ya mtshan du 'dzin pa rnams," literally "brahmins who hold things as worthy of contempt or disdain." The term is a recurring designation in the story for aggressive or contemptuous brahmins. The line rendered "O daughters of gluttons!" translates a somewhat contemptuous address; the Tibetan reads literally "daughters of the woman who eats." This is a conventional insult in the Vinaya literature referring to greedy persons, here directed at the attendants.

The episode of the girl and the sesame — the mange on the hand, the head-shaving, and the split tongue — appears to recount consequences suffered by someone who sought a teaching from the six groups of monks in exchange for sesame, though the Tibetan is elliptical. The translation renders what the grammar most naturally supports.

The phrase rendered "prepared food" and "cooked food" corresponds to two standard Vinaya categories of edibles subject to specific rules on food remaining after a meal has been formally concluded; the five items in each category are standard Vinaya lists not enumerated here in the Tibetan itself. The phrase rendered "great prioress" for སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི is literally "great mistress of beings Gautamī," an honorific title for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the first nun and the Buddha's aunt and foster mother; "great prioress" follows established Vinaya convention.

The sentence about Sthulanandā stating that "she bathed a bodhisattva" is a notable doctrinal detail: the Vinaya tradition here identifies the infant previously bathed by Sthulanandā as a bodhisattva, implying she had a legitimate or extraordinary reason in that unique case — a reason that cannot be generalized to justify nuns bathing ordinary children.

The final anatomical passage concerning Sthulanandā's pubic hair is rendered plainly as the text requires in a Vinaya context; the term རྨོངས here means pubic or lower-body hair, not "confusion," a distinct lexical item in this medical-hygienic context. The phrase rendered "consecration of the Dharma robe" translates a term that literally means "blessing" or "consecration" applied to monastic robes; in Vinaya context this refers to a fortnightly ritual acknowledgment or marking of one's robes as properly belonging to one's allowance, keeping track of their status. The precise ritual is a matter of Vinaya commentary.

The "seven kinds" of robes is a standard Vinaya enumeration of the allowable types of monastic cloth; the text does not enumerate them here. The phrase rendered as "dance-teacher's costume in exchange" translates a passage involving Sthulanandā accepting or exchanging a garment associated with a dancing-woman, used as a Dharma robe. The precise nature of the exchange is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan, but the meaning is clear enough in context. The term "stiff extension" in the verse summary is a provisional rendering of a technical term for a type of padding or extension attached to garments; the exact referent within monastic textile usage is not entirely certain from this passage alone. The term rendered "rhubarb" translates a word that may refer to a medicinal root or plant product used as a purgative in the ancient Indian context; the precise identification of the substance is uncertain, but "rhubarb" or a similarly purgative medicinal root is the traditional understanding. The commentary's gloss equating "causes to present rhubarb" with "the Saṅgha's robe-cloth" is unusual and may reflect a different referent in the base rule versus its explanatory gloss; this structural tension is present in the Tibetan itself. The term སྲ་བརྐྱང (rhubarb) is used throughout as a gloss for the Saṅgha's robe-cloth in the exegetical sections, following the established convention from the preceding passage, where the rhubarb presented by the sick man stands metonymically for the Saṅgha's property. The summary verse at the end condenses four preceding training rules; the line "a spell not to be accepted or installed" renders རིག་པ་མི་བླང་མི་གཞུག, referring to rules about accepting or inserting a spell or formula, which will be elaborated in subsequent sections. The precise referent of "come here and be calmed" for the first rule is consistent with a standard Vinaya formula inviting a party to settle a dispute or matter peaceably. The string "sar phu, bi si ri phu, si ri bi svāhā" is transliterated directly as it appears in the Tibetan; it is a garbled or vernacular mantra formula, and no standard Sanskrit reconstruction can be offered with confidence. The passage is preserved as a phonetic transcription.

The name rendered throughout as "Stomā Gāmī" transliterates སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ; this is a nun's name occurring in Vinaya narratives and is kept consistent with the preceding rendering convention. The repeated phrase rendered as "however little... in every case" reflects the Vinaya formula indicating that any instance of the action, no matter how slight, constitutes a full transgression — a standard juridical formulation in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya.

The mantra syllables are transliterated phonetically as they appear in the Tibetan; they carry no standard Sanskrit reconstruction.

The phrase rendered "shaven-headed woman" translates an insult literally meaning "one whose head has been touched" or "shaved-headed one," a contemptuous reference to the tonsure of a nun. The phrase rendered "set a seat to grow" in the summary verse is unusual. The Tibetan reads "sstan ni skyid du mi gzhug," literally "not inserting a seat for comfort" or perhaps "not setting up a seat in a garden or nursery." This is an abbreviated verse rubric summarizing a rule whose full narrative has not been provided in this passage; the precise idiomatic meaning awaits the corresponding rule's narrative for full clarification.

The exchange about calves and milk is a colloquial way for Stomā Gāmī to probe why the householder's wife is unhappy, drawing on the woman's agrarian context. The subsequent remark comparing her to "a needle" reflects a somewhat sardonic question about whether the wife too has only one kind of work in a household, as a needle does one thing — the idiom is terse and its exact nuance is slightly uncertain. The name rendered "Stomā Gāmī" appears here again as the protagonist of the first rule in this passage, consistent with the preceding context. The name "Tsugga'mo" (Tib. གཙུག་དགའ་མོ) is kept in transliterated form as no established Sanskrit equivalent is provided; it appears to be a Tibetan name for a nun who figures in several of these Vinaya rules. The phrase rendered "causes seats to be experienced" reflects the somewhat elliptical Vinaya commentary language where "experiencing" a communal item means privately appropriating or benefiting from it. The "seven kinds" of thread is a standard Vinaya enumeration whose specific contents are not enumerated in this passage. The phrase rendered "the sinister one, the rough one, and the wanton one" represents three Tibetan epithets used as informal designations for the prostitute's former clients: གཡོན་ཅན (the deceitful or sinister one), ནལ་ཕྲུག (the rough or unruly one), and རྒྱན་པོ (the wanton or dissolute one). These appear to be character-type epithets rather than proper names, and the exact nuances are uncertain; the renderings given reflect the most plausible interpretations.

The name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, transliterated here as Bombagamo, is a Tibetan rendering of a proper name; the exact Sanskrit original is uncertain. The phrase rendered "one who wanders everywhere" in the summary verse translates a term that in context appears to refer to a wandering woman or vagrant, parallel to the preceding rules about various categories of women giving massage. The verse is a mnemonic summary and its terms are intentionally compressed.

The phrase "trainee nun" renders the Tibetan term for a woman undergoing the two-year probationary training period before full ordination as a nun, the śikṣamāṇā in Sanskrit; the text's explanation confirms this.

"Charnel grounds" in the nuns' disparaging remark about Bombagamo is a conventional insult implying she is unclean or of low character, associating her with a polluted place. "Wandering woman" renders ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུ་མོ, a female parivrājikā — a female ascetic of a non-Buddhist school, here specified as Sāṃkhya (གྲངས་ཅན, "Sāṃkhya," literally "those who enumerate"). The identification with Sāṃkhya is explicit in the text.

"Turushka" (ཏུ་རུ་སྐ) is a fragrant resin, sometimes identified as frankincense or a similar aromatic substance used in Indian ritual and cosmetic contexts.

The phrase "twelve groups of monks" (བཅུ་གཉིས་སྡེ་དག) refers to the stock Vinaya designation for the misbehaving faction whose conduct prompts new rules; it is a conventional formulaic reference, not a literal count. The name rendered as "Stomāgāmā" is a phonetic reconstruction of the Tibetan "སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ" (Sbom dga' mo).
